Initially created: 2026-01-30T19:54:38.048+09:00 by CH Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: The ancients did not write books;
the ancients never discussed principle (lǐ) apart from affairs (shì).
The Six Classics (Lìu Jīng) are all the governing statutes (zhèng diǎn) of the former kings.
Someone might ask:
Concerning the Shī, Shū, Lǐ, Yuè, and Chūnqiū,
we have already received instruction.
But the Yì elucidates Yīnyáng,
I wish to hear how it is considered a governing statute (zhèng diǎn),
and the meaning of classifying it with history. Reply:
I have heard the words of the Master (Fūzǐ).
"The Yì opens up things and accomplishes tasks,
covering the Way (Dào) of the world."
"It knows the future and conceals the past;
good and ill fortune share the woes of the people."
Its Way (Dào) generally encompasses what governmental instruction (zhèng jiào) and statutes (diǎn zhāng) cannot reach.
By imitating Heaven and modeling the Earth,
"it causes spiritual things to arise,
thereby making use of the people’s resources."
Its instruction generally precedes governmental instruction (zhèng jiào) and statutes (diǎn zhāng).
The Tàibǔ (Grand Diviner) in the Zhōu Guān was in charge of the methods of the Three Yì:
In the Xià dynasty, it was called Liánshān;
in the Yīn dynasty, it was called Guīzàng;
and in the Zhōu dynasty, it was called Zhōu Yì.
Each had its images (xiàng) and numbers (shù),
each differed in its changes (biàn) and divination (zhān),
and they were not inherited from one another.
However, the Three Yì each had their foundation.
The Dà Zhuàn (Great Commentary) mentions Páo Xī, Shén Nóng, Huáng Dì, Yáo, and Shùn.
This is what is meant: The Guīzàng was based on Páo Xī; the Liánshān was based on Shén Nóng; the Zhōu Yì was based on Huáng Dì.
Viewing them from their foundations,
not only were the Three Kings (Sān Wáng) non-inheriting of each other,
but the Three Sovereigns (Sān Huáng) and Five Emperors (Wǔ Dì) also did not follow each other's customs.
For when the Sages (Shèngrén) first emerged to govern the world,
they innovated sight and hearing,
establishing instruction through the Divine Way (Shéndào),
thereby embracing that which Rites (Lǐ), Music (Yuè), Punishments (Xíng), and Government (Zhèng) could not reach.
This was fundamentally based on the natural principles (Tiān Lǐ) of Heaven,
unlike later generations who rely on the strange and marvelous, the demonic and the auspicious,
prophecies (chèn wěi) and magical arts (shù shù),
in order to fool the world.
The Master (Fūzǐ) said:
"I have observed the Way (Dào) of Xià.
Qǐ is insufficient to verify it.
I obtained the Xià Shí (Xià Calendar)."
"I have observed the Way (Dào) of Yīn.
Sòng is insufficient to verify it.
I obtained Kūn and Qián."
Now, Xià Shí,
is the book of the Xià calendar.
Kūn and Qián,
are categories within the Yì.
The Master (Fūzǐ) regretted that the documents (wén xiàn) of Xià and Shāng were unverifiable;
yet Kūn and Qián, together with the book of the Xià calendar, were what he obtained from observing Xià and Shāng.
Therefore, that which served to enrich the lives of the people and benefit their usage (mín yòng),
generally functioned, alongside regulating the calendar and defining the seasons,
as the legal institutions (fǎ xiàn) of that era.
It was not the personal idea of a single Sage (Shèngrén),
who, separated from affairs (shì wù), specifically authored a book,
claiming to elucidate the Way (Dào).
Now, observing the celestial images and establishing instruction,
along with regulating the calendar and granting the seasons,
is the Way of Heaven (Tiāndào).
Rites (Lǐ), Music (Yuè), Poetry (Shī), and History (Shū),
together with punishments (xíng), government (zhèng), instruction (jiào), and decrees (lìng),
are the affairs of humanity (Rénshì).
When Heaven and humanity interact,
this is the great authority (dà quán) of the King (Wáng Zhě) in ruling the world.
When Hán Xuānzǐ visited Lǔ,
he observed the books in the keeping of the Grand Scribe (Tàishǐ Shì).
He was able to see the Yì Xiàng (Images of the Yì) and the Chūnqiū,
and believed that the Rites of Zhōu (Zhōu Lǐ) were preserved in Lǔ.
Now, the Chūnqiū was an old statute established by Zhōu Gōng.
To say that the Rites of Zhōu (Zhōu Lǐ) were preserved in Lǔ is acceptable.
The Yì Xiàng was also referred to as a Rite of Zhōu (Zhōu Lǐ).
That it constituted governmental instruction (zhèng jiào) and statutes (diǎn zhāng),
closely related to the people's usage and not merely empty words of a single individual,
established by the ruling dynasty itself and not simply inherited from previous systems,
is therefore also clear.
The Master (Fūzǐ) said:
"The flourishing of the Yì,
was it perhaps during the Middle Antiquity (Zhōng Gǔ)?
The one who created the Yì,
did he perhaps experience sorrow and hardship?"
Gù Shì Yánwǔ once said that Liánshān and Guīzàng
were not named Yì.
The so-called Three Yì maintained by the Tàibǔ (Grand Diviner)
were named retroactively because of the Zhōu Yì.
Now, observing that the Eight Trigrams (Bā Guà) originated with Fú Xī,
the Liánshān was composed by the Successors of Xià,
yet the Master (Fūzǐ) said the Yì flourished in the Middle Antiquity (Zhōng Gǔ),
and the person who created the Yì exclusively refers to Wén Wáng,
then the fact that Liánshān and Guīzàng were not named "Yì,"
is further proof of this.
Someone might ask:
Wén Wáng was imprisoned in Yōu;
he never attained the position to enact the Way (Dào).
How can he be said to have created the Yì to establish governing statutes (zhèng diǎn)? Reply:
The Eight Trigrams (Bā Guà) were common to the Three Yì.
Wén Wáng himself took the Eight Trigrams (Bā Guà) and appended texts to them.
When the Way (Dào) of Shāng declined,
Wén Wáng shared the sorrow and hardship with the people.
Therefore, he repeatedly explored the Way (Dào) of handling distress
and aimed for faultlessness (wú jiù).
This was not a founding of institutions.
When Zhōu Wǔ stabilized the world,
he then named it the Zhōu Yì
and established the fundamental doctrines and instructions of that era.
This was not something Wén Wáng initially intended or calculated.
The Master (Fūzǐ), throughout his life, did not gain high office.
He could not found institutions or establish laws
to serve the people’s usage.
Because he saw that the Zhōu Yì, in its principles and methods (dào fǎ),
was beautiful and perfect beyond measure,
and fearing that it might eventually be lost,
he composed the Commentaries, such as the Tuàn, Xiàng, and Wén Yán,
to elaborate on its profound meanings.
This is what is meant by "transmitting but not creating" (shù ér bù zuò).
It was not that his ability was lacking,
but that principle and circumstance inherently dictated it should not be done.
Later Confucians (Hòu Rú) who attempted to imitate the Yì,
were truly reckless and unthinking!
Did the principles (lǐ) and numbers (shù) they referred to
contain anything that surpassed the Zhōu Yì?
If they did not surpass it,
and they merely changed its images, numbers, methods, and patterns,
simply to show that they did not inherit the ancient style,
this is akin to a King (Wáng Zhě) controlling the world
and introducing novelties to sight and hearing,
much like the Hàn system which stated that the color was yellow and the number was five—
an act that is the same category as reforming the calendar and changing the color of vestments.
Yáng Xióng, not understanding this, created his work
by using 9x9=81
to change the 8x8=64 structure.
Great Confucians (Dà Rú) of later generations
mostly praised him,
reasoning that his numbers corresponded to the regulation of the calendar
and that his yarrow-stalk divination matched good and ill fortune.
Now, numbers (shù) are common to ancient and modern times.
Anyone who understands calendrical studies
can derive them.
Why must it be the Tài Xuán before they align?
As for yarrow-stalk divination matching good and ill fortune,
this is the ultimate principle (zhì lǐ) inherent in Yīnyáng itself.
Where sincerity (chéng) is achieved,
drawing bamboo slips or drilling tiles
can all be used to know good and ill fortune.
Why must one elaborate the text,
and make the characters difficult and profound,
before one can know good and ill fortune?
The Yuán Bāo recklessly claims connection to the Guīzàng;
it is not worth discussing.
Sīmǎ's Qián Xū
further used 5x5 to alter 9x9,
which cannot avoid being the overly busy work of a worthy man.
Therefore, the Six Classics (Lìu Jīng) must not be imitated.
The argument made by earlier Confucians (Xiān Rú) merely stated that one should fear the former Sages (Xiān Shèng) and recognize the necessity of respect and awe.
This refers to Yáng Shì’s Fǎ Yán
and Wáng Shì’s Zhōng Shuō,
which indeed hit upon the specific faults.
As for the Six Classics (Lìu Jīng),
they are all the traces of the former kings (xiān wáng) who attained high office and practiced the Way (Dào),
ordering and governing the cosmos and the world,
and they were not reliant on empty words.
Therefore, even with the sagehood of the Master (Fūzǐ),
he still transmitted but did not create.
If one foolishly attempts to create without knowledge,
not only is there the suspicion of imitating a Sage (Nǐ Shèng),
but one also incurs the crime of presumptuously usurping royal statutes (wáng zhāng).
How can one not be careful!
Kǒng Zhòngdá said:
"The 《Yì》
is the general name for change and transformation,
the distinct appellation for alteration and replacement."
Among the interpretations of the meaning of the 《Yì》 by earlier Confucians,
none has been as clear and penetrating as that of Mr. Kǒng (Kǒng Shì).
Taking his explanation and extending it further,
the 《Yì》 is a monumental canon for rulers implementing systemic reforms (gǎizhì);
its affairs are inextricably linked with regulating the calendar (zhìlì) and clarifying seasons (míngshí);
its meaning is thus revealed plainly.
Xǔ Shūzhòng, interpreting the character "Yì,"
said:
"It is the lizard (*xīyì*),
the gecko (*shǒugōng*),
being a pictograph.
Secret treatises state,
'The sun and moon form *Yì*,'
symbolizing Yīn and Yáng."
The Grand Diviner (*Tàibǔ*) of the 《Zhōuguān》
oversaw the methods of the Three 《Yì》s.
Zhèng Shì commented:
"The *Yì*
refers to the numbers derived from manipulating the milfoil stalks, which are capable of divination."
Zhū Zǐ held that "the 《Yì》 has the meanings of interchange (*jiāoyì*) and change/alteration (*biànyì*)."
These are all explanations derived from the character itself,
each speaking only to one facet,
and not the ultimate intent for naming it the 《Yì》 at that time.
Although the name "Three 《Yì》s"
began with the 《Zhōuguān》,
and the 《Liánshān》 and the 《Guīzàng》
can be collectively named the 《Yì》,
the 《Yì》 cannot be attached to the 《Liánshān》 and the 《Guīzàng》 and called the "Three Liáns" or "Three Guīs."
This is truly because the meaning of the 《Yì》
actually encompasses the procedural numbers (fǎshù) that have not been merely copied since the time of Xī and Nóng.
The first appearance of *Yì* in written form
is in the Imperial Canon (Dìdiǎn) phrase: "Píng zài Shuò Yì" (The equinox lies on the beginning of the month's change);
Kǒng’s Commentary (*Kǒng Zhuàn*) stated that the year changes (gǎiyì),
and the people of Zhōu immediately took this to name the book for manipulating the hexagrams.
Thus, the great meaning of a ruler changing systems and renewing (gǎizhì gēngxīn)
is clearly discernible.
The 《Dà Zhuàn》 says:
"That which generates life upon life is called *Yì*."
Hán Kāngbó said that "Yīn and Yáng shift and change (zhuǎnyì),
thereby completing transformation and generation."
This is the source from which Zhū Zǐ's meanings of interchange (*jiāoyì*) and change/alteration (*biànyì*) arose.
Although the texts of the Three 《Yì》s are not transmitted,
looking now at the methods recorded for the Grand Diviner in the 《Zhōuguān》,
and the divination records containing their words in the 《Zuǒ Shì》,
then the 《Liánshān》 and the 《Guīzàng》
all contain the meanings of interchange (*jiāoyì*) and change/alteration (*biànyì*).
Thus, since the time of Xī and Nóng,
although the name 《Yì》 was not yet established,
the concept of 《Yì》 was already active within them.
In high antiquity, being simple and unadorned,
written characters were few;
naturally, there were those things which had the reality but lacked the defined name.
Later generations, based on this reality, fixed the name,
then applied it throughout past and future,
and all took this as the principal meaning,
as if the name had always been prominent—
this is just one instance of that phenomenon.
The idea of solemn illumination (*qīnmíng*) being reverence (*jìng*),
the idea of sincerity and stability (*yǔnsài*) being truth (*chéng*),

and the regulating of celestial appearances (*lìxiàng*) being the calendar (*lì*) [The calendar aspect of regulating celestial appearances is interpreted as calculating movements, not the name of a calendar book.]:
these are all names defined later after the reality already existed.
The Image (*Xiàng*) of the *Gě* (Revolution) hexagram in the 《Yì》 says:
"Fire in the midst of the marsh—
the superior person uses this to regulate the calendar (*zhìlì*) and clarify the seasons (*míngshí*)."
Its Judgment (*Tuàn*) says:
"Heaven and Earth revolutionize, and the four seasons are completed.
Tāng and Wǔ revolutionized the mandate (gémìng),
following Heaven and responding to humanity."
Since the time of Huángdì, the calendar
has been altered generation by generation,
yet the Master (Fūzǐ) took the image from the fire in the marsh,
and moreover took the changing of the seasons by Heaven and Earth, and the revolution by Tāng Wǔ, as the meaning of the *Gě* hexagram.
If this is so, then does the way (*dào*) of the 《Yì》,
rising and falling according to the times, differ at all?
The 《Yì》 began with Xī and Nóng,
and was fully developed in Chéngzhōu (the established Zhōu);
the calendar began with Huángdì,
and was successively altered in later generations.
High antiquity emphasized the Way of Heaven (*tiāndào*),
while the Middle Antiquity and afterward emphasized the great principles of human affairs.
However, although the theory of Hexagram Qi (*guàqì*)
was initiated by Hàn Confucians,
the hexagram sequence and hexagram positions
already fully contained the beginning and end [of the cycle].
Therefore, one suspects that before Dà Náo created the *jiǎzǐ* cycle,
Xī Nóng already used the hexagram diagrams for celestial reckoning (*lìxiàng*),
which is what is meant by Heaven and humanity uniting as one.
The 《Dà Zhuàn》 says:
"In ancient times,
when Páoxī Shì ruled the world,
he looked up to observe the celestial appearances in Heaven,
looked down to observe the patterns on Earth,
observed the markings of birds and beasts and the suitability of the terrain.
Nearby, he drew analogies from himself;
distantly, he drew analogies from things.
It was then that he began to create the Eight Trigrams (*Bāguà*),
in order to comprehend the virtues of the spirits and deities,
and to classify the nature of all things."
This was created before Huángdì instituted the cyclical stems and branches (*gānzhī*).
Observing the separate mandates given to Xī Hé,
then the celestial appearances, patterns, markings, and suitabilities—
their underlying principle (*dào*) was fully contained without exception,
and all were used to bestow the proper seasons upon the people.
Thus, we know that the sages of high antiquity,
who opened the sky and initiated systems,
establishing laws to govern the world,
the creation of the 《Yì》 and the creation of the calendar (*lì*)
sprang from the same source;
it is not appropriate to force a separation of which came first or last.
Therefore, the 《Yì》 says:
"It opens up things and accomplishes tasks,
encompassing the Way of the world."
The 《Shū》 (Classic of History) says:
"Regulate and arrange them respectfully and grant them (the seasons),
correct the errors and bring about change (*yì*)."
Both describe the same principle.
The Master (Fūzǐ) said:
"Grant me a few more years,
to study the 《Yì》 at fifty,
and I might be free from great errors."
He also said:
"I study the Rites of Zhōu (*Zhōulǐ*);
now I apply them.
I follow Zhōu."
To study the 《Yì》
is therefore to study the Rites of Zhōu.
When Hán Xuānzǐ saw the Images (*Xiàng*) of the 《Yì》 and the 《Chūnqiū》 (Spring and Autumn Annals),
he considered the Rites of Zhōu to be preserved in Lǔ.
The Master studied the 《Yì》 and compiled the 《Chūnqiū》—
this is what is meant by studying the Rites of Zhōu.
The Master told Yán Yuān:
"Use the seasonal calendar of Xià,
ride in the carriage of Yīn,
wear the ceremonial cap of Zhōu,
and let the music be the *Shàowǔ* dance."
This was weighing and deliberating among a hundred kings,
modifying and augmenting the systems of the four dynasties,
serving as the standard for ten thousand generations.
Although celestial reckoning was successively altered,
the Master exclusively adopted the time system of Xià.
Although methods of milfoil divination differed,
the Master exclusively adopted the 《Zhōu Yì》.
These are the things that, subsequent to the Three Dynasties,
are still followed and have not been abolished today.
However, after the Three Dynasties,
the calendar (*lì*) became prominent while the 《Yì》 became subtle;
the calendar was preserved in official custody,
while the 《Yì》 spread through private scholarly transmission.
Therefore, Confucians dared to emulate the 《Yì》,
but did not dare to fabricate a calendar.
The thinness, eclipses, fullness, and waning of the calendar
have visible appearances that can be verified,
but the fortune/misfortune, remorse/distress of the 《Yì》
have no verifiable trace to be constrained by.
Therefore, officials in charge of the calendar could not arbitrarily manipulate it with private intelligence,
while masters of the 《Yì》 each formed their own theories,
leading to endless confusion.
Therefore, those who study the 《Yì》
cannot afford to be ignorant of Heaven.
The symbolism (*xiàng*) of the 《Yì》,
and the associative imagery (*xīng*) of the 《Shī》 (Classic of Poetry),
involve transformation and cannot be fixed by physical definitions.
The organizational structure (*guān*) of the 《Lǐ》 (Classic of Rites),
and the established precedents (*lì*) of the 《Chūnqiū》,
are strict and cannot be distorted.
The Master said:
"The world returns to the same destination though by different paths;
the ultimate goal is one, though the considerations are a hundred."
For the superior person regarding the Six Arts,
to comprehend them by a single thread
is sufficient.
When things are mixed together, they form patterns (*wén*);
when affairs are compared, they yield categories (*lèi*).
Knowing that the names and meanings of things and affairs arise mixed together and are placed through comparison,
without literary patterns (*wén*), they cannot be expressed;
without categorization (*lèi*), they cannot be connected.
The literary patterns of the Six Arts
can be exhausted in a single phrase.
Now, be it symbolism (*xiàng*),
or associative imagery (*xīng*),
or precedent (*lì*),
or structure (*guān*)—
though they are as unrelated as horses and oxen driven far apart—
their expressions can be called patterns (*wén*),
but their underlying principle is simply connection through category (*lèi*).
Therefore, the essential point for a student
is to value the knowledge of categories.
The scope encompassed by Xiàng (Image/Symbolism) is vast.
It is not limited merely to the *Yì* (The Changes).
It includes all of the Liùyì (Six Arts).
It is the manifestation of the Dàotǐ (Substance of the Way) before it becomes fully visible.
The Jūjiū (osprey) symbolizing a noble match (hǎo qiú),
the Jiūmù (curved tree) symbolizing constancy and purity (zhēn shú),
and even the bear and the snake symbolizing male and female offspring,
these show how Xiàng pervades the *Shī* (Odes/Poetry).
The Wǔxíng (Five Phases) signaling the Wǔshì (Five Affairs),
Jī (Sieve) and Bì (Net) constellations verifying rain and wind,
and even Fù Yán (Fu Yue) being brought forth by a dream (lài),
these show how Xiàng pervades the *Shū* (Documents/History).
Ancient officials recorded things by clouds and birds,
the *Zhōu Guān* (Rites of Zhōu) regulated heaven, earth, and the four seasons,
extending to the patterns of dragons and pheasants (zhái) on ceremonial robes,
and bears and tigers marking archery skill (zhì shè),
these show how Xiàng pervades the *Lǐ* (Rites/Ceremonies).
Songs harmonized Yīnyáng,
dances distinguished Wén (civil) and Wǔ (martial),
extending to the chime stone (qìng) recalling the limits of the hexagrams (guà jiāng),
and the drum summoning thoughts of generals and commanders (jiāng shuài),
these show how Xiàng pervades the *Yuè* (Music).
The editing (bǐ xuē) did not discard calamities and anomalies,
the *Zuǒ Shì* (Zuǒ’s Commentary) further expanded on omens and portents (yāo xiáng),
these show how Xiàng pervades the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals).
The *Yì* is congruent with Heaven and Earth;
thus, it is able to encompass completely the Dào of Heaven and Earth.
All things and myriad creatures,
when they move from stillness,
before their forms and traces are evident, the Xiàng (Image) is already seen.
Therefore, the Dào cannot be seen;
those who seek the Dào and feel as though they perceive something,
are seeing its Xiàng.
There are the Xiàng naturally produced by Heaven and Earth,
and there are the Xiàng constructed by the human mind.
Regarding the Xiàng naturally produced by Heaven and Earth,
the statements in the *Shuō Guà* (Discussion of the Trigrams), such as "Heaven is round,"
are broadly sufficient to exhaust them.
Regarding the Xiàng constructed by the human mind:
the cart in the Kuí (Separation) hexagram carries ghosts,
the wild pheasant's cry (hàn yīn) ascends to Heaven.
Wherever intention reaches,
nothing is impossible.
However, while the mind is empty and its function is spirit-like,
humans are bound up between Heaven and Earth,
and cannot avoid being affected by the waxing and waning of Yīnyáng.
The constructions of the mind
are due to the changes and variations of human emotions (qíng).
The changes and variations of emotions
are stirred by interaction and structure in the human world,
and are enabled by the reliance and concealment (yǐ fú) inherent in Yīnyáng.
Thus, the Xiàng constructed by the human mind
also originate from the Xiàng naturally produced by Heaven and Earth.
Although the Xiàng of the *Yì* encompasses the Liùyì,
it is especially closely connected to the Bǐ Xìng (comparison and stimulation) found in the *Shī*.
They are particularly integrated (as inner and outer).
Now, the various schools of the *Shī*,
flourished in the humanistic culture of the Zhànguó (Warring States) period.
It is said that they excelled at satire and metaphor (fěng yù).
If one does not study the *Shī*,
then one has no means to speak (See the chapter on *Shī Jiào*).
However, the literature of the Zhànguó period
deeply utilized Bǐ Xìng,
which is precisely its deep application of taking Xiàng.
In the allegories of *Zhuāngzǐ* and *Lièzǐ*,
the snails (chù mán) could establish a state,
and a deer of plantain leaves (jiāo lù) could settle lawsuits.
When the *Lí Sāo* vents its indignation,
the palace of the sovereign can ascend to the Jiǔtiān (Nine Heavens),
and the conditions of ghosts can be scrutinized in the Jiǔdì (Nine Earths).
Other examples include the scholars of the Zònghéng (Vertical and Horizontal) school who offered unrestrained counsel,
the practitioners of Fēiqián Bǎihé (Flying Clamping and Opening/Closing),
schemes involving moving snakes and leading tigers,
and dialogues between a peach figurine (táo gěng) and an earth idol (tǔ ǒu).
The more they appeared, the more bizarre they became,
defying imagination.
Yet, in pointing out delusion and following the Dào,
they certainly have their achievements;
but in disguising treachery and selling deceit,
they also inflict harm.
Therefore, the Xiàng constructed by the human mind
can be auspicious or inauspicious.
One should observe the Xiàng naturally produced by Heaven and Earth,
and conform them to Lǐ (Principle/Reason).
This is why the teachings of the *Yì* set the standard for the world.
As for the various masters and the Bǎijiā (Hundred Schools),
they did not conform perfectly to the Great Dào.
The reason why their ideas had a basis (chí zhī yǒu gù) and their words formed a coherent rationale (yán zhī chéng lǐ),
is that their origins
were all within the scope of the canons and duties preserved in the *Zhōu Guān*.
Those parts that were fragmented and failed to align with the Dào,
arose because teachers lost their official duties (guān shǒu),
and the resulting schools of later ages
followed their private intentions, indulging in their own theories.
It is not that they gained nothing
at all from the Dào of the Former Kings,
and then established their own separate school of thought.
Regarding the teachings of the Fó Shì (Buddhists),
they came from the Xīyù (Western Regions).
Regardless of the fact that they were not remnants of hereditary official duties (shì guān diǎn shǒu),
and also that (the language they used) originated outside Zhōngguó,
their speech was incomprehensible,
and even though they flourished in Zhōngguó,
their script was not yet fully understood.
Yet, what they spoke and their written texts,
whose ideas had a basis and whose words formed a coherent rationale,
were perhaps even more robust than those of the Bǎijiā.
Repeatedly examining them,
we realize their origin lies in the teachings of the *Yì*.
For what they call Xīn (Mind), Xìng (Nature), Lǐ (Principle), and Dào (Way),
though the terminology differs,
if we trace their essential meaning,
they are initially no different from the words of the Sages.
Where they differ from the Sages
is only that they discard affairs and things (shì wù) and seek a separate concept of the so-called Dào.
As for the Zhàngliù Jīnshēn (eighteen-foot-tall golden body),
the solemn and magnificent physical manifestations (sè xiàng),
extending to the brightness and clarity of Tiāntáng (Heaven),
the gloom and misery of Dìyù (Hell),
celestial maidens scattering flowers,
and Yèchā (Yakṣas) with disheveled hair—
all these kinds of strange illusions,
which are unseen by men—
Rú zhě (Confucians) denounce them as baseless delusion.
They do not know that the Buddhists use Xiàng as instruction (Xiàng jiào),
which is comparable to the "dragon blood, black and yellow" (lóng xuè xuán huáng) in the *Yì*,
or the drawing of a bow (zhāng hú) and the carrying of ghosts (zài guǐ).
Therefore, the varying appearances of Yánmó (Yama)
are spoken of based on the Xiàng constructed by the human mind;
they are not fabricated falsehoods intended to deceive the world.
As for later generations losing the proper transmission,
carving them out and making them literal,
even the ignorant among men and women,
occasionally seeing manifest shapes or hearing relying sounds,
then fabricating interpretations to match them,
resulting in the claim that beneath the bright sky,
there exists a separate realm.
The Rú zhě, furthermore, do not investigate the root and the branch (běn mò),
rolling up their sleeves to argue,
enraged as if they cannot coexist under the same heaven,
yet they do not realize that these (Buddhist concepts) are not strictly literal.
If their teachings,
and the objects designated by their texts,
were simply applied closely to the daily practices of human relationships (rén lún),
then they would be the Dào of the Sages.
Using Xiàng as instruction
is not without foundation.
The Xiàng of the *Yì* pervade the Bǐ Xìng of the *Shī*;
the words (Cí) of the *Yì* pervade the precedents (Lì) of the *Chūnqiū*.
Strictly dividing Heaven and the marsh (tiān zé), the second line often receives praise (duō yù),
and the fourth line often experiences fear (duō jù).
Carefully considering the juncture between order and chaos,
the solid line (Yáng) symbolizes the Jūnzǐ (superior person),
and the broken line (Yīn) symbolizes the Xiǎorén (petty person).
Blocking the beginning of gradual decay:
In Gòu (Encountering), just one Yīn line appears,
yet there is already the warning of "the woman is mighty" (nǚ zhuàng).
In Lín (Approaching), two Yáng lines appear,
and immediately there is concern about the eighth month (bā yuè).
Being cautious about the loaning of names and ritual vessels (míng qì):
Line Five warns against the weak Yīn,
and Line Three often faces danger and warning (wēi tì).
Furthermore, regarding the Four Virtues (Sì Dé): Zūn (honorable)
Yuán (sublime) has no alternative designation;
Hēng (success) may be Xiǎo Hēng (minor success);
Lì Zhēn (benefit and constancy) may be Xiǎo Lì Zhēn (minor benefit and constancy);
Zhēn (constancy) may be Zhēn Jí (constancy is auspicious) or Zhēn Xiōng (constancy is inauspicious);
Jí (auspicious) may be Yuán Jí (supremely auspicious);
Huǐ (regret) may be Huǐ Wáng (regret vanishes);
Jiù (fault) may be Wú Jiù (no fault).
The addition or omission of a single character
is even more strict and rigorous than in the *Chūnqiū*.
This is because the Sages, concerning the juncture between Heaven and humanity,
deemed it profoundly fearful.
The *Yì* uses Tiāndào (the Way of Heaven) to closely relate to human affairs (rén shì);
the *Chūnqiū* uses human affairs to harmonize with Tiāndào.
The principle and precedent (yì lì) revealed in their language,
show the cautionary intent of the Sages.
of the *Zhōu Guān* (Rites of Zhōu),
manages the documents of the Sān Huáng (Three Sovereigns) and Wǔ Dì (Five Emperors).
Now, only the records of Yú, Xià, Shāng, and Zhōu remain;
of the Wǔ Dì, only two exist,
and the Sān Huáng are not known.
That which Zuǒ Shì called the *Sān Fén* and the *Wǔ Diǎn*,
is now unknowable.
We do not know if these were those very documents or not.
Using the chapters on Oaths (Shì), Announcements (Gào), Tributes (Gòng), and Regulations (Fàn) of the Sān Wáng (Three Kings)
to deduce the precedents and principles of the Sān Huáng and the various Dì (Emperors),
then high antiquity was simple and plain.
The era of knot-tying was not far removed;
writing had just begun to flourish,
and records merely served to convey subtle obscurities and to connect form and name.
Chapters were named based on the events they covered,
fundamentally lacking fixed methods.
They could not be expected to be exhaustive in scope, like later historians,
or restricted by definite nomenclature.
The Master (Fūzǐ) compiled and narrated them,
selecting those that were clearly understood and reached far,
sufficient to establish teachings.
Scholars of later generations do not comprehend this.
They hold that the progenitor
of historical writing truly lies in the *Shàngshū* (Venerated Documents).
Thus, those who take the fixed historical methods of later ages
and frantically try to imitate the *Shū*
are all mistaken.
The way history was written before the Sān Dài (Three Dynasties),
compared with the way history was written after the Sān Dài,
the reasons for their similarities and differences can be known.
Before the Sān Dài,
records and notes had established methods,
but the compositions lacked fixed names;
after the Sān Dài,
compositions had fixed names,
but records and notes lacked established methods.
Now, if records and notes lack established methods,
then gathering source material is difficult;
if compositions have fixed names,
then compiling documents is easy.
If compiling documents is easy,
then literary form prevails over substance.
If gathering source material is difficult,
then falsehood corrupts the truth.
If falsehood corrupts the truth and literary form prevails over substance,
historical scholarship, though seemingly preserved, is lost.
The talent of a good historian
appears once in an age;
patching up deficiencies and remedying defects,
they are exhausted and cannot sustain it.
It is not that the learning and knowledge of later generations are inferior to those of earlier ones,
but because the system of the *Zhōu Guān* is lost,
and the teaching of the *Shàngshū* is severed.
The circumstances inevitably lead to this.
The *Zhōu Guān* lists three hundred and sixty offices,
detailing the minutiae of all beneath Heaven.
However, the regulations were vested in the offices,
and the offices maintained their own documents.
Observing the principle of the overlapping duties of the Liù Qīng (Six Ministers),
one knows that the ancients, regarding their canons and documents,
did not shrink from complexity, duplication, and comprehensiveness,
ensuring the completeness of their records and notes.
Take, for example, the text of the Liù Diǎn (Six Canons):
they are intricate and numerous like this.
The Tài Zǎi (Grand Administrator) managed them,
the Xiǎo Zǎi (Junior Administrator) assisted,
and the Sī Huì (Director of Accounts), Sī Shū (Director of Documents), and Tài Shǐ (Grand Historian) each also kept duplicates of the auxiliary records.
Thus, the text of the Liù Diǎn
was perhaps quintupled in its primary and auxiliary copies,
and preserved in the archives.
Other chapters and documents
must have followed the same pattern.
Therefore, if one office failed in its duties,
or if one canon faced unforeseen disaster by water or fire,
other departments could consult the auxiliary records for verification.
Are these not established methods
for records and notes, more detailed than those of later ages?
By the Hàn dynasty, between the Yuán and Chéng eras,
the canons and documents could be considered complete.
However, Liú Shì's *Qī Lüè* (Seven Summaries),
although tracing the classifications derived from the Liù Diǎn,
was already unable to list all the relevant offices;
Furthermore, while statutes and ordinances were stored in the judicial bureaus (Fǎ Cáo),
regulations were kept in the ancestral archives (Gù Fǔ),
and court protocols were maintained by the Tài Cháng (Grand Minister of Ceremonies),
it is not heard that Shí Qú (Stone Channel Pavilion) and Tiān Lù (Heavenly Favor Pavilion) separately stored auxiliary copies
for the verification of the editing department (Jiào Sī).
This can truly be called a lack of established method.
The administration of Hàn
was the closest to antiquity, yet it was already so sketchy.
How much more astonishing is it that the writings and classical accounts
of later ages should be confused, disorganized, and without order?
Méngzǐ (Mencius) said:
"When the traces of the true King ceased, the *Shī* (Odes) perished;
after the *Shī* perished, then the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals) was composed."
This generally speaks of the decline of the Kingly Way (Wáng Huà),
tracing the origin of the function of the *Chūnqiū*.
But they do not know that when the system of the *Zhōu Guān* was abolished, the *Shū* (Documents) perished;
after the *Shū* perished, then the *Chūnqiū* was composed.
This speaks of the failure to establish Kingly Regulations (Wáng Zhāng),
and through this, the structure (Tǐ) of the *Chūnqiū* can be discerned.
How could they not know that when the system of the *Zhōu Guān* was abolished, the *Shū* perished?
This is because the official ritual system was rigorous,
and only then did records and notes have established methods;
when records and notes had established methods,
then compositions could be without fixed names.
It means that the minutiae were completely and intricately prepared,
and the responsible offices already possessed complete documents.
I (Confucius, implicitly) specifically selected the important and great ones,
committed them to writing,
to illustrate the broad strategies by which the Dì Wáng (Emperors and Kings) governed the world.
As for the categories of Canons (Diǎn), Counsels (Mó), Instructions (Xùn), Announcements (Gào), Tributes (Gòng), Regulations (Fàn), Offices (Guān), and Punishments (Xíng),
whether detailed or summarized, kept or discarded,
depended solely on the dictates of intention,
and it was unnecessary to establish them as fixed precedents.
This is how the *Shàngshū* governs the world.
When the official ritual system was abolished,
the records and notes were insufficient to cover everything.
The *Chūnqiū* links events with words,
and Zuǒ Shì had no choice but to use the archives of the various offices,
along with the precious documents of the various states,
to complete the beginning and end of the events.
The circumstances made it necessary.
From Mǎ Qiān (Sīmǎ Qiān) and Bān Gù onward,
they expanded upon Zuǒ Shì and further elaborated its branches.
This is what is meant by
records and notes lacking established methods, but compositions having to adopt fixed names.
Therefore, it is said:
When the traces of the true King ceased, the *Shī* perished,
showing the function of the *Chūnqiū*;
when the system of the *Zhōu Guān* was abolished, the *Shū* perished,
showing the structure of the *Chūnqiū*.
The *Jì* (Record of Rites) says:
"The Zuo Shǐ (Left Scribe) records words,
the Yòu Shǐ (Right Scribe) records actions."
Their offices are not seen in the *Zhōu Guān*,
and their documents are not transmitted to later generations.
Perhaps this is an error in the texts of the Rites scholars?
Later scholars failed to observe this,
and divided the *Shàngshū* as belonging to the recording of words,
and the *Chūnqiū* as belonging to the recording of events.
This is a severe mistake.
If the *Chūnqiū* cannot dispense with the commentary (zhuàn) and exist solely as a catalogue of events,
then the words recorded by Zuǒ Shì
number no fewer than tens of thousands.
In the chapters of Canons and Counsels (Diǎn Mó)
in the *Shàngshū*, events are recorded and words are also present;
in the chapters of Instructions and Announcements (Xùn Gào),
words are recorded and events are also visible.
In antiquity, people's affairs were manifested in their words,
and words constituted affairs.
They never separated affairs and words into two distinct things.
Liú Zhījǐ, due to the intermingling of the chapters on the Two Canons (Èr Diǎn), Tribute (Gòng), and Regulations (Fàn),
in turn criticized the lack of purity in the principles and precedents of the *Shàngshū*.
Did he not perhaps use the empty rhetoric of later ages
to cast doubt on the genuine events of the ancients?
The *Jì* says:
"Clear understanding that reaches far
is the teaching of the *Shū*."
How could this simply mean recording words?
The Liù Yì (Six Arts) stood together.
The *Yuè* (Music) perished and entered into the *Shī* and the *Lǐ* (Rites);
the *Shū* perished and entered into the *Chūnqiū*.
These were all results of heavenly timing and human affairs,
happening without conscious design.
Regarding the events in the *Chūnqiū*,
such as Qí Huán and Jìn Wén,
the decree of Zǎi Kǒng to the Marquis of Qí,
and the decree of Wángzǐ Hǔ to the Marquis of Jìn,
are all texts of instructions and announcements (Xùn Gào).
Zuǒ Shì appended them to the commentary (zhuàn) to support the Classic (Jīng).
The Master (Fūzǐ) did not compile them in the same chapter as the *Wén Hóu zhī Mìng* (Decree to Marquis Wén).
This is clear proof that the *Shū* entered the *Chūnqiū*.
Mǎ Qiān inherited the method of the *Chūnqiū*,
but he edited and polished the Canons and Counsels (Diǎn Mó),
inserting them into the Basic Annals (Jì) and Biographies (Zhuàn).
Bān Gù succeeded Mǎ Qiān and created his work.
The *Yǔ Gòng* (Tribute of Yǔ) was placed first in the Treatise on Geography (Dì Lǐ),
and the *Hóng Fàn* (Grand Plan) was specifically recorded in the Treatise on the Five Phases (Wǔ Xíng).
Thus, the *Shū* and the *Chūnqiū* inevitably merged into one.
Later scholars failed to observe this,
and insisted that the chronological-biographical style (Jì Zhuàn) follows the *Shàngshū*,
while the annual compilation style (Biān Nián) follows the *Chūnqiū*.
This, in forcing a separation and classification,
how is it any different from rigidly separating the Left Scribe recording words and the Right Scribe recording events?
The *Shū* (Book/Document) had no fixed structure,
thus it was easily lost in transmission;
precisely because the *Shū* had no fixed structure,
many attributed (their works) to it.
In the late Zhōu period, culture flourished,
and the official rites (guānlǐ) lost their function and responsibility.
Consequently, the scholarship of the Hundred Schools (bǎijiā)
often competitively attributed (their texts) to the writings of the Sānhuáng (Three Sovereigns) and Wǔdì (Five Emperors).
Arts of cultivation were attributed to Shénnóng,
military strategies and medical classics were attributed to Huángdì.
Enthusiasts
transmitted them as lost texts of the *Sānfén* and separate transmissions of the *Wǔdiǎn*.
They did not realize that while the documents certainly arose from attribution,
the content was not entirely without sources or lineage;
(they were) the institutional history (zhǎnggù) preserved by people when official rites (guānlǐ) and governance were implemented,
passed down through generations of clans and teachers.
Only the remnants of the “Three”
and the “Five”
that remain
are largely preserved in the responsibilities described in the *Zhōu Guān* (Rites of Zhōu officials).
Thus, the books managed by the Outer Scribe (wàishǐ)
must be separately compiled records,
similar to the system where the Six Statutes (liùdiǎn) each maintained their duplicate copies.
What Zuǒ Shì referred to as the *Sānfén* and *Wǔdiǎn*,
might have been a generalized naming,
or perhaps it was a separate theory;
this is unknowable.
To insist on precisely identifying what constitutes the *Fén* of the Sānhuáng,
and what constitutes the *Diǎn* of the Wǔdì,
would be overly forced (zuó).
The *Yì Zhōu Shū* (Lost Book of Zhōu), in seventy-one chapters,
consists mostly of separate records of official rites (guānlǐ) and external chapters (wàipiān) of the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals).
Those studying the *Shàngshū* probably gathered them randomly to serve as collateral evidence for the Classics.
Liú [Xiàng] and Bān [Gù] believed they were the remnants of the hundred chapters discussed by Kǒngzǐ.
This would imply they are lost chapters,
originally forming one book along with the Statutes (*diǎn*), Counsels (*mó*), Instructions (*xùn*), and Announcements (*gào*),
(already translated above)
but Kǒngzǐ merely edited them, deleting some and preserving others.
Setting aside the fact that the writing styles of these documents are dissimilar
and that purity and confusion are interspersed,
even looking at interpretations such as those in *Zhífāng* and *Shíxùn*,
they clearly employ the language of historical records and classics.
The *Tàizǐ Jìn Jiě*,
clearly draws upon events from the *Chūnqiū* period.
That they are external chapters (wàipiān) and separate records
can be determined without extensive discussion.
However, there truly exist within them canonical statements and valuable teachings,
recognized as remnants of the oaths and announcements of the Former Kings (xiānwáng),
which are not necessarily outside the scope of the hundred chapters' intent,
and therefore should not be hastily regarded as remnants of deletions and abridgements.
The Master (Fūzǐ) said:
“I transmit but do not innovate. I am truthful and love antiquity.”
If the canonical announcements (diǎngào) of the Former Kings,
still existed during the declining Zhōu dynasty,
and the Master deleted them,
how could he be considered one who loves antiquity?
It is only because the *Shū* had no fixed structure,
that the separate records and external chapters (wàipiān) of the *Chūnqiū* and official rites (guānlǐ)
were all able to be appended and incorporated into it.
This also clarifies the different branches of the *Shū* tradition.
Since the *Shū* had no fixed structure,
those who appended material were numerous and varied.
Later people wrongly tried to imitate the *Shū* to establish a fixed structure,
thus their adherence became rigid.
Ancient people did not speak idle words;
how could there be a specialized book dedicated only to recording speeches?
Hàn Confucians mistakenly believed the description in the *Yùzǎo*
and regarded the *Shàngshū* as a specialized book for recording speeches.
Consequently, later generations “cut their toes to fit the shoe,”
selecting texts where events and writings matched,
cutting out the events and compiling only the texts,
to serve as sequels to the *Shàngshū*;
examples include Kǒng Shì's *Hàn-Wèi Shàngshū* and Wáng Shì's *Xù Shū*.
Lacking the reality,
but merely resembling the appearance of the ancients,
it is like a painted rice cake which cannot satisfy hunger.
Furthermore, the *Shàngshū* fundamentally did not limit itself merely to recording speeches,
so what Kǒng Yǎn and Wáng Tōng imitated
failed even to capture the superficial resemblance of the ancients.
Liú Zhījǐ once worried that within historical records of events,
lengthy literary passages were suddenly interspersed.
He wanted to take the imperial edicts and announcements (zhàogào)
and the memorials (zòuzhāng) of officials,
separate them into a category,
and arrange them within the historical biographies (jìzhuàn),
roughly like the system where treatises (shū zhì) have separate chapters and titles.
This shows that Liú also understood how the *Shàngshū* tradition blended into the *Chūnqiū* tradition.
However, if events and speeches must be strictly divided into two,
given that events and speeches are intertwined and that there is a relationship between substance (zhì) and literary expression (wén xuān),
if they are made into separate chapters,
they become inconvenient to review;
if they are still recorded together,
the methodology is inconsistent.
This is why, although Mr. Liú had this proposal,
later generations ultimately did not implement it.
As for memorials and essays discussing governance (zhāngshū),
they are fundamentally the same as oral reports;
letters addressing difficulties and challenges,
are no different from face-to-face discussions.
Their inclusion in the historical biographies (jìzhuàn),
without separating events and speeches,
is acceptable, and later historians adhered strictly to this established method.
However, as for the rhymed prose (*cífù*) of Yáng [Xióng] and Mǎ [Róng],
which were originally not political discourse,
and the presented texts of Yán [Zhù] and Xú [Fú],
which were also essentially dedicatory odes (xiànsòng);
the strategizing (zònghéng) of Zōu Yáng and Méi Chéng;
and the embellishments (fùhuì) of Dù Qīn and Gǔ Yǒng—
they fundamentally had no relation to canonical essentials (diǎnyào).
Mǎ [Qī] and Bān [Gù] included them to demonstrate the national brilliance.
If they were cut out, the literary splendor would vanish;
if they were kept, the historical biographies (jìzhuàn) become bloated and excessive.
It is thus not surprising that Mr. Liú wished to discuss reforms.
Dù Shì’s *Tōngdiǎn* comprises two hundred scrolls,
and the Canon of Rites (*Lǐdiǎn*), being one of the eight divisions,
already occupies one hundred scrolls.
This is because his work is fundamentally a remnant of official rites (guānlǐ),
so it is reasonable that he elaborated in detail on matters of ritual.
However, when narrating statutes and governmental systems (diǎnzhāng zhìdù),
it is not unlike the writing style of other historians.
But when ritual texts are ambiguous or contradictory,
or when situational changes create inconsistencies,
the erudites (bóshì) and Classicists (jīngshēng)
seek compromises and discuss in detail.
Sometimes decisions are made and immediately implemented,
sometimes they are shelved and not yet used.
If these were included in the main text,
the excessive complexity would be unbearable;
if they were cut and discarded,
the principles and context would be incomplete.
Dù Shì collected and compiled all these texts,
appending them after the Ritual section.
A total of more than twenty scrolls,
which can be said to exhaust the bounds of Heaven and Earth,
and comprehend the changes of past and present.
The book by Shǐ Qiān,
after the *Qín Jì* (Annals of Qín),
preserved and recorded the original text of the Qín history.
Unfortunately, his editorial method was not widely extended,
and later generations did not follow suit.
This marks the limit of both recording speeches and recording events,
(and) a separate method of adaptation and flexibility
which later virtuous scholars should consult and adopt.
A ladle-full source (lànshāng) flows into rivers (jiānghé);
matters begin simply but end massively.
Since the Eastern Capital (Dōngjīng) [period],
literature flourished and texts multiplied.
Historians could not generally present them in the historical biographies (jìzhuàn),
so they compiled them into the *Wényuàn* (Garden of Literature) chapters.
Literary figures often had few governmental accomplishments,
(so the chapters) only listed their official ranks and family lineage,
similar to the annotations of names in the *Wénxuǎn* (Selections of Literature)
or the biographical records of examination lists.
Although the chapter title suggests beautiful writing,
the literary brilliance felt diminished.
Thus, we know that the flourishing literature of an era
cannot be entirely covered by historical writings.
Since Xiāo Tǒng's *Wénxuǎn*,
many have created such anthologies.
Those particularly prominent today are
Yáo Shì's *Táng Wén Cuì*,
Lǚ Shì's *Sòng Wén Jiàn*,
and Sū Shì's *Yuán Wén Lèi*.
All sought to encompass an entire dynasty,
serving as supplements to the histories.
This actually somewhat resembles separating documents based on speech and events,
but in reality, these various selections are the spring blossoms,

while the standard histories are the autumn fruit. (The standard histories and literary anthologies each contain both speeches and events, thus they can only be divided into "blossom" and "fruit," not into "speech" and "event.")
Once the Four Divisions (sìbù) were established,
the field of collected works greatly expanded.
When literary men were charged with drafting announcements (gào),
collections of court decrees (nèizhì) and external pronouncements (wàizhì)
formed their own compilations.
When prime ministers offered opinions and reflections,
or remonstrance officials submitted blunt critiques (báijiǎn),
or departmental officials reported on specific matters,
or military commanders outside the pass estimated the enemy and planned good strategies,
the chapters of Lù Zhì's *Zòuyì* (Memorials and Deliberations),
and Sū Shì's presented strategies,
were recorded in their respective collections.
When aggregated, there are works like *Míngchén Jīngjì* (Statesmanship of Famous Ministers) and *Cèfǔ Yìlín* (Forest of Discussions from the Strategy Library)—
volume after volume, page upon page,
how can they be fully counted!
Generally, previous authors recorded them
under the two categories of Individual Collections (biéjí) and General Collections (zǒngjí),
based on the perspective of an individual person's writings.
In reality, they should belong to the History Division (shǐbù);
tracing their source, they belong to the *Shàngshū* tradition.
However, instructions and announcements (*xùn gào*) are only one aspect of the *Shàngshū*,
and it is not permissible, like the Hàn people, to simply categorize the *Shàngshū* as a history solely recording speeches.
Famous ministers' memorials and petitions,
are categorized under the Shàngshū,
to be likened to didactic pronouncements (xùn gào),
which people easily understand.
Those who compiled these memorials and petitions,
should know that the record of words in didactic pronouncements,
must narrate the corresponding events,
to provide the full context of what was said.
Therefore, the Shàngshū contains no empty words;
when there are words, they must be situated within events.
Later compilers of memorials and petitions,
merely selected those discussions that were clear and lucid,
and whose sentiments and rhetoric were fervent and incisive,
considering these the best memorials,
but they did not provide the full beginning and end of the events.
Although there were excellent pieces,
what use were they intended for?
This common practice of literati valuing flowery rhetoric,
cannot be spoken of regarding the Classics and Histories (jīng shǐ).
In Bān Shì’s biographies of Dǒng [Zhòngshū] and Jiǎ [Yì],
he treated the scholarship of the Chūnqiū as the Shàngshū—this is proof that the Shàngshū branched into the Chūnqiū.
When narrating the life and deeds of Jiǎ and Dǒng,
he had no intention of seeking detail,
the context before and after being merely a few scattered words,
serving only to provide the context for their various political memorials and the Three Strategies concerning Heaven and Man (tiān rén sān cè). Alas!
Those who observe the methods of historical composition,
must understand this intention,
and only then can one discuss the respective ultimate appropriateness of the scholarship of the Shàngshū and the Chūnqiū,
unlike later generations who categorize and copy excerpts to cite events,
knowing only how to be comprehensive, seeking both the square and the round aspects.
The Yì says:
“The virtue of the text is round and spiritual,
the virtue of the hexagrams is square and intellectual.”
I have occasionally privately adopted this meaning,
to categorize the records of antiquity and the present:
Historical composition (zhuàn shù) seeks the round and spiritual,
while record-keeping (jì zhù) seeks the square and intellectual.
Now, intellect (zhì) serves to preserve the past,
and the spiritual (shén) serves to foresee the future.
Record-keeping aims for past events not to be forgotten,
while historical composition aims for future generations to be inspired.
Thus, record-keeping preserving the past resembles intellect,
and historical composition foreseeing the future emulates the spiritual.
Preserving the past seeks comprehensiveness without omission,
thus its structure is fixed,
and its virtue is square;
foreseeing the future seeks judgment, selection, and rejection,
thus its methods are not restricted by convention,
and its virtue is round.
The three hundred and sixty offices of the Zhōu Guān [Rites of Zhōu],
can be said to contain nothing incomplete concerning the matters of Heaven, man, and official procedure.
However, all historians merely managed record-keeping,
and there was never an official responsible for historical composition.

The office of prayer and history produced commands and announcements, which were not entirely unrelated to composition, but there was no person designated as a composing historian. Thus, the task of transmitting knowledge through generations and far afield,
cannot be constrained by specific official duties,
but must wait for the right person before it can proceed.
Unless one is a sage, a wise philosopher, or possesses spiritual clarity,
deeply understanding the profound subtlety of the Two Emperors and Three Kings (Èr Dì Sān Wáng),
one is not fit for this task.
This is why the Shàngshū has no fixed method (dìng fǎ).
The Shàngshū and the Chūnqiū,
are both canons created by the Sages.
The Shàngshū has no fixed method,
while the Chūnqiū has established precedents (chéng lì).
Therefore, the branch lineage of the Shū [Shàngshū],
folded into the Chūnqiū,
but the Shū itself had no heir.
That which has established precedents is easy to follow,
but that which has no fixed method is difficult to continue.
This is what people know.
However, the round and spiritual, and the square and intellectual,
ever since records have existed,
these two aspects have never been abandoned in favor of the other.
It is merely that people cannot fully investigate the profundity of the Six Arts (Liù Yì),
yet none have failed to obtain their lingering intention.
Among historians who followed the Chūnqiū and produced works,
none are superior to Mǎ [Qiān] and Bān [Gù].
Mǎ is closer to the round and spiritual,
while Bān is closer to the square and intellectual.
The Shàngshū underwent one transformation to become Zuǒ Shì’s Chūnqiū [Zuǒ Zhuàn],
the Shàngshū having no established methods while Zuǒ Shì had fixed rules,
serving to elaborate upon the Classic.
Zuǒ Shì underwent one transformation to become Sǐ Qiān’s Basic Annals and Biographies,
Zuǒ Shì followed the years and months, while Sǐ Qiān’s work classified by category,
in order to gather what was missed.
Sǐ Qiān’s work underwent one transformation to become Bān Shì’s chronological history,
Sǐ Qiān’s work encompassed transformation,
while Bān Shì adhered to rules,
in order to demonstrate comprehensiveness.
Speaking of the external form,
Sǐ Qiān’s work is greatly different from Zuǒ Shì’s,
but Bān Shǐ’s history is close to Sǐ Qiān’s work.
This is because Zuǒ Shì’s structure is linear,
making him the originator of the annals style,
while Mǎ and Bān arranged events extensively,
both being the originators of the basic annals and biographies style.
Extending this discussion to the subtle and profound,
then Sǐ Qiān’s work is closer to Zuǒ Shì’s,
while Bān Shǐ’s history is further from Sǐ Qiān’s work.
This is because Sǐ Qiān’s work employs the round structure and the spiritual application,
largely preserving the heritage of the Shàngshū;
Bān Shì employs the square structure and the intellectual application,
largely preserving the intention of the official rites.
Sǐ Qiān’s work, with its Basic Annals, Tables, Treatises, and Biographies,
is fundamentally based on Zuǒ Shì but shows slight differentiation,
and is not strictly bound by topic titles.
The Biography of Bó Yí,
is actually a preface/guide for the seventy chapters,
and is not solely a biography of Bó Yí.
The Biographies of Qū [Yuán] and Jiǎ [Yì] serve to condemn the slander of Jiàng and Guàn,
and the text that narrates Qū [Yuán],
is not intended to declare Qū Shì's loyalty,
but is rather an elegy lamenting Jiǎ [Yì].
The Biography of Cāng Gōng records his medical cases,
The Biographies of the Money-Makers (Huò Zhí) also record natural resources,
The Treatise on Tortoise Shells and Divining Stalks (Guī Cè) merely discusses divination,
all having the intention of naming the chapter based on the event or topic,
and originally not meticulously providing the full context for a single person.
In the biographies of Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú,
through one, the other can be understood.
The Biographies of Mèngzǐ and Xún Qīng,
merely summarize the writing of traveling scholars.
The titles based on names,
often disregard standard categorization,
merely serving to name the chapter.
Just like Guān Jū and Lù Míng [chapters of the Shījīng],
the actual focus is on the esteemed guests and virtuous ladies,
and yet some mock the placement as illogical (like Mèngzǐ with the Three Zōu Masters),
or criticize the repetition as lacking oversight (like Zǐgòng already in the Biographies of Disciples, yet appearing again in Huò Zhí).
They do not understand the central purpose of the ancients in writing,
but instead use the established rules rigidly adhered to by later generations,
to criticize the ancients’ flexibility and adaptability.
Do they not know that Sǐ Qiān’s work uses the round structure and the spiritual application,
still possessing the heritage of the Shàngshū?
Sǐ Qiān’s history cannot be taken as a fixed method,
but Bān Shì’s work adopted the structure of Sǐ Qiān,
and created a definitive set of principles,
thereby becoming the perpetual standard for later generations.
Since the Three Dynasties (Sān Dài),
historical talent has not been constantly appearing,
so carefully adhering to the rules,
waiting for the right person before proceeding,
is an unavoidable circumstance.
However, Bān Shì’s work is fundamentally historical composition rather than record-keeping,
so even within its tendency toward the square and the intellectual,
there is still the round and spiritual element,
used to shape and govern the work.
This is why it was able to establish a school,
and be transmitted through generations and far afield.
Later historians lost the original intention of Bān Shǐ’s history,
and treated the Basic Annals, Tables, Treatises, and Biographies,
as equivalent to examination formats,
or official government registers.
Thus, regarding both record-keeping and historical composition,
they resemble neither,
and the fundamental purpose of the ancients in writing,
can no longer be spoken of.
The history does not establish a school,
and both the events and the text are obscured,
yet they still rigidly adhere to established methods,
claiming that their work follows Mǎ [Qiān] as ancestor and Bān [Gù] as model,
but the true historical scholarship has been lost for a long time!
Calendar methods, when ancient, must be flawed;
observational calculations, when later, are increasingly meticulous.
This is why former people discussed regulating heaven (Sītiān).
And the study of history is also similar to this.
When the *Shàngshū* changed and became the *Chūnqiū*,
then by naming chapters according to events,
and not adhering to standard regulations,
it became slightly more meticulous by arranging narratives based on comparable events.
When the *Zuǒ* and *Guó* [commentaries] changed and became the annals and biographies (jìzhuàn),
then those who, having years as warp and events as weft,
could not make lateral connections,
gained greater meticulousness by classifying and differentiating them by category.
The system of annals and biographies has been practiced for over a thousand years,
and scholars have inherited it,
much like wearing linen in summer and fur in winter,
drinking when thirsty and eating when hungry,
without change.
However, it lacks unique insight or conception,
which is the means by which things can be transmitted through the ages and travel far;
instead, it is meticulous like adhering strictly to the form of the imperial examinations (Kējǔ),
daring not to change slightly;
like managing the documents and records of petty officials (xūlì),
too voluminous to be pruned.
If speaking of square intellect (fāng zhì),
then it is redundant, repetitive, crude, and faulty,
difficult to serve as an authoritative source;
if speaking of round spiritual efficacy (yuán shén),
then it is disorganized, overly broad, and vast,
impossible to recite or memorize.
This is because historians (zúshǐ) only know how to seek completeness within the established rules of annals, tables, treatises, and biographies (jì biǎo zhì zhuàn),
and the writings are restricted by structure and format,
merely desiring to be perfectly square and round,
unaware that annals and biographies fundamentally originated from the *Chūnqiū*,
and the *Chūnqiū* originally aligned with the initial meaning of the *Shàngshū*.
The *Yì* [or *Yìjīng*] says:
“When exhausted, there is change;
when changed, there is permeability;
when permeable, there is permanence.”
The annals and biographies system was indeed a good method after the Three Dynasties (Sāndài),
but having been practiced for a long time,
the great principles and great methods of the former kings
have instead been obscured by the annals and biographies system, which is strictly adhered to in later generations.
How can one not consider the way of change and adaptation?
Zuǒ Shì's chronological arrangement (biānnián),
could not fully categorize and group events;
thus, the annals, tables, biographies, and treatises of the *Shǐ* [Sīmǎ Qiān's *Shǐjì*] and *Hàn* [Bān Gù's *Hànshū*],
were used to remedy the limitations of categorization and grouping.
Historians (zúshǐ) have in turn become restricted by categorization and grouping,
leading to voluminous books and obscure events;
this is also like textual exegesis and commentaries (xùngǔ zhùshū),
which are used to explain the Classics (jīng),
but common teachers (súshī) are instead immersed in xùngǔ zhùshū and obscure the meaning of the Classics (jīng zhǐ).
If the Classics are obscured by explanations,
one should seek the beginning before explanations existed;
if history is restricted by format,
one should seek the beginning before formats existed.
Formats began with the *Zuǒ Shì* commentary on the *Chūnqiū*;
why not seek the original meaning of the *Shàngshū* before it entered the *Chūnqiū*?
The miraculous changes into the rotten,
and the rotten returns to the miraculous.
Those who interpret the writings of Zhuāng [Zhuāngzǐ]
believe that heaven and earth naturally possess change,
and humans merely follow suit by calling things miraculous or rotten.
Affairs repeatedly change and then revert to the beginning;
excessive refinement reaches its limit and returns to simplicity.
This is the natural principle of the world.
The *Shàngshū* is round and spiritual;
regarding historical records,
it can be called the ultimate expression of Heaven.
If the right person is not present, it will not be practiced;
thus it diverged into the *Zuǒ Shì*,
and then merged into the schools of Mǎ [Sīmǎ Qiān] and Bān [Bān Gù].
Indeed, since Liú Zhījǐ
onward, all have believed that the tradition of the *Shàngshū* was broken,
and historians could not carry on its thread.
Furthermore, since the record in the "Treatise on Classics and Literature" (*Jīngjí Zhì*) of the *Suí* [Dynasty] was registered,
treating annals and biographies as the standard history (zhèngshǐ),
and chronological arrangement (biānnián) as ancient history (gǔshǐ),
subsequent dynasties have followed this,
consequently dividing them into primary and secondary,
and none fail to prioritize annals and biographies and demote chronological arrangement.
Thus, the histories of Mǎ [Sīmǎ Qiān] and Bān [Bān Gù],
though secondary sons, inherited the *Chūnqiū*;
while Xún Yuè and Yuán Hóng,
whose schools were the main lineage of the *Zuǒ Shì*,
were reduced to collateral branches.
Sīmǎ [Guāng's] *Tōngjiàn* objected to the fragmentation of the annals and biographies system,
and combined it using chronological arrangement (biānnián).
Yuán Shū's *Jìshì Běnmò* in turn objected to the synthesis of the *Tōngjiàn*,
and divided it according to event categories.
Examining the structure of the *běnmò* (records of events from beginning to end),
it names chapters according to events,
not adhering to standard formats;
without deep knowledge of the general principles of antiquity and the present,
and the management of the world,
one cannot comprehensively summarize and encompass events,
leaving nothing out nor including anything superfluous.
The writing is more concise than the annals and biographies,
and the events are clearer than in chronological arrangement;
by decisively selecting what to remove and what to keep,
its form is round (complete) and its function is spiritual (efficacious).
This is truly the remnant of the *Shàngshū*.
Yuán Shū initially did not have this intention,
and furthermore, his scholarship was insufficient for this task,
nor does his book entirely match what is claimed here.
Therefore, various scholars who cataloged works throughout the dynasties
ranked his book under miscellaneous histories (záshǐ).
It naturally belongs to the category of compilation and recording,
merely facilitating viewing and reading.
But if one takes this established method,
reflects deeply and searches inwardly,
and adds divine, spiritual changes,
then the origin of ancient history
will become faintly discernible.
There are books where the author's meaning is very shallow,
yet the observer's understanding is very deep;
this work is of that type.
Therefore it is said:
The miraculous changes into the rotten,
and the rotten returns to the miraculous;
fundamentally, it is but one principle.
History is a book that records events.
Events vary infinitely and are inconsistent;
if the historical text is flexible and exactly matches the event,
then one must name chapters according to events,
not being restricted by standard formats,
and only then can the beginning and end be handled freely,
without a single word being omitted or superfluous.
This is why the *Shàngshū* exhibits divine, spiritual changes
and cannot be limited by fixed forms.
Descending to the commentary of Zuǒ Shì,
it already could not avoid making the text subservient to the format;
the nature of circumstances made this unavoidable.
To demand the methods of the divine sages of high antiquity
from the historians of recent times,
is this not utterly unrealistic?
One should know that the Classics (jīng) cannot be mastered merely by study,
but the intention (yì) can certainly be followed and imitated.
Furthermore, the *Shàngshū* is certainly not something that can be entirely studied and mastered;
even the *Jìshì Běnmò*,
is merely a small compiled book,
and it should not be entirely adopted as a historical method,
but specifically because its underlying principles are close [to the original intent],
one should not allow the wording to obscure the meaning.
By deliberating upon the historical writings of antiquity and the present,
and determining the middle path between refinement and simplicity,
one should follow the intention (yì) of the *Shàngshū*,
apply the structure and format (yìlì) of Qiān's (*Sīmǎ Qiān's*) *Shǐ* [the *Shǐjì*],
and connect the framework (cáizhì) of the *Zuǒ Shì*.
This is how to remedy the extreme failings of the annals and biographies system,
not merely indulging in arbitrary reform.
Although the Annular Records and Biographies (Jìzhuàn) were first established by Sīmǎ Qiān,
they were also based on prior material.
If one examines the Tàigǔ Niánjì, the Xià Yīn Chūnqiū, and the Zhúshū Jìnián,
then the model of annular records (Běnjì) and chronological arrangement (Biānnián)
has existed
since the invention of writing.
The Shàngshū (Book of Documents) represents a distinct category of historical writing.
If we apply the method of the Zuǒshì (Zuǒ Zhuàn)
and combine it with chronological arrangement,
that is the Biography (Zhuàn).
If the principles of the Shàngshū
were used as the commentary (Zhuàn) for the Chūnqiū (Spring and Autumn Annals),
then the Zuǒshì would not have been forced to subordinate the text to the model,
and much verbose or superficial writing would have been eliminated.
If the principles of the Shàngshū
were used as the commentary (Zhuàn) for Qiān’s Shǐjì,
then the eight Treatises (Bā Shū) and thirty Hereditary Houses (Shìjiā)
would not need to be separately categorized;
they could all follow the Zuǒshì model and be uniformly called Biographies (Zhuàn).
Some Biographies would examine canonical statutes and institutions;
others would narrate the entirety of human affairs;
others would investigate the conduct of a single person (this is the core form of the Lièzhuàn);
others would combine affairs of a similar nature;
others would record the sayings of a period, like injunctions and precepts (Xùngào);
others would record the writings of an era,
naming the chapters according to the subject,
to serve as the warp threads for the annular records (Běnjì).
Compared to the Zuǒshì supporting the classic,
this would avoid the burden of being confined to the sequence of years and months;
compared to the separate classifications in Qiān’s Shǐjì,
this would avoid the annoyance of diverging classifications and overlapping appearances.
The text would be concise, but the events would become even clearer;
the model would be simple, but the meaning would become even more refined.
Is this not the appropriate balance between substance and form (wén zhì),
the Middle Way between antiquity and the present?
As for names of people and categories of events,
when they are combined within the narrative framework (běnmò),
making verification and inspection difficult,
then they should be separately compiled as Tables (Biǎo),
to coordinate the framework.
As for celestial phenomena and geographical features,
chariots and clothes, ritual implements and instruments,
which cannot be fully covered by the narrative framework,
and which are difficult to record through writing,
they should be separately drawn as Illustrations (Tú),
to make them clear.
This would penetrate the origins of the Shàngshū and Chūnqiū
and remedy the shortcomings of the books by Mǎ (Sīmǎ Qiān) and Bān (Bān Gù).
There is no better way than this approach.
As for establishing new designs,
delineating separate categories,
comparing the works of ancient and modern times,
and determining the structure of a single historical work,
I have separately established the Yuántōng chapter (Piān);
I will not discuss it here.
Shào Jìnhán (Shào Jìnhán) said:
“The historical model of Annular Records and Biographies,
when compared and referenced with that of Yuán Shū (Yuán Shū),
is similar in appearance but different in essence.
When tracing it back to the traditions of the Shàngshū,
it is different in appearance but similar in essence.
What this chapter promotes,
is a secondary branch of the Six Arts (Liù Yì),
but the grand tradition of historiography (Shǐxué);
it is the central pillar for previous histories,
and the pioneer (Cáncóng kāishān) for later scholars.”
When the Zhōu declined and literature decayed,
the Dao of the Six Arts ceased,
and the Hundred Schools contended.
It was in the Warring States period (Zhànguó) that the variations in literary style were exhausted,
in the Warring States period that the work of writing and compiling became specialized,
and in the Warring States period that the literary forms of later ages were completed.
Therefore, by discussing literature in the Warring States period,
the reasons for its rise, fall, prosperity, and decline can be known.
The literature of the Warring States period
was characterized by the bizarre and the perverse,
and diverged from the Dao—
people know this.
But its origins all came from the Six Arts—
people do not know this.
The literary forms of later ages
were all completed in the Warring States period—
people do not know this.
Their origins mostly came from the teachings of the Shī (Classic of Poetry)—
people know this even less.
Only by knowing that literary forms were completed in the Warring States period
can one begin to discuss the literature of later ages.
Only by knowing that the various schools originated from the Six Arts
can one discuss the literature of the Warring States period.
Only by knowing that the Warring States literature mostly came from the teachings of the Shī
can one discuss the literature of the Six Arts.
Only by being able to discuss the literature of the Six Arts
can one separate the literature to see the Dao.
Only by being able to separate the literature to see the Dao
can one uphold the Dao and refute the literature of the various schools.
Why is it said that
the literature of the Warring States period
all originated from the Six Arts?
The Dao essence encompasses everything;
the Six Arts are sufficient to exhaust it.
The books created by the various schools (Zhū Zǐ),
if their arguments were based on facts and their discourse was reasonable,
must have obtained a piece of the Dao essence (Dào Tǐ);
only then could they freely and extensively put forth their theories,
to form the doctrines of a single school.
This “piece” (yī duān)
is invariably encompassed by the Six Arts.
Therefore, by tracing them back, their sources can all be found.
This does not mean that the various schools truly followed the teachings of the Six Arts
and ensured that their expressions were always consistent with them.
Lǎozǐ’s (Lǎozǐ) doctrines are based on Yīn and Yáng;
Zhuāng and Liè’s (Zhuāngzǐ, Lièzǐ) use allegories and metaphors—
these are the teachings of the Yì (Classic of Changes).
Zōu Yǎn (Zōu Yǎn) extensively discussed Heaven and Earth;
Guān Yǐn (Guān Yǐn) elaborated on the Five Phases (Wǔ Xíng)—
these are the teachings of the Shū (Classic of Documents).
Guǎn (Guǎn Zhòng) and Shāng’s (Shāng Yāng) legal systems,
whose purpose lay in governmental ordinances—
these are the teachings of the Lǐ (Classic of Rites).
Shēn (Shēn Bùhài) and Hán’s (Hán Fēi) concepts of names and reality (Xíng Míng),
whose core intent was reward and punishment—
these are the teachings of the Chūnqiū (Spring and Autumn Annals).
As for the doctrines of Yáng (Yáng Zhū), Mò (Mò Dì), and Yǐn Wén (Yǐn Wén),
and the strategies of Sū (Sū Qín), Zhāng (Zhāng Yí), Sūn (Sūn Wǔ), and Wú (Wú Qǐ),
by discerning their origins and developments,
and grasping their main objectives,
the sections into which the Nine Streams (Jiǔ Liú) were divided,
and the categories discussed in the Qī Lù (Seven Records),
all achieved consistency
by relying on specialized functions (wù qū rén guān)
without realizing that they were remnants of the Six Canons (Liù Diǎn).
Since the literature of the Warring States period
originated from the Six Arts,
why is it also said that it mostly came from the teachings of the Shī?
I answer:
The Warring States period
was an age of Vertical and Horizontal Alliances (Zònghéng).
The doctrines of Vertical and Horizontal Alliances
originated from the ancient office of the Traveling Emissary (Xíng Rén).
Looking at the diplomatic language (cí mìng) in the Spring and Autumn period,
the high officials of the various states,
when exchanging inquiries with the feudal lords
and acting as plenipotentiaries for negotiations,
simply sought to make their language eloquent to convey their intent.
However, in the Warring States period, they struck their palms and made estimations (dǐ zhǎng chuǎnmó),
putting forth their theories to obtain wealth and status.
Their language was elaborate, extravagant, and forceful (yáng lì),
changing their source material and adding grandiosity and novelty.
It cannot be said that this was not the extreme development of the traveling emissaries’ diplomatic language.
Kǒngzǐ (Confucius) said:
“If a person recites the three hundred odes of the Shī,
but when given a task in government,
they cannot achieve results;
or if sent to various regions,
they cannot conduct independent negotiations (zhuān duì)
—what use is their knowledge, however extensive?”
This shows that the purport of allegory and comparison (bǐ xīng),
and the significance of remonstrance and persuasion (fěng yù),
were precisely what the traveling emissaries practiced.
The followers of the Vertical and Horizontal schools
developed and elaborated upon this,
thus they were able to negotiate subtly and appeal to emotions,
being nuanced and skilled in persuasion.
The doctrines of the Nine Streams,
inheriting specialized functions from the Six Canons,
though they might have originated from the Shū, Yì, or Chūnqiū,
their substance (zhì) was mostly rooted in the teachings of the Lǐ (Classic of Rites),
because their form had general applicability.
When they emerged to engage with the world,
they invariably combined them with Vertical and Horizontal rhetoric,
in order to refine their substance.
In antiquity, substance and form were unified;
in the Warring States period, each possessed its own substance.
When put into practice,
they necessarily utilized the rhetoric of the Vertical and Horizontal Alliances to refine it.
This was the result of the decline of the Zhōu and the decay of literature.
Therefore, it is said:
The Warring States period
was an age of Vertical and Horizontal Alliances.
. What is meant by this? The answer is:
When the forms of the Zǐ (Masters) and Shǐ (Histories) declined, the form of the Wénjí (Literary Collections) flourished
; when formal Zhùzuò (scholarly works) declined, the study of Cízhāng (Rhetoric and belles-lettres) arose
. Wénjí
are those [collections] where Cízhāng did not adhere to specific schools
, but rather gathered literary writings
, making a jumble of dragons and snakes (a literary miscellany)
