. The fact that later worthies inherited [this form] and did not discard it
, is because the rivers had flowed forth, and the current could no longer be blocked
. Scholarly study of the Jīng (Classics) did not adhere to specific schools
, yet the Wénjí contained Jīngyì (interpretations of the Classics)
; scholarly study of History did not adhere to specific schools
, yet the Wénjí contained Zhuànjì (biographies and records)
; formal philosophical assertion (Lìyán) did not adhere to specific schools
, yet the Wénjí contained Lùnbiàn (disquisitions and debates)
. The Wénjí of later generations
, setting aside the three forms of Jīngyì, Zhuànjì, and Lùnbiàn
, the rest all belong to the category of Cízhāng
. And Cízhāng was truly fully established during the Zhànguó period
, [later generations] inherited its current and adapted its style and structure
. Scholars, being unaware of this
, trace back only to the *Liúbié* (Classification of Literary Forms) compiled by Zhì Yú
, and some even take the *Wénxuǎn* (Selections of Literature) of Xiāo Liáng
, and proclaim it as the ancestor of Cízhāng
. They truly do not understand the meaning of the flow and classification of ancient and modern literature
. Now, relying on the various forms found in the *Wénxuǎn*
, we will demonstrate the comprehensive readiness [of these forms] in the Zhànguó period
. The various Fù (rhapsodies) concerning capital cities
, trace their origin to Sū [Qín] and Zhāng [Yí] campaigning across the six states
, in the legacy of elaborately describing strategic topographical situations
. Works like *Shànglín* and *Yǔliè*
, stem from Ānlíng following the hunt
, and Lóngyáng participating in the fishing
. Works like *Kènán* and *Jiěcháo*
, follow Qū Yuán’s *Yúfù* and *Bǔjū*
, and Zhuāng Zhōu’s debates with Huì Shī
. Hán Fēi’s *Chǔ Shuō*
, comparing events and seeking symmetry
, is the origin of the *Liánzhū* (linked pearls) form
. Yet some believe it began with the likes of Fù Yì
; this is not the fundamental truth
. Mèngzǐ asked the King of Qí about his great desires
, enumerating soft warmth, rich flavors
, sounds, and varied colors
, which was the inspiration for the *Qīlín* (Seven Forests) style
; yet some believe it was created by Méi Chéng
, forgetting its ancestor
. Zōu Yáng defending himself against slander before the King of Liáng
, Jiāng Yān presenting his defense to Jiànpíng
, are all like Sū Qín defending himself after being wronged despite his loyalty and trustworthiness
. Discourses such as *Guò Qín*, *Wángmìng*, *Liùdài*, and *Biànwáng*
, rising and falling, moving back and forth
, embody the intent of the poets' critiques and admonitions
, the method Mèng [zǐ] and Xún [zǐ] used to praise their predecessors
, and warn the rulers of their time
. The retainers of Huáinán
, and the literati of Liáng Yuàn
, were grand gatherings like those of [Wèi] Yuán, [Zhào] Cháng, [Píng] Shēn, and [Yú] Líng
. Dōngfāng [Shuò] and Sīmǎ [Xiàngrú]
, served in attendance at the Western Capital
; Xú [Gān], Chén [Lín], Yīng [Yáng], and Liú [Zhèn]
, pursued literary careers at Yèxià
. This was the spectacular phenomenon of discussing Heaven and carving dragons
. Fortunes rise and fall
, and eras experience success and failure
. Extraordinary talents gathered in later ages
, and official profit gathered their natures and spirits
. Whether in court halls or mountain forests
, by rivers and lakes or before palace towers
, though separated by generations, they mutually responded
, not knowing whether their grief or joy originated
. The profound feelings of the literati in relation to the *Shī* (Odes) and the *Sāo* (Lament)
, have been the same throughout history
. By the Zhànguó period, the literary transformations were complete
, and by the Zhànguó period, the forms of later writing were fully established
. This statement is reliable and verifiable
. By the Zhànguó period, the task of formal composition (Zhùshù) became specialized
. What is meant by this? The answer is:
In ancient times, there was never a specific task of Zhùshù
. Officials and teachers guarded their statutes and documents
, and the historians recorded their duties
. The Way of writing
, was used by all officials to govern
, and by the myriad people to examine [matters]
, and its function was thereby already fulfilled
. Therefore, the sage kings standardized writing (shū tóng wén) to pacify All Under Heaven
. Writing was never used outside of government, education, and official statutes
, nor was writing considered the formal composition of a single individual
. When the Way ceased to be practiced, masters and literati established their teachings
, this is how our Master (Kǒngzǐ) achieved merit equal to Yáo and Shùn
. Yet, [Kǒngzǐ said], "I wish to speak no more"
, and "I transmit, but do not innovate"
. The Liù Yì (Six Arts/Classics) preserve the ancient statutes of Zhōu Gōng
, the Master never formally composed [a work of his own]
. The *Lúnyǔ* records the subtle words of the Master
, but Zēngzǐ and Zǐsī
, both had works of transmission and composition (Shùzuò) to hand down instruction
. It was only by the time of Mèngzǐ that their writings became broad and unrestrained
. This is clear proof that Zhùshù only began to specialize during the Zhànguó period
. During the Chūnqiū period
, Guǎnzǐ supposedly had a book
. The works *Yùzǐ* and *Yànzǐ*
, were attributed to them by later people
. However, since they record the statutes, governance, and teachings of a specific time
, they are analogous to Zhōu Gōng’s official ritual texts (*Guānlǐ*)
. Records of Guǎnzǐ’s words and actions
, were compiled by those who studied the methods of the Guǎn lineage
, and were not formally composed by Guǎn Zhòng himself
. The military strategists had the *Tàigōng Yīnfú*
, the medical practitioners had the *Huángdì Sùwèn*
, and the agriculturalists had the *Shénnóng* and *Yělǎo*
. Earlier scholars considered these to be forgeries composed by later people
, and attributed them falsely to the ancients
. Their reasoning seems correct
, but upon investigating the deeper meaning
, there is still something incomplete [in that view]
. Since these minor arts and lesser techniques
, all originated with the sages
, if there had been no transmission of subtle words and essential principles
, they could not have been useful for thousands of years
. During the flourishing eras of the Sāndài (Three Dynasties)
, each line (shì) guarded its own specific knowledge concerning people, offices, and objects
, and thus transmission was conducted orally
. Therefore, before Kǒngzǐ and Mèngzǐ
, their books were never seen
. By the Zhànguó period, the Way of official guarding and master-disciple transmission had been abandoned
. Those who mastered this learning
, recounted what they had heard in the past and committed it to bamboo and silk
. Though there may have been gains or losses in the process
, fundamentally, concerning their origins
, they cannot be quickly dismissed
. [The belief that] Zhànguó people
, composed the doctrines of Huáng [Dì] and Nóng [Shénnóng]
, led earlier scholars to critique their literary style
, and conclude that they were forgeries
. They failed to realize that in ancient times there was no Zhùshù
, and the Zhànguó period was the first to replace oral transmission with bamboo and silk
. They were genuinely not forgeries
. Therefore, the specialization of Zhùshù began in the Zhànguó period
, this must have been due to the necessity of the circumstances
. Zhùshù inevitably evolved into Cízhāng (belles-lettres)
, and Cízhāng inevitably produced a taste for stylistic preference
. Later people lacked the compulsion faced by their predecessors
, focusing only on stylistic preferences in Cízhāng
. Nevertheless, they still called their works Zhùshù
. Thus, while the Zhànguó period was the zenith of literary writing (Wénzhāng)
, the beginning of its decline was already apparent in the Zhànguó period
Someone asked:
Is it the case that after the *Sān Dài* (Three Dynasties),
among the *Liù Yì* (Six Arts), only the teaching of the *Shī* (Odes/Poetry) became extremely widespread?
I venture to ask, regarding the utility of literature,
is nothing grander than the *Shī*? I replied:
How can it be that this is true only after the *Sān Dài*?
Before the *Sān Dài*,
the teaching of the *Shī* was never not widespread.
The Master (*Fūzǐ*) said:
“If one does not study the *Shī*,
there is no means by which to speak.”
In antiquity, there were no writings by private schools,
yet there was never a lack of speech that conveyed sincere feelings.
It was merely entrusted to sound and rhythm,
and was not recorded in written characters.
Therefore, when the *Qín* people banned the *Shī* and the *Shū* (Documents),
the *Shū* suffered lacunae,
but the chapters of the *Shī* were not scattered and lost.
In later ages, the efficacy of bamboo slips and silk scrolls
surpasses oral tradition;
but in antiquity, the transmission through sound and rhythm
surpassed written characters;
thus, antiquity and the present differ in time,
and the underlying principles and conditions are also distinct.
From antiquity, the sage kings governed the world through ritual (*Lǐ*) and music (*Yuè*).
The literary grace and essential substance of the *Sān Dài*
originated from a single source.
When the age flourished,
the statutes and documents were preserved by official custodians—
this was the substance of *Lǐ*;
feelings and intent harmonized with rhythmic verses—
this was the literary grace of *Yuè*.
When the age declined,
statutes and documents were scattered,
and the various masters gained fame through specialized methods.
Thus, specialized administrative methods
were all variations of the *Guān Lǐ* (Official Rituals).
Feelings and intent became extravagant,
and reclusive scholars engaged in reckless debate,
thus the Hundred Schools (*Bǎijiā*) indulged in expansive theories,
which were all variations of the rhythmic *Shī*.
The literature of the *Zhàn Guó* (Warring States) period
was a variation of the *Lǐ Yuè* (Ritual and Music) of the former kings.
Yet, the reason we say specifically that the teaching of the *Shī* became widespread during the *Zhàn Guó* is that
specialized occupations were few,
but discourse based on sweeping, expansive theories was abundant.
In later ages, specialized works by the Masters disappeared, but literary anthologies flourished.
Although they differed in purity, quality, superiority, and inferiority,
their ultimate purpose was nothing more than expressing one’s own feelings and intent.
Therefore, I say:
The literary styles of later ages
were all fully present during the *Zhàn Guó* period,
and the teaching of the *Shī* can thus be considered to have reached its extreme breadth.
If scholars can truly read widely in the anthologies of later ages,
and imagine the beginning state of the *Lǐ Yuè* of the former kings,
they will perhaps have a stable foundation and be able to speak,
and thus participate in the instruction of studying the *Shī* and studying the *Lǐ*.
Scholars merely restrict the *Shī* to works that observe sound and rhyme,
but they do not realize that literature which expresses feelings and conveys intent,
which spreads forth admonishment and satire,
and which possesses cadence and lingering charm,
all originates from the teaching of the *Shī*.
This is why later literary collections are numerous,
but the confused literature that is inherited and used
mutually follows its form,
yet there is no way to know its overall essential principles.
As for literature based on sound and rhyme,
ancient people did not entirely equate it with the *Shī*,
and the types of poetry and *fù* (rhapsody) inherited and used by later ages
do not entirely derive from the teaching of the *Liù Yì*;
the reasons for this are also fully present in the *Zhàn Guó* period.
Therefore, by understanding the shifting forms and circumstances of the *Zhàn Guó* period,
afterward, the distinction between *Lǐ* and *Yuè* can become clear,
and the teachings of the *Liù Yì* can be differentiated;
the discourse of the *Qī Lüè* (Seven Summaries), the *Jiǔ Liú* (Nine Schools), and the *Zhūzǐ Bǎijiā* (Various Masters and Hundred Schools),
can have its sources traced and its streams dredged;
the literature of the *Liǎng Liú* (Two Dynasties), the *Liù Cháo* (Six Dynasties), the *Táng*, *Sòng*, *Yuán*, and *Míng* Dynasties,
can be divided into plots and distinguished by ridges;
official songs, specialized crafts,
rhythmic poetry, and prose theories,
and the transitions between oral tradition and written text (bamboo and silk),
can be settled while seated.
Calculating the Great Plan (*Hóng Jí*),
which is the rhyming portion of instructional pronouncements,
served to facilitate recitation,
so that intention was not forgotten.
The six images supporting the words,
which are the rhyming portions of the *Yáo* (Lines) and *Xì* (Appendices) [of the *Yì Jīng*],
served to facilitate divination,
and expound the mysterious and profound.
The *Liù Yì* cannot all be equated with the *Shī*,
yet rhymed language was not discarded.
Therefore, the harmony of sound and the accordance of rhythm
cannot be exclusively attributed to the teaching of the *Shī*.
Historical narratives like the *Zuǒ* (Commentary of Zuo) and *Guó* (Discourses of the States),
and descriptive theories like *Lǎo* (Laozi) and *Zhuāng* (Zhuangzi),
their composition often follows sounds and achieves harmony,
their phrases match rhythm and instantly accord.
How could they necessarily conform to the suggestive imagery (*Bǐ Xīng*) of the *Shī* teaching?
The *Yì Lín* (Forest of Changes) by *Jiāo Gòng*,
the *Jí Jiù* (Quick Success) by *Shǐ Yóu*,
are rhymed texts within the Classics section that do not involve the *Shī*.
The seven-character lines of the *Huáng Tíng Jīng* (Yellow Court Classic),
the broken phrases of the *Cān Tóng Qì* (Kinship of the Three),
are rhymed Masters' technical texts that do not involve the *Shī*.
In later ages, among the Hundred Schools of miscellaneous arts,
when reciting lists of names and numbers,
they generally used five-character and seven-character lines,
developing them into chants and mnemonic verses,
all intended for ease of memorization and recitation,
and none conform to the meaning of the poets.
However, when the literary intent resides in extended sighing/chanting,
and the adopted meaning is close to *Bǐ Xīng* (Analogy and Arousal),
whether extensive, flowing for ten thousand words,
or concise, being just a few phrases,
it does not necessarily harmonize rhyme and tone,
yet those who understand it elegantly appreciate it as a residual model of the *Fēng* (Airs) and *Sāo* (Lament).
Therefore, those skilled in discussing literature
value seeking the author's intent,
and must not be restricted by external form.
The Commentary states:
“That which is recited but not sung is called *fù* (rhapsody).”
Master *Bān* (*Bān Gù*) firmly stated:
“The *fù* belongs to the stream of ancient poetry.”
Master *Liú Xié* said:
“What was dependent on the *Liù Yì*
flourished and became a great state.”
This is generally a change in the form of extended speech and chanting,
and unrhymed literature that can be equated with poetry,
also became increasingly widespread because of this.
The twenty-five chapters by Master *Qū* (*Qū Yuán*),
recorded by *Liú* (Xiàng) and *Bān* (Gù),
were considered the *Qū Yuán Fù* (Rhapsodies of Qū Yuán).
The verses of the *Yú Fù* (Fisherman),
never rhymed in harmony,
yet entered the category of *fù*.
Therefore, the diverging streams of inherited literary forms
must be understood in their gradual development.
Literature that is elaborately presented and loftily expressed
are all transformed styles of the *fù*.
It is not only that the dependent state became a great nation,
but also like the descendants of *Chén Wán*
leaving the old capital of *Wǎn Qiū*,
and greatly expanding their territory on the shores of the Eastern Sea.
Later ages, among the Hundred Schools of miscellaneous arts,
also used the *fù* style for selection and recitation,
which generally sprang up outside the *Liù Yì*, alongside chants and mnemonic verses.
However, the schools of *fù* writers
still retained the lingering intent of the various Masters,
and boldly claimed their doctrines as the discourse of a school,
wherein each had its own central purpose.
This is quite different from the stream of poetry and *fù* in later ages,
which were constrained by form but lacked substance,
and whose divergent streams cannot be vaguely discerned.
This is why *Liú* (Xiàng) and *Bān* (Gù), in the *Shī Fù* section [of the bibliography],
divided them into five categories,
and designated *Qū Yuán*, *Lù Jiǎ*, and *Xún Qīng*
as establishing the doctrine of three schools.
The two historians, *Mǎ* (Qiān) and *Bān* (Gù),
regarding the *fù* written by masters like *Xiāng Rú* and *Yáng Xióng*,
all recorded them in detail in the Biographies,
and ever since *Liú Zhī Jǐ*,
those who have attacked, rejected, and ridiculed them
have been too numerous to count,
but essentially, none of them truly understand this discourse.
This marks the origin of the later Literary Garden (*Wén Yuàn*),
and the Literary Garden must lead to actual achievements in literary flourish.
Compared with the historical records starting from *Fàn Shǐ* (Fan Ye's History),
which designated a Literary Garden but only briefly recounted the deeds of literary figures,
this is far superior.
However, the *fù* of the *Hàn* court
were truly not casually composed.
Recording long pieces within the complete biographies
fully shows the author’s extreme dedication.
Their utility, perhaps, differed from the memorials of *Jiǎ* (Yí) and the policies of *Dǒng* (Zhòngshū),
but their purpose was the same:
they both aimed at transmitting the person through literature.
Thus, the stream of *fù* writers
represented a branch of sweeping, expansive discourse,
while also retaining the lingering influence of the various Masters.
This is why they differ from the literary scholars of later ages.
Therefore, when discussing literature from the *Zhàn Guó* period onward,
one must value seeking the author's intent,
and must not be restricted by external form.
reached its peak
in the literary anthologies of later generations.
This is probably due to the compilers being ignorant,
as well as being unaware of the ancient people's distinctions between genres,
and the authors' intentions,
thus they were forced to discuss writings by restricting them to outward form.

Although collecting writings began in the Jiàn'ān (建安) period when Wèi Wén (魏文) compiled the writings of Xú (徐), Chén (陳), Yīng (應), and Liú (劉) into one anthology (this was the beginning of the literary anthology, while Zhì Yú’s (摯虞) 《Liú Bié Jí (流別集)》 was even later),
it truly flourished during the period between Qí (齊) and Liáng (梁);
the impossibility of restoring ancient learning

was probably complete and utter only after the Qí and Liáng eras (Zhì Yú’s 《Liú Bié Jí》 was compiled by later people collecting the works of earlier people. Self-compiled anthologies began with the Qí dynasty’s 《Wáng Wénxiàn Jí (王文憲集)》, and Zhāo Míng’s (昭明) 《Wén Xuǎn (文選)》 marked the flourishing of general anthologies).
In the histories of Fàn (範), Chén (陳), Jìn (晉), and Sòng (宋)
, the biographies of literary figures,
when summarizing their compositions,
invariably state "such-and-such number of chapters of Shī (詩), Fù (賦), Bēi (碑), Zhēn (箴), Sòng (頌), and Lěi (誄)," but never say "such-and-such number of volumes of literary anthologies";
thus, it is known that the writings of the ancients
were scattered throughout various texts
and were not forcibly divided by category.
Sūn Wǔ’s (孫武) writings
originally comprised eighty-two chapters (The details are in the discussion of military writings in the Hàn Records section of the external chapter 《Jiào Chóu Lüè (校讎略)》),
but Hé Lǘ (闔閭) said, "Your thirteen chapters
I have already obtained and seen."
This is clear evidence that the thirteen chapters starting with 《Jì (計)》
were separately transmitted and circulated at that time,
and only later generations combined them.
Hán Fēi’s (韓非) writings
now preserve fifty-five chapters.
But the King of Qín (秦王), upon seeing his 《Wǔ Dù (五蠹)》 and 《Gū Fèn (孤憤)》,
regretted that he could not live at the same time as the author.
This is clear evidence that 《Wǔ Dù》 and 《Gū Fèn》
were separately transmitted and circulated at that time,
and only later generations combined them.
The preface to 《Lǚ Shì Chūn Qiū (呂氏春秋)》
states that noble men inquired about the Twelve Jì (紀),
meaning that the Bā Lǎn (八覽) and Liù Lùn (六論)
were never included in that sequence.
The chapters by Mr. Dǒng (董), 《Qīng Míng (清明)》, 《Yù Bēi (玉杯)》, and 《Zhú Lín (竹林)》,
Bān Gù (班固) recorded their titles alongside 《Fán Lù (繁露)》.
This shows that these chapters
were not included in the book 《Fán Lù》 at that time.
Now, the writings of the various Masters and specialists
had focused subjects without extraneous content,
yet their chapter sequencing could still not be forcibly aligned with category rules;
how much more so for the contents collected in literary anthologies,
where the structures are not uniform,
and the intentions differ widely
—if one does not deeply seek out the original intention,
how can one wish to restrict them rigidly by chapter title and external form!
The Fù (賦) precedes the Shī (詩),
and the Sāo (騷) is distinct from the Fù.
That the introductory dialogue structure of the Fù
was mistakenly categorized as Fù Xù (賦序, preface to the Fu)
—these are obvious points raised by earlier scholars when discussing the 《Wén Xuǎn (文選)》.
As for the 《Fēng Shàn (封禪)》, 《Měi Xīn (美新)》, and 《Diǎn Yǐn (典引)》,
they are all Sòng (頌, odes).
If writings that celebrate merit and virtue by citing auspicious signs
are separately categorized as Fú Mìng (符命, Auspicious Signs),
then Wáng Zǐyuān’s (王子淵) ode celebrating a harmonious gathering when a sage ruler acquired worthy ministers
should also be separately categorized as Zhǔ Chén (主臣, Ruler and Minister).
The rhymed verses of Bān Gù
constitute the self-preface of the 《Hàn Shū (漢書)》.
His statements, "Relating the First Chapter of the Annals of Emperor Gāo (Gāo Dì Jì, 高帝紀)"
and "Relating the First Biography of Chén Shèng and Xiàng Yǔ (Chén Xiàng Zhuàn, 陳項傳),"
were meant to preface his original intention for writing the book:
since Shǐ Qiān (史遷) had already composed earlier works
(the *Shǐ Jì*), Bān Gù deferred by merely 'relating' them.
If, now, outside of the category of historical discourses,
one creates a separate genre called Shǐ Shù Zàn (史述贊, Historical Narrative and Eulogy),
then the self-preface of Shǐ Qiān's book
where he stated "Composing the First Chapter of the Annals of the Five Emperors (Wǔ Dì Jì, 五帝紀)"
and "Composing the First Biography of Bó Yí (伯夷傳),"
should also be separately categorized as Shǐ Zuò Zàn (史作贊, Historical Composition and Eulogy).
Hàn Wǔ’s (漢武) imperial edict (zhào) concerning policy questions (cè) for the worthy and good (Zhào Cè Xián Liáng, 詔策賢良)
was essentially a policy question (cè wèn).
Now, because it originated from an imperial decree
, it is given a separate name, Zhào (詔), outside the Cè Wèn category
. If so, then the replies to those policy questions
should be separated from the general Cè (策) category and be newly named Biǎo (表, Memorial).
Jiǎ Yí’s (賈誼) 《Guò Qín (過秦)》

was probably a chapter title within the 《Jiǎ Zǐ (賈子)》 (The currently transmitted 《Jiǎ Shì Xīn Shū (賈氏新書)》 lists the two chapters of 《Guò Qín》 at the beginning; this later arrangement by subsequent compilers is not sufficient evidence. The 《Hàn Zhì (漢誌)》 lists fifty-eight chapters by Jiǎ Yí plus seven Fù, with no other categories mentioned, thus it is clear that 《Guò Qín》 was a chapter title within 《Jiǎ Zǐ》).
Because Lù Jī’s (陸機) discussion in 《Biàn Wáng (辨亡)》
modeled itself after 《Guò Qín》,
people subsequently cited Zuǒ Sī’s (左思) statement, "his composition of a discourse (Lùn) was based on 《Guò Qín》"
and thus labeled its genre as Lùn (論, Discourse) (The statement about Zuǒ Sī writing a Lùn must be interpreted flexibly, not rigidly).
Wèi Wén’s 《Diǎn Lùn (典論)》
was probably like Huán Zǐ’s (桓子) 《Xīn Lùn (新論)》 and Wáng Chōng’s (王充) 《Lùn Héng (論衡)》, which used Lùn to name the entire book.
《Lùn Wén (論文)》
was merely a chapter title within it.
Now, 《Lùn Wén》 is categorized together with chapters like 《Liù Dài (六代)》 and 《Biàn Wáng》
, under Lùn.
If that is the case, Zhāo Míng’s preface
stated that works like those of Lǎo (老) and Zhuāng (莊)
and the schools of Guǎn (管) and Mèng (孟)
prioritize the establishment of ideas
and are not fundamentally based on fine writing,
and therefore his selection criteria excluded works by the various Masters (Zǐ);
can it be that just because a piece of writing (Wén) is borrowed,
its chapter title can be forced into the Lùn category,
thereby changing the Zǐ works into Jí (集, Anthology) works?
The writings in the 《Qī Lín (七林)》
all consist of posed questions.
Now, because Méi Shēng (枚生) posed seven questions
, the work is titled Qī (Seven).
If so, should 《Jiǔ Gē (九歌)》, 《Jiǔ Zhāng (九章)》, and 《Jiǔ Biàn (九辨)》
also be labeled Jiǔ (Nine)?
《Nàn Shǔ Fù Lǎo (難蜀父老)》
is also a sequence of posed questions.
Now, because the chapter title uses Nàn (難, challenge/difficulty)
, a separate Nàn Tǐ (難體, Challenge genre) is created.
If so, then 《Kè Nàn (客難)》 should be compiled with it,
and 《Jiě Cháo (解嘲)》 should be separately classified as the Cháo Tǐ (嘲體, Mockery genre),
and 《Bīn Xì (賓戲)》 should be separately classified as the Xì Tǐ (戲體, Scoffing genre).
The 《Wén Xuǎn》
is the standard of literary writing
and the model for anthologies,
yet its disorder and confusion
cannot be fully enumerated.
If this is the case, then among those who browse through these anthologies
and the intentions of the authors?
, who has truly deeply investigated and grasped
If those compiling the writings of others
still fail to grasp their intent,
why are there so many people
who hastily collect their own writings and title them literary anthologies?
As for the principles governing general anthologies (Zǒng Jí) and individual anthologies (Bié Jí),
the merits and drawbacks of editing and compiling sequences,
the appropriate balance between detail and brevity, ancient and modern,
and the suitability of recording, selecting, critiquing, and copying,
there are separate dedicated chapters to discuss these points
, and they will not be fully described here.
The Six Jīng (經, Classics) do not speak of Jīng,
and the Three Zhuàn (傳, Commentaries) do not speak of Zhuàn;
this is like a person each having a self (wǒ) but not allowing that self to be 'I-ed.'
Only when relying on the Jīng are there Zhuàn,
and only in contrast to others is there a self (wǒ).
Thus, the names Jīng, Zhuàn, person, and self
arose out of necessity imposed by circumstance,
and were not their original essential nature.
The 《Yì (易)》 (Book of Changes) says:
"In high antiquity, they governed by tying knots;
later generations of sages replaced this with written contracts,
by which the hundred officials were governed
and the myriad people were examined."
Now, governing and examining
served to reveal the hidden and communicate titles and forms,
and to disseminate policies and teachings and standardize laws and measures,
and there were never writings that were treated as the private discourse of a single school.
The 《Yì》 says:
"Clouds and thunder assemble (Tún, 屯).
The noble person uses this to structure and regulate (jīng lún)."
The phrase Jīng Lún
means to structure and regulate the cosmos.
Zhèng Shì’s (鄭氏) (Zhèng Xuán) commentary
states that it means "discussing and composing the rites and music for writing
, and implementing political affairs."
Is this where the name Jīng (Classic) originated!
However, it merely refers to warp and woof, or administration (jīng jì),
and never clearly designated the Six Arts, such as the 《Shī (詩)》 and 《Shū (書)》, as Jīng.
When the Three Dynasties (Sān Dài) declined
and governance and teaching were separated,
the Master (Fū Zǐ) was born in the Eastern Zhōu (Dōng Zhōu).
Possessing virtue but lacking official position,
he feared that the methods established and the Way perfected by the former sage kings
, which culminated in the flourishing of Zhōu (Chéng Zhōu),
might be lost because there was no one to continue and succeed them.
Therefore, he took the statutes of Zhōu Gōng (周公)
, which embodied the compositions concerning Heaven and Humanity and preserved the records of governance and transformation,
and solely, with his disciples,
elaborated and clarified them.
This is why the Six Arts, though losing their official custodianship,
still relied on transmission by teachers.
However, in the Master’s time,
they were still not called Jīng.
When the Master had died,
the subtle words were cut off and the profound meanings were about to be lost.
Consequently, his disciples and followers,
each according to what they had seen, heard, or heard reported,
sometimes finalized written records,
or sometimes conveyed knowledge orally,
recording the texts and raising interpretations.
《Zuǒ Shì Chūn Qiū (左氏春秋)》
and the chapters like Zǐ Xià’s (子夏) 《Sāng Fú (喪服)》
were all named Zhuàn (Commentary/Tradition).
Furthermore, lost texts from previous generations
that were not part of the Six Arts
were all referred to as Zhuàn when cited or narrated,
such as the reply Mèng Zǐ (孟子) gave regarding Tāng (湯), Wǔ (武), and King Wén’s (Wén Wáng) parks
Therefore, the name Jīng arose because of the Zhuàn,
just as the title Fù (Father) is established because of the Zǐ (Son).
When the offices of the officials and the teachers were already separated,
unemployed scholars debated widely,
the various Masters (Zhūzǐ) arose in great numbers,
writing books and establishing doctrines.
Consequently, texts began to contain private theories,
not entirely derived from canonical regulations or governmental teachings.
The school of Rújiā (Confucianism),
then honored the Six Arts (Liù Yì) and revered them as Classics (Jīng).
This naming, therefore, was not solely used in contrast to Commentaries (Zhuàn).
Xúnzǐ said:
“Study begins with reciting the Jīng,
and concludes with practicing the Rites (Lǐ).”
Zhuāngzǐ said:
“Kǒngzǐ spoke of governing through the six Classics: the *Shī* (Poetry), *Shū* (Documents), *Lǐ* (Rites), *Yuè* (Music), *Yì* (Changes), and *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals).”
He also said:
“By turning over the twelve Jīng,
one may perceive Lǎozǐ.”
Since both Xúnzǐ and Zhuāngzǐ were students of Zǐxià's followers,
and what they said was as such,
it is clear that the name Six Classics (Liù Jīng)
originated with Kǒngzǐ's disciples.
However, the specific reference to the Six Classics
was based on the governmental teachings and canonical regulations of the former kings,
which served as the guiding principles for the world.
Therefore, the *Jīng Jiě* (Exposition of the Classics) distinguishes the Six Classics,
holding that upon entering a state, one could know its teachings through them.
The *Lúnyǔ* (Analects) narrates the words and actions of the Master (Fūzǐ).
The *Ěryǎ* serves as the glossary and exegetical commentary for the collective Classics.
The *Xiàojīng* (Classic of Filial Piety), furthermore, was narrated by the second generation of disciples,
and is intermingled with the various records like the *Zī Yī*, *Fāng*, and *Biǎo*.
Followers of Liú Xiàng and Bān Gù,
ordered the categories into nine,
but named the Arts (Yì) as six.
They firmly considered these three to be Zhuàn (Commentaries/Appendices),
and appended them to the Classics (Jīng).
These were known as Zhuàn separate from the Jīng,
and were not grouped alongside the Zhuàn appended directly to the Classics.
At that time, when the various Masters wrote books,
they often categorized their own texts into Jīng and Zhuàn,
such as those who compiled the *Guǎnzǐ*, distinguishing the Jīng statements.
The *Mòzǐ* also contains 'Jīng' chapters.
The *Hánfēi* contains the 'Jīng' and 'Zhuàn' of the *Chǔ Shuō*.
This was presumably establishing definitions according to the times,
using their own theories to mutually interweave (as warp and weft).
They were not imitating others and usurping the name.
Jīng was a shared honorific title;
its meaning was simply taken to mean comprehensive essentials,
not having the strictness it held in later generations.
Even a sage like the Master
did not necessarily write a Jīng himself.
The various Masters had Jīng
to structure their Zhuàn (Commentaries).
The meaning of the term was appropriate in each context.
Later catalogers,
due to the great proliferation of texts,
which did not all pertain to the essential principles,
therefore took the subtle words of the former sages,
and the supporting wings of the collective Classics,
and designated all of them as Jīng.
Such as the *Lúnyǔ*, *Mèngzǐ*, and *Xiàojīng*,
and the Elder and Younger *Dài Jì* (Records of Dài) separated from the *Lǐ* (Rites),
and the *Zuǒ Shì*, *Gōng* (Gōngyáng), and *Gǔ* (Gǔliáng) separated from the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals),
were all titled Jīng.
Thus there came to be the Nine Classics, the Ten Classics, and the Thirteen or Fourteen Classics,
forming a dedicated section.
This was presumably to honor the Classics while simultaneously including their branches and descendants.
However, when Rú scholars wrote books,
they began to strictly regulate the name Jīng,
daring not to violate it.
This was honoring the teachings of the sages and carefully avoiding a name that might seem presumptuous,
similar, perhaps, to how after the Three Dynasties (Sān Dài),
only the sovereign was allowed to refer to himself as *zhèn*.
Therefore, what is now called Jīng (Classic),
is largely what the ancients called Zhuàn (Commentary).
What the ancients called Jīng
were the canonical regulations and statutes
during the flourishing periods of the Three Dynasties,
made manifest in the reality of governmental teachings and actions,
and were not intentionally composed as texts by the sages to be transmitted to later generations.
Events have actual basis,
but principles have no fixed form.
Therefore, when the Master (Fūzǐ) transmitted the Six Classics,
he drew entirely upon the canonical regulations of the former kings,
never setting aside events in order to establish principles.
Later Rú scholars regarded the words and deeds of the sage teachers as models for the world.
Thus, they also named their books Jīng.
This is simply the natural course of affairs and principles.
However, if one honors it by intention,
then one can also usurp it by intention.
Since the separation of officials and teachers,
officials possessed administration;
the humble masses certainly dared not forcefully interfere with it,
because it had basis (in law/authority).
Teachers possessed instruction;
the unworthy readily dared to set themselves up as authorities in great numbers,
because it lacked basis (in law/authority).
In Mèngzǐ's time,
Yáng (Yáng Zhū) and Mò (Mòzǐ) were already considered heterodox teachings.
The Yáng school had no books.
Mò Dí's book (the *Mòzǐ*),
was originally not titled Jīng. (Though there are 'Jīng' chapters and 'Jīng Shuō,' the whole book was not named Jīng.)
Yet Zhuāngzǐ said:
“People like Huò and Dèng Líng
all recited the *Mò Jīng* (Mohist Classic).”
Thus, his followers mutually revered it and titled it Jīng.
When Qín Jǐng of the Eastern Hàn was sent on a mission to Tiānzhú (India),
the *Sìshí'èr Zhāng* (Forty-Two Sections),
was not named Jīng.
All Buddhist Classics were translated in China; Indian books did not use the word *jīng*. Afterwards, when receiving translations into Chinese,
the term Jīng was conveniently attached,
which was also merely an embellishment of language.
The two chapters of the *Lǎozǐ*,
when cataloged by Liú (Xiàng) and Bān (Gù),
were initially not called Jīng.
The *Suí Zhì* (Treatise on Literature in the History of Suí) followed Ruǎn’s *Lù* (Catalogue),
calling it the *Lǎozǐ Jīng*.
The reason is likely that Ruǎn’s *Lù* originated during the Liáng dynasty,
when Emperor Wǔ of Liáng revered foreign doctrines,
so Buddhism and Daoism (Lǎo) were both categorized under Jīng.
This was what was imitated.
And the additions like *Dàodé Zhēnjīng* (True Classic of the Way and Virtue),
and the *Zhuāngzǐ* being called the *Nánhuá Zhēnjīng* (True Classic of Nánhuá),
and the *Lièzǐ* being called the *Chōngxū Zhēnjīng* (True Classic of Vacuity),
occurred when the Daoist doctrine established formal curricula during the Kāiyuán era.
This was further ornamentation and elaboration,
becoming even more excessive later.
Hán Tuìzhī said:
“The Way they profess as the Way
is not what I call the Way.”
If the doctrines and teachings are different,
why prevent them from designating their own Jīng,
even if it is not what we call Jīng?
As for state institutions and regulations,
they inherently constitute the Jīng system.
Lǐ Kuī's *Fǎ Jīng* (Classic of Law)
was the origin of later statutes and ordinances.
The Táng people established legal studies as a curriculum.
The founding emperor of the Míng (Míng Zǔ) promulgated the *Dà Gào* (Great Edict).
Masters and scholars lectured on and studied it,
treating it as a required statute.
This captures the meaning of *jīng lún* (governance/ordering) taken from the *Yì* (Classic of Changes).
State educational canons,
revered as Jīng by officials and commoners,
are meanings not contrary to antiquity.
Mèngzǐ said:
“Implementing humane governance
must begin with rectifying the field boundaries (jīngjiè).”
When speaking of land boundaries as Jīng,
the meaning of management and arrangement (jīng jì) is taken.
Therefore, books on geography
are often named Jīng.
The *Hàn Zhì* (Treatise on Literature in the History of Hàn) lists the *Shānhǎi Jīng* (Classic of Mountains and Seas).
The *Suí Zhì* lists the *Shuǐ Jīng* (Classic of Waterways).
Later geographies of prefectures and commanderies
were often called *tú jīng* (Illustrated Classics).
The meaning is all rooted in land surveying (jīngjiè).
These books also preserved factual information themselves,
not falling into the same category as doctrinal writings.
Therefore, regarding the texts of the Six Arts (Liù Yì),
there was naturally no conflict of terminology.
Regarding the various schools of techniques and calculations (shù shù),
they all originated from the creations within the school of the Sages.
Zhōu Gōng (Duke of Zhōu) managed and established regulations,
which were all maintained by officials regarding personnel, governance, and detailed matters,
and their transmission was not lost.
When these offices lost their duties,
the Way scattered and the categories perished.
Thus, those who practiced these doctrines
studied and transmitted them among themselves,
which was just like the necessary transmission and practice within the Kǒng school.
However, learning transmitted orally
cannot last long without error.
Therefore, recording it on bamboo and silk,
to hand down to people (details explained in the chapter 'On Poetry Teaching, Part I'),
was also a natural necessity.
Thus, when it came to the Warring States (Zhànguó) period, books attributed to Xī (Fúxī), Nóng (Shénnóng), and Huángdì (Yellow Emperor)
appeared mixed together simultaneously.
These books all claimed ancient sages as authors.
For example, the astronomical *Xīng Jīng* (Classic of Stars) by Gān (Dé) and Shí (Shēn).
And the technical medical texts like the *Líng* (Shū), *Sù* (Wèn), and *Nán Jīng* (Classic of Difficulties).
Their categories were truly numerous.
This is comparable to craftsmen making offerings to Lǔ Bān,
or soldiers making offerings to Chī Yóu.
It is not necessary that the writers of these books were truly sages,
but those who practice these techniques
revere them as guiding principles.
Therefore, they must also respectfully regard them as Jīng statements.
Furthermore, concerning texts after the *Hàn Zhì*,
a mixture of books from the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods appeared,
such as Shī Kuàng’s *Qín Jīng*,
Bó Lè’s classic on *Xiàng Mǎ* (Horse Physiognomy),
and their categories are also numerous.
They are merely the works of enthusiasts,
who attached them to those historical figures,
or by those who generally understood the methods,
and claimed ancient authorship to elevate their status.
This is just like the Ru scholars transmitting Měi Shì’s *Shàng Shū*,
and Zǐ Xià’s *Shī Dà Xù*.
Others include Lù Shì’s *Chá Jīng*,
Zhāng Shì’s *Qí Jīng*,
for wine there is the *Gān Lù Jīng*,
and for goods there is the *Xiàng Bèi Jīng*.
These are merely literary pleasantries,
fundamentally irrelevant to the purpose of formal record-keeping.
For example, Máo Yǐng (the brush) can have a biography,
the crab can have a record,
the qín (lute) can have a history,
and the lychee and the peony can have a genealogy.
All these are half-real, half-unreal,
and not worth discussing.
Now, let us discuss these various types.
The classics (*jīng*) of heterodox teachings,
are like the Six States, each ruling its own kingdom,
ignoring the Son of Heaven of Zhōu.
However, the proper names and status established in the *Chūn Qiū*,
are known to everyone,
and they cannot usurp or claim them.
The classics of institutions and regulations,
are the laws of the reigning sovereign.
Unifying paths and aligning customs,
they do not necessarily all carry the name *Jīng*,
but observing ritual and time is paramount.
Since one is a subject of the current generation,
one must follow and not transgress them;
even adhering wholeheartedly to the Six Arts,
is merely one aspect of complying with the sovereign's system.
For the classics of specialized skills and arts,
each has its own followers,
who mutually uphold them,
so there is naturally no fear of them straying beyond their boundaries.
As for mere pleasantries also being titled *Jīng*,
this is what Zhào Tuó meant by falsely usurping the title of Emperor,
just for self-amusement.
It is harmless to treat them as jokes,
the Way of the Six Classics,
is like the sun at noon,
how could this be a defect?
Heterodox schools calling their works *Jīng* to compete against the Six Arts,
is foolish.
Ru scholars presumptuously calling their works *Jīng* to imitate the Six Arts,
is baseless.
The term Six Classics was not originally an honorific title;
the meaning comes from the notion of organizing and weaving to establish laws for the world.
The Six Arts were all government statutes established by Zhōu Gōng,
hence they were designated *Jīng*.
The sagehood of the Master (Kǒngzǐ),
was not inferior to Zhōu Gōng,
yet the chapters of the *Lún Yǔ* are not called *Jīng*,
because they are not government statutes.
Later Ru scholars honored them because they were venerable,
classified them under the classics,
believing that the commentaries surely assisted the classics.
The books of Buddhism (Fó) and Daoism (Lǎo),
are fundamentally doctrines of a single school;
they do not contain principles for governing affairs.
If their followers wish to honor their teachings,
and using the doctrine of their own school,
honor them more highly than the Six Classics,
there is no fault in that.
But forcefully imposing the name *Jīng* to imitate them,
how is that different from an actor imitating the Chancellor of Chǔ?
It is also foolish.
Yáng Xióng and Liú Xīn,
were Ru scholars who mastered the classics.
Yáng Xióng’s *Fǎ Yán*,
is said to consist of people of the time asking questions,
and he answered them using the principles.
This, too, may be acceptable.
But to say that it imitated the *Lún Yǔ*,
how ridiculous is that?
Nevertheless,
this is still the doctrine of one school,
and its fault is minor.
What is greatly strange,
is that he composed the *Tài Xuán* to emulate the *Yì* (Classic of Changes).
People only know to criticize him for presuming to write a classic,
but they do not know that the *Yì* is a government statute of the former kings, not mere empty words.
Yáng Xióng essentially committed the crime of presumptuously stealing royal ordinances,
he did not reflect deeply enough (detailed in the chapter *Yì Jiào*).
Wèi Shì’s *Yuán Bāo*,
and Sīmǎ’s *Qián Xū*,
were also composed in imitation of the *Xuán*,
not realizing that the *Xuán*’s imitation of the *Yì* was already wrong.
Liú Xīn wrote the *Dà Gào* for Wáng Mǎng.
The deeds by which he offended the moral codes,
are certainly indefensible.
But to imitate the *Shàng Shū*,
why stoop so low?
The six treatises of Héfén,
some say, were elaborations by enthusiasts;
Wáng Tōng may not have been so immediately baseless.
But if such an event truly occurred,
then the criticism that the Six Classics were his slaves,
still does not capture the reality of the situation.
A slave has never failed to serve his master.
Where does Wáng Shì’s Six Classics,
show service to Kǒng Shì?
Where is it?
Shù Xī’s *Bǔ Shēng Shī* (Supplement to the Shēng Odes),
Pí Rìxiū’s *Bǔ Jiǔ Xià* (Supplement to the Nine Xias),
Bái Jūyì’s *Bǔ Tāng Zhēng* (Supplement to Tāng's Campaign)—
if treated as playful jokes by literary figures and not malicious,
and designated as imitative works,
that would perhaps be acceptable.
But when titled "Supplement,"
why bother with the words of mere literary stylists,
to mend the deficiencies of the *Shī* and the *Shū*?
As for the *Xiào Jīng*,
although titled *Jīng*,
it is actually a commentary (*zhuàn*).
Ru scholars valued the surviving words of the Master,
so they appended it to the classics section.
Mǎ Róng sincerely had the ambition to promote loyalty.
If he used Mǎ Shì’s own doctrines,
citing the classics and referencing the commentaries,
analyzing back and forth at length,
pushing his ideas to their limit, that would be acceptable.
But to insist on titling it the *Zhōng Jīng* (Classic of Loyalty),
is already strange.
Furthermore, to divide it into eighteen chapters,
citing the *Fēng* and appending the *Yǎ*,
imitating the model precisely,
how is this different from Zhāng Zài’s *Nǐ Sì Chóu* (Imitation of Four Sorrows),
or the *Qī Lín* imitating the *Qī Fā*?
Truly, this is not Mǎ Shì’s book,
but rather a fabrication by common Ru scholars.
Sòng Shì’s *Nǚ Xiào Jīng* (Classic of Filial Piety for Women),
and Zhèng Shì’s *Nǚ Lún Yǔ* (Analects for Women)—
if they are meant to praise the ambitions of women of talent,
that is acceptable.
But if they wished to clarify women’s teachings,
they should simply establish their arguments based on their own ideas.
To invent a dialogue between Bān Shì and Huì Jī,
in which they ask and answer questions with various women,
is to treat the book as a canonical instruction,
while first fabricating its authorship among the likes of Zǐ Xū and Wáng Shì.
How is one supposed to follow it?
Their intent was merely to make it resemble a classic or a commentary,
but how can a classic be merely similar?
If a classic merely seeks resemblance,
then fraudulent divination has its hexagrams (as seen in *Chuò Gēng Lù*),
and when boots start making noise,
there will be a *Yuè Lìng* (Almanac) (These are all jests).
Now, as for Qū Yuán expressing his indignation,
there were twenty-five chapters of lyrics.
When Liú Xiàng and Bān Gù cataloged them,
they generally titled the collection *Qū Yuán Fù*.
However, when Wáng Yì created his commentary,
the chapter *Lí Sāo*,
already had the name *Jīng*.
Wáng Shì interpreted *Jīng* as *jìng* (path/way),
but he did not explain who first titled it *Jīng*.
Who was the originator?
When the Sòng dynasty scholars annotated Qū Yuán,
they said, "One version has the character *zhuàn* (commentary) after *Jiǔ Gē*."
Although we do not know when this naming began,
it is essential that the name *zhuàn* was established based on the pre-existence of a *jīng*,
and should not have started in the Sòng period.
The rhapsodies of Master Qū,
were certainly centered on the *Lí Sāo*.
From Sǐ Qiān onward,
people even took *Sāo* to name the entire collection,
and this is still the case today.
However, the essence of the various chapters,
was fundamentally without distinction.
Only because the first chapter was held in high regard,
did people forcibly divide them into *Jīng* and *Zhuàn*,
wishing to imitate the precedent of classifying the Orthodox *Yǎ* as *Jīng*,
and the Variant *Yǎ* as *Zhuàn*.
By this reasoning, the seven chapters of *Mèngzǐ*,
ought to be divided into the *Liáng Huì Wáng* Classic,
and the various commentaries like *Gōng Sūn* and *Téng Wén*.
. Zhuāngshēng
considered it discussion without judgment.
This is because its meaning is contained within its events and its text
, and it does not explicitly assign rewards and punishments.
From the Hàn and Wèi Dynasties onwards
, those who imitated the *Chūnqiū*
were indeed numerous.
Among these, some succeeded and some failed
, and a relay of servants could not count them all.
Later commentators
went so far as to compare the works of Qiān and Gù (Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù) and their successors
to the *Shàngshū*;
and the chronological histories (biānnián) of various schools
they compared to the *Chūnqiū*.
They do not realize that the basic annals (běnjì) of Qiān and Gù
were originally scholarship rooted in the *Chūnqiū* school;
the treatises (shū), monographs (zhì), tables (biǎo), and biographies (zhuàn)
are perhaps merely the means by which the inner and outer teachings of the *Zuǒzhuàn* and *Guóyǔ* were fully revealed, providing the beginning and the end.
The *Yángqiū* of various schools
appeared mixed together, one after the other.
Some used the name but changed the form (such as the *Shíliù Guó Chūnqiū*)
. Others avoided the name but emulated the substance (such as the *Tōngjiàn Gāngmù*)
. Essentially, they all fail to understand that the writings of Qiān and Gù
originally carried on the scholarship of the *Chūnqiū*
, and were absolutely not modeled after the *Shàngshū*.
Therefore, those who understand the principles of the *Chūnqiū*
should only compare and correct the meanings embedded within the texts and events
of Qiān and Gù and their successors.
If one wishes to gather the events
and compile them chronologically by year
, then the examples of Xún Yuè and Yuán Hóng are fully extant
, and there is no reason why they cannot be imitated.
But if one insists on creating a separate *Chūnqiū*
outside of the annal-biography and chronological forms
, then this would merely be a continuation of the Wáng family's *Yuánjīng*.
As for heretical doctrines that resist the Classics
, they are unworthy of discussion.
If a scholar (rúzhě) studies and practices the Six Classics
yet does not know that the Classics cannot be imitated
, then he is but a shallow scholar!

The great origin of the Dào comes from Heaven (Tiān)
. Does Heaven therefore instruct it painstakingly? I reply:
Before Heaven and Earth existed
, I cannot know.
When Heaven and Earth gave birth to humanity
, there was the Dào
, but it was not yet manifest.
When three people dwell in a room
, the Dào becomes manifest
, yet it is not yet clearly displayed.
When people increase from groups of five or ten to hundreds and thousands
, whom a single room cannot hold
, and they are separated into divisions and sections
, then the Dào becomes clearly displayed.
The names of benevolence (rén), righteousness (yì), loyalty (zhōng), and filiality (xiào)
, and the systems of punishment (xíng), governance (zhèng), ritual (lǐ), and music (yuè)
, all arose only out of necessity.
When a person is born, the Dào is present
, but the person does not realize it.
When three people dwell in a room
, they must open and close their doors morning and evening,
and their food and drink must be supplied by gathering firewood and drawing water.
Since they are not one person
, there must be those who divide the responsibilities.
Some individually manage their affairs
, or they rotate their shifts
. This is what is meant by the necessity of circumstance,
and thus the principles of fairness, equality, and order emerge.
Furthermore, fearing mutual neglect and conflict
, they must choose the eldest person to maintain fairness.
This, too, is the necessity of circumstance,
and thus the distinction between elder and younger, and the honoring of the venerable, becomes manifest.
When it comes to groups of five or ten, or hundreds and thousands
, separated into divisions and sections
, there must also be leaders for each group of five or ten.
When they accumulate into thousands and hundreds
, the population is large and relies on competence and management,
so they must choose the most outstanding talents to handle the complexities.
Since the circumstances are intricate and require leadership and guidance,
they must choose the person whose virtue is greatest to oversee the transformation.
This, too, is the necessity of circumstance;
and thus the concept of establishing rulers (jūn) and teachers (shī)
, marking out lands and dividing provinces (zhōu)
, and the ideas of the well-field system (jǐngtián), enfeoffment (fēngjiàn), and schools (xuéxiào) become clearly displayed.
Therefore, the Dào
is not something that the wisdom and strength of the Sages (Shèngrén) could create.
It is entirely a natural outcome of circumstance
, gradually becoming manifest and clearly displayed,
emerging only out of necessity
. Hence, we call it Heaven.
The *Yì* (Classic of Changes) states
: "One Yīn and one Yáng—that is the Dào."
This means that before humanity existed, the Dào was already complete.
That which follows it is goodness (shàn)
; that which completes it is nature (xìng).
This is Heaven manifesting in humanity
, and principle (lǐ) adhering to vital energy (qì).
Therefore, that which can be given form and named
is all the effect of the Dào
, but it is not the Dào itself.
The Dào
is the reason why all ten thousand affairs and ten thousand things are so
, but it is not what all ten thousand affairs and ten thousand things ought to be.
What people can perceive
is merely what ought to be.
From the beginning of human life
, up to groups of five, ten, hundreds, and thousands
, and extending to the establishment of rulers and teachers
, and the division of provinces and marking of lands
: it must be that something was needed, and then it was supplied;
something was repressed, and then it was released;
something was deficient, and then it was rectified.
The creations and institutions of Xī, Nóng, Xuān, and Zhuān
were initially nothing more than this.
The systems accumulated and became beautiful and complete
, reaching absolute perfection during the time of Táng (Yáo) and Yú (Shùn).
The Yīn followed the lessons of the Xià
, and reached an unblemished state during the time of Chéng Zhōu.
It is analogous to a mere wine-cup flowing (lànschāng) accumulating and gradually becoming rivers
, or small mounds accumulating and reaching the scale of mountains.
This, too, is the natural course of principle and circumstance,
and it is not that the sageliness of Yáo and Shùn
surpassed Xī and Xuān,
or that the divinity of Wén and Wǔ
triumphed over Yǔ and Tāng.
Later Sages imitate earlier Sages
. They do not imitate the earlier Sages themselves
, but they imitate the Dào as it gradually became manifest and clearly displayed.
The Three Sovereigns (Sānhuáng) achieved transformation through non-action (wúwéi)
; the Five Emperors (Wǔdì) initiated things and completed affairs;
the Three Kings (Sānwáng) established systems and handed down laws.
Later generations, seeing the governance and transformation, distinguish them in this way.
When the Sages created systems in those days
, it was just like the necessity of making light robes (gě) in summer
and warm furs (qiú) in winter,
and there was no conscious intention
to say, "I must act like this so that I can differ from the Sages,"
or "I must act like this so that I can stand equally with the former Sages."
These occurrences are all inevitable results of the reciprocating cycle of One Yīn and One Yáng
, but they cannot immediately be taken as the Dào of One Yīn and One Yáng.
The reciprocating cycle of One Yīn and One Yáng
is like a carriage wheel.
The systems created by the Sages
, which resemble light robes for summer and furs for winter
, are like the tracks and ruts left by the wheel.
The Dào possesses spontaneity (zìrán);
the Sage (Shèngrén) possesses necessity (bùdé bù rán).
Are their affairs the same? The answer is:
They are not the same.
The Dào does nothing and yet is spontaneous;
the Sage acts based on what he perceives, and thus possesses necessity.
The Sage perceives something,
hence he possesses necessity;
the common person perceives nothing,
and thus acts spontaneously without knowing why he acts so.
Which is closer to the Dào? The answer is:
Acting spontaneously without knowing why one acts so
is the Dào itself.
It is not that there is nothing perceived,
but that it is imperceptible.
The necessity (bùdé bù rán)
is the means by which the Sage accords with the Dào,
it cannot simply be taken as the Dào.
When the Sage seeks the Dào,
and the Dào is imperceptible,
it is precisely the spontaneity of the common person (zhòngrén) who “acts without knowing why he acts so”
that the Sage uses as a foundation to perceive the Dào.
Therefore, acting spontaneously without knowing why one acts so
is the manifestation (jī) of Yīnyáng.
Learning from the Sage
makes one a worthy person (Xiánrén).
Learning from the worthy person
makes one a noble person (Jūnzǐ).
Learning from the common person
makes one a Sage.
It is not that the crowd (zhòng) itself is something to be learned from,
but seeking the Dào must be done through the manifestations of Yīnyáng.
From the beginning of Heaven and Earth
up to the eras of Táng, Yú, Xià, and Shāng,
the manifestations were many, and the principles of comprehensive change and perpetual continuity (Qióng Biàn Tōng Jiǔ) were fully established.
Zhōugōng, with his heaven-bestowed innate wisdom,
happened to live at a time when accumulated antiquity was passed down
and the methods of the Dào (dàofǎ) were fully perfected.
Therefore, his organizational endeavors and creations
represented the great compilation (dàchéng) of a thousand ages.
This, too, was due to the opportune time and circumstances (shíhuì),
it was not the Sagely intelligence of Zhōugōng that necessarily made it so.
Indeed, the Sages of ancient times
all learned from the spontaneity of the common people;
but Zhōugōng, moreover, reviewed thoroughly the necessities of all Sages throughout antiquity,
and thus understood the underlying principle (qí rán).
Zhōugōng was indeed a Sage with heaven-bestowed innate knowledge,
but this was not within the capacity of Zhōugōng’s wisdom and strength;
the opportune time and circumstances made it so.
Consider the analogy of Spring, Summer, Autumn, and Winter:
each governs one season,
but the winter culmination signifies the completion of the year.
This is also due to the opportune time and circumstances,
and not because the winter culmination surpasses the other three seasons.
Therefore, the Sage who institutes ordinances and demonstrates achievements
is the same throughout the ages.
The one who compiled the great completion
was uniquely Zhōugōng.
The opportune time and circumstances made it happen when the time was right,
and Zhōugōng himself did not necessarily know why it happened.
Mèngzǐ said:
“Kǒngzǐ is what is meant by the great compilation.”
If we now say that the one who accomplished the great compilation was Zhōugōng,
is this not perhaps contradictory to Mèngzǐ’s intent? The answer is:
The meaning of the word ‘compilation’ (jí)
is to gather everything that the multitude possesses and unify it.
From the beginning of Heaven and Earth
up to Táng, Yú, Xià, and Shāng,
all Sages attained the position of the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ).
Their organizational governance and transformation
all derived from the inherent spontaneity of the Dào's substance (Dàotǐ).
Zhōugōng completed the virtue of Wénwáng and Wǔwáng.
He happened to be in an era where the Imperial systems were complete and the Royal systems were perfected,
following the models of Yīn and Xià,
reaching a point where nothing further could be added.
Thus, he was able to rely on this foundation to create institutions and regulations,
and thereby, using the ways of Zhōu (Zhōudào), compile the achievements of the ancient Sages.
This is what is meant by the great compilation.
Kǒngzǐ possessed virtue but lacked position (wèi).
Consequently, he had no means of obtaining the authority to institute systems.
If he could not be ranked as an accomplishment (yī chéng),
how could there have been a great compilation for him to achieve?
It is not that Kǒngzǐ's Sageliness
was inferior to Zhōugōng's,
but that the opportune time and circumstances made it so.
What Mèngzǐ meant by the great compilation
was spoken in contrast to Bóyí, Yī Yǐn, and Liǔxià Huì.
Fearing that scholars might suspect Kǒngzǐ’s Sageliness
was the same as that of the three masters,
and having nothing suitable for comparison,
he compared him to the great completion achieved in the performance of music.
Therefore, the description of Kǒngzǐ as the great compilation
is appropriate when contrasted with the three masters,
but it cannot fully describe Kǒngzǐ himself.
To use it to fully describe Kǒngzǐ
is, conversely, to belittle Kǒngzǐ.
Why is this?
Zhōugōng compiled the great accomplishments dating from Xī (Fúxī), Xuān (Xuānyuán), Yáo, and Shùn onward.
Zhōugōng certainly learned from the preceding Sages and compiled their works.
Without the methods of the Dào established by the preceding Sages,
he certainly could not have become Zhōugōng.
Kǒngzǐ did not compile the great accomplishments of Bóyí, Yī Yǐn, or Huì (Liǔxià Huì).
Kǒngzǐ certainly never learned from Bóyí, Yī Yǐn, or Huì.
Moreover, if the deeds of Bóyí, Yī Yǐn, and Huì were lacking,
would Kǒngzǐ then be unable to become Kǒngzǐ?
Now, Mèngzǐ’s words
were appropriate for their specific context only;
how can one damage the true meaning by adhering strictly to the wording?
The villagers of Dálàng said:
“How great is Kǒngzǐ!
He is broadly learned, but has achieved no recognized name (chéng míng).”
Today, everyone mocks these villagers for not understanding Kǒngzǐ;
but do they truly know what name Kǒngzǐ ultimately achieved?
Some claim he was a Sage with heaven-bestowed innate knowledge,
incapable of being described in words or analyzed by reason,
and thus incapable of having a fixed designation.
They consequently invoke Heaven and the Spirits (shén),
believing that the Sage is simply unknowable.
In this perspective,
how do they differ from the villagers?
Though Heaven and Earth are great,
they can be summarized in a single statement.
Although Kǒngzǐ is great,
he does not exceed Heaven and Earth;
can he alone not be summarized in a single statement?
If someone asks how he can be summarized in a single statement,
the answer is:
He merely studied Zhōugōng.
Was there nothing else to study
apart from Zhōugōng? The answer is:
It is not that there was something to study that Kǒngzǐ failed to reach;
since Zhōugōng had already compiled the accomplishments of all Sages,
then apart from Zhōugōng,
there was nothing further to be called ‘learning.’
Zhōugōng compiled the great accomplishments of all Sages,
and Kǒngzǐ studied and fully mastered the Dào of Zhōugōng.
This single statement
is sufficient to encompass the entirety of Kǒngzǐ.
“I model myself upon Yáo and Shùn”
was the ambition of Zhōugōng.
“I follow the pattern of Wénwáng and Wǔwáng”
was the work of Zhōugōng.
In one instance, he said:
“Since Wénwáng has died,
is not the culture (wén) vested here?”
In another instance, he said:
“Extreme is my decline!
I no longer dream of Zhōugōng.”
He also said:
“I learned the Rites of Zhōu (Zhōulǐ),
and now I apply them.”
And he also said:
“How richly displayed is the culture!
I follow Zhōu.”
When Āigōng asked about governance,
he replied:
“The government of Wénwáng and Wǔwáng
is spread throughout the official records (fāng cè).”
When someone asked, “Where did Zhòngní (Kǒngzǐ) learn?”
Zǐgòng believed that “the Dào of Wénwáng and Wǔwáng
had not yet fallen to the ground.”
“Transmitting, not creating” (Shù ér bù zuò),
this was the established tradition of Zhōugōng.
“Loving antiquity and diligently seeking knowledge” (Hào gǔ mǐn qiú),
this was the inheritance left by Zhōugōng.
The villagers, living at the same time and not knowing him,
said he achieved no recognized name.
Yet, this was not entirely without insight.
Later generations read the records
but fail to know what the Master studied;
this means their insight is inferior to that of the villagers.
Yet they still mock the villagers for their lack of knowledge—
is this not merely the ridicule of fifty paces by a hundred paces?
Therefore, among the Sages of antiquity,
though their Sageliness was the same,
the means by which they became Sages
were not necessarily entirely the same;
the opportune time and circumstances made it so.
Only Kǒngzǐ and Zhōugōng
were born after the systems were accumulated, the Dào was perfected, and nothing further could be added.
Zhōugōng compiled these accomplishments in order to practice his Dào,
and Kǒngzǐ fully mastered this Dào in order to clarify his teachings.
Their tallies matched perfectly,
as if they issued from one person,
leaving not even the slightest difference or variation.
If this is the case, those who wish to honor Kǒngzǐ—
why must they invoke Heaven and the Spirits
and create vague and unreliable theories?
Someone asked:
Since Kǒngzǐ already shared the same Way (Dào) as Zhōugōng,
Zhōugōng achieved the Great Synthesis (Dàchéng),
why is Kǒngzǐ alone not considered a Great Synthesizer? I reply:
The Great Synthesis of Kǒngzǐ,
was also not what Mèngzǐ spoke of.
It is fundamentally the same as Zhōugōng’s synthesis of the achievements of Xī, Nóng, Xuān, Xù, Táng, Yú, and the Three Dynasties,
but it was not a synthesis of the achievements of Yí, Yǐn, or Liǔxià.
The reason why the ruler and the teacher were separated, and governance and instruction could not merge into one,
is due to the natural patterns (qìshù) emanating from Heaven.
Zhōugōng synthesized the achievements of the governing system (zhìtǒng),
while Kǒngzǐ clarified the pinnacle of establishing instruction (lìjiào).
These were all matters of principle that necessarily had to be so,
and not because the Sages were different from those who preceded them.
This is due to the constraints of the Way and the Law (Dàofǎ) emanating from Heaven.
Therefore, prior to the Suí and Táng dynasties,
the schools simultaneously sacrificed to Zhōu and Kǒng,
taking Zhōugōng as the Former Sage (Xiānshèng),
and Kǒngzǐ as the Former Teacher (Xiānshī).
This signifies that creation and institution (zhìzuò) make one a Sage,
while establishing instruction makes one a Teacher.
Therefore, Mèngzǐ said:
“The Way of Zhōugōng and Zhòngní is one.”
If that is the case, Zhōugōng and Kǒngzǐ
established the ultimate standard of the ruling lineage based on timely circumstances.
Do Sages necessarily rely upon timely circumstances?
Zǎiwǒ considered the Master “more worthy than Yáo and Shùn,”
Zǐgòng considered that “since the creation of mankind, there has never been anyone like the Master,”
Yǒuruò, when comparing the Master to the ancient Sages,
said he “stood out from his kind and rose above the common herd.”
These three disciples all set aside Zhōugōng,
and exclusively honored the Kǒng lineage.
Zhūzǐ considered that their actual achievements (shìgōng) were different,
which is correct.
However, governance is manifested in actual deeds,
while instruction relies on transmitted words alone.
Later generations, influenced by the words of these three disciples,
lavishly extolled Kǒngzǐ,
surpassing Yáo and Shùn,
and consequently revered inner nature and destiny (xìngmìng) while slighting actual achievements.
Thereupon, the great statecraft of a thousand Sages,
was not deemed worthy of the seated discussions of Confucian scholars.
Those who honor the Master,
should approach him most closely through human nature.
If they do not know the reality of the matter,
but merely strive to exalt him,
then he becomes Mysterious upon Mysterious,
and the Sage becomes merely a general designation for divinity or Heaven.
What help is this to the instruction of the world?
Therefore, Zhōu and Kǒng cannot be ranked as superior or inferior.
If one uses dust, dirt, husks, and chaff,
to mold and cast Yáo and Shùn,
even Zhuāngshēng called that an ‘allegory.’
Should Confucian scholars then adopt such a theory?
Therefore, those who wish to know the Way,
must first know why Zhōu and Kǒng were Zhōu and Kǒng.
Hán Tuìzhī said:
“From Zhōugōng upwards,
those above were Rulers,
thus their deeds were accomplished;
From Zhōugōng downwards,
those below were Ministers,
thus their teachings (shuō) endured.”
Now, that which endures through teaching,
is how the Way is illuminated,
but that which endures through teaching,
is also how the Way is obscured.
The Master clarified instruction for ten thousand generations,
but the Master never created a theory himself.
He authenticated the Six Classics,
preserving the former statutes of Zhōugōng.
Therefore he said:
“Transmitting and not creating,
believing in and loving the ancients.”
He also said:
“There may be those who create without knowing (the principles),
I do not have this fault.”
“What the Master regularly spoke of,
were the *Shī*, the *Shū*, and the observance of *Lǐ*,”
which is what is meant by clarifying the Way of the Former Kings to guide people.
It was not that the Master exalted the Former Kings,
with the intention of being humble and yielding and therefore not creating himself;
the Master fundamentally had nothing to create.
Having virtue but lacking position,
meant he lacked the authority to institute new systems.
Mere empty words cannot instruct people;
this is what is meant by “nothing is trustworthy without verification.”
The affair of instruction,
since the time of Xī and Xuān,
has fundamentally existed.
Looking at what is stated in the *Yì Dàzhuàn*,
we know that the Sages demonstrated the law through their very persons,
establishing instruction based on actual events,
and never, outside the sphere of promulgating governance and administering order,
had a separate thing called “methods of instruction.”
In the court of Yú, instruction,
had specialized officials.
What the Sītú respectfully spread,
and what the Diǎnyuè was consulted about;
down to the establishment of schools,
was consistent across the Four Dynasties.
The duties of the Sīchéng, teachers, and guardians,
are detailed in the *Zhōuguān*.
However, since these were listed among the regular offices,
the studies conducted resided within official administrative precedents.
What they practiced,
was the Way of cultivating oneself, regulating the family, ordering the state, and bringing peace to the world,
and those whom they took as teachers,
were people who upheld the official statutes and laws.
Governance and instruction were not separate;
official and teacher were combined into one.
How could there be empty words used to preserve private theories?
The school of Rú,
venerates Kǒngzǐ,
as if intending him to be the private Grand Master of the Rú scholars.
If so, they do not understand Kǒngzǐ.
Kǒngzǐ established the ultimate standard of the Human Way;
Did he possibly intend to establish the ultimate standard of the Rú Way?
The *Rú* (scholar) is,
a worthy man who does not meet with an era of enlightened rulers and worthy ministers,
who, failing to obtain a position to widely implement his Way,
consequently upholds the Way of the Former Kings,
to await later students.
This arises purely from circumstances that leave him with no alternative.
What ought to be done according to the Human Way,
is broad,
and vast.
How can it be that one meets with no opportunity in one's lifetime,
and must necessarily resort to preserving the past and awaiting the future,
not again involving oneself in the human world?
Studying the *Yì* originates from the trigrams of Xī,
but one does not necessarily have to replicate his grass clothing and dwelling in the wilderness.
Observing the *Shū* begins with the canons of Yú,
but one does not necessarily have to replicate his crying out to Heaven with lamentations.
This is because the environments in which they found themselves,
were each different.
If that is the case, those who study the Master,
how can they say they should set aside actual achievements,
and anticipate that the Way will not be practiced, thereby hanging up his teachings?
The *Yì* says:
“That which is above physical form is called Dào,
that which is below physical form is called Qì.”
Dào does not leave Qì,
just as a shadow does not leave the form.
Later generations who adhered to the teachings of the Master (*Fūzǐ*) relied on the Six Classics (*Liùjīng*),
considering the Six Classics to be the books that contained the Dào,
yet they did not know that the Six Classics are all Qì.
The book of the *Yì*,
which serves to disclose things and complete affairs,
was managed by the Grand Diviner (*Tàibǔ*) of the Office of Spring (*Chūnguān*).
Thus, it inherently had official duties attached and was listed among the historical records.
The *Shū* [Book of Documents] belonged to the Outer Scribes (*Wàishǐ*),
the *Shī* [Book of Odes] was governed by the Grand Master (*Dàshī*),
the *Lǐ* [Book of Rites] originated with the Minister of Ancestral Affairs (*Zōngbó*),
music (*Yuè*) had the Director of Education (*Sīchéng*),
and the *Chūnqiū* [Spring and Autumn Annals] belonged to the respective State Historians (*Guóshǐ*).
Before the Three Dynasties (*Sāndài*),
the *Shī*, the *Shū*, and the Six Arts (*Liùyì*)
were always used to teach people,
but were not revered as the Six Classics (*Liùjīng*) by later generations,
separated into a distinct school of Rú Learning (*Rúxué*),
and exclusively called the books that contained the Dào.
This is because what scholars studied
did not go beyond the institutional responsibilities of officials,
and the governmental teachings of the state;
and their function
also did not go beyond the daily norms of human relationships (*rénlún rìyòng*).
Therefore, they only saw them as unavoidable necessities,
and never separately perceived the Dào contained therein.
When the Master (*Fūzǐ*) narrated the Six Classics to instruct later generations,
he also meant that the Dào of the former Sages and former Kings (*xiānshèng xiānwáng*) could not be seen,
but the Six Classics were the visible Qì thereof.
Later people do not see the former Kings,
so they ought to rely on the preservable Qì to contemplate the invisible Dào.
Therefore, he highlighted and elucidated the governmental teachings of the former Kings,
along with the institutional duties of officials, to show them to the people,
without creating his own writings or theories,
thereby avoiding speaking of the Dào separately from the Qì.
When the Master (*Fūzǐ*) himself explained why the *Chūnqiū* was written,
he said:
“If I wished to entrust it to mere empty words,
it would not be as profound, incisive, and clearly manifest as presenting it through actual historical events.”
Thus, beyond governmental teachings and statutes,
and the daily norms of human relationships (*rénlún rìyòng*),
there is no separate way to write or articulate the Dào—
this is already clear.
The Qín people prohibited private discussion of the *Shī* and the *Shū*,
and said: “If one wishes to study laws and decrees,
let officials be the teacher.”
The Qín’s transgression against antiquity
was only in prohibiting the *Shī* and the *Shū*.
As for the statement that those who study laws and decrees
should take officials as their teacher,
this is also the ultimate principle (*zhìlǐ*) of Dào and Qì being unified,
where official duties (*guānshī*) and governance/teaching (*zhìjiào*)
have never branched off into two separate things.
Afterward, scholarship and governance separated;
they could not be unified.
This was the will of Heaven (*Tiān*).
Officials managed the historical records of the current era,
while classical scholars (*jīngshī*) transmitted and received the textual chapters and phrases.
This was also an unavoidable consequence of circumstances.
Nevertheless, across successive generations,
Rú scholarship (*Rúyè*) was not abandoned,
because what they preserved was the Dào of the former Kings.
Yet the followers of the Rú School (*Rújiā*),
holding fast to their Six Records (*Liùjí*),
claimed that these were merely the books containing the Dào.
How can there possibly be Dào spoken of apart from Qì in this world,
or a shadow existing apart from its form?
If they abandon all things in the world and the daily norms of human relationships (*rénlún rìyòng*),
and hold fast only to the Six Records (*Liùjí*) in order to speak of Dào,
then assuredly, one cannot discuss Dào with them.
The *Yì* says:
“The benevolent (*rén*) see it and call it benevolence (*rén*);
the wise (*zhì*) see it and call it wisdom (*zhì*);
the common people use it daily but are unaware of it.”
However, when the Dào is not known, the Dào persists;
when it is seen and named Dào, the Dào vanishes.
The hiding of the Great Dào (*Dàdào*)
is not concealed from the common and the foolish,
but is concealed from those of the talented and wise class who constantly claim to see it.
Since official duties and governance/teaching were unified,
the wisdom and intelligence of the world were confined within one standard;
therefore, the Dào existed within the Qì,
and the human heart had no divergent thoughts.
When official duties and governance/teaching separated,
wisdom, intelligence, talent, and ability
were no longer contained within the standards.
Then the single *yīn* and single *yáng*
entered the partiality of received nature,
and each took what they perceived to be inherently correct.
This was also the result of circumstance.
In the case of the Director of Rites (*Lǐsī*) and the Music Officer (*Yuèzhí*),
each maintained their specialized office.
Even if they possessed the clarity of Lílóu
or the keen hearing of Shīkuàng,
they could not avoid adhering to the standard and following the rules.
Now it is said that the official duties have been lost in transmission,
and that we should use Dào and Dé to illuminate the teachings;
but then every person considers themselves to possess Dào and Dé.
Therefore, the Master (*Fūzǐ*) narrated but did not create,
and highlighted the Six Arts (*Liùyì*),
in order to preserve the old institutions of Zhōugōng,
not daring to abandon the Qì and speak of the Dào.
However, the various masters (*zhūzǐ*) were numerous
and already spoke of the Dào.
Master Zhuāng (*Zhuāngshēng*) compared them to ears, eyes, mouths, and noses;
Sīmǎ Tán divided them into Six Schools (*Liùjiā*);
Liú Xiàng categorized them as Nine Streams (*Jiǔliú*).
All considered themselves to have reached the ultimate standard,
and intended to use their Dào to transform the world.
From the perspective of the noble person (*jūnzǐ*),
they are all perceptions of benevolence (*rén*) and wisdom (*zhì*) that give rise to these claims,
and not that the Dào is truly so easily defined.
The Dào becomes manifest due to the Qì;
it is not named because of a person.
Since people began to speak of Dào,
the Dào began to have its name differentiated based on the person.
The benevolent perceive it and call it benevolence (*rén*);
the wise perceive it and call it wisdom (*zhì*);
this is what happens.
People naturally follow the Dào and act;
the Dào is not something people can seize and possess.
Since people individually claim their own Dào,
and each acts according to their claim,
the Dào thereby becomes possessed by man.
The Dào of the Mò School (*Mòzhě*),
the Dào of Master Xǔ (*Xǔzǐ*),
all such examples are of this type.
The Dào manifested itself in the three individuals living together,
and was fully perfected by Zhōugōng and Kǒngzǐ.
Throughout the line of sages, it was never separately named the Dào,
perhaps like a single family
not needing to identify its own surname.
It was not until the Hundred Schools (*Bǎijiā*) emerged mixed together and spoke of Dào,
