that the Rú scholars (*Rúzhě*) were compelled to honor the source from which they came.
First, they called it the Dào of Yáo and Shùn;
then they called it the Dào of Zhōugōng and Zhòngní.
Therefore, Hán Tuìzhī said that “Dào and Dé are empty titles.”
That Dào and Dé are empty titles
is the decline of Dào and Dé.
When people gather together,
the name of the master (zhǔ) is established because of the guests (bīn).
When words burst forth prolifically,
the name of the right (shì) is established because of the wrong (fēi).
Since the various masters (zhūzǐ) spoke confusedly about the Dào,
it became a sickness for the Dào.
The followers of the Rújiā (Confucian school)
then honored the Dào of Yáo, Shùn, Zhōu, and Kǒng,
taking it to be "Our Dào."
The Dào fundamentally has no "Ours" (wú),
but people themselves make it "Ours,"
believing that it might perhaps be distinguished as the Dào that is separate from the non-Dào.
Yet they do not realize that each makes their own "Ours,"
just as the multitude of the three armies
can be called "Our Army,"
referring to it as "Ours" in contrast to an enemy state;
but when not facing an enemy state,
the three armies each again have their own "I" (wǒ).
Now, concerning the six arts (liùyì),
the Sàngrén (Sages) preserved the Dào by adhering to the implements (qì);
but regarding the three schools’ version of the Yì (Changes),
and the four families’ versions of the Shī (Odes),
those who attack and practice them
cannot bear their entering as the master and exiting as the slave.
They do not realize that the ancients, regarding the six arts,
wore and practiced them like clothing and food,
with everyone practicing them as a matter of course,
and they were never specialized to gain fame for a school.
Later Confucians (hòurú) only focus on a corner or restricted part of one classic,
and exhaust their energy and strength throughout their lives,
yet still fear they will not attain a single correct insight.
How can this not be due to the difference between ancient and modern people?
The circumstances necessitate it.
In ancient times, the Dào resided in the implement (qì);
the officials (guān) and teachers (shī) were combined into one.
What the scholars studied
was either the statutes and regulations of the state,
or the precedents of the governing officials (yǒusī).
Their eyes and ears were accustomed to these things, and there was no need for deep investigation,
hence they attained it easily.
Later Confucians sought the Dào through the implement (qì);
they had teachers but no officials.
Matters came from hearsay and tradition,
not from what was seen firsthand.
The texts required interpretation of ancient meanings (xùngù), not direct statements (zhìyán).
Therefore, attainment was difficult.
Now, the six arts are equally important,
and one should not stop at adhering to a single classic.
The profound meaning of the classics is vast,
and cannot be confined to a corner or restricted part.
Yet the various Confucians specialize in one corner of one classic,
and must exert double the capacity of the ancients who comprehended all six arts.
Thus, given the long distance from the Sages,
this situation is certainly not strange.
But since they have exhausted the intellectual power of their minds, thoughts, eyes, and ears,
they must inevitably see the height and depth of Heaven and Earth uniquely within their field,
and thus claim that in the vastness of Heaven and Earth,
no one surpasses them—
this, too, is human nature.
Yet they do not realize that specializing in a corner of one classic
is insufficient to glimpse the complete form of the ancients.
Explanations of ancient meanings and sentences (xùngǔ zhāngjù),
commentaries and elucidation of principles (shūjiě yìlǐ),
and examination of names and things (kǎoqiú míngwù),
are all insufficient for speaking of the Dào.
If one adopts these three and uses them concurrently,
then with the power of concentrated effort,
one may supplement the accomplishment of remote tracing,
and perhaps come close.
However, the masters of the classics themselves cannot avoid contradictions,
and those who transmit their teachings
further divide themselves into different schools and factions,
no less distinct than the dispute between Rú and Mò;
then, having established the master based on the guests,
there are again guests within the master;
and having established the right based on the wrong,
there is again wrong within the right.
The pathways become increasingly divergent,
and the Great Dào becomes increasingly obscured.
“In high antiquity, government was conducted by tying knots.
Later Sages replaced this with written characters (shūqì).
By them, the hundred officials were governed,
and the myriad people were clearly understood.”
The use of written characters,
for governance and for clarity (zhì-chá),
was never taken by the ancients for the purpose of writing books.
Using written characters for writing books
began with the separation of duties between officials and teachers,
and the division of the paths of governance and education.
Kǒngzǐ said:
“I wish to speak no words.”
That he wished to speak no words
means he could not help but speak something.
Mèngzǐ said:
“Am I fond of disputation?
I am compelled to do it.”
Later writers (zàibǐ zhī shì),
who compose essays (wénzhāng),
intend to establish credibility for the present and transmit to the future.
May they still bear in mind the principle of wishing to speak no words,
and the feeling of compulsion,
that perhaps the words issue from me,
but the reason for speaking
was fundamentally not determined by me.
Now, the Dào is fully contained in the Six Classics (Liùjīng).
For the profound meanings hidden in earlier times,
sentence commentary and textual interpretation (zhāngjù xùngǔ) are sufficient to illuminate them.
For changes in affairs that arise later,
which the Six Classics cannot speak of,
it is indeed valuable to summarize the principles of the Six Classics
and compose writings according to the times in order to fully explore the Great Dào.
The highest accomplishment is establishing virtue (lìdé);
the next is establishing achievement (lìgōng);
the next is establishing words (lìyán).
Establishing words is commensurate with establishing achievement.
For writings must follow and supply what is needed,
follow and articulate what is suppressed,
follow and remedy what is detrimental,
and not merely boast of sounds, emotions, colors, and styles,
to gain fame for oneself.
The Yì says:
“The divine (shén) knows the future;
wisdom (zhì) conceals the past.”
Knowing the future
is yáng.
Concealing the past
is yīn.
One yīn and one yáng
is the Dào.
The use of wénzhāng
is either to narrate events
or to clarify principles.
Events that oppose what is already past
are yīn.
Principles that unfold toward the future
are yáng.
When it reaches the utmost,
then when narrating events, principles are illuminated,
and when speaking of principles, events serve as models.
Then the focus is not biased,
and the writing (wén) conforms to the Dào.
The histories of Qiān and Gù,
and the writings of Dǒng and Hán—
may they perhaps have been compelled to speak?
Those who do not understand this reason
but merely drown in literary phrases (wéncí),
are not worth discussing.
Even those who present high-minded arguments,
saying that writing should primarily clarify the Dào,
and why should one care for sounds, emotions, colors, and styles just for pleasure,
do not speak words of those who know the Dào.
Now, the governance of non-action (wúwéi) is rewarded with the gentle breeze (xūnfēng);
the accomplishment of the spirit-tower (língtái) is celebrated with bells and drums;
and extending to playing the qín and encountering Wén,
and speaking of aspirations during the Spring Purifications (fēng yú);
then the Sages who brought forth governance,
and the Worthies who cultivated merit,
never lacked the pleasure of delighting the eyes and cheering the heart.
So, how can one say that the use of wénzhāng
must be devoid of the effect of chanting and soaring emphasis?
Zǐgòng said:
“The Master’s literary achievements (wénzhāng),
we can hear about.
The Master’s discussions of nature (xìng) and the Way of Heaven (tiāndào),
we cannot hear about.”
In essence, what the Master spoke of,
was nothing but nature and the Way of Heaven,
but he never explicitly declared and manifested it, saying:
“This is nature, this is the Way of Heaven.”
Therefore, he did not say that nature and the Way of Heaven
could not be heard;
but rather, he said that speaking about nature and the Way of Heaven
could not be heard.
That what he spoke of was nothing but nature and the Way of Heaven,
yet he did not clearly manifest this nature and the Way of Heaven,
was out of fear that people would abandon the vessel (qì) and seek the Way (dào).
The rites of Xià (Xià Lǐ) can be spoken of,
the rites of Yīn (Yīn Lǐ) can be spoken of,
and all (scholars) say, “Without verification, there is no belief.”
Therefore, what the Master spoke of
must draw evidence from concrete affairs and things (shìwù),
and not merely rely on empty words,
to illuminate the Way.
When Zēngzǐ practiced earnestly and persevered for a long time,
he said:
“It is unified by one principle.”
When Zǐgòng learned much and remembered,
he said:
“It is unified by one principle.”
If one has neither practiced earnestly and persevered for a long time,
nor learned much and remembered,
then there is fundamentally no basis upon which to ground the unified thread.
The interpretation of words and phrases (xùngǔ) and the naming of things (míngwù)
are intended to seek the traces left by the ancient sages,
but those who boast of memorization
are like merchants in the marketplace.
Compiling and writing literary works
is intended to elucidate the minds of the ancient sages,
but those who drown in brilliance and ornamentation
are like playing with treasured trinkets.
Heterodox doctrines and distorted learning,
which describe what they describe,
and value what they value,
are certainly insufficient to determine the gains or losses of this Way.
The learning of memorization,
and the talent for literary expression,
cannot but take this Way as their ultimate master,
yet the bustling merchants and players forget their origins.
The Sòng Confucians (Sòng Rú) arose and argued against this,
holding that these people were all submerged in the vessel (qì) and did not know the Way (dào).
Now, for those who are submerged in the vessel and do not know the Way,
it would be sufficient to use the vessel itself to show them the Way.
This would be acceptable.
But their fault,
was wanting to make people abandon the vessel and talk about the Way.
The Master taught people to study literature broadly (bóxué yú wén),
yet the Sòng Confucians said:
“Playing with things (wánwù) leads to the loss of aspiration (sàng zhì).”
Zēngzǐ taught people to reject crude and contradictory language (cí yuǎn bǐ bèi),
yet the Sòng Confucians said:
“Skill in literature (gōng wén) harms the Way.”
Indeed, are the words of the Sòng Confucians
not excellent medicine for later degenerate trends?
However, medicine is intended only to attack diseases in the internal organs.
The intent of the Sòng Confucians
seems to be that seeing the disease is in the internal organs,
they subsequently wished to remove the internal organs entirely.
If one intends to seek nature and Heaven (xìngtiān),
but disdains memorization and rejects literary composition,
how is this different?
Nevertheless, the precision of their analysis of principle (lǐ),
and the earnestness of their practice,
were things the Confucians of Hàn and Táng
had not yet heard of.
Mèngzǐ said:
“The delight of principle and righteousness (yìlǐ) to my heart,
is like the delight of meat and grain (chú huàn) to my mouth.”
Principle and righteousness cannot be empty words;
broad learning solidifies it,
and literary composition conveys it.
When these three converge into one,
it is almost as if the Way of Zhōu and Kǒng (Zhōukǒng), though distant,
is communicated without the need for multiple translations.
Yet, the masters of the Classics (jīngshī) disparage one another,
literary scholars undervalue each other,
and among the various scholars of nature and principle (xìnglǐ zhū rú),
there are also the agreements and differences of Zhū [Xī] and Lù [Jiǔyuān],
and those who follow Zhū and those who follow Lù attack each other,
and those who talk about scholarship and literature
chase popular trends and remain unenlightened.
This is what Zhuāngshēng called: “The hundred schools go on and never turn back;
they will certainly not reach agreement.”
Alas!
Shào Jìnhán said:
“When this essay first came out,
the draft circulated in the capital (Jīngshī).
All my colleagues who usually admired the writings of Mr. Zhāng [Xuéchéng] were dissatisfied,
saying that it stepped into the conventional style of the Sòng scholars’ recorded conversations (yǔlù),
unavoidably stale and unpopular,
and unlike his usual writing style,
to the extent that some sent letters to admonish him.
I carefully examined it,
and said to Zhū Shàobái (Míng Xīgēng):
‘This clarifies all that is written in his Tōng Yì.
His original statements and separate discussions
all arise naturally,
without artificial pretense.
Although the language is broad and simple (húnchéng),
the ideas are mostly profound and penetrating,
and it cannot be criticized.’ ”
My nephew Tíngfēng said:
“My uncle’s Tōng Yì
is normally popular and highly praised (kuàizhì rénkǒu),
but does everyone truly grasp its core meaning?
It is merely that his refined sayings and lofty discussions
are mostly novel and pleasing,
perhaps only serving as conversational aids in hand.
They do not know that my uncle once regretted that his famous brilliant expressions (míng jùn) were too numerous,
losing the ancient spirit.
The topic of this essay,
though seemingly overly lofty and impractical (yūkuò),
actually contains many newly created and pioneering meanings.
For instance, stating that the Way began with three people living together,
and that rulership, tutelage, governance, and instruction (jūn shī zhèng jiào)
all originate from Heaven;
that the worthy and the wise learn from the sage;
that the sage learns from the common people (bǎixìng);
that the one who synthesized the great achievements
was Zhōugōng, not Kǒngzǐ;
that scholars must not arbitrarily separate Zhōu and Kǒng;
that those who study Kǒngzǐ
should not first take the transmission of teachings for ten thousand generations as their goal;
that the greatness of Kǒngzǐ,
in the single phrase, “learning the Rites of Zhōu” (xué Zhōu lǐ),
can cover his entire essence;
—all these ideas are utterly strange when first heard,
but utterly accurate upon deep reflection.
Before the Tōng Yì,
they were never spoken by anyone.
How can they be called stale and unpopular?
The gentlemen who criticized it as stale and unpopular that day,
I fear, had read the title too casually,
and had not carefully examined the text itself.”
The *Yì* says:
"Achieving the pattern is called *Qián*,
Following the model is called *Kūn*."
Learning,
is defined as following the model.
The *Dào*,
is defined as achieving the pattern.
The Master (*Fūzǐ*) said:
"Study below and reach above."
This refers to studying the implements that are below form,
and naturally reaching the *Dào* that is above form.
The *shì* hopes to be *xián*,
the *xián* hopes to be *shèng*,
the *shèng* hopes to accord with Heaven.
Hoping to be *xián* and hoping to be *shèng*,
this certainly has a rationale.
"The operations of High Heaven
are without sound and without smell,"
How then does the *shèng* hope to accord with Heaven?
Generally, when Heaven gives birth to humanity,
none are not endowed with the nature of *rén*, *yì*, *lǐ*, and *zhì*;
this is *tiāndé*;
none are not placed within the human relationships of ruler and minister, father and son, husband and wife, brothers, and friends;
this is *tiānwèi*.
By employing *tiāndé* to cultivate *tiānwèi*,
even where matters and things have not yet intersected in subtle and hidden ways,
there is already a perfect suitability for what is proper,
and there is a standard that is neither excessive nor deficient,
this is what is called achieving the pattern.
On ordinary days, one embodies this pattern,
and when affairs arrive and things intersect,
one consistently proceeds by that standard to meet them,
this is what is called following the model.
This is how the *shèng rén* hopes to accord with Heaven,
this is the *shèng rén*'s studying below and reaching above.
*Yī Yǐn* said:
"When Heaven gives birth to these people,
it makes the first to know awaken those who come later,
it makes the first to awaken awaken those who awaken later."
Humanity receives *qì* unevenly in life,
thus there are naturally those who cannot spontaneously know the standard of perfect suitability,
therefore, the people who know first and awaken first
proceed to point it out to them.
This is what is called *jiào*.
*Jiào*,
teaches people to spontaneously know the standard of perfect suitability,
it does not teach them to abandon their own inherent nature and follow me.
Thus, the *shì* hopes to be *xián*,
the *xián* hopes to be *shèng*,
hoping to follow the model found in achieving the pattern,
and not abandoning their own inherent nature in order to pursue it.
If this is the case, how can they be made to know the standard of perfect suitability?
How can they be made to know achieving the pattern and following the model?
They must then observe those, since the birth of humanity,
who fully possess the purity of *tiāndé*,
and who reached the pinnacle of *tiānwèi*.
They must seek their former words and past deeds,
the means by which they handled the transformations in extremity and endurance through permanence, and know them extensively,
and only afterwards will they spontaneously obtain that which is called achieving the pattern,
and perfect their following of the model.
Therefore, following the model
must be manifested in actions and affairs.
Reciting and reading the *Shī* and the *Shū*,
is the means by which to seek the resources for following the model,
but it cannot immediately be considered the following of the model itself.
However, why did the ancients not consider actions and affairs as learning,
but instead considered reciting and reading the *Shī* and the *Shū* as learning?
Why is this?
It generally means that if one does not investigate things (*gé wù*) and extend knowledge (*zhì zhī*),
then one cannot make the intention sincere (*chéng yì*),
and action must proceed forth according to that knowledge.
Thus, those who consider reciting and reading as learning,
speak by extrapolating the scope of the teacher's instruction,
not meaning that there is no learning outside of this scope.
*Zǐlù* said:
"There are the common people,
there are the altars of earth and grain (*shè jì*),
why must one read books,
before being considered learned?"
The Master (*Fūzǐ*) rebuked him for being glib,
generally because *Zǐgāo* was a steward (*zǎi*),
and would not speak like this,
it does not mean that learning must solely focus on reciting and reading.
To focus solely on reciting and reading when discussing learning
is the narrow view of worldly *rú*.
of the ancients
did not abandon practical affairs and concrete matters.
This was probably because governance and education had not yet been separated,
and the officials and teachers were unified,
which made their practice relatively easier. The Sītú
spread the Wǔjiào,
the Diǎnyuè taught the Zhòuzǐ,
and the schools of the Sāndài
were all manifested in the institutions and systems. Those
who were engaged in scholarship at that time,
when indoors, reinforced their readings and studies,
and when outdoors, immediately saw the execution of political governance, education, and codified laws.
Because of this, their learning was entirely trustworthy and verifiable,
and not merely empty words passed down mutually.
However, while their knowledge was easy to acquire,
their actions were difficult to match (the standard),
which has been the case since antiquity. When Yáo
banished Gònggōng,
he said:
“He speaks smoothly when still, but his actions are contrary.” Now, being
still yet able to speak well,
means that he was not unlearned.
To test him in practical affairs and find contradiction,
shows he differed from those who merely imitate existing models. When Fù Yuè
enlightened Gāozōng,
he said:
“It is not the difficulty of knowing;
it is the difficulty only of acting.” Gāozōng
had studied previously under Gānpán,
and had long labored outside (in the field).
How could he be unlearned?
But since he had not yet been tested in practical affairs,
there was fear that his actions would not be trustworthy (or effective).
He also said:
“Men seek much learning (multi-directional listening);
when it is time only to establish affairs,
then learning from the ancient instructions yields success.” Although this saying
comes from the ancient text,
its meaning must have been received (from a prior source).
Now, seeking much listening and verifying it by establishing affairs,
then what is called learning the ancient instructions,
is not merely recitation and discussion;
this too is evident.
If governance and education are unified and the officials and teachers are not separated,
seeking knowledge is easy, but practical implementation is already difficult;
how much more so when officials and teachers are separated,
and what scholars practice
are all merely the obsolete traces of former men? The Fūzǐ
said:
“To learn without thinking is bewilderment;
to think without learning is peril.”
He also said:
“I once spent the entire day without eating,
and the entire night without sleeping,
in order to think.
It was of no benefit;
it is better to learn.” Thinking
is also the work of a learner,
yet he separates thinking from learning,
as if to say that thinking cannot be called learning.
This implies that one must certainly be experienced in practical affairs
before one can speak of learning.
This, then, is the Fūzǐ's method of instructing people in the unity of knowledge and action. The doctrines
of the various masters and the Hundred Schools
arose from mere contemplation without practical learning.
Thus, although their core principles all had something inherited and received,
they could not avoid errors and defects. What Liú Xīn
called the lineages of certain schools (jiā),
their source emerged from the duties of a certain official position in antiquity;
their branching became the scholarship of a certain school;
and their failing became the defect of a certain matter. Now, the duties
of a certain official position
are precisely the ordinances, statutes, and standards of the former kings.
Branching into the scholarship of a certain school
meant that the official duties were lost in transmission,
and each (scholar) used the limit of his own thinking
to create his own different lineage. Failing
and becoming the defect of a certain matter
meant that they exhausted their thought but were not experienced in practical affairs.
Although their arguments were based on precedent,
and their words formed a coherent theory,
they could not know the flaws in their execution. Thus,
during the flourishing of the Sāndài,
learning originated from a single source.
What was called learning
referred entirely to the accomplishments achieved by men. Speaking
generally,
at ten years old it was called 'yòuxué' (junior learning);
this is correct.
Speaking analytically,
then at thirteen one learned music,
and at twenty one learned ritual;
this is correct. When the state
used names based on the achievements of men
to name its institutions,
then it spoke of Xiāngxué and Guóxué.
Learning, in this sense, was common to the Sāndài;
this is correct. There
was no instance where learning was attributed to an individual
and distinguished by names based on their personal rank or attainment. When
officials and teachers separated and the doctrines of the various masters and Hundred Schools arose,
then learning began to be named based on the personal rank and attainment of individuals.
What is called the school of so-and-so (Jiǎ),
or the school of so-and-so (Yǐ),
is this. Learning
having different names because of people,
learning thereby went astray.
This was not due to an excess of action leading to this,
but rather arose from an excess of thinking. Therefore,
when the Fūzǐ spoke of the defects of neglecting either learning or thinking,
he immediately continued by saying:
“Devoting oneself to Yìduān (heterodox doctrines),
this is indeed harmful.” Now, the rise
of Yìduān
is entirely due to an excess of thinking
without practical experience in affairs.
originated from thinking but not studying;
the ailment of contemporary Confucian scholars (shìrú),
originated from studying but not thinking;
this is because the official role and the teaching role were separated, and study differed from that of the ancients.
Later monarchs (hòu wáng) believed that Confucian methods (Rúshù) could not be abandoned,
thus establishing Erudites (Bóshì),
setting up disciples,
and setting up examination systems to select scholars,
believing that reciting and modeling themselves on the former kings (xiān wáng) was encouragement.
In the beginning,
they used profit and emoluments (lìlù) to encourage Confucian methods,
but ultimately,
they used Confucian methods to curry favor for profit and emoluments.
This, of course, is not worth discussing.
Yet, leading Confucian masters (rú zōng shuò shī),
emerged from this group,
so it cannot be said that this was not cultivated by the court's (cháotíng) cultural and ethical policies (fēngjiào).
Now, human nature (rén zhī qíng)
cannot move without being drawn to something desirable;
once something is done,
one strives to fully achieve its substance
and seeks to match the reputation.
Those who are above average,
can be encouraged to aspire to it.
Schools and the examination system (kējǔ),
attract thousands of talented individuals (cáijùn);
how could there not be one in ten who emerges from those above average?
Being far removed from antiquity,
they cannot study what the ancients studied;
therefore, they take the recitation and practice of Confucian studies (rúyè),
as the ultimate goal of learning.
Moreover, the difficulty of mastering and succeeding
is inherently double that of the ancients.
Therefore, for those who specialize in mastering Confucian studies,
if they truly have something distinctive to show for themselves,
and are not accessible to all mediocre commoners,
I have nothing to criticize them for.
Those whose learning is broad excel at verification and research (kǎosuǒ);
is this not genuine accumulation within the Way (Dào)?
Yet those who chase breadth,
exhaust their essence and weary their spirits throughout their lives to pursue it,
without considering what value that breadth has.
Those whose talent is exceptional are skilled at writing literature (shǔ wén);
is this not the manifestation of the body of the Way (Dàotǐ)?
Yet those who are masterful in literature,
agonize their hearts and burn their thoughts throughout their lives to construct it,
without considering what use that literature has.
Those who discuss moral principles (yìlǐ) seem capable of thinking,
yet they do not realize that if moral principles are held suspended and lack substance,
then moral principles are also irrelevant to the Way.
All these people know *that* it is so,
but they do not know *why* it is so.
Master Chéng (Chéngzǐ) said:
"In all matters, thinking about why they are so,
is the foremost learning (xuéwèn) under Heaven."
Why do people not also seek out that which explains *why* it is so and think about it?
The world cannot be without cultural trends (fēngqì);
cultural trends cannot be without circulation.
The principle of one Yīn and one Yáng (yī yīn yī yáng zhī Dào),
is evident in the cycle of cosmic forces (qìshù).
What is valued in the learning methods of the noble person (jūnzǐ)
is the ability to sustain the world and rectify imbalances.
The principle of one Yīn and one Yáng,
is naturally suited for moderation and adjustment.
When a cultural trend begins,
it must have something that recommends it;
thus, learning, literary language, and moral principles,
cannot avoid being disproportionately emphasized or neglected.
When a cultural trend matures,
it must have something that spoils it;
human sentiment conforms to the times and loves reputation,
pursuing the trivial and neglecting the fundamental.
Therefore, though the originating trend cannot avoid imbalance,
its essence must be grasped
to welcome the new ethos;
and although the spoiled trend is nominally orthodox,
those who follow it surely imitate its falseness
as a reliance for the declining current.
This, too, is the natural course of events.
Yet the scholars of the world (shì zhī yán xuézhě),
do not know how to maintain cultural trends,
but only know how to conform to cultural trends,
and moreover claim that without doing so, they cannot invite renown.
Then they simply fail to think.
Shěn Fēngchí wrote a letter inquiring about learning.
He confessed that he was ashamed
of being unable to engage in Q&A with educated people in large assemblies.
I replied to him that learning lies in self-establishment,
and what others are capable of,
I do not necessarily need to be ashamed of being incapable of.
I then drew an analogy to commodity trading:
those who deal in cloth and silk
do not need to concern themselves with grain and beans;
those who store medicines
do not need to inquire about gold and pearls.
The real worry is failing to establish one's own specialized field.
For example, if one markets cloth but is lacking in tailoring materials,
or sells medicine but is deficient in medical prescriptions,
then that is unacceptable.
Someone asked:
“This is the method Sū Zǐzhān taught people for reading the *Hàn Shū*,
and many students today are already aware of it.”
I replied:
“The words are similar but the meaning is different.
A slight divergence, even by a hair's breadth,
leads to an error of a thousand *lǐ*.”
Someone once asked Sū Jūn:
“Can your extensive knowledge
also be learned?”
Sū Jūn replied:
“Yes.
I once read the *Hàn Shū*,
and completed it in just a few passes.
I focused on specific subjects like military affairs, agriculture, ritual, and music,
and in each pass, I sought out one subject with deliberate intent.
After a long time, I achieved thorough understanding.”
He then used the analogy of marketing goods,
implying that while goods are inexhaustible,
the capabilities of the merchant are finite,
so one must know what to choose.
Many students recite Sū Shì’s words
and regard them as an excellent method,
unaware that this is merely the common practice of extracting sentences,
like recent compilers of categorized reference books.
The inquirer merely sought extensive knowledge,
so there was naturally no deep intention behind the question.
Sū Shì’s answer,
therefore, was no more than the task required of classical scholars seeking to pass examinations.
Anyone who pays a little attention to examination preparation today
can perform this task;
it cannot yet be called learning (*xuéwèn*).
Yet, students consider it an excellent method,
which shows how few true scholars there are.
Now, learning must involve specialization.
Was Sū Shì's intention
to take Bān Shū as his sole field of study?
If so, he could never complete that work in his lifetime.
How could a few passes suffice to complete it?
Or, was he taking the subjects he sought—ritual, music, military, and agriculture—as his field of study?
If so, each category has its own profound depths,
and how could one pass be sufficient to master one category?
If we follow Sū Shì’s analogy,
comparing it to a merchant seeking goods,
then 'seeking out one subject with deliberate intent in each pass'
means that in the first trip one intends to trade in gold and pearls,
in the second trip to trade in cloth and silk,
and then successively, grain, millet, and medicines.
He seeks them out one category after another.
If he intends to seek out and master all categories,
then even the wealth of Táo Zhū and Yī Dùn
would be insufficient to cover the cost of the goods.
If he merely takes a rough estimate of the cost
and provisionally collects a small amount of each kind,
then he fails to complete any store of goods.
Sū Shì’s words
are untenable regardless of whether one advances or retreats.
Yet, students today are rushing to follow Sū Shì without delay.
This is because Sū Shì’s method,
while insufficient for seeking true learning,
is more than adequate for pursuing examination work.
Examination work is known and recited by every household,
yet few can accomplish what Sū Shì did.
When it is occasionally encountered,
it truly stands out among common practices,
and people look upon it with awe.
Consequently, the person who achieves this claims it for themselves,
asserting that it is learning (*xuéwèn*),
not mere examination work,
without realizing their error.
Sū Shì’s learning
originated from the school of Vertical and Horizontal Alliances.
His strength
lay in assessing worldly affairs and
being practical, closely aligned with utility,
and what he relied upon for development
was policy essays (*cè lùn*).
Policy answers must have distinct points,
and argumentative essays must cite historical facts.
If one does not have specialized prior scholarship,
they must consult records and check facts.
If one truly applies the effort involved in Sū Shì’s method of reading the *Hàn Shū*,
then they can respond to sudden needs and anticipate questions,
finding no difficulty in the matter.
Hán Chānglí said:
“The recorder of events must grasp their essentials;
the compiler of words must hook their profundity.”
‘Hooking the profound and grasping the essential’
has been praised for a thousand years.
However, the profound and essential statements Hán Shì compiled for himself
are not only invisible today,
but absolutely no copies circulated back then.
They must have been merely selections of phrases and sentences
prepared for ready reference when composing texts.
Yet, people try to imitate the idea of ‘hooking the profound and grasping the essential’ for their own writing.
This, too, is taking Sū Shì’s categorical seeking
and mistakenly treating it as learning (*xuéwèn*);
it can be viewed as an analogous case.
Someone asked:
“If what you say is true,
are Hán and Sū not worth modeling ourselves after?” I replied:
“Hán and Sū used their effort
to aid their literary composition,
not to define it as learning.”
Someone else asked:
“Examination work is what allows us to gauge a person's learning.
The separation between examination work and learning,
is an error of later trends.
If one has preparations ready to meet the examination,
that is what the *Jì* calls 'broad learning and strong memory ready to meet inquiries.'
How can it be denied the name of learning?”
I replied:
“Broad learning and strong memory
are indeed the duty of a scholar.
But I argue that the basis of self-establishment
does not lie in this.
Learning values breadth but also the ability to be concise.
There has never been anyone who was not broad yet could be concise.
This applies to crude and unsophisticated scholars
who confine themselves to the teachings of one master and establish their own boundary;
they cannot be called specialists.
However, there has also never been anyone who was not concise yet could be broad.
This applies to common scholars whose memorization is vague and diffuse,
reaching endlessly,
seeking knowledge of all things in vain,
which even the wisdom of Yáo and Shùn could not achieve.
Broad learning and strong memory
can certainly prepare one to meet inquiries.
But if one does not know how to maintain focus
and merely sets it up as preparation for inquiries,
then if there is no inquirer,
will the scholar have no learning?
Moreover, the inquirer will certainly seek my substance upon hearing my name.
A name must be established through a foundation;
without specialized, accomplished learning, it is impossible.
Therefore, no learning can be accomplished without specialization.
Someone asked:
“Sū Shì’s categorical seeking
and Hán Shì’s hooking the profound and grasping the essential
are both studies aimed at meeting inquiries.
You say they are insufficient to establish a specialized field.
Wáng Bóhòu collected and extracted information,
exploring the obscure and subtle to the utmost.
Regarding the Classics, Commentaries, Masters, and Histories,
and things like names, objects, systems, and numbers,
he connected and synthesized them extensively,
truly able to investigate what previous scholars had left incomplete.
The books he compiled
are still relied upon by scholars today.
How can we overlook them by calling them studies aimed at meeting inquiries?”
I replied:
“Wáng Bóhòu
was one who sought substance based on reputation.
People of old said that Hán Chānglí saw the Way through literature,
and once he saw the Way,
he transcended literature.
Wáng Shì sought learning through preparation for inquiries,
and once he knew learning,
he transcended preparation for inquiries.
However, Wáng Shì’s various books
may be called compilations,
but they cannot be called original writings (*zhùshù*).
They may be called the effort and exertion of a scholar seeking knowledge,
but they cannot yet be called the scholarship (*xuéshù*) of an established specialist.
The reason why broadly cultured gentlemen today
exhaust their energy and weary their spirits on the Classics, Commentaries, Masters, and Histories,
yet gain nothing in their learning throughout their lives,
is precisely that they honor Wáng Shì
and mistakenly regard the effort of seeking knowledge
as learning itself.
Learning and effort
are indeed similar but different.
Learning cannot be achieved quickly;
people should apply their efforts to the exertion of seeking knowledge.
However, pointing to the effort and calling it learning
is like pointing to sorghum and millet and calling them wine.”
Indeed, study includes innate nature,
which, amidst reading books and adhering to the ancients,
is the initial understanding that enters one's consciousness,
and is that which cannot be changed throughout one's life.
Study also includes ultimate feeling,
which, amidst reading books and adhering to the ancients,
is the heartfelt experience of joy and melancholy,
and is that which suddenly makes one unaware of the origin of one's song or tears.
If the power of effort is sufficient,
but nature and feeling are lacking,
it cannot be called learning.
If nature and feeling are inherent,
but one does not deepen them with the power of effort,
this is called having fine potential but not having studied.
The Master (Fūzǐ) said:
“He is so eager that he forgets to eat,
so happy that he forgets his worries,
and does not know that old age is approaching.”
I do not know what counts as the power of effort,
and what counts as nature and feeling.
If this truly is the ultimate state of study,
how did the Master attain this?
The answer is:
“He is one who loves antiquity and seeks it diligently.”
The conventional scholars of today
regret that they cannot see the “Spring and Autumn Annals” (Chūnqiū) before the Master revised it,
and also regret that Dài Gōng obtained the “Hymns of Shāng” (Shāng Sòng),
but did not preserve the missing titles of the seven chapters,
believing that such profound feeling and superior taste
are worthy of mutual praise.
Extending their narrow views,
they even imply that the Master’s editing and revision
was not as skillful as Wáng Bóhòu's (Wáng Bóhòu) ability to search for lost relics.
This is because they are driven by temporary trends,
and mistakenly believe that stitching up and mending gaps is sufficient to exhaust all the great capabilities of Heaven and Earth.
Fortunately, they were born in later ages;
if they had been born before the destruction by the fires of Qín (Qín),
when all classics and documents existed,
and there was no need for supplementation or compilation,
they would have had no use for their learning.
Someone asked:
You speak of scholarship,
saying that the power of effort must necessarily be combined with nature and feeling;
as for the method of learning,
you do not establish fixed rules,
but merely instruct scholars to recognize what their natural endowment inclines toward and what their strength enables them to strive for,
and then apply their power of effort.
This perhaps echoes the lingering thought of Wáng's (Wáng Shì) innate knowledge (liáng zhī).
In antiquity, teaching
from mathematics and names of directions,
to reciting poetry and performing the “Spoon Dance” (wǔ sháo),
each had a fixed curriculum,
regardless of whether a person’s endowment inclined towards it or not,
or whether their strength enabled them to strive for it or not.
Yet you say that each person has things they can do and things they cannot do,
and should not be forced into conformity.
Could it be that the teaching methods of ancient and modern people are different?
I reply:
If modern people do not study,
they cannot be the same as the ancients;
it is not that their talents are unequal,
but that circumstances dictate it.
Since the official teachers (guān shī) were separated,
the teaching methods ceased to be unified;
scholars privately transmit and receive instruction based on their respective abilities;
this is the first difference.
Furthermore, once the official teachers were separated,
studying relies solely on bamboo slips and books;
the Way is not manifested through material objects,
and affairs are not guarded by professional occupations;
this is the second difference.
Therefore, learning lacks the official pedagogical inheritance;
the Six Scripts (liù shū) and the Nine Divisions (jiǔ shù),
which the ancients mastered thoroughly in elementary schooling,
are all clearly understood;
but later generations of established masters and seasoned scholars,
specializing families and famous schools,
exhaust their lifelong energy seeking them,
yet still cannot fully conform to the ancient ways;
this is the third difference.
Heavenly timing and human affairs
cannot be forced to be the same between ancient and modern times;
this is not something human wisdom or strength can achieve.
Nevertheless, the great principles of the Six Classics (Liù Jīng)
are as bright as the sun and stars;
the enhancements and deletions (sǔn yì) of the Three Dynasties (Sān Dài)
can be projected for a hundred generations.
The brilliant ones proceed from the broad outline to seek accomplishment,
while the profound ones follow the measured steps to slowly achieve realization.
That which one's natural endowment inclines toward and which one's strength enables one to strive for
is possessed by every person;
thus, everyone can attain self-realization;
how can one cling to fixed molds and force others into conformity?
Wáng Shì's (Wáng Shì) doctrine of extending innate knowledge (zhì liáng zhī)
is exactly the lingering words of Mèngzǐ.
Since innate knowledge is said to be extended (zhì),
then naturally the power of effort is not omitted.
Zhū Zǐ (Zhū Xī) desired people to follow what is manifested and thereby become enlightened;
Mèngzǐ called this discerning the starting points and expanding upon them (kuò chōng zhī);
both refer to this same Way.
Yet conventional scholars today, when speaking of study,
often treat innate knowledge as a taboo,
perhaps due to caution against the errors of later developments,
and thus believe that the fundamental aim truly differs from what the ancients spoke of?
Someone asked:
What Mèngzǐ called expansion (kuò chōng)
certainly attains the complete substance of benevolence (rén), righteousness (yì), propriety (lǐ), and wisdom (zhì).
Yet you want people to recognize their strengths,
so that they may specialize in their field and establish their school,
and you even caution people against pursuing side interests;
how can this be considered the teaching of the universal Way (tōng fāng zhī dào)?
I reply:
Statements cannot be so rigid.
The Way seeks universality,
but the occupation must be specialized and focused;
these two doctrines proceed simultaneously and do not conflict.
Among the disciples of the Sage (shèng mén), seventy-two people mastered the Six Arts (liù yì),
yet even among Yán (Yán Huí), Zēng (Zēng Shēn), Cì (Duān Mù Cì), and Shāng (Pú Shāng),
the paths they followed were not identical.
After two generations,
Xún Qīng (Xún Qīng) specialized in the “Rites” (Lǐ),
and Mèngzǐ excelled in the “Odes” (Shī) and the “Documents” (Shū);
some were expansive, some detailed;
the pathways differed,
but they all culminated in the Way.
The paths that later scholars utilize as their starting points
are broadly categorized into
meaning and principle (yì lǐ),
systems and numbers (zhì shù),
or literary expression (wén cí).
To achieve one of the three,
one cannot help but be slow regarding the other two;
this is the nature of principle and circumstance.
If one knows that what is achieved is but one aspect of the Way,
and does not consider the two areas that are temporarily slower to be negligible,
then one is not far from this Way.
If one clings solely to one aspect,
and claims that nothing in the world can surpass it,
then one is merely switching between being a slave and being a master (chū nú rù zhǔ),
alternately conquering and being defeated by others;
this is what is called being fixated on things and not being transformative.
Therefore, study must seek one's own realization,
occupation must value specialization and refinement,
categories must necessarily be expanded upon,
the Way must reach its full capacity,
nature and feeling must be understood through sorrow, joy, indignation, and pleasure,
principle and circumstance must be understood through change in extremity and enduring through universality,
broad yet not cluttered,
concise yet not missing anything;
only then can scholarship perhaps be pure and firm,
and the method of upholding the past and awaiting the future (shǒu xiān dài hòu zhī dào)
will seem as though it is about to be seen.
The words of the ancients,
were thus meant for the public good,
and they never boasted of their literary refinement,
nor privately claimed them as their own possession.
Their aim was focused on the Dào (Way),
their words served to clarify that aim,
and the writings served to complete the words.
If their Dào was truly made clear to the world,
and their aims were fully extended,
it was unnecessary for their words to truly belong to them.
The Yú Shū (Book of Yú) states:
"Present petitions through words,
test their effectiveness clearly through deeds."
This was the beginning of observing men based on their speech.
If people are employed and convinced only after testing their deeds,
then what is valued does not lie in the words themselves.
The structure of oaths and pronouncements (shì gào),
is that of words compiled into documents.
If they suffice to establish governance and administer order,
the ruler and the ministers never divide the merit of establishing the words.
Zhōu Gōng (Duke of Zhōu) said:
"The King speaks thus to the numerous regions."
This is the text of the proclamation to the four states.
Commentators believe that Zhōu Gōng transmitted the King's command,
not realizing that these words fundamentally originated with Zhōu Gōng,
and when Chéng Wáng (King Chéng) permitted and enacted them,
they became the words of Chéng Wáng.
Generally, when a sagely minister establishes words for a worthy ruler,
this is called allowing the worthy and capable to serve the sage;
this is also the governance of a sage.
Zēng Gǒng (Mister Zēng) said:
"The Diǎn and Mó (Canons and Counsels) record the merits and achievements of Yáo and Shùn,
and record their subtle and profound intentions as well,
how could this be achieved by ordinary people?
The historians who wielded the brush at that time
were also disciples of the sages."
Viewing it this way,
when a worthy minister narrates deeds for a sage ruler,
this is called the worthy and capable understanding the sage;
this is also the words of the sage.
Writing and the Dào are interconnected as one,
words and deeds share the same category,
just as the eight musical sounds rely on each other to create harmony in music,
and cannot be attributed solely to the excellence of one instrument.
The five flavors mix together to create harmony in the cauldron,
and cannot be designated merely by the sweetness of one ingredient.
Therefore it is said:
The words of the ancients,
were thus meant for the public good,
and they never boasted of their literary refinement,
nor privately claimed them as their own possession.
Sīmǎ Qiān said:
"The three hundred pieces of the Shī (Odes),
were generally composed by worthy men and sages acting out of indignation."
Thus, the words of mutual admiration between men and women
are the vehicles for longing for the sovereign or cherishing friends.
The grievances of marching husbands and separated wives
are the vessels for loyalty to the state and worry about the times.
If one adheres strictly to the words,
and takes them as the literal speech of those people,
then the "Chī Xiāo" (Owl) poem is truly the sorrowful sound of a bird,
and why should one be surprised that the Girdle-fish angrily admonished Zhuāng Zhōu?
If "Cháng Chǔ" (The Long Winding Vine) is truly a happy song about a rootless plant,
why should one be surprised that the female wind (cí fēng) lamented to Sòng Yù?
Now, the purpose of the poets
is gentle and generous,
primarily literary but serving as indirect remonstrance.
Those who speak are blameless,
and those who hear have enough to take warning from.
Expressing their frustrations,
and benefiting moral instruction in some small measure—
this is their aim.
If they were to establish fame based on this,
they would be competing in the technical skill of literary arts;
the ancients did not do this.
Therefore it is said:
The words of the ancients,
were thus meant for the public good,
and they never boasted of their literary refinement,
nor privately claimed them as their own possession.
The Master (Fūzǐ) said:
"I transmit but do not innovate."
The Six Arts were all old standards established by Zhōu Gōng;
the Master had no need to innovate anything.
The Lúnyǔ (Analects) records the Master's words.
When he said, "He does not constantly possess his virtue,"
arguing against diviners and doctors,
he never explicitly stated it was a text from the Yì (Book of Changes).
When he praised Jì Lù (Zǐ Lù)
with "having no rancor, seeking nothing,"
or sighed about Yí (Bó Yí) and Qí (Shū Qí)
that "truly they were not distressed by wealth,"
he never stated that the words came from the Shī (Odes).
When he related the words of Yáo,
saying, "Sincerely hold fast to the Mean,"
or related the Oath of Tāng,
saying, "The dark bull is clearly announced,"
he never stated that the words came from the Shū (Book of Documents).
The Lúnyǔ records the Master's subtle words,
yet initially makes no distinction between the Shī and the Shū.
This reflects the principle that transmission and innovation are not different.
The Master’s words,
appearing in the narratives and citations of various schools,
yet the Lúnyǔ did not include all of them;
this also reflects the principle that detail and brevity are mutually entrusted.
Now, the Six Arts are the originators of writing,
and the Lúnyǔ is the culmination of sagely words.
Innovating the new or transmitting the old,
there was never any self-serving intent;
they merely took what was sufficient to clarify the Dào and establish instruction,
and the sagely innovations and clear transmissions
never divided the merit of establishing the words.
Therefore it is said:
The words of the ancients,
were thus meant for the public good,
and they never boasted of their literary refinement,
nor privately claimed them as their own possession.
When the Zhōu declined and the literary arts deteriorated,
the various schools of philosophers contended,
generally after the Master had passed away,
when subtle words ceased and the great principles had already diverged.
Nevertheless, the various philosophers intended to reform the world with their teachings,
and they certainly sought to prove that their so-called Dào
was unsurpassed in the world,
yet regarding their language and writing,
they never concealed its origin.
The former people's old statutes,
were preserved and recorded without attribution:
the chapters on "Yòu Guān" (Junior Officials) and "Dìzǐ" (Disciples),
and the instructions in "Yuè Lìng" (Monthly Ordinances) and "Tǔ Fāng" (Soil Methods) are examples of this.
In compiling their words and deeds,
not everything recorded was necessarily discussed and narrated by the person himself:
Guǎn Zhòng’s narration of events following his death,
and Hán Fēi’s inclusion of Lǐ Sī’s "Bó Yì" (Disputing Opinions) are examples.
Regarding the chapters of
"Ràng Wáng" (Yielding the Throne) and "Yú Fù" (The Fisherman) in Zhuāngzǐ,
Mister Sū (Sū Shì) called them forgeries;
they are not forgeries,
but were merely added later by scholars of the Zhuāng school.
Concerning the Yànzǐ Chūnqiū,
Mister Liǔ (Liǔ Zōngyuán) claimed it was the words of the Mò school (Mòzhe).
It is not that Yànzǐ was Mò (Mohist),
but rather that Mohist scholars narrated the affairs of Yànzǐ
to name their book,
just as Mèngzǐ (Mencius) named his chapters after Gào Zǐ and Wàn Zhāng.
The Lǚ Shì Chūnqiū (Spring and Autumn Annals of Lǚ),
was discussed by earlier Confucians alongside the Huáinán Hóngliè (Master of Huáinán),
generally meaning that they were compiled by gathering many retainers,
and thus could not claim to be the words of a single expert.
This is certainly true.
However, Lǚ Shì and Huáinán
never made a secret of their collective compilation,
unlike later generations who concealed others' strengths and claimed them as their own.
These two schools certainly used the authority of editing and defining
to designate the works as the words of their respective houses,
thus their fundamental purpose
always conformed to one standard.
This, moreover, was something in which the retainers had no part.
The vigorous rise of the various philosophers
was due to the splitting of the Dào and its arts.
Each, relying on the biased aspect of his intelligence and talent,
often gained an insight into one corner of the Great Dào,
and thereupon wished to reform the world with it.
Those whose doctrines were well-founded
and whose words were rationally constructed
naturally sought to elaborate their scholarship
and transmit it to their disciples.
If it was sufficient to demonstrate their technique and establish their school,
then those who cited previous works
and those who supplemented later expansions
never divided the merit of establishing the words.
Therefore it is said:
The words of the ancients,
were thus meant for the public good,
and they never boasted of their literary refinement,
nor privately claimed them as their own possession.
. Mèngzǐ said
: "Its matters concern Qí Huán and Jìn Wén
, its literary style is that of history"
. Kǒngzǐ himself claimed merely to have borrowed its righteousness/principles (*yì*)
. Scholars who take up the brush
, and who aspire to the great work of the *Chūnqiū*
, must certainly seek only the righteousness/principles (*yì*)
; its matters and its style
are merely the means used to preserve the righteousness/principles (*yì*)
. Those in the world who criticize Sīmǎ Qiān
, fault him for segmenting and fragmenting the texts of the *Shàngshū*, the *Zuǒ Shì*, the *Guó Yǔ*, and the *Guó Cè*
, claiming the division was inappropriate
. (This quote is from Sū Míngyǔn’s *Shǐ Lùn*.) Those in the world who criticize Bān Gù
, fault him for inheriting/plagiarizing Sīmǎ Qiān's writings concerning the period before Xiàowǔ (Emperor Wǔ)
, claiming it was shameless theft
. (This quote is from Zhèng Yúzhòng’s *Tōng Zhì*.) These are entirely illogical arguments regarding literary structure and principle
. Sīmǎ Qiān's history begins with the Five Emperors (*Wǔ Dì*)
, and continues through the Three Dynasties (*Sān Dài*), the Zhōu, and the Qín
. If he were to abandon the *Shàngshū*, the *Zuǒ Shì*, and the *Guó Yǔ*
, would he then rely on nothingness, composing works based on non-existent facts
? If it must be insisted that the contents following the *Zuǒ Shì* and the *Guó Yǔ*
were composed by Sīmǎ Qiān himself
, then Lù Jiǎ’s *Chǔ Hàn Chūnqiū*
, and the biographies (*zhuàn*) of Gāozǔ and Xiàowén
were all sources that Sīmǎ Qiān selected and collected
. Those books were not transmitted to later generations
, but merely based on the *Shàngshū*, the *Zuǒ Shì*, and the *Guó Yǔ* that people *did* see
, they criticized him for fragmentation
. This can be called knowing ten minus one but not knowing five times two
. Bān Gù's writing covers only the period of the Western Capital (*Xījīng*)
. If, concerning the period before Xiàowǔ
, he did not use Sīmǎ Qiān's history
, would he then write different prose on the same subject, just like scholars preparing for imperial examinations
? If it must be insisted that the contents following Xiàowǔ
were composed by Bān Gù himself
, then the records (*jì*) of Féng Shāng and Yáng Xióng
, and the writings (*shū*) of Liú Xīn and Jiǎ Hù
were all original sources for Bān Gù
. Those books were not seen by later people
, but merely based on the history of Sīmǎ Qiān that people *did* see
, they criticized him for shameless theft
. This can be called knowing the white entry but not knowing the black exit
. To regard recording speech as mere fabrication
? The rhymed prose (*cí fù*) of Yáng (Xióng) and Mǎ (Xiāngrú)
, were especially empty and lacking in substance
. Sīmǎ Qiān (Mǎ) and Bān Gù (Bān) did not create a Biographies of Literati (*Wén Yuàn Zhuàn*) section
, but by this means, preserved elegance and literary splendor
, which is the greatest aspect of narrating events
. To regard narrating events as merely demanding factual evidence
? The Chronological Tables (*Nián Biǎo*) and the sectional headings of the Biographies (*Zhuàn Mù*)
, are especially substantial but lacking in literary style
. The headings like "Qū Yuán and Jiǎ Yí," "Mèng Zǐ and Xún Zǐ," and "Lǎo Zǐ, Zhuāng Zǐ, Shēn Bùhài, and Hán Fēi"
, and the distinct tables for "Marquis-Kings of the Imperial Clan (*Tóng Xìng Hóu Wáng*)" and "Marquis-Kings of Different Surnames (*Yì Xìng Hóu Wáng*)"
, do not initially contain any explicit elaboration
, but merely preserve the topic headings
. The meaning of praise and censure
is implicitly contained within them
, which is the greatest aspect of establishing literary principles (*lì yán*)
. In writing history, it is vital to understand the intent
; it is not the same as mere historical records (*zhǎng gù*)
, which seek only the trivial details of events and style
. Fūzǐ said
: "If I desired to rely on empty words
, it would be better to reveal them through actions, which is profound, explicit, and clear."
This is the fundamental principle of the historian
. If the righteousness/principles (*yì*) can be grasped and the purpose (*zhì*) made clear
, then the sequence of events and the composition of the essays
have never failed to contribute to the accomplishment of establishing literary principles
. Therefore it is said
: The words of the ancients
are meant to be shared by all (*gōng*)
; they never boasted of their literary refinement
, or privately claimed them as their own
. The masters of the classics (*jīng shī*) in the early Hàn dynasty
, clinging to fragments and preserving incomplete texts
, used their lifelong energy
to illuminate the residual words (*xù yán*) of the former sages
. The profound origins of their transmission from teacher to disciple
are equivalent to the lineage and genealogy of a clan
; by observing the scholarly achievements of the disciples
, the transmission and inheritance from the teacher
is as distinct as the black and white of ducks and swans, impossible to confuse
. Scholars must exert their utmost effort in this regard
. Regarding the *Chūnqiū*, the schools of Gōngyáng and Gǔliáng
, later people believed that they established hypothetical questions and answers merely to elaborate on the core meaning
. They do not realize that the ancients first had oral transmission
, and only afterwards committed it to bamboo and silk
. It was not like later people composing commentaries on the classics (*jīng yì*)
, where if one desires to establish a famous school (*míng jiā*)
, one must rely on written works for achievement
. Shāng Qú received the *Yì* (Classic of Changes) from Fūzǐ
. Five generations later, it reached Tián Hé
. Shī, Mèng, and Liángqiū
were all disciples of Tián Hé
. However, from Tián Hé backwards
, there had never been any written text
. Therefore, the *Yì* of these three schools
, recorded in the *Yì Wén Zhì* (Treatise on Literature)
, are all fundamentally derived from the orally transmitted learning existing prior to Tián Hé
. From this, we know that even if the ancients did not write books
, their words were certainly transmitted
. Those who study Hán’s version of the *Shī* (Classic of Poetry)
do not mix it with the Qí and Lǔ versions
; those who transmit Fú’s version of the *Shū* (Classic of History)
do not know Kǒng’s learning
. For the various schools studying chapters, verses, and exegetical interpretation (*zhāng jù xùn gǔ*)
, there are specialized books
. When disciples and followers
quote, cite, and narrate
, and their statements appear mixed in biographies, records, and memorials (*zhuàn jì zhāng biǎo*)
, they do not entirely come from the transmitted books
, yet the fundamental principles ultimately do not contradict the teacher's doctrine
. Thus, besides the books written and completed by the various scholars
, there were distinct subtle words (*wēi yán*) and supplementary discussions (*xù lùn*)
orally imparted to their followers
. And the scholars, having mastered their intent
, expanded and elaborated upon them
, and recorded them in writing
. One no longer distinguishes whether it was instructed by the teacher
or derived by the disciple
. And when people observe this
, they determine it to be the learning of that specific school (*jiā*) based on the individual
, no longer distinguishing which came from the teacher’s doctrine
, and which came from the disciple’s doctrine
. Since the goal is sufficient to comprehend the classic (*jīng*) and transmit the learning (*xué*)
, then oral transmission, auditory learning, bamboo slips, and silk scrolls
have never been separated in their contribution to establishing principles (*lì yán*)
. Therefore it is said
: The words of the ancients
are meant to be shared by all (*gōng*)
; they never boasted of their literary refinement
, or privately claimed them as their own
When the instruction of the
world declines,
if the Way (Dào) is insufficient and people compete based on rhetoric,
then speech (yán) can be obtained and privatized;
if substance (shí) is not sufficient and people compete based on reputation (míng),
then rhetoric (wén) can be obtained and boasted about.
If speech can be obtained and privatized,
and rhetoric can be obtained and boasted about,
then the spirit of contention arises, and the methods of the Way (dàoshù) are fractured.
The words of the ancients
were intended to enlighten the world;
but the words of later people
are intended to deceive the world.
It is not that their hearts are content with deceiving the world,
but having something they privatize and boast about,
they cannot avoid acting in this manner.
The words of the ancients
were intended to improve others;
the words of later people
are intended to display themselves.
It is not that the ancients did not wish to display themselves,
while later people are particularly keen to do so,
but having deficiencies and insufficiencies,
they cannot avoid acting in this manner.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Is the fletcher necessarily unkind compared to the armorer?
The practice of skills must be handled with caution."
The ancients established their words by adopting what is easy;
later people establish their words by adopting what is difficult.
How can this be made clear?
What the ancients desired to communicate
was the Way (Dào).
They spoke only when unavoidable,
like happiness within making one unable not to laugh,
or illness afflicting the body making one unable not to groan.
How could they calculate skill, clumsiness, quickness, or slowness,
and deliberately force themselves to imitate a model?
As for where the Way resides,
learning moves toward it;
where learning resides,
people of the same kind gather toward it.
When the ancients spoke,
if someone first attains the same understanding in their heart
as mine, that is the same as my own words.
Why?
Because their Way is the same.
When transmitted to others,
if they can grasp my explanation and flexibly apply it,
that is the same as my own words.
Why?
Because their Way is the same.
Exhausting a lifetime of learning, questioning, reflection, and debate upon the fixed Way,
and communicating upwards with people of the same Way through the ages to serve as a foundation,
and waiting downwards for people of the same Way through the ages to serve as assistance—
their establishment of words,
is it not easy?
But as for those whose wisdom is without a teacher,
who are keen to produce rhetoric without substance,
they force a smiling expression when unhappy,
and deliberately groan when they are not ill;
they are already overcome by effort and exhaustion;
much less when they harbor selfish intentions
fearing exposure, and steal and occupy an undeserved reputation they claim for themselves.
Having no foundation ahead
and no support behind,
their position is isolated, perilous, and insecure—
is this not difficult?
The words externally embellished,
versus the words arising from within—
the measure of their difficulty and ease can be known.
The words that do not seek to compete for fame,
versus the words that absolutely seek to compete for fame—
the measure of their difficulty and ease
can also be known.
Words that span antiquity and the present, before and after,
and are made public for all to share;
versus words that are privately claimed, uniquely possessed,
and must be declared to originate from oneself—
the measure of their difficulty and ease
can also be known.
Will the scholar who establishes words
intend to focus on the Way (Dào),
and follow what is public and easy?
Or will they merely compete in rhetoric (wén),
and follow what is private and difficult?
Between public and private,
difficult and easy, there must be a distinction.
Alas!
How can one find a scholar who truly knows words
and encourage them to advance along the Way?
In antiquity, there were instances of stealing another person’s words and claiming them as one's own.
Bó Zōng’s reply concerning Liáng Shān
not only received the reprimand of having no descendants,
but also incurred the guilt of obscuring the worthy.
In antiquity, there were instances of stealing another person’s writings and claiming them as one's own.
When Qū Píng was writing a draft that was not yet finalized,
Shàngguān Dàfū saw it and tried to seize it;
he not only intended to deceive the sovereign,
but also slandered a friend.
Stealing the excellence of others
is equivalent to the crime of a thief stealing property;
Lǎo Shì spoke of this with great certainty.
This fault arises from privatizing one's own talent and wisdom,
and not knowing how to attribute it publicly to the Way (Dào).
If Bó Zōng had recommended the worthiness of the carriage driver,
and used the established idea of weeping in plain silk at the shrine,
those would have been Bó Zōng’s words for reviving the state,
and his merit would not have been limited to the affair of Liáng Shān.
If Shàngguān Dàfū had treated Qū Píng well and supported the laws he formulated,
those would have been Shàngguān’s words for founding the state of Chǔ,
and his merit would not have been limited to the excellence of the laws.
Hán Qí was Chancellor,
and Ōuyáng Xiū was a Hanlin Academician.
Someone claimed that Lord Hán had no literary skill (wénzhāng);
Hán replied, "Qí is Chancellor and employs Xiū as an Academician;
of all the literary skill in the world,
whose is greater than Qí’s?"
Alas!
A man like Hán Shì
can be said to have understood the ancient meaning of publicizing words.
For those who steal the words of others
and claim them as their own,
the desire for fame (hàomíng) is the worst offense,
and competing for merit is secondary.
Merit deceives for a time,
but fame deceives for a thousand ages.
For those who take their own compositions
and falsely attribute them to the ancients,
illegal profit (jiānlì) is the worst offense,
and seeking amusement is secondary;
seeking amusement limits the crime to the individual,
but illegal profit encourages imitation and corrupts the public morality.
Qí Qiū stole the *Huà Shū* from Tán Qiào,
and Guō Xiàng stole the commentary on *Zhuāngzǐ* from Xiàng Xiù;
the superior man considers them shallow, frivolous, and without integrity.
If the original authors were conscious,
they would only desire their teachings to be clearly understood throughout the world,
and not necessarily demand that they be clearly attributed to themselves.
However, one cannot help but be grieved by those who steal,
because the cunning of breaking through walls and prying open boxes
necessarily involves altering and rearranging the work to cover up the theft,
and thus losing the original intent.
Liú Xuàn’s *Lián Shān*
and Méi Zé’s *Gǔwén Shàngshū*
were presented upon imperial command,
intending to seek official position and profit.
Insulting the words of the sages,
and secretly comparing oneself to the researches of Héjiān and Hénèi—
the superior man considers their crime too great for punishment.
Since the *Fén Diǎn* [ancient texts] have already perished,
the compilations and patchworks of forgers may not lack one-tenth of the originals surviving.
Nevertheless, one cannot but profoundly detest the forgers:
lost passages and scattered phrases,
when appended to existing fragments,
still preserve their meaning;
but when they are fabricated into complete books,
their meaning is utterly lost.
If they had exchanged the mental effort used for forgery
and claimed the compilation and patching as their own merit,
would their achievement have been inferior to the *Lǐ* (Rites) of Héjiān
or the *Shū* (Documents) of Hénèi?
Wáng Bóhòu’s *Sānjiā Shī Kǎo* and Wú Cǎolú’s *Yì Lǐ*... Guō Xiàng’s interpretations of *Qiū Shuǐ* and *Dá Shēng*,
are not without insightful sayings and renowned principles that could rank second only to Xiàng [Xiù];
had he clarified and elaborated upon their central ideas,
and had them circulate alongside
the commentary written by Xiù,
observers would not have been able to distinguish which belonged to Xiàng [Xiù] and which to Guō [Xiàng].
Why resort so quickly to the techniques of a housebreaker?
Not knowing the meaning of publicizing words,
but wanting to privatize and profit for oneself and claim it as merit,
causes the Great Way (Dà Dào) to be obscured, and the integrity of the mind can no longer be trusted.
There are no scholars who do not aspire to immortality,
but do they truly know that immortality fundamentally has its own way (Dào)?
Speaking generally in the world,
books sometimes perish,
but the learning contained within does not immediately cease.
This is because the learning forms a school (jiā),
and those who propagate it endure,
and observers who investigate and seek it out can recognize it.
Although the Ancient Text (Gǔwén) tradition of the Kǒng Shì clan perished,
Shǐ Qiān inquired about the past from Ān Guó.
Now, Shǐ Qiān’s writings are fully extant,
and the *Shū* (Classic of Documents) of the Kǒng Shì clan,
has not entirely perished.
Although the *Shī* (Classic of Poetry) tradition of the Hán Shì clan perished,
Xǔ Shèn studied the *Shī* while including the Hán Shì school;
Now, the *Shuōwén* is fully extant,
and the *Shī* of Hán Yīng,
has not entirely perished.
Liú Xiàng’s *Hóngfàn Wǔxíng Zhuàn* (Commentary on the Five Phases in the Great Plan),
and the *Qīlüè Biélù* (Seven Summaries and Separate Catalogue) may have perished,
but Bān Gù’s historical scholarship originated from Liú Xīn;
Liú Xīn’s *Hàn Jì* was the basis for the *Hàn Shū*. Now, the two monographs, *Wǔxíng* and *Yìwén*, are fully extant,
and the learning of the Liú Shì clan has not perished.
There are also later scholars who rely on earlier masters,
Chǔ Shàosūn borrowed the brilliance of Mǎ Qiān,
Péi Sōngzhī leaned on the light of Chén Shòu;
if they did not attach themselves to the swift horse,
their own power would be insufficient for survival.
There are also those whose Dào is similar and whose methods are close,
whose writings, unfortunately, perished or were lost,
but who survived through fellow practitioners of the Dào:
the *Lièzǐ* is fragmented and incomplete,
half of it is recounted in the work of Master Zhuāng (Zhuāng Shēng);
the writings of Yáng Zhū perished,
much of it is preserved in the *Hánzǐ*;
This is because Zhuāng and Liè both emerged from the Dàojiā school,
and Yáng Zhū emphasized “for myself,”
his methods were inherently close to the School of Names and the School of Law.
There are also those whose talent and wisdom displayed themselves,
but were not sufficient to establish a school (jiā),
yet, because their Dào found an affinity,
they were fortunate to preserve the substance of their carving and cutting:
Gào Zǐ’s arguments concerning the Qǐ willow and rushing water,
were transmitted thanks to Mèngzǐ;
Huì Shī’s discussions on the white horse and three legs,
became prominent because of Master Zhuāng;
although they served as targets for the archers,
they also revealed unconstrained talent,
and were not utterly lost.
There are also trivial remarks,
which originally had no lofty theories,
but were fortunate to enter into accord with a perceptive mind,
and eventually set down classical precepts.
The song of the child washing his feet,
communicates principles concerning the family and the state;
the common saying of the time about crops growing large,
is attested to by the body and mind.
For those that illustrate principles,
even the shallow can become profound;
and for those that are preserved,
nothing coarse fails to become refined.
In all such cases,
it is not necessarily that the ancients found it easy while later people found it difficult,
or that the ancients were skillful while later people were clumsy,
or that the ancients were right while later people were wrong.
The circumstances surrounding fame and substance are different,
the nature of public versus private motivations differs,
and those who intended their words versus those who did not intend their words,
cannot be spoken of in the same breath.
Therefore, it is said:
Words written without intending to write survive,
words written with the intention to write perish.
Now, when common people have a lawsuit,
both parties submit their statements,
and the official in charge receives them.
They must base rewards and punishments for rightness or wrongness on the statements.
The statements submitted,
how could they necessarily have been composed by the rustic commoners themselves?
Yet the rewards and punishments for rightness or wrongness,
are not imposed upon the one who composed the statement,
but upon the litigants,
because the intent behind the spoken word is prioritized,
and the origin of the words need not be considered.
Regarding tombs, fields, pathways,
ancestral temples, and lineage branches,
when investigating and examining stelae and tablets,
no matter how crude or vulgar the text is,
it is said that to compare and discuss rightness and wrongness,
there is no other way to grasp the crucial facts.
Is it that there are no bronze vessels and tripods from the Three Dynasties (Sāndài),
or stone carvings from Qín and Hàn,
whose inscriptions are wonderfully archaic,
and whose characters are refined and profound,
things that later generations cannot obtain?
If they are used to clarify the facts of an event,
though they are commonplace, they cannot be discarded;
if they have no relevance to the matter,
though they are marvelous, they are not worth arguing over.
If this is the case, then later scholars,
who strive for technical skill in the trivialities of writing,
and who desire to claim it for their private use,
are truly unworthy to discuss the Dào.
Someone might say:
“The meaning must be far-reaching and the rhetoric elegant,”
this is the teaching of the *Dàzhuàn*.
“If the rhetoric is far-fetched, it is vulgar and contrary (to reason),”
this is the statement of the worthy and accomplished.
“If words are not ornate,
they will not travel far.”
Therefore, rhetoric cannot be abandoned.
Now you say that those who strive for technical skill in the trivialities of writing are wrong—
what, then, should be the standard for establishing one’s words?” I reply:
That is not what I meant.
The *Yì* (Yìjīng) says:
“Refine the rhetoric to establish sincerity (chéng).”
Sincerity does not necessarily require the ultimate achievement of perfect sincerity (zhìchéng) by a sage,
before it is worthy of refining the rhetoric and establishing it.
When scholars engage in literary expression,
regardless of how the expression is constructed,
if they adhere to it, there must be a reason for it,
and it was not merely produced for the sake of literary form—
that is all sincerity.
If there is a reason for it,
and the rhetoric is refined to accord with that reason,
then the striving for technical skill therein,
is the means by which they seek to express their sincerity.
“The *Yì* is strange yet standard,
the *Shī* is correct yet flowery,”
the *Yì* expresses the Yīnyáng,
the *Shī* expresses human nature and emotions (xìngqíng).
The reason why they were refined to be strange or flowery,
is fundamentally because they believed that if they were not so,
they could not manifest the principles of Yīnyáng or the emergence of xìngqíng.
Therefore, I say:
It is not merely striving for skill.
If there is the writing but no substance,
even the rhetoric of the Six Classics (Liù Yì),
would still have nothing worthy of adoption,
how much less so regarding other writings?
Writing (wén),
is an empty vessel; the Dào,
is the genuine target.
That writing should be skillful,
is like a bow and arrow needing to be good quality.
A bow and arrow can defend against invaders,
but can also be used by invaders.
This does not concern whether the bow and arrow are good quality or poor quality.
Writing can elucidate the Dào,
but can also oppose the Dào.
This does not concern whether the writing is skillful or unskillful.
Chén Lín drafted a declaration for Yuán Shào,
proclaiming the crimes of Cáo Cāo.
Its literary quality was never anything but magnificent and vigorous.
Later, when he met Cáo,
he likened himself to an arrow that must follow the bowstring.
If he had written the declaration for Cáo Cāo against Yuán Shào,
his skill would certainly have been the same.
If this is the case, merely possessing excellence in literary rhetoric,
but lacking relevance to the Dào,
is analogous to a good quality boat or carriage;
it is indeed convenient for the passenger,
but whether one is heading towards Yān or Yuè,
cannot be known.
The words of the Shèng Rén (Sages),
are recounted by Xián Rén (Worthies),
but sometimes their meaning is lost.
The words of the Xián Rén,
are recounted by common people,
but sometimes their meaning is lost.
The hearts of men differ,
just like their faces.
Yet, why is it said that words entrusted to the public sphere (gōng)
do not necessarily all originate from oneself?
What is the reason?
It is likely because if the Dào (Way) is the same and the virtue (dé) accords,
the ultimate result will not lead to divergence.
Furthermore, when citing stanzas from poetry (fù shī duàn zhāng),
