it is no different than if they issued from one's own mouth,
yet the original intent is not constrained.
When arguments are introduced and mutually debated,
though their meaning might sometimes be contradictory,
the ancients allowed them both to exist and did not discard them.
When previous generations had words,
and later generations cite them to gain weight,
this is equating the ancients with oneself.
When previous generations had words,
and later generations follow and expand upon them,
this is attaching oneself to the ancients.
The Rén (Benevolent) see benevolence (rén),
the Zhì (Wise) see wisdom (zhì).
Regarding words that derive difference from similarity,
and similarity from difference,
they are probably like the feathers of autumn birds,
impossible to list completely.
This is why later generations recount the words of former generations,
yet do not discard the original works of those former generations.
Thinking that both should coexist under heaven and earth,
while right and wrong, loss and gain,
are left to the wise (zhì zhě) to differentiate and select,
this is precisely the principle of public fairness (gōng).
The Jūn Zǐ (Gentleman) hates those who steal others’ words,
and swiftly erase their traces,
thereby achieving the selfish act of concealing their authorship.
As for cases where the works of former generations have already been lost,
and one is compelled to rely on the accounts of later generations,
this is truly unavoidable;
it is comparable to an ancestor whose sacrifices are lost,
but whose kinsman is found to conduct the rites,
which can also communicate with the ancestor's spirit (hún pò).
Unless one understands the purpose of the Analogy of Public Fairness (Yán Gōng),
it is insufficient to grasp this.
Therefore, one should extensively peruse the forest of literature (Wén Lín),
and circle through the garden of arts (Yì Yuàn);
Separating the form to gain the semblance,
loosening the reins and removing the bridle;
Above, observing the intent of the author,
below, absorbing the writings of contemporary trends.
Once the learning derived only through mouth and ear (oral transmission) wanes,
the merit of bamboo and silk (written texts) becomes evident.
When a dwelling place is found for the feet,
then carved jade (Xuán Diāo) begins to appear;
Hairy leaves protect against the cold,
leading eventually to compilation and organization.
Names and words (míng yán) were forgotten in remote antiquity (Tài Chū),
while differing schools (liú bié) arose in recent times.
Like water bubbling vigorously poured from a flask,
thus one lifts one's robe to cross the ford;
If dikes and defenses are needed to rescue against floods,
then square boats must be used to cross the turmoil.
By extending the fundamental principle of public fairness (Yán Gōng),
we attain the single thread (yī guàn) of our Dào.
Only by using it daily without realizing it,
like the owl forgetting the projectile aimed at it.
If you try to observe the stream's course,
it is luxuriantly green like a spring garden bed.
When the nine layers (imperial palace) stand lofty,
and the six directions (the world) share the same custom.
The royal utterances (wáng yán) are imperial decrees (lún fú),
the primordial essence (yuán qì) fills the universe.
The ministers who grasp the handles of government,
assist the plans in the imperial hall (Diàn Bǎi);
The scholars who wear writing brushes and hold writing slips,
receive the command under the imperial maple (Chén Fēng).
Thus, in the Western Wing (Xī Yè), decrees are drafted,
and by the Northern Gate (Běi Mén), drafts are reviewed.
The celestial wind (tiān fēng) spreads to the four directions,
the deep thunder (yuān léi) shakes the eight cardinal points.
Spreading the overflowing sounds of virtue (dé yīn),
recounting the inner feelings of anxiety and diligence (yōu qín).
If culture (wén) is honored, it is like the music of Sháo and Huò filling the mountains and seas (Shān Sháo Hǎi Huò),
if military might (wǔ) is strengthened, it is like grand preparation and forceful driving (Tài Mò Pà Qū).
When administration (zhèng) is spread, clouds and dragons follow the rhythm (yún lóng jiù lǜ),
when disasters are relieved, doves and swans return to plumpness (jiū hú huí rú).
These things are all stored in the Stone Chamber and Metal Coffer (Shí Shì Jīn Téng),
and held in honor by officials managing historical records (Shǐ Chéng Zhǎng Gù);
While in blue cases and yellow scrolls (piǎo hán xiāng zhóu),
scholars compile them as family records (jiā shū).
The records kept by the Left Scribe and Right Scribe,
the sovereign (wáng zhě) holds nothing back;
The collections of internal (nèi zhì) and external decrees (wài zhì),
are not monopolized by the literary ministers (cí chén).
Although the archives (mù tiān) are quiet and secret,
public declarations (gōng yán) have designated officials;
and in humble dwellings (zhú diàn máo yán),
mutual preservation does not obstruct external transmission—this is the public nature of decrees (zhì gào zhī gōng).
Turning to supporting literature and examining the past (yòu wén jī gǔ),
purchasing classics and inviting talents (gòu diǎn yán yīng).
The Luán Tái (Phoenix Terrace) recounts history,
the Hǔ Guān (Tiger Gate) discusses the classics.
Discussing scales and regulating standards,
the theories regarding the Six Heavens (Liù Tiān), Five Emperors (Wǔ Dì), Three Sequences (Sān Tǒng), and Nine Divisions (Jiǔ Chóu),
are upheld by various specialized scholars;
The grievances over the Lǐ (Rites) and disputes over the Shū (Documents),
the theories regarding Qí dialects (Qí yán), Lǔ traditions (Lǔ gù), Kǒng’s wall finds (Kǒng Bì), and Liáng tombs (Liáng Fén),
are adjudicated by imperial regulation (chēng zhì) to achieve balance.
The Zhèng Yì (Correct Meanings) were definitively established by one school,
and the Jìn Shǐ (History of Jìn) was condensed to a hundred scrolls.
Six hundred years of commentaries and detailed notes,
and eighteen schools of compiled annals and biographies.
Like the Zhāng River splitting and the Jiāng River merging,
the Jǐ River flowing underground and the Hé River cutting across,
the Huái, Shēn, and Miǎn Rivers winding,
all swiftly converging toward the mighty sea;
Jadeite green and sky blue,
dark blue and purplish fungus,
water jasper and cinnabar red,
splendidly manifested in glorious colors.
All this is to unify standards of writing and laws (tǒng chē shū), and standardize sight and sound (yī shì tīng),
to regulate musical scales and suppress heterodoxy and excess.
Although generally named as being fixed by imperial edict (chì dìng),
the task was actually carried out by Confucian ministers (rú chén).
The leaders of the high ranks (chóng bān),
had their names listed on the first slips when presenting the work;
But the names of the mass of workers who gathered to work,
were all obscured at the time.
When a new temple is dedicated with merit,
how can one calculate the hurried efforts of all the craftsmen,
and record their individual contributions?
When a grand sacrifice (míng yīn) completes the ritual,
why discuss the cook preparing the offerings,
while the invoker (shī zhù) presents the prayer?
Furthermore, in the Three Terraces (Sān Tái) and Eight Seats (Bā Zuò),
and the hundreds of offices and subordinate departments,
The military commissioners (jié zhèn) governing their sectors,
and the commanderies and counties (jùn xiàn) administering separately.
Arranged like clustered stars in the autumn sky (qiū mín),
growing the hundred grains in the fields of the east (dōng zī).
Account books (bù shū) are densely packed,
documents and registers (juǎn dié) are scattered widely.
The brilliance of the Bureau of Civil Affairs (Wén Chāng), the Military Arsenal (Wǔ Kù),
the Department of Rites, and the Office of Music (Lǐ Sī Yuè Shǔ),
is like spokes converging to rotate the axle of a wheel;
The regulations concerning weapons (jiǎ bīng), legal cases (àn sòng),
money and goods (qián huò), and agricultural fields (nóng tián),
are like chess pieces placed neatly on a lined board.
They proceed in a line, presenting the documents from Lán Tián,
following the prescribed formula (lìng shì) and literary style;
The leader summons his followers from Píng Yuán,
following the precedents (gù shì) and nodding assent.
Thus, ordering the brush is like issuing a knife,
and the document is called Lì (Clerical script/Clerks).
The issuing of words originates from the clerks (xū tú),
but the success or failure belongs to the chief officials (cháng lì).
For when all the officials govern and the myriad people are examined,
this is the reason why knotted cords were replaced by written documents (shū qì).
The ignorant merely argue about the minor details,
but the wise (zhī zhě) understand the original intent—this is the public nature of official documents (wén yí zhī gōng).
the marquises, kings, generals, and chancellors,
the regional governors (yuè mù) and high officials (qún gōng). The bell gates (líng gé)
initiate matters,
the halberd gates (jǐ mén) manage military affairs. They possess
the wealth and eminence of high status,
and embody the majesty of civil and military authority. Then there are
the graceful secretaries (shū jì),
the elegant renowned scholars (míng shì),
the staff and guests (bīn kè) of the headquarters (mù fǔ),
and the literary clerks (yuàn shǐ). Like the sparrow hawk
striking the seaside,
Zhèng Zhòng (Zhòng Lián) sends a flying letter (fēi shū) to the desert;
like the eagle soaring over the region north of the Yellow River (Hé Shuò),
Chén Lín (Kǒng Zhāng) rushes a declaration (chí xí) at Dāng Tú. Wáng Càn
was impassioned and relied upon Liú (Liú Biǎo),
his rhymes were spread throughout the watchtowers (jué) of Jīng (Jīngzhōu);
Bān Gù was unconventional and followed Dòu (Dòu Xiàn),
his inscription was carved at Láng Jū (Lángjūshān). When the straw is
trampled and the road destroyed,
the departed soul is moved by Xiè Huì Lián’s (Huì Lián) lament;
when the oriole sings and the flowers bloom,
the living soul returns via Fàn Xī Fàn’s (Xī Fàn) letter. These writings sometimes
penetrate the hardness of metal and stone with sincerity,
and arouse the spirit of loyalty and valor like wind and clouds. When
emotions are conveyed, green grass springs up in the springtime;
when arguments surge forth, yellow waves boil in the summer. When they move
the hidden world, mountain spirits weep at night;
when they manifest clearly, sea spirits clear the dawn sky. They are all capable of
pursuing the remote and entering the dark,
conveying the heart and reaching the intent. They change
according to the person,
bending and twisting as desired. Because
the path to profit and salary is wide,
the skill of speculation (chuǎi mó) subtly achieves its goal. The collections of
writers in the Middle and Late periods
are mostly skills of the ghostwriter (zhuō dāo). Since they
harmonize the carriage and match the bells,
how can they separate the road and fight for the banner? It is heard that
when one is satisfied with wealth and nobility,
one yearns for the immortals (shén xiān). When
the art of alchemy (huáng bái zhī shù) fails,
the esteem for literature (wén zhāng) then prevails. Considering
the immortality of living people,
longevity is not as good as having one’s name transmitted; Since they
punish the foolish and glorify the wise,
they subsequently surpass the past with the later. Thus, there are those
whose rank commands seven sable tails (qī diāo),
or whose households are allotted ten thousand fiefs, who,
during their dignified retirement from office,
or during their days off (xiū mù) and leisurely banquets. They feel ashamed
of being obscured by worldly glory,
and thus elegantly yearn for narrative praise (shù zàn). Therefore,
refined scholars gather in the Western Garden (Xī Yuán),
and literati are hosted in the Eastern Pavilion (Dōng Gé); Pencils are
laid out and writing boards set up,
black ink is spread and red corrections are revealed. Seeking
the magnificent achievements of the forest of arts (yì lín),
they consequently combine their strength and plan together. Some
carry the unpolished jade of Jīng Shān,
some boast of the pearl of Suí Hóu, Some treasure
the stone from the marketplace of Yān (Yānjì),
and some fraudulently play the reed pipe (yú) at the gate of Qí (Qímén); They all
harbor private motives and flatter themselves,
watching the master’s signal and rushing forward. Since they
gather much and use it widely,
this is like stacking grain and collecting straw. They rely
on great strength to include all that exists,
providing material for skillful study and research. Establishing achievement
is indeed equal to establishing words (lì yán);
how could it ever be inferior to the original creations of the specialist? Turning to matters such as

Expressing words based on personal realization and comprehension,

Establishing rules based on innate conscience,

All these divisions and categories [Qūfēn Lèibié],

Delicate flowers beautify spring,

They reach the extreme of shallow and profound differences,

When they are hidden, they are almost universal;

The capable have nothing to compete for regarding fame,

The Historian's Virtue [Shǐdé]
The three qualities of talent [Cái], learning [Xué], and insight [Shì],
obtaining even one is not easy,
and possessing all three is especially difficult.
Throughout the ages there have been many literary men but few good historians [Liángshǐ];
this is the reason why.
Formerly, Liú Shì Zǐxuán [Liú Shì Zǐxuán],
perhaps believed this explanation was sufficient to exhaust the principle.
Although this is so,
what the historian values is meaning [Yì],
what is prepared is facts [Shì],
and what is relied upon is literary style [Wén].
Mèngzǐ said:
"The facts concern Qí Huán [Qí Huán] and Jìn Wén [Jìn Wén],
the style is historical,
but the meaning [Yì] is what the Master [Fūzǐ] himself claimed to have appropriated."
Without insight [Shì], there is no means to judge the meaning [Yì];
without talent [Cái], there is no means to perfect the style [Wén];
without learning [Xué], there is no means to refine the facts [Shì].
These three naturally have their specific points of application,
but among them there are inherent similarities that are not the genuine article.
Memorization [Jìsòng] is taken for learning [Xué],
rhetorical flourish [Cícǎi] is taken for talent [Cái],
decisive judgment [Jīduàn] is taken for insight [Shì]—
these are not the talent, learning, and insight of a good historian [Liángshǐ].
Even the so-called talent, learning, and insight of Liú Shì [Liú Shì],
is still insufficient to fully exhaust the principle.
Liú Shì [Liú Shì] believed that having learning but no insight,
is like an ignorant merchant handling gold,
not understanding how to trade or transform it.
Extending this point to verify Liú Shì's [Liú Shì] intent,
it means nothing more than wanting to know how to select
and make decisions among the memorized facts,
in order to achieve coherent literary style.
Therefore, it is said:
Ancient historians who aimed to establish a school [Chéngjiā],
dismissed retired scholars and promoted cunning heroes,
rejected those who died for their principles and embellished the faults of rulers—
they also claimed this was the way of their particular school.
This is still the insight of a literary man [Wénshì],
not the insight of a historian [Shǐshì].
One who possesses the insight of a historian,
must understand the historian’s virtue [Shǐdé].
What is virtue?
It refers to the historian’s mental disposition [Xīnshù].
One who writes corrupt history thereby corrupts himself,
one who writes slanderous books thereby slanders himself.
If one’s normal conduct is shameful to others,
how can one's writing be deemed important?
The false accusations of Wèi Shōu [Wèi Shōu],
and the secretive wickedness of Shěn Yuē [Shěn Yuē]—
those who read their books
first disbelieve the men themselves,
and the harm caused is not extreme.
What is truly troublesome regarding mental disposition [Xīnshù]
refers to those who possess the mind of a superior person [Jūnzǐ],
but whose cultivation has not yet reached purity.
Now, having the mind of a superior person [Jūnzǐ],
but lacking pure cultivation,
is something
from the great worthies downward,
that cannot be avoided.
If even this is considered problematic regarding mental disposition,
then apart from the Master's [Fūzǐ] *Chūnqiū* [Chūnqiū],
nothing is worthy of comparison.
To demand this standard of others,
is that not too difficult?
Indeed, one who wishes to be a good historian [Liángshǐ],
must carefully distinguish between the realm of Heaven and the realm of Man [Tiānrén Zhījì],
exhausting the natural [Heavenly] aspect without adding the human element.
To exhaust the natural without adding the human element—
although one may not achieve this completely,
if one sincerely understands it,
it is also sufficient to be called the proper mental disposition [Xīnshù] of a writer.
Yet the literati and historical scholars [Wénshǐ Zhī Rú],
compete to discuss talent, learning, and insight,
but do not know how to distinguish mental disposition [Xīnshù] in order to evaluate the historian's virtue [Shǐdé].
How can this be acceptable?
while disapproving of Jié and Zhòu,
everyone is able to say that. To venerate the Kingly Way (Wángdào) and reject the achievements of Hegemony (Bàgōng),
this is further the traditional habit of scholars.
As for honoring the good and hating the evil,
praising the upright and detesting the perverse,
all those who wish to entrust their written compositions
to achieve immortality
possess this mindset. However, the reason why the disposition of the mind (xīnshù) must be carefully considered
is that Heaven and Man participate equally,
and the starting points (of thought) are extremely subtle,
not something that this paltry intelligence
can rely upon. Now, what history records is deeds;
deeds must rely on writing to be transmitted.
Therefore, there is no good historian who is not skilled in writing,
yet they do not realize that writing also suffers from being enslaved by the deeds themselves.
For deeds cannot be without success and failure, right and wrong;
once there is success or failure, right or wrong,
then inclusion and exclusion, granting and seizing, contend and clash.
If the contention and clashing does not cease,
then vital energy (qì) accumulates therein.
Deeds cannot be without flourishing, decline, gain, or loss;
once there is flourishing, decline, gain, or loss,
then going back and forth, lamenting the past, causes attachment and lingering.
If the attachment and lingering does not cease,
then emotion (qíng) deepens therein.
Generally, writing is not sufficient to move people;
that which moves people
is the vital energy.
Generally, writing is not sufficient to penetrate people;
that which penetrates people
is the emotion.
When vital energy accumulates, the writing flourishes;
when emotion deepens, the writing is sincere;
when vital energy flourishes and emotion is sincere,
this is the ultimate writing in the world.
However, within this, there is Heaven and there is Man,
which must be differentiated.
Vital energy attains the strong masculinity of Yáng,
and emotion aligns with the gentle femininity of Yīn.
Man is situated between Yīn and Yáng,
unable to depart from them.
Vital energy conforming to principle (lǐ)
is Heaven;
vital energy being able to violate principle to act arbitrarily
is Man.
Emotion rooted in nature (xìng)
is Heaven;
emotion being able to overwhelm nature to indulge arbitrarily
is Man.
The essential meaning (yì) of history originates from Heaven,
but the writing (wén) of history
cannot but rely on human effort
to accomplish it. Man suffers from the maladies of Yīn and Yáng,
and if the historical writing subsequently clashes with the fairness of the Great Way (Dàdào),
the subtle influence it invokes is profound.
Now, writing cannot be established without vital energy,
but vital energy values balance (píng).
The vital energy of a person,
when dwelling in repose, is invariably balanced.
When emotion arises due to deeds,
if vital energy is lost, it becomes expansive;
if vital energy is lost, it becomes aggressive;
if vital energy is lost, it becomes arrogant;
this tends toward Yáng.
Writing is not deep without emotion,
but emotion values uprightness (zhèng).
The emotion of a person,
when placed in emptiness, is always upright.
When emotion arises due to deeds,
if emotion is lost, it becomes flowing (excessive);
if emotion is lost, it becomes indulgent;
if emotion is lost, it becomes biased;
this tends toward Yīn.
The calamity of hidden Yīn and Yáng afflictions,
riding upon the vital energy (xuèqì) and entering the heart-mind and understanding,
silently operating and secretly shifting within it,
appears impartial but actually indulges self-interest,
appears Heavenly but is actually obscured by Man;
when manifested as written composition,
it goes so far as to harm righteousness (yì) and violate the Way (Dào),
yet the person themselves still does not realize it.
Therefore, it is said that the disposition of the mind (xīnshù) must be carefully guarded.
Now, when vital energy dominates and emotion is biased,
this is still said to be motion originating from Heaven but influenced by Man.
Men of talent and skill,
furthermore, become obsessed with literary expression,
regarding it merely as a vehicle for aesthetic viewing,
without knowing that this is unacceptable.
History’s reliance on writing,
is like clothes needing color,
or food needing flavor.
Color cannot avoid being ornate or plain,
and flavor cannot avoid being rich or mild;
this is inherent tendency.
If the ornate and the plain contend, there will inevitably be false colors;
if the rich and the mild contend, there will inevitably be strange flavors.
False colors harm the eyes,
and strange flavors please the mouth,
both arising from the contention between the ornate/plain and the rich/mild.
Literary expression has skillfulness and clumsiness,
and historians currently use this as a source of competition;
this is abandoning the root and pursuing the branch.
To use this for writing,
one has yet to see its ultimate realization.
To use this for history,
how can one comprehend the fundamental principles of the ancients?
Hán Yù
said:
"The speech of a person embodying Benevolence (Rén) and Righteousness (Yì)
is gentle and harmonious." Rén is the universality of emotion;
Yì is the successful deployment of vital energy.
Chéngzǐ once said:
"Only possessing the spirit of the *Guān Jū* and *Lín Zhǐ*
can one then carry out the laws and measures of the *Zhōu Guān*."
I would therefore say that only by thoroughly understanding the intent of the analogy and metaphor (bǐ xīng) within the Six Arts (Liù Yì)
can one then lecture on the text concerning the King's Spring and First Month (Chūn Wáng Zhēng Yuè).
This essentially means that the disposition of the mind (xīnshù) is valued in cultivation.
Sīmǎ Qiān’s
130 chapters,
(and) the *Bào Rèn Ān Shū* (Letter to Rèn Ān),
state that he "investigated the boundaries between Heaven and Earth,
understood the changes of antiquity and the present,
and perfected a school of thought."
His self-preface says that he intended to "carry on the legacy of renowned ages,
correct the commentary of the *Yì Zhuàn* (Commentary on the Book of Changes),
and establish the principles of the *Shī*, *Shū*, *Lǐ*, and *Yuè* (Odes, Documents, Rites, and Music),"
this being his original purpose. What is said about writing his book out of indignation (fāfèn zhùshū)
was merely a narrative of his distress and sorrow,
used fictitiously as an excuse.
Later generations clung rigidly to the idea of "writing out of indignation,"
and thus claimed that the 130 chapters
were all motivated by resentment and slander.
Wáng Yǔn also denounced his writings as books of libel.
Consequently, later generations, in discussing literature,
took Sīmǎ Qiān
as the master of sarcasm and slander,
and treated subtle writing (wēiwén) as the great authority of the historian's duty.
Some followed this path with admiration and imitation;
this is directly taking the mindset of treacherous ministers and wicked sons
and falsely attaching it to the editing and cutting of the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals)—
is this not absurd? Now, observing the writings composed by Qiān,
such as the chapters on *Fēng Shàn* (Imperial Sacrifices) being confused by spirits,
and *Píng Zhǔn* (Stabilization of Prices) calculating against merchants and traders,
these were the flawed policies of Emperor Xiàowǔ.
When later generations read the writings of Xiāngrú
or the discourses of Huán Kuān,
how could they have waited for Sīmǎ Qiān
before recognizing these flaws? In the chapters like *Yóu Xiá* (Wandering Knights) and *Huò Zhí* (The Growers of Wealth),
it is impossible not to have feelings of strong emotion;
wise men being curious about the unusual
is indeed truly the case.
The rest (of the work) interweaves antiquity and the present,
arbitrates among the Six Arts;
how could he have dared to malign his superiors?
Zhūzǐ once said
that the *Lí Sāo* (Encountering Sorrow) does not heavily resent the ruler,
and that later generations exaggerated this point through forced interpretation.
I, therefore, believe that Sīmǎ Qiān dared not slander the sovereign;
it is merely that the readers’ own minds are unbalanced.
Now, if a person, due to personal misfortune and frustration,
extends resentment and slander to the ruler and father,
and furthermore wishes to use this to seek fame throughout the ages,
this is but the foolishness of those dissatisfied with their lot,
a criminal within the scope of the Teachings of Names (Míng Jiào),
deserving execution by Heavenly Principle (Tiānlǐ)—
what composition of theirs could possibly be transmitted?
Indeed, the *Sāo* (referring to the *Lí Sāo*) and the *Shǐ* (referring to the *Shǐ Jì*)
are the ultimate writings of a thousand ages.
The reason their writing reached this ultimate status
is that they both lifted their aspirations to the heroes of the Three Dynasties,
and interwove the principles between Heaven and Man.
Their circumstances were both distressed;
naturally, they could not be without strong emotion.
But the kind of people who are unlearned and without insight
even claim that slandering the ruler and attacking the sovereign
is acceptable and worthy of being honored as the founding principles of literary composition.
How, then, can Great Righteousness (Dàyì) be clarified,
and how can the disposition of the mind (xīnshù) be rectified?
The Master (Kǒngzǐ) said:
"The *Shī* (Odes) can inspire."
Commentators take this to mean inspiring the heart to love the good and hate the evil.
Regarding the heart that loves the good and hates the evil,
one fears that it may resemble righteousness without actually being it;
thus, it is valued that one cultivates it habitually.
The *Sāo* and the *Shǐ*
are both those profoundly versed in the *Shī*.
Their words are subtle and rich in implied meaning (fēng);
neither departs from the Teachings of Names (Míng Jiào),
yet those constrained by literary form do not differentiate this.
Therefore, it is said that one must thoroughly understand the intent of the analogy and metaphor (bǐ xīng) within the Six Arts
before one can lecture on the text concerning the King's Spring and First Month (Chūn Wáng Zhēng Yuè).
Explanation of History.
Someone asked: Is there a difference in meaning between the *shǐ* (史) in *fǔshǐ* (府史, governmental clerk) in the *Zhōuguān* (周官, Offices of Zhōu)
and the *shǐ* (史) in *Nèishǐ* (內史), *Wàishǐ* (外史), *Tàishǐ* (太史), *Xiǎoshǐ* (小史), and *Yùshǐ* (御史)?
The reply is:
There is no difference in meaning.
The *shǐ* in *fǔshǐ*
refers to commoners serving in official positions who supply clerical labor;
they are what are now called *shūlì* (書吏, scribal clerks).
The Five *Shǐ* (Wǔshǐ),
however, are composed of *qīng* (卿), *dàfū* (大夫), and *shì* (士),
who manage matters of archival records, historical compilation, decrees, and legal codes.
They are what are now called the various divisions of the *Nèigé* (內閣, Grand Secretariat), the Six Departments (*liùkē*), the *Hànlín* (翰林) Academy, and the Central Secretariat (*Zhōngshū*).
The distinction between officials (*guān*) and service personnel (*yì*),
the barrier between high and low,
and the separation of their streams of responsibility
are as vast as heaven and earth.
However, the reason there is no difference in meaning
is that both uphold the statutes and precedents (*zhǎnggù*)
and thereby preserve the Way of the Former Kings through the methods (*fǎ*).
If a *shǐ* merely guards statutes and precedents without knowing how to select among them,
it is like a *fǔ* (steward) guarding the treasury without knowing how to calculate.
The Former Kings believed that the *Tàizǎi* (太宰, Grand Steward) who controls the national expenditure,
and the *Sīkuài* (司會, Controller of Accounts) who verifies the annual achievements,
both embody the principle of balancing surplus and deficiency, and harmonizing order and fairness.
If they were not chosen for their virtue, morality, wisdom, and ability,
they could not be entrusted with the duty,
thus they were appointed with the gravity appropriate to *qīngshì* (卿士) and *dàfū*.
As for those who guard the treasury,
they dare not act autonomously in disbursements and receipts;
commoners serving in office
are sufficient to fulfill their duties without inadequacy.
However, while *qīngshì* and *dàfū*
discuss national policy
and grasp the long-term perspective,
if one asks about the minutiae of the treasury,
they must refer to the *fǔ*.
The Five *Shǐ* relate to texts and writings
just as the *Tàizǎi* and *Sīkuài* relate to finance and goods.
Concerning the *Diǎn* (典, Canons), *Mó* (謨, Counsels), *Xùn* (訓, Instructions), and *Gào* (誥, Announcements),
Zēng Shì (曾氏) suggested that “during the flourishing eras of Táng (唐), Yú (虞), and the Three Dynasties,
those who held the writing brushes and kept records
were also among the disciples of the Sages.”
His view can be called profound.
The Five *Shǐ*, selected from *qīngshì* and *dàfū*,
discuss subtle principles;
whereas the general *shǐ* merely guards the documents, records, regulations, and precedents,
and dares not act autonomously.
However, if one asks about the details and turns of the statutes and precedents,
they must refer to the *shǐ*.
The Master (Fūzǐ) said:
“The people can be made to follow (the Way),
but they cannot be made to understand it.”
The Way and the Law of the Former Kings
are not two separate things.
The *qīngshì* and *dàfū* are capable of discussing the Way,
while the *fǔshǐ* merely guards the Law.
Human knowledge
can be divided into that which can be mastered and that which cannot be mastered.
It is not that there is a separate Way of the Former Kings
apart from what the *fǔshǐ* uphold.
The Master said:
“I have heard about matters concerning the sacrificial vessels (*zǔdòu*).”
Zēngzǐ (曾子) then said:
“There are three things the gentleman values in the Way.
As for the matters of the bamboo and wooden vessels (*biāndòu*),
the officials are responsible for them.”
Zēngzǐ’s words are not different from the Master’s.
The Master was advancing the Way,
while Zēngzǐ feared people would become fixated on the methods (*fǎ*).
Zǐgòng (子貢) said:
“The Way of Wén (文) and Wǔ (武)
has not fallen to the ground;
it resides in people.
How could the Master fail to learn anything?
And how could he have a fixed teacher?”
“When he entered the Grand Ancestral Temple,
he asked about everything.”
Thus, humble service personnel (*jiànyì*),
shamans, priests, and various artisans (*wūzhù bǎigōng*),
were all those from whom the Master learned.
When asking about ritual (*lǐ*) and offices (*guān*),
how could he not be learning from those who uphold the statutes and precedents (*zhǎnggùzhě*)?
Therefore, the Way cannot be assessed abstractly,
and texts cannot be written abstractly.
Before the Three Dynasties, the Way was never specifically named as a teaching,
yet the Way was wholly present;
there was no empty principle.
Before the Three Dynasties, writing was never specifically named as composition or authorship,
yet the writings produced were unmatched by later generations;
there were no empty words.
It was only after the functions of officials (*guān*), masters (*shī*), governance (*zhì*), and teaching (*jiào*) were separated
that private authorship (*sīmén zhī zhùshù*) of texts began.
Consequently, literary studies (*wénzhāng xuéwèn*)
became distinct from the statutes and precedents managed by officials (*guānsī zhǎnggù*),
and those who established teachings could then speak of the essence of the Way (*dàotǐ*) detached from the Law.
The *Yì* (易, Book of Changes) says:
“If it is not the right person,
the Way will not proceed in vain.”
Scholars revere the Six Classics,
believing the Sages composed these texts to establish teachings for posterity.
They do not realize that during the flourishing periods of the Three Dynasties,
everyone simply upheld the statutes and precedents of their specialized office,
and the Sages did not deliberately create literary compositions.
The *Zhuàn* (傳, Commentary) says:
“In ritual,
timeliness is paramount.”
It also says:
“The writing shall be uniform (*shū tóng wén*).”
This speaks of the importance of the institutions and regulations of the temporal king.
Scholars merely recite the inherited words of the Former Sages
without understanding the institutions of the temporal king.
Thus, literature becomes a mere toy, like embroidered purses, towels, and fine silks,
and learning becomes a means for competitive novelty and guessing games (*dòu qí shè fù*),
no longer considering its practical application.
Therefore, when the Way is obscured and difficult to know,
the learning and literature of *shìdàfū*
may not be sufficient to meet the needs of the nation.
When the Law is manifest and easy to uphold,
the statutes and precedents preserved by the *shūlì*
are, in reality, where the nation’s institutions reside,
and they are also the practical traces of adaptation, reform, reduction, and augmentation
since Yáo (堯) and Shùn (舜).
Therefore, if one has no aspiration for learning, so be it.
If a gentleman truly aspires to learning,
he must seek out the canonical regulations of the present age
to apply them intimately to daily human conduct;
he must seek out the statutes and precedents of the offices
to achieve a thorough understanding of the subtleties of classical scholarship.
Only then is learning grounded in practical matters (*shíshì*),
and literature is not empty rhetoric.
This is what is meant by having substance must necessarily lead to utility.
To be ignorant of the present age yet claim fondness for antiquity,
or to be unfamiliar with statutes and precedents yet claim classical scholarship,
then the literature of embroidered purses
and the learning of guessing games,
no matter how refined and skillful,
will certainly prove irrelevant to practical application.
Mèngzǐ (孟子) said:
“One may be able to lift a hundred *jūn* (鈞, 30,000 catties)
yet be unable to lift a single feather.
One’s sight may be sharp enough to discern the tip of an autumn down,
yet one may not see a cartload of firewood.”
To find difficult what is easy,
and easy what is difficult,
is called losing the proper measure of judgment (*quándù*).
Scholars ignore the present and extensively study the past,
they neglect statutes and precedents yet master classical scholarship.
This means they can accomplish what is difficult for the *qīngshì* of the *Zhōuguān*,
but they fail to seek out what is easy for the *fǔshǐ*.
Therefore, abandoning the concrete implements (*qì*) to seek the Way,
abandoning the present to seek the past,
and abandoning daily human conduct to seek subtle scholarship,
all derive from a failure to understand that the meaning of the *shǐ* in *fǔshǐ* is connected to that of the Five *Shǐ*.
Taking the official (clerk, *lì*) as teacher
is the ancient custom of the Three Dynasties.
What the Qín (秦) people did that violated antiquity
was prohibiting the *Shī* (詩, Odes) and *Shū* (書, Documents) and merely taking the laws as teacher.
During the flourishing times of the Three Dynasties,
all learning throughout the realm
took the official as teacher.
The three hundred and sixty offices of the *Zhōuguān*
encompassed all learning, heavenly and human.
Those who upheld their offices and performed their duties
without causing heavenly work to fail
were all mentors and teachers to the realm.
From the Eastern Zhōu (Dōngzhōu) onward,
the functions of ruler, teacher, administration, and education were no longer unified.
Consequently, human scholarship
did not entirely derive from the canonical custodianship of official offices.
The Qín people, by taking the official as teacher,
initially restored an ancient system.
But people grew accustomed to their existing habits
and instead deemed the Qín practice wrong.
The Qín dynasty committed many violations against antiquity,
but one aspect that aligned with antiquity
was taking the official as teacher.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"One who is born into the world of today,
but returns to the way of antiquity,
disaster will surely befall his person."
Lǐ Sī requested the banning of the Shī (Classic of Poetry) and the Shū (Classic of History),
believing that the Rú (Confucian) scholars praised the ancient and condemned the present.
Their words seem similar,
but their intentions are greatly contradictory.
Gentlemen of later ages
must investigate this.
The Sān Wáng (Three Kings) did not adopt identical rites,
and the Wǔ Dì (Five Emperors) did not follow the same music.
If one does not realize that fitting the rites to the time is paramount,
and constantly speaks of loving antiquity,
he certainly does not genuinely understand the ancient systems.
This is reckless behavior that disregards the law,
hence the Master (Fūzǐ) despised it.
However, regarding the Yīn following the Xià rites,
this can be known for a hundred generations.
Although increase and decrease are said to accord with the times,
there has never been anyone who disparaged Yáo and Shùn,
and then reviled Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, Wǔ, and Zhōu Gōng, yet was able to govern successfully.
Lǐ Sī’s request to ban the Shī and Shū,
gentlemen deemed the height of foolishness.
Later ages are separated from Táng, Yú, and the Sān Dài (Three Dynasties)
by an even greater distance.
Essentially, the canonical institutions of any single dynasty,
which can be handed down through generations and achieve temporary peace and order,
have never failed to derive
some likeness from the way of the ancient sage kings.
Therefore, the established norms of the current age,
and the precedents kept by government officials,
there are none that cannot be understood through the traditions transmitted by the Shī, Shū, and the Liù Yì (Six Arts).
Yet scholars, oblivious to knowing the proper time,
constantly pride themselves on broad knowledge of antiquity,
which is like studying the sericulture of Xīlíng
or discussing Shénnóng’s cultivation methods,
believing they can ward off hunger and cold without needing actual clothing and food.
Historical Commentary.
Formerly, when the Master composed the Chūn Qiū (Spring and Autumn Annals),
after the selection and editing were complete,
he further transmitted the subtle words and profound principles
orally to his disciples.
The creation of the Sān Zhuàn (Three Commentaries)
resulted from each author basing their work on what they had heard and seen,
elaborating upon the hidden meaning of the classic.
Thus, the Chūn Qiū was clarified.
The various schools and hundred masters (Zhūzǐ Bǎijiā),
having written down their theories,
also had their followers who together preserved them,
only then did their theories become prominent throughout the world.
As for historical matters,
the ancients treated it as a profession passed down through their families;
scholars would go to those families to receive the transmission of the craft (Kǒngzǐ, when inquiring about rites, invariably sought out the Guardian of the Archives).
This is because the three great things within the realm
cannot be completed by the hand of a single person,
nor can success be judged merely by the field of writing and ink.

Shǐ Qiān compiled one hundred and thirty chapters (The Hàn Shū [Book of Hàn] was titled Tàishǐ Gōng [Grand Scribe] until the Suí Zhì [Suí Dynasty Record] first called it Shǐ Jì [Records of the Grand Historian]).
He said:
"Store it in a famous mountain,
transmit it to the right person."
Afterwards, his grandson Yáng Yùn
first made his book public.
Bān Gù’s Hàn Shū,
after Bān Gù died,
scholars of that time
were unable to fully comprehend it.
Mǎ Róng then waited beneath the canopy,
receiving instruction from Bān Gù’s younger sister,
and only then did his scholarship become prominent.
The works of Mǎ and Bān,
people today see them completely,
but in those days, their transmission certainly required the right person,
and the recipient of the reading had to have a legitimate source.
The specialized scholarship of the ancients
surely contained unwritten methods of heart-to-heart transmission,
beyond the capabilities of the written word and editing.
Thus, they transmitted it orally to their disciples,
who mutually practiced and preserved the craft,
in order to pass it down permanently.
Shǐ Qiān's book was first annotated by Péi Yīn,
and Bān Gù's book was first interpreted by Yīng Shào.
Afterwards, there were still several families
who provided commentaries;
these all elaborated on the scholarship of their own lineage.
Since the period of Wèi and Jìn,
writings have been numerous and chaotic,
lacking instruction from previous masters,
and without subsequent students to follow them.
Moreover, when they composed these writings,
the style was both diffuse and rambling,
utterly lacking the rigorous principle of selection and editing found in the ancients;
the purpose, furthermore, was shallow and superficial,
and also lacked the subtle and hard-to-explain points of the ancients.
Naturally, they could only rely on their own limited ability
to circulate in the world in isolation.
Regarding the keeping of historical records,
there have been suitable people in every generation,
but ancient scholarship was lost in transmission,
leaving history as a mere collection of facts.
Only in the arrangement of official declarations and documents,
and the sequence of daily and monthly records,
is there endless confusion,
and the text is also overly detailed and repetitious,
completely losing the former style of Shǐ Qiān and Bān Gù.
Is this entirely due to the inadequacy of the authors' talent and ability,
or is it because history lacks a system of annotation,
making it inevitable that it tends daily toward excessive complexity?
An ancient book
was transmitted by several families.
In later ages, several people
collaborated to complete one book.
If the transmitters are numerous,
the method of maximizing conciseness and revealing subtlety is preserved.
If the authors are many,
the defect of contradiction and repetition arises.
Once the stream flows on and daily forgets its source,
how can ancient scholarship be recovered,
and how can historical records be made concise?
This is why the Táng Shū (Book of Táng) is twice the size of the Hàn Shū,
and the Sòng Shǐ (History of Sòng) is twice the size of the Táng Shū.
Those who examine them cannot bear the burden,
and how can the tradition of transmission
avoid being lost?
Those who heard the same things but related them differently
saw differing perspectives and followed separate paths.
Those whose source was correct but whose streams diverged
lost authenticity over time.
In the case of the nine masters of the Yì (Classic of Changes),
and the four lineages of the Shī (Classic of Poetry),
teachers and scholars stood like a forest,
and the transmissions were already overwhelmingly complex.
If a scholar, born after the three ancient ages,
is able to achieve his own comprehension of the ancients
and compile the work of a single school,
he will inevitably wander between the two extremes,
isolated and without followers.
If he wishes to embrace this small body of learning
and wait for it to be brought to light by Zǐcháng’s grandson
or Mèngjiān’s younger sister,
this is a sure impossibility.
The Grand Scribe’s composition of the Zì Xù (Author's Preface)
was perhaps the beginning of self-annotation?
Clarifying the original purpose of the composition,
showing the origins of what was selected and rejected,
it already seems as though he feared later generations would not know what he meant,
and so he specially wrote it to mark the intent.
The saying, "does not depart from the ancient texts,"
and "verifies according to the Liù Yì," and so forth,
are all the core principles of the one hundred and thirty chapters,
sometimes placed at the end of the scroll,
sometimes prefixed at the beginning of the chapter,
never failing to repeatedly clarify themselves.
Bān Gù’s book includes ten chapters of annual tables,
and the two treatises Jì Lǐ (Geography) and Yì Wén (Literature), all of which are self-annotated.
This established the rules for outlining main principles and subsidiary details.
The histories by Chén Shòu and Fàn Yè
still had Sōngzhī (Pèi Sōngzhī) and Zhāng Huái (Lǐ Xián) to annotate them.
Down to Xí Huìmíng annotating the Qín Jì,
and Liú Xiàobiāo annotating the Shì Shuō Xīn Yǔ,
which are secondary branches of miscellaneous history,
they still had subsidiary commentaries.
This is proof that the historical methodology of the Liù Cháo (Six Dynasties) had not yet perished.
Since then, the authority over history became dispersed,
and the biographic records became vast and numerous.
Only Xú Wéifāng's annotation of the Wǔ Dài Shǐ (History of the Five Dynasties),
though already brief,
still preserved a glimmer of the rites.
But the various historians of the Táng and Sòng dynasties
were vaguely unaware of the limits (of their records).
Fàn Chōng of the Sòng dynasty, when compiling the Shénzōng Shí Lù (Veritable Records of Emperor Shénzōng),
separately compiled five chapters of Kǎo Yì (Investigation of Differences)
to clarify the meanings.
This shows that lacking capable successors,
he provided the explanations himself.
This should, alongside works like the Tōng Jiàn Jǔ Yào (Essentials of the Comprehensive Mirror) and Kǎo Yì,
be considered an excellent method of recent times.
Liú Zhī jǐ’s Shǐ Tōng (Generalities on History)
delineated three categories for supplementary annotation.
Those referred to as records of minor personalities, such as Sān Fǔ Jué Lù and Huá Yáng Shì Nǚ,
and those referred to as compilations by the historians themselves, such as Luòyáng Qiélán Jì and Guāndōng Fēng Sú,
although designated as two grades,
are in reality one category.
All of these are practices that the historians of recent generations, when discussing history, must urgently restore.
Only the category concerning the expansion of diverse hearings, such as Sōngzhī’s Sān Guó Zhì and Liú Zhāo’s Hòu Hàn Shū annotation,
is the old method of historical scholarship,
which, compared to works like Suǒ Yǐn and Zhèng Yì,
is broadly similar but subtly different.
literary and historical works, grow
increasingly abundant day by day. Once
a volume is edited and finalized, the books from which the
materials were selected, within
not many decades, tend to lose five or six
out of ten [parts of their content] through loss. The established rules of
compiling history during the Sòng and Yuán [dynasties], can
be reviewed and examined in this regard. If
the system of self-annotation were allowed to be practiced, then,
by means of the citations used, it would be possible to preserve the general outline of the
private libraries of previous generations, and thereby
correct the errors and omissions in the records of literary works (Yì Wén Zhù Lù).
This is also an aid to historical methodology. Furthermore,
the human heart grows degenerate day by day, and
trends (fēng qì) change daily. The meaning of
gaps in the text is not understood, and the practice
of forced interpretation and amalgamation, is
becoming ever more prevalent and refined. In
government-compiled books, the only
hope is to fulfill the duty cursorily; in
private scholarship, [authors] respectfully
embellish vain reputation, perhaps
plagiarizing established books, or
settling for poor quality and simplicity. If their
techniques are slightly clever, they can
deceive the senses of their contemporaries, and the way
of authorship further declines. If one
could truly use self-annotation to indicate what was selected or discarded, then the breadth
or narrowness of one's reading, the thoroughness
or slightness of one's effort, and the sincerity
or deceitfulness of one's motives, would be clearly
visible the moment the book is opened, and the general trend
could gradually return to ancient simplicity. This
is yet another particularly great benefit. If so,
examining past generations, the
established systems were as described; measuring
against future generations, the weight
of the issue is thus significant; the
writing brush is used less than before, yet the efficacy
is greater than the old way—what
could surpass self-annotation? Biographies and Records (Zhuàn Jì)
The literature of
biographies and records, its origin
is ancient, having
emerged mixed among the Six Arts (Liù Yì) in sequence. Ancient
writing had no fixed form, and Classics
and Histories were not separated into distinct categories. The commentaries (zhuàn) of
the three schools of the Chūn Qiū, each recorded
what they heard, establishing interpretations
based on the Classic. Even if they were
called Records (Jì), it would be acceptable. The Records (jì) of the
two Dài concerning the Classic of Rites (Lǐ), each transmitted
their own explanations, circulating
alongside the Classic. Even if they were
called Commentaries (Zhuàn), it would be acceptable. After this,
branches separated into different schools, until
recent times, when those
recording individuals (rén wù), were distinguished
as Biographies (Zhuàn); and those
narrating events (shì jì), were distinguished
as Records (Jì). This likely
arose because the Collection category (Jí Bù) flourished greatly, and people
spontaneously created this distinction. Not knowing
why it happened thus, it happened thus, and consequently
it became like an immutable law of nature. There
are many such instances. Scholars
born in later generations, provided
it does no harm to principles of righteousness (yì lǐ), may
follow the general consensus. However, consider examples
like Yú Yù’s Dù Jì and the Xiāngyáng Qí Jiù Jì: when narrating
people, were they not called Records (Jì)? The Zhuàn (Commentaries/Biographies)
concerning Guī Cè and Xī Yù, when describing
events, were they not called Commentaries (Zhuàn)? Generally,
works designated Diǎn or Jīng, are all
those produced by individuals possessing virtue and high status, regulating
human relations and societal structure. The
current Six Arts are examples of this. Kǒngzǐ
had virtue but no status, thus
he transmitted but did not create. Therefore,
the Lún Yǔ and the Xiào Jīng, were both
considered commentaries (zhuàn) and not classics (jīng), and the Yì Xì (Appended
Treatises of the Book of Changes) was only called the Dà Zhuàn (Great Commentary). Later,
they were all listed as Classics (Jīng). The scholars
honored Kǒngzǐ's writings, and made
them distinct from the records (zhuàn jì) of later scholars. Scholars
at the end of the Zhōu Dynasty, extending
to the beginning of the Hàn Dynasty, all knew
that the task of writing, could
not claim the status of Jīng Lún (classical frameworks), stepping
into reckless composition. They also
believed that establishing their own theories, must
rely on the Sacred Classics (Shèng Jīng) as the governing principle. Thus,
they wrote down what they saw and heard, each
writing it down in a book as a commentary or record (zhuàn jì). Examples
include the various Records (Jì) of the two Rites, and the various Commentaries (Zhuàn) of the Shī, Shū, Yì, and Chūn Qiū. They
all established interpretations based on the Classics (Jīng), but in reality,
they were independent works, naturally
different from the annotations and commentaries (jiān zhù) of later generations. In later
generations, specialized learning declined, and the style
of collected works (jí tǐ) flourished. Narrating
people or describing events, each
consisted of scattered essays, which also
took the name of Zhuàn Jì, adhering
to the meaning of the specialized Zhuàn Jì of the ancients. In the Míng Dynasty,
starting after the Jiājìng period, discussions
on literature were divided into different schools. Those
who enjoyed making lofty arguments, frequently
asserted that the Zhuàn (Biography) was a historical duty, and if one
was not a historiographer (shǐ guān), how
could one write a biography for others? People
in the world who lack stable judgment yet insist on interpreting matters, gathered
together to echo this, claiming
it had never been heard of in antiquity. Now, the
writings of later generations, which
did not exist in antiquity, yet which
people proceeded to create collectively, are numerous
in the Collection category (Jí Bù); most
of them are like this. As for the Zhuàn (Biography),
it was fundamentally not invented by historians. Before
Mǎ [Qiān] and Bān [Gù], such writings

already existed. (Mèngzǐ, responding to a question about parks and the affairs of Tāng and Wǔ, repeatedly said, “It is contained in the Zhuàn.” At that time, there were no histories using the chronicle-biography style. How could this be the writing of a historiographer?) If
one insists now that holding no historical office, means
one should not write a Zhuàn, then try
asking what the difference is between Zhuàn and Jì. If one
is not a master of the Classics (Jīng Shī), how
can one write a Jì (Record)? If the Jì
causes no offense, but the Zhuàn
is strictly forbidden, then
this is honoring History while slighting the Classics. The
essential purpose of literature, and the form
and style of writing,
are called established rules (lì yì). Among
present-day writers, many
are ignorant and fail to observe these. Yet, concerning
these matters which are beyond doubt, they frequently
engage in baseless adherence. This is almost
like ignorant village shamans and old women, who make up
arbitrary taboos regarding Yīn Yáng, making
the actions of the common people difficult. The people
of the late Míng Dynasty, thought
without learning; their
blind talk, how
could one endure spitting upon it! Those
who discuss literature today, conversely,
learn without thinking, instead
adopting those theories, to boast
of being insightful. This
is being fooled by antiquity. The argument
distinguishing professional roles (biàn zhí), is
especially lacking in understanding of principle. If
we consider standard Zhuàn Jì, anyone
can write them, regardless
of whether they are Classics Masters (Jīng Shī) or Historiographers (Shǐ Guān). If one
strictly adheres only to the Biographies (Liè Zhuàn) in the Standard Histories (Zhèng Shǐ), and only
then considers one qualified to write a Zhuàn, then even
if one holds the office of historiographer, unless
one is specifically compiling a history, how
can one separately write a private Zhuàn? If one
merely responds to another person's request, and proceeds
to compose a Zhuàn, it is
no different from what common people compile. Only if
others do not hold that office, and are
therefore generally prohibited from writing, while
oneself holds the office, and
is therefore permitted to write, this
is like official documents that require a seal. This
reduces the historiographer to a clerk, and treats
the requested biography, as a tool
for manipulating texts by relying on official status. This
explanation is even more untenable. Those
who merely listen to street gossip, claim
that this argument comes from Master Zhū of Dàxīng. They do not
realize that this was a spurious argument from the late Míng period,
using sectionalism (mén hù) to attack Wáng [Shìzhēn] and Lǐ [Pānlong]. Master
Zhū once said: “For people
still alive, one
should not write a Zhuàn.”
This is a sound principle. However,
looking at the ancients, it
was not entirely so. According
to the Sān Guó Zhì, the mother of Páng Yù, Zhào É, murdered
someone to avenge her father. The
annotation quotes Huángfǔ’s Liè Nǚ Zhuàn (Biographies of Exemplary Women) as saying: “Liáng Kuān
of Āndìng, formerly a Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gates, wrote a biography for her.” Thus,
for people who were still alive, the
ancients certainly wrote biographies. Lǐ Áo compiled
the Yáng Liè Fù Zhuàn (Biography of Exemplary Woman Yáng); at that
time, [Madam] Yáng was still alive. I suspect
that such cases among the ancients were not rare. Now,
covering a person's entire life to write a Zhuàn, is the style
of the Biographies (Liè Zhuàn) in the Shǐ [Jì] and Hàn [Shū]. While
taking up an incident to write a Zhuàn, is the
style of the Commentary (Zhuàn) of Zuǒ [Qiūmíng] on the Classic. Master
Zhū's statement, refers
exclusively to the Liè Zhuàn style.
Shào Niànlǔ and Jiā Tàizhān,
once debated about ancient writers compiling private biographies (sī zhuàn), saying:
"Do you alone not hear of the biography of Dèng Yǔ,
that Fàn Shì indeed had a source for it?"
Examining this, it is not limited to Fàn Shì;
Chén Shòu's *Sān Guó Zhì* (Records of the Three Kingdoms),
in the commentary (zhù) by Péi Sòngzhī, cites private biographies from various authors of the Dōngjīng, Wèi, and Jìn eras to provide mutual confirmation,
totaling several dozen families (authors).
Even those seen in the Súi and Táng catalogs of bibliography (*Jīngjí* and *Yìwén Zhì*),
such as *Dōngfāng Shuò Zhuàn* and *Lù Xiānshēng Zhuàn*,
are too numerous to list completely;
the matter certainly needs no further debate.
Those who cling to rabbit-garden (elementary) texts,
seeing only that *Zhāomíng Wénxuǎn* and the Eight Masters of Táng and Sòng rarely included this genre,
then claim that the books of the world
can no longer be used for collateral evidence.
Previously, when I was hired to compile the *Húběi Tōng Zhì* (General Gazetteer of Húběi),
relying on the deep understanding of the Governor-General (dūfǔ),
I proceeded to use a distinctive, original method,
organizing it into the Learning of the Three Schools.
The section on Figures (*Rénwù*),
entirely followed the standard format of biographies (liè zhuàn) in the official histories,
compiling chapters.
As for those from before the Súi and Táng dynasties,
whose historical biographies were clearly documented,
and for which there was no need to cross-reference details or apply editorial revision (bǐxuē),
I simply listed their names,
creating the *Rénwù Biǎo* (Table of Figures). (The explanation is detailed in the *Xù Lì* of this work.)
The original biographies found in various histories
were all included in the *Wén Zhēng* (Collected Writings),
for ease of reference and inspection. (What is called the Learning of the Three Schools: the *Wén Zhēng* is modeled on the *Wénxuǎn*.)
Regarding the principles and methods of compilation,
they were precise and appropriate.
At that time, there was a malicious person (qiānrén),
poor due to his inadequacy in official life,
who requested me to recommend him into the Bureau of Compilation (shūjú),
allowing him to collect a salary without doing any work.
When the Governor-General was demoted (zuǒqiān),
this petty man (xiǎorén), drooling for profit, fabricated slander,
and a swarm of criticisms arose.
The officials in charge were misled by this,
and issued a proclamation appointing that person to revise and correct the work.
I, on the other hand, was relying on the fact that he was recommended by me,
and did not anticipate him turning against virtue and biting the hand that fed him (fǎnshì),
forgetting what he had previously acknowledged and respected,
and creating chaos and deceit to deceive his superiors. (There is a separate, specialized essay debating this principle.)
He then claimed that the structure of *Wén Zhēng* imitated *Wénxuǎn* and *Wényuàn* (Yīnghuá),
but that *Wénxuǎn* and *Wényuàn* fundamentally did not contain the biography genre (zhuàn tǐ).
He proceeded to cite the biographies of Hé Fán, Lǐ Chì, Máo Yǐng, and Sòng Qīng,
saying they originated from playful exercises (yóuxì) or complimentary presentations (tóu zèng),
and thus could not be included in proper biographies.
The superior officials immediately praised him for his learning and insight,
and secretly supported his argument,
concealing it and not allowing me to know. Alas!
*Wényuàn Yīnghuá* contains five volumes of biographies (zhuàn),
covering roughly [chapters] 792,
up to 796.
Among them, the forms of genuine biographies include:
for high officials, the Minister of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū), Duke Liáng, Lǐ Xiàn,
and for regional commanders (jiéyuè), the Military Governor (Jiédù) of Dōngchuān, Lú Tǎn (both biographies written by Lǐ Huà).
For literary figures, such as Chén Zǐ'áng (biography written by Lú Cángyòng).
For integrity and character, such as Lǐ Shēn (biography written by Shěn Yàzhī).
For chastity and heroism, such as Lady Yáng (Lǐ Áo) and Maiden Dòu (Dù Mù).
Those that conform to the standard biographical structure used by historians
amount to more than ten chapters.
To claim that *Wényuàn* contains no genuine biographical form
is truly senseless!
The Sòng people, when compiling *Wényuàn*,
certainly had classifications that were incomplete,
but this is not something that petty slanderers can understand.
Even among the biographical styles adopted,
there are those that are ornate and stately like stone inscriptions (bēizhì) (like Yǔ Xìn's *Qiū Nǎifū Dūnchóng Zhuàn*),
self-narratives that are not the standard form (like *Lù Wénxué Zì Zhuàn*),
statements with figurative meaning (jìtuō) (like *Wáng Chéngfú Zhuàn*),
using borrowed names for satire (fěngcì) (like *Sòng Qīng Zhuàn*),
complimentary pieces resembling prefaces or introductions (xù yǐn) (like *Qiáng Jūshì Zhuàn*),
humorous pieces written for amusement (yóuxì) (like *Máo Yǐng Zhuàn*),
all of which are arranged after the genuine biographies.
It is not as good as Lǐ Hàn's collection of Hán Yù's writings,
where he placed *Hé Fán Zhuàn* under miscellaneous writings (zázhù),
and placed *Máo Yǐng Zhuàn* under miscellaneous literature (záwén).
In that case, the organizational principle is perfectly clear.
Xí Gù
Where does debate (biànlùn) arise?
It arises from the mind's discernment of right and wrong (shìfēi).
Where does the mind's discernment of right and wrong arise?
It arises between doubt (xián), scruple (jiè), and semblance (yísì).
Where does it reach its limit?
It reaches its limit in affirming Yáo and condemning Jié.
The world does not debate the right and wrong of Yáo and Jié,
just as the world does not debate the height and lowness of heaven and earth.
Vision is strained by the down of an autumn hair (the minutest detail),
hearing reaches its limit at the sound of an ant in a hole.
Being able to see Tàishān,
is not considered sharp vision;
being able to hear thunder,
is not considered keen hearing.
Therefore, Yáo and Jié
are names for right and wrong,
but they are not the means by which right and wrong are debated.
Doubt, scruple, and semblance
are not yet as clearly divided as Yáo and Jié.
But when analyzed, there is nothing that cannot be divided as clearly as Yáo and Jié;
it begins with the minute details of right and wrong,
and culminates in the essence of debate.
Therefore, Yáo and Jié
are the limit reached by debate;
while right and wrong
are where the obscure and minute differences begin.
The original insight (chuàng jiàn) into the obscure differences,
is what debaters value and treasure.
If, upon analysis, it does not lead to Yáo and Jié,
there is no reason to value the original insight.
But once the analysis reaches Yáo and Jié,
people will naturally settle into the established Yáo and Jié and rest in that certainty.
Therefore, the right and wrong derived from original findings,
ultimately cease to be seen as right and wrong.
Yáo and Jié require no further analysis.
Those who settle into the accumulated right and wrong of antiquity and the present, treating them as Yáo and Jié,
are all those who have accumulated and fully analyzed the obscure original insights of people throughout time.
Those who settle into the analyzed extreme of right and wrong
do not know where right and wrong truly reside.
Those who do not know where right and wrong reside,
are not completely forgetting right and wrong;
they merely assume them to be self-evident and thus unworthy of focusing their intention upon.
When they encounter something of that nature and their thoughts are stirred,
they then arrive at a perspective they deem to be truly correct—
affirming what they affirm and denying what they deny.
They value and treasure this,
believing it to be an original insight into the obscure.
When they analyze and synthesize it,
compare and equate it,
and bring it to its limit,
it is exactly the same Yáo and Jié that they previously rested in as self-evident.
Previously, they did not know the reason why,
but now they know the reason why.
Therefore, their current perception differs from their previous perception,
yet what they say is fundamentally no different from what was said before.
Therefore, for those who do not focus their thought on right and wrong,
the original insights they value
are all commonplace and nothing remarkable.
A liquor seller brewed wine that turned sour.
He wrote in large characters on the door, "Sour wine, reduced price,"
hoping for a quick sale.
There was a man who could not read.
He went in, drank the wine, and found it sour.
He supposed that the owner did not yet know of this.
After leaving, he forgot an item.
The owner chased after him and returned it.
The man again commented on the owner's great generosity toward him.
He drew the owner aside and said:
"Your family's wine is sour.
Why not reduce the price and sell it quickly?"
When the owner heard this, he merely chuckled (yǎrán).
Therefore, those who do not focus their thought on right and wrong,
the original insights they value,
are simply telling the owner that his wine is sour.
Yáo and Jié certainly need no debate.
However, one who experiences the benevolence of Yáo
must approach a point (jī),
where they are almost incapable of speaking about Yáo—
that is truly a person of Yáo.
One who encounters the tyranny of Jié
must approach a point,
where they are almost incapable of counting the faults of Jié—
that is truly a person who condemns Jié.
The self-evident Yáo and Jié of a thousand ages,
still began by being analyzed from that "nearness" (jī),
that point where one is almost unable to speak or count [the faults],
and only then were the self-evident natures of Yáo and Jié established.
Therefore, those who truly know right and wrong
cannot immediately speak of right and wrong.
Those who truly know to affirm Yáo and condemn Jié,
their learning lies prior to right and wrong,
and not in affirming Yáo and condemning Jié.
Affirming Yáo and condemning Jié,
valuing the Kingly Way (wáng) and despising the Hegemonic Way (bà),
venerating Zhōu and Kǒng (Confucius) and rejecting heterodoxy (yìduān),
upholding Chéng and Zhū (Chéng Yí/Hào and Zhū Xī) and marginalizing Lù and Wáng (Lù Jiǔyuān and Wáng Yángmíng)—
I do not say that these are incorrect;
but those who habitually treat them as self-evident and speak of them easily,
I know that they do not possess true knowledge.
Zhū Lù
The principles of Heaven, Human Nature, and Destiny,
are fully covered in the Classics and Commentaries (jīng zhuàn).
The Classics and Commentaries are not the words of a single person,
yet their essential aims have never been divergent;
this is because their principles are manifested in concrete affairs and objects (shì wù),
and are not entrusted to empty rhetoric.
When teachers and scholars (shī rú) explain principles to guide later students,
only by manifesting them in concrete affairs and objects
will there be no contention between different schools (mén hù) of thought. Principles,
can be likened to water.
Concrete affairs and objects,
can be likened to vessels.
Vessels have size, shallowness, and depth,
and water is poured in according to the capacity,
without excess or deficiency.
If one now desires to use water to fill the vessel,
but temporarily sets aside the vessel,
and discusses the drawing, pouring, filling, and emptying of water,
along with the principles of measuring emptiness and gauging reality,
debating endlessly for years,
the dispute will never cease,
and the vessel will certainly have become useless.
The disciples of Zǐxià
asked Zǐzhāng about friendship.
Scholarly governance separated, and teachers and scholars honored knowledge in order to spread their conduct and reputation;
if not for the Master (Kǒngzǐ),
the division was inevitable given the circumstances.
The different ways of being elevated and brilliant (gāo míng) versus profound and subtle (chén qián),
can be likened to cold and heat, day and night;
those who understand their meaning
mutually contribute to success,
but those who do not understand their meaning
mutually cause harm.
Among the Sòng Confucians were Zhū [Xī] and Lù [Jiǔyuān];
their similarities and differences are such that they cannot be reconciled for a thousand generations,
yet their similarities and differences are also such that they cannot be absent for a thousand generations.
Later followers who lack understanding
viciously contend and curse each other,
and those who strive to resolve the disputes
by mediating and finding a compromise acceptable to both sides,
are all unnecessarily making trouble.
However, to say that Mǎster Zhū (Zhūzǐ) focused excessively on pursuing inquiry and study (dào wèn xué),
and therefore the scholars of the Lù clan (Lù Shì)
attacked the Zhū clan for being close to fragmentation and tedious detail (zhī lí);
or to say that the Lù clan focused excessively on honoring the virtuous nature (zūn dé xìng),
and therefore the scholars of the Zhū clan
attacked the Lù clan for drifting into emptiness and nihility (xū wú);
each faction using what it unduly prioritized
to contest their school’s position,
this is also the natural course of human affairs.
But since they already claim to inherit the teachings of the Zhū clan,
and attack Lù and Wáng,
they must be broadly learned and widely informed,
thoroughly understand the Classics, and conform to antiquity,
like the diligent works of gentlemen such as Xīshān, Hèshān, Dōngfà, and Bóhòu,
and only then, having fully developed their insights,
should they condemn rhetoric about virtuous nature as emptiness and nihility.
Now, the scholars who attack Lù and Wáng
are not learned and knowledgeable Confucians,
but rather crude, unsubstantiated pedants (xué jiū);
thus, their target of attack
is contrary to their own practice.
If you ask them why they do not pursue inquiry and study,
they reply, "It is fragmented and tedious (zhī lí)."
If you press them on why they adhere to narrow and crude views,
they reply, "It is about nature and destiny (xìng mìng)."
Thus, those who attack Lù and Wáng
have not even come close to approximating Zhū [Xī's teachings],
they are merely using spurious Lù and Wáng [ideas] to attack the genuine Lù and Wáng [ideas],
which can also be described as failing to gauge their own ability.
Xúnzǐ said:
“Disputation arises from inferior scholarship (mò xué).”
Zhū [Xī] and Lù [Jiǔyuān] were fundamentally different,
how much more so the babbling of later students?
But once the schools (mén hù) are divided,
those who wish to attack Zhū [Xī]
must appropriate the superficial resemblance of Lù and Wáng;
those who wish to attack Lù and Wáng
must appropriate the superficial resemblance of Mǎster Zhū.
The superficial resemblance of Zhū [Xī] must necessarily be detailed and elaborate,
and the superficial resemblance of Lù and Wáng must necessarily be empty and ethereal—
this is an immutable principle.
However, the mutual attacks between schools throughout history
are all characterized by clinging obstinately to one's own deficiencies,
piling up books without reading them,
and yet still speaking loftily about nature and Heaven (xìng tiān).
Therefore, those who claim to follow Lù and Wáng to attack Zhū [Xī]
are certainly spurious Lù and Wáng followers;
likewise, those who claim to follow the Zhū clan to attack Lù and Wáng
are also spurious Lù and Wáng followers,
and should not be called spurious Zhū followers.
Though belonging to the same school,
the reason Lù and Wáng have spurious followers
while Zhū does not have spurious followers
is that empty talk is easy,
but practical learning (shí xué) is difficult.
Huáng, Cài, Zhēn, and Wèi
all inherited Mǎster Zhū’s teachings and dedicated themselves to practical learning;
thus, they naturally had no time to entertain views on the differences between schools,
nor would they follow the trend of rise, fall, prosperity, or decline.
In this respect, the offshoots of Mǎster Zhū [Xī's school]
are superior to those of Lù and Wáng.
Yet, the spurious Lù and Wáng followers who falsely claim to be Zhū scholars
are still accepted by some as colleagues sharing the same path;
I fear the followers of the Zhū clan
would reject them with a shout.
It is said that there are beautiful afflictions,
and also medicinal stones.
The attacks of Lù and Wáng against Zhū [Xī]
are sufficient to achieve mutual completion, but not sufficient to cause mutual harm.
But the spurious Lù and Wáng followers who claim to study and honor Zhū [Xī]
are the misfortune of Zhū [Xī's] scholarship.
The integration of nature and destiny (xìng mìng), practical achievement (shì gōng), inquiry and study (xué wèn), and literary expression (wén zhāng)
into a unified whole
is the scholarship of Mǎster Zhū.
To seek unification through extensive study and knowledge,
and to restrain oneself with ritual (lǐ) based on broad learning,
is to encompass both fundamental and subsidiary aspects.
It is inevitable that the explanations of the various Classics contain successes and failures,
and that textual commentary and verification contain omissions and errors;
how can this damage the Great Rites (dà lǐ)?
Moreover, those who transmitted his learning,
such as Huáng, Cài, Zhēn, and Wèi,
were all pure scholars (chún rú) who thoroughly understood the Classics, conformed to antiquity,
and personally acted upon and practiced the teachings;
if Mǎster Zhū made errors,
they did not twist their adherence to agree with him,
and this is sufficient to establish instruction.
Yet there are those who highly esteem nature and destiny (xìng mìng) but minimize practical achievement (shì gōng),
discarding all inquiry, study, and literary expression,
and adhering only to the aims of one or two sections of collected commentaries;
consequently, they denounce Lù and mock Wáng,
with such hatred as if they cannot coexist under the same sky,
believing that they have inherited Zhū [Xī's] transmission.
This turns the Mǎster Zhū who comprehended antiquity and modern times and managed the structure of the universe
into a Mǎster Zhū who is rustic, ignorant, unknown, arrogant, and self-righteous.
Furthermore, explanations of meaning cannot avoid successes and failures,
and verification and textual commentary cannot avoid omissions and errors;
since the capture of the Qílín and the cessation of writing,
no one has been exempt from this.
Now, those who have acquired the spuriousness of Lù and Wáng
and yet claim to follow Zhū [Xī],
say:
To obstinately adhere to Mǎster Zhū,
even knowing there is poison,
one still must consume it.
They also say:
Mǎster Zhū actually combines the strengths of Kǒngzǐ, Yán [Huí], Zēng [Shēn], and Mèngzǐ. Alas!
The rightness or wrongness of such statements
need not be debated.
If Mǎster Zhū has awareness [in the afterlife],
how distressed must he be?
Gàozǐ said:
“If one does not grasp something through words,
do not seek it in the mind.
If one does not grasp something through the mind,
do not seek it in the vital energy (qì).”
The person whose mind is unshakable (bù dòng xīn)
does not seek where righteousness rests—
this is the beginning of obstinate adherence (mò shǒu) through the ages.
The mind that judges right and wrong (shì fēi zhī xīn)
is possessed by everyone.
If one cannot fully develop it through righteousness and principle (yì lǐ),
and furthermore refuses to accept the goodness of others,
this obstinate adherence resembles Gàozǐ.
However, borrowing the right and wrong of others to determine one's own right and wrong
is inferior to Gàozǐ's self-satisfaction.
Borrowing the right and wrong of others to determine one's own right and wrong
is like being hired to assist in a fight,
knowing how to compete for victory but not knowing the reason for competing.
Therefore, when attacking others, they spare no effort,
but when questioned about the successes and failures of the teachings they uphold,
they are unable to fully articulate them.
Hence the saying:
Though clearly known to be toxic,
it must be consumed.
The minor streams lose their origin,
and the various schools tracing back to Zhūzǐ,
believe themselves superior to Lù [Jiǔyuān] and Wáng [Yángmíng].
If that is the case, those who uphold the sacrificial offerings of the Zhū clan [Zhūzǐ's teachings],
must they necessarily be without error? I say:
How can they be without it?
Today, there are scholars who disparage the Zhū clan [Zhūzǐ];
these are precisely those who arose several generations after Zhūzǐ.
Their opposition to the Zhū clan [Zhūzǐ]—
their learning is a hundred times superior to the minor streams of Lù [Jiǔyuān] and Wáng [Yángmíng],
and their thinking is even deeper than the followers of the Zhūmén (Zhū school).
If they achieve their maximum potential,
Zhūzǐ himself would inevitably feel fear before these latter-day scholars.
However, upon investigating the source of their learning,
it truly arose several generations after Zhūzǐ,
but the people themselves do not realize this.
And those in the world designated as enlightened scholars and influential figures (tōngrén dáshì),
have almost hitched up their robes to follow them.
When observed by those with discernment,
it is like the people of Qí fighting over drinking water from a well.
The discourse on Nature and Destiny (Xìngmìng)
easily lapses into emptiness and nothingness (xūwú).
Zhūzǐ sought unity and consistency (yīguàn) through extensive study and memory,
and embodied adherence to ritual (yuēlǐ) within broad learning (bówén).
His methods were intricate and thorough,
and his accomplishments were substantial and difficult [to achieve];
although what Zhūzǐ sought
I dare not definitively say was without error.
However, those who followed his learning,
the first generation included Miǎnzhāi and Jiǔfēng;
the second generation included Xīshān, Hèshān, Dōngfā, and Hòuzhāi;
the third generation included Rénshān and Báiyún;
the fourth generation included Qiánxī and Yìwū;
the fifth generation included Níngrén and Bǎishī.
All of these adhered to ancient ways and mastered the Classics (tōngjīng),
seeking correctness in their studies,
and were not the type
who rely solely on themselves, clinging to fragments, and speaking idly about Xìngmìng.
Outside of this line of transmission,
writing fell into mere rhetoric (cízhāng),
and scholarship flowed into broad but shallow erudition (bóyǎ).
If one seeks the location of their fundamental principles (zōngzhǐ),
there might be some who are unaware of it themselves.
Born in the present age,
due to hearing of the style of Níngrén and Bǎishī,
one traces back the writings and achievements, past and present,
and thereby knows their intent in his heart.
This is the remnant thread of mastering the Classics and adhering to the ancients,
and he has inherited their voice.
