However, this person's intelligence (huì) surpasses his discernment (shí), and his vitality (qì) overwhelms his purpose (zhì);
instead, he criticizes Zhūzǐ,
thus forgetting his own origins.
True learning (shíxué) that seeks correctness
is not in the same category as empty talk about Nature and Heaven (xìngtiān).
Researching antiquity easily leads to error;
interpreting Classics easily leads to omission,
just as celestial phenomena cannot be exhausted by a single perspective.
In the study of astronomical records and phenomena (lìxiàng),
later people must surpass earlier people;
the natural progression makes it so.
If one criticizes Xī and Hé [astronomers] because of the precision of later people,
one fails to recognize that this precision is the transmitted method of Xī and Hé themselves.
Now, having succeeded Zhūzǐ after several generations,
one’s understanding surpasses that of the preceding generations,
but one does not realize that this is precisely the remaining legacy of those preceding generations.
This is like using later calendrical science to criticize Xī and Hé.
Indeed, that their insight
can surpass their predecessors
is due to an excess of intelligence (huì).
Moreover, this is only what should be expected of the intellect and understanding of a later age.
The failure to recognize that this is precisely the transmitted knowledge of their predecessors
is due to insufficient discernment (shí).
Their initial intention may not have been quite like this,
but their words are sufficient to awe the tōngrén dáshì of their generation,
and those who follow their well-fighting [contention]
are swept away by vitality (qì).
Subsequently, those who accept this without doubt
have their purpose (zhì) swayed by their vitality (qì).
Those who attack Lù [Jiǔyuān] and Wáng [Yángmíng]
only criticize spurious versions of Lù and Wáng.
Their own learning is coarse and shallow,
and is not sufficient to be a fault of Lù or Wáng.
But those who criticize Zhū [Zhūzǐ] emerged from the Zhū school itself,
and their strength is deep and profound.
If we do not mutually compare the source (yuán) and the stream (liú),
and cross-reference their words and actions;
in the world, those who love learning but lack true discernment (zhēnshí),
few fail to be swept away by this trend.
What the ancients inscribed on bamboo and silk
were all the words they proclaimed by mouth and ear.
Once the words were finalized, those who observed them
interpreted them in thousands of ways,
thus it was inevitable that some adhered to them while others opposed them.
The clever ones of today are not like this.
Using their strengths,
they are able to move the knowledgeable people of the world.
Knowing that their shortcomings
cannot be concealed,
they appear to treat [the knowledgeable] with disdain.
The serpent that moves across the swamp
even treats lesser beings as divine rulers.
When they encounter those who are capable of knowing but who are not necessarily true knowers,
they ignore their strengths,
believing that they cannot be conversed with;
and yet they embellish their shortcomings,
claiming that there is nothing they cannot do.
They use thunder and lightning to render it mystical,
ghosts and spirits to make it profound,
locked coffers to secure it,
and banners and signs to market it.
Consequently, there were none like them before,
and none will come after them.
Those who truly know in the world are few,
but those who are not necessarily true knowers are numerous.
The true knowers are definite and unchanging,
but those who are not necessarily true knowers change a thousand times without limit.
Therefore, they use the brush (writing) to gain the trust of the knowers,
and use the tongue (speech) to deceive those who are not necessarily deep knowers.
The world consequently rushes to follow them.
Now, ignoring their shortcomings and adopting their strengths—
since their surviving writings are all extant,
the majority of them should be followed and not abandoned.
If the world rushes to follow them,
why should that be a cause for concern!
They do not realize that the severity left by their words and tongues,
deeply penetrating the minds of those who seem to know but do not truly know,
causes them to accept or reject the ancients
based on their biased feelings (piǎnzhōng), thus harming the Way (Dào).
The saying goes:
"If the father murders to avenge,
the son will certainly carry out robbery."
That person, concerning Zhūzǐ, has essentially drunk the water and forgotten the source.
Yet when committing it to writing,
there are merely subtle remarks and veiled glimpses of criticism,
not daring to outright repudiate him.
This is why he is not hated by the true knowers.
But those who are not necessarily deep knowers,
having become accustomed to hearing [these criticisms] through speech,
wantonly attack and disparage without scruple,
believing that since such a person said these words,
then Zhūzǐ truly cannot be left uncriticized.
Therefore, those who follow his trend
invariably take attacking Zhū [Zhūzǐ] as their chief skill.
It is not that they hate Zhū [Zhūzǐ];
they fear that if they are unlike this person [the critic],
they will not be able to be regarded as a tōngrén.
Now, the material that Zhūzǐ provided for others to criticize
mostly comes from the *Yǔlù* (Recorded Sayings).
The *Yǔlù* originated from the miscellaneous notes compiled by his disciples and followers,
and it may not be entirely free from errors regarding his original intent.
However, the main substance is genuinely consistent with the books he wrote,
so what Zhūzǐ inscribed on bamboo and silk
is the same as the words he proclaimed by mouth and ear.
This internal and external consistency
was the learning of the ancients.
If we use this standard to judge that person,
we can also know that he falls far short of Zhūzǐ,
so why debate over the trivialities of written language and spoken words?
【Appendix】
〈Postscript to the Chapter on Zhū [Zǐ] and Lù [Jiǔyuān] (Based on volume two of the Liú edition of the *Yíshū*) 〉
Dài Jūn’s
scholarship deeply perceived the main principles of the ancients;
he was worthy of being called a great scholar of his generation.
However, his moral conduct (xīnshù) was not pure,
which became a rather severe affliction for scholars of recent times.
Therefore, I wrote the chapter “Zhū Lù” to correct this.
Dài Jūn passed away more than ten years ago.
That certain contemporaries aggressively slandered and abused him
certainly does not diminish Dài Jūn.
But those who honored and upheld him excessively,
even to the point of calling him the one man after Mèngzǐ,
were also inevitably fooled by Dài.
After one’s death, grievances and favors are both laid to rest,
and it is proper that public opinion should emerge.
Yet, up to now, no one has been able to definitively assess Dài Shì’s quality,
which shows how few people truly possess virtue (dé) know how to evaluate others.
All that Dài Jūn studied
deeply understood textual interpretation (xùngǔ),
investigating names, objects, and institutions (míngwù zhìdù),
and grasping the reasons why they were so,
intending thereby to illuminate the Way (dào).
People of that time valued broad knowledge and textual research (bóyǎ kǎodìng).
Seeing his command of textual interpretation and names and objects,
which suited the popular taste,
they believed Dài’s ultimate achievement lay in this.
When Dài authored the chapters like “Lùn Xìng” and “Yuán Shàn,”
discussing the principles and vital force (lǐ qì) of Heaven and Man,
he genuinely revealed things that his predecessors had not disclosed.
The people of the time, however, said that he was merely speaking empty doctrine and principle (yìlǐ),
and that these writings could have been left unwritten.
These people surely did not understand Dài’s scholarship.
Dài, seeing the understanding of people at that time,
then presented his views in a bizarre fashion, saying:
“Regarding textual interpretation, phonology, celestial phenomena, and geography—these four things—
I am like the servants carrying the sedan chair.
The Way I illuminate
is the great person riding in the carriage.
Those considered accomplished scholars (tōngrén) today
are merely qualified to exchange greetings with my sedan chair servants.”
Although his words were not without reason,
they ultimately harmed refined conduct (yǎdào).
However, they were prompted by the fact that the world lacked true appreciating friends (zhī jǐ).
Thus, he inevitably went to an extreme,
but this still did not violate righteousness (yì).
In his self-aggrandizement of his own field of study,
he claimed that if scholars did not investigate this area,
they would have no means of hearing the Way.
He failed to recognize that textual interpretation and names and objects
are also just one aspect.
If the ancients who studied literature and rhetoric (wéncí)
and sought principle (yìlǐ)
did not follow his method,
such as scholars like Hán, Ōu, Chéng, and Zhāng,
and he completely denied them permission to have heard the Way,
then that is also excessive.
However, this was still merely presenting his own views,
wishing others to follow only him.
In terms of his doctrines, he was not yet deceitful.
But regarding the principles of historiography (shǐxué yìlì) and the methods of ancient prose (gǔwén fǎdù),
he genuinely lacked understanding.
Having long traveled the world (jiānghú),
he was ashamed of knowing nothing,
and often forced himself to act knowledgeable,
responding to people’s requests.
Furthermore, he was uncomfortable with adhering to old habits,
and recklessly boasted of unique judgments.
For instance, when compiling the “Fénzhōu Fǔzhì,”
he asserted that Buddhist monks (sēngliáo) should not be listed among the category of humans,
and consequently took the names of famous monks from the old gazetteer and placed them under ‘Historical Sites.’
He also claimed that the important thing in compiling a gazetteer is researching historical evolution,
and that everything else could be arbitrary.
This shows that his understanding was gradually descending into vulgar delusion.
However, this was merely deceiving himself;
he did not yet have the deliberate intention of deceiving others.
I once encountered Dài Jūn at the Ningbō Circuit Administration office.
The host was Fēng Jūn Tíngchéng from Dàizhōu.
Fēng was already from a prestigious family,
and had long respected Dài’s reputation.
At that time, Fēng Shì’s brothers and cousins
were all circumspect, conscientious, and devoted to learning,
and admired Dài Jūn’s words
as if they were divine pronouncements.
Dài Jūn, in turn, deliberately offered lofty discourses,
ranging between heaven and the abyss,
making it impossible for others to fathom or comprehend him.
When people inquired about the relative merits of the histories by Bān and Mǎ,
he completely plagiarized Zhèng Qiáo’s criticisms of Bān
and claimed them as his own original insight.
When someone else asked to study ancient prose (gǔwéncí),
he replied:
“Ancient prose can be mastered without study.
I, throughout my life, did not understand ancient prose.
Later, I suddenly wished to write it but did not know the method.
So, I took the writings of the ancients,
and pondered over them repeatedly,
forgetting sleep and food for several days.
One night, I suddenly experienced an epiphany.
The next day,
I took up the material I wished to write about,
set the brush flying, and wrote
without needing deliberation,
and the resulting prose far surpassed that of the ‘Zuǒ’ (Zuo Commentary), ‘Guó’ (Discourses of the States), ‘Shǐ’ (Records of the Grand Historian), and ‘Hàn’ (Book of Han).”
Although the Fēng family had long respected and believed him,
hearing this, they were also quite suspicious.
His original intention was likely nothing more than hearing Mr. Zhū from Dàxīng and others discuss how writing prose should not intentionally seek skillful refinement,
though he himself had never experienced the difficulties of it.
He also felt that Mr. Zhū’s words were too plain and unremarkable,
so he presented it in an exaggerated and bizarre way,
hoping to capture people’s attention.
He failed to realize that descending into such recklessness and exaggeration,
starting from self-deception and reaching the point of deceiving others,
his heart had already become hardened (rěn).
Yet, he had not yet sinned against the doctrines of orthodox teaching (míngjiào).
Dài Jūn’s academic methods
were actually derived from Zhū Zǐ’s emphasis on textual learning (wèn xué).
Therefore, his warning against speaking of principle without foundation (záokōng yán lǐ)
was a theory that deeply probed the fundamental origins
and cannot be easily altered.
However, on account of certain instances in textual interpretation and definitions (xùngǔ míngyì)
where he happened to surpass Zhū Zǐ,
he consequently disparaged and belittled Zhū Zǐ,
even denouncing him as perverse and absurd,
and criticizing him for baseless fabrication.
Furthermore, he said:
“Since the appearance of Dài Shì,
Zhū Zǐ’s fortuitous status as the venerated master of the world,
which has lasted five hundred years,
must also gradually decline.”
This is utterly mistaken and absurd!
In what Dài Jūn committed to writing,
regarding his points of agreement or disagreement with Zhū Zǐ,
his phrasing was similar to that of Gù Shì Níngrén and Yán Shì Bǎishī.
He dared not offer any direct mockery or criticism,
which was certainly upholding the scholarly tradition (jiāfǎ) of Zhū learning.
Where he differed from Gù and Yán and other gentlemen,
was that he occasionally included subtle criticisms (wēicí) of Zhū Zǐ,
though he still dared not openly and explicitly reject him.
But the absurdity of his oral statements
reached this extreme,
harming righteousness and injuring doctrine—
how could this be trivial?
Some might say that words spoken by mouth leave no trace,
and since he is dead,
and his writings contain no major contradictions,
why must one insist on exposing this to damage generosity (hòudào)?
I respond that no one has yet been inspired by reciting Dài’s extant writings,
but those who have become increasingly extreme after hearing Dài’s oral statements
are flowing ceaselessly.
Even today, in the areas between Huī and Shè,
those who claim to be masters of the classics and adherents of antiquity,
if they do not despise Zhū Zǐ,
they are not considered accomplished scholars (tōngrén).
And their slandering of sages and attacking of worthies
shows absolutely no scruples.
This pervading trend (liúfēng) is greatly alarming.
Formerly, while in Wéiyáng,
I once presented my view to Shěn Jìtáng Xiānshēng, saying:
“How does Dài Jūn’s self-cultivation and personal conduct (lìshēn xíng jǐ)
compare to that of Zhū Zǐ?
As for their scholarship and writings,
since the dispute between them has not been resolved,
can we perhaps postpone a definitive judgment?”
This statement seems crude but is in fact subtle;
it seems shallow but is in fact profound.
Dài Dōngyuán said:
"Often, those who speak eloquently and dominate a discussion
leave behind writings and biographies
that might ironically be inferior to those of people who stammer and cannot express themselves well."
Although this statement is not entirely true,
it is fundamentally inevitable according to reason and circumstances.
However, since Lord Dài knew this principle,
yet spent his life striving to win arguments verbally,
sometimes causing heated disputes that harmed elegance (yǎ),
could it be that his downfall was knowing the truth but failing to maintain it through benevolence (rén)?
Generally, Lord Dài's lifetime conversational style
had about three types:
When dealing with powerful, highly esteemed officials in the central court (zhōng cháo),
he often agreed or disagreed ambiguously with their views,
occasionally expressing his own ideas,
but always judging what that person could comprehend.
He would merely hint at the sharpness of his thought
and refuse to finish his argument.
When dealing with his disciples (jí mén zhī shì),
he taught lessons and resolved doubts,
offering real assistance and benefit;
when dealing with those who admired his style and reputation,
but had not yet become formal students,
his speech often became vague and baseless,
mysterious upon mysterious (xuán zhī yòu xuán),
making it impossible for others to grasp,
causing them to doubt Heaven and doubt Destiny (mìng),
and ultimately remain unsettled.
Therefore, after his death,
successful gentry and officials all said:
"Lord Dài follows the same Way as I do;
I once set the definitive form for a certain book or writing of his."
Or they would say:
"Lord Dài finalized a certain matter with me;
I approved it, and he agreed to follow it."
But they did not know that Lord Dài merely ambiguously agreed with their words that day,
and the foundation upon which he established himself
was not in those things.
As for his disciples,
those who were truly brilliant
often surpassed Dài.
When Lord Dài saw them approaching his level,
he, conversely, would not greatly approve of them,
though Lord Dài surely knew those individuals deeply.
Later scholars, yearning for his teachings,
upon hearing his vague, mysterious, and ethereal words,
doubted and dared not make a judgment,
and even today have been unable to definitively establish what kind of person Dài was.
Meanwhile, those who believed excessively
subsequently spread the notion that he surpassed the Rú (Confucian scholars) of the Hàn, Táng, and Sòng Dynasties, being the sole successor to Mèngzǐ.
These people do not truly understand Dài.
Literary Virtue (Wéndé)
Whenever discussing doctrine or principle (yì lǐ),
there are cases where previous generations left things sparse, and subsequent generations made them denser and more intricate;
one must not fail to give this careful consideration.
The ancients, when discussing literature,
merely discussed literary style and diction.
When Lord Liú Xié appeared,
he built upon Lord Lù Jī’s theory and greatly championed discussing the Mind of Literature (wén xīn);
when Lord Sū Zhé appeared,
he built upon Lord Hán Yù’s theory and greatly championed discussing the Vital Force of Literature (wén qì);
this may be called progressing towards greater and greater refinement.
I have not yet seen anyone discuss the Virtue of Literature (wéndé).
This is what scholars ought to deeply reflect upon.
The Master (fūzǐ) once said, "He who has virtue must have words,"
and also said, "In refining language, establish sincerity."
Mèngzǐ once discussed "understanding words" (zhī yán)
and "nourishing the vital force" (yǎng qì),
grounding it in the accumulation of righteousness (jí yì).
Master Hán also spoke of
"the path of benevolence and righteousness (rén yì),"
and "the source of the *Shī* and *Shū* (Classics),"
all referring to Virtue.
Now, the reason I say no one has discussed Literary Virtue
is that what the ancients spoke of
combined root and branch,
encompassing inner and outer,
uniting Virtue, the Way (Dào), and literature into one whole;
they never specifically spoke, within the context of literary style,
of talent,
of learning,
of knowledge,
and also of the virtue of the writing itself.
must employ reverence (jìng) and forbearance (shù).
To approach writing with necessary reverence
is not what is meant by cultivating virtue.
To discuss the ancients with necessary forbearance
is not what is meant by leniency or tolerance.
The reverence that is not the cultivation of virtue
means keeping the vital force restrained, not giving it free rein;
if it is given free rein, it certainly cannot accord with moderation.
The forbearance that is not leniency
means being able to put oneself in the position and circumstances of the ancients.
Alas!
Few know Virtue.
If one knows that approaching writing cannot be without reverence and forbearance,
then one knows Literary Virtue.
In the past, Chén Shòu's *Sān Guó Zhì*
recorded Wèi in the main annals and relegated Wú and Shǔ to biographies.
Xí Záochǐ wrote the *Hàn Jìn Chūn Qiū*
and rectified the legitimate lineage (tǒng).
Sīmǎ's *Tōng Jiàn* still followed Lord Chén’s view,
but Master Zhū’s *Gāng Mù* then arose and rectified it again.
"The sense of right and wrong
is possessed by all men."
It should not be that Lord Chén erred first,
and Sīmǎ erred again afterward,
while the intellectual power of Lord Xí and Master Zhū
alone resides in superiority.
Yet those who criticize the *Guó Zhì* and the *Tōng Jiàn* today and throughout history
almost give free rein to their mouths and heap abuse;
I wonder if, were we to raise the ancients from the Yellow Springs (jiǔ yuán),
they would submit willingly to our views?
Lord Chén was born in the Western Jìn,
and Sīmǎ was born in the Northern Sòng.
If they were to reject the abdication (shàn ràng) of Cáo Wèi,
where would they place their sovereign and father?
Conversely, Xí and Master Zhū
were certainly men who had crossed the river south of Jiāngdōng,
concerned only that the Central Plain might contest the heavenly mandate (tiān tǒng) (This view has been stated by others before.).
All these worthies would have done the same had they switched positions;
it is not necessarily the case that their knowledge was inferior to today’s pedants.
Therefore, if one does not know the era of the ancients,
one must not rashly critique the writings of the ancients.
Even if one knows their era,
if one does not know the personal circumstances of the ancients,
one still cannot hastily critique their writings.
The circumstances one is in
naturally vary in glory and disgrace, obscurity and prominence, constraint and expansion, sorrow and joy.
And when words are spoken, there is always an intention behind the speaking.
Even Yǒu Zǐ did not fully grasp what the Master meant,
much less those born a thousand ages later?
The discussion of forbearance (shù) in the Sage's school is:
"What you do not desire,
do not impose upon others,"
and its Way (Dào) is vast.
Now, merely being a literary person,
when criticizing the ancients, one must first put oneself in their place;
this is what constitutes the forbearance aspect of Literary Virtue.
Lord Hán, discussing literature, said:
"Meet it and then reject it,
observe it with a tranquil mind."
He compared the vital force (qì) to water,
and speech to floating objects.
Lord Liǔ, when discussing literature, spoke of:
"not daring to approach it casually or throw it away,"
"dealing with it negligently,"
"creating it with boastful vital force,"
or "producing it with muddled vital force."
Now, when these various worthies discussed the mind (xīn) and discussed the vital force (qì),
they did not immediately reach the ultimate meaning of Kǒng and Mèng,
nor the subtlety of Heaven and Man, or nature and destiny (xìng mìng).
However, though literature is abundant and cannot be wholly done away with,
and though their expressions vary, each has its appropriateness.
To summarize their main point, it is 'to approach writing while maintaining reverence (zhǔ jìng),'
which covers everything in a single phrase.
If one maintains reverence, the mind is tranquil (píng),
and the vital force is restrained;
thus, one can naturally undergo transformation and proceed calmly, aligning with proper measure.
Now, history has three excellences:
talent (cái), learning (xué), and knowledge (shí).
If ancient prose and writing do not stem from history,
it is like food and drink not originating from farming and cultivation.
Now, knowledge is born from the mind,
and talent emerges from the vital force.
Learning,
is concentrating the mind to nourish the vital force,
and refining knowledge to perfect one's talent.
An empty mind is difficult to rely upon,
and a floating vital force is easily slackened.
One who maintains reverence
constantly inspects and controls both the mind and the vital force,
and carefully guards against the flaw of proceeding recklessly and failing to draw back.
"Brightening and reverently ceasing" (jī xī jìng zhǐ)
is how the sages achieve both beginning and end;
its meaning is vast.
Now, for the purpose of approaching literature,
controlling the mind and vital force,
this constitutes the reverence aspect of Literary Virtue.
Literary Principle (Wénlǐ)
I
saw a manuscript copy of the *Shǐjì*. I took it
to examine it. It turned out
that it used five colors of circles and dots, each marking different sections
and categories. I repeatedly
scrutinized it, but did not understand
what it meant. I asked
Liángyǔ. He burst
out laughing, saying that he himself was also tired
of looking at it. He said
the book originated from Guī Zhènchuān during the previous Míng dynasty. The five colors
used for marking, each represented a different category
or principle, and they were
not mixed up. One color was for the structure
of the entire piece, another was for the outstanding points
of each section, another was for the momentum
and flow of the ideas, and another was for the spiritual
vitality and strength. Classified according
to these examples, it facilitated diligent practice
and deep study. It was known
as the Secret Transmission of Classical Prose. The elders who spoke
of classical prose, valued it highly for instruction
and transmission, and would not lightly show
it to others. He also
said: "This is like the Fifth Patriarch transmitting
the lamp, or the *Língsù* receiving
the talismanic register. That which emerges
from this source, is the orthodox
school; that which does not emerge
from this source, even if it involves extraordinary
writings, is ridiculed by Buddhists
as ‘wild fox Chan.’ I studied
this in my youth, but when I traveled
to the capital, and my knowledge
and experience broadened somewhat, I realized
that the path of literature, did not originally
depend on this. However, I suspect
that there might be one or two useful points within it, which is why I did not
discard it immediately; it is not that
I treasure it." I
replied: The path
of literature, before
the Yuán dynasty, was decaying
and ailing, but had not
yet perished. In the Míng dynasty, people
initially inherited the remnants of the Sòng and Yuán, and roughly maintained
the conventions. By the time of the Jiājìng
and Lóngqìng eras, it had become obscure,
confused, and blocked, and literature was nearly
extinct. Guī Zhènchuān
was born during this time. He lacked the strength
to oppose the likes of Wáng and Lǐ, but knew in his heart
that they were wrong. Therefore, he criticized Fèngzhōu
for being mediocre and reckless. He stated that Fèngzhōu created
a counterfeit Qín and Hàn style, to the extent that even official titles
and place names, were changed
to ancient appellations, making it impossible for people
to distinguish what era he was writing about. Thus, when he directly
criticized him saying, "His writing is illogical," it was not reckless
talk. However, Guī's
prose, while clear
in essence and style, when examining the substance
of what he achieved, cannot be
forcefully demanded. Therefore, I once wrote
a note afterward, stating that the reason the Master served
as a bulwark in the current stream, was simply that his writing
followed convention and his words were smooth, preventing him from being submerged
by vulgar trends. But regarding what the ancients
referred to as having profound interiority and unrestrained exterior expression, where words vocalize
what the mind has attained, that, I have
not heard of. Nevertheless, he must
be called a hero of that time. However, regarding
Guī's skill in examination essays (zhìyì), he is like Zǐcháng
of the Hàn dynasty, or Tuìzhī
of the Táng dynasty, a great master revered for a hundred
generations. Therefore, among modern writers
of contemporary prose who discuss classical prose, many take Guī
as their model. The selection of the Eight Masters
of Táng and Sòng, is almost treated by people
with the same reverence as the origins of the *Wǔjīng* and the works of the Four Masters. Only in the collected works
of Guī and Táng, are their discussions
on writing all based on the *Shǐjì*; yet the extent
to which they drew strength from the *Shǐjì*, is surprisingly
unlike it. Generally, the style
of the *Shǐjì* is inherently vast and plain, but Sīmǎ's talent
was immense, hence he wielded
it with lightness and spirit. Now, what Guī and Táng
call ‘unconstrained, rugged, and fluctuating,’ is lacking
in substance, and consequently
becomes merely shallow and facile, thereby initiating a trend
among later generations for superficial imitation. Therefore, I suspect
that Guī, Táng, and others, gained only surface
benefit from the *Shǐjì*, only its superficial
aspects, and had not seen
the profound essence of the ancients.
Now, looking at this five-color
annotated edition passed down by gentlemen, I then realize the reason
Guī was unable to reach the level of the ancients, is precisely
due to this method. Indeed, the essential point
of establishing one's words, lies in having
substance. When the ancients created
literature, it was all based
on what they perceived internally, not originally because they liked
to be ostentatious and brilliant, like weavers and embroiderers who boast
of their colors. A rich
and noble young man, even in a drunken
dream, cannot speak
the pathetic words of a beggar; a person suffering
from illness and hardship, even if placed in a setting
of music and lavish feasts, cannot exchange their groans
for laughter. This is why one's voice
reflects one's mind, and why writings cannot
be mutually exchanged, but must each form
their own style. Now, abandoning
what one seeks oneself, and merely copying
the external form of the ancients, is like Qǐ Liáng's
wife, who was adept
at weeping for her husband, yet the elderly wife
in the western house, also learns
her sad wailing; Qū Zǐ drowned
himself in the Mìluó River, yet the officials
of a unified and harmonious court, should also produce
the lamentations of Chǔ; Is that
not absurd? As for
writing, the ancients never
failed to desire skillfulness. Mèngzǐ
said: "Hold fast
to your resolution (*zhì*), and do not harm
your vitality (*qì*)." Learning and knowledge
are the foundation for establishing one's words, which is analogous
to *zhì*; while literature is the instrument
for illuminating the Way, which is analogous
to *qì*. Seeking internal attainment
through learning and knowledge, is certainly the root
of writing; seeking excellence
in literature, is also the demonstration
of learning. Therefore, Sòng Confucian scholars
respected moral principle and slighted literary ornamentation. Master Yīchuān
said that being skilled in writing harms the Way, and Master Míngdào
said that memorization is merely playing with objects and losing one's resolution. Although they spoke
to those who forgot the root and chased the branch; yet inferring the original intention
of the two masters, those who hold fast
to their resolution, do not necessarily
have to fail to restrain their vitality. If one's utterances and vital force
were removed from vulgarity and error, and one desired
one's words to be understood, then Kǒng and Zēng
would both have failed to hear the Way. However, the excellence
and superiority of literature, truly depends on the reader's
own internal acquisition; just as with delicious
food and drink, and light
and warm clothing. The experience of those
who wear and eat them, is known
only to themselves, and is difficult
to explain to others. If you wish to convey
the principle of clothing and food to someone, you should point to fine cuisine
and let him taste it himself, then he will obtain
the sweet flavor; point to fox and badger fur
and let him wear it himself, then he will obtain
the lightness and warmth—this is the proper
way. But to spit out what one
has tasted and feed it to another to give them the sweetness, or to embrace
another's body and press them against one's chest to give them warmth, there is no such
principle.
said:
"Those who record events must extract their essentials,
and those who compile words must capture their mystery."
The writings that supposedly 'capture the mystery and extract the essentials,'
are not only unavailable for later generations to hear of,
even those of the time, such as Jí and Shí’s followers,
have not been heard to have seen them.
What exactly are they?
They are probably nothing more than searching through chapters and plucking out phrases,
to serve as material assistance for writing.
This type of recorded knowledge,
the ancients must certainly have possessed.
For example, Zuǒ Sī spent ten years composing the Rhapsody on the Three Capitals (《Sāndū Fù》).
He had brushes and paper hung up all around his gateway, courtyard, fences, and privies;
everywhere he placed paper and brushes,
and whenever an idea came, he immediately wrote it down.
Now observing his rhapsody,
there are no extraordinary or wondrous thoughts,
that stir the mind or shock the soul,
that required ten years of intense contemplation and effort to complete.
What he meant by 'writing down immediately when an idea came,'
must also have involved marking down the meaning of existing texts,
first collecting the essence of the ancients,
and only then having enough material to put to use.
However, what one gains from reading a book,
resides in the person themselves,
and they do not interfere with each other.
Therefore, when the ancients discussed writing,
they often spoke of the merit of reading and cultivating vitality (qì),
the essential nature of broad knowledge of antiquity and mastery of the classics,
the benefit of close association with teachers and friends,
and the methods for gathering material and seeking assistance—
this is the proper path.
As for discussing the skill or crudeness of literary language,
they provided one corner and expected three others to be inferred,
matching emotion and comparing categories,
such as Lù Jī’s Rhapsody on Literature (《Wén Fù》),
Liú Xié’s The Literary Mind and the Carving of Dragons (《Wénxīn Diāolóng》),
Zhōng Róng’s Gradings of Poets (《Shī Pǐn》);
or sometimes citing an excellent character or a fine line,
or judging the merits and faults of an entire piece,
allowing the reader to gain insight from the text itself,
and understand the spirit beyond the words.
This way, their thoughts regarding literary expression are more than half revealed.
As for making excerpts into books out of necessity,
and marking them for categorization,
this is merely what the mind grasped at a specific moment,
and does not necessarily derive from the inherent nature of the source text.
For example, when missing someone, one sees the moon and begins to muse;
must the moon necessarily signify distant longing?
When a long-term sojourner hears the rain and feels sadness,
must the rain necessarily contain sorrowful circumstances?
Yet, the feelings under the moon,
and the emotions amidst the rain,
are they not the utmost literature of Heaven and Earth?
If one wishes to take these specific feelings and longings,
and hide them away as secrets,
or perhaps desire to benefit future learners,
by saying that whenever one faces the bright moon or listens to continuous rain,
one must adopt this particular sorrow and feeling
in order to comprehend,
then those who happen to meet a dear friend after a long time,
or those newly married enjoying their peace,
will certainly not believe it.
Therefore, concerning the matter of studying literature,
what can be transmitted and received are the compass and square (rules and standards);
what cannot be transmitted and received is the spontaneous creation of the mind and intention.
As for books that compile categories and compare excerpts,
and volumes that mark and critique,
they are fundamentally the minor aspects of writing,
and should not be revealed to others,
but only used for self-record.
A father must not give them to his son,
nor a teacher transmit them to his pupil.
This is because there is fear that the boundless writings of the ancients
will be confined by the limited mind and hand of one particular time.
For regulated verse (lǜ shī), one must understand level (píng) and oblique (zè) tones;
for ancient verse (gǔ shī), one ought to know the rhythmic pattern (yīnjié).
However, píng and zè are obvious and easy to know,
while yīnjié is subtle and difficult to discern.
If one is skilled in gǔ shī,
one should grasp it naturally.
If one insists on using gǔ shī to fix the rhythmic patterns for others,
then the changes in yīnjié,
are distinctly beyond what a fixed set of poems can restrict.
When Zhào Shēnfú compiled the poems of the ancients into the Manual of Tonal Patterns (《Shēngdiào Pǔ》),
learned men mocked him.
I cannot defend Master Zhào.
However, for someone who does not understand rhythmic patterns,
it is not impossible that it might inspire their enlightenment;
it is just improper to hold it up as the universal standard or law.
For contemporary prose (shí wén), one must understand structure and rules (fǎdù);
for ancient prose (gǔ wén), one must also know structure and rules.
The fǎdù of shí wén are obvious and easy to discuss,
while the fǎdù of gǔ wén are subtle and hard to explain.
If one is skilled in gǔ wén,
one should grasp it naturally.
If one insists on using gǔ wén to demonstrate structure and rules to others,
then the changes in writing,
are not limited by a fixed piece of writing.
Guī Zhènchuān took text from The Records of the Grand Historian (《Shǐ Jì》),
marked it with five colors,
to show its meaning and structure.
Learned men of today,
upon hearing of this, would surely laugh in secret.
I cannot defend Master Guī.
However, for someone who does not understand structure and rules,
it is not impossible that it might aid their comprehension;
it is just insufficient to be regarded as a secret method for transmission.
If it is regarded as a secret method for transmission,
it is like the man of Yǐng treating common swallow-stones (yàn shí) as treasure.
Indeed, writing is difficult to exhaust in a single aspect.
The benevolent see benevolence,
the wise see wisdom.
The rhythmic patterns of poetry,
and the structure and rules of prose,
the superior person believes can be attained without formal study,
like the restraint and release in weeping and laughing,
and the modulations and undulations in singing and sobbing.
If one insists on revealing these to others,
people will instead become constrained and fail to achieve the genuine emotions of singing, sobbing, weeping, and laughing.
However, if one's own insights,
do not involve forced interpretation or excessive pursuit,
but arise from casual reading,
with something grasped by the mind,
and committed to writing to record it,
for self-reflection and recognition,
it is not impossible that it may aid in refining rhetoric.
But if one takes their own insights,
and argues that all people in the world,
must model their minds and hands after mine,
later generations might perhaps follow me,
but if we raised the ancients and asked them,
they would say:
"What I ordained (or intended),
was not this!"
Would this not be an injustice?
Literary Collection
The rise of the collection (jí)
Was it perhaps at the juncture when writing (wénzhāng) was ascending and declining?
In antiquity, the court had the canons and counsels (diǎnmó);
officials maintained the statutes and laws (fǎlìng);
the folk songs (fēngshī) were collected from the hamlets;
memorials (fūzòu) ascended to the ancestral halls (miàotáng).
There was no one who wrote books merely for themselves,

nor families who preserved just one specific doctrine (yīshuō). When Liú Xiàng (劉向) collated books and cataloged the various Masters and Hundred Schools (zhūzǐ bǎijiā), he consistently said they originated under the supervision of a certain ancient official or clan (mǒu guān mǒu shì zhī zhǎng). This is evidence that in antiquity, there was no private authorship.
Since scholarship was separated into different paths,
and the Hundred Schools (Bǎijiā) arose like the wind,
the doctrines of the various Masters of the Zhōu (周) and Qín (秦) periods
were too numerous to count;
the discerning already lamented the fragmentation of the Way and its arts (dàoshù).
However, those professional studies passed down through families
never sought literary fame (wén míng).
If they were sufficient to manifest their craft
and could be transmitted to their disciples,
then their doctrines (shuō) ceased there
and never involved inconsistent or complex miscellaneous writing (cēncī pángzá zhī wén).
Writing flourished gradually during the two Hàn (漢) dynasties,
marking the beginning of the decline of true authorship (zhùzuò).
However, the memorials and discussions of Jiǎ Shēng (賈生)
were compiled into the *Xīn Shū* (新書);
Sīmǎ Xiāngrú’s (司馬相如) rhymed prose (cífù)
were merely recorded as titles:
All formed the doctrines of a single school (yī jiā zhī yán),
not far removed from the various Masters (zhūzǐ).
Initially, there was no practice of gathering various styles together,
collecting them into what is known as a literary collection (wénjí).
From the Eastern Capital (Dōngjīng) onwards,
ending around the Jiàn'ān (建安) and Huángchū (黃初) eras,
writing became voluminous.
Yet, in the biographies of literary figures (wényuàn zhuàn) recorded by the two historians Fàn [Yè] (範) and Chén [Shòu] (陳),
the compiled biographies of scholars (wénshì)
recognized their writing style,
and all stated that they authored a certain number of poems (shī), rhymed prose (fù), steles (bēi), admonitions (zhēn), eulogies (sòng), and funeral elegies (lěi),
but did not say ‘a certain number of volumes of literary collections’ (wénjí).
Thus, the substance of the literary collection was already present,
but the name ‘literary collection’ (wénjí) had not yet been established.
Since Zhì Yú (摯虞) first created the *Wénzhāng Liúbié* (文章流別),
scholars found it convenient.
Consequently, they separately gathered the works of the ancients
and labeled them as individual collections (biéjí).
Therefore, the term ‘literary collection’ (wénjí)
was actually modeled on the Jìn (晉) dynasty, when Chén Shòu (陳壽) compiled the collection of Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮).
In later generations, writings composed for social obligation or expediency,
and trivial, disorderly writings produced for examination success,
also spread profusely and chaotically,
contending to attach themselves to the name of 'individual collection' (biéjí).
This truly could not be encompassed by Liú’s *Liè* (略),
nor attached to Bān’s *Zhì* (誌).
Furthermore, the writings thus created
were also full of affected sentiment and polished appearances,
inconsistent and contradictory,
no longer the words of specialized masters, which permit no extraneous content.
When scholarship divided, the various Masters (zhūzǐ) emerged—
that was the juncture of public and private spheres.
When speech and action diverged, the literary collections (wénjí) arose—
that was the separation of sincerity and falsehood.
If the trend repeatedly changes, it repeatedly declines;
if writing becomes increasingly numerous, it becomes increasingly chaotic.
If there were truly scholars fond of learning and deep in thought,
seeking the essence of established doctrines through writing,
and seeking the return to unity from dispersion,
then, after three such changes, ancient scholarship (gǔxué) might flourish again.
Alas, those who follow the streams forget the source,
and those drowning in fame lose the substance.
If two earthenware vessels can still be mistaken for bells,
how much more so the overwhelming flood that has no limit?
In the past,
the detailed classification by Liú Xiàng (向) and Liú Xīn (歆), father and son,
was surely the surviving methodology of the *Zhōu Guān* (周官).
They gathered writings old and new and distinguished their schools (jiā);
they unified the learning of the realm and entrusted it to officials.
Had there not been a fixed system passed down through generations,
then at the end of the Western Hàn (Xī Hàn),
there would have been no way to trace directly back to the origins in the Zhōu (周) and Qín (秦) dynasties.
After Bān’s *Zhì* (誌),
those who compiled catalogs frequently
sometimes combined and sometimes separated works,
without understanding the main essentials.
Since their books have not all been transmitted,
the merits or flaws of their arrangement by section (bù cì),
and the quality of their descriptions (xùlù),
cannot be fully examined either.
Xún Xù’s (荀勖) *Zhōng Jīng* (中經) had four divisions;
poetry, rhymed prose, illustrated texts, and encomiums
were placed in Division Dīng (丁 Bù), along with the books from the Jí Tomb (Jí Zhǒng).
Wáng Jiǎn’s (王儉) *Qī Zhì* (七誌)
designated poetry and rhymed prose as the Wénhàn Zhì (文翰誌),
placing it between the collected Masters (Zhūzǐ) and military books (jūnshū).
Thus, the category of Collections (Jí Bù) gradually began to open up,
but was still not explicitly listed as a separate, specialized heading.
It was not until Ruǎn Xiàoxù (阮孝緒) compiled the *Qī Lù* (七錄)
that only Techniques (Jìshù), Buddhism (Fó), and Daoism (Dào) were separated into three categories,
while the four records of Classics (Jīngdiǎn), Historical Biographies (Jìzhuàn), Masters and Military texts (Zǐbīng), and Literary Collections (Wénjí)
were already completely the precursor to the four divisions of Classics (Jīng), Histories (Shǐ), Masters (Zǐ), and Collections (Jí) used by the Táng (唐) people.
Therefore, the cataloging of the Collections Division (Jí Bù)
was actually modeled after the Xiāo Liáng (蕭梁) period,
and the tradition of ancient scholarship (gǔxué yuánliú)
underwent a transformation at this point,
which was also necessitated by the prevailing circumstances.
Alas!
When true authorship (zhùzuò) declined, literary collections (wénjí) appeared;
when sources and precedents (diǎngù) were exhausted, classified anthologies (lèishū) appeared.
Scholars became greedy for the ease of brief reading
but were unaware of the decline of substantial learning (shíxué).
They were habituated to easily attained fame
but were unaware of the dispersal of the Great Way (Dà Dào).
Rivers decline day by day.
How can heroic scholars,
after the raging torrent has already collapsed,
who wish to block the hundred streams flowing eastward,
avoid being mocked and ridiculed by the entire world,
or being targeted and cited for their rhetoric?
How can this be achieved?
Furthermore, the name (míng)
is the guest of the substance (shí).
Classification (lèi)
arises from precedent (lì).
The ancients possessed specialized scholarship,
and only afterward were there specialized books.
Once there were specialized books,
only afterward was there specialized instruction and transmission.
By seeking books based on classification,
and tracing the source from the stream,
if the method of sectional arrangement (bù cì zhī fǎ) is clear,
even the *Sān Fén* (三墳) and *Wǔ Diǎn* (五典)
can be obtained while sitting down.
Since the tradition of textual collation (jiàochóu) has been lost,
the contents of literary collections (wénjí) and classified anthologies (lèishū)
within a single compilation
are themselves overwhelmingly chaotic and inconsistent.
How can later generations, who arise,
gain insight into the grand structure of the ancients?
Now, the *Chǔ Cí* (楚詞)
is the work of Qū Yuán’s (屈原) single school.
Since the *Qī Lù* (七錄) first included it in the Collections Division (Jí Bù),
the *Suí Zhì* (隋誌) specifically featured the Chǔ Cí (楚詞) category,
and thus classified General Collections (zǒngjí) and Individual Collections (biéjí) together as three categories,
which became the established method for catalogers.
If we fully extend this principle,
then the rhymed prose (fù) of Sīmǎ Xiāngrú (相如),
the five-character poetry (wǔyán) of Sū [Wǔ] (蘇) and Lǐ [Líng] (李),
and Méi Shēng’s (枚生) *Qī Fā* (七發),
should also be separately marked with headings
and become the Fù Category, the Wǔyán Category, and the Qī Fā Category.
How can the labels General Collection (zǒngjí) and Individual Collection (biéjí)
be adequate to categorize them?
The misuse of the source
truly began when rhymed prose (cífù) was not listed as a specialized school
and literary writers began having individual collections.
The *Wén Xīn Diāo Lóng* (文心雕龍)
is a specialized work by Liú Xié (劉勰).
Since the *Jí Xián Shū Mù* (集賢書目) classified it as a General Collection (zǒngjí),
the *Táng Zhì* (唐誌) subsequently grouped it with the *Shǐ Tōng* (史通), the *Wénzhāng Guī Jiàn* (文章龜鑒), and the *Shǐ Hàn Yì Yì* (史漢異義) as one category.
This became the common rule for the various Masters (zhūzǐ) cited by Zhèng [Qiáo]’s *Liè* (鄭略) and Mǎ [Duānlín]’s *Kǎo* (馬考).
If we fully extend this principle,
then the *Diǎn Lùn* (典論) by Wèi Wén [Dì] (魏文),
Gě Hóng’s (葛洪) *Shǐ Chāo* (史鈔),
and Zhāng Zhì’s (張騭) *Wénshì Zhuàn* (文士傳)
should also be mixed together and put into General Collections.
How then can the headings for the History Division (Shǐ Bù) and Masters Division (Zǐ Bù) be distinguished?

The *Diǎn Lùn* (典論) belongs to the Masters category (Zǐ Lèi). The *Shǐ Chāo* (史鈔) and the *Wénshì Zhuàn* (文士傳) belong to the History category (Shǐ Lèi). This confusion of principles is truly due to the difficulty of defining specialization within literary collections,
and things that merely look alike can masquerade as the genuine article.
Since cataloging lacked a clear source and tradition,
authors’ titling
subsequently followed no fixed rule.
Láng Wèizhī’s (郎蔚之) *Zhū Zhōu Tú Jīng Jí* (諸州圖經集)
is Geography within the History Division (Shǐ Bù) but bears the name ‘Collection’ (Jí).
Wáng Fāngqìng’s (王方慶) *Bǎo Zhāng Jí* (寶章集)
is Philology (Xiǎoxué) within the Classics Division (Jīng Bù) but bears the name ‘Collection’ (Jí).
Xuán Jué’s (玄覺) *Yǒngjiā Jí* (永嘉集)
is Buddhist texts (Shìjiā) within the Masters Division (Zǐ Bù) but bears the name ‘Collection’ (Jí).
Regarding the later streams of the Hundred Schools and miscellaneous arts (bǎijiā záyì),
their knowledge was mediocre and murky,
and their writing was crude and rustic.
They either plagiarized the ancients
or merely demonstrated petty skills.
They fundamentally do not belong to the Collections category,
yet the numerous works that call themselves ‘Collection’ (Jí)
are too many to enumerate.
However, once the three types of Collections (Sān Jí) arose,
the Nine Streams (Jiǔ Liú) were inevitably mixed up.
The confusion in scholarship
is not merely a case of a ghost on Lí Qiū (黎丘)
or losing a sheep at a fork in the road!
End of Chapter/Volume.
The *Yì* says:
"Keep still the jaws (gěn qí fǔ),
speech will have order."
The *Shī* says:
"Words uttered have structure (yǒu zhāng)."
For the ancients regarding speech,
they only sought that it have structure (yǒu zhāng) and order (yǒu xù).
When recorded in writing,
there were bamboo slips and tablets (jiǎn cè).
Marking their beginning and end,
this was called a piān-zhāng.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Regarding the *Wǔchéng*,
I only took two or three slips."
This is proof that connected slips formed a piān.
The *Yì Dàzhuàn* says:
"The slips of the two piān [parts]
number eleven thousand five hundred and twenty."
This is proof that the beginning and end constitute a piān.
When Zuǒ Shì quoted the *Shī*,
he cited its piān name,
and when quoting it sequentially,
he would say, "a certain zhāng says so-and-so."
This is proof that the piān is the main completion,
and the zhāng (stanza) is the sectional division.
The essence lies in the writing being sufficient for the speech,
forming structured sections (chéng zhāng) and having order,
so that it can travel far and be understood.
Piān-zhāng or bamboo slips,
were not the primary consideration.
Later generations had a proliferation of writings,
leading to the establishment of the study of textual collation (jiào chóu zhī xué).
And when Liú Xiàng (Xiàng) and Liú Xīn (Xīn) recorded these works,
they mostly used piān (sections) and juàn (scrolls) for counting.
Generally, piān followed the bamboo slips,
and juàn followed the silk cloth (jiān sù);
names were determined by the material,
with no other meaning.
Writing on silk cloth [jiān sù]
came later than bamboo slips,
thus during the Zhōu and Qín dynasties they were called piān,
and it was only upon entering the Hàn dynasty that the term juàn (scroll) appeared.
However, at that time, bamboo and silk were used simultaneously,
and a named piān necessarily had a beginning and end;
juàn did not have a definition for beginning and end,
and often a juàn was created based on the piān;
therefore, the number of piān recorded in the *Hàn Zhì* [History of the Hàn]
generally corresponds to the number of juàn in later generations,
this being the main correlation.
However, the *Shījīng* consists of three hundred piān,
but only twenty-eight juàn;
the *Shàngshū* and the *Lǐjīng*,
also both have fewer juàn than piān.
Thus, we also know that when books were transferred to silk cloth [jiān sù] at that time,
they were still called piān.
The designation piān
specifically emphasizes the beginning and end of the textual meaning,
whereas juàn is related to the length of the connected silk cloth.
This has no other meaning,
it is simply that the term piān for a book
is older than juàn.
Therefore, different piān could be in the same juàn,
but the division into juàn was not used to mark a beginning or an end.
Furthermore, in Bān Shì’s [Bān Gù's] Treatise on the *Wǔxíng* [Five Phases]
and the Biography of the *Yuánhòu*,
if the piān was long and the juàn was short,
it was divided into sub-juàn (zǐ juàn).
This means the piān cannot be easily changed,
but the juàn can be divided or combined.
Following this,
up through the Suí and Táng dynasties,
books counted by juàn were many,
while those counted by piān were few.
Among the various authors,
what they called "one juàn,"
often corresponded to what the ancients called "one piān";
thus, things change with time,
and people often do so unknowingly.
Only Sīmǎ Biāo’s *Xù Hòu Hàn Zhì* [Continuation of the Treatise on the Later Hàn]
had eight piān of text
divided into thirty juàn.
Splitting piān to fit juàn,
this greatly altered Bān [Gù]’s method of sub-juàn,
setting a bad precedent (zuò yǒng) for the historical biographies of the Táng and Sòng dynasties,
and losing the meaning intended by the ancients.
As for designations where the name is slightly different but the reality is the same:
The Dàoist texts use cè [volume],
which is just another name for juàn,
and the Yuán dynasty people used it in the *Shuō Fú*.
Kuǎi Tōng’s *Jùn Yǒng* uses shǒu [head],
which is another name for zhāng (section),
and the people of the Liáng dynasty used it in the *Wénxuǎn*.
This, however, was just creating new and different labels;
the reality of the names was therefore harmless.
Since the Táng and Sòng dynasties,
books that were scrolls [juǎn zhóu]
again changed into paper booklets (zhǐ cè);
thus, the ease of compiling books,
compared to the ancients,
was more than fivefold (bèi xǐ).
What the ancients referred to as heavy bundles of bamboo slips [jiǎn zhì],
which could not be combined into one piān,
can now be doubled in volume
and easily contained within the same booklet (tóng cè).
Therefore, before the Táng dynasty,
the division of juàn was very short.
What the collections of writings from the Six Dynasties and Táng scholars
comprised as ten juàn,
modern people would consider only three or four juàn.
Since the Sòng dynasty,
the division of juàn has consequently become longer.
Since the ancients’ juàn followed the scroll [juǎn zhóu] format,
they naturally could not be excessively long;
when later people used paper booklets for books,
they merely preserved the name juàn,
and thus, following their own preference,
they had no difficulty recording works in giant volumes (jù cè).
Using paper booklets (zhǐ cè) while retaining the name juàn derived from silk cloth (jiān sù)
is exactly like the Hàn people using silk cloth while retaining the name piān derived from bamboo slips;
the principle is fundamentally the same.
However, since piān is used to measure the beginning and end of the text,
this is something that cannot be changed forever,
and one might even say that its definition is independent of bamboo slips.
Juàn, conversely, is limited by the length of the scroll roller,
and there is no standard rule for its beginning and end.
Now that silk cloth is no longer used and paper booklets are employed,
the boundaries should naturally be set according to what the paper booklet can reasonably bear.
Whether one prefers the antique and labels it juàn,
or follows the material and labels it cè (booklet),
neither is inherently wrong;
but one should not take the number of juàn and the number of cè [volumes]
and deliberately mismatch them (cān cī),
causing people to search for piān using the juàn,
and then again causing people to seek the juàn using the cè,
merely adding confusion.
Now, the length, brevity, beginning, and end of a text
cannot be rigidly fixed;
and the weight of square tablets and slips (fāng cè)
is no longer in use today.
Thus, a piān naturally cannot stand alone;
it must necessarily rely on the juàn for continuous compilation;
this is the reality.
Juàn is not fixed and unchangeable.
If one wishes to encompass piān to consolidate them,
and also wishes to break up the cè to divide them,
causing people to have an extra layer of searching beyond combination and division,
and yet having no relevance to principles of meaning or structure,
is this not merely bothersome busywork?
Therefore, when compiling a book, one should only discuss the piān,
and should not count the juàn.
If one must count juàn,
allow it to be determined by the length of the cè [volume],
and arrange the apportionment accordingly.
To ignore the physical cè [volume] being contained,
yet meticulously divide it into juàn
merely for the aesthetic beauty of the title label and catalogue entry,
is all about clinging to the past and forgetting reality.
In the *Chóngwén* [Catalogue] and the *Sòng Zhì*,
there are cases where the cè is listed but the juàn are not detailed.
The Míng dynasty *Wényuān Gé Mù* [Catalogue of the Wényuān Pavilion]
only counts the cè and has no juàn listed.
Although this is a deficiency in cataloging procedures,
if the juàn and the cè were consistently matched,
why would this fault arise?
The Analogy of Heaven
Heaven is vast and formless (hún rán ér wú míng).
The Sān Yuán, the Qī Yào, the Èrshíbā Xiù, the Twelve Stations (Yī Shí'èr Cì), the three hundred and sixty-five degrees, the ecliptic (Huáng Dào), and the celestial equator (Chì Dào) —
these are merely names forcibly imposed by calendar specialists (lì jiā) to keep count.
Since ancient times,
when combined, they form refinement (wén), substance (zhì), reduction, and increase (sǔn yì);
when divided, they form academic pursuits (xué yè), practical achievements (shì gōng),
literary style (wén zhāng), and moral nature (xìng mìng).
When they began,
there was only insight into what was proper (dāng rán),
and they acted upon what they inevitably had to do,
being vast and without fixed names.
The act of dividing things into categories
and naming them wén or zhì,
naming them xué yè or shì gōng,
wén zhāng or xìng mìng,
and declaring them incapable of merging,
all arose from addressing specific flaws (piān jiù bì),
holding something up to instruct and show others,
and reluctantly imposing names
to fix a direction.
Later generations did not observe the reason for this and clung to the names,
believing they could thereby designate their own schools and classifications,
leading to the widespread tendency of acknowledging one master and dismissing others as mere servants (rù zhǔ chū nú).
The mutual mockery between Hànxué (Hàn Learning) and Sòngxué (Sòng Learning),
the reciprocal slandering between textual commentary (xùngǔ) and literary rhetoric (cí zhāng),
and the conflicts over virtue and nature (dé xìng) versus pure scholarship (xué wèn) —
all stem from knowing *what* is the case but not knowing *why* it is the case.
to manage the affairs of the world (jīngshì).
For example, those who study calendrics (zhì lì zhě)
exhaust human effort to seek convergence with the movements of Heaven, and nothing more;
they fundamentally do not rely on their own subjective intentions or preconceptions.
That which former generations overlooked, later generations elaborate upon;
that which former generations lacked, later generations originate;
that which former generations habitually practiced, later generations alter.
For instance, the stars mentioned in the *Yuèlìng* cannot be the same as those in the *Yáodiǎn*;
the calendar system of the *Tàichū Lìfǎ* cannot be the same as that of the *Yuèlìng*.
The essential point is that they must appropriately suit their context, and then they are acceptable.
Zhōu Gōng succeeded Kings Wén and Wǔ,
and personally served as Grand Administrator (zhǒngzǎi);
therefore, he established the Rites and Music (lǐyuè),
serving as the established statute for an entire era.
Kǒngzǐ was born into a declining age,
possessing virtue but lacking position;
therefore, he transmitted (shù) but did not create (zuò),
thereby clarifying the Great Way of the former kings.
Mèngzǐ lived during a time when hermits and scholars engaged in widespread argumentation;
therefore, he strenuously resisted Yáng and Mò
to uphold the transmission of Kǒngzǐ.
Hánzǐ lived during a time when Buddhism (Fó) and Daoism (Lǎo) flourished greatly;
therefore, he promoted and clarified the Way of the Sages (shèngdào),
thereby correcting the learning and scholarship of the realm.
Chéng and Zhū lived at the juncture when later learning had forgotten its roots;
therefore, they distinguished and clarified the Principle of Nature (xìnglǐ),
thereby retrieving the hearts of the common populace.
Their undertakings and achievements
were all unique and did not copy one another,
yet all spoke to the management of the world (jīngshì).
Therefore, learning and scholarship
are the means by which social trends (fēngqì) are opened up.
If social trends have not yet been opened,
learning and scholarship provide the means to open them.
If social trends have already become corrupt,
learning and scholarship provide the means to retrieve them.
Human hearts and social customs
cannot endure forever without becoming corrupt,
just as the methods of Xīhé and Bǎozhāng
cannot endure forever without error.
Addressing their corruption and implementing remedies
is like calendrists discussing alterations when errors arise in the calendar.
The errors in calendrical law
are either excess (guò) or insufficiency (bùjí).
The corruption in social trends
is either undue emphasis (piān zhòng) or undue neglect (piān qīng).
The bias of undue emphasis, neglect, excess, or insufficiency
cannot be addressed unless one moves away from the extreme
to obtain the propriety of the Central Mean (zhōngzhèng).
Scholars who crave fame
are merely chasing social trends and calling it scholarship;
this is like trying to rescue a fire with fire,
or rescuing water with water.
It is established that Heaven overcomes humanity,
but established human effort (réndìng) can also overcome Heaven.
The Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions (Èrshíbā Xiù),
and the Twelve Divisions (Shí'èr Cìshě),
which map the celestial degrees surrounding Heaven,
encompass all the capital cities of Zhōngguó during the Spring and Autumn period (Chūnqiū).
Now, Zhōngguó (China) is within the Great Earth,
merely a single southeastern corner.
Yet the celestial degrees of the entire heavens,
when applied to prognostications (zhānyàn),
have never failed to correspond.
This perhaps cannot be inferred solely by reason;
it is likely due to established human effort (réndìng) overcoming Heaven.
Furthermore, consider the method of Zǐpíng for predicting a person's life based on the year, month, day, and hour of birth.
It is entirely based on the sixty sexagenary cycles (liùshí jiǎzǐ),
allocating them according to the generative and restrictive cycles of the Five Phases (Wǔxíng).
Now, the years, months, and hours
were fundamentally not recorded by the jiǎzǐ system,
and the ancients never spoke of this method.
But since later generations established this method,
when they extrapolate good and ill fortune (xiūjiǔ), there is nothing that fails to correspond.
Is this not established human effort overcoming Heaven?
The *Yì* (Classic of Changes) states, "Act before Heaven, and Heaven will not contravene,"
this is probably what it means.
Learning and inquiry also follow the principle that established human effort overcomes Heaven.
Principle (lǐ) is divided into the Unlimited (Wújí) and the Great Ultimate (Tàijí);
Numbers (shù) are divided into Prior Heaven (Xiāntiān) and Later Heaven (Hòutiān);
Diagrams include the *Hétú* and the *Luòshū*;
Nature (xìng) is divided into the Principle of Righteousness (yìlǐ) and Physical Temperament (qìzhì).
When the Sages' intentions
are inferred by later worthy scholars using their own intentions,
it turns out as if the Sages might well have been interpreted in this way.
If one follows these explanations,
one can aspire to become a Sage;
one can also aspire to embody Heaven.
Is this not established human effort overcoming Heaven?
To venerate and believe too strongly,
and hold that one has truly grasped the Sages' intentions, is certainly wrong;
yet to argue and refute too strongly,
and regard other scholars as abusive and malicious,
how could that be appropriate either?
On Teachers (Shī Shuō)
Hán Tuìzhī said:
"The teacher
is one who transmits the Way (dào), imparts knowledge (yè), and resolves doubts (huò)."
He also said:
"The teacher is not necessarily more worthy than the disciple,
and the disciple is not necessarily inferior to the teacher."
"Where the Way exists,
there the teacher exists."
He also said:
"Shaman-doctors and artisans of all trades
are not ashamed to teach one another."
He then expressed surprise that the people of his time
considered it shameful to learn from one another,
and were thus inferior even to shaman-doctors and artisans.
Hán Shì (Mr. Hán) was speaking regarding the corrupt customs of his time;
he had not yet reached the ultimate meaning of the Teacher.
The *Jì* (Record of Rites) states:
"Among the things people serve, there are three,
and they should be served as one:
the ruler (jūn), parents (qīn), and teacher (shī)."
This is spoken regarding the transmission of the Way.
Imparting knowledge and resolving doubts,
however, involves differences in rank (chāděng).
Knowledge has refined and crude aspects;
doubts also have major and minor aspects.
Those who impart and resolve certainly act as teachers;
that is undeniable;
however, there is a distinction between this and the transmission of the Way.
The mutual teaching among shaman-doctors and artisans
cannot be viewed generally (as equivalent).
There are teachers who can be replaced
and teachers who cannot be replaced;
the difference between them
is incomparable.
One who understands the meaning of the Teacher
does he understand Heaven?
Indeed, people all follow the Mandate of Heaven;
Heaven has neither sound nor smell (chòu),
yet it causes the ruler (jūn) to govern them.
People are all begotten by Heaven;
Heaven does not individually beget each creature,
but parents (qīn) beget them.
People all learn from Heaven;
Heaven does not instruct tirelessly,
but the teacher (shī) teaches them.
If this is so, then for a noble person (jūnzǐ) who contemplates serving Heaven,
it lies simply in diligently serving these three.
When a person loses their Dào,
they lose that by which they are human,
just as if one is without a body,
then one is without that by which one lives.
Therefore, that parents give birth and teachers instruct,
the principles underlying them are fundamentally not different.
This is why the seventy disciples serving Kǒngzǐ
could die with him,
could live with him,
and traveling east, west, south, or north,
dared not claim ownership of their own bodies.
This was not due to emotional kinship,
but because the natural order and circumstances dictated it so.
As for the transmission of knowledge and resolving confusion,
there are differences in hierarchy.
The transmission and reception of canonical teachings
involving chapter arrangement, sentence structure, and exegetical commentary;
the profound origins of historical studies,
involving selection, omission, principles of justice, and formal precedents;
all are encompassed by the substance of the Dào.
The ancients said, "Writing does not fully express the words,
and words do not fully express the intentions."
Beyond bamboo and silk,
there is a separate transmission of the mind,
received through the mouth and ear in succession.
One must clearly understand the source,
just as the order of ancestral and collateral branches of a lineage cannot be confused.
For this, one must follow the person and only then receive the teaching.
If they are not that person,
one already has nothing to receive.
This is the teacher who cannot be replaced (Bùkě Yì zhī Shī).
Specialized scholarship,
literary works that manage the world—
the urgency, gradualness, sweetness, and bitterness within them
can be apprehended through intuition
but cannot be verbally transmitted.
This also houses the ultimate Dào;
one must follow the person and only then receive the teaching.
If one does not follow that person,
one already has nothing to receive.
This is the teacher who cannot be replaced.
If this is the case,
while alive, one should serve diligently,
attending constantly without fixed direction;
upon death, one should offer the person the seat of the deceased and sacrifices on the sacrificial vessel,
like the seventy disciples did for Kǒngzǐ.
As for discussing and practicing classics and commentaries,
the main intent holds no place for individual interpretation;
correcting literary compositions,
the principle does not warrant independent status;
things that people commonly know and are able to do,
which someone happens to obtain and teaches to me;
if I do not finish with A,
it does not prevent me from leaving and turning to B;
if A does not inform me,
B can also be asked.
This does not delve into the Dào,
and thus this is a teacher who can be replaced (Kě Yì zhī Shī).
Even scholarship and literature
are but minor arts.
The methods one adopts from them
are no different from the carpenter advising on carving and sculpture,
or the weaving woman transmitting techniques for fine silk and embroidery.
If they confer a single day's worth of skill,
one may bow and treat them with propriety,
follow them in their movements and sit in a corner,
and show increased affection and respect.
But if one insists on strictly adhering to the three solemn duties of service
and equates their significance with that of parents who gave birth,
then the one who demands is deluded,
and the one who gives is not sincere.
The teachers of shaman-doctors and the hundred artisans
certainly cannot be compared to the Dào of the Jūnzǐ,
yet there is also an explanation for them.
Regarding the excellence of technical skills,
the ancients who professionally specialized
also had subtle points understood only by the individual,
which were transmitted if they found the right person,
and not transmitted if they did not.
This is also a teacher who cannot be replaced,
and should also be served diligently while alive,
and offered the seat of the deceased upon death.
When the ancients ate or drank,
they always sacrificed to the person who first made food and drink,
not forgetting the origin.
How much more so concerning the person who perfected my morality, Dào, and arts,
and from whom I inherently could not have received it otherwise?
As for the saying that disciples are not necessarily inferior to the teacher,
and the teacher is not necessarily superior to the disciples,
it depends on what is gained.
If the contention lies in the Dào,
then why haggle and compare superiority or inferiority
concerning the mastery of mere techniques, tricks, and professions?
Alas!
The Dào of the teacher has been lost for a long time.
A person of aspiration
searches throughout the world
but does not see the teacher who cannot be replaced.
Yet, observing the past and present,
there is something that stirs their heart within.
Unconsciously, they smile broadly,
and then sorrowfully do not know where the tears come from—
this is also my teacher.
Though I do not see the person,
I receive a secret transmission from them.
It is like an orphan seeing their deceased father in a portrait:
even if no one tells them,
they will surely have a realization in their dreams.
Yet, some people say that the conduct of the ancients
is not entirely worthy of emulation
and need not be offered the seat of the deceased.
However, Yǔ surely sacrificed to Gǔn,
honoring his origin.
Soldiers sacrifice to Chīyóu,
revering the originator of the methods.
If one must select a person to revere,
Zhōu Gōng and Kǒngzǐ would have no regrets.
When a son serves his parents,
is there a practice of assessing their merits and virtues
and excluding the grandfather from ancestral rites in favor of the great-grandfather?
Some years ago,
a guest was discussing scholarship,
saying that books became voluminous in later generations,
but human lifespan cannot increase beyond that of antiquity.
Therefore, talent is not equal to that of the ancients.
If those who possess books now
could live for five hundred years,
scholars would have no regrets.
It is estimated that after a thousand years,
books will surely be several times more numerous than today,
so one should correspondingly be granted a lifespan of a thousand years.
This was even transmitted as a famous saying.
I say that this is the remark of a fool who does not understand learning.
If it were as he said,
even if the Creator granted him five thousand years,
he still would not achieve realization.
Learning, concerning one's mind and body,
is like hunger and cold concerning clothing and food.
To fail to satisfy one's life with sufficient warmth and fullness,
but wish to extend one's years to exhaust all the clothing and food in the world—
this is either foolishness or delusion.
The commentary says:
"The utmost sincerity enables one to fully realize one's own nature,
which then enables one to fully realize the nature of others;
being able to fully realize the nature of others
then enables one to fully realize the nature of things."
What distinguishes humans from things
is the purity of Rén, Yì, and the Dào and Dé;
the capacity to perceive things clearly and distinguish relationships;
the ability to form a triad with Heaven and Earth and assist them—
these are not fully possessed by things.
As for consciousness, movement,
the mind, perception, and blood-vitality endowed by Heaven,
how are these different from things?
What is great in substance cannot be used for small purposes;
what is small in substance does not require assistance from others.
Each thing has its limit.
Humans are also one type of thing.
The lifespan of the Kūn Pèng is billions of years;
even a thousand years is still childhood for them.
The cicada (Huìgū) does not know spring or autumn;
one season makes it aged.
Man, situated between Heaven and Earth,
is a creature whose term is a hundred years.
The mind, perception, and blood-vitality
are sufficient to supply the needs of a hundred years,
and this cannot be forcibly changed.
Fūzǐ set his mind on learning at fifteen,
"at seventy, I could follow my heart's desires
without transgressing what was right."
The Sage (Shèngrén),
is the ultimate attainment of the human Way (Dào).
For people who study to become a sage,
they may put in ten times or a hundred times the effort,
but I have never heard of them needing ten times or a hundred times the years.
The skill gained from a single accomplishment,
or the mastery of a single technique,
also has its beginning where the mind is set on learning,
and its ultimate realization where nothing is transgressed.
That they cannot reach sageliness
is limited by their inherent quality (zhì),
not constrained by the years.
Yánzǐ died young at thirty,
Fūzǐ said:
"Alas!
I saw him advance,
but never saw him stop."
This surely lamented that he was unable to fully realize the ultimate end of a hundred years.
He also said:
"The younger generation is formidable.
If a man reaches forty or fifty and is still unknown,
then he is not worth fearing."
It is true that human life inherently spans eighty, ninety, or up to a hundred years,
yet now, not waiting until one has reached the end of their natural lifespan,
but judging at forty or fifty,
and saying that he is not worth fearing—
this is also based on estimating his life by the hundred years allotted,
and measuring the expenditure of his mental faculties, knowledge, vitality, and energy (xīnzhī xuèqì),
which can surely be obtained by reasoned calculation.
If one is unknown at fifty,
even if granted another thousand or a hundred years,
it would still be the same.
The theory of immortal spirits (Shénxiān) and eternal life,
is indeed vague and remote.
That beings of the same species possess different abilities,
is also something that reason allows;
therefore, the accounts of arranged immortals (Lièxiān) and cave spirits (dònglíng),
might have one or two tenths of truth among thousands,
and are not entirely false.
However, a thousand-year-old immortal spirit (Shénxiān),
is never heard to surpass an accomplished scholar (tōngrú) of a hundred years—
this is clear evidence that borrowed years are insufficient to encourage learning.
Yǔ (The Great) cherished even the smallest fraction of time,
and Kǒngzǐ (Confucius) "became so excited that he forgot to eat,
so joyful that he forgot his troubles,
not knowing that old age was approaching."
He also said:
"If I were granted a few years,
I would study the *Yì* (*Yì Jīng*) at fifty."
He surely feared that he would not fully exhaust the potential achievements of a hundred years,
thinking that if something could be achieved by human effort,
and yet he failed to achieve it,
then he would have failed his life.
If the cicada (huìgū) were granted the lifespan of the Kūnpéng,
it would still be capable only of chirping.
The years may be borrowed,
but the inherent quality and nature (zhìxìng) cannot be changed.
This is why Sages (Shèng) and Worthies (Xián) cherished time and strength,
but could not regret the shortening of the hundred-year span—
this is what is called "fully exhausting one's nature" (jìn xìng).
In the world, there are those who are brilliant in childhood,
whose reading and recitation abilities are doubled or quintupled compared to others, and yet they do not stop;
they should naturally be greatly different from ordinary people.
When they achieve success,
comparing them to the hundredfold effort put in by the dull and weak,
they cannot immediately surpass them.
Thus, although quickness and dullness differ,
they are ultimately all limited by the potential achievements of a hundred years,
and the use of the mental faculties, knowledge, vitality, and energy (xīnzhī xuèqì),
can clearly be constrained by reason.
Now, people do not know how to study for themselves (wéi jǐ),
but rush into broad learning to show off to others.
The things seen and heard under Heaven cannot be exhausted,
and the preferences and tastes of people cannot be the same.
To use a finite life
to pursue inexhaustible sights and sounds;
to use one person’s body
to pursue limitless preferences and tastes—
even Yáo and Shùn could not achieve this.
Mèngzǐ (Mencius) said:
"The wisdom of Yáo and Shùn
did not extend to every single thing.
The benevolence of Yáo and Shùn
did not extend to loving every single person."
Now, to take one's ordinary and vulgar abilities,
and desire to exhaust what Yáo and Shùn could not encompass,
and furthermore, wish to borrow a natural lifespan of five hundred years—
fortunately, this is impossible.
If one were able to do so,
it would merely be an ominous monstrosity.
My nephew Tíngfēng said:
"Whenever my uncle meets scholars,
they complain that they severely lack memory,
and immediately forget texts after reading them once,
and thus excuse themselves from learning.
