My uncle always replies:
'You yourself are simply not good at learning.
If you were truly good at learning,
there is absolutely no reason why your memory would be insufficient for use.
Books are vast like a sea of smoke;
even a Sage cannot exhaust them all.
The reason the ancients valued breadth
is precisely because one must first be able to specialize in a field,
only then can one discuss breadth.
For specialization leads to becoming an expert (chéngjiā),
and once an expert, one is already established.
Among the names and objects in the universe,
those that pertain closely to oneself,
even the tiniest detail should not be omitted.
Those that do not pertain closely to oneself,
even if they are Mount Tài, one should not regard them.
If one applies the mind in this way,
even with extremely dull abilities,
there is no way one cannot remember.
To not know how to specialize and become an expert,
but indiscriminately pursue what the Sage could not exhaust—
this is the wisdom of Yúgōng (The Foolish Old Man) trying to move a mountain,
and is identical to the view of the utterly narrow-minded.'"
This essay was surely written with a specific purpose,
and serves as a critique for those who boast of breadth and compete in extravagance,
administering a painful needle.
Therefore, its language is both serious and playful,
causing people to spontaneously engage in deep reflection,
and when compared with what has been discussed previously,
it is sufficient to corroborate the experiences of scholars.
Encountering Circumstances (Gǎn Yù)
In ancient times, the officials (guān), teachers (shī), administration (zhèng), and instruction (jiào) all originated from one source,
if a distinguished person (xiù mín) did not cultivate their hundred *mǔ* (acres),
they were fed (xì) in the schools (xiáng xù).
Having no fixed occupation was called the occupation of learning (xué yè).
They necessarily possessed fixed property (héng chǎn),
so there was nothing left fallow.
When the Zhōu declined and official positions were lost (guān shī),
the Way (Dào) was transmitted privately through teachers (shī) and scholars (rú).
At this point, scholars (shì) who had lost their official posts first appeared,
what Mèngzǐ called those who prize aspiration (shàng zhì).
When advancing, they could not enjoy the emoluments (lù) of their constant occupation;
when retreating, they could not plow and harvest their fixed property (héng chǎn).
Living in the world, they were isolated and precarious.
This is how it came to be.
If the sages and worthies (shèng xián) were committed to this world,
then there were occasions when they could serve as publicly supported officials (gōng yǎng zhī shì).
The Way (Dào) of thrice approaching and thrice leaving,
the timing of meeting and fitting in,
is indeed hard to speak of.
When the Master (Fūzǐ) was about to go to Jīng,
he sent Zǐxià ahead;
he reaffirmed this through Rǎnyǒu.
Xiè Liǔ and Shēn Xiáng,
if they had no support beside Duke Mù (Mù Gōng),
then they could not secure their own persons.
When Mèngzǐ left Qí,
Shízǐ offered words of concern and guidance,
and there was a guest who offered advice on staying or leaving.
The earnestness of mutual need,
combined with the scarcity of mutual encounters,
necessitates introduction and lateral communication,
maintenance and careful protection—
this arises inevitably from the circumstances of the time.
The sages and worthies (shèng xián) advanced according to ritual (lǐ);
they retreated according to righteousness (yì).
They were not provoked externally,
thus, their self-possession (zì dé) was complete.
The scholar (shì) had no fixed property (héng chǎn);
when he studied, his emolument (lù) was contained therein.
It was not that he feared being starved by plowing,
but that circumstances made it impossible for him to attend to it.
Nevertheless,
if one was without a lord (jūn) for three months,
the dead had no ancestral temple sacrifices (miào jì),
and the living had no feasts or merriment.
Frost and dew pierce the heart;
cold and desolate, they mourned each other.
How could the sages and worthies (shèng xián) necessarily be far removed from human feelings?
The noble person (jūnzǐ) stands firm in poverty;
they would bend a foot (chǐ) to straighten eight (xún).
They are ashamed to associate with crooked defenses;
they are not contending over rites and details (lǐ jié),
but rather fearing they cannot complete their self-possession (zì dé).
Those in antiquity who did not meet their time,
retreated and lived in obscurity in lower positions.
In later ages, lower positions,
cannot be attained by chance.
Those in antiquity who did not serve as officials,
personally plowed and delighted in the Way (Dào).
In later ages, land for cultivation,
cannot be sought by chance.
The state of integrity and retreat achieved by ancients,
later generations seek it by exhausting greedy and opportunistic methods,
yet still do not attain it.
Therefore, in holding the noble person (jūnzǐ) of antiquity responsible,
we only demand that they clearly understand the principles of advancing and retreating,
and not carelessly covet glory and profit (róng lì).
In holding the noble person (jūnzǐ) of later times responsible,
they must possess the steadfastness of an aspirant (zhì shì) who embraces dying in a ditch (gōu hè) and is brave enough to lose their head—only then will it suffice.
The circumstances encountered by a sage (shèng rén),
certainly contain no concept of difficulty or ease;
but for those below the great worthy (dà xián),
demanding that they fully embrace losing their head or dying in a ditch (gōu hè) before it suffices,
is also difficult for human nature.
Shāng Yāng superficially tested the Way of the Emperor (dì dào);
Jiǎ Shēng discussed matters concerning ghosts and spirits (guǐ shén).
One grew weary of obscurity,
the other met a welcoming summons to the front seat.
Their intentions each had a purpose.
Yet one met with success and the other did not:
Shāng (Yāng) relied on what Duke Xiào (Xiào Gōng) desired,
while Jiǎ (Shēng) handled what Emperor Wén (Wén Dì) found difficult.
Hán Fēi expressed frustration in *Shuō Nán* (The Difficulty of Persuasion),
Màn Qiàn (Dōngfāng Shuò) spoke allegorically through playful obscurity.
They knew that learning was not difficult,
but that the means by which to deploy that learning was difficult.
However, Hán Fēi ultimately died because of his persuasion,
while Màn Qiàn was still employed as a jester (pái).
Why?
One exposed his blade and incurred jealousy;
the other sheathed his point and was luckily preserved.
Thus, it is not difficult for the noble person (jūnzǐ) to use their learning (xué shù) to serve the world,
but difficult to use the learning (xué shù) needed to employ their learning (xué shù).
Ancient and modern times are different, and circumstances vary greatly,
this cannot go unexamined.
The learning (xué shù) of antiquity was simple and easy;
one merely needed to ask whether it was appropriate or not.
The learning (xué shù) of later times is convoluted and difficult.
Even if one’s learning (xué shù) is appropriate,
one still may not be able to use it.
One must possess the learning (xué shù) needed to employ one’s learning (xué shù),
and within this, there are skilled and unskilled aspects (gōng zhuō).
Regarding one's personal encounters in life,
we do not first criticize whether it is appropriate or not,
but first criticize its skilled or unskilled nature (gōng zhuō).
If the learning (xué shù) is appropriate but the approach and avoidance are not skillful,
one is rejected by contemporaries.
If one is skillful in encounters but one’s adherence is inappropriate,
one is mocked by later generations.
The danger of dying in a ditch (gōu hè) presses close in front,
and the consequences of skill and clumsiness (gōng zhuō) drive one from behind.
Alas!
For the scholar (shì) who cultivates and clarifies their learning (xué shù),
desiring to minimize faults,
and to be able to complete their self-possession (zì dé),
how difficult is it not!
Furthermore, revelation and obscurity are matters of timing (shí);
poverty and prosperity are matters of destiny (mìng).
Talents born of Heaven have their unique strengths,
and learning (xué) accomplished by man has its superior points.
The use required during temporary urgency or relaxation,
and the trends favored by an entire era,
do not necessarily happen to coincide—
this is also a matter of circumstances (shì).
Liú Xīn, with his classical scholarship (jīng shù), did not meet Emperor Xiàowǔ;
Lǐ Guǎng, the flying general (fēi jiàng), did not meet Emperor Gāo (Gāo Huáng).
For a thousand ages, this has been considered a pity.
A person in the Zhōu studied military arts (wǔ),
but the ruler of the time esteemed literary arts (wén).
He changed and studied literary arts (wén),
but the ruler again valued military arts (wǔ).
While still young, the ruler preferred to employ the old;
having become old, the ruler preferred to employ the young.
That gray-headed people weep by the roadside,
is certainly fitting.
As for cases where what the subordinate possesses,
is exactly what the superior seeks,
yet the mutual need is extremely urgent,
but the mutual encounter remains distant—
these are too numerous to recount.
Emperor Xiàowén slapped his thigh and thought of Pō (Po) and Mù (Mu),
yet Wèi Shàng was not spared from punitive labor.
Emperor Lǐzōng sat solemnly and praised Chéng and Zhū,
yet Zhēn and Wèi were not spared from being alienated and distant.
Thus, it is not the difficulty of learning (xué shù),
but the learning (xué shù) required to employ one’s learning (xué shù),
which is truly difficult!
One who gazes upon a distant mountain,
finds its height and beauty admirable;
but upon entering it, one does not perceive this.
One who reflects on past events,
finds sorrow and joy without end;
but while in that situation, one is unaware.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn read the *fù* (rhapsody) of Xiāngrú,
lamenting that he was soaring and piercing the clouds,
regretting that he could not have lived in the same time.
Yet when he finally met Xiāngrú,
we have never heard that Xiāngrú was placed above the multitude of attending officials of that time.
It is inherent in people that they may love the person but not understand their learning (xué),
or love their writings (wén) but not understand the person.
In the Táng dynasty, there were the factions of Niú and Lǐ.
Those who disliked Bái Jūyì,
sealed up the works of Master Bái (Bái Shì),
believing that seeing them would cause people to develop affection,
fearing a change of original intent.
This shows a distinction between loving and hating a person’s writing (wén) and their conduct (xíng).
The daughter of Zhèng Tián,
chanted and recited the poems of Luó Yǐn,
even desiring to commit herself to serving him.
Later, upon seeing Luó Yǐn’s unattractive appearance,
she consequently stopped speaking of him entirely.
This shows a division between accepting and rejecting a person’s talent and appearance (cái mào).
Distinguishing love and hate based on writing and conduct,
surely stems from factional selfishness;
dividing acceptance and rejection based on talent and appearance,
is the perspective of women and girls.
Nevertheless, the world values learning (xué shù) highly,
and when reading the books of the ancients,
one often sighs that one was not born at the same time.
Should an encounter actually occur,
they are then drawn into views based on factional support, difference, and similarity,
or worse, they imitate Zhèng Tián’s daughter in making distinctions based on appearance.
Thus, for the scholar (shì) who cultivates and clarifies their learning (xué shù),
desiring to minimize faults,
and to be able to complete their self-possession (zì dé),
how difficult is it not?
Chúnyú Liàng drank from the measure of a *dǒu* and a *shí*,
and the treatise on 'No Ghosts' was examined through dogs and horses.
This is what is meant by reciting *Guān Jū* to arouse thoughts of a virtuous lady,
or singing *Lù Míng* to convey the sentiment toward honored guests.
There must be something relied upon to initiate the inspiration,
intending to move from the shallow to the deep.
This is not only the subtly reserved style of poets,
but is truly the essence of the presentation of lambs and wild geese by gentlemen of the world.
Those who wish to implement their learning,
cannot but gauge what ordinary people understand and enter gradually.
However, those in the world who observe others,
when they hear *Guān Jū*, they seek the river island,
when *Lù Míng* is mentioned, they look for the duckweed fields,
while the virtuous lady and the honored guests are cast aside and not mentioned.
The tendency of average people,
is to enjoy ease and fear difficulty,
delight in conformity and hate difference.
Those who listen to words but fail to discern the meaning of those words,
are often eight or nine out of ten.
There are base individuals,
who, knowing that opportunity and acceptance are thus difficult,
then abandon their strengths,
and force their weaknesses.
They vigorously pursue current trends,
not necessarily seeking satisfaction in their hearts.
How could current trends be entirely without merit?
Those who initiated them,
surely had a reason;
but those who follow them,
merely imitate their falsehood.
Now, refined music (*yǎ yuè*) does not perish due to the local songs of Xiàlǐ,
but perishes due to the sounds of Zhèng (*Zhèng shēng*).
The sounds of Zhèng are artful.
Good seedlings are not destroyed by weeds,
but are destroyed by deceitful grass.
Deceitful grass is similar.
Learning and arts (*xuéshù*) are not lost to vulgar customs,
but are lost to false learning (*wěi xué*).
False learning is clever.
When the world does not know learning and arts,
they never fail to empty their hearts and wait for it.
When false learning appears,
the world no longer knows of the genuine learning that comes from self-realization.
This is why Kǒngzǐ hated the village worthy (*xiāng yuàn*),
and why Mèngzǐ deeply resented that which resembles the truth but is not.
However, those who practice this falsehood,
claim that this is merely how they apply their learning and arts.
In the past, the Master never failed to partake in the hunting sacrifice (*liè jiào*),
and the regulations for official record-keeping were ultimately not abandoned.
He only departed after the omens were insufficient for the undertaking.
Thus, the skill of applying one's learning and arts,
is not abandoned by the sages and worthies.
If learning and arts cannot adapt to changes in current trends,
then it need not be limited to sages and worthies;
even carpenters and wheelwrights,
are the same way.
Therefore, the gentleman borrows from omens (circumstances) to implement his learning,
but whether he meets acceptance or not is determined by Heaven.
In the past, Yáng Zǐyún gained recommendation early on through 'carving insects' (elaborate literature),
but in his later years, drafting *Xuán* was lonely.
Liú Zhījǐ first became famous through poetry and rhymed prose (*cífù*),
but later lost reputation due to compiling historical works.
Truly knowing that nothing could be done about it,
they accepted it as fate.
Discerning Likeness
People conceal their minds,
which cannot be fathomed.
Words are the sound of the mind.
Those skilled at observing people,
observe what they say, and that is all.
People are not necessarily all good,
yet there are no words spoken that are not based upon goodness.
Those skilled at observing people,
merely investigate the reasons for the goodness of their words.
The Master said:
"Originally, concerning people,
I listened to their words and believed their actions;
now, concerning people,
I listen to their words and observe their actions."
(He feared) that what was spoken did not genuinely issue from the intent of the mind.
Now, words that do not come from the heart,
are like a lawsuit lacking genuine facts,
when the language is exhausted, the true feelings are easily seen.
This is not what the gentleman worries about.
The affliction of learning and arts,
is none greater than that the words are the same as those of a gentleman,
and the words are the same as those spoken by someone accomplished.
But if one seeks the reason for which those words were spoken,
within the distance of a foot,
there is a separation between sky and earth (a vast difference),
it resembles the truth but is not.
The words of the world,

are fundamentally few. Words may undergo a thousand changes and ten thousand transformations, but the essential principles can be exhausted in a few points, hence it is said that words are fundamentally few.
People, however, are constantly changing and unequal.
For people who are constantly changing and unequal,
to utter words that are few in number,
it is fitting that while their outward traces (actions) differ, their words must be the same.
For example, if a city has only four gates,
and there are thousands and tens of thousands of people inside the city,
when they leave the gates to go somewhere,
there must be more than four paths,
but the place from which they exit,
is limited to four gates.
Thus, although their destinations may differ,
yet when they set out, they cannot but start from the same point.
It is not that they intentionally imitate each other,
nor is it pretending to go West while heading East,
the circumstances compel it.
Cultivating the five grains,
is intended for the livelihood of the common people.
Yí Dí said:
"The five grains must not fail to ripen."
If you ask why he prays for a good harvest,
then he will say:
"If they don't ripen, there will be nothing to make wine and liquor."
Teaching the people sericulture and growing mulberries,
is intended for providing silk clothes for the elderly.
Chī Yóu said:
"Silkworms and mulberries must not fail to be planted."
If you question why he desires to plant them,
then he will say:
"If they are not planted, there will be nothing to make banners and flags."
Now, Yí Dí and Chī Yóu,
is it not truly necessary for them to have grain and silk?
However, if they thus treat clothing and food the same way (as secondary means),
they cannot be relied upon.
The *Yì* says:
"That which is unfathomable in the Yin and Yang is called spiritual (*shén*)."
It also says:
"The spiritual,
is that which makes all things marvelous when spoken of."
Mèngzǐ said:
"To be great and transformed is called sagehood (*shèng*);
to be sage-like yet incomprehensible is called spiritual (*shén*)."
This is the origin of the theories of spiritual transformation and spiritual marvel.
Now, the unfathomable nature of Yin and Yang,
does not depart from Yin and Yang.
Making all things marvelous when spoken of,
does not depart from the myriad things.
The incomprehensible nature of the sage,
does not depart from fullness, substantiality, and radiance.
However, to speak of sagehood, spirituality, and marvel,
is to prevent people from being stuck on the outward traces (form),
and to use what is known and seen to conceive of what cannot be known and seen.
Learning, arts, and literature,
have realms of spirituality and marvel.
Those who engage in superficial studies,
cling to the outward traces in seeking it.
Those who truly know it,
believe that there is spirituality and marvel within,
which can be grasped by the mind but cannot be conveyed in words.
Those who are unlearned and lack insight,
are blocked in their minds and find no entry,
are exhausted in debate and find no way out,
they also say that it can be grasped by the mind but cannot be conveyed in words.
Therefore, the gentleman hates that which resembles the truth but is not.
Bóhūn Màorén said to Liè Yǔkòu:
"People will certainly cherish you,
it is not that you are able to make people cherish you,
but rather that you are unable to make people not cherish you."
Thus, one who cannot make people cherish him is inferior,
one who can make people not cherish him is superior,
and the middle position is to be cherished by others.
Therefore, in the world, only the middle realm is easy to distinguish;
the superior realm surpasses the middle, while the inferior realm does not reach the middle,
and they constantly resemble each other.
At the start of learning,
one cannot yet memorize.
When extensive study has become deep,
one will transcend memorization.
Therefore, memorization,
is the boat and carriage of learning.
When a person has somewhere to go,
he must rely on a boat and carriage;
when they reach their destination,
they put aside the boat and carriage.
One who does not take a single step,
will also not use a boat and carriage.
The person who does not use a boat and carriage,
falsely claims those who have put aside the boat and carriage as being of the same disposition.

Therefore, the gentleman hates that which resembles the truth but is not. Chéngzǐ saw Xiè Shàngcài having extensive knowledge of the Classics and Commentaries, and immediately said that he was ‘playing with things and losing his will,’ which ultimately does not resemble Kǒngzǐ’s principle of ‘pervading unity.’
When principle (lǐ) is first perceived,
regardless of whether one is wise or foolish, worthy or unworthy,
the difference is not great.
If one thinks about it a second time,
it becomes vague and unreliable.
If one thinks about it a third time,
it becomes confusing, as if snatched away.
The effort of thinking repeatedly
might actually be worse than the initial perception.
The initial perception stands outside of the matter,
hence the spirit is whole;
the repeated thinking enters into the matter,
and the self already follows its twists and turns.
One must completely exhaust these twists and turns,
and only then can one recover the ultimate state of the initial perception.
Therefore, learning (xuéwèn) must not shrink from tedious effort.
However, when the self is following the path of twists and turns,
the spirit lacks the wholeness of the initial perception.
One must constantly recall that initial perception
to serve as a guide amidst the vagueness and confusion;
it is only then that one might perhaps recover the origin.
I see today's earnest learners:
they did not initially perceive something and then act upon it,
nor do they later expect to reach the ultimate goal.
They exert themselves and endure hardship,
believing only that their learning (xué) can surpass others.
Like a drifting boat without moorings,
even if it sails a thousand lì a day,
how can it be put to use?
Yet they still say that learning must not shrink from tedious effort.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ detests that which is similar yet not correct.
Now, speech (yán) is used to illuminate principle (lǐ),
and refined language (wéncí) is the vessel used to contain it.
A vehicle that is empty and merely decorated,
while the passenger (or master) is absent;
thus, those who drown in refined language
are not worth discussing refinement (wén) with.
The Yì states:
“Things mingle,
hence it is called pattern (wén).”
It also states:
“Its purpose is far-reaching,
its wording is refined (wén).”
The Shū states:
“In governance, valuing constancy is precious;
in expression (cí), upholding essential structure is important.”
The Shī states:
“When the language (cí) is harmonious,
the people are settled.”
The Jì states:
“Do not plagiarize explanations,
do not repeat others blindly;
thus, by ancient standards,
one is praised by the former kings.”
The tradition (zhuàn) says:
“Language (cí) only needs to convey the meaning.”
Zēng Zǐ said:
“When putting forth language and demeanor,
one avoids vulgarity and perversity.”
The words of the sages and worthies in the Classics and Commentaries
have never failed to value refinement (wén).
This is because refinement (wén) fundamentally serves to carry principle (lǐ);
if the refinement is incomplete,
the principle is not made clear.
Moreover, refinement (wén) also has its own principle.
Beauty and ugliness, good and bad—
those who perceive them
have a shared feeling without having agreed upon it beforehand.
This shared feeling, which does not relate to the principle being conveyed,
is precisely the principle of refinement (wén) itself.
Therefore, for those who reach the ultimate stage of refinement,
the refined language (wéncí) is not what they emphasize;
yet, it is not that they lack refined language.
But narrow-minded scholars do not study,
and crudely say, "Skill in refinement harms the Way (dào)."
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ detests that which is similar yet not correct.
Lù Shìhéng said:
“Even if the loom and spindle are in my heart,
I fear that others have preceded me;
if it compromises integrity or violates righteousness,
then even though I love it, I must discard it.”
This means that a scholar of writing (wénzhāng),
having exhausted the gains of his mind,
is constantly afraid that the ancients have preceded him in saying the same thing.
If his words truly match those of the ancients,
it becomes a compromise of integrity and a violation of righteousness;
even though it is deeply cherished,
it must be cut away.
Hán Tuìzhī said:
“Only in antiquity was writing necessarily original;
later generations, unable to be original, merely plagiarized.”
This expresses the same idea.
The scholar who establishes discourse (lìyán)
takes intention (yì) as his foundation;
this naturally places him in a different class from mere rhetoricians.
Humans share this heart,
and the heart shares this principle (lǐ).
The universe is vast,
and ancient records are numerous and tangled;
how can one guarantee that what one says has absolutely never been said by the ancients?
This is the first reason why it is harmless.
Moreover, human hearts are different,
just like their faces.
If one unintentionally happens to agree,
then in the nuances of presentation (wěizhé) and emphasis (qīngzhòng),
there must be points of difference;
people can discern this for themselves.
This is the second reason why it is harmless.
The fundamental aims (zōngzhǐ) of writing a book are not numerous,
but the words used are ten thousandfold and never-ending.
If one happens to agree with the ancients,
it is merely one or two points;
what is different
is sufficient to overshadow what is coincidentally the same.
This is the third reason why it is harmless.
I see today's scholars who establish discourse:
they fundamentally have no particular aim (zōngzhǐ);
they cite the words of the ancients and expound upon them,
but the intent of their exposition
is already entirely contained in what the ancients provided.
Nevertheless,
this is the work of those whose talent is weak;
people recognize it at a glance,
and it ultimately ends up discarded (used to cover jars).
In this case, there is certainly no real harm done.
However, there are cunning individuals:
they change the outer form of the ancients' words
while plagiarizing their intentions.
If a contemporary colleague has an original theory,
they expound upon its meaning while concealing its source.
Or perhaps, having heard someone speak of their insights
before they were committed to writing,
they hastily steal the idea and claim it as their own;
later, when the originator publishes the book himself,
the plagiarist's work ironically appears before it.
Moreover, their private cleverness and small wit
are sufficient to patch up the gaps,
making it difficult for others to clearly discern the underlying facts.
Unless the person who was stolen from confronts them directly
and challenges them on points they have failed to reach,
their deceit is not easily exposed.
Furthermore, only if those who share the same Way
have also thoroughly researched and investigated the matter repeatedly
and checked its origins and conclusions,
can the hidden plagiarism be attacked.
And yet, stealing reputation and deceiving the world
has been a severe plague for a long time.
And the people of that time
even say, "Scholar X's learning
is no less than Master Y's,"
or "Scholar X's achievements
surpass Master Y's."
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ detests that which is similar yet not correct.
He who gained the trust of ten thousand generations
is Fūzǐ (Kǒngzǐ) alone.
The words of Fūzǐ are not singular in focus;
the worthy attain what is excellent,
while the unworthy are misled by what is merely similar.
“Teaching without weariness”
was not meant to insult the ignorant.
“I wish to speak no more”
was not meant to stop teaching.
“Loving antiquity and diligently seeking”
was not meant to pursue mere breadth.
“To be unified by one thread”
was not meant to abandon specific matters.
If one statement could encompass everything,
then even with the sageliness of Fūzǐ,
it would not be possible.
To grasp one of his sayings,
yet not seek what is correct but seek what is similar—
whether one is worthy or unworthy
depends on the individual;
Fūzǐ could do nothing about it.
Mèngzǐ was skilled at learning from Kǒngzǐ.
Fūzǐ spoke of benevolence (rén) and knowledge (zhī),
while Mèngzǐ spoke of benevolence (rén) and righteousness (yì).
Fūzǐ served in Dōng Zhōu,
while Mèngzǐ sought to counsel the kings of Qí and Liáng.
Fūzǐ was “trusting and loved antiquity,”
yet Mèngzǐ said:
“If one believes everything in the Classics (Shū) entirely,
it would be better to have no Classics at all.”
Yet those who seek Kǒngzǐ
must begin with Mèngzǐ.
Therefore, he who attains what is correct
does not seek similarity.
He who seeks to attain similarity
is certainly not one who has attained what is correct.
Yet all those in the world who are misled by similarity
claim, “I have attained what is correct.”

Shuō Lín (Discourse Forest)
The Dào
is public. Learning
is private.
The Jūnzǐ studies in order to achieve the Dào,
intending to exhaust human capacity to reach Heaven (Tiān).
What is the human capacity (rén)?
It is intelligence, talent, and strength,
which are divided by the privacy of physical form and vital energy (qì).
What is Heaven (Tiān)?
It is balanced, upright, even, and straight,
rooted in the public nature of spontaneity (zìrán).
Therefore, it is said that the Dào is public but learning is private.
Regarding the Dào being the same but the methods (shù) being different:
Hán Fēi has the books *Jiě Lǎo* and *Yù Lǎo*;
*Lièzǐ* has the chapter on Yáng Zhū;
the Mòzhě (Mohists) recount the affairs of Yàn Yīng.
The resulting actions are dissimilar,
but the principles are interlinked.
Regarding the methods (shù) being the same but the inclinations (qù) being different:
Zǐzhāng criticized Zǐxià's association;
Xún Qīng rejected Mèngzǐ’s theories;
Zhāng Yí defeated Sū Qín’s system of vertical alliance (zòng).
The main aims were not disparate,
but the guiding principles they upheld mutually differed.
A colt from Wòwā
can carry one hundred jūn (a unit of weight) and travel a thousand lǐ,
but uniting the strength of two Wòwā horses
still cannot enable them to travel two thousand lǐ.
This speaks of unique learning and solitary attainment,
where innate spirit arrives independently.
Even if there are biases or deficiencies,
it is not something others can assist.
Two Wòwā colts
cannot travel two thousand lǐ;
but uniting the strength of two Wòwā horses
is not necessarily incapable of bearing two hundred jūn, each traveling a thousand lǐ.
This speaks of great strategies and ultimate achievements,
where each exerts their own strength.
Even if there are contradictions,
they are not things that others can privately seize.
Literary expression was not valued by the ancients.
Initial drafting and discussion,
refinement and polishing,
certainly involved combining the efforts of many to create the expression.
The expectation was to be perfectly good,
not to boast of private authorship.
When Dīng Jìnglǐ had Cáo Zǐjiàn polish his text,
thinking, "In later generations, who will know who finalized my text?"
this shows an intention to deceive the world.
To preserve the text while also preserving the quality of those who participated and finalized it,
is to allow later generations, reading the writing of one person,
to gain the benefit of two excellences.
Is not the resulting contribution immense?
When Sīmǎ Qiān incorporated the texts of the *Shàngshū*, the *Zuǒ* (Commentary), and the *Guó* (Discourses),
it was not because he liked conformity;
it was necessitated by principle and circumstance.
When Sīmǎ Qiān revised and interspersed words into the texts of the *Shàngshū*, the *Zuǒ*, and the *Guó*;
and when Bān Gù revised and interspersed words into Sīmǎ Qiān's text,
it was not because they liked deviation;
it was necessitated by principle and circumstance.
If there is an event,
and one asks people for the details,
must one insist that they personally heard or saw it?
When Zhāng Jiǎ recounts what he heard from Lǐ Yǐ,
is that plagiarism?
Human hearts are dissimilar,
just like their faces.
When Zhāng Jiǎ recounts Lǐ Yǐ's words,
but the voice, demeanor, smile, and expression
cannot entirely become Lǐ Yǐ's,
is this deliberate deviation?
Kǒngzǐ learned from Zhōugōng;
Zhōugōng observed the two dynasties;
the two dynasties were based on Táng and Yú;
Táng and Yú followed the ancient past.
Therefore, it is said:
"The great origin of the Dào comes from Heaven (Tiān)."
I have observed the springs emerging beneath the mountains,
where sand and stone appear and disappear,
and the flow is winding or straight.
Due to the subtle becoming gradually apparent,
one understands the origin of rivers, streams, boats, and oars.
I observed the babbling of infants,
with sound but no words,
their form is measured and meaning is sought,
and thus know the very beginning of literature and composition.
There is the history of a dynasty,
there is the history of a state,
there is the history of a family,
there is the history of an individual.
Arranging historical events
and the meaning of specialized scholarship are unclear (details are found in *Shì Tōng* and *Dá Kè Wèn*). ,
yet regarding the history of a dynasty,
few are those who understand it.
Local gazetteers of prefectures and counties,
and the meaning of historical records of various states are unclear (details are found in the *Fāng Zhì* chapter). ,
yet regarding the history of a state,
few are those who understand it.
Genealogies do not accept the established rules of the official historian (shǐguān).
(Details are found in the *Jiā Shǐ* chapter).
Yet regarding the history of a family,
few are those who understand it.
The literary structure of the various masters (Zhūzǐ) is unclear,
and collections of essays are privately composed by each author.
Yet regarding the history of an individual,
few are those who understand it.
Zhǎn Xǐ received instructions from Zhǎn Qín;
thus, the rejection of Qí’s proposal,
to say it came from Zhǎn Qín is acceptable,
to say it came from Zhǎn Xǐ is also acceptable.
Disciples write books based on the master's teachings;
friends establish explanations after consultation and inquiry;
later people elaborate on ancient principles.
It is unnecessary to conceal the source,
and they should naturally feel no shame in having authored the words.
Zǐjiàn (Cáo Zhí) liked people to critique his writings;
if there was anything flawed,
he revised it immediately.
The words of critique can be preserved,
and the revised text can also be preserved.
For those whose ideas are superior but whose expression falters,
polish the artistic expression with a brilliant pen;
for those whose expression is rich but whose learning is shallow,
draw upon scholarly texts and knowledge (fùsì).
What is essential is the substance that achieves immortality,
and drawing upon resources should not be concealed.
Chén Lín wrote a letter for Cáo Hóng to the Heir Apparent of Wèi,
discussing the advantages and disadvantages of defeating the rebels.
If this idea sincerely came from Cáo Hóng,
and explicitly employed Chén Lín's language,
including it in Cáo Hóng’s collected works would be acceptable.
Now it is said:
"[I] wanted to have Chén Lín write the letter,
but Lín has been busy lately,
so I exerted the thoughts of this old man."
And it is also said:
"It is strange that [he] undervalues his own clan
and calls it employing others."
This is the shame of concealment,
and it should not be included in Cáo Hóng’s collected works.
Compare this to a bird:
The ambition and insight (zhìshí) are its body,
and the literary expression (wéncí) is its wings.
Only by possessing the body of the great Pèng bird that travels a thousand lǐ
can one utilize wings that cover the sky.
If a small sparrow (yànquè) borrows the wings of an eagle (diāo'è),
its strength will fail before it even takes flight,
let alone the Pèng’s wings!
Therefore, refining one’s expression should not fear temporary borrowing,
but what is valued is possessing the insight (zhìshí) to carry the expression,
and the ability of one's own power to overcome. Alas!
This is difficult to discuss with those who drown in the trivialities of literary expression.
The fundamental aim of the schools of the Masters (Zhūzǐ)
is that their literary style is strict and pure,
yet they can incorporate the language of others.
Collected works (wénjí),
which are general collections of miscellaneous writings,
have comprehensive structures,
but dare not include the writing of others.
What is the reason for this?
It is not that their literary grace and expression
are inferior to the Masters;
but that the Masters' ambition and insight (zhìshí) are outstanding,
such that they can stand independently and achieve immortality apart from the written characters—
something the others dare not aspire to.
If a collected work truly stands out and establishes a school,
even if the language of others is included,
what harm is there?
Regarding Zhuāng Zhōu’s chapters, such as *Ràng Wáng* and *Yú Fù*,
distinguishing whether they are genuine or false;
and Qu Yuán’s rhapsodies (*fù*), *Zhāo Hún* and *Dà Zhāo*,
disputing whether they are jade (genuine) or a lesser stone (cuō);
certainly!
This is the view of literary scholars.
Lǐquán (Sweet Spring)
is water that resembles sweet wine (lǐ).
Everyone under Heaven drinks sweet wine (lǐ),
yet they uniquely regret not being able to drink Lǐquán.
How extreme!
The world values that which resembles the truth but is not.
Regarding the style of creative writing (zhùzuò zhī tǐ),
when citing ancient meanings,
or reusing established phrases,
if the source is not marked,
it is not done to steal credit (luè měi);
it is because the overall structure and flow sometimes do not allow for it.
It is also necessary to ensure that one's own resolve and insight (zhì shí) are sufficient to stand independently,
without relying heavily on the words cited;
moreover, if the cited material
is vastly different,
and I do not object to its being seen again,
then one may speak of the matter of creative writing.
Regarding the style of textual research (kǎozhèng zhī tǐ),
every single character and phrase,
the source must be marked.
If the source work
is found in more than one or two places,
then the earliest source must be marked (for example, if both Mǎ and Bān contain the item, use Mǎ and not Bān).
If the original source work has been lost,

then the work that cites it must be marked (for example, if Liú Xiàng’s 《Qī Lüè》 has been lost, but its arrangement appears in the 《Hàn Yìwén Zhì》, and Ruǎn Xiàoxù’s 《Qī Lù》 has been lost, but its gaps are noted in the commentary to the 《Suí Jīngjí Zhì》, then citations from 《Qī Lüè》 or 《Qī Lù》 must specify 《Hàn Zhì》 or 《Suí Zhù》).
This is the established method for speaking cautiously about remaining works.
If a text appears in multiple sources,
but the original is not listed,
it is crude.
Citing lost texts (yì shū) without marking the source
is deceptive.
Using the standards of textual research,
to wrongly invoke the principles of creative writing,
in order to justify one's own plagiarism (piāoqǐe zhī sī),
is absurd.
Literary expression (wén cí)
is like the three armies;
resolve and insight (zhì shí)
are their commander.
When Lǐ Guǎng entered Chéng Búshí’s army,
the flags and ramparts were entirely reorganized;
yet, he certainly did not change every single object,
nor revise every single affair.
One who understands this meaning
can reuse established phrases
without having to generate them themselves.
Literary expression
is like a boat or a carriage;
resolve and insight
are the passenger.
Wheels should be solid,
sails should be swift—
whoever uses a boat or carriage
must have it so.
East, West, South, or North,
is determined by the passenger.
One who understands this principle
can make literature serve them,
and will not be enslaved by literature.
Literary expression
is like various goods;
resolve and insight
are the artisan.
Oranges, tangerines, hawthorns, and plums—
when the cook obtains them,
they select the sweet and crisp ones to serve as sacrificial fruits;
when the physician takes them,
they prepare their medicinal properties to treat illness and fever.
One who understands this principle
can take different meanings from the same text,
or take the same source but apply it differently,
without leaving obstructive traces.
Literary expression
is like metal and stone;
resolve and insight
are the furnace and hammer.
The marvelous can be transformed into the rotten,
and the rotten can be transformed into the marvelous.
One who understands this principle
need not cling to a single, established theory.
Literary expression
is like wealth and goods;
resolve and insight
are the shrewd merchant.
If others discard, I take;
if others take, I give—
then the art of commerce is connected to the spiritual intelligence (shén míng).
One who understands this principle
can weigh the prevailing trends (fēng shàng) and establish their statements.
Literary expression
is like medicine and poison;
resolve and insight
are the medical practitioner.
If coldness is treated with heat,
excessive heat causes greater severity than the cold;
if heat is treated with cold,
excessive cold causes greater severity than the heat.
A good physician, when the condition is acute,
already worries about a relapse into deficiency (fǎn xū zhī yōu);
therefore, treatment of imbalances must not be extreme,
after which there will be no lingering trouble.
One who understands this principle
can rescue the ailing and maintain the Mean (chù zhōng).
He who turns the mechanism of the draw-well crane (jiégāo zhī jī)
must operate it comprehensively across top and bottom, front and back.
Pushing upward and pulling downward
are where the strength applies.
Directly forward and directly backward
are where the strength fails.
Double the push,
and the front feels like it drops;
double the pull,
and the back feels like it leaps—
by increasing the effort applied,
one reaches the place where the force would otherwise fail.
In human intelligence and knowledge,
there must be areas where strength fails;
one must not fail to know where to increase effort to establish one's ground.
In the blending of the five flavors,
and the performance of the eight musical notes,
simultaneous use is valued.
Tasting them one after the other,
or listening to them one after the other,
will not produce flavor or sound.
In the arrival of postal relays (yóu chuán),
and the accuracy of the clepsydra (kèlòu),
continuity is valued.
If they ride side-by-side and stop together,
or measure time together and cease together,
it will not function as postal relays or a clepsydra.
For books completed by several people,
passing through subsequent generations makes them increasingly refined,
but receiving simultaneous help makes them increasingly sparse;
those working sequentially harbor no competitive spirit,
but those working simultaneously possess a desire to surpass;
those working sequentially can hand down and receive,
but those working simultaneously find mutual understanding difficult;
those working sequentially can complement and remedy,
but those working simultaneously seldom achieve order and leisure.
That humans have capabilities and incapacities,
regardless of whether they are commoners, worthies, or sages,
is inescapable.
By using what one is capable of to remedy what one is incapable of,
then what is sought
can be invariably obtained.
Those focused on moral principles (yì lǐ) are awkward in literary rhetoric (cí zhāng);
those skilled in literary expression (wén cí) are negligent in evidentiary research (zhēng shí);
these three mutually criticize one another endlessly.
Moral principles rely on insight,
literary rhetoric relies on talent,
and evidentiary research relies on learning;
this is the reasoning behind Liú Zǐxuán’s theory that the three strengths are difficult to possess simultaneously.
If one person cannot possess them all,
and instead consults others to achieve the result,
it is not the case that the outstanding works of the ancients cannot be continued.
If selfish motives dominate,
and one fears that fame will not be monopolized by oneself,
then the three strengths will not benefit each other,
but will instead become defects against each other.
What is meant by “loving the ancient” (hǎo gǔ),
is not that the ancient must necessarily surpass the present;
it is precisely that the present is no different from the ancient,
and in the midst of evolution, change, differences, and similarities,
one seeks their balancing point (zhé zhōng).
The dross of the past
can become the essence of the present.
It is not valuing the dross and directly treating it as essence,
but because the dross exists,
one can imagine the source of the essence.
The flaws of the past
can become a model for later generations.
It is not taking the flaws and directly treating them as a model,
but because the flaws exist,

one can imagine where the model resides (For instance, the 《Lùn Héng》 is the most biased and contradictory work, yet the accounts it mentions, which were lost to later generations, are preserved through it).
Therefore, the reason learning values evidentiary research (kǎozhēng)
is to illuminate moral principles (yì lǐ).
When uttering words and expressions (chū cí qì),
one must keep far from vulgarity and absurdity.
Absurdity is the culprit against eloquence;
but why must one keep far from vulgarity?
If it is not refined, it is not expression;
if the expression is insufficient to endure,
then that which gives rise to the expression will also perish.
Among the various masters and the hundred schools (zhū zǐ bǎi jiā),
there are those that were absurd in principle yet survived,
but there are none that were vulgar in expression yet survived.
If the principle is not absurd but the expression is vulgar,
the power cannot endure;
if the expression is not vulgar but the principle is absurd,
it is what is called “the five grains fail to ripen,”
which is inferior to weeds and tares.
Principle is primary and expression is secondary;
this is the universal principle throughout history.
However, if vulgar expression cannot overcome absurd principle,
it is because the public mind regarding beauty and ugliness, preference and dislike,
never fails to stem from principle.
Waves are the wind of the water;
wind is the wave of the emptiness;
dreams are the flowers of the mind;
literature is the partiality of the Way (Dào).
Still water has no waves;
calm emptiness has no wind;
the perfect person (zhì rén) has no dreams;
perfect literature has no partiality.
Those who perform vocal mimicry,
can simultaneously produce myriad sounds and attitudes of humans, animals, water, fire, men, women, the old, and the young within a moment.
It is not that one mouth truly makes ten thousand poses.
The myriad sounds and attitudes,
when reaching human ears,
must inherently have a limit.
They take those sounds that meet the ear as the limit,
thus the technique is simple yet achieves numerous sounds.
Skilled painters,
can simultaneously show myriad shapes of far and near, shallow and deep, front and side, interlocking and revolving, within a small canvas.
It is not that a small canvas truly contains myriad shapes.
The myriad shapes, when meeting human eyes,
must also inherently have a limit.
They take those shapes that meet the eye as the limit,
thus the brushwork is simple yet portrays many forms.
Now, sounds and colors reaching the ear and eye,
and principles (yìlǐ) reaching the human heart,
are equivalent.
If one truly grasps where the principles meet,
and takes that as the limit for literary expression (wéncí),
one can then speak of literary creation.
In the world, there are things of which half can be done,
but the entirety cannot be achieved.
Medicine for partial paralysis (piānkū)
can cure partial paralysis;
doubling the medicine for partial paralysis
cannot revive the dead. (This saying is found in the *Lǚshì Chūnqiū*.)
In the world, there are things of which the entirety can be done,
but half cannot be achieved.
A woodcutter carrying firewood weighing two *jūn* walks quickly;
remove half of it, and he cannot proceed.
This is not because his strength is insufficient,
but because the balance (shì) is inconvenient.
Wherever fashionable trends (fēngshàng) tend,
they must lead to abuses.
The *jūnzǐ* establishes his words to remedy these abuses,
and returns them merely to the mean and correct (zhōngzhèng).
Fearing that this is insufficient to counteract the prevailing trend,
and correcting it perhaps excessively,
is like doubling the medicine for partial paralysis and hoping to revive the dead.
Merely attempting to remedy the abuse,
without fully clarifying the entirety of the Way (dào),
is like taking away half the wood being carried,
and intending to pity the woodcutter’s strength.
Ten *cùn* make one *chǐ*;
eight *chǐ* make one *xún*.
Measuring eighty *chǐ* yields ten *xún*,
but measuring eight hundred *cùn* may not yield ten *xún*—
accumulating small units easily leads to error.
The strength of one man
can cultivate a hundred *mǔ*;
but combining the strength of eight men can cultivate nine hundred *mǔ*—
gathering strengths easily develops the land.
In the matter of scholarship (xuéwèn),
if one can gather strengths
and not cling rigidly to minute details,
that is excellent.
Where the flow of trends (fēnghuì) tends,
even common people can strive to follow;
where the flow of trends has departed,
even heroes (háojié) find themselves unable to recover it.
When the Hàn court valued classical techniques (jīngshù),
even the petty clerical officials (zúshǐ) could understand the Six Scripts (liùshū).
When officials and common people submitted memorials,
errors were immediately reported and impeached.
In later generations, many scholars of literature
do not practice the principles of the Six Scripts. (Wáng Xīzhī’s vulgar script was criticized by Mr. Hán. Mr. Hán also said: “When writing essays, one should know the characters slightly.”)
How could the scholars of literature in later generations,
in terms of intelligence and mental capacity,
be inferior to the petty clerical officials of the Hàn court?
It is the force of the trends (fēnghuì) that made it so.
The people of Yuè boast among themselves about Yān speech.
Those who can speak Yān speech
must have frequently visited the metropolises,
be experienced,
and have a speaking skill superior to others.
But upon arriving in Yān,
even common servants and lowliest maids,
young girls and children with tufts of hair,
all speak Yān speech.
To boast about the men of Yuè speaking Yān speech based on this,
how can that be a general principle?
At Zhòngní's (Kǒngzǐ's) gate,
a five-foot-tall boy was ashamed to speak of the Five Hegemons (wǔ bà).
If one insists that the five-foot-tall boy
surpassed in talent and knowledge such worthies as Guǎn Zhòng, Hú, and Zhào,
that is something the Master (Fūzǐ) would not allow.
Between the five grains (wǔgǔ) and the weeds (tíbài),
the ranking of their value
is fixed.
Nevertheless, unripe five grains
are inferior to weeds harvested in autumn.
And those who rely on a momentary trend (fēnghuì),
proudly boast of their own path and rut,
claiming that their acquisition of a single inch of wood
is genuinely superior to someone else’s tall tower (cénlóu)—

they can only be described as lacking understanding. (They value Hàn scholarship, esteem Zhèng and Xǔ. Today's trend is like this. This is merely learning from antiquity, not the actual learning of antiquity. They openly discard everything else, as if secretly having something to rely on.)
The servants and grooms (púyǔ) of princes and dukes (wánggōng)
are not necessarily held in higher regard than the close attendants of scholar-officials (shìdàfū).
Yet these servants and grooms,
entering and exiting vermillion gates and grand mansions,
proudly display their connection and boast to the scholar-officials, saying:
“My master’s house is great.”
They fail to realize that the scholar-official is fully entitled to shout at and bind them,
to request that the prince or duke punish them.
The prince or duke will surely also beat and punish them severely,
in apology for the lack of discipline in his household.
Those who pursue scholarship (xuéwèn) without seeking actual attainment,
but boast of what they rely on as being superior,
are of the same kind as the servants and grooms of the princes and dukes.
“In mourning, desire quickly to become poor;
in death, desire quickly to decay.”
Yǒuzǐ believed this was not the saying of a *jūnzǐ*.
If so, statements made for a specific purpose (yǒuwéi zhī yán),
which deviate from the standard meaning,
cannot be entirely avoided even by the Sages (shèngrén).
Those today who rigidly adhere to literary phrasing (wéncí),
without examining the intent behind the established words,
and hastily determine right and wrong,
are effectively demanding talent superior to Kǒngzǐ.
The *Chūnqiū* criticizes flatterers (nìng rén). (*Gōngyáng Zhuàn*.)
The Master (Fūzǐ) once said:
“I detest those with glib tongues (nìng kǒu) who overthrow states and families.”
Thus, *nìng* (glibness/flattery) is a name for wickedness and perversity.
Yet someone suggested, “Yōng is benevolent but not glib.”
Even if that person was very foolish,
why would he praise a benevolent man for being incapable of wickedness?
Moreover, the ancients humbly referred to themselves as *bù nìng* (not glib).
How could they use the inability to be wicked as a form of humility?
Therefore, *nìng* is also a general term for intelligence and verbal eloquence.
Xúnzǐ wrote the *Xìng È* (Human Nature is Evil)
and stated that the Sages (shèngrén) achieved “transforming nature and initiating artifice (wěi).”
*Wěi* (artifice) in the Six Scripts (liùshū)
is the correct name for human endeavor.
The intent of Xún Qīng
was probably to say that natural endowment (tiānzhì) cannot be relied upon,
and scholarship must rely on human effort (rénwéi).
It did not refer to the *wěi* of deceit, falsehood, and deception.
Yet those in the world who fault Xún Qīng
claim that he slandered the Sages as being deceptive.
This is failing to examine the meaning intended by the ancients,
and hastily determining right and wrong.
In antiquity, there were not many characters,
and characters were used interchangeably based on meaning (zhuǎnzhù tōngyòng);
their meanings often overlapped.
When the various philosophers (zhūzǐ) wrote books,
in adopting and using characters,
each had their own primary meaning (zhǔyì).
Like orders in the army
or regulations in official departments,
they established their own codes and precedents.
The interpretations they set forth
did not necessarily harmonize with one another.
Qū Píng's *língxiū* (spiritual cultivation),
Zhuāng Zhōu's *yīnshì* (conforming to this),
Hán Fēi's *cānwǔ* (checking correspondence),
Guǐ Gǔ's *bǎihé* (opening and closing).
Sū and Zhāng's *zònghéng* (vertical and horizontal alliances)—

if moved to another person’s book, no one would know what they meant. (The Buddhist terms *gēn*, *chén*, *fǎ*, *xiāng*, and the legal terms *yǐ*, *zhǔn*, *jiē*, *gè*, *jí*, *qí*, *jí*, *ruò*, are all examples of this.)
Féng Xuǎn asked Mèngcháng Jūn,
after collecting debts and returning to report,
what should be purchased before coming home?
He replied:
“Look for what my household lacks.”
Scholarship (xuéwèn) for governing the age,
and literature (wénzhāng) for imparting instruction,
like a physician’s medicine for partial paralysis,
should likewise merely look at what the age lacks.
To use scholarship and literature
to cater to what the world values
is like serving rich meat (liángròu) to someone already full,
or adding fur coats (húháo) to someone already warm.
If something is not one's strong point
yet one forces oneself to cater to it,
it is like serving husks and chaff (kāngbǐ)
to someone who is just full of rich meat,
or serving coarse short robes (shǔhè)
to someone who is just covered in fur coats.
As for those who need fur coats in summer and linen robes in winter,
I have rarely seen them.
Those who treasure bright pearls
inevitably accumulate fish eyes.
Those who admire beautiful jade
inevitably compete for *wǔfū*.
Thus, when the body has one shadow,
the *wǎngliǎng* occupy two or three positions.
Nevertheless, fish eyes and *wǔfū* are easily sold;
compared to bright pearls and beautiful jade, they are twice as swift (to sell).
Pearls and jade are selfless,
but *wǔfū* are intentional (or have intent).
Intentional things are easy to offer.
Pearls and jade are difficult to change,
but *wǔfū* can follow (adapt).
Adaptable things are easy to harmonize with.
Pearls and jade use their own standards,
but *wǔfū* submit to being used.
Things that submit to being used are easy to satisfy.
Pearls and jade hold the power of the three difficulties yet have no fixed price,
while *wǔfū* seize the opportunity of the three ease-factors and seek cheap prices.
How can *wǔfū* not be sold,
and how can pearls and jade not be abandoned?
Against the poison of the *zhèn* bird,
the rhinoceros horn can counteract it.
Against the plague of miasma (*zhàng*),
the betel nut relieves it.
Where the *zhèn* bird exists,
there must be rhinoceros horn.
In regions plagued by miasma,
there must be betel nuts.
The benevolence of Heaven and Earth in creating things
ensures that there is a fixed principle of ebb and flow, control, and transformation.
Hàn Confucians valued specialization in transmitting the Classics;
specialization ensures that the origins and flow are not confused.
The drawback is that they confined themselves to their own branch and maintained remnants,
leading to the flaw of narrowness.
Liú Xīn’s (*Liú Xīn*) *Qī Lǜe*
discussed and categorized the distinctions among various schools,
and promoted the remnants of the *Guān Lǐ* (Official Rites),
thereby counteracting the miasma-plague of narrow specialization.
During the Táng Dynasty, books were compiled and official bureaus were established;
these bureaus allowed each person to utilize their specific strengths.
The drawback was that there was no overall system or coherence,
leading to the flaw of disorder.
Liú Zhījǐ’s (*Liú Zhījǐ*) *Shǐ Tōng*
assessed the merits and defects of ancient and modern works,
and established standards for methodology and law,
thereby curing the miasma-plague of scattered disorder.
Scholarship and writing,
following the prevailing trends and fashions,
sometimes breed plagues of miasma;
thus, one cannot fail to know the use of betel nuts and rhinoceros horn.
What is concerning about medicines
is that they are specialized for treating illness:
the sick who take them can be cured,
but if ordinary people take them,
they might instead fall ill.
The world has no complete merit,
and the Sage has no use that is universally applicable.
The five grains are excellent and valuable,
but if eaten beyond their limit,
they are certainly capable of killing people.
Therefore, one who knows how to preserve health
can consume all things.
One who knows how to embody the Dào
can preserve all schools of thought.
The Six Classics and the Three Histories
are the deep origins of scholarship.
I see the miasma-plague caused by those who are not skilled at governing (or using) them.
Scholarly knowledge and literature,
intelligence, talent, and rhetoric,
are insufficient to sustain the world;
what sustains the world
lies in insight (*shí*).
What is valued in insight
is not merely the ability to hold back the excesses of prevailing trends;
it is knowing that within those excesses,
there are things that must not be discarded.
It is not merely the ability to employ one's unique specialized strengths;
it is knowing that one's own specialized strengths
are also insufficient to encompass everything.
Regarding that which must not be discarded:
be strict in removing falsehoods
and cautious in curing the partiality of those who truly have attainment;
then there will be no flaw.
Regarding that which is insufficient to encompass everything:
leave gaps for what one does not know,
and skillfully promote those who are capable;
if such people do not exist,
then clarify one's own shortcomings
and suspend judgment while waiting for the right person;
then one can be free from deceiving the world.
If the Dào is public yet I monopolize it privately,
that is inhumane (*bù rén*).
The trends of fashion
cycle and recur,
and cannot be overcome by force.
If I am unable to maintain the balance of the Dào,
and also enter into the cycles of recurrence,
yet attempt to overcome them by force,
that is unwise (*bù zhì*).
Being inhumane and unwise,
one is insufficient to speak of scholarship.
Although insufficient to speak of scholarship,
those who boastfully speak of it are numerous.
Is it difficult to achieve knowledge?
Is it difficult to practice it?
Is it difficult to know it?
That by which people claim to know a person
is not knowing their surname and given name,
nor is it knowing their voice, appearance, laughter, or demeanor;
it is reading their writings,
knowing what they say,
and knowing the reason why they say it, and that is all.
Those who read their writings
are everywhere in the world;
those who know what they say
are fewer than a hundred out of a thousand.
Those who know what they say
are few and far between in the world;
those who know the reason why they say it
are fewer than one out of a hundred.
Nevertheless, everyone in the world says:
"I can read their writings
and know the reason why they say it."
This is the difficulty of knowledge.
People know the *Yì* (Book of Changes) is a book of divination;
but the Master (Kǒngzǐ) read it,
and knew that the author harbored anxiety and distress.
This is a Sage knowing a Sage.
People know the *Lí Sāo* is the ancestor of poetic prose (*cífù*);
but Sīmǎ Qiān (*Sīmǎ Qiān*) read it,
and grieved for the author's aspirations.
This is a worthy man knowing a worthy man.
If one does not possess the aspirations of Sīmǎ Qiān,
yet wishes to know the aspirations of Qū Yuán (*Qū Yuán*);
if one does not possess the distress of the Master,
yet wishes to know the distress of King Wén (*Wén Wáng*);
then one is nearly blind (to the truth).
If that is the case, among the ancients,
there were those who possessed that same distress and those same aspirations,
yet unfortunately failed to find later generations who could grieve their grief
and realize their aspirations,
and thus were submerged and unheralded—
surely these were not few.
Liú Yànhé (*Liú Yànhé*) said:
"When the *Chǔ Shuō* first appeared,
and the *Zǐ Xū* was initially completed,
Qín Huáng (*Qín Huáng*) and Hàn Wǔ (*Hàn Wǔ*) regretted not living at the same time (as the authors).
Yet when they did live at the same time,
Hán (Fēi) was imprisoned and Mǎ (Sīmǎ Qiān) was held in contempt."
This mourns the fact that kindred spirits living contemporaneously cannot necessarily be relied upon.
Lǐ Sī's (*Lǐ Sī*) severe fear of Hán Fēi (*Hán Fēi*),
and Emperor Xiàowǔ's (*Xiàowǔ*) treating Sīmǎ (Qiān) as an entertainer—
these were deep knowledge
and appropriate handling,
arising from circumstances making it unavoidable.
This is what is called appearing ignorant in action but deeply knowing in heart.
Jiǎ Shēng (*Jiǎ Shēng*) was far exiled to Chángshā (*Chángshā*).
Afterwards, he was summoned to an audience in the Xuān Shì (Hall).
Emperor Wén Dì (*Wén Dì*) even said:
"It has been a long time since I saw Shēng.
I thought I had surpassed him,"
but upon seeing him, knew he was still inferior.
The relationship between sovereign and minister
can be called an opportune encounter.
However, the Emperor did not understand Jiǎ's memorials concerning governing the nation,
but understood his discourse on ghosts and spirits.
This is what is called appearing to know in action but being ignorant in heart.
Liú Zhījǐ (*Liú Zhījǐ*), relying on his peerless scholarship,
was viewed lightly by his contemporaries.
When he was appointed court historian three times
and entered the Dōngguān (Imperial Library) twice,
this can be called an opportune encounter.
Nevertheless, when discussing historical talent, he was relegated a thousand miles behind;
and when debating matters of history, not a single word was agreed upon.
This is what is called appearing to know, but being ignorant in heart.
As for those who know in action,
if they are not like Jiǎ (Shēng), known but not utilized,
then they are like Liú (Zhījǐ), utilized but not trusted.
As for those who know in heart,
if they are not like Mǎ (Sīmǎ Qiān), treated intimately yet held in contempt,
then they are like Hán (Fēi), slandered and put to death.
When a great man seeks to be known by the world,
to achieve a recognition like that of Hán, Mǎ, Jiǎ, and Liú,
is already considered glorious.
Yet their attainment was like that,
and their failure was like this.
It seems reliable,
yet it seems unreliable;
it seems knowable,
yet it seems unknowable.
This is why the knowledge gained through opportune encounters is difficult to speak about.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
“Those in the world who master methods and arts,
all believe that their achievements cannot be surpassed.”
Now, “ears, eyes, mouth, and nose,
each have their own clarity,
but they cannot communicate with each other.”
Yet everyone takes that which they have mastered,
to be unsurpassed;
this is the fault of not knowing oneself.
In the world, there are few who know themselves,
therefore, those who truly understand one another are few. Anyone who defends their past actions and refuses to acknowledge merit in others is one who does not truly know themselves.
It is traditionally said that Xiāo Yǐngshì was able to recognize Lǐ Huá's poem *Gǔ Zhànchǎng Wén*,
claiming that writings have a true connoisseur.
But words are rooted in the mind,
and their differences are like faces.
If Yǐngshì could not determine it was Huá upon a single viewing,
but vaguely said that Huá was capable of reaching this level,
this cannot be called true understanding.
Moreover, those in the world who possess the recognition of Mr. Xiāo,
are already one in ten thousand;
as for the learning and achievement of people,
there are certainly those who do not stop at Lǐ Huá's level,
so upon whom can the world rely?
All things that receive a completed form,
cannot be without unique characteristics.
All things endowed with blood and vitality,
cannot be without a competitive spirit.
When there are unique characteristics,
the flaw of treating newcomers as masters and those who leave as slaves,
or forming factions to attack dissidents, arises.
When there is a competitive spirit,
the seeds of holding fears of being exposed,
and jealousy, envy, and slander are sown.
Huìzǐ said:
“He who runs goes east,
and he who pursues also goes east;
although the eastward movement is the same,
the intention behind their eastward movement is different.”
Now, those traveling together are numerous,
but can one know the intentions of those moving in synchronization?
Whether reliable,
whether not reliable,
whether knowable,
whether not knowable—
this is why the knowledge of those who share the same path is difficult to speak of.
Ōuyáng Xiū once lamented that in the four sections of the *Qī Lüè*,
the titles remained while the books vanished,
considering this the misfortune of those authors.
He was saddened that writings cannot be fully relied upon.
However, since the capture of the Qílín,
the business of literary composition,
reached its height with Mǎ Qiān and Bān Gù.
Mǎ Qiān hid his work in a famous mountain,
and passed it on to a specific person;
Bān Gù's younger sister completed his work,
and Mǎ Róng knelt by the curtained doors to receive his writings.
Their works are still like the sun and moon today.
Nevertheless, reading the books of the *Shǐjì* and the *Hànshū*,
and examining the commentaries and explanations of various scholars like Xú Guǎng, Péi Yīn, Fú Qián, and Yīng Shào,
those interpretations that fail to capture the intent of Mǎ Qiān and Bān Gù,
often constitute three or four tenths.
Even with specialized study and practice,
they still failed to reach the subtlety of the ancients,
how much more so when the extent of general reading,
allows love and hate to be determined by oneself?
For those works that are not transmitted,
there is the sorrow of having titles and categories existing in vain;
for those that are transmitted,
there is the affliction of investigation losing the original intent,
and the constant variability of personal love and hate.
Whether reliable,
whether not reliable;
whether knowable,
whether not knowable;
this is why posthumous recognition is difficult to speak of.
That by which humans differ from wood and stone,
is emotion (*qíng*).
That by which emotion is valuable,
is mutual understanding and resolution.
The worthy, failing to achieve prominence and needing companions to carry out their will,
will also find partners to enjoy their way when they are in distress;
failing to achieve flourishing encounters and contemporary recognition while alive,
they will also wait after death for true understanding in later generations.
However, that which has the principle,
does not necessarily have the resulting event;
those who connect through external traces,
do not necessarily connect through the heart.
Whether reliable,
whether not reliable;
whether knowable,
whether not knowable.
How the future regards the present,
is just like how the present regards the past.
Alas!
This is why Bó Yá snapped his strings and stopped playing,
and why Biàn Shēng cried mournfully while holding the jade.
When sparrows and magpies chirp,
many respond harmoniously.
When reeds and rushes turn yellow and white,
many bend and sway.
The Phoenix soars high above a thousand *rèn*,
the Paulownia stands solitary over a hundred *xún*.
Knowing they have few responders and no peers,
yet being unable to yield or conform to the masses,
is also dictated by circumstance.
Therefore, the *jūnzǐ* (noble person) exerts himself so much he forgets to eat,
and quietly cultivates himself,
unaware that old age is approaching;
this is merely seeking to achieve his own purpose.
How can he use his bounded life,
to pursue boundless slander and praise?
The explanation of *tōng*
in the *Yìjīng* states:
“Only the *jūnzǐ* is capable of penetrating the will of the world.”
Commentators say that the *jūnzǐ* takes civilization and enlightenment as virtue,
and during the time of *Tóng Rén* (The Gathering of Men hexagram),
he can reach the will of the world.
The *Shūjīng* (Book of Documents) says:
“Thereupon, Chóng and Lí were commanded,
to sever the communication between Heaven and Earth.”
Commentators say this meant that humans and spirits should not interfere with each other,
and each should maintain their proper order.
The former kings feared that people might harbor hidden intentions,
thus they established governance based on civilization and enlightenment,
penetrating and clarifying ethical categories,
thereby extending the capacity of *Tóng Rén*.
The former kings feared that the world might have disordered governance,
thus they assigned official posts to individuals with divided duties,
severing connections to prevent penetration,
and strictly guarded against betrayal and support of illicit actions.
Since the Six Ministers divided the administration,
and the Five Historians managed documents,
learning was specialized to specific teachers,
and officials adhered to their regulations;
this is the meaning of severing communication between Heaven and Earth.
Mathematical methods converged in the nine divisions,
and written records were summarized in the six categories;
various objects were compiled based on virtue (classification),
writing was unified, and track widths were made uniform;
this is the meaning of reaching the will of the world.
When the Master (Kǒngzǐ) died, subtle words ceased;
when the seventy disciples passed away, the great principles diverged.
At the beginning of the Hàn Dynasty,
the *Chūnqiū* was divided into five traditions,
and the *Shī* (Book of Odes) was divided into four schools;
yet those who studied the *Gōngyáng* tradition,
did not discuss the *Zuǒ* or the *Gǔ* traditions;
those who practiced Hán’s *Shī*,
did not mix it with the Qí or Lǔ schools;
specialized professional study,
was at its height then.
Afterward, the master-disciple traditions gradually declined,
and scholars' intelligence flowed out laterally,
causing various theories to arise tumultuously.
Thereupon, gentlemen of profound insight and far-reaching view,
feared that the chapters of linguistic exegesis in the *Ěryǎ*,
were insufficient to exhaust the isolated phrases of previous eras,
where the reality was the same but the designations were different,
and that mere compilers of learning,
would have no means to synthesize their essential points;
therefore, they summarized the essentials of the *Wǔ Jīng* (Five Classics),
and clarified the texts of the Six Arts.
Works such as the *Shíqú Záyì*,
began to separate from the Classics and become independent books;
this is the practice from which the meaning of *tōng* (penetration/generalization) originated.
Liú Xiàng comprehensively collated the *Wǔ Jīng*,
and compiled the Three Rites.
Regarding the various records collected by the Dài family,
he distinguished and categorized them by subject,
grouping them according to type,
such that the meaning was not specialized to one area.
For chapters like *Tángōng* and *Lǐ Yùn*,
all were titled as *Tōng Lùn* (General Discussions).
This is where the definitive name *tōng* was established.
*Bān Gù* (班固) received the imperial edict of *Jiànchū* (建初),

and composed the *Báihǔ Tōngyì* (白虎通義) (The *Rúlín Zhuàn* calls it *Tōngyì*; *Gù*'s biography calls it *Tōngdélùn*; later generations removed the character *yì* and called it *Báihǔ Tōng*, which is incorrect.).
*Yìng Shào* (應劭), lamenting the failings of the trends of his time,
composed the *Fēngsú Tōngyì* (風俗通義).
This is because the methods of textual analysis and exegesis,
eventually declined,
and thus scholarly interpretations of the Classics and personalized doctrinal arguments
arose to remedy them.
The books created by these two men
were the origin of later generations labeling works as "Comprehensive."
From this point, interpretations based on the Classics
included Collected Commentaries (*jíjiě*): *Dù Yù*'s (杜預) *Zuǒzhuàn* (左傳), *Fàn Níng*'s (範寧) *Gǔliáng* (穀梁), and *Hé Yàn*'s (何晏) *Lúnyǔ* (論語).

Collected Annotations (*jízhù*): *Xún Shuǎng*'s (荀爽) *Jiǔjiā Yì* (九家易), *Cuī Líng'ēn*'s (崔靈恩) *Máoshī* (毛詩), *Kǒng Lún* (孔倫) and *Péi Sōngzhī*'s (裴松之) *Sāngfú Jīngzhuàn* (喪服經傳). Similarities and Differences (*yìtóng*): *Xǔ Shèn*'s (許慎) *Wǔjīng Yìyì* (五經異義), *Hè Yáng*'s (賀玚) *Wǔjīng Yìtóng Píng* (五經異同評). Affirmation or Negation (*ránfǒu*): *Hé Xiū*'s (何休) *Gōngyáng Mòshǒu* (公羊墨守), *Zhèng Xuán*'s (鄭玄) *Bóyì* (駁議), *Qiáo Zhōu*'s (譙周) *Wǔjīng Ránfǒu Lùn* (五經然否論). These are the various titles;
works written apart from the Classics

included categories such as Six Arts (*Liùyì*) (e.g., *Zhèng Xuán*'s treatise), Sacred Proofs (*Shèngzhèng*) (e.g., *Wáng Sù*'s treatise), Rectification of Errors (*Kuāngmiù*) (e.g., *Táng Yán Shīgǔ*'s (唐顏師古) *Kuāngmiù Zhèngsú* (匡謬正俗)), and Comprehensive Illumination (*Jiānmíng*) (e.g., *Sòng Qiū Guāngtíng*'s (宋邱光庭) *Jiānmíng Shū* (兼明書)).
Although these works were not explicitly labeled "Comprehensive,"
their substance actually contained the meaning of comprehensiveness.
The classifications within the Classic division
must not be left unexamined.
As for the records of *Yáo* (堯) and *Shùn* (舜),
they were collectively named the *Xià Shū* (夏書);

(*Zuǒzhuàn* calls *Yú Shū* the *Xià Shū*. The three schools of *Mǎ Róng*, *Zhèng Xuán*, and *Wáng Sù* all titled the first chapter *Yú Xià Shū*. *Fú Shēng*'s *Dàzhuàn* also titled the first chapter *Yú Xià Zhuàn*.) The *Guóyǔ* (國語) and the *Guócè* (國策),
do not follow the historical records of the *Zhōu* (周);
the *Tàishǐ* (太史) in one hundred and thirty chapters,
named itself a single work (Its original name was *Tàishǐ Gōng Shū*, not *Shǐjì*.).
*Bān Gù*'s *Wǔxíng* (五行) and *Dìlǐ* (地理),

trace back to the *Xià* and *Zhōu* dynasties (*Dìlǐ* begins with the *Yǔ Gòng*; *Wǔxíng* integrates with the *Chūnqiū*). They supplement the omissions of *Sīmǎ Qiān* (司馬遷), and do not necessarily use the *Hàn* (漢) dynasty as a cutoff point.
The personalized doctrines of the ancients,
once the text was complete and the structure established,
were analyzed and categorized
solely according to principle.
Thus, they were never specifically given separate titles
or divided into categories.
*Liáng Wǔdì* (梁武帝), seeing that historians from *Qiān* and *Gù* onward
wrote histories covering individual dynasties,
then started from the Three Sovereigns above,
and ended with the *Liáng* dynasty below,
compiling a single work titled *Tōngshǐ* (通史) (Comprehensive History),
wishing to encompass all historical narratives.
The labeling of historical records as "Comprehensive"
began with this work.
Following this,
the branches and sources gradually diverged.
Summarizing the scholarship of ancient and modern times,
and making the Annals and Biographies conform fully to the model of the Grand Historian *Sīmǎ Qiān*,

*Zhèng Qiáo*'s (鄭樵) *Tōngzhì* (通誌) was written (The essence of *Tōngzhì* lies in its organizational principles. It is the doctrine and learning of an individual scholar housed within the rules of various histories, and was not originally intended to excel in verification and textual research. It is incorrect for later generations to criticize its shortcomings.).
Unifying the treatises of previous histories,
and basing the composition method on the Official Rites,
*Dù Yòu*'s (杜佑) *Tōngdiǎn* (通典) was written (*Tōngdiǎn* originates from *Liú Zhì*'s *Zhèngdiǎn*.).
Combining the interrelated texts of the Annals and Biographies (The text of the Annals and Biographies elaborate on each other),

and arranging the compilation in the manner of *Xún* (荀) and *Yuán* (袁) (*Xún Yuè*'s (荀悅) *Hàn Jì* (漢紀) in thirty volumes and *Yuán Hóng*'s (袁宏) *Hòuhàn Jì* (後漢紀) in thirty volumes, both changed the Annals and Biographies into chronological style),
*Sīmǎ Guāng*'s (司馬光) *Zīzhì Tōngjiàn* (資治通鑒) was written.
Gathering private and public compositions,

and compiling the collection roughly following the style of *Kǒng* (孔) and *Xiāo* (蕭) (*Kǒng Huàn*'s (孔逭) *Wényuàn* (文苑) in one hundred volumes and Crown Prince *Xiāo Tǒng*'s (蕭統) *Wénxuǎn* (文選) in thirty volumes),
*Péi Lín*'s (裴潾) *Tàihé Tōngxuǎn* (太和通選) was written.
These four men:
some preserved the structure of the Standard Histories (This is the *Tōngzhì*. Since the *Suí Zhì*, all works of the Annals and Biographies type are considered Standard Histories.),
some rectified the chronological method (The *Tōngjiàn*).
some used institutional history as the framework (The *Tōngdiǎn*),
and some preserved literature through literary essays (The *Tōngxuǎn*).
The comprehensive works in the History Division,
reached their zenith here (Large-scale general anthologies intended to preserve historical precedents ought to belong to the History Division, not grouped with works of literary criticism.).
As for works like *Gāo Shì*'s (高氏) *Xiǎoshǐ* (小史) (during the *Yuánhé* era of the *Táng*, by *Gāo Jùn* and his son *Jiǒng*) and *Yáo Shì*'s (姚氏) *Tǒngshǐ* (統史) (*Táng Yáo Kāngfù*),
they curtailed the lengthy texts
and summarized them themselves.
