Works like *Luō Shì*'s (羅氏) *Lù Shì* (路氏) (*Sòng Luō Mì*) and *Dèng Shì*'s (鄧氏) *Hánshǐ* (函史) (*Míng Dèng Yuánxī*),
possessed their own unique styles

and formed their personalized doctrines (*Qiáo Zhōu*'s *Gǔshǐ Kǎo*, *Sū Zhé*'s *Gǔshǐ*, and *Mǎ Sù*'s *Yìshǐ* all selected materials from the Classics and their commentaries, differing from Comprehensive Histories.).
*Fàn Shì*'s (範氏) *Wǔdài Tōnglù* (五代通錄) (*Sòng Fàn Zhì* used chronological style to record the facts of the *Liáng*, *Táng*, *Jìn*, *Hàn*, and *Zhōu*),

and *Xióng Shì*'s (熊氏) *Jiǔcháo Tōnglüè* (九朝通略) (*Sòng Xióng Kè* combined *Lǚ Yíjiǎn*'s *Sāncháo Guóshǐ*, *Wáng Guī*'s *Liǎngcháo Guóshǐ*, and *Lǐ Táo*, *Hóng Mài*, etc.'s *Sìcháo Guóshǐ* to create a book of nine dynasties in chronological style),
were labeled "Comprehensive" but were limited by dynasty (The change of surname defines the dynasty; the tradition defines the imperial court.).
*Lǐ Shì*'s (李氏) *Nán-Běishǐ* (南·北史) (*Lǐ Yánshòu*),
and *Xuē* (薛) and *Ōu*'s (歐) *Wǔdài Shǐ* (五代史) (*Xuē Jūzhèng* and *Ōuyáng Xiū* both wrote one),

were dynastic histories that nonetheless followed the comprehensive style (The above two categories, although covering several dynasties, still have limits and breaks, unlike *Liáng Wǔdì*'s *Tōngshǐ*, which integrates ancient and modern times.).
The remaining categories of Annals, Biographies, and Historical Narratives,
and works compiled to supplement and gather records,
arose in confusion.
Although they cannot be judged by a single standard,
they essentially all imitated the meaning of *Xiāo Liáng*'s (蕭梁) *Tōngshǐ*,
merely for the convenience of the eyes and ears.
The classifications of the History Division,
must not be ignored.
When proper scholarly methods are lost,
human nature hesitates to return to antiquity.
When the subsequent trends gradually decline,
scholars are constrained by what they see and hear.
Exegesis flows into scholarly interpretations of the Classics,
transforming once to enter the category of Ruist works in the Masters Division (like *Yìng Shào*'s *Fēngsú Tōngyì* and *Cài Yōng*'s (蔡邕) *Dúduàn* (獨斷)).

Transforming twice to enter the recorded conversations of conventional scholars (*Chéng* and *Zhū*'s recorded conversations contain parts not rigorously selected by the recorders, and upon being transmitted twice, they gradually decline, hence they are called conventional scholars.),
and transforming thrice to enter the lecture notes of mediocre teachers (Works intended for the ignorant and shallow, which are overly fragmented and worse than the recorded conversations).
Those who do not understand become accustomed to them,
while those who do understand despise and reject them,
not realizing that they originated from the comprehensive nature of scholarly interpretations of the Classics,
but have lost their original purpose.
Historical writing gathered together resulted in Comprehensive History,

transforming once to become Historical Abstracts (Works like *Xiǎoshǐ* and *Tǒngshǐ*, which merely condense the Standard Histories without unique structure, should be classified as Historical Abstracts. Previous records categorized them as Comprehensive History, which is incorrect. The Historical Abstracts category in the History Division began with the *Sòng Shǐ*.),

transforming twice to become the categorized summaries used by policy experts (Works like *Wénxiàn Tōngkǎo* (文獻通考)—although modeled on the *Tōngdiǎn*, their analysis and arrangement make them essentially *lèishū* (encyclopedias). These books lack unique comprehensive scholarly discernment and are useful for answering policy questions.),
and transforming thrice to become the simple excerpts and comparisons of superficial scholars (Works like *Gāngjiàn Hézuǎn* (綱鑒合纂) and *Shíwù Cèkuò* (時務策括)).
Those who do not understand become accustomed to them,
while those who do understand despise and reject them,
not realizing that they originated from the comprehensive nature of the History Division,
but have lost their fundamental source.
Furthermore, when the *Qīlüè* (七略) flowed into the Four Divisions,
the categories and rules became clear,
and there was no longer any need to deeply seek the methods of the ancient scholars.
However, with the mixing of recorded conversations and lecture notes,
the Classics cease to be Classics,
and the Masters cease to be Masters.
With the confusion caused by categorized policy summaries and simple excerpts,
History ceases to be History,
and Collections cease to be Collections.
The Four Divisions cannot contain them,
the Nine Schools have no way to distinguish them.
They arise in a confusing mixture,
attempting wrongly to attach themselves to comprehensive historical records.
Their distinctions must be rigorously drawn.
When the ancients wrote books,
they took old records
and applied their own creative structure,
thereby establishing a specialized field of study.
Later generations combined and simplified the general categories,
seeking convenience for reference,
which is why they fell into the crudity of mere memorization.
Classical scholars, merely by differentiating textual analyses,

immediately established their own school (e.g., *Fèi Zhí*'s (費直) *Yì* (易) and *Shēn Péi*'s (申培) *Shī* (詩). The *Rúlín Zhuàn* states they had no separate writings or commentaries, and the *Yìwén Zhì* lists *Fèi Shì Shuō* and *Shēn Gōng Lǔ Shī*, which must have been their orally transmitted textual analyses.).
Historical works that follow established tradition
can exist concurrently without harm;

(e.g., *Sīmǎ Qiān* based his work on the *Chūnqiū* and *Guócè*; *Hàn Shū* was based on *Sīmǎ Qiān*'s records and *Liú Xīn*'s writings; the two existed simultaneously without the issue of plagiarism). Specialized works,
have unique, individual structures,
and are not criticized even if they appear similar.
Plagiarized lecture notes,
when habitually used for a long time, lose their original purpose (The *Míng* Dynasty scholars who compiled the *Dàquán* modified the established theories of earlier Ruists to suit their own views.).
When historical facts are excerpted and compared,
if the original source appears, the errors cannot be concealed.
The crudity of mere memorization,
spreads without any scholarly discipline,
and is easily plagiarized.
However, the excellence of specialization
and the crudity of plagiarism
are distinguished from one another,
often lying in a subtle difference.
Therefore, one must be extremely careful in making distinctions.
The compilation of comprehensive histories ([Tōngshǐ]),
has six benefits:
First, avoiding repetition;
second, standardizing classifications and precedents;
third, facilitating selection and arrangement;
fourth, balancing right and wrong;
fifth, eliminating contradictions;
sixth, detailing neighboring affairs.
It has two advantages:
first, possessing skill in editing and selection ([Jiǎncái]);
second, establishing a systematic method ([Jiāfǎ]).
It has three shortcomings:
first, lacking distinction between importance and unimportance;
second, retaining original titles;
third, forgetting classification headings.
What is meant by avoiding repetition?
When dynasties change ([Dǐnggé zhī jì]),
persons and facts
emerge simultaneously and are seen together.
The vanquished kingdom having no signs [of divine approval],
while the new king manifests auspicious omens,
is precisely one and the same event.
The former court's stealthy banditry,
and the new ruler's advance guard,
refer to precisely the same person.
Dǒng Zhuó and Lǚ Bù,
Fàn [Yè] and Chén [Shòu] each compile separate biographies for them.
The imperial edicts announcing the abdication,
the [history of] Liáng and the [history of] Chén both record the full text,
this is what is called repetition.
When the Tōngzhì compiles and integrates [these records] into one book,
events can be cross-referenced,
and texts do not need to reappear—
is this not excellent?
What is meant by standardizing classifications and precedents?
Mǎ [Qiān] established the Tiānguān [Treatise],
Bān [Gù] initiated the Dìlǐ [Treatise].
The Tiānwén section of the Qí Zhì
does not record astronomical calculations;
the Yìwén section of the Tángshū does not narrate the origins;
following ancient practices,
discrepancies like these exist.
Although Zhèng Qiáo compiled the Lüè [Treatises],
altering the standards of historical monographs,
thereby establishing his own systematic method;
however, the Six Scripts ([Liùshū]) and Seven Tones ([Qīyīn]) [sections]
were fundamentally not about evolutionary changes,
and why must creatures, plants, and trees
necessarily remain constant across dynastic changes?
Only by linking the past and present to compel the establishment of a single system,
will the principles arise from the underlying meaning,
and naturally conform to comprehensive standardization.
The Monographs of the Five Dynasties in the Suí Shū (covering Liáng, Chén, Běi Qí, Zhōu, and Suí)
ultimately surpasses the works of Shěn, Xiāo, and Wèi (referring to Shěn Yuè’s Sòng Zhì, Xiāo Zǐxiǎn’s Nán Qí Zhì, and Wèi Shōu’s Wèi Zhì, all of which are inconsistent and uneven).
What is meant by facilitating selection and arrangement?
Encompassing all histories,
systems and institutions generally remain constant.
However, distinguished individuals
each follow their respective eras.
Regarding empresses, consorts, and imperial clansmen,
their dynastic titles are clearly marked;
as for subjects,
they are generally arranged chronologically,

and placed in sequence for comparison (The Nán Běi Shǐ separated imperial clansmen above all other officials for identification, and Ōuyáng [Xiū]'s Wǔ Dài Shǐ first began marking different dynasties).
Nevertheless, descendants are attached to their ancestors,
and aristocratic families gather together their lineage branches (The biographies of the Wáng and Xiè clans in the Nán Běi Shǐ are not entirely segmented by dynasty).
The bloodline inheritance of a single family,
and the rise and fall of their fortunes over time,
can thus be observed.
Even placing Qū Yuán of Chǔ
in the same biography as Jiǎ Shēng of Hàn,
or the Grand Historian of Zhōu
alongside the noble sons of Hán in the same section,
the ancients surely had profound intentions.
By appending them they are clarified,
and the meanings are determined singularly.
How can superficial later scholars
follow this and make unwarranted critiques?
What is meant by balancing right and wrong?
The determination of crookedness and straightness,
is established during the change of dynasties.
However, the Jìn History must ultimately treat Wèi as the legitimate dynasty,
and the subject Hán Tōng of Zhōu cannot be given an official biography.
Although the compiler may be distinguished,
caution regarding national taboos is necessary,
so there is nothing that can be done.
Only when events are separated by several generations,
and judgment is absolutely impartial,
can the act of historical writing be fair and balanced,
and the final decision be settled.
What is meant by eliminating contradictions?
When histories are written covering specific dynastic periods,
each has its own methods of composition.
What is detailed, summarized, omitted, or included
does not interfere with one another.
However, when the beginnings and ends overlap,
and there are mutual inclusions and exclusions,
then the source of contradictions
becomes apparent.
Regarding the events of the Provisional Regency ([Jūshè]),
Bān [Gù]'s account differs from Fàn [Yè]'s;
regarding the start and end of the Two Liú (Liú Biǎo and Liú Yān),
Fàn [Yè]'s account differs from Chén [Shòu]'s.
Integrating them into one compilation
might hopefully avoid this.
What is meant by detailing neighboring affairs?
Records of usurping states,
and foreign states on the four frontiers,
cannot possibly share the same beginning and end dates as a single dynasty.
However, when orthodox chronologies and biographies
are compiled dynastically,
then the historical accounts of the central court are complete,
while the records of vassal states are only partial.
Only in the Comprehensive History of the North and South ([Nánběi Tǒngshǐ])
are the beginnings of Hòu Liáng and Dōng Wèi fully recorded,
and in the Collected Compilation of the Five Dynasties ([Wǔ Dài Huìbiān]),
the records of Wú Yuè, Jīng, and Tán reach their conclusion.
These six points
are what are called the benefits.
What is meant by possessing skill in editing and selection?
In integrating all histories,
it is not merely about standardizing the general rules,
but also supplementing deficiencies,
cutting out superfluous rhetoric,
smoothing out abrupt changes and filling in gaps,
thereby conforming to the measure of a unified system.
For example, the Two Histories of the North and South ([Nán Běi Èr Shǐ]) by the Lǐ clan (Lǐ Yánshòu),
uses more concise language than previous authors,
and details events found in earlier records,
hence it is called a good history.
This is because those born in later generations,
possess the things they hear and see,
and naturally have supplements for their predecessors.
This is what is called having access to resources,
making the effort easier.
What is meant by establishing a systematic method?
If existing compilations are complete,
why bother with the serious task of re-compilation?
A specialized undertaking
naturally requires its own structure and essentials.
For example, the Tōngzhì by the Zhèng clan (Zhèng Qiáo),
demonstrates outstanding insight and clear principles,
possessing unique viewpoints and distinctive editing.
The ancients could not anticipate its innovations,
and later generations cannot exceed its standards.
Although the facts do not differ from older records,
the rectification of names and clarification of things,
embodying the ideas of the philosophers ([Zhūzǐ]),
are integrated into the historical compilation,
ultimately forming an imperishable achievement.
These two points
are what are called the advantages.
What is meant by lacking distinction between importance and unimportance?
In compiled and edited books,
if the contents are merely compared chronologically,
without essential additions or deletions,
and only the headings are changed,
then it falls under what Liú Zhījǐ referred to: "Scholars would rather study the original text
than peer into the new record."
What is meant by retaining original titles?
What is meant by retaining original titles?
Various histories have similarities and differences,
and each has its categories and titles.
If the author does not revise them,
they merely apply a new method of organization.
The Nán Shǐ has the Xiàoyì [Section] but lacks the Liènǚ [Section] (refer to the Liènǚ chapter for details).

The Tōngzhì uses Shǐjì when denoting the era (In the Tōngzhì, people from Hàn and Wèi are marked with Hàn and Wèi, referring to the era, not the historical book. But people recorded in the Shǐjì are also marked Shǐjì, not marking the era, which is mistakenly retaining the original text).
Following one corner to deduce three,
there are many instances of inappropriate inclusion or omission.
What is meant by forgetting classification headings?
Emperors, empresses, consorts, imperial clansmen, and aristocratic families,
have their dynastic titles marked,
making the distinction easily visible.
In the biographies of subjects and officials,
there are those whose affairs coincide with the times,
which are evident in the text.
Although they lack specific markings,
by observing the narrative sequence,
the dynasty naturally becomes clear.
As for sections like Dúxíng (Solitary Conduct), Fāngjì (Arts and Techniques), Wényuàn (Literature), and Liènǚ (Eminent Women),
the people therein are not entirely involved in political affairs.
When they are arranged uniformly,
such as Wú Kuí and Hán Língmǐn in the Nán Shǐ,
how often does one read their accounts without knowing their era?
These three points
are what are called the shortcomings.
defines *tōng* (通, permeation/thoroughness) as *dá* (達, reaching).
It means going from one point to another.
*Tōng*
is that which makes universal what is not yet universal throughout the world.
Reading the *Yì* as if the *Shū* did not exist;
reading the *Shū* as if the *Shī* did not exist.
The *Ěryǎ* governs textual exegesis (*xùngǔ*);
Elementary Learning (*Xiǎoxué*) illuminates the Six Scripts (*Liùshū*);
this is what is meant by *tōng*.
Ancient people compiled and authored texts by combining and separating concepts,
which were self-evident without needing explanation.
Hàn people used *tōng* as a title marker,
and during the Liáng era, *tōng* was incorporated into historical compilation methods.
Therefore, the styles and systems
are clearly distinct and cannot be intermingled.
Dù Yòu considered Liú Zhì’s *Zhèngdiǎn* incomplete,
and thus extended it upwards to the Sānwǔ (Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors).
This is why his *Diǎn* (Canon) is named *Tōng* (Thorough).
How is it that Wèi Liǎowēng took the institutional history of the Zhào Sòng dynasty alone,
and also named his work the *Guócháo Tōngdiǎn* (Thorough Canon of the National Dynasty)?
Since he called it "National Dynasty,"
marking a break at that specific period,
how can it be *tōng*?
This is also following the name without contemplating its meaning.
The Six Ministers jointly handled affairs.
Books concerning official posts
also carry the meaning of *tōng*.
How is it that Pān Dí took the duties of the Censors (*Yùshǐ*) of the Yuán dynasty,
and also titled his book the *Xiàntái Tōngjì* (Thorough Record of the Censorate)?
Furthermore, the study of geography
has its own specialization.
Gazetteers of prefectures and commanderies
should belong to the external histories (wàishǐ). (See details in the *Wàipiān: Bózhōu Zhì Yì*).
The former Míng dynasty changed the Yuán dynasty's Provisional Administrations (*Xíngshěng*) into Thirteen Provincial Administration Commissions (*Bùzhèngshǐ Sī*).
The prefectures (*fǔ*), departments (*zhōu*), counties (*xiàn*), and guards (*wèi*) under their jurisdiction
each had their own original gazetteers.
Since the area governed by the Commission was vast,
the various prefectures and counties within it,
fearing that their individual records
would not follow a single consistent path,
compiled and integrated all the subordinate regions
and separately created a *tōngzhì* (thorough gazetteer).
*Tōng*
is that which connects the prefectures, departments, counties, and guards that were individually unconnected.
How is it that those who compile the *tōngzhì*,
take the prefectures, departments, counties, mountains, rivers, people, and objects,
organize them into categorized sections,
use the prefecture to lead the counties,
use the county to lead the factual records and cultural achievements,
and list them separately,
without combining them?
If the books are created this way,
then readers need only read the original gazetteers of the prefectures and counties.
What use then is the *tōng*?
Now, historical and cultural comprehensiveness (*tōng shǐ rénwén*)
spans thousands of years,
but where the principles and systems are connected,
there is no aversion to combining compilations across different eras.
The Commission's jurisdiction covers
merely several dozen departments and counties,
yet they meticulously delineate borders,
fearing only that they might cross boundaries.
This is truly because their knowledge lacks comprehensive ability (*tōngcái*),
causing the books to be like mere clerical records.
*Héngtōng* (Lateral Thoroughness).
The term *tōngrén* (thorough person)
cannot be uniformly applied.
Some possess expertise in specialization,
others possess broad knowledge from general observation.
Each has something that cannot be changed;
if changed, it cannot be good.
Each has something that should not be coordinated;
if coordinated, it cannot be beneficial.
However, the term *tōng*
is used metaphorically, like roads:
four major crossroads and eight directions,
nowhere is inaccessible.
This is called *tōng*.
It also refers to the knowledge stored in the mind,
which, though differing in height and depth, partiality and completeness, size, and scope,
can all reach the Great Way (Dàdào).
Hence, it is called *tōng*.
Nevertheless, there are some that cannot be four major crossroads and eight directions,
cannot reach the Great Way,
yet still must be called *tōng*.
This is called *Héngtōng*.
*Héngtōng* and *tōngrén*
are similar yet different,
close yet far,
unified yet separated.
Old merchants are skillful at selling books;
old families are rich in book collections;
enthusiasts are keen to engrave books.
All these are people with whom broadly learned celebrities (*Bóyǎ míngliú*) link arms and enter the forest [of scholarship].
"When propriety is lost, seek it in the countryside" (*Lǐ shī qiú yě*).
Their knowledge and experience can significantly supplement what the broadly learned celebrities lack;
thus, the noble person (*Jūnzǐ*) must certainly visit them.
However, these people are merely zither makers and stele artisans,
whose crafts allow them to connect with the refined (*wényǎ*).
Since they connect with many celebrities,
they habitually hear pure speech and famous discourse.
But if their minds lack the pearl of wisdom,
then what they relay is mere hearsay (*dàotīng túshuō*).
The shallowness of their foundation
is not difficult to discern.
Academician Zhōu Chángfā
called people of this sort *Héngtōng*.
His words are extraordinary yet accurate.
Therefore, the noble person
takes what is advantageous in them and disregards their shortcomings,
just as zither makers and stele artisans are sufficient for practical use.
Unfortunately, scholars
are narrow in their knowledge and experience.
When they encounter the discussions of the *Héngtōng*, it is like a fierce thunderbolt splitting a mountain,
thus leading to fish eyes being mixed with pearls (falseness being confused with truth),
and the pure stream (*Qīngliú*) having no distinction.
And these people consequently boast and self-proclaim,
not realizing that their thoroughness (*tōng*) arises from the lateral (*héng*).
Speaking glibly in the mundane world (*jiānghú huīzhǔ*),
they create a distinct style belonging to the zither makers and stele artisans.
The noble person should be cautious about this difference in origin.
Master Xú was skilled in ritual demeanor;
Master Zhì knew the sounds of music (*kēngqiāng*).
When the Hàn court discussed rites and music (*lǐyuè*),
even seasoned scholars and elders
sometimes fell short compared to Master Xú and Master Zhì.
How could those who discuss rites and music
fail to interact with them?
However, the discourses held at Shíqú (Stone Channel) and Tiānlù (Heavenly Blessings)
were not something Master Xú or Master Zhì could participate in.
These, too, are the *Héngtōng* of rites and music.
Can people who are *Héngtōng* be dispensed with?
They cannot be dispensed with.
Their lateral thoroughness (*héng*) is used
to assist the verticality (*zòng*) of the noble person.
The noble person also does not suppress the lateral resources they rely upon.
Thus, the ritual demeanor of Master Xú
and the musical resonance of Master Zhì,
when used as supplements to rites and music,
how can they be minor?
The misfortune is that they do not realize their lateral position,
and the noble person also fails to discern their lateral position.
This is like: where Rites involve jade and silk,
the weavers and jade carvers
may participate in the high hall's assembly;
where Music involves bells and drums,
the metal casters and leather workers
may debate the records of Héjiān.
Therefore, the noble person must not be unaware of the distinction of origins,
and the *Héngtōng* must not forcefully attach themselves to the pure stream.
If so, there will be no trouble.
When criticizing the poetry and prose of women,
there is much undue leniency.
When writing prefaces and postscripts
for the *Héngtōng*, there is much praise and commendation.
The former is out of pity for their beauty;
the latter is to utilize their practical function.
Suppose, like Ruǎn Jí’s examination practice of covering names and swapping papers,
one allows someone who has some understanding of the substance
to thoroughly and clearly distinguish them,
then they cannot be deceived.
Nevertheless,
the poetry and prose of women
typically deal only with wind, clouds, moon, and dew,
and their shortcomings are easily seen.
The prefaces and postscripts of the *Héngtōng*,
however, commend scholarship.
Whether a single statement indicates wisdom or lack thereof—
the noble person, in this regard,
should exercise caution.
People who are *Héngtōng*
all love fame.
Those who love fame
are generally crude in understanding intentions.
Those they rely upon and attach themselves to
are certainly not of the first rank.
If someone possesses the hearing of Shī Kuàng,
whose discernment reaches to ghosts and spirits,
he would detest this.
Therefore, when the noble person interacts with the *Héngtōng*,
they do not fully express their pleasure,
nor fully exhaust their sincerity.
They treat them with moderate praise
and reserve their ultimate judgment;
then they are sufficient for mutual coexistence.
Extensive Enumeration.
I once read the *Zuǒshì Chūnqiū* (The Spring and Autumn Annals of Zǔo Qīumíng),
and was troubled that its method of writing people's names and courtesy names,
did not establish a fixed standard.
Now, receiving a given name (míng) in childhood,
receiving a courtesy name (zì) upon capping,
being referred to by seniority (bó zhòng) at fifty,
and receiving a posthumous title (shì) upon death,
this was the way of the Zhōu dynasty.
This refers to terminology used in ritual texts,
not the convention for historical writing recounting events.
Zǔo Shì, however, cited them randomly and arbitrarily,
without rules or consistency;
moreover, besides the given name, courtesy name, posthumous title, and seniority,
he further included official titles, noble ranks, and feudal estates.
Within a single passage,
they appeared mixed up and referenced interchangeably;
were it not for commentaries passed down,
having been continuously transmitted until now,
one would no longer recognize who the person was.
This is why later historical writings,
though none failed to diligently revere Zǔo Shì,
nevertheless, specifically concerning this matter,
they did not follow his precedent again.
Sǐ Mǎ Qiān initiated the structure of the Categorized Biographies (Lièzhuàn).
The meaning of "liè" (categorized) is,
to arrange various people from beginning to end,
thus distinguishing it from the chronological narratives.
However, the naming conventions for the listed people,
were also inconsistent.
Sometimes they used the noble title, such as Huái'yīn Hóu (Marquis of Huái'yīn).
Sometimes they used the official rank, such as Lǐ Jiāngjūn (General Lǐ).
Sometimes they simply wrote the given name.
Although this was not the same type of confusion as Zǔo Shì's,
it ultimately resulted in an impure standard of convention.
Some say:
Sǐ Mǎ Qiān had a subtle intention.
Now, recording events factually, where the good and bad become evident automatically,
is the essence of the *Chūnqiū*.
If one must explicitly title chapters to indicate praise or censure,
how can we fault the works of Shěn Yuē, Wèi Shōu, and others,
for directly using the headings frivolously!
Moreover, in the seventy Categorized Biographies,
those referred to by office or rank,
are only occasionally seen;
the rest simply record the full name,
and they were not cases that deserved censure by convention;
thus, at the beginning of Sǐ Mǎ Qiān's innovation,
it is merely that he could not avoid error.
If one insists on finding reasons for it,
that harms the principle (dào).
The literary style of the late Táng and Five Dynasties period was bizarre.
People were referred to without their given name or surname,
often using hidden jokes and allegories.
An observer, upon first viewing the text,
did not know who the person referenced was.
For instance, calling a person named Lǐ "Lǒngxī,"
or marking a person named Wáng as "Lángyá."
Although this was quite inappropriate,
one could still say it emphasized their commandery origin (jùnwàng).
If someone with the surname Zhuāng was called "Qīyuán,"
or someone with the surname Níu was called "Tàiláo,"
then it was merely ridicule, mockery, and jest,
and the prose no longer maintained coherence.
All examples of this type,
originated in ornate, parallel, and flowery prose,
developed through letters and casual fiction (xiǎoshuō),
and then unlearned scholars,
used them in their historical writings.
It is no wonder that the prose of examination essays,
deteriorated into roughness and crudeness,
and the entire field of literature fell into chaos.
Since gentlemen like Ōu Yáng Xiū and Zēng Gōng,
clarified and swept away the bizarre deviations of the late Táng and Five Dynasties,
over the few centuries of the Sòng and Yuán dynasties,
although the quality of the prose varied,
the spirit of the style favored clarity and authenticity (qīngzhēn);
this is commendable.
However, the Sòng people themselves opened a door to excessive bizarreness:
every person had a nickname (hào),
and not just one nickname,
but often three or more.
Now, in high antiquity, people were simple and substantial,
and they only had a given name.
The Zhōu way valued refinement (wén),
so a child received a given name and an adult received a courtesy name.
Therefore, those of lower status, when addressing those of higher status,
mostly avoided the given name and used the courtesy name.
Hence the saying, "The courtesy name expresses virtue."
If these were insufficient, and nicknames were added,
what is the justification?
Extending into recent ages,
customs daily grew decadent.
Initially, people dropped the given name and referred to others by the courtesy name.
Gradually, they dropped the courtesy name and referred to others by the nickname (hào).
Consequently, those of lower status, when addressing those they revered,
not only tabooed the given name,
but also tabooed their courtesy name,
viewing it as an offense.
Is this not both sycophantic and disrespectful?
Kǒngzǐ said:
"If names are not correct,
then speech will not flow smoothly."
Using nicknames and tabooing courtesy names,
are these not the most extreme examples of incorrectness and un-smoothness?
The origin of the nickname (hào)
did not begin in Sòng.
During the Chūnqiū and Zhànguó (Warring States) periods,
its beginnings were already visible.
Táo Zhū and Chī Yí Zǐ Pí
were names used to conceal themselves while escaping.
The masters Hè Guān and Guǐ Gǔ and others,
concealed their own names and courtesy names,
and people then bestowed nicknames upon them based on what they wore or where they lived.
None of these occurred without reason.
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
Daoism was greatly esteemed.
Thus, there were perfect beings (zhēnrén) bestowed titles like Nán Huá or Chōng Xū.
Dharma masters (fǎshī) were bestowed titles like Yè Jìng Fǎshī.
Daoist priestesses (nǚguān) were bestowed titles like Tài Zhēn Yù Fēi.
Buddhist monks (sēngqié) were bestowed titles like Sān Zàng Fǎshī. (Sān Zàng lived during Tàizōng's time, not starting in Kāiyuán, but is cited here as an example of the category.)
These were titles advertised by followers of the two teachings (Buddhism and Daoism).
Later, it extended to hermits like Chén Tuán and Lín Bū,
and soon spread to the scholarly class.
However, since they originated from bestowals by the imperial court,
although they lacked canonical importance,
they were still not nicknames coined by the person themselves.
Considering the intent behind the honor and favor granted at that time,
for those already deceased, it was similar to posthumous titles (shìfǎ);
for those still living, it was similar to official designations (tóuxián).
It was simply a way of rewarding people with empty words.
The proliferation of self-coined nicknames,
imitated the commandery origin (jùnwàng) trend,
and was an extreme extension of this deviation in later ages.
This stemmed from the fact that since the Six Dynasties, prominent families (méndì) competed to advertise their commandery origins,
whenever names were mentioned,
they did not use the ancestral registry (běnguàn) where the person actually lived,
but only emphasized the fame of the clan surname,
placing it at the head of the inscription.
This is why Líu Zǐxuán was conversely mocked by the historians.
After this was practiced for a long time,
commandery origin became merely a literary term of the time.
Once literary terms needed to be fresh and novel,
people competed in seeking strangeness and novelty,
names followed their arbitrary intentions,
and they created their own titles.
Therefore, the beginning of the alternative nickname (biéhào),
mostly derived names from mountains, springs, forests, and marshes.
This sufficiently proves it was a variation of the commandery origin trend,
resulting from attaching oneself to the place where one resided.
Gradually, it changed to halls (táng), verandas (xuān), pavilions (tíng), and gardens (yuàn);
this was a variation based on residence,
resulting instead from attaching oneself to the rooms where one resided.
Initially, one based it on the actual location,
but later, it was no longer necessary to actually possess the place—
they created mountains and rivers of private fancy.
Initially, one might actually have the room,
but later, it was no longer necessary to actually possess the room—
they constructed towers and pavilions in the air.
Discerning people only realized that the human mind prized novelty and oddity,
but did not know it started with the initial overflow of the commandery origin trend.
This is why the noble person (jūnzǐ) detests those who initiate harmful practices.
Peaks, springs, streams, and bridges,
towers, pavilions, verandas, and halls,
were already numerous, repetitive, and tiresome.
Then there emerged names derived from homophones or hidden puns.
This trend had not yet been initiated by the Sòng or Yuán people,

but the fashion became truly rampant from the former Míng dynasty up until recent days (sometimes taking a homophone of a character as the nickname, sometimes taking separated or combined parts of a character as the nickname).
Bandits who coin their own titles,
intend to deceive the masses. (The Red Eyebrows (Chìméi) and Yellow Turban (Huángjīn) are numerous examples.)
Prostitutes and actors who coin their own titles,
intend to charm customers. (Examples like the swallows, orioles, beauty, and plain white silk are numerous.)
Yet, the literati and officials (shì dà fū) conversely are dissatisfied with their given names and courtesy names,
and rush to adopt nicknames;
this is simply thoughtlessness.
Escaped prisoners often change their names,
fearing recognition.
A maid sold off must change her name,
to suit her new master.
Thus, a frequently escaped prisoner,
or a frequently resold maid,
must have many names,
which is said to be unavoidable.
Since scholars have already abandoned the courtesy name and established a nickname,
if there were an underlying meaning,
it would be necessary.
One would be enough.
But they deem one nickname insufficient,
and proceed to have three or even five! Alas!
It can be said they are utterly unafraid of unnecessary complications.
Ancient people, when writing books,
often did not label the chapter titles.
Later people, when collating and editing,
then named the chapters using the first phrase or sentence of the chapter.
If the book title was not labeled,
later generations, during collation,
then named the book after the author;
this shows that the ancients had no intention of advertising themselves.
For those that did have chapter titles and book titles,
they were all clear and easy to understand,
and never intentionally meant to be paradoxical.
However, if a single book had two names,
or if the refined (wén) and plain (zhì) elements appeared in varying order,
and could not be fixed definitively,
then the collators
would easily change the name in the record.
Following this practice without careful examination,
a divergence subsequently arose.
This was fundamentally not because the author of the book
sought novelty themselves
or intended to be paradoxical.
There are cases where the original name was plain (zhì) but the catalog followed the ornate (wén);
there are cases where the original name was ornate but the catalog followed the plain;
there are cases where the book was originally complete but others only cited parts;
there are cases where the book was originally partial but others referred to the complete work;
scholars must be aware of these things.
Examples of the original name being plain (zhì) but the catalog following the ornate (wén):
The *Lǎozǐ* (Lǎozǐ) fundamentally had no canonical title,
but the book is revered as the *Dàodé* (Dàodé);
The *Zhuāngzǐ* (Zhuāngzǐ) was fundamentally named after the person,
but the book is recorded under the class of *Nánhuá* (Nánhuá).

This is the case (The Hàn (Hàn) referred to it as *Zhuāngzǐ* (Zhuāngzǐ). During the Táng, it was officially honored as the *Nánhuá Zhēnjīng* (Nánhuá Zhēnjīng). In the Kāiyuán (Kāiyuán) era, the *Suí Zhì* (Suí Zhì) already included the title *Nánhuá* (Nánhuá)).
Examples of the original name being ornate (wén) but the catalog following the plain (zhì):
The book by Liú Ān (Liú Ān)
was originally titled *Hóngliè Jiě* (Hóngliè Jiě),
but the *Hàn Zhì* (Hàn Zhì) only recorded it as *Huáinán Nèiwài* (Huáinán Nèiwài);
The book by Kuǎi Tōng (Kuǎi Tōng)
was originally titled *Juànyǒng* (Juànyǒng),
but the *Hàn Zhì* (Hàn Zhì) only recorded it under the original name of *Kuǎi Tōng* (Kuǎi Tōng).
This is the type of case (*Juànyǒng* (Juànyǒng) has eighty-one sections, mentioned in the biography, which does not match the treatise).
Examples of the book title being originally complete but others only citing parts:
The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* (Lǚshì Chūnqiū) contains the Twelve Annals, Eight Surveys, and Six Discourses,
but later people sometimes referred to it only as the *Lǚ Lǎn* (Lǚ Lǎn);
The works of Qū Yuán (Qū Yuán) comprise twenty-five chapters,
and *Lísāo* (Lísāo) is specifically the leading chapter,

but later generations ultimately called the entire genre the *Sāofù* (Sāofù). This is that type of case (Liú Xiàng (Liú Xiàng) named it *Chǔcí* (Chǔcí), and later generations made it a dedicated literary section).
Examples of the book title being originally partial but others referring to the complete work:
The *Shǐ Jì* (Shǐ Jì) is the general name for records and documents,
but later people specifically named the whole work the *Tàishǐgōng Shū* (Tàishǐgōng Shū);
Sūn Wǔ (Sūn Wǔ) had over eighty chapters,
including diagrams and text,
but later people referred to just the thirteen chapters as the *Sūnzǐ* (Sūnzǐ).
This is that type of case.
These are all things that the collators and catalogers should pay attention to (already detailed in *Jiàochóu Tōngyì* (Jiàochóu Tōngyì)).
Although the shifting emphasis between the plain and the ornate
sometimes occurs naturally,
if the catalogers
do not differentiate clearly,
then the resulting error
is no different from the paradoxical practice of using alternative names or titles.
For books belonging to the Masters (Zǐ) and Histories (Shǐ) categories,
the identity or divergence between name and reality
is truly unavoidable due to transmission.
The rise of the Collections (Jí) category
all came from the subsequent compilation by later people.
Therefore, names were established based on the person
to indicate differentiation;
the Eastern Capital works entrusted to the Early Táng
have no other divergence.
Literati of the middle period,
when establishing their own collected works,
often labeled the collection title,
such as *Huìchāng Yīpǐn* (Huìchāng Yīpǐn) or Yuán Bái’s (Yuán Bái) *Chángqìng* (Chángqìng).
This is also somewhat redundant.
However, mentioning the era
is still acceptable.
Or naming it after a place (such as Dù Mù’s (Dù Mù) *Fánchuān Jí* (Fánchuān Jí), or Dúgū Jí’s (Dúgū Jí) *Pílíng Jí* (Pílíng Jí)),
or naming it after an official position (such as Hán Wò’s (Hán Wò) *Hànlín Jí* (Hànlín Jí)),
still has some basis.
As for those titles that are jocular or mocking,
named simply according to whim,

such as *Jǐnnáng* (Jǐnnáng) by Lǐ Sōng (Lǐ Sōng), *Wàngquán* (Wàngquán) by Yáng Huáiyù (Yáng Huáiyù), *Pīshā* (Pīshā) by Lǐ Xiányòng (Lǐ Xiányòng), *Túlóng* (Túlóng) by Xióng Jiǎo (Xióng Jiǎo), *Áoshū* (Áoshū) by Shěn Yán (Shěn Yán), or *Mànbian* (Mànbian) by Yuán Jié (Yuán Jié),
they are named arbitrarily.
And the style of the great elegance (Dàyǎ)
cannot be restored.
For books of the Masters and Histories categories,
the names are established based on their content (reality),
which is generally done out of necessity.
Collections, however, are scattered writings passed down.
When poems and articles are scattered,
they are all issued in response to events,
each having its own title,
and fundamentally there is no worry that the main point cannot be discerned.
Therefore, when compiling poetry and prose,
because they were scattered writings categorized as the words of one person,
then naming the collection after the person
is sufficient for identification.
In the higher examples,
although the writings are scattered, the main point derives from a single source;
this is surely the surviving model of the specialists in the Masters and Histories categories.
In the secondary examples,
the excellence of the writing
is gathered into one,
which is also a single achievement of the skill of literary embellishment.
Since their prose and poetry
already possess their individual titles,
it is fundamentally unnecessary to give the compiled poetry and prose a separate name.
The human mind enjoys difference,
and people compete to create titles,
which is certainly extravagant.
As for when one name is insufficient,
and they divide the collection into front and back parts,
separating the chapters,
perhaps taking official posts held as criteria,
or perhaps taking travel routes as criteria—
if rich and noble, they boast of their glory and distinction;
if poor and humble, they cultivate an air of destitution;
they skillfully invent names
and arbitrarily divide titles.
Consequently, the poetry and prose of a single person
ends up having countless collection names,
the record of titles
is squandered on flowery words,
the chapters and volumes cannot be made uniform,
and the catalog records cannot be summarized or unified.
Yet if one inquires into their main point
and examines their literary brilliance,
they are nothing more than yellow reeds and white rushes,
not differing by a single hair.
Such works ought to be generally consigned to the fire,
how can they be vulgarly entered into the superior categories?
Correcting Errors (Kuāng Miù):
The existence of prefaces in books
is intended to clarify the purpose of writing the book,
not merely for aesthetic presentation.
Prefacing the chapters
is intended to clarify the purpose of that chapter.
As for chapters succeeding one another
in sequence and order,
the ancients generally sometimes derived this from thematic principles (yì lì),
and sometimes did not derive it from thematic principles.
It is done according to the book’s main purpose,
and there is no room for forced arrangement.
The two chapters of the *Xù Guà* (Xù Guà) (Order of the Hexagrams) in the *Zhōu Yì* (Zhōu Yì)
sequence the meaning of the sixty-four hexagrams following one another.
Starting with *Qián* (Qián), *Kūn* (Kūn), *Tún* (Tún), *Méng* (Méng), and so forth,
the succession has its own explanation for each.
Although the meaning of the *Yì* (Changes) is not entirely contained here,
this is also naturally embodied within the meaning of the *Yì* (Changes),
and is not forcibly added.
When I look at how later people order books,
I cannot understand their reasoning.
The fundamental purpose of the book
originally has no sequential thematic arrangement of chapters.
They observe the ancients and admire them,
and thus they also create chapter sequences.
They vulgarly fill it with general phrases,
and forcibly connect rhyming language,
claiming that, "Therefore, such-and-such chapter is made first,"
and, "Therefore, such-and-such chapter is narrated second."
They equate themselves with Huáinán (Huáinán), the Grand Historian (Tàishǐ), Bān Gù (Bān Gù), and Yáng Xióng (Yáng Xióng)—
how deluded they are!
That they wrote and narrated them
is certainly understood.
But the “therefore first” and “therefore second,”
where is the explanation for that?
Furthermore, in the *Xù Guà* (Xù Guà), *Tún* (Tún) follows *Qián* (Qián) and *Kūn* (Kūn),
which must have its inherent meaning.
Filling the space between Heaven and Earth is the creation of the myriad things;
this is the meaning of *Tún* (Tún) following *Qián* (Qián) and *Kūn* (Kūn).
Therefore, the reason it is followed by *Tún* (Tún)
is precisely to say that it cannot be followed by hexagrams like *Xū* (Xū) or *Sòng* (Sòng),
but must be followed by *Tún* (Tún).
From *Méng* (Méng) and *Xū* (Xū) downwards,
it is merely the same principle.
This is why the *Xù Guà* (Xù Guà) is referred to as sequencing.
When later people sequence chapters,
they merely state that this chapter must be written.
They insist that A must precede B,
forcibly connecting them into text.
How can there be a principle that they cannot be interchanged,
like the necessary sequence of *Tún* (Tún) and *Méng* (Méng)?
Those who imitate the sequence of the *Yì* (Changes)
would be better off following the sequence of the *Shī* (Odes) or the *Shū* (Documents).
The chapter order of the *Shī* (Odes) and the *Shū* (Documents),
is it entirely without thematic principles?
But the rule that a certain chapter must necessarily follow another certain chapter does not exist there.
The Six Arts establish teachings,
and their governing principle is unified.
Why must one prioritize the sequence of the *Yì* (Changes)
and find the sequences of the *Shī* (Odes) and the *Shū* (Documents) lacking?
Now, books created based on symbolic numbers and mathematical structures
can have their chapters and sections sought out using symbolic numbers and mathematical structures.
If a book was not originally related to symbolic numbers and mathematical structures,
and one insists on seeking symbolic numbers and mathematical structures to substantiate it,
then it is forced and artificial.
The Yì (易) has the two fundamental principles (Liǎngyí), the four phenomena (Sìxiàng),
and the eight-times-eight generations,
totaling sixty-four hexagrams,
all deriving naturally from the Heavenly Principle.
The Tàixuán (太玄) uses nine-times-nine to make eighty-one,
and the Qiánxū (潛虛) uses five-times-five to make twenty-five.
Books that emulate the Yì (易),
having their numerical structures predetermined
before the text is composed,
therefore have chapters and sections
analogous to the organized formations of military strategy,
which can be roughly calculated.
Sīmǎ Qiān (司馬遷) authored one hundred and thirty chapters,
claiming to carry on the tradition of the illustrious eras and succeeding the Chūnqiū (春秋).
Truly,
it is an unparalleled masterpiece since the Three Dynasties (Sāndài).
However, his self-comparison
also contains flaws.
The twelve Basic Annals (Běnjì)
subtly follow the twelve dukes of the Chūnqiū (春秋).
He divided the Records of Qín (Qínjì) before the time of Zhuāngxiāng (莊襄),
making it a separate volume,
and ending the later part with the reign of Hàn Wǔ (漢武),
for which he composed the Basic Annals of the Current Emperor (Jīnshàng Běnjì),
clearly intending to strategically divide the space
to fulfill the number twelve.
The Chūnqiū (春秋) compiled by the Master
established literary style and codified laws;
the twelve years it chronicles
happened to be the way things were at that time,
not that thirteen was excessive
or twelve was lacking.
Hàn Confucians, in seeking antiquity,
were often constrained by superficialities.
Even a scholar of Sǐmǎ Qiān's (司馬遷) caliber
could not entirely avoid this;
this instance is such a case.
However, this only applies to the Basic Annals (Běnjì);
he did not necessarily have this intention for the other chapters.
Yet, scholars studying Qiān's (遷) work often confusingly insist on forced associations,
arguing that the twelve Basic Annals
follow the twelve months,
the eight Treatises (Shū) follow the eight winds,
the ten Tables (Biǎo) follow the ten Heavenly Stems,
the thirty Hereditary Houses (Shìjiā) follow the thirty days of a month,
the seventy Biographies (Lièzhuàn) follow the seventy-two seasonal markers (hòu),
and the one hundred and thirty chapters follow the inclusion of a leap month in a year.
This is disjointed and difficult to understand.
Even if we accept this argument,
if the Tables (Biǎo) follow the ten Heavenly Stems,
the Basic Annals (Běnjì) should follow the twelve Earthly Branches.
How could the Imperial Annals instead use earthly numbers
while the royal houses use heavenly numbers?
If the year is not yet three years old,
how can it symbolize a leap month?
If there are seventy-two seasonal markers,
why are two missing?
Examining the meaning based on the names,
contradictions appear at every turn.
Nevertheless, many schools of thinkers and historians
follow this theory,
sometimes referencing the odd and even numbers of Yīn and Yáng,
sometimes referencing the production cycle of the Five Phases (Wǔxíng).
If the numbers are small, they are combined into three or five;
if large, they are matched up to one hundred or one hundred and ten.
They would rather lengthen a duck's leg or shorten a crane's leg
than fail to achieve concordance with symbolic numbers and mathematical structures.
They insist that the seven chapters of Mèng (孟) follow the seven luminaries (Qīzhèng),
and that Qū Yuán’s (屈原) Jiǔgē (九歌)
is difficult to match with the Nine Chapters (Jiǔzhāng).
More recently, there are Dèng’s (鄧) Hánshǐ (函史) with its Old Yáng and Young Yáng,
and Jǐngyuè Quánshū (景嶽全書) with its eight directions and eight military formations.
How far is this from being child's play?
When the ancients composed books and titled chapters,
the names were taken merely to distinguish the items (A and B);
they held no deep significance.
The texts of the Six Arts (Liùyì)
are now generally recognizable.
Whether they have fixed titles
or non-fixed titles,
they are all named merely to distinguish the items (A and B),
without deep significance.
Examples of fixed titles

include the Dǐan (典), Mó (謨), Gòng (貢), and Fàn (範) (The Dì Dǐan, Gāoyáo Mó, Yǔ Gòng, and Hóngfàn are all fixed names in the ancient classics. Other examples like Duōfāng, Duōshì, and Zǐcái are not fixed names.)
Examples of non-fixed titles
include the Fēng (風) poems and the Yǎ (雅) and Sòng (頌) sections (All are named after the first two characters of the chapter).
Books of the various philosophers and historical records
also have fixed titles and non-fixed titles;
they follow the text to set the pattern,
which is too numerous to list.
However, the naming convention, which is merely for distinction
and holds no deep significance,
is largely the same (Books based on symbolic numbers and mathematical structures are not included in this category).
After the Master died, the subtle words ceased.
The twenty chapters of the Lúnyǔ (論語)
are certainly the ultimate domain of the Six Arts.
However, chapter titles like Xuéér (學而) and Wéizhèng (為政)
were all named after the first words or phrases of the chapter;
they hold no other meaning.
The seven chapters of Mèngzǐ (孟子)
are sometimes said to be recorded by Wàn Zhāng’s (萬章) disciples,
and sometimes said to be authored by Mèngzǐ (孟子) himself.
Regardless, the book emulates the Lúnyǔ (論語).
The chapter titles Liáng Huì Wáng (梁惠王) and Gōngsūn Chǒu (公孫醜)
were also the initial words or phrases of the chapter,
taken to be the title.
How could there be any other intention?
Commentators fail to seek the principles within the chapters
but excessively seek meaning outside the chapter titles.
This is a forced interpretation of the meaning.
Question-and-answer sessions between a master and disciple
are ordinary occurrences.
The fact that someone happens to be at the beginning of a chapter and is used to name the chapter,
what is so strange about that?
Commentators believe that Wèi Líng Gōng (衛靈公) and Jì Shì (季氏)
were the feudal lord and grandee of that era,
and that Kǒngzǐ's (孔子) morality qualified him to be a king's teacher.
Therefore, they are used to name the chapters,
just as Gōngyě (公冶) and Yǒngyě (雍也)
are included among the disciples.
Mèngzǐ (孟子) has chapter titles Liáng Huì Wáng (梁惠王) and Téng Wén Gōng (滕文公),
both feudal lords of that era,
listed alongside chapters like Wàn Zhāng (萬章) and Gōngsūn Chǒu (公孫醜).
This follows the same pattern.
This, however, can be called forced and irrational.
Even if we follow this argument,
the Lúnyǔ (論語) has a chapter Tàibó (泰伯),
an ancient sage.
And Yáo Yuē (堯曰),
an ancient sage emperor.
Should we also infer that the Master was the teacher of Yáo (堯) and Tàibó (泰伯)?
Wēi Zǐ (微子)
was an ancestor of Kǒngzǐ (孔子).
If Wēi Zǐ (微子) names a chapter,
is he implying that his ancestor was his disciple?
Furthermore, among the feudal lords,
were not Qí Huán (齊桓) and Jìn Wén (晉文)

superior to Wèi Líng (衛靈)? (Disciples are naturally spoken of in relation to contemporaries. Therefore, Lǔ Āi and Qí Jǐng were also more worthy than Wèi Líng and should not have been selected.) And were not Yàn Yīng (晏嬰) and Qú Yuàn (蘧瑗)
superior to Jì Shì (季氏)?
They appear in the chapter;
why were they not elevated to the chapter title,
but instead rejected in favor of the others?
As for Mèngzǐ's (孟子) interaction with Gào Zǐ (告子),
Gào Zǐ (告子) is too lowly to be mentioned.
Yet, to list him alongside Gōngsūn (公孫) and Wàn Zhāng (萬章)
shows a lack of a sense of right and wrong.
If one insists on using this principle to interpret books,
it is no wonder that subsequent authors,
who rashly imitate the ancients without grasping their true meaning,
are endlessly numerous.
Someone might say:
Attaching names to chapters/sections arbitrarily,
and forcefully creating titles/labels,
is characteristic of the way Hànrú (Hànrú) (Han Confucians) interpreted the classics,
in seeking explanations, they inevitably went too far.
But the reason Hànrú did this,
could it be that they had completely no basis [for their views],
and simply stretched their own arbitrary conjectures?
I say:
I fear that the base scholars (jiànrú) of the end of the Zhōu (Zhōu) Dynasty
had already initiated this trend.
The flourishing of writing books,
was greatest during the Zhànguó (Zhànguó) (Warring States) period;
making a living by writing books as a means to seek official stipends
also began in the Zhànguó period.
Therefore, when Qū Píng (Qū Píng)'s draft manuscript [was written],
Shàngguān (Shàngguān) wished to seize it,
and the Guócè (Guócè) often records cases of writing memorials on behalf of others;
thus, writing was valued,
and book-writing opened the door to appropriation and borrowing.
When the Qín Wáng (Qín Wáng) saw the chapters Wǔdù (Wǔdù) and Gūfèn (Gūfèn),
he saw them,
and was so regretful that he could not have lived at the same time [as the author],
then those below used this writing to seek favor,
and those above also used this writing to select [officials].
When many sought selection,
prideful labeling arose,
and the trend of adorning and falsifying also began.
I examined the Hàn Yìwén Zhì (Hàn Yìwén Zhì),
in the stream of the Rújiā (Rújiā) school,
there is the book Wèi Wén Hóu Yǔ Píngyuán Jūn Shū (Book of Wèi Wén Hóu and Píngyuán Jūn).
If readers do not investigate thoroughly,
they might consider how the princely sons of the lords of the Zhànguó period
could be included in the Rújiā school?
They do not realize that the person who wrote the book,
himself attributed it to the Rújiā school,
and recounted the princely sons of the lords requesting instruction and posing questions,
and therefore used the name of the person asking the question to title the chapter and place it first.
That book is not extant,
later generations were misled by the title name,
and thus concluded that Wén Hóu and Píngyuán Jūn themselves authored it.
Those who, for a time, chased the prevailing trends and wrote books,
how could they possess the morality fit to be teachers of others,
while the lords, ministers, and chancellors,
indiscriminately and without selection or judgment,
generally followed them to request instruction?
There must have been instances where the events did not happen,
but were attributed to relationships with the noble and prominent in order to deceive the world.
The book Guócè (Guócè),
mostly records the strategies and wisdom of the strategists of the time,
but there are also occasionally strange plots and cunning schemes
that were not used at the time,
yet the scholar who compiled the book,
loved them too much to discard them,
and fabricated hypothetical questions and answers between lords and ministers to satisfy his own wishes,
such as the stories concerning Sūzǐ (Sūzǐ), Xuē Gōng (Xuē Gōng), and the Chǔ Tàizǐ (Chǔ Tàizǐ);
these are clear proofs.
If that is the case, then those who were poor and humble attributed their words to exchanges with the noble and prominent,
and those who were foolish and crude associated themselves with the highly enlightened as companions.
The trend of boasting and deceit among strategists,
coupled with a time when rhetoric was valued and praised,
had long spread throughout the land.
And those who interpreted the classics, seeing the current affairs of that time to be like this,
then asserted that the flourishing morality of the sages and worthies
must rely on the lords, ministers, and chancellors honoring them as masters,
only then could they rise above their generation.
Alas!
This originates from being limited by the prevailing trend.
As for fabricating questions and answers to write a book,
did this happen in antiquity? I answer:
There are examples that start from reality and become fictitious.
The parables in Zhuāng (Zhuāng) and Liè (Liè)
describe the questions and answers of Yáo (Yáo), Shùn (Shùn), Kǒng (Kǒng), and Yán (Yán);
one can tell immediately that they are parables.
There are examples that start from fiction and become concrete.
The Yú Fù (Yú Fù) and Zhān Yǐn (Zhān Yǐn) mentioned in the Qū Fù (Qū Fù) (Qū's Rhapsodies)
were originally not real people,
but Qūzǐ (Qūzǐ)'s own words were incorporated into them.
This means those figures were fictitious, but Qūzǐ's words were real.
One can also tell immediately that they are allegorical.
There are examples that are fabricated purely for literary effect.
These are the Chǔ Tàizǐ (Chǔ Tàizǐ) and the Wú Kè (Wú Kè),
and Wūyǒu Xiānshēng (Wūyǒu Xiānshēng) and Zǐxū (Zǐxū).
There are examples that are fabricated based on content/substance.
This is when the Gōng (Gōng) and Gǔ (Gǔ) commentaries transmit the classics,
setting up hypothetical questions and challenges,
but without recording personal names.
This is that example.
The scholars of later generations, when elaborating words and displaying ornate language,
often resorted to deceitful attribution,
knowing that readers would not cling to the specifics.
To examine and scrutinize difficult questions,
one must know the true name.
If one cannot find the person,
and infers them based on conjecture,
then one should use the phrase "Someone asked" (huò wèn),
fearing that the fabricated statements
might mislead later generations.
Regarding the writings and books of recent times,
I cannot help but be confused.
Things that are easily observed principles
do not need to be stated.
If one must state them,
writing them plainly in the book
is also acceptable.
If the author insists on setting up a question,
that is already roundabout.
If they must set up a question,
either by attributing it to Jiǎ Yǐ (Jiǎ Yǐ) (A and B),
or calling it "Someone asked" (huò wèn),
all are permissible.
But if they insist on naming a real person to substantiate it,
then what is the reasoning behind that?
Furthermore, the person attributed [as the questioner]
must be chosen from those who were contemporaries and interacted with the author,
and had at least some fame,
otherwise they would not be sufficient for labeling and promotion.
If one were to take what that person actually wrote,
and then interrogate them about the attributed questions,
and that person knew nothing about it originally,
is this not slanderous?
Moreover, in the form of question and answer,
the questioner must be shallow,
and the answerer must be profound;
the questioner holds error,
and the answerer must hold truth.
Now, to falsely attribute [dialogue] in the form of question and answer,
is always to grant oneself the profound and the correct,
and to assign the shallow and the erroneous to others.
Is this not mean-spirited?
When a Jūnzǐ (Jūnzǐ) (gentleman) engages in writing,
if it is sufficient to illustrate his meaning,
and to judge the truth/falsity correctly,
even if such a person truly existed,
they would still conceal the name to preserve integrity and benevolence.
How much more so when the statement originally does not exist and is forced upon someone else?
Slandering a person to gain fame,
how is this different from robbing a person to seek profit?
In what way are they different?
Furthermore, writing has rising and falling movements,
and often uses the pretense of questions and answers inherent in the meaning;
in this case, it is due to the requirements of the literary momentum,
and initially has nothing to do with any hidden meaning in the content.
If, regarding this matter, someone still needs to ask questions,
that person must be truly foolish and crude.
Now, to impose foolishness and crudeness upon someone,
and use it to supply the rising and falling movement of one's own writing,
is like falsely using the Tuīguān (Tuīguān) (Judicial Commissioner) to complete a rhyme.
In the past, there was a man serving in a low position who recited a poem to slander his superior.
The superior summoned him,
and he happened to be seen at the same time as a certain Tuīguān (Tuīguān).
The superior questioned him,
and the man recited another poem to explain himself,
and the concluding line was,
"Ask the certain Tuīguān (Tuīguān)."
The Tuīguān (Tuīguān) had not known about this beforehand,
and was terrified, unable to clear himself.
He retreated and questioned the man about why he had been slandered.
The man replied:
It was for no other reason;
I merely borrowed your title to complete the rhyme.
The structure of inquiry and rebuttal,
necessarily involves the questioner being put down while the answerer expands the response.
Therefore, unless the principles and doctrines are of utmost importance,
the *jūnzǐ* does not wish to reveal the surname and given name of the one who was put down.
Mèngzǐ rejected Yáng [Zhū] and Mò [Dí],
he necessarily took the theories of Yáng and Mò and refuted them,
thus focusing not only on the individuals but on their teachings.
Therefore, quoting the words of Yáng and Mò,
only illuminates the school doctrines of Yáng and Mò,
and does not necessarily refer exclusively to the individuals Yáng Zhū and Mò Dí.
This shows the depth of his rejection;
he wished to thoroughly eradicate their branches and descendants.
This is because they and we cannot coexist;
if it were not like this,
it would not be sufficient to illuminate the Great Dào of the Former Kings.
When those heterodox schools viewed us Rú (Confucians),
how could they have felt otherwise?
When Hán Fēi practiced the doctrines of Xingmíng (laws and terminology),
then both Rú (Confucians) and Mò (Mohists) were subjected to rejection.
The words of the Mohists were few,
but the Rú had the *Shī* (Odes), the *Shū* (Documents), and the Six Arts,
all of which were praised and narrated by Rú scholars,
therefore, when he criticized the actions and affairs of Yáo, Shùn, Wén, and Zhōu,
he necessarily borrowed the words of Rú scholars to debate against them.
Therefore, in the various chapters titled "Difficulties" (Nàn),
he often singled out Rú scholars,
making them the targets for shooting practice.
This was unavoidable for them,
but it is what the *jūnzǐ* disdains to compare himself against.
However, their writing is brilliant and argumentative,
their intentions harsh and profound;
scholars of literature in later generations
mostly enjoy reading them.
If one regards only the literature and not the individual,
then it is not impossible to consult and adopt from them.
Wáng Chōng, in his *Lùn Héng* (Discourses Weighed in the Balance),
imitated the writing style of the various "Difficulties" chapters.
His imitation of the writing
was not due to adopting their teachings;
he also singled out Rú scholars and challenged them.
Furthermore, the things he challenged,
which were confused historical records and biographies,
were also not entirely derived from Rú scholars.
He forcefully attributed these to Rú doctrines,
making them the signposted targets for shooting.
What enmity did Wáng Chōng have with the Rú?
Moreover, his polemics and rebuttals in chapters like *Wèn Kǒng* (Questioning Kǒng) and *Cì Mèng* (Attacking Mèng),
which held that Rú doctrines were wrong,
had a style similar to Hán Fēi.
Hán Fēi denounced the Rú
in order to promote Xingmíng.
What did Wáng Chōng intend
to promote?
Considering that he deeply criticized Hán Fēi's analogy of the deer and the horse in order to honor the Rú,
and furthermore, in his own preface,
he sought to distinguish popular customs and erroneous transmissions,
wishing to rectify people's minds and customs;
this is precisely the fundamental aim of Rú scholars.
If so, did Wáng Chōng, being a Rú scholar, reject Rú scholars?
Hán Fēi's fundamental purpose
certainly existed.
The sharpness of his writing
did not lie merely in his ability to denounce the Rú.
Wáng Chōng was bogged down by that style,
believing that if one did not denounce the Rú,
the writing would not be sharp?
When ordinary people exchange insults,
they often turn the opponent's words back on them to insult them—
that is human nature.
When one denounces a name and heaps abuse,
the person abusing in return must necessarily change that name—
that is the necessary consequence.
Now, Wáng Chōng's rejection of the Rú
is like denouncing one's own counter-abuse,
while still using one's own name.
Regarding fundamental nature:
The Three Virtues of the *Hóng Fàn* (Great Plan)—
Uprightness, Firmness, and Central Harmony—
in which the firm and the soft mutually moderate,
to balance the excessive and the deficient.
This summarizes the minds, knowledge, vitality,
intelligence, talent, and strength of all people under Heaven;
nothing falls outside these three.
Kǒngzǐ's instruction to his disciples:
If the path of the Central Constant cannot be attained,
then seek the Ardent (Kuáng) or the Scrupulous (Juàn).
This also draws its material from the Three Virtues.
However, those who belong to the stream of the "Village Worthies" (*xiāng yuàn*),
who superficially resemble the Central Constant but mock the Ardent and the Scrupulous,
are not summarized by the Three Virtues.
Kǒng and Mèng detested them as the thieves of virtue;
this is because, together with the Central Constant, the Ardent, and the Scrupulous,
they corrupt the three and make them four.
But people's hearts are no longer like those of antiquity,
and prevailing trends descend;
not only do the false Central Constants
corrupt the three into four,
but the streams of the false Ardent and the false Scrupulous
also corrupt the four into six;
not only is the Central Constant path unobtainable,
but even seeking genuinely Ardent or Scrupulous individuals—
how can they be found?
Mèngzǐ, in discussing the discernment of words,
held that the generation of thoughts and the initiation of governance
were harmful to the endeavor.
I have profoundly investigated the reasons
in the writings of various schools.
Those that ramblingly spread into books
and originally lacked the aim of establishing doctrines
can be disregarded.
However, there are those who claim to have founded a school,
and examining their fundamental aims,
they are not entirely meaningless;
but measuring them against the reality of the Three Virtues,
they have lost their essential nature,
and do not correspond to the essential Dào of the ancients—
this is what is called "similar but wrong."
If scholars seek the great principles from the ancients
but fail to make distinctions in this regard,
then those who started by corrupting the three into six,
will eventually cause the Three Virtues to perish due to the three falsities.
Alas!
How can the discourse on fundamental nature
be neglected?
The *Yì* (Classic of Changes) says:
"Words have substance, and conduct has constancy."
The *Shū* (Classic of Documents) says:
"Poetry expresses intent (*zhì*)."
I observe the *jūnzǐ* who establish doctrines
and the poets who sing verses—
why are they so numerous and confused?
If we seek their substance, it is not found;
if we probe their intent, it is vague.
Yet they all say:
I have established doctrine,
I have composed poetry.
To have words where there are no words,
to have poetry where there is no poetry—
this is precisely their so-called substance and intent.
However, confusion arises from this point forward.
A man of serious intent,
prizes his mind
and develops his intention,
believing that his words are not spoken haphazardly.
His learning must be rooted in natural disposition,
his interest must converge on *rén* (benevolence) and *yì* (righteousness),
his assertions must conform to the *Shī* and the *Shū*,
and his achievements must reach the people and all things.
He affirms Yáo and Shùn but rejects Jié and Zhòu;
he honors Kǒng and Mèng but rejects Yáng and Mò.
What he speaks
cannot be altered
even if a sage were to rise again.
Yet, seeking the reason why he speaks,
the fundamental purpose remains vague.
For instance, concerning the *Tóng Gōng* and *Zhàn Lù* odes,
when they are played at a guest banquet,
the listeners believe that this is achieved through consistent practice.
Some say:
It seems they are free from blame.
Yet Zǐ Mò grasps the Central Way here,
and the Village Worthy finds no fault here.
Huìzǐ said:
"The runner runs east,
and the pursuer also runs east;
although the eastern running is the same,
the nature of their eastern running is different."
Observing the words of this type of person,
is his running the east of the runner,
or the east of the pursuer?
This cannot yet be known.
However, from this point, confusion arises again.
When heroes and exceptional talents emerge,
they consider that their words are not spoken aimlessly;
they genuinely possess ambition.
Things cry out when they cannot find their balance.
Observing how they name things and point out analogies,
some are like the comparisons and imagery of the poets (shīrén),
and some are like the allegorical hidden meanings of the persuaders (shuōkè).
They use the small to illustrate the great,
lament the past while grieving for the present,
their playful laughter is more intense than glaring rage,
and their sorrowful singing can substitute for weeping.
Truly, there are things they cannot help but speak of.
They believe that worthy men (xiánzhě) who fail to realize their ambitions in their time
express their indignation by writing books to make themselves known.
Generally, the core intent
does not deviate from the style of the Lisāo.
I have read the words of the Sāorén:
“Indeed I possess this inner beauty,
and further, I emphasize cultivated ability.”
Sīmǎ Qiān (Tàishǐ Qiān) said:
“When I read the Lísāo,
I grieved over its aspiration.”
He also said:
“He elucidated the vastness and loftiness of virtue (dàodé),
and the framework of order and chaos.
His ambition was pure,
his conduct was honest,
and he was immaculate, unstained by mud;
it would be acceptable for him to contend for brilliance with the sun and moon.”
This is why Jiǎ Yí (Jiǎ) lamented Qū Yuán (Qū),
and why Sīmǎ Qiān (Qiān) wrote the biography of Jiǎ Yí (Jiǎ);
these were all heroes of the Three Dynasties.
As for those who rely on the style of the Lísāo (Sāo) to proclaim themselves,
when seeking the reason for their melancholy (láosāo), one finds only confusion.
Alas, they sigh over poverty and old age,
while others are rich and noble, they are poor and humble,
others gain high degrees, while they are rejected and dropped.
They seek favor from those in power but are met with drawn swords.
They compete for power and profit and are overthrown and crushed.
Because of this failure to realize ambitions,
they seek to express their writing in the style of the Sāo and the Yǎ,
claiming it to be the aspiration of the ancients.
They do not realize that they are merely people of middle or lower talent,
who are described as “uniting their hearts in the same wish,
holding intentions that have not been expressed.”
If
the civil examinations elevate a hundred or ten high-ranking scholars,
there must be several thousand Jiǎ Yís
who weep bitterly lamenting the Xiāngjiāng River;
the river does not hear them.
If the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù) promotes a thousand or a hundred officials with positions,
there must be ten thousand Qū Yuáns
scratching their heads to compose the Tiānwèn;
Heaven finds it tiresome.
Mèngzǐ said:
“If one possesses the ambition of Yī Yǐn (Yī Yǐn), it is acceptable;
if one does not possess the ambition of Yī Yǐn (Yī Yǐn), then it is usurpation.”
I say that for those suffering melancholy (láosāo),
if they possess the ambition of Qū Yuán (Qū) and Jiǎ Yí (Jiǎ), it is acceptable;
if they do not possess the ambition of Qū Yuán (Qū) and Jiǎ Yí (Jiǎ), then it is vulgar.
Nevertheless, those who proclaim themselves Sāorén
are already numerous.
There are those who adopt a broad perspective (kuàngguānzhě),
and they proceed to explain:
“Why should this matter?
I have something to say,
and I do so simply to satisfy my own mind.
If people agree with me,
I am not pleased,
if people disagree with me,
I am not angry.
The right and wrong of the past and present,
I do not wish them to be too clear;
the opinions between myself and others,
I do not wish to hold onto them excessively.
If one insists on believing in the present,
what is one accomplishing?
Having words is not better than having no words at all.”
The aim of this perspective is probably to rely on Zhuāng Zhōu’s (Zhuāng Zhōu) doctrine of the Equivalence of Things (Qíwù).
I heard Zhuāng Zhōu’s (Zhuāng Zhōu) words stating:
“The learning of inner sageliness and outer kingship (nèishèng wàiwáng)
is obscure and unclear,”
and “The hundred schools go forth and do not return,
the Way (dàoshù) is about to split apart,”
and “Allegorical speeches (yùyán) are nine out of ten,
goblet speeches (zhīyán) emerge daily.”
However, they are profusely appropriate and profoundly successful,
richly fulfilling and cannot be stopped.
Thus, he was not without something to stand by,
and did not aimlessly adopt a detached view (dáguān)
to disregard worldly affairs.
Now, those who attach themselves to Zhuāng Zhōu (Zhuāng) and call themselves detached,
is their true intent really to claim that words are useless?
Even if their teaching of uselessness
cannot be preserved,
is their teaching of uselessness
intended to pass down instruction?
Yet, we have never heard that peddlers and servants (fànfū zàolì)
must necessarily desire usefulness.
With their greedy pig-bellies (shǐfù tāotāo)
and their cautious goat-horns (yángjiǎo jíjí),
how have they ever sought to clarify the right and wrong of the past and present,
or insist on the opinions between themselves and others?
The reason why the timid (qiè) overcome the brave (yǒng)
is that they have abundant strength but do not use it.
The reason why the slow-of-speech (nà) overcome the eloquent (biàn)
is that they have abundant wisdom but do not compete.
When flood dragons battle in the abyss,
earthworms and ants do not know the victory or defeat;
when tigers and leopards fight on the mountains,
civets and wildcats do not know their relative strength;
they are unable to know,
it is not that they do not wish to.
To claim that one does not wish to, based on one's inability,
then the foolishness of ordinary people (fūfù zhī yú)
could be equated with the highest wisdom.
Nevertheless, those who hide within this perspective
are also numerous.
The Yìjīng says:
“One Yin (Yīn) and one Yang (Yáng) is called the Way (Dào).”
The transformation of Yang and the convergence of Yin,
cycling endlessly,
is the pneumal transformation of Heaven and Earth.
Humans, born endowed with the pneuma of central harmony (zhōnghé),
become intelligent, enlightened, wise, and discerning.
When Yin (Yīn) and Yang (Yáng) assist each other,
they should be regulated by firmness (gāngkè) and regulation by yielding (róukè).
This is why learning (xuéwèn) is valued.
If fierce Yang (Yáng) harms Yin (Yīn),
affecting one’s disposition (qìzhì),
and the scholar cannot overcome himself,
and takes what resembles right but is wrong as learning,
then it is better not to learn at all.
Kǒngzǐ said:
“If I cannot find people who walk the central way (zhōngxíng) to associate with,
I must take the ambitious (kuáng) and the reserved (juàn)!
The ambitious advance and strive,
the reserved refuse to do certain things.”
Zhuāng Zhōu (Zhuāng Zhōu) and Qū Yuán (Qū Yuán),
are their writings those of the ambitious and the reserved?
Qū Yuán (Qū Yuán) could not allow his pure self (shēn zhī chá chá)
to endure the defilement of the world (wù zhī wèn wèn);
he was the reserved type who disdained impurity.
Zhuāng Zhōu (Zhuāng Zhōu) alone associated with the spirit of Heaven and Earth (tiāndì jīngshén),
and yet was not arrogant towards the myriad things;
he was the ambitious type who advanced and strived.
The ancients said that the writings of Zhuāng (Zhuāng) and Qū (Qū)
had sorrow and joy that surpassed others.
This means that although Nature (xìng) cannot be seen,
the extremes of feeling (qíng zhī qí zhì) like those of Zhuāng (Zhuāng) and Qū (Qū),
is the reason why the ambitious and the reserved (kuángjuàn) are immortal.
Those belonging to the class of hypocritical villagers (xiāngyuànzhě),
who adopt the central way (zhōngxíng) to speak of Nature and Heaven (xìngtiān),
their deceitfulness is easily seen
and is not worth mentioning.
If one can see the person through their learning,
and their feelings are manifested in their writing,
then perhaps the ambitious and the reserved (kuángjuàn) can be associated with!
Nevertheless, those who proclaim the Lísāo (Sāo) are vulgar,
and those who proclaim Zhuāng Zhōu (Zhuāng) are deluded.
The ambitious and the reserved (kuángjuàn) are nowhere to be seen,
yet the vulgar and the deluded
are numerous in their self-proclamations.
Feelings (qíng) are rooted in Nature (xìng),
and talent (cái) follows pneuma (qì).
Those affected by the interplay of Yin (Yīn) and Yang (Yáng)
cannot avoid the mechanism of waxing and waning (yíng xū xiāoxī).
Talent and feelings are inseparable from blood and pneuma (xuèqì);
without learning to sustain them,
they cannot avoid being shifted by Yin (Yīn) and Yang (Yáng).
Joy, sadness, anger, and worry (táo wǔ wèn qī)
within one's body
revolve endlessly
without self-awareness.
If one fully explores this principle,
even the cycle of indignation and joy experienced by the Master (Fūzǐ)
is nothing more than this.
Those below him,
each have things they reach,
and each have things they understand.
Generally, when joy reaches a deep and absorbing point,
and one regrets the passing of time (guāngjǐng),
it inevitably turns into sorrow;
when worries and suffering deepen,
and one realizes there is nothing that can be done,
it reverses into detachment and broad-mindedness (kuàngdá).
Qū Yuán (Qū Yuán), at the extreme of worry,
therefore composed rhapsodies about lightly ascending, distant travels, feeding on mist, and drinking dew (cānxia yǐnxie zhī fù);
Zhuāng Zhōu (Zhuāng Zhōu), at the extreme of joy,
