therefore possessed the sorrow that later generations would not see the purity of Heaven and Earth, nor the grand design of the ancients (tiāndì zhī chún, gǔrén dàtǐ zhī bēi);
this is also the ultimate principle of interdependence and reversal (yǐfú zhī zhìlǐ).
As for those inclined towards Yin (Yīn),
they presumptuously make promises to themselves,
and emotions of lament arise boundlessly;
these are the destroyers of the Sāo style.
As for those inclined towards Yang (Yáng),
they are frantic and uncontrollable,
constantly invoking Nature (zìrán);
these are the destroyers of the Zhuāng style.
Nevertheless, this cycle will continue ceaselessly.
My nephew Tíngfēng said:
"To discuss historical talent (cái) and historical learning (xué),
but not discuss historical virtue (dé);
to discuss literary sentiment (qíng) and literary intent (xīn),
but not discuss literary character (xìng)—
The ancients certainly had omissions in their principles.
This, along with the chapter 'Shǐdé,'
is enough to bring to light what the ancients failed to address."
Cunning and crudeness:
gathering rushes from Dǒngzé;
inheriting validation from 'Chángyáng';
boasting of familiarity with high officials;
recording responses in the diviner's booth—
people call this cunning (xiá);
it is not cunning,
it is crudeness (lòu).
Fame is the guest of reality (shí).
Pursuing fame (míng) while forgetting reality
will result in losing the very fame one seeks;
when substance departs, ornamentation cannot survive alone.
The highest (person) forgets fame,
knowing only what is necessary to do,
not caring what others say of him.
The next level is to regard fame and contemplate principle (yì).
There is no circumstance in the world where fame is simply planted for one's benefit;
rather, based on where fame resides,
one contemplates how it came to be so,
then one knows what must be done and can spur oneself on.
The next is to fear fame and not act recklessly.
He exhausts what he knows and what he is capable of,
but does not force what he does not know or cannot do.
When the cunning regard him,
he seems clumsy (zhuō);
it is not clumsiness,
but mutually supporting achievements.
The lowest pursues fame while forgetting reality.
What does "gathering rushes from Dǒngzé" mean?
Those who discuss literature honor the Zuǒ and the Shǐ.
The Zuǒ and the Shǐ, in terms of literature,
are like the compilation and editing (shān shù) of the Six Classics.
The Zuǒ relies on the cherished records of a hundred states;
the Shǐ relies on the records of the Shàngshū, the Guóyǔ, as well as the Shìběn, the Guócè, and the Chǔ Hàn Chūnqiū;
what they themselves authored was one-tenth,
and what they preserved through editing and compilation was nine-tenths.
The superior person does not consider this wrong.
The essential purpose of their writing
was fundamentally to excel at editing and compilation.
Therefore, those who succeeded the Chūnqiū to create their own school of thought
were diligently
focusing on the matters (shì) and placing literary style (cí) second.
The ancients did not boast privately about their literary style;
moreover, historical writing cannot be fabricated from nothing and constructed separately.
Furthermore, the sources upon which they relied
are suspended between heaven and earth.
If one examines the literary style used in their compilations,
it still possesses its ultimate quality in each part;
this is truly the result of being molded and fused with the creative forces of Nature.
When I observe recent literary collections,
I cannot but feel confused.
Biographical writings (zhuàn jì),
the ancients formed them into independent volumes,
and did not include them in collections;
later people scattered them and included them in collections—
this is a change in literary practice.
Since they are biographies contained within a collection,
they are no longer specialized works based on editing and compilation;
they should record what has been heard and seen,
in preparation for the compilation efforts of later generations.
This might perhaps be fitting.
Those who are cunning in seeking fame but crude in understanding intent
catch a glimpse of the scholarly knowledge and literature of the current age,
and cannot but be moved by it,
yet measuring their own talent and capacity,
they know they are insufficient to achieve it;
consequently, seeing the reliance on precedent among historians,
they cunningly organize texts into biographies,
planning to make their collections profound and vast,
but they do not know that this is inappropriate.
The calendrical calculations of the Méi clan of Xuānchéng—
their family possessed the relevant books.
Gathering and recording discussions on the calendar,
the text fills two volumes.
Why make this a biography and place it in a literary collection?
What is the purpose?
Retreating and examining the individual (author),
we have not heard that he had any understanding of musical rhythm (lǜ) or calculation (suàn).
The medical principles of the Zhū clan of Dānxī—
people widely transmit their learning.
Extracting and transcribing medical cases,
the text amounts to tens of thousands of words.
Why make this a biography and place it in a literary collection?
What is the purpose?
Going further and seeking his explanation,
we have not heard that he distinguished between various magical or medical techniques (fāng shù).
Bān Gù relied on the transmission of the Hóngfàn to narrate the Wǔxíng (Five Phases);
he relied on the records of the Qīlüè to describe the Yìwén (Treatise on Literature).
Bān Shì had never been deeply versed in omens and calamities,
nor skilled in textual collation,
yet the superior person considers that Bān Shì’s compilation and editing
had accomplishments that supplemented Mǎ Qiān;
They also praised Bān Shì’s compilation and editing
as being adept at relying on others and not seeking to impose his own views.
For the Hànshū was regarded as the ancestral temple (miàotáng),
and the scholarship of the various schools
was comparable to the display of the great bells (yōng) and large drums (fén gǔ).
Now, those who write biographies for Méi and Zhū
seem to envy the beauty and richness of the ancestral temple and the hundreds of officials,
and yet they secretly take the courtyard torch and the spittoon tray,
to use them as decorations for their simple thatched door.
Even so,
it may also be called clumsy (zhuō).
The transmission of the classics by teachers,
and the specialization in techniques by various masters (zǐ shù),
were the lifelong undertakings of the ancients.
If one can simply hunt down the essence
to enrich one's own writing,
then the classics and records in the Siku (Four Treasuries)
are like the rushes in Dǒngzé.
Why be so focused only on these specific examples?
What is meant by "inheriting validation from the Chángyáng"?
If there is good, attribute it to the parents;
if there are mistakes, attribute them to oneself.
This is the conduct of a filial son,
and also the proper structure for an essay.
The matters narrated in the Shī and the Shū
are far distant.
After the Three Dynasties,
Shǐ Qiān and Bān Gù were both hereditary historians,
and the achievements of Tán and Biāo
are also briefly mentioned in the accounts by Qiān and Gù.
Later people, however, claimed that Gù stole his father's book,
while Qiān praised his father’s goodness.
Viewing it now,
how can this necessarily be true?
Tán's general discourse
only briefly mentions the tenets of the Six Schools.
As for the story of being detained south of Zhōunán,
where father and son held hands weeping,
and the history was passed on—
this is merely stated as empty words,
without actual basis.
As for Biāo's authorship of the 'Hòuzhuàn' (Continuation of the Biographies),
the origins and development are completely extant,
and in the discursive praises (lùn zàn) of the three annals (jì),
Biāo's explanations are clearly stated,
showing that the family learning had been transmitted;
How could it be as later people said,
thus provoking Zhèng Qiáo's accusation that Bān Shì committed plagiarism?
However, Shǐ Qiān's narration concerning Tán
was not intentionally brief;
nor was Bān Gù's account of Biāo
intended to be detailed.
A filial son deeply loves his parents,
and when recording his parents' deeds and work in a book,
he must portray the parents as they were in their daily lives,
and avoid associating with the circumstances he personally encountered.
When I observe recent literary collections,
I cannot but feel confused.
If their parents have nothing worthy of praise?
Omit it, and that is acceptable.
If their parents only possessed minor virtues?
Record them according to their measure.
One must not abbreviate them, causing omissions,
or exaggerate them, causing misrepresentation.
Those who are cunning in seeking fame but crude in understanding intent
lavishly display their own achievements,
filling pages without being able to stop themselves,
yet when the melody ends and the 'ya' tune is played (i.e., when concluding with propriety),
they say, "This is the teaching of my ancestors."
Even more so, when they elaborate on their own glorious opportunities,
recounting their words with relish,
and the essay concludes in confusion (i.e., the climax),
they say, "This is the reward for the virtue of my ancestors."
Now, self-narrating essays,
if they excessively extol achievements,
Liú Zhījǐ still criticized them for being boastful in stating their intentions,
and they are lightly ridiculed.
How much more so when praising one’s parents,
should it become a means for self-praise?
That Zhāng Tāng had descendants (who achieved prominence),
the historian recorded this to encourage those who recommend worthy people;
but if it came from Ānshì’s own mouth,
it would be perverse.
That Bóqǐ had hereditary virtue,
the historian recorded this to be fortunate for those who are clean and loyal;
but if it came from the writings of Bǐng or Cì,
it would be contradictory.
The ancients said of the 'Chángyáng' and 'Shànglín' (Rhapsodies)
that they lavishly described tours and sights,
but contained veiled admonishments at the end,
meaning they obliquely criticized one thing while encouraging a hundred.
As for the writings of these people,
do they perhaps boast of themselves a hundred times,
and praise their parents only once?
Praising the access granted by the usher,
what does this mean?
The National Historian (Guóshǐ) narrates the *Shī* (Book of Songs),
elucidating the Six Arts (Liùyì).
Indeed, the *Shī* contains no plain words;
the intent of the author,
if not explained by a preface (xù),
then that which was composed,
cannot be discerned as to what it means.
Regarding the present *Shī Xù*,
to say that its transmission has lost the original meaning
is acceptable;
to say that there is no need for a preface
is unacceptable.
As for the preface(s) of the *Shū* (Book of Documents),
perhaps the Outer Historian (Wàishǐ), who managed the books of the Three Sovereigns (Sān Huáng) and Five Emperors (Wǔ Dì),
must have had chapter titles?
The present *Shū Xù*,
I suspect, is also the product of words transmitted from master to disciple,
created by imitating the *Shī Xù*?
When the reader finishes the chapter,
the facts and rationale naturally become clear;
therefore, even if the *Shū* had no preface,
the meaning of the text would never be hindered.
Furthermore, the *Shū* inherently had prefaces,
for the texts of instructions and admonitions (xùngào), which record words throughout the chapter,
must record the events on the first slip (jiǎn),
in order to show the circumstances under which the instructions and admonitions were composed.
This means that texts of the *Shū* that record events do not require a preface,
but texts that record sayings inherently have prefaces.
Viewing it from this perspective,
whether a preface exists or not
is rooted in the clarity or obscurity of the writing,
and this, too, is evident.
I observe the literary collections (wénjí) of recent days,
and I cannot help but be confused.
In writings that establish meaning,
perhaps the topic has already been discussed by previous people,
or perhaps the right and wrong of it were inherently easy to see,
and the author was certainly not unaware of this,
yet insisted on composing a treatise on it—
in such cases, there might also be subtle intent hidden within,
or perhaps something is borrowed to serve as satire,
or perhaps something is felt and thus expressed;
Since the reason for writing is not clearly stated,
it is necessary to preface it by describing the era and circumstances when the treatise was composed,
along with the general gist of what the author saw and heard,
only then can later generations compare and verify the information,
and thus perceive the true meaning of why the treatise was written.
This is also the legacy of the prefaces of instructions and admonitions in the *Shū*.
But observing treatise writings,
those that discuss what need not be discussed
often account for seven out of ten;
how can it be that among these there are not one or two instances stemming from words written for a specific purpose?
However, like the *Fēng Shī* (Airs) without a preface,
how can we know their subtle intent?
Moreover, if discussions and arguments had prefaces,
then writings lacking substance, similar to those formulaic essays produced by classical scholars,
could also be somewhat eliminated,
yet people generally practice this without noticing the deficiency.
As for writings that narrate events,
the ancients presented them according to the events themselves.
But observing later literary collections,
when responding to requests to write biographies and memorial inscriptions (zhuàn zhì),
they often preface it by describing the person who made the request,
and furthermore, elaborate in detail the words used in the request.
If done occasionally,
it is certainly harmless;
but if it becomes a pervasive custom,
then it is a preface beyond the preface.
Nevertheless,
that is still acceptable.
Those who are clever in seeking fame but crude in understanding purpose,
when prefacing the words of a request,
deliberately elaborate and exaggerate them in order to flatter themselves.
In one instance, they quote the request saying:
“Your virtue and morality are profound and lofty,
your words are a model for the world;
if we cannot obtain your writing,
the deceased will not rest in peace.”
In another instance, they quote saying:
“Your literary skill and scholarship
make you a Grand Master of the present age;
if we can obtain a single word from you,
it will be trusted and verified by later generations.”
The author, in turn, declines repeatedly in various ways,
while the requester insists earnestly, beating his forehead.
All such descriptions
are included in the writing,
providing not the slightest benefit to the matter at hand,
but serving only to use others to show off oneself—
how utterly shameless is this?
Moreover, if the writing does not merit such praise,
this is slandering the dead;
if the requester never originally spoke such words,
this is slandering the living.
If one argues that the origin of the event
must be detailed,
then the person coming to make the request should first be announced by the gatekeeper for an audience,
the calling card should be delivered beforehand,
upon entering the seat, greetings should be exchanged,
and the package of gifts presented afterward.
These are also origins;
why not also detail and record them?
And can the words of praise exchanged when requesting the text
be considered different from these?
The response concerning the fortune-telling stall (Bǔ Sì),
what does it mean?
Writings (zhù zuò) decline and become literary collections (wén jí).
This involves heavenly fate (tiān yùn),
and it involves human affairs (rén shì).
If morality (dào dé) is not cultivated,
scholarship (xué wèn) has no means to establish itself independently.
The root is severed, and the branches and leaves wither.
This is the necessary decline caused by human affairs.
Worldly affairs differ, and literary quality changes.
Social interaction in the human world (chóu zuò),
rites, laws, and systems,
those things absent in antiquity but present today,
all appear in writings (wén zhāng).
Therefore, if one remains deep in the mountains and does not emerge, that is one thing.
But if one involves oneself in the human world,
then one must satisfy needs and requests.
The uses of writing increase, and literary styles differentiate.
When they differentiate, they inevitably appear in literary collections (wén jí).
For those whose morality (dào dé) is lofty and profound,
and whose scholarship (xué wèn) is refined and pure,
they treat their literary collections (wén jí) as their definitive writings (zhù zuò),
which is what is called "establishing discourse based on affairs" (yīn shì lì yán).
However, even they cannot avoid mixing in matters of social interaction (chóu zuò),
and practical uses fulfilling requests.
If they cannot become specialists in the Masters (Zǐ) or Histories (Shǐ),
their words will not be universally relevant.
Those who mistakenly take writings intended for social interaction and fulfilling requests as self-established works, and frequently label them collections (jí),
their number is perhaps uncountable.
This occurrence is due to destiny and circumstance (yùn huì),
and is not entirely related to human affairs (rén shì).
When I observe the literary collections (wén jí) of recent days,
I cannot but feel confused.
When historical studies (shǐ xué) decline,
biographies (zhuàn jì) frequently emerge mixed in [with other styles].
For example, starting from the Eastern Capital (Dōngjīng, i.e., Eastern Hàn),
the various biographies like the *Xiānxián* and *Qíjiù* (records of Worthies and Elders),
and the various records like *Shíyí* and *Sōushén*,
are all examples of this.
When historical studies (shǐ xué) are abandoned,
literary collections (wén jí) incorporate biographies.
For example, since the Táng and Sòng dynasties,
the epitaphs (zhì míng) by Hán [Yù] and Liǔ [Zōngyuán],
and the prefaces and accounts (xù shù) by Ōu [Yáng Xiū] and Zēng [Gǒng],
are all examples of this.
One who possesses historical talent (shǐ cái) but cannot personally undertake the duty of a historian
to fully realize their ability,
should also collect what is heard and seen,
verify its accuracy,
and write a book of their own,
attaching themselves to the specialists of biography (zhuàn jì).
When it is absolutely unavoidable,
and due to requests from others,
one composes various forms such as steles (bēi), inscriptions (míng), prefaces (xù), and accounts (shù),
one then inevitably must use language meant for social interaction and fulfilling requests,
which mixes the intent of the writing.
This is what Hán [Yù], Liǔ [Zōngyuán], Ōu [Yáng Xiū], and Zēng [Gǒng] referred to as having no choice (wú rú hé).
Those who are clever in seeking fame but ignorant of true intent,
judging that their literary talent is insufficient to move people,
and their scholarship is insufficient to establish themselves,
then contemplate finding something to rely upon to attach themselves to the enterprise of immortality.
They see the renowned figures and achievements of the current era
being universally praised and exaggerated,
and consequently believe they can borrow their reputation.
To borrow it [the reputation],
seems plausible.
But they do not know that the specialized composition of biographies (zhuàn jì)
is understood in a way that does not surpass the literary collections (wén jí) of Hán [Yù] and Ōu [Yáng Xiū].
They assume that if they are not epigraphs (bēi zhì), they are not permissible.
Epigraphs (bēi zhì) must necessarily arise from the requests of descendants,
but when the descendants of these people have never requested them,
they falsely compose epigraphs to include in their collections (jí),
making it seem as if the descendants had requested them,
claiming to be nearly equal to Hán [Yù] and Ōu [Yáng Xiū].
Now, Hán [Yù] and Ōu [Yáng Xiū] composed these works in response to requests from others,
doing so out of necessity (bù dé yǐ).
Therefore, Ōu Yáng [Xiū] considered himself bound by the history of the Five Dynasties (Wǔ Dài),
and Master Hán [Yù] desired to punish falsehood and flattery even after death,
to reveal the hidden light of obscured virtue,
and to establish a standard Classic for the Táng dynasty,
yet he still regretted relying on mere empty words.
Now, [these current writers] look up to those works produced by necessity
and gaze upon them with excessive admiration,
going so far as to imitate them like Yōu Mèng (a famous impersonator).
This is equivalent to the examination candidates drafting edicts,
though they did not originate from the imperial mandate (sī lún),
or the seven sages answering questions in the woods (Qī Lín),
when such words were not necessarily spoken.
How then will they verify [these records] against metal and stone [inscriptions],
and make them manifest for future generations?
By abandoning the direct transmission of biographies (zhuàn jì)
and imitating the indirect communication of epigraphs (bēi zhì),
is it because they seek to resemble Hán [Yù] and Ōu [Yáng Xiū]?
If so, this is the action of Pín Lǐ (the frowning neighbor).
Or is it because they seek the literary prestige that comes from responding to others’ requests?
If so, this is the fortune-telling stall (Bǔ Sì).
In the past, Xī Shī suffered from a heart ailment and frowned (pín).
An ugly woman in the neighborhood (lǐ),
believed it to be beautiful and imitated her;
the rich man [seeing this], closed his door and refused to come out,
while the poor man took his wife and children and departed.
A humble artisan selling fortunes (bǔ) in the city market,
when no one passed by to ask for a reading,
would say:
“A certain princely descendant (wáng sūn) favors me deeply,
a certain nobleman (guì qīng) believes my art to be divine.”
Common people detest
The difficulty of navigating the world through writing,
is due to the many common taboos.
When Tuìzhī [Hán Yù] encountered Lǐ Sù destroying the stele inscription (The Stele Commemorating the Pacification of Huáixī), the original text had not actually diminished Lǐ Sù's achievements.
When Ōuyáng [Ōuyáng Xiū] had to defend the epitaph of Shīlǔ [Shī Xù],
it has been rare since antiquity to find anyone capable of resolving such issues.
Formerly, I studied ancient prose with Master Zhū.
The Master wrote the Epitaph for the *Jǔrén* Lǚ.
Lǚ had long struggled and failed the examinations.
Every night he studied in great distress.
A neighboring woman remarked concerning his shortcoming:
"Student Lǚ's reading voice is loud,
but the rhythm and cadence are mournful and tragic.
Is it possible that he harbors some dissatisfaction within himself?"
Her husband told Lǚ.
Lǚ cried until his voice failed him, saying:
"That woman understands me.
If the person presiding over the writing [the examiner],
possessed that woman's insight,
how could I still have failed the examinations for so long?"
Because of this, every time he read, he bowed three times towards the neighboring wall.
This essay deeply expressed Mr. Lǚ's grief over his misfortune;
but people at the time considered it frivolous and inappropriate,
(because it lacked any suspicion of illicit relations between men and women,)
so they gathered and criticized it.
He also wrote an epitaph for a certain woman (Fūrén).
Her husband was teaching his nephew to study, but the nephew was disobedient,
and he beat him until he bled.
The Old Mistress (Tàifūrén) protected the nephew and became angry,
refusing to eat.
The woman knelt and begged her to take food.
The Old Mistress was angry
and slapped her cheek.
The woman’s amiable expression only intensified,
and she eventually won her mother-in-law's happiness.
That writing, concerning kindness, filial piety, friendship, and harmony,
originally contained no separation or breach [of these virtues];
but people at the time believed that a woman being slapped by her mother-in-law
was a humiliation that must be tabooed,
and that beating a nephew and slapping a woman
both violated kindness and love.
Therefore, they deleted and removed the passage.
I once drafted the Inscription for the Repair of the Chán'ān County Wall.
In it, I recounted that the wall had long been decayed and ruined,
and that at the time there were other projects that were more urgent,
which is why the high officials examined it and decided to postpone the work;
now, however, more time has passed,
the collapse and damage are even worse,
and it cannot be postponed further.
This was written based on the facts,
and it seemed as though it should be unobjectionable.
However, readers at the time
believed that since the inscription recounted the necessity of repairing the wall,
it should not further mention the official review that postponed the work, thereby exposing their shortcoming.
I initially suspected that person was overly cautious,
but afterward, when I questioned those in the current generation known as experts in writing,
they all expressed this same opinion,
agreeing spontaneously.
I also once composed a Biography of a Virtuous Widow for someone,
in which I recounted that she lived amidst hardship and poverty,
and her relatives offered no support or assistance,
so she was able to work hard to support herself
and raise her orphan son until he was established.
But her son then said:
"At that time, my relatives were not all destitute;
they simply did not pity my mother and me.
If we write this now,
I fear they will feel shame,
and it will create resentment and bad blood.
Please only describe my mother's hardships,
and do not mention the relatives' lack of support."

Such fastidiousness is abundant, and one cannot list them all. Occasionally, there are situations that are too close (sensitive), making it truly difficult to write according to the rules; these cases are not entirely due to mere fastidiousness. I also drafted the Inscription for Master Zhū's Birthday Screen, saying:
"Since retiring from the position of Education Intendant in the *Guǐsì* year and returning home,
the students who followed him
began to be extremely numerous."
But among his colleagues,
there were those who had followed him before the *Guǐsì* year,
who angrily changed color and said:
"If it must be that the flourishing period only occurred after this,
does that mean our group is not worth valuing?"
I also proofread and annotated the Chronological Biography of Liáng Wéndìng, saying:
"The Duke (Gōng) remembered that his elder brother's wife (Sǎofūrén) had become a widow young,
and throughout his life, he respected her with the rites due to a mother.
Whenever she was displeased,
he would try in every way possible to gain her happiness."
But someone then said:
"An elder brother's wife should naturally be respected.
Now, saying that he respected her because he remembered she became a widow young,
implies he was preventing her from failing to maintain her virtue (jié),
which is not genuine respect."
Other trifling matters,
which were criticized by others,
cannot be fully discussed here;
I will merely summarize the main points.
One can thus see that navigating the world through writing
is indeed difficult to speak of.
Now, regarding the utility of writing:
if internally it is not based on learning and scholarship,
and externally it does not concern world teachings (ethical instruction),
it has already lost the essence of being an essay;
and if one harbors a petty mind,
maligns individuals,
or even worse, attacks and exposes private matters,
and slanders the innocent;
such a person is a criminal against the ethical teachings (Míngjiào),
and even if they fortunately escape legal punishment,
heavenly retribution will surely reach them.
As for the location of right and wrong,
writing employs suppression and praise (yìyáng);
in the remainder of comparisons,
there are conventional host and guest roles (bīnzhǔ);
if someone is generous, one must say they are not stingy;
if someone is pure, one must say they are flawless;
this is almost like composing poetry: one must harmonize the level and oblique tones (píngzè)
to achieve musicality;
and in arranging words, one must use auxiliary particles
to convey the meaning clearly.
Now, when writing about someone who is pure and generous,
the only fear is that they might be suspected of having flaws or being mean;
this is like literary sentences that must exclude the particles *yān*, *zāi*, *hū*, and *yě*
and poetic lines that must use entirely oblique or entirely level tones.
Even if Zhōu Gōng and Kǒngzǐ were resurrected,
they could not utter a single word that would be called completely perfect.
Alas!
The work of ordering the world
cannot be used as a means of navigating the world through writing.
Unforeseen praise
and fault-finding condemnation
have been thus since antiquity.
Reading ancient folk songs (Yuèfǔ),
which describe the difficulty of the Shǔ road
and the winding nature of the Tàiháng Mountains,
people suppose that the paths they point to are narrow
and symbolize the dead end of a road;
they do not know that the path of writing
is also rugged like this.
Therefore, truly insightful scholars remain silent and somber.
They reserve their works for inscribing upon famous mountains,
intending to wait for those who understand to reveal them.
Why would they compare their joys and hardships with the flattering crowd?
Censure of Names:
Name (míng)
is the guest of Reality (shí).
When Reality is achieved, the Name follows;
this is the natural principle,
but it is not necessarily bound to happen.
The superior person (Jūnzǐ) follows the natural principle
and does not seek things that are necessarily bound to happen.
The learning of the superior person
lies only in knowing what is necessary to be done;
if they do not know what is meant by Name,
how can they perceive it as Reality?
Those who crave Name
pursue Name and forget Reality,
and then only those who do not forget are seen as possessing Reality.
Those who are perceptive lament this,
and thus wish people to prioritize Reality and put Name second.
Although this is the case,
they still have not forgotten the distinction between Name and Reality.
The superior person does not have this.
The superior person's actions (Chūchù, engaging or retiring)
must stem from righteous principle (Míngyì).
The means by which the former kings enlightened the world and guided the people
were inseparable from the ethical teachings (Míngjiào).
Since antiquity,
there has never been anyone who could achieve governance by abandoning the Name.
Why is it that craving Name leads to forgetting Reality? The answer is:
Righteousness (Yì) inherently has no Name,
but because we want those who do not know righteousness to follow righteousness,
we call it Righteous Principle (Míngyì).
Teaching (Jiào) inherently has no Name,
but because we want those who do not know the teaching to follow the teaching,
we call it Ethical Teaching (Míngjiào).
To reveal something as a Name
is what is meant by seeking Reality.
For example, people do not know how to eat,
so the name of "cultivating plants" is revealed to encourage farming;
people do not know how to clothe themselves,
so the name of "rearing silkworms and reeling silk" is revealed to encourage sericulture;
those who are warmly dressed and fully fed
do not seek the name of "farming and sericulture."
Now, if we ignore farming and sericulture,
and merely boast and show off about being well-fed and warm,
there will surely be those who stop plowing and weaving and endure hunger and cold,
borrowing husks and chaff to simulate fullness,
and secretly wrapping themselves in rags to feign warmth.
This is the vice of craving Name.
Therefore, the Name used in Míngjiào (Ethical Teaching) and Míngyì (Righteous Principle)
is Farming and Sericulture (the essential action).
The Name sought by those who crave Name
is fullness and warmth (the superficial result).
If one insists on pursuing the Name of fullness and warmth,
there has never been anyone who did not have to forcibly endure hunger and cold.
those who covet fame lose fame,
is a principle of nature,
not a matter of necessity.
In the past, when Jiè Zhītuī
did not speak of emolument, emolument still did not reach him.
When reality arrives and fame returns,
fame may not necessarily return rapidly.
The fame of the world
is determined by those who truly know,
and is bolstered by those who seem to know but in fact do not know deeply.
Now, those who truly know
must first know themselves.
Few people in the world
know themselves, thus those who can truly know others are not numerous.
Those who seem to know but in fact do not know deeply are numerous.
Because they seem to know,
they can interact and establish reputation.
Because they have not truly
known deeply, those who covet fame are able to sell their deception.
Moreover, when cunning intellect is employed and skillful methods are managed,
exhausting all the thought and effort of one's lifetime,
how can we say that nothing proper has been gained therein?
Therefore, those who covet fame often
gain temporary fame, just as those who covet profit do not necessarily lack temporary profit.
Furthermore, those who covet fame
certainly act for the sake of some benefit.
It is like a merchant benefiting from the market;
the merchant must bring forth their stock
and only then can gain profit;
those who covet fame,
must also dilute their reality (substance)
and only then can pursue temporary fame.
Since the hearts of people differ like their faces,
thus those who pursue substance,
cannot make everyone praise them as good.
A person who covets fame,
however, focuses on guessing what is common in human sentiment,
which does not necessarily proceed from what their heart truly considers genuine.
Moreover, those who covet fame
must follow the fashion of the moment.
Fashions cycle,
like the mutual change of spring orchids and autumn chrysanthemums,
not adopting each other.
When a person lives among them,
their superior talent and nature
do not necessarily happen to align with them.
Those who covet fame,
must certainly bend and conform to pursue them,
therefore their mental methods are often questionable.
If the lips are gone, the teeth are cold;
Lǔ wine was thin, and Hándān was besieged—
this speaks of circumstances that are bound to arrive,
and principles that are inherently so.
The Way of learning
involves no jealousy or envy toward others,
but concerning that which fame relates to,
envy and jealousy are bound to arise.
The Way of learning
involves no affectation toward the world;
but where fame resides,
affectation is inevitable.
Therefore, those who covet fame
are the thieves of virtue.
As for those who truly know,
their self-knowledge is certain;
they do not seek to be known by the human world.
As for those who seem to know but in fact do not know deeply,
they disdain to share the same path.
Perhaps looking back a hundred generations,
they find one person
and lament that he was distant and peerless,
yet they never fail to wait for me to be their support as a later successor.
Or perhaps far away beyond a thousand *lǐ*,
they find one person
and regret that he was distant and their traces were unjoined,
yet they never fail to share the intimacy of close neighbors with me.
Based on this, if we ask about recognition in the current generation,
it is sparse,
but the noble person does not consider it a worry.
When superficiality subsides
and fashions flatten,
how could there be no one
who truly knows in the vastness of the world?
When this point is reached, the skill
of coveting fame also reaches its limits.
Therefore it is said:
When reality arrives, fame returns;
those who covet fame lose fame—
these are all principles of nature,
not matters of necessity.
Ultimately, however, the matter also does not depart from the principle.
Critique of Anomalies
(shì),
and never sought to be different from others. For those whose learning reached its height,
others gazed upon them but could not attain it;
only then was their difference perceived,
not because they deliberately possessed something different. Fūzǐ said:
"In matters of frugality (jiǎn),
I follow the majority.
In matters of grandeur (tài),
though I violate the majority,
I follow those below (humble practices)."
The Sages were actually seeking commonality with others.
Sometimes being different from the multitude
was the Sage's necessity (a situation he could not avoid).
In the world, there is a public standard of correctness (gōng shì);
it forms when the multitude follows a course unknowingly but inevitably,
and the Sages cannot differ from it.
The virtuous and wise scholars
deeply investigate the reasons,
and believe that it is so.
The ordinary and foolish
have never had knowledge,
yet they also rest content in accepting that it is so.
However, those who pride themselves on their talent
are ashamed to share the same conclusion with the ordinary and foolish,
and therefore deliberately twist their theories to argue that it is not so. Take, for example, those skilled in cooking:
their delicious food earns the shared preference of others;
even those who do not understand flavor
have never failed to call it sweet.
Now, if one is ashamed to share preferences with those who do not understand flavor,
they must sip fermented dregs and discard sweet wine,
abandon fine roasted meat and seek weeds and wild vegetables,
and only then can they be different from the common crowd.
The saying goes:
"If later generations were not impartial,
there would be no Sages or Worthies surviving today."
The one trusted by ten thousand generations
is only Fūzǐ.
That Fūzǐ is trustworthy,
by whom was this determined?
It is the public standard of correctness (gōng shì) that does not tolerate violation.
Fūzǐ discussed and cataloged the divine, sage, and worthy people of antiquity,
and there were many.
Bóyí sought benevolence and attained benevolence;
Tàibó yielded the throne;
had Fūzǐ not clarified the obscure and revealed the subtle,
people would have had no means of knowing them.
Even without the accolades of Fūzǐ,
how could people not know Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, Wǔ, and Zhōu Gōng?
Given the sageliness of Fūzǐ,
when he praised Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, Wǔ, and Zhōu Gōng,
we do not hear of his selections or rejections differing from the masses.
If so, then truly there is no scope in the world for seeking difference.
The sense of right and wrong (shì fēi zhī xīn),
everyone possesses it.
Regarding sound, sight, smell, and taste (shēng sè chòu wèi),
the ears, eyes, mouths, and noses of the world
are all similar.
That which the heart universally approves
is principle (lǐ)
and righteousness (yì).
However, the world diverges into different paths,
all because of arguments over principle and righteousness,
and consequently, the sense of right and wrong
is also shifted.
How can the heart's universal approval
be inferior to that of the ears, eyes, mouths, and noses?
Sound, sight, smell, and taste have material evidence (yǒu jù), while principle and righteousness are formless (wú xíng).
Where there is material evidence, even the ordinary and foolish know how to follow and comply;
where there is no form, even the virtuous and wise cannot avoid self-application (relying solely on one's own judgment).
Therefore, seeking to be different from others
has never failed to stem from self-application.
To remedy the flaw of self-application,
nothing is better than using verifiable (yǒu jù) learning
to substantiate the formless principle and righteousness (lǐ yì),
and only then will one’s course not enter divergent paths.
When the interior is weighty, the exterior is regarded lightly;
when reality is achieved, reputation is forgotten.
Generally, those who seek to be different from others
do so because of internal insufficiency.
They know their own insufficiency,
but cannot overcome their desire for fame;
hence they seek difference in order to surpass others,
yet ultimately others are not surpassed by them.
If the interior is insufficient,
one must display pride externally;
if reality is not attained,
one must eagerly chase fame;
this is also generally true of human nature.
Since this is generally true of human nature,
and those who seek difference certainly cannot avoid manifesting this tendency,
then how have those who seek difference ever differed from others?
They merely differ from the open and generous gentlemen (jūnzǐ).
Take horses:
their coats and manes are similar,
they graze on grass and drink water,
they are fed fodder and grain,
and they are saddled and bridled;
nothing about these things is different.
Yet some travel a hundred lǐ in a day,
and some travel a thousand lǐ in a day;
achieving unique difference from within commonality—
that is how Sages, Worthies, and Heroes (shèng xián háojié)
differ from ordinary people.
If one does not follow what the majority holds in common,
but first seeks difference,
they will certainly be like the horse that fakes holding the bit and steals the reins,
kicking, bucking, biting, and chewing—
unusable for riding or driving.
Writings that criticize common practice
claim that compositions for birthday screens and funeral hangings
are almost equivalent to market stalls,
and should not enter the halls of scholars (xuéshì). In reality, they are done for the needs of the time.
When dealing with the world, one cannot abolish social customary practices (yìngchóu gùshì).
When offering standardized phrases for congratulations
or habitual expressions for condolences and elegies,
there is no way to express one's true nature or spirit (xìng líng).
If one still meticulously focuses on these,
calculating merit and debating clumsiness,
how is that different from dreaming about interpreting dreams?
Literature (wén) is used to convey one’s intention.
If the intention has no means of expression
and simply follows the generalized commonality,
then the ancients would not have specially created texts,
such as the felicitations for a man’s capping ceremony
or the charges for a woman’s wedding ceremony;
they would simply have cited pre-written official documents.
Due to the habit of emphasizing literary flourish (wén shèng),
people invariably wish to create texts.
When texts are created, how can they be without some merit?
They then mutually display pride in their intentions and creations,
mutually admire and imitate each other,
and the small spring quickly flows into rivers,
which can no longer be dammed or blocked.
Literature originates from substance (zhì).
Those who first created it
had not yet grasped transformation (biàn),
thus their methods were easily exhausted.
This is why those who merely follow and copy
make no good progress. Since we have inherited uncontrollable rivers,
we ought to plan measures for channeling and embankment,
utilizing them for irrigation
and for navigation,
only then realizing their divine, pervasive, and lasting utility.
In the way of literature (wén zhāng zhī dào),
everything that antiquity lacked but modernity possesses
should be treated in this manner.
Birthday congratulations (chēng shòu) were not seen in antiquity,
but in narrating a person’s life story,
one must uniformly employ the methods of historical documentation.
If this is done to ensure the person's immortality,
then the text must be like the histories and biographies written on bamboo and silk.
Elegies and sacrificial texts originally stem from literary rhetoric (cí zhāng),
but in tracing a person's life achievements,
one must uniformly employ the intent of eulogies and posthumous titles (lěi shì).
If this is done to honor the person's beginning and end,
then the text must be like inscriptions carved on metal and stone.
Literature is born from substance (zhì);
depending on the nature of the substance, we apply our writing to it.
This is not without benefit to worldly instruction (shì jiào).
Furthermore, why should we doubt the comparison to market stalls,
or why should scholars (xuéshì) disdain to mention it?
Now, for the living there are birthday felicitations (shòu yán),
and for the dead there are sacrificial laments (jì wǎn).
These are the rituals of modern people who have lost touch with true ritual (lǐ).
Ritual should follow appropriateness (yí);
practices should follow custom (sú).
If they do not contradict the way of the ancients,
the *jūnzǐ* (gentleman) should not abandon them.
Those who specialize in literature
look down upon birthday felicitations and laments,
failing to realize the spiritual clarity of their methods.
This deficiency has certainly reached this point.
Even worse,
they keep sacrificial laments (jì wǎn) but are ashamed to record birthday felicitations (shòu yán).
When recent literati
compile their own collections,
those who cannot bear to discard such writings and occasionally keep them
must also segregate them into separate volumes,

just as the *Yǎ* (Elegant) and *Zhèng* (Vulgar) songs cannot be spoken of together in the same breath. (*Wāng Dùn Wēng*, who styled himself a master of classical prose, constantly chastised others. In reality, he had talent but no insight, and enjoyed making unnecessary taboos, yet prided himself on having insight. Most people are like this.)
This can be called knowing the number ten (yī shí) but being ignorant of two times five (èr wǔ).
They merely see that the collected works of earlier writers contain eulogies (āi lěi) but no birthday felicitations (shòu yán),
and thus conclude that eulogies are consistent with antiquity,
whereas writings for blessings and congratulations (zhù guǎ zhī cí)
were absent in antiquity.
They do not know that tomb inscriptions (mù zhì) began in the Six Dynasties (Liù Cháo),
and stele texts (bēi wén) flourished in the Eastern Hàn (Dōng Hàn);
neither was commonly practiced in the deepest antiquity.
The stele inscriptions of *Zhōng Láng* (Cài Yōng),
and the epitaphs and inscriptions of *Chāng Lí* (Hán Yù),
have been highly praised by scholars.
Now, looking at the collected works of the two masters, *Cài* and *Hán*,
among them are praises for those lacking virtue,
retaining only rhetorical skill.
Are the persons with whom they associated and interacted
essentially different from the birthday felicitations of recent times?
To be lenient when accepting the ancient
but strict when judging the modern,
the *jūnzǐ* considers this having ears but no eyes.
If one insists that the category of inscriptions and epitaphs
truly originated in antiquity,
then the writings of blessings and congratulations (zhù guǎ zhī wén)
surely began in the *Zhōu Guān* (Rites of Zhōu),
where the texts of the Six Blessings (liù zhù zhī cí)
served to pray for fortune and auspiciousness.
To differentiate their categories
simply because they were written by literary scholars at a later time,
how can this be considered understanding the changes of the age?
Literature is born from substance (zhì).
Birthday blessings (shòu zhù) and eulogies (āi lěi),
when applying rhetoric (wén) based on the substance (zhì) of the person,
then change occurs without fixed rules.
The writings composed by later generations
can thus surpass those of earlier generations.
That which is dependent on the person:
the person changes ten thousand ways, and the writing also changes ten thousand ways.
That which is dependent on the event:
the event does not change, and the writing also does not change.
The address for the capping ceremony (jiào nǚ zhī cí) of a daughter,
and the eulogy for the crowning ceremony (guān nán zhī sòng) of a son—
these all use fixed texts and ancient precedents.
The ancients did not compose separate writings for these,
and those recorded in traditions and histories
are indeed numerous.
The formalized procedures of bows and courtesies (yī ràng zhī yí wén),
and the rhythms of drums and music (gǔ chuī zhī jié zòu),
are things ritual (lǐ) and music (yuè) do not abandon.
However, if the substance (zhì) is not present,
even if divine sages compose them,
there is no point in taking the formalized procedures and rhythms
as something uniquely outstanding or marvelous.
Later generations who follow the stream but fail to distinguish the source
write generic texts for everything.
This is what is meant by verbal extravagance.
The steles inscribing the names of the *jìnshì* (Imperial Scholars)
must have records (jì);
(This was a fault of the Míng people, but is absent now.) The registers presented during imperial examinations and rituals (kē jǔ bài xiàn zhī lù)
must have prefaces (xù).
(This still exists today. It seems advisable to request adopting a fixed format, like the example of the congratulatory memorials (hè biǎo).)
Since the Táng and Sòng Dynasties,
passing the autumnal examinations and gathering for the spring examinations,
and the *jìnshì* succeeding in the examination,
is equivalent to transferring grain supplies or submitting budgetary reports,
it is not an event requiring unique composition or exceptional talent.
For inscribing names and presenting registers,
established procedures are followed.
Even if one employed *Lǐ Sī* (referring to the inscribed steles)
or *Liú Xiàng* (referring to the submitted registers),
how could they, beyond the ordinary flow of ink,
compose a unique text?
and the unskilled feel ashamed,
valuing the writing but not the event.
This is what is called delusion.
When a house is completed and the ridgepole is raised (chéng shì shàng liáng),
there must be a text for it.
When marriage proposals and gifts are exchanged (hūn yīn tōng pìn),
there must be a formal communication (qǐ).
These are the same basic structures (táng gòu),
and the same fundamental relationship between male and female.
Even if *Lǔ Bān* issued the commands,
or *Gāo Méi* presided over the guests,
how could they, beyond the ordinary flow of ink,
compose a unique text?
Yet the talented boast about it,
and the unskilled feel ashamed,
valuing the writing but not the event.
This is what is called delusion.
But contemporary literati
still criticize that and praise this.
Why is this so?
In the great standard regulations of the state,
for the sacrificial prayers (zhù bǎn) at the suburban altars and ancestral temples (jiāo miào),
which are performed annually as regular events,
there is a fixed format,
and no modification is allowed.
For extending imperial favor based on precedent,
the imperial mandates (gào chì) given to officials,
when the rank is the same,
there is a fixed format,
and no modification is allowed.
For the grand celebration of the emperor’s longevity (wàn shòu qìng diǎn),
and on auspicious dates and excellent festivals,
the congratulatory memorials (hè biǎo) from officials
all have a fixed format,
and no modification is allowed.
When the sages composed works
and created the Classics of Ritual (lǐ jīng),
whether simple or ornate,
they always ensured it was appropriate.
Writing depends on the event:
if the event changes ten thousand ways, the writing also changes ten thousand ways;
if the event does not change, the writing also does not change.
Even if *Zhōu* (Zhōu Gōng) and *Kǒng* (Kǒng Zǐ) composed the works,
how could it be different?
The formalized procedures of bows and courtesies,
and the rhythms of drums and music—
what ordinary men cannot diminish,
divine sages cannot increase.
Yet literati, following habitual practices,
insist on boasting about volume and competing in extravagance.
It is no wonder that collections of literature are so numerous and disordered.
The *Lǐ* (Classic of Rites) says:
“Before burial, the *jūnzǐ* reads the rites of mourning (sāng lǐ);
after burial, he reads the rites of sacrifice (jì lǐ);
when mourning ceases and life returns to normal, he reads the musical scores (yuè zhāng).”
The mourning rites (sāng lǐ) distinguish between closeness and distance
and are differentiated by rhetoric (wén) and substance (zhì).
This is fundamentally based on utmost sincerity.
But contemporary literati
have sacrificial texts (jì wén) composed when mourning parents and donning mourning clothes,
sacrificial texts for the hall sacrifice (táng jì) when burying parents,
and biographical sketches (xíng shù) distributed to guests offering condolences.
A commentary says:
“When a filial son mourns his parents,
his weeping is not drawn out (bù yī);
in ritual there is no composed bearing (wú róng);
his speech is not ornate (bù wén).
Alone amidst the straw mats and dirt clods (shān kuài),
he relies on a staff to rise.
He weeps morning and evening without fixed times.”
How can there still be people
who can take up the brush and compose flowery texts,
to be recorded on bamboo and silk?
How is this different from the man of *Cāng Wú* (Cāng Wú Rén) who gave away his wife,
or Grand Master *Huà* (Huà Dà Fū) who praised his own ancestor?
Someone might say:
The writing is not necessarily done by the person himself;
it is composed by the assistant mourner (xiāng sāng zhě) on his behalf.
But literature is born from substance (zhì).
When texts are composed on one's behalf,
the person must still be capable of expressing those sentiments.
When the owl (chī xiāo) finds itself displaced and precarious,
it does not produce the pleasing chirping of the *xiàn huǎn*.
When the crucian carp (fù yú) is trapped in a dry rut,
it cannot help but flash an indignant color.
Even when speaking on behalf of birds and fish,
one must still express their true sentiments.
How can one say that because the text is written on their behalf,
one can forget the position in which the filial son places himself?
Some say that when writing on behalf of others,
those who have living parents
should not write eulogies for others' deceased parents (kǎobǐ).
The instructions written by Yán Shì,
likely meant that a filial son avoids suspicion (xián),
listening to the soundless and seeing the formless—
being extremely earnest.
Nevertheless,
this does not clarify the principles of speaking on behalf of others (dàiyán).
The greatest of suspicions
is none greater than that between ruler and minister;
when Zhōu Gōng issued edicts to officials and commoners on behalf of Chéng Wáng,
he did not consider facing south (nánmiàn, ruling) a source of suspicion.
The most intense suspicion
is none greater than that between men and women;
when Gǔ Yǒng reported to Yuán Dì on behalf of Empress Xǔ,
he did not consider kinship within the inner court (nèiqīn) a taboo.
Considering the famous ministers of antiquity,
when drafting documents for enfeoffment, prayers, and imperial pronouncements (zhìgào),
they posthumously conferred titles (zhuīshì) on previous dynasties,
enfeoffed empresses, established heirs,
and even issued instructions and edicts to subordinates—
which one of these acts was not speaking and writing on the emperor's behalf (dàidì zhì)?
How could there be suspicion (xián)?
If one insists on avoiding suspicion in worldly affairs,
differentiating it from official duties (guānshǒu),
must the orphan in the *Yuèfǔ* poem
necessarily be a mourning relative wearing a white cap?
Why were the laments of the ancient widow
not written by a man with beard and eyebrows?
If a scholar writing a son's eulogy for his parent
must necessarily be an orphaned son before it is permissible,
then in writing a husband's eulogy for his wife,
must it necessarily be done by a eunuch before it is permissible?
As for ritual that is not truly ritual (fēilǐ zhī lǐ),
and righteousness that is not truly righteousness (fēiyì zhī yì),
the superior person (jūnzǐ) does not engage in them;
this is probably the reason.

Defending Zhèng (Shēn Zhèng)
Since Zǐcháng (Sīmǎ Qiān) and Mèngjiān (Bān Gù) ceased writing,
specialized historical scholarship (shǐxué) has declined.
Those who followed Chén (Shòu) and Fàn (Yè)
sometimes succeeded and sometimes failed,
but were generally sufficient to be called master historians (míngjiā).
When the Táng people established bureaus and supervisors,
compiling the narratives of Jìn and Suí,
they also named their works a single history;
scholars mistakenly inherited these classifications,
no longer distinguishing and correcting their forms (tǐ),
thus the aims of the ancients in writing books
became obscure and unclear.
As for literary stylists who expanded on the writing style,
and memory specialists who refined the investigations and verification (kǎohé),
regarding historical scholarship,
it seemed they made minor contributions;
but following the stream and forgetting the source,
ignorant of the grand principles (dàtǐ),
the more diligent their efforts,
the further the understanding they reached
drifted from antiquity and the more irrelevant it became.
Zhèng Qiáo, born a thousand years later,
profoundly perceived the source of ancient composition and writing,
knowing that the author's intent
was not merely to treat literary style as writing
or textual research (kǎojù) as scholarship.
Therefore, he sought to correct Shǐ Qiān (Sīmǎ Qiān),
augmenting him with broad erudition (bóyǎ),
and to criticize Bān Gù,
mocking his repetition and imitation,
while uniquely drawing upon three thousand years of
surviving writings and old records,
applying his own unique discernment and methodology (biéshí xīncái).
This was inheriting the tradition of the comprehensive history (tōngshǐ),
creating his own framework,
and establishing a unique school of thought.
Scholars, seeing little and finding much strange,
did not investigate his establishment of general rules (fāfán qǐlì),
his extraordinary insights and expansive discussions,
which allowed him to weigh various statements
and create the essential compilation of historical studies.
Instead, they merely picked out flaws in his sparse citations,
and imperfections in his preliminary organization,
attacking him widely,
as if they could not coexist under the same heaven.
If the ancients were resurrected,
how would these attacks amount to more than a brief sigh of contempt?
Regarding the Twenty Categories (*Èrshí Lüè*),
the three categories of the *Liùshū* (Six Scripts), the *Qīyīn* (Seven Sounds), and *Kūnchóng Cǎomù* (Insects, Grasses, and Trees),
which are known as "using history to assist the Classics" (yǐ shǐ yì jīng),
they were fundamentally not books covering disconnected periods
that could be continuously succeeded and exhausted by others.
They are truly unique, specialized achievements,
which the various scholars of the Hàn and Táng dynasties
could not have conceived of.
He established categories and formulated rules,
creating a monumental structure and grand compilation,
thereby clarifying his school of thought through thematic classification.
In this undertaking, he could not avoid relying on books completed at the time
and making a rough summary.
Originally, he did not intend to compare strengths and weaknesses
with specialists in minor studies (xiǎoxué)
who dedicated themselves exclusively to a single book;
nor did he wish for later generations
to adhere to his established theories
without making any adaptations.
Now, what Zhèng Shì emphasized lay in the grand framework (hónggāng),
but later scholars found fault
in minor details.
How is this different from mocking the famous generals Hán (Xìn) and Péng (Yuè)
for not being skilled in the formal stepping and bowing of Zōu and Lǔ;
or faulting the great scholars Fú (Shēng) and Kǒng (Ānguó)
for not being adept at frivolous calligraphy (diāochóng zhuànkè)?
Shǐ Qiān's exceptional scholarship
stands alone after the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals),
being only one person.
The reason he encompassed all ages and confined all schools of thought
lies solely in his creation of rules and establishment of general principles (chuànglì fāfán),
his outstanding vision and unique insights,
which allowed him to trace the source of ancient authors,
naturally possessing the scholarship of the *Chūnqiū* school.
As for the lack of evidence in his facts,
the inappropriateness of his selection and rejection,
and the immaturity of his arguments—
had he lived after the Táng or Sòng dynasties,
before the ancients had settled their views;
or had the collections he relied on at the time—the treasures of the Stone Chamber and Golden Casket (shíshì jīnguì),
and works like the *Shìběn*, *Diéjì*, and *Chǔ Hàn Chūnqiū*—
not been entirely lost;
later generations who indulge in literary style and cling to textual research
would have gathered to nitpick (zīzhū ér jiào) and compare,
scrutinizing inch by inch,
and who knows what kind of renewed attacks they would have launched.
How are those who criticize Zhèng Qiáo today
different from this hypothetical situation?
When Kǒngzǐ wrote the *Chūnqiū*,
he essentially said that the events were those of Qí Huán and Jìn Wén,
the writing style was historical,
but the significance (yì) was what Kǒngzǐ himself found valuable.
Events are what later textual researchers value,
and style is what later literary stylists emphasize.
However, what the Master valued
was not those, but the significance (yì).
Therefore, in the method of historical writing,
how can one fail to seek the underlying significance and intention?
Since Qiān (Sīmǎ Qiān) and Gù (Bān Gù),
historians have lacked unique discernment and methodology (biéshí xīncái);
what they sought was merely the event and the style.
Only Zhèng Qiáo showed a slight intention to seek significance (yì),
and yet the followers of minor, trivial scholarship
noisily rose up to dispute it.
If their argument were fully adopted,
then all the compositions for the imperial examinations,
and the ledgers of petty officials,
because they are clear, flawless,
accurate, and documented,
would ironically be judged far superior to Qiān and Gù.
Nevertheless,
Zhèng Jūn (Zhèng Qiáo) could not be entirely faultless either.
Mǎ (Sīmǎ) and Bān (Bān Gù), father and son, passed down their profession,
serving as official historians their whole lives;
this is naturally beyond comparison.
Sīmǎ Wēngōng's (*Sīmǎ Guāng*) *Zīzhì Tōngjiàn*
took nineteen years from beginning to end,
with a dedicated editorial office accompanying him,
and assistants he personally appointed.
Those with whom he discussed the work
were also famous figures of the time;
hence, he was able to shape a unique achievement
and become a master model for the world.
Zhèng Jūn, relying on his meager self,
residing in a humble and remote place,
dared alone to do what Mǎ (Sīmǎ) and Bān (Gù) had not dared to do since their time.
His establishment of high and far-reaching arguments
did not match the reality of his output,
and he was also unfortunate enough to be mentioned concurrently with Mǎ Duānlín's *Wénxiàn Tōngkǎo*
during the same era.
However, the flaws and deficiencies of the *Tōngkǎo*
were conversely not as severe as this.
Later, superficial scholars,
inherently lacking fixed judgment,
proceeded to praise and criticize both,
presumptuously comparing them,
thus linking his work with mere categorization and compilation efforts
and speaking of them in the same breath.
When weighing their shortcomings and discussing their strengths,
it was as if a skyscraper was being compared unfavorably to an inch of wood—
is this not a distortion?
Reply to a Guest (Part One)
In the *Guǐsì* year (1773), while in Hángzhōu,
I heard that Dài Zhēngjūn Zhèn, during a discussion with the recluse Wú Chǔshì Yǐngfāng,
fiercely criticized Zhèng Jūn’s *Tōngzhì*,
their words were utterly bizarre and laughable,
and I thought they were not worth debating seriously,
so I set it aside without discussion.
Subsequently, scholars
rather often attacked and slandered it.
Therefore, I borrowed the narrative of a certain gentleman
to clarify the origins and trajectory of historical writing.
I myself believed that regarding conventional and shallow opinions,
this effort had largely succeeded in breaking down and clearing away fallacies.
However, that essay traced history upward to Mǎ Qiān and Bān Gù,
and downward distinguished the *Tōngkǎo*,
all of which were key principles of historical study,
and were not entirely written solely to address the *Tōngzhì*.
Yet, those who did not understand this raised new issues to challenge me,
so I composed the three chapters of *Dákèwèn*.
A guest who had seen Zhāng Zi’s *Xù Tōngzhì Xùshū Hòu*
asked Zhāng Zi, saying:
"That the *Tōngzhì* should not be lightly criticized
I have already heard and received your instruction.
However, in your distinguishing arguments, Sir,
the writing is extensive and cannot be condensed,
and the scope of your reasoning,
assessing and judging the ancients,
often does not align with the category of scholars esteemed by the world.
Is this merely intentional depreciation or praise,
intended to assist your argument?
Or does the Master have a separate theory?
Now, scholars all refer to the Twenty-Two Histories,
and cataloguers
all take the histories from Mǎ Qiān and Bān Gù onward,
up to the Yuán and Míng dynasties,
and classify them as the single category of standard histories (*zhèngshǐ*).
Now, you alone contend that the Táng dynasty writers compiled and organized the narratives of Jìn and Suí,
and these books are also named as ‘A History,’
but scholars mistakenly followed this tradition and categorization,
and no longer properly distinguished their form.
How can it be that the histories starting from Jìn and Suí,
should not be named as ‘A History’?
Observing their established format of tables and treatises,
and the fixed structure of annals and biographies,
they are never different from the histories written by Mǎ Qiān and Bān Gù.
(Continuation of 44)
Establishing offices and setting up supervising officials,
gathering many people to compile the books,
was merely dictated by circumstances and timing.
If we seek the substance,
they are all the same category.
Now you say scholars mistakenly followed the tradition and categorization.
I venture to ask, for the histories starting from Jìn and Suí onward,
what is the reason they should be distinctly separated
from the histories of Chén Shòu and Fàn Yè and earlier?"
Zhāng Zi replied:
"The great origin of history
lies fundamentally in the *Chūnqiū*.
The significance of the *Chūnqiū*,
is clearly manifested in its editing and selection (*bǐxuē*).
The significance of *bǐxuē*
is not merely that events possess beginning and end,
and the writing has attained fixed form and rule.
If we view it through the Master's principle of 'stealing the meaning where righteousness resides,'
(Continuation of 63)
it is certainly intended to govern the world,
and illuminate the Great Way.
The means by which one grasps the transformations of antiquity and the present,
and thereby completes one's own distinctive intellectual tradition (*yījiā zhī yán*),
necessarily involves detailing what others abbreviate,
differing from what others share,
emphasizing what others neglect,
and overlooking what others hold important—
which cannot be constrained by fixed standards,
or rigidly adhered to by category precedents.
Only then, in moments of slight and subtle transition,
can one establish a unique judgment from one's own mind.
And when the book is completed,
it can naturally participate with Heaven and Earth and be verified by gods and spirits,
correspond with past sages and await future ones.
This is why a distinctive scholarly tradition (*jiāxué*) is valuable.
Since Chén Shòu and Fàn Yè,
if measured by the principle of the *Chūnqiū*,
I dare not say they made no errors.
Nevertheless, their mental selection and unique insights,
demonstrate that their scholarly tradition is fully present.
Even if one were to argue against them,
perhaps alleging that Mǎ Qiān's book demoted recluses and promoted wicked heroes,
or that Bān Gù's book excluded loyal heroes and excused the failings of the rulers,
ultimately, their combinations, separations, and changes,
ensured the meaning never deviated from the main path,
being sufficient to establish a recognized scholarly tradition and accord with the principles of the classics.
They were fundamentally unlike the later practice of compilation and classification,
where writers emulate Zǐ Mò's rigid adherence to the Mean,
seeking the non-controversial safety of the 'village worthy,'
boastfully claiming to surpass Mǎ Qiān and Bān Gù.
As for the records of rulers and ministers,
the statutes of various offices,
the transfer of the Mandate of Heaven and change of surname by a new ruler,
comprehensively reviewing previous dynasties,
and compiling and classifying records
in order to preserve the old materials of a given era—
this is what is called the task of compiling and organizing narratives.
Establishing offices,
setting up supervising officials, and gathering many people to compile the books,
is precisely when one should apply precedents in reasoning,
adhere to fixed standards,
and await the final verdict of later generations. That would suffice.
How could this be compared to the category of specialized scholarly works?
The *Yì* says:
'If reverence is not accorded to the right person,
the Way cannot proceed vainly.'
Historical talent is rarely produced in the world,
and the changes of the era cannot be constant.
To timely compile what has been heard and seen,
and not make the distinguishing of one's own scholarly tradition or the decisive choice of inclusion/exclusion the urgent task,
how can this be true only for the histories of Jìn and Suí?
Before Bān Gù,
there were the *Shǐjì* written by Liú Xiàng, Liú Xīn, Yáng Xióng, and Jiǎ Kuí.
Before Fàn Yè,
there were the *Hànjì* written by Liú Zhēn, Lǐ Yóu, Cài Yōng, Lú Zhí, and Yáng Biāo.
Why would these books not follow the established rules of tables and treatises,
or fail to employ the fixed structure of annals and biographies?
However, the older narratives which preserved the past and awaited the future,
and the specialists who established unique judgments through editing and selection,
their functions were sufficient to complement each other,
but their categories could not be conflated.
This is certainly the case.
Tracing further back,
the precious records of the hundred states compared to the *Chūnqiū*,
or the *Shìběn* and *Guócè* compared to the *Shǐjì*,
the underlying principle is still the same.
After the Táng dynasty, historical scholarship declined,
and there were no specialist authors.
Later people did not understand the scholarly tradition of the *Chūnqiū*,
but rashly took the older narratives compiled officially by many hands
and placed them alongside the books of Mǎ Qiān, Bān Gù, Chén Shòu, and Fàn Yè,
grouping them together as standard histories (*zhèngshǐ*).
Consequently, historical writing became equivalent to the formula of the imperial examinations,
or the official documents of petty clerks,
and could not tolerate the slightest variation or adaptation.
Occasionally, there are scholars who are fond of learning and deep thinking,
capable of finding their own teachers in the ancients,
establishing a precedent of meaning outside the fixed rules,
and manifesting a unique judgment of their own mind.
Yet, the common multitude of the world gathers to mock and curse them,
pointing fingers and dragging forth their words,
just as the weasel or ape seeing hats and robes,
would not stop until they have chewed, torn, ruined, and ripped them apart,
until utterly destroyed.
The slander suffered by Zhèng Shì’s *Tōngzhì*
is entirely due to this.
Alas!
The Way has been obscured for a long time.
The *Liù Jīng* (Six Classics) are all histories.
That which is metaphysical is called the Way (*dào*);
that which is physical is called the Vessel (*qì*).
When Kǒngzǐ composed the *Chūnqiū*,
he probably meant:
'If I sought to entrust it to empty words,
it would be inferior to demonstrating it through actual events, making it profound, urgent, and clear.'
Therefore, the statutes, documents, and facts of events
are what the author dares not neglect,
because they intend to use the Vessel to illuminate the Way.
If the book is sufficient to illuminate the Way,
then matters of ceremonial vessels and ritual implements
are handled by the responsible officials;
the gentleman does not consider these trifles.
When the Way is obscured but people argue about the Vessel,
when the substance is inadequate but they compete over the writing style,
the failing is barely an inch different
from those who use empty words to gain victory,
or whose flowery rhetoric harms reason.
Yet those absorbed in worldly matters fail to notice this.
The Grand Historian (Tài Shǐ Gōng) said:
'Fond of learning and deep thinking,
the mind knows the true meaning.'
In the world today,
how can we find people who know the meaning
and discuss the principles of historical writing with them?"
From the *Dákèwèn*
The Guest said:
Kǒngzǐ (Confucius) called himself:
"A transmitter and not a creator,
faithful to and fond of antiquity."
He also said:
"Fond of antiquity, diligently seeking it."
The rituals of Xià and Yīn,
the Master could speak of,
yet if there was no evidence, he would not accept them,
lamenting the insufficiency of historical documentation (wénxiàn).
Now you, Sir, say that the authors possess profound meaning and intent (yìzhǐ),
and that details like the number of ritual vessels (biāndòu qìshù),
should not be considered trivial matters.
Does this not contradict the teachings of the Master?
The exhaustive completeness of Mǎ Shì's (Mǎ Duānlín's) *Tōngkǎo*,
and the loose errors of Zhèng Shì's (Zhèng Qiáo's) *Tōngzhì*,
are known even to three-foot-high children.
You, Sir, exclusively adopt its profound meaning and intent (yìzhǐ),
without requiring its practical utility,
and thus seek to champion Zhèng Qiáo and criticize Mǎ Duānlín.
Is this argument not inclined toward bias?
Zhāngzǐ (Zhāng Xuéchéng) said:
The words in the world,
each have their appropriate place;
the words in the Classics and Commentaries,
are simply the same.
When reading the books of the ancients,
if one cannot grasp and integrate their core intent (zhǐ),
but merely clings to seemingly similar or questionable doctrines,
seeking victory in a limited sphere,
then the arguments from that limited sphere,
cannot be exhaustively applied.
In the world, there are books of compilation and arrangement (bǐcì zhī shū),
there are studies based on independent judgment (dúduàn zhī xué),
and there are efforts dedicated to comprehensive research (kǎosuǒ zhī gōng).
These three approaches each have their priorities,
and cannot necessarily overlap perfectly.
The Six Classics (Liù Jīng) relative to the canonical texts (diǎnjí),
are like the sun and moon in the sky.
Reading the *Shū* (Classic of History) as if there were no *Shī* (Classic of Poetry),
reading the *Yì* (Classic of Changes) as if there were no *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals),
even if they are the records of the Sages,
it is impossible for one book,
to encompass the methods of inquiry of several schools.
The *Yì* says, "One cannot make them into fixed regulations or essentials (diǎnyào),"
while the *Shū* distinctly states that "the language should still adhere to the fundamental essentials (tǐyào)."
When reading the *Shī*, one must not allow the words (cí) to harm the intent (zhì),
yet the *Chūnqiū* precisely uses a single phrase to determine right and wrong.
If, hypothetically, we were to insist on the imagery of 'dragon's blood' or 'demon carts,'
and apply them to verify the phrase 'Yù Ruò Jī Gǔ' [from the *Shū*],
or rely on dreams of bears, snakes, and fish banners (Zhōu Gong's dreams),
to record the command of the New Year decreed by the Spring King,
then the achievements of the Sages would be neglected,
and the core intent of mastering the Classics would be violated.
If you speak of being fond of antiquity and diligently seeking it,
and verifying beliefs through historical documentation (wénxiàn zhēngxìn),
I do not suggest that past conduct and former words should be discarded lightly.
One should listen widely but make selections,
study extensively but aim for conciseness.
What one chooses must have a basis for one's own assertions,
and cannot be generally restricted by established doctrines.
When the Great Way (Dàdào) became obscured,
the various masters (zhūzǐ) contended loudly,
each having grasped one aspect of the former kings' teachings.
This is what Zhuāngshēng (Zhuāngzǐ) meant by saying: "Ears, eyes, mouth, and nose,
each have something they illuminate,
but they cannot communicate with each 68]other."
The eye can discern the tip of an autumn hair,
but cannot see thunder.
The ear can distinguish the five notes,
but cannot observe Mount Tàishān.
To say that the ears and eyes have capabilities and incapacities,
is acceptable;
but to say that what the ear hears and the eye sees is insufficient to constitute thunder and mountains,
how can that be?
Since the time of the Hàn dynasty,
scholars, based on what they attained,
who relied on their writings to manifest their own views,
were quite numerous.
Those who are lofty and brilliant often engage in studies of independent judgment (dúduàn zhī xué);
those who are deep and reserved value the effort of comprehensive research (kǎosuǒ zhī gōng).
The scholarship of the world,
cannot help but encompass these two paths.
It is analogous to the sun for the day and the moon for the night,
heat for summer and cold for winter.
When they alternate and complete the year's cycle,
there is the benefit of mutual need;
but if one restricts oneself and establishes boundaries,
there is the drawback of mutual harm.
Thus, Mǎ (Mǎ Qiān) and Bān (Bān Gù) were ancestors of historiography (shǐzǔ),
while Fú (Fú Shèng) and Zhèng (Zhèng Xuán) were masters of the Classics (jīngshī).
If they switched their roles, they would not be excellent,
as they travel their own paths without opposing each other.
If Fú Shèng and Zhèng Xuán were made to jointly annotate a Classic,
there would inevitably be the flaw of contradiction.
If Mǎ Qiān and Bān Gù were made to compile one history together,
there would inevitably be the suspicion of inconsistency.
From this, we know that specialized scholarship (zhuānmén zhī xué),
never fails to follow its intent independently.
Even if peers argue against it, it does not waver;
even if the whole world condemns it, it pays no heed.
This is why Shǐ Qiān (Sīmǎ Qiān) absolutely desired to transmit his work to a specific person,
and why Bān Gù had to wait for Mǎ Róng to receive instruction from his younger sister,
before his scholarship truly became prominent.
Sīmǎ Qiān’s work had Xú Guǎng, Péi Yīn, and others to transmit his legacy;
Bān Gù’s work had Fú Qián, Yīng Shào, and others to transmit his legacy.
Specialized scholarship,
is transmitted orally and passed on mentally,
no less than how Masters of the Classics (jīngshī) have their chapter and verse commentaries (zhāngjù).
Thus, the meaning of the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals) for managing the world (jīngshì),
must contain details that cannot be fully expressed in written characters,
and standards that cannot be measured by the compass and square (róngmò).
Yet today’s scholars,
whenever they encounter the writings of the ancients based on independent judgment (dúduàn),
and their views are not satisfied,
clamorously rise up and attack them,
which shows they merely love discussion but do not seek successful achievement.
As for books of compilation and arrangement (bǐcì zhī shū),
they are the itemized lists of officials (zhǎnggù lìngshǐ),
the established format for registers, records, and notes.
Although their origins stem from what was stored beneath the pillars [in the archives],
their utility is limited to preparing for consultation and providing material for selection,
and originally they possess no other remarkable qualities.
However, studies of independent judgment (dúduàn zhī xué),
do not derive decisions without them;
the effort of comprehensive research (kǎosuǒ zhī gōng),
does not establish evidence without them.
It is like fine wine (zhǐjiǔ) not being separate from the dregs (zāopò),
or excellent grain (jiāhé) not being separate from the dirt and fertilizer (fèntǔ).
Therefore, books concerning official posts, historical precedents, documents, maps, and records,
