cannot be lightly criticized.
Nevertheless, studies of independent judgment (dúduàn zhī xué),
and the effort of comprehensive research (kǎosuǒ zhī gōng) desire wisdom,
whereas books of compilation and arrangement (bǐcì zhī shū) demand simplicity (yú, i.e., adherence to facts without interpretation).
This is like how wine can be used to fill the *zūnyí* ritual vessels,
but dregs (zāopò) cannot fill the *zūnyí*;
grain can be offered in the *fǔguǐ* ritual vessels,
but dirt and fertilizer (fèntǔ) cannot be sought for the *fǔguǐ*.
The principle is perfectly clear.
The ancients said:
"If words are not ornate,
they will not travel far."
"If writings are not refined and elegant (yǎxún),
gentlemen scholars (jiànshēn xiānshēng) will find it difficult to speak of them."
Because records of official posts, precedents, documents, maps, and tallies are difficult to gather and travel far,
there arose the method of compilation and arrangement (bǐcì).
It does not claim to be a specialized school (jiāxué),
it does not establish specialized interpretations,
it uses this method to organize precedents,
and waits for later generations to make decisions—
this is the effectiveness of compilation seeking simplicity (yú).
If one raises it up and places it in the hall of creative writing,
and furthermore labels it as specialized scholarship (jiāxué),
how easy is that to say?
Furthermore, Bān Gù's talent,
can be called ultimate.
Yet, when he, along with Chén Zōng, Yǐn Mǐn, and their peers,
compiled the 'Basic Annals of Emperor Shìzǔ,'
and the biographies of Xīnshì and Pínglín,
these could not stand equally alongside the *Hàn Shū* [which he primarily wrote],
and one must take Fàn Wèizōng's (Fàn Yè's) book [the *Hòu Hàn Shū*] as the true orthodox standard;
this shows clearly that the compilation of precedents managed by multiple officials,
and the historical judgments based on specialized independent scholarship,
do not align with one another.
Since that time,
the original source and tradition have been lost.
Zhèng Qiáo lacked the effort of comprehensive research (kǎosuǒ zhī gōng),
yet his *Tōngzhì* is sufficient to clarify the studies of independent judgment (dúduàn zhī xué);
thus, the superior person finds value in it.
Mǎ Guìyǔ (Mǎ Duānlín) lacked the studies of independent judgment (dúduàn zhī xué),
and his *Tōngkǎo* is insufficient to fulfill the achievement of compilation and arrangement (bǐcì zhī gōng),
because his wisdom (zhì) has nothing to be praised for,
and in the way of simplicity (yú),
he was also incomplete.
Moreover, he took the *Tōngdiǎn* and further subdivided its categories,
merely for the convenience of reference.
He relied on historical treatises (shǐzhì) to gather his discussions and arguments,
merely making it easy to reconcile opinions.
These are just strategies and summaries used by classicists (jīngshēng) for passing examinations.
He dared not express a single unique insight,
or mark an idea outside the accepted standards,
but humbly flattered the world and became a village worthy (xiāngyuàn).
Regarding the profound meaning and intent (yìzhǐ) of the ancients' writings,
it cannot be heard from him.
Superficial scholars found the arrangement of categories easy to follow,
and liked his arguments for being balanced and appropriate,
and together they unanimously praised it,
but they did not know that the origin and tradition of the work lacked true merit.
This is like a grating, discordant melody,
that nonetheless attracts the response of ten thousand people.
Response to the Guest (Part Two)
The Guest said:
The studies of independent judgment (dúduàn zhī xué),
and the effort of comprehensive research (kǎosuǒ zhī gōng),
I have now received instruction on these.
May I ask, regarding books of compilation and arrangement (bǐcì zhī shū),
why did you, Sir, compare them to dregs (zāopò) and dirt (fèntǔ)?
What do you mean?
Zhāngzǐ said:
This is not a derogatory phrase.
There is unpolished jade before carving is applied;
there is substance before the axe is wielded.
The relationship between priority and weight,
its principle is easily understood.
The Master (Fūzǐ) had not yet abridged the Shī (《詩》) and Shū (《書》),
nor finalized the Yì (《易》), Lǐ (《禮》), and Chūnqiū (《春秋》).
These were all old canons of the former kings.
However, had they not been discussed and settled by the Master,
they could not have been transmitted to students.
Lǐ Táo said, "When Zuǒshì was about to transmit the Chūnqiū (《春秋》),
he first gathered the historical records of various states,
arranged them separately by state as narratives,
in order to prepare material for culling in the Nèichuán (《內傳》)."
Although this is an inference,
ancient people, when writing books,
never wholly lacked a source upon which to draw.
Based on this, we know that the task of compilation (bǐcì)
must be discussed.
The methods of compilation
generally fall into three categories:
First, those who collect and compile in a timely manner
and await the final determination of later generations,
such as the Shǐjì (《史記》) by Liú Xīn and Yáng Xióng,
and the Hànjì (《漢記》) by Bān Gù and Chén Zōng.
Second, those who aspire to writing,
first hunt through various books
to use as fuel (xīnyǒu),
such as Wángshì’s Yùhǎi (《玉海》)
and Sīmǎ’s Chángbiān (《長編》).
Third, those who refine specialized sources
and force them into monumental works,
such as Qiān recording Cānggōng’s methods,
and Gù editing Liú Xiàng’s Wǔxíng (《五行》).
Now, for timely compilation awaiting determination,
the selection, omission, and inclusion of detail
must be focused solely on meticulous organization.
For first hunting through various books
to use as fuel,
one must distinguish similarities and investigate differences,
focusing solely on careful verification.
For refining specialized sources
and forcing them into monumental works,
one must extract the profound and summarize the essentials,
focusing solely on mastering the general scope.
Since the task of compilation
has these differences;
the authors' intentions
must also distinguish and select based on appropriateness.
But today's scholars
hold that the Way of the world
lies merely in comparing the similarities and differences of names and numbers,
and distinguishing whether pronunciations and meanings are correct or not,
and nothing more than this;
How is this different from gazing at the sky from the bottom of a well,
measuring the water in a shallow depression,
and then hoping to exhaust the movements of the universe (liùhé)
and gauge the waves of the four seas,
believing they can be completed?
The ages of the Hàn emperors
are fully recorded in the Biélù (《別錄》);
the names of Fú Shēng and Wén Wēng,
are verified on stone carvings;
Gāozǔ’s founding of Xīnfēng
is detailed in the Liújì (劉記);
Xiàowǔ’s preference for incognito travel
is recorded in the outer biographies;
Yet the two books by Qiān and Gù,
did not record them.
Thus, the abundance of compilation
does not necessarily hinder the author's brevity.
Cáo Pī’s abdication memorial
is detailed in the Xiàndì Zhuàn (《獻帝傳》);
Empress Zhēn’s admirable conduct
is highly praised in the Wèishū (《魏書》);
The account of Āiláo
is verified by the census clerks;
the register of former worthies
was recorded in the Huángchū era;
Yet the two histories by Chén and Fàn
did not include them.
Thus, the private nature of compilation
must await the public spirit of the author.
However, classicists practice their trade,
thus compiling a forest of canons;
literati probe their brushes,
thus collecting refined compositions.
The decadent habit of recent times
is to take convenience as a guideline,
each making their own private "rabbit garden" manuals,
to provide material for vulgar students to pick up and carry;
If the task of compilation
is merely like dregs and dung,
how can one hope that corruption will transform and produce the miraculous?
It cannot be achieved!
If village books and vulgar learning
already lack good material,
then the task of compilation
is difficult to rely upon—this is the first reason.
The facts collected
are often not the original text,
and there is a tendency to change characters and phrases,
diluting their essence,
leading scholars to prefer studying the original books
rather than bothering to look at the new records;
Thus, the task of compilation
is difficult to rely upon—this is the second reason.
Grouping items by category
is fundamentally not authorship,
yet when collecting old documents,
the source book is not cited,
making it seem as if the compiler obtained it solely,
leaving people unable to verify the credibility;
Thus, the task of compilation
is difficult to rely upon—this is the third reason.
When transmitted words differ
and records appear separately,
unable to gather and record them all
to await the author’s selection and decision,
but instead privately exercising cleverness
and self-determining what to keep and what to discard;
Thus, the task of compilation
is difficult to rely upon—this is the fourth reason.
The study of drawings and paintings
is not admitted into historical criticism,
and inscriptions on metal and stone
are only referenced in catalogs,
making it impossible for later generations to examine and
verify the credibility;
Thus, the task of compilation
is difficult to rely upon—this is the fifth reason.
Specialized books
that have already formed massive compilations
are not collected or recorded,
generally neglecting measures to prevent their loss, allowing them to circulate independently,
gradually leading to their obliteration;
Thus, the task of compilation
is difficult to rely upon—this is the sixth reason.
Restricting oneself to established categories and precedents,
merely collecting enough to complete the book,
and not procuring extensively
beyond the established rules
to await the author's discernment and judgment—
if the net has only one mesh,
the day a bird is caught is far off;
Thus, the task of compilation
is difficult to rely upon—this is the seventh reason.
All these various points
were things the ancients did not fully detail,
and are especially unfamiliar to later students.
If one is anxious about having only three months' worth of stored grain,
then how can study and practice not be prepared in advance?
Yet the scholars of this generation
do not know how to assess their virtues or measure their abilities,
all clamorously proclaiming themselves authors,
unwilling to perform the foundational work of trap, snare, and sounding arrow.
This is what Liú Xīn called "harboring the private intention of fearing being discredited,
and lacking the public spirit of following goodness and submitting to righteousness."
How can technical work be appropriate?
And how can the Way of authorship
ever be set right?
Response to Question (Dáwèn)
Someone asked:
May the writings of previous generations
be revised and altered to be made into one's own work?
The answer was:
Why would that not be permissible?
In ancient times, writing was considered a public instrument.
If the words of previous generations are considered exhausted,
later generations narrate but need not create anew.
Cutting a stanza from a poem
is no different from seeming as if it came from one's own mouth.
The emphasis is on the underlying reason for the writing,
not on the written words themselves.
If one truly grasps the essence of that underlying reason,
there is no need for any revision or alteration,
and the writings of the predecessors are no different from one's own.
If one lacks that underlying intention but seeks to conform to the written words,
then even if the phrases and characters are untouched,
but one secretly imitates what the predecessor said,
a gentleman would scorn it as "theft."
Someone said:
Chén Lín (陳琳) wrote the memorial for Cáo Hóng (曹洪) reporting to the Prince of Wèi (魏),
and he kept secret that the words were by Chén Lín.
Dīng Jìnglǐ (丁敬禮) asked Cáo Zǐjiàn (曹子建) to polish his writing,
who replied, "In later generations, who will know who revised my writing?"
Hán Shì (韓氏) of the Táng (唐) dynasty said:
"Only the ancients always produced their writings from themselves;
those who fall short and cannot do so are engaging in plagiarism."
The ancients surely wished their writings to be exclusively their own creation;
how can it be said that they merely valued the underlying intention?
The answer was:
The writing of a literary man
and the writing of scholarly authorship
cannot be spoken of in the same breath.
Scholarly authorship must have an intention established prior to the writing;
it merely borrows the written words to convey that intention.
For example, when conducting rites in the ancestral hall,
one must use embroidered silks and jade pendants.
The person conducting the rites
does not concern himself with how the silks and pendants were made.
The writing of scholarly authorship is like this.
The silk worker and the jade craftsman
have never practiced the rites;
they only rely on weaving the silk and carving the jade to claim merit.
If they pass off what others have made as their own creation,
then everyone considers it theft.
The writing of a literary man is like this.
Therefore, to use the perspective of a literary man
to critique the writing of scholarly authorship
is like a silk worker or jade craftsman
critiquing the rituals of the ancestral hall.
Someone said:
The proclamations and mandates of the ancients were initially drafted
and then subject to revision and polishing.
In later generations, poetry and prose
also acknowledged a "master of a single character."
If the emphasis is truly on the underlying intention,
and the words themselves are not a concern—
for instance, in conducting rites in the ancestral hall,
although one may not fuss over the silks and pendants,
if the silks and pendants are worn out and torn,
and fail to conform to the standard pattern,
how can the rites proceed?
The answer was:
This is discussing writing purely from the perspective of writing,
which is a separate domain altogether.
When discussing writing from the perspective of writing,
our former master (Confucius) provided the instruction that "words must convey the meaning" (cí dá),
and Zēngzǐ (曾子) issued the warning against crude and defiant language (bǐ pèi).
When the Sage's school established disciplines,
literature (wénxué) and speech (yányǔ) existed side-by-side.
Oratory, too, was valued as requiring skill.
The writings of the ancients
never failed to strive for refinement.
But that is not the point of contention here, concerning those who delineate boundaries
and insist that writing must originate solely from oneself,
thereby boasting of their private achievements.
Since the periods of Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉) onward,
the discussion of writing has also become a specialty.
The Music Bureau (Yuèfǔ) revised the musicality of old compositions,
the Wén Xuǎn (文選) edited the works of predecessors—
both prioritizing sound, emotion, color, and style,
which is not the same category as scholarly authorship.
In the preface to the Huìchāng Zhì Jí (會昌制集),
Zhèng Yà (鄭亞) excised the richness of Yìshān's (義山) work;
in the Yuánhé (元和) "Song of the Lunar Eclipse,"
Duke Hán (Hán Gōng) selected the strange elements of Yùchuān's (玉川) work.
Sometimes the original text was preserved and attributed to the author,
and sometimes the title was changed and included in one's own collection.
Although discussing writing belongs to minor skills,
there are those who are expert in it.
When their understanding becomes deep,
they no longer bother to haggle over the trivialities of other people's words and phrases.
Someone said:
In the past, Yuè Guǎng (樂廣) was skilled in speech,
while Zhì Yú (摯虞) had a marvelous pen.
Yuè (樂) could talk, but Zhì (摯) could not seal the documents;
Zhì (摯) could write, but Yuè (樂) could not reproduce it.
Everyone has their particular strengths.
If so, is it not permissible for someone who is capable in speech but not in writing
to borrow someone else to wield the brush?
The answer was:
Pān Yuè (潘嶽) also drafted the document of resignation for Yuè Guǎng (樂廣).
He must have obtained Guǎng's (廣) meaning and intention
before arranging it into a famous piece of writing.
The histories never failed to praise both of them.
From the period of the Two Hàn (兩漢) onwards,
few people possessed multiple talents.
They might be strong in scholarship but deficient in rhetoric,
or skilled in writing but careless in recording.
Furthermore, even within the domain of scholarship,
there are specialized strengths,
and in the area of writing,
there are particular specialties.
Originally, they could assist each other to achieve success,
but the world tends toward mutual criticism and denigration,
which is why the Great Way ultimately cannot be fully manifested.
Writing is a minor skill.
If one removes the boundaries and pools specialized strengths,
there can still be outstanding and immortal achievements,
let alone advancing from scholarship to seek the grand essence of the ancients!
However, from antiquity until now,
such a person has not existed.
This is an irremediable situation.
Someone said:
If what you say is true,
that literature and scholarship
can rely on each other.
If there is a cunning person
who fundamentally lacks talent
but falsely claims to be committed to public principles
in order to exploit the system (like the musician Nánguō),
how should we distinguish them?
The answer was:
A thousand-jūn (鈞) cauldron
lifted by two men—
the one who cannot carry five hundred jūn
will fall over.
Lǐ Guǎng (李廣) entered Chéng Bùshí's (程不識) army,
and the banners, flags, and encampment walls
were immediately transformed.
If his talent and wisdom had been inferior to Chéng's (程),
the entire army would have fallen into chaos.
A wealthy man traveling far
does not carry a single coin,
yet when he needs something and asks for a loan,
people eagerly grant it.
Why cannot others do the same?
Only by being rich in money
can one borrow money from others.
Therefore, if literary achievement is truly devoted to public principles,
those without substance
cannot feign it.
Someone said:
The writings of predecessors
may not be entirely perfect.
If later generations revise and polish them to demonstrate a model standard,
is this also permissible?
The answer was:
That is difficult to discuss.
In scholarly authorship, revising and altering predecessors' work
has a different guiding intention,
so there is no harm.
In discussing writing (lùn wén), revising and altering predecessors' work—
the literary mind is different,
just like a person's face.
One cannot abruptly declare that one's own views
are superior to those of the predecessor.
Liú Shì's (劉氏) Shǐ Tōng (史通)
includes the chapter "Diǎn Fán" (點煩, Pointing out Redundancy).
Since Zuǒ (左) and Mǎ (馬) (Zuǒ Qíu Míng, 左丘明 and Sīmǎ Qiān, 司馬遷),
there have been revisions and corrections,
which some criticized as knowing history but not literature.
However, Liú Shì (劉氏) did what he did with a specific purpose,
and the gains and losses can still be seen mutually.
But when specifically engaging in discussing writing,
one should be cautious.
The intelligence and wisdom of antiquity and the present
are difficult to fully grasp;
what people today see
is not necessarily inferior to what the ancients saw.
Generally, when an accidental insight arises unconsciously,
it achieves the merit of turning stone into gold;
but when one deliberately seeks to change things,
it often incurs the ridicule of drawing on a muddy wall.
This is because discussing writing values the spontaneous presentation of natural genius
and dislikes artificial human interference.
Someone asked:
In recent times, figures like Fāng Bāo,
who cut and revised the great masters of the Táng and Sòng dynasties—
did this provide any benefit?
Now, Fāng Shì was merely a literary man;
what he gained was fundamentally not very profound.
Furthermore, he added subjective bias and arrogance.
Not only was this of no benefit to literature,
but it conversely inaugurated the dangerous trend of unrestrained audacity among the younger generation.
Minor cleverness and selfish ingenuity,
partial understanding and superficial knowledge,
might not prevent one from criticizing the flaws of the ancients
or picking up what previous generations missed.
If this is discussed in terms of scholarship,
it can be categorized as a case of "unwise but knowledgeable in small things,"
and the argument may be preserved for the selection of later generations.
However, if discussed in terms of literary composition (wéncí),
it holds no connection to major principles,
and can all be set aside without discussion.
This means that people's minds differ just as their faces do,
and there is no need to forcibly standardize them.
If, regarding right and wrong, success and failure,
later generations indeed have new insights,
they naturally cannot remain silent.
It must be expressed as if done out of absolute necessity,
after reviewing and scrutinizing it repeatedly.
Just as when the state discusses old regulations,
or renowned ministers counsel on benefits and drawbacks:
unless there is a glaring discrepancy of ten or a hundred times [in effectiveness],
it is better to maintain the old ways than rashly introduce changes.
If one does not deeply understand this principle,
yet lightly criticizes the ancients,
this is the height of mediocrity and presumption.
Even if there might be small gains,
these are insufficient to compensate for the great losses.
When Fāng Shì cut and revised the great masters,
was there absolute necessity?
Were there rights and wrongs, gains and losses,
that clearly differed by a factor of ten or a hundred?
Did he possess the fundamental intention
—like the state discussing old regulations,
or renowned ministers counseling on benefits and drawbacks—
of preferring to stick to the old ways rather than rashly making changes?
Therefore, subjective bias and arrogance,
seeking to surpass the ancients—
this is why Fāng Shì ultimately failed to reach the level of the ancients.
Anyone who can truly merge with the ancients
must first adhere strictly to the rules and standards of the ancients and dare not overstep them.
For unless one believes wholeheartedly and adheres strictly,
one cannot enter deeply into the ancient tradition;
if one does not enter deeply, one cannot merge with it.
For example, among friends,
to be able to fully realize the trust and shared wealth exemplified by Guǎn and Bào,
one must first be rigorous in the specific rules of taking and giving;
otherwise, it is impossible.
Therefore, studying the ancients but daring not to slavishly cling to them
is precisely the utmost form of respect and solemn reverence for the ancients,
not slighting them.
Fāng Shì did not understand the intent of the ancients,
but only catered to literary style,
and what he gained from literary style
was fundamentally not very profound.
His selfish ingenuity and minor cleverness
were only enough to glimpse what the ancients *ought* to have written,
but he did not know where they *did not* write according to his expectations.
It is understandable that he would readily take up his brush and make alterations.
The established forms of ancient literature
and the origins and development of ancient literary structures
must be the first things a beginner identifies
when entering the field.
Sū Zǐzhān’s *Biǎo Zhōng Guān Bēi* (Stele for the Temple of Manifesting Loyalty)
fully recorded Zhào Biàn’s memorial,
without any additions or deletions to the text,
and immediately appended a verse inscription below it.
This was a common practice for Hàn dynasty stelae;
examples seen in epigraphic works
are too numerous to list.
Even among the works of the Eight Great Masters of Táng and Sòng,
such as Liǔ Zǐhòu’s *Shòuzhōu Ānfēng Xiàomén Bēi*,
this method was also used,
and is fundamentally not surprising.
Wáng Jièfǔ was astonished and claimed it imitated the "Tables of the Feudal Lords" in the *Shǐ Jì*—
truly the words of a petty scholar.
Lǐ Qíqīng said its literary style imitated the *Hàn Shū*;
this, too, is completely inexplicable.
This is an extremely ordinary thing seen by everyone;
why should these gentlemen find it so strange and peculiar,
treating it like an antique curiosity?
Furthermore, consider recent examples in markets and villages:
if there are benefits or drawbacks, gains or losses,
and the public discusses initiating or prohibiting something,
and requests officials to establish regulations,
and a stele is erected to endure forever,
that stele will engrave the original text of the government document or proclamation,
without the need to add or delete words or phrases.
This is also an ancient method.
Is it possible that Jièfǔ and the others
had never seen such stelae?
The astonishment and criticism voiced by Wáng Shì’s retainers at the time
are not even worth a laugh.
Judging purely by literary style,
Zhào Qīngxiàn’s original memorial requesting the restoration of the Temple of Manifesting Loyalty
was perhaps not as classical and refined as Sū Shì’s stele inscription.
Historians, when recording events and statements,
often adopt existing texts,
and originally employed methods of polishing and revising.
Although Sū Shì’s stele
appears to be a simple transcription,
it actually required meticulous planning and structure.
However, while literary style can be polished,
institutional form must follow the contemporary standard.
The three characters “Chén Biàn yán”
at the beginning of the memorial,
and the three characters “Zhì yuē kě”
at the end,
I fear, do not conform to the style used during the Sòng dynasty for presenting memorials or issuing imperial decrees.
But in Sū Shì’s mind,
the phrases like “Chéngxiàng Chén Sī mèi sǐ yán”
and “Zhì yuē kě”
from the *Qín Běnjì* were too familiar,
and thus he inevitably drew the criticism leveled by Liú Zhījǐ:
that the appearance is the same, but the spirit is different.
When I previously compiled the *Hézhōu Zhì*,
there was the *Yǐhài Yìliè Zhuàn*,
specifically recording the events of the eighth year of Chóngzhēn at the end of the Míng dynasty,
when the Chuang 'rebels'
attacked and breached Hézhōu,
and officials, gentry, and common men and women perished as martyrs.
I used the method of comprehensive narrative:
taking events as the warp [main structure]
and people as the weft [supporting threads],
recording everything in detail.
But controversy erupted within the prefecture.
This was because the Chuang 'rebels,'
angered by the resistance, massacred the city.
The descendants of those massacred
blamed the person who first proposed defending the city, claiming he
endangered the lives of everyone in the city.
Others wrote essays criticizing the defender's illegal deployment,
which led to the city's fall.
There were even slanders claiming that the person who proposed the defense
tried to escape by rope over the wall
and was captured and killed by the 'rebels,'
and was not a true martyr.
I searched and found the memorial submitted by Zhū Dàdiǎn, the Governor of Fèngyáng,
reporting the fall of Hézhōu
and the details of the martyrdom of officials and gentry.
This report was based on the submission of the Prefectural Sub-Administrator for River Defense,
who in turn relied on the firsthand accounts of refugees who had been in the besieged city and escaped.
The loyalty and heroism of the officials and gentry
could not be falsely accused.
Therefore, I fully transcribed the memorial,
using it as the preface to the biography.
The wording within the body of the memorial, which I polished,
had many excellent points.
However, the beginning of the piece had to state:
“On a certain day in the second month of the ninth year of Chóngzhēn,
Your Minister Zhū Dàdiǎn, Governor of Fèngyáng, Director-General of Military Affairs, and Right Vice Censor-in-Chief of the Censorate, respectfully submits this memorial,
concerning the city of Hé being captured by 'rebels,'
the pitiful martyrdom of officials and gentry,
and requesting bestowal of commendation
to manifest their righteous and heroic deeds.”
And the end of the piece stated:
“By Imperial Edict:
Having read the memorial, We feel sorrow and compassion.
Let the relevant ministry investigate the precedent and act accordingly.”
This was the actual contemporary format for submitting memorials and reporting decrees.
Some suggested that since the text of the memorial in the middle
had already been revised to be classical and elegant,
the beginning and end seemed suitable for similar refinement.
I responded that the phrasing of the memorial text
did not have a strictly fixed style,
so it could be polished to be classical and elegant
without obstructing the facts.
However, the beginning and end were definitely the institutional formulas of the time.
How could one use the attire of the Qín and Hàn dynasties
to depict the likeness of a Míng dynasty person?
Regarding Sū Shì’s *Biǎo Zhōng Guān Bēi*,
that previous scholars did not understand it
and collectively expressed astonishment
was certainly the fault of their lack of study.
Sū Shì’s writing
was fundamentally beyond criticism.
However, the part that people became accustomed to and did not find strange,
but which is actually illogical,
is only the six characters at the beginning and end that did not follow the institutional form.
If literary style fails to investigate proper principles and rules
and only caters to being classical and elegant,
then how are the three characters “Chén Biàn yán”
more ancient than the three characters “Yuè yuē wū”
How are the three characters “Zhì yuē kě”
more ancient than the three characters “Dì yuē yú”
Abandoning Táng and Yú to emulate Qín and Hàn,
I do not see how this demonstrates a love for the ancient.
Wāng Dùnwēng compiled the “Preface to the Eulogy for the Memorial Arch of the Chaste and Ardent Woman Tāng in Suīzhōu” (《睢州湯烈婦旌門頌序》).
The document begins by recording the memorial submitted by the Inspecting Censor (xún'àn yùshǐ),
which is merely standard practice,
nothing to criticize,
nor anything to boast about.
However, Wāng Shì did not realize that while the writing must follow ancient methods,
the official format (gōngshì) must adhere to contemporary regulations;
the format for memorials and reports during the Qín and Hàn dynasties
cannot be used to replace modern writing styles.
To start the essay with the words “The Supervising Censor Chén Cuìrán says,”
shows that this author is too familiar with the three characters “Chén Biàn says” (臣抃言)
from reading the “Stele of the Temple Commending Loyalty” (《表忠觀碑》),
but is unaware that Sū Shì’s use was already considered incorrect practice.
In modern official memorials (zhāngzòu),
when listing the titles at the beginning of the text,
none fail to mention the surname;
this is also standard procedure.
What is Cuìrán’s surname?
How could Wāng Shì omit it merely by imitating ancient style?
Furthermore, in modern official memorials,
below the titles and name,
one must write *jǐn zòu* (謹奏, respectfully memorialized),
not using the term *yán* (言, says or speaks).
A phrase that is only four characters long
yet violates standard procedure twice—
how can this be considered “ancient prose” (gǔwéncí)?
If a woman has a given name, refer to her by her name;
if she does not have a given name, refer to her by her surname,
saying “Zhāng Shì” or “Lǐ Shì” is acceptable.
In modern official documents
and commoners' legal petitions,
it is often the case that the surname is omitted, and they are simply referred to as *yuē shì* (曰氏, Ms. so-and-so),
or even referred to as *gāi shì* (該氏, the said woman)—
this is truly vulgar and unrefined.
However, if there is no clear regulation forbidding it,
and the yamen clerks (xūlì), if they possess some knowledge,
still refer to them as Zhāng Shì or Lǐ Shì,
and the officials do not prohibit it,
then this is still an accommodating rule of grammar.
Wāng Shì, regarding the fixed and immutable official procedures,
deliberately changed them to the ancient format of the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
which is already similar in appearance but different in spirit.
As for the generally accepted and correct appellations,
he again favors the common practice over the correct one.
How extremely convoluted!
The concluding sentence again says, “Your servant respectfully risks death to report” (臣謹昧死以聞),
which is also not the modern system.
Wāng Shì normally prides himself highly on his ancient prose,
yet he is this mediocre and vulgar—
why is this the case?
Wāng’s preface,
immediately after the phrase “Your servant Chén Cuìrán says,”
starts abruptly with, “Zhūshēng Tāng Mǒu’s wife Zhào Shì from Suīzhōu,
during the calamity of Lǐ Zìchéng’s downfall in the late Míng”
and so on.
This is also not good.
It should say, “Zhāo Shì, the wife of the former Míng *zhūshēng* Tāng Mǒu from Suīzhōu,
during the calamity of Lǐ Zìchéng,”
which flows more smoothly in terms of phrasing.
Starting abruptly makes it sound like the person is contemporary,
and only in the following sentence is it supplemented with “during the calamity of Lǐ Zìchéng in the late Míng,”
making the flow of the writing rather stagnant.
Those who study literature
should pay attention to and discern matters like these.
Ten Flaws of Ancient Prose
I have discussed the principles (yìlì) of ancient prose
in letters to gentlemen who share my interests,
totaling several tens of communications.
As for written treatises,
there are also the chapters “Literary Virtue” (Wéndé), “Literary Reason” (Wénlǐ), “Innate Quality” (Zhìxìng), “Cunning Vulgarity” (Xiálòu), “Common Dislike” (Súxián), and “Common Taboo” (Sújì)—
in which I have also elaborated in detail.
However, I mostly discussed the ancients,
and rarely addressed recent times.
Now, observing the authors of today,
there are quite a few statements and compositions
that feel uneasy to the mind (i.e., problematic).
I have therefore selected the most superficial and common issues
and categorized them into ten general points,
hoping to discuss and clarify them with like-minded gentlemen.
What has been covered in other chapters will not be repeated;
readers may cross-reference them.
This is insufficient to fully uncover the hidden aspects of literature,
but by citing one corner and deducing the other three (yī yú sān fǎn),
it may perhaps come close.
First:
In all attempts at writing ancient prose,
one must first understand the general principles (dàtǐ) of the ancients;
the skill or awkwardness of the writing itself
is secondary.
If one does not understand the general principles,
then the distinctions between right and wrong in the heart
cannot be relied upon,
and the things they discuss and organize
may not align with facts and principles.
If the facts and principles themselves are sound,
they, conversely, see them as flawed and attempt to remedy them,
thereby leading the people of the world into harming benevolence and righteousness.
A famous scholar submitted an account of his mother’s life (xíngshù)
and requested Mr. Zhū from Dàxīng to write a commemorative biography (zhì).
In describing his mother’s chastity and filial piety,
he related that when his grandfather was old, sickly, and confined to bed,
urinating and defecating uncontrollably,
and there were no male servants in the house,
his mother did not avoid the filth and contamination,
but personally washed and cleaned him.
That act was already admirable.
He then went on to relate that his grandfather felt distressed and uneasy at the time,
and his mother solemnly replied:
“I am fifty years old.
I am now serving an eighty-year-old elder.
What is there to dislike or doubt?”
Alas!
The mother’s conduct is commendable,
but the son’s writing is extremely inferior.
If there was fundamentally no mental barrier (jièdì),
why would there be dislike or doubt?
The chaste mother, having understood the great righteousness,
certainly knew better than to utter such words.
This gentleman, without cause, invented dislike and doubt,
specifically adding this note to mediate the situation.
He himself thought he had grasped the proper form,
but he was unaware that it was exactly like fair, unblemished skin
being carved into ulcers and sores,
which will inevitably show more scars the more one tries to wash it away.
If a person does not understand literature,
when encountering such situations,
they merely need to state the facts plainly
and must not needlessly add arbitrary embellishments.
Adding arbitrary embellishments
is called “carving flesh to create a wound” (wānròu wéicāng);
this is a common flaw among literati.
Second:
The *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals) does not conceal minor wrongs within its narrative.
Only when the year turns cold does one know that the pine and cypress wither last.
Therefore, if one wishes to illustrate the constancy of the pine and cypress,
one must clarify the harshness of the frost and snow;
this is the inevitable consequence of logic and circumstance.
But since the world harbors many taboos and sensitivities,
when seeking to illustrate the pine and cypress,
people worry that the frost and snow might feel ashamed,
so everything they touch becomes thorny.
However, great wrongs are concealed,
but minor wrongs are not—
the way the *Chūnqiū* records events
has its own balance and measure.
An old family in Jiāngnán
compiled a genealogy (zōngpǔ).
One of their ancestors in a collateral line arranged a marriage for his son with a certain Miss Mǒu.
Later, because the distance was great and the family was poor,
they lacked the means to hold the wedding.
Fearing they would miss the appropriate time for the marriage,
they falsely reported that their son had died young (shāng),
so that the woman could marry elsewhere.
The woman subsequently starved herself to death,
unaware that their son was still alive.
This means that the circumstances surrounding her upholding chastity and sacrificing herself for virtue
are ambiguous.
However, the woman's conduct
truly deserves the praise of chastity and ardor,
and they could not bear to let it be erased.
If the facts were recorded plainly,
the paternal elder (wēng) would inevitably appear culpable.
But the *Zhōuguān* (Rites of Zhōu) states that the Matchmaker official (méishì) prohibits marriage to one who has died young.
Thus, the woman was fundamentally not obliged to die.
In the *Zēngzi Wèn*,
if a day has been set for marrying a woman,
and her parents die,
a messenger is sent to deliver the news to the woman’s family.
The commentary notes that this is done so as not to miss the opportune time for the family’s joyful event.
This indicates that in ancient times, there was a rite for withdrawing from a marriage.
Under current regulations,
if the husband travels far away
and is unheard of for three years,
the wife is permitted to report to the authorities and marry elsewhere.
This means the law includes a stipulation for divorce due to prolonged separation.
Therefore, the grandfather’s deceitful claim that his son died young,
when judged by analogy and original intent,
is still not a grave offense that absolutely must be concealed.
Yet his clansmen changed color and warned each other,
insisting that it must not be recorded plainly.
Thus, they hid the true account and wrote:
“They sent a letter reporting the early death of a young child,
and the woman’s family mistakenly heard it to mean the fiancé.”
Now, reporting the death of a young child without reason,
thousands of miles away,
and without mentioning the upcoming marriage date for the man and woman,
anyone discerning knows that such an explanation is unreasonable.
Thus, the writing is flawed.
Since humans are not sages,
how can they be without fault?
When the ancients narrated a person’s deeds,
they did not object to showing both achievements and failures.
If one now narrates the deeds of a single person
and also wishes to ensure that all the people above, below, around, front, and back of that person
are without minor blemish,
it becomes difficult.
This is called seeking perfection from all eight sides (bāmiàn qiú yuán),
which is another common flaw among literati.
Third,
the writing should aspire to match the facts,
but I have never heard of the facts aspiring to match the person [being written about].
I once saw a famous scholar write a tomb inscription (zhì) for someone.
This person probably had strong bonds of friendship and honor,
so the inscription mimicked the inscription for Liǔ Zhōu written by Hán Chānglí,
following every step and every movement,
only fearing that it might miss something.
In the middle [of the inscription], there were lamentations about the fickle nature of the world;
I already felt that this was needless moaning without any illness.
Finally, it recounted how the funeral expenses were borne by a nobleman,
and how the deceased's close relatives exhausted themselves handling the affairs.
When I inquired of the family,
the nobleman had given a somewhat generous condolence gift,
but he was not able to cover all the funeral expenses.
As for the close relatives, they merely attended the interment,
and did not handle the affairs either.
Furthermore, the sons of the deceased were all grown up,
not like Liǔ Zhōu's young, exposed, and orphaned children
who necessarily needed others to manage their affairs.
When I questioned why the facts were distorted to such an extent,
he replied:
“I was mimicking the end of Hán’s inscription for Liǔ’s grave, which says:
‘The expenses for returning the body for burial were provided by Surveillance Commissioner Péi Jūn Xínglì.
Furthermore, his cousin, Lú Zūn,
after burying Zǐhòu,
is also going to manage his family's affairs.’"
“The recording of these two individuals [in Hán’s text]
makes the writing clear, deep, and substantial.
The current inscription merely wished to resemble it.”
I once brought this up when speaking to others,
and many laughed at it.
Little do they know that when writing and imitating the ancients,
people compromise and shift the importance [of facts],
and often end up resembling this example.
This is called trimming the toes to fit the shoe (unnatural adjustment),
and it is another common failing among literati.
Fourth,
even becoming a sage through benevolence and wisdom,
Fūzǐ dared not claim for himself.
Regarding the honorable vessel of the *hú liǎn* (sacrificial vessel),
how could Zǐgòng assign that name to himself?
In praising the virtues of others,
one still fears failing to capture the truth;
how can self-promotion and critical appraisal [of one's own work]
be appropriate to become a widespread habit of boasting?
I once saw a famous scholar write a biography for someone [else].
He said of himself, “Among the scholars in my hometown,
few know the fundamentals,
only I and Mǒu Jiǎ,
have achieved success in classical scholarship.”
The aforementioned Mǒu Jiǎ
certainly had contemporary fame,
but it was not evident that he necessarily excelled in classical scholarship.
The author merely wanted to drag him in to claim fame,
highly promoting himself.
Shameful!
There was also an itinerant scholar (jiānghú yóushì)
who was famous for his poetry,
but in reality, he was not sufficient to bear the title.
However, someone whose fame and merit were far beneath that scholar
wrote a preface for his poetry collection,
relating the words used when he was asked to write the preface, saying:
“You are equally famous as Mǒu Jiǎ.
Since Mǒu Jiǎ has already written an introductory essay,
how can you not provide an appraisal?”
If the equal fame originally had no basis,
then the petitioner certainly would not have used those words,
but [the author] boasts of equal fame,
using others to advertise himself.
His face no longer knows shame!
Moreover, in classical studies, drawing comparison to Fú and Zhèng,
or in poetry, climbing up to Lǐ and Dù,
can still be excused as admiring a high mountain;
but if Mǒu Jiǎ's classical scholarship
and Mǒu Jiǎ's poetry
are fundamentally unreliable,
yet one still uses them to claim fame.
This is called privately bestowing titles upon oneself,
and it is another common failing among literati.
Fifth,
things are valued because they are rare,
and the same should be true for people.
If everyone under heaven were sages and worthies,
Kǒng and Mèng would also not be highly respected.
Pure conversation (*qīng yán*) can certainly break away from vulgarity,
but during the time of Diǎn Wǔ [the Jìn Dynasty],
it flowed everywhere.
The ancients criticized the *Jìn Shū* (History of Jìn)
for having biographies that resembled fictional narratives,
precisely because it collected many *qīng yán* [pure conversations],
but selected few of them.
Maintaining integrity in court,
being stubborn and daring to speak out—
former historians widely regarded this as praiseworthy.
After the middle of the Míng Dynasty,
due to factions and cliques,
and mutual agitation of public opinion,
who was not a scholar daring to speak?
When judging people based on this,
a superior person must be discerning.
It is certainly not appropriate
to immediately label them as possessing integrity
just because they stubbornly assert their power; this is the principle.
Our Xiàn Huángdì purified the administration,
eliminated corrupt regulations,
rectified officialdom,
and punished corruption.
This was truly a rare moment in a thousand years.
Officials serving at that time,
whether highly virtuous or merely moderately honest,
nearly became the norm;
the greedy and covetous,
all changed their ways at the mere mention of it.
This was due to the circumstances of the time.
Now, looking at biographies, inscriptions, tablets, and records,
when describing prefects, departments, and county magistrates during the Yōngzhèng years,
they highly praise them for completely refusing gifts,
rooting out long-standing abuses,
maintaining personal honesty and hardship,
and abolishing extraordinary expenditures.
These texts are indeed worthy of the Biographies of Upright Officials.
They fail to realize that at that time, being pressured by administrative ordinances,
they had no choice but to act this way.
This behavior was common to tens of thousands of people,
and is not sufficient to constitute great integrity.
How can one praise a eunuch for not being lustful?
People living in the mountains do not value firewood;
people wading through water do not treasure fish and shrimp.
Everyone knows this reasoning does not hold true,
yet those who praise others alone act otherwise.
This is called failing to comprehend the circumstances of the time,
and it is another common failing among literati.
Sixthly, it is said:
When historical writing has become an established tradition,
the existing texts are mutually cross-referenced.
There are examples like the Combined Biography of Guǎn and Yàn (Guǎn Yàn Lì Zhuàn),
yet the achievements are detailed in the Hereditary House of Qí (Qí Shìjiā);
Zhāng Ěr is given a separate heading,
but his affairs are summarized in the Biography of Chén Yú (Chén Yú Zhuàn).
It is not only that the authorial intent differs,
but also that the structure requires appropriate degrees of detail and brevity.
As for works within an anthology or collection of writings,
where biographies appear individually,
whenever related events are touched upon,
and there is no other cross-referencing chapter,
it must necessarily be detailed further,
which is also logical.
But one must weigh the facts and principles involved,
so that they are sufficient to match the person [described],
only then will it not suffer from being excessive or cumbersome.
For example, when the Táng pacified Huái Xī,
the Hán Stele (Hán Bēi) attributed the merit to Péi Dù,
which can be called appropriate.
Later, being subject to slander,
it was reassigned to Duàn Wénchāng,
causing sighing and regret for a thousand ages.
But Wénchāng deferred to Lǐ Sù,
and Sù’s achievement fundamentally cannot be ignored,
so his fault was still not extremely severe.
Suppose that on that day an unnamed minor general,
a person irrelevant to the success or failure,
had a memorial inscription erected after death,
lavishly listing the merits of Huái Xī,
then that would be utterly illogical.
Mr. Zhū (Zhū Xiānshēng) once wrote a memoir for the deceased Compiler, Lord Jiǎng (Jiǎng Jūn),
in which he narrated the essential summary of the nation’s pacification of Zhǔn and Huí, both before and after.
This was because Lord Jiǎng was the chief editor of the military strategy records,
worked diligently alone,
died just as the book was finished,
and therefore did not receive recognition for his achievements.
However, the memoir's writing was elegant and vigorous,
and scholars admired it.
Later, I saw that a certain Mid-Official Secretary (zhōng shū shè rén) died,
and someone composed a family biography for him,
which entirely plagiarized the original text of the Jiǎng Memoir.
This was because that person had served as an assistant compiler for several months,
and according to custom, was allowed to list his title and name,
but in reality, had never actually seen the book.
How is this different from the unnamed minor general
claiming the achievement of Huái Xī?
How are they different?
Yet literary men delight in collecting facts,
nearly equivalent to military officials stealing merit.
How can this be tolerated?
This is what is called the ‘same village’ burial streamer (tóng lǐ míng jīng).
In the past there was a bragging man
who never received a single appointment in his life
but liked to usurp titles.
When he was about to die,
he summoned all his acquaintances
to devise the inscription characters for his burial streamer.
Some deferred to his wishes
and borrowed high-sounding ranks, such as titles granted by precedent, or posthumous honors like Cultivated Officer (xiū zhí) or Ascended Scholar (dēng shì),
but he shook his head, displeased.
Finally, there was a humorous man
who took the names of the noble and prominent figures in his village.

He wrote in large letters: 'The coffin of so-and-so, from the same village (tóng lǐ) as the Duke of a certain state, who holds merit rank, Grand Mentor/Guardian, Palace/Cabinet positions, and Board/Court positions.'
People spread this as a joke.
Therefore, anyone who gratuitously attaches himself to the shadow [of others]
is called a tóng lǐ míng jīng.
I did not expect literary men would also imitate this;
this is another common failing of literary men.
Seventhly, it is said:
When Chén Píng assisted the Hàn dynasty,
his ambition was seen in how he distributed the sacrificial meat (shè ròu).
When Lǐ Sī caused the downfall of Qín,
the omen began with the privy rats (cè shǔ).
Deducing the conspicuous from the subtle
is indeed the profound technique of assessing men;
discovering the slight details to capture the spirit
is also the skillful application of literary writers.
But one must obtain the location of the spirit and ambition;
then it is like a famous painter
skillfully adding a single hair to the cheek.
If one merely admires the quality of ancient literary style,
and forcibly seeks out trifling details
in order to achieve similarity;
it is like seeing peach blossoms and achieving enlightenment,
and then taking peach blossoms to make rice.
How can there be any spiritual marvel remaining in that?
Furthermore, scholars recently
delight in seeking verifiable proof.
Whenever they see incomplete steles or broken stones,
or remaining texts and surviving characters,
even those not related to the main meaning,
they often use them to research ancient systems and institutions
and supplement historical omissions.
This is certainly good.
Because of this practice in writing,
they greedily seek much information,
clearly knowing redundancy is unnecessary,
yet believing it beneficial for future generations,
they research and deduce without worrying about excessive wording.
This not only means the writing lacks structure and focus,
but also consider living in this age and trying to prepare for the verification of future generations:
it is exactly like the resources of Dǒng Zé—
how can one successfully reach the end of them?
For those narrating a person, the writing should match the person;
for those narrating an event, the writing should match the event;
that is sufficient.
If anything relates to verification,
it must necessarily be inherent to the substance.
Even if it is a casual sentiment escaping [the pen],
it is precisely to capture the spirit of the person.
If one does not focus on this,
but only seeks to increase the market weight of the vegetables,
this is called drawing a snake and adding feet,
which is another common failing of literary men.
Eighthly, it is said:
Literary men are certainly capable of writing,
but the person about whom the literary man writes
is not necessarily fully capable of writing.
Writing that narrates events
is the words of the author.
Whether polished or plain,
it is dependent on what he desires,
provided it matches the event, that is all.
Writing that records speech
is not the words of the author;
whether polished or plain,
it must strive to exactly match the person's own words,
which the author cannot arbitrarily control.
Chaste and virtuous women
who understand poetry and practice rites
certainly exist.
There are those who have never studied,
perhaps originating from villages or narrow alleys,
or even hired servants or sold slave girls,
whose chastity, fidelity, filiality, and righteousness
all stem from outstanding natural disposition.
Though their substance does not shame the ancients,
their language is difficult to expect to be Confucian and refined.
Whenever I see biographies of this kind,
describing their speech,
the source is originally the Lúnyǔ and the Xiàojīng,
they incorporate the Máoshī and the Nèizé.
The writings of Liú Xiàng's Biographies,
or Cáo Zhāo's Admonitions,
it is as if these words came from their mouths,
it can be called literary.
But consider: those who are good at assisting their husbands,
why must they all know the stories of the deer carriage and the raised tray (lù chē hóng àn)?
Those who are good at teaching their sons,
must they all memorize the stories of drawing on reeds (huà dí) and making pills from bear fat (wán xióng)?
Since the literary man has a clear concept in his heart,
he makes the conduct of the inner chambers
all appear as if printed from the same block.
Rather than being polished and losing reality,
why not be plain and convey the truth?
Extending this reasoning,
famous generals rise from the ranks of the soldiers,
righteous heroes sometimes emerge from the common populace.
Their words need not be those of classical scholars;
the narrative should value exact resemblance.
Yet authors in the world
often fail to consider this point;
this is called the performance of actors (yōu líng yǎn jù).
The songs and tunes of actors,
even if performed by farmers, ruffians, servants, or slaves,
when they open their mouths, all fit the musical modes.
This is why it is called 'theatrical play' (xì).
If the pen of historians and biographers
follows and imitates this,
it is another common failing of literary men.
Ninthly:
The writings of the ancients developed into established forms
but never adhered to fixed structures.
To transmit a person's life required that it fit the person;
to narrate an event required that it fit the event.
Within the absence of fixed rules,
there was a certainty.
He who grasps the intention
will encounter it morning and evening.
He who does not grasp the intention,
but merely imitates the external form,
will fail to capture the spirit.
Previously, I compiled the biography, *Chéngxìng Zhìzhuàn* (The Chronicle of Cultivating Nature), for the former Court Attendant of Hézhōu,
Chéng Xìng. Xìng was renowned for his counsel and remonstrations,
so I gathered and recorded his memorials and proposals.
However, Xìng suffered greatly during times of chaos in his youth;
his entire family was killed.
His remembrance and mourning of his ancestors
are frequently evident in his writing.
The chapter titled *Měngxǐng* (Sudden Awakening) is especially profound and moving,
serving as a lesson in filial piety.
Therefore, I included the entire essay at the end of the biography.
A well-known scholar from his hometown praised my work, saying:
"Although the beginning contains so many memorials,
if the chapter *Měngxǐng* were absent,
it would be like a traveling ship
where the figurehead is heavy and the stern deck light.
Now, this coda
may be called skillful planning of the structure."
I playfully retorted:
If Lord Chéng originally had not composed this piece,
would this ship never be able to sail?
Generally, when private tutors lecture on the meaning of the *Four Books* and essays,
they call them "timely compositions" (shíwén),
which must follow fixed rules to conform to the format.
Since these rules are difficult to explain through abstract language,
they often use analogies to instruct the naive students.
When compared to a house,
there are the so-called framework and structure (jiānjià jiégòu);
when compared to the human body,
there are the so-called eyes, brows, muscles, and joints;
when compared to painting,
there are the so-called dotting the eyes and adding fine hairs;
when compared to geomancy (fēngshuǐ),
there are the so-called coming dragon and final resting spot (jiélǜè).
Analogies are drawn as needed.
However, to show the method to beginners
it is indeed unavoidable,
and there is no need for blame.
It is only when the ingrained habit of shíwén
is deeply embedded in the mind,
and one proceeds to examine all ancient books and writings
with this shíwén understanding,
and constantly employs the arguments used by tutors for elementary instruction,
it is then like using a chessboard to arrange pieces for the game of wéiqí (Go)—
it inevitably becomes incompatible.
This is called 'viewing the heavens from the bottom of a well,'
and it is another common failing among literati.
Tenthly:
Timely compositions (shíwén) may be critically selected and judged,
but ancient prose (gǔwén), which deals with governance and statecraft,
cannot be critically selected and judged.
If the ancients' works are to be selected and judged,
it should merely be an assessment of the writing based on the writing itself.
However, those who perform the selection and judgment
are often not people with a profound understanding of gǔwén.
The writings of the ancients
are not fully extant today.
Their preserved writings are found in historical records and biographies,
and selectors and judges
mostly gather excerpts from these records.
Yet, the editorial conventions of historical records
often involve cutting and condensing the original texts
to fit the summary format,
hence, the full scope of the textual style
is not entirely preserved.
The selectors and judges,
unaware of this fact,
mistakenly believe the original text was thus,
and proceed to comment on it.
They praise instances where the introductory material is absent
and the text abruptly starts mid-passage
as 'bizarre and extraordinary beginnings';
and instances where the remaining text has been trimmed
and immediately enters the main narrative
as 'sharp and precipitous conclusions to the chapter.'
Consequently, those who are curious but lack true knowledge
praise and admire these examples to each other,
and painstakingly strive to imitate them.
This is nearly what Zuǒ Shì (Master Zuǒ) described:
"It is not what you seek,
but what you find in Pú."
Since the middle of the Míng dynasty,
a certain type of prose, devoid of emotion and reason, yet claiming to be gǔwén, emerged.
Its beginning is unknown;
its ending is unknown.
Such authors exclusively use these inexplicable elements
to boast of their strangeness and uniqueness.
Thus, thorns and thistles grow
on the broad and level path.
Indeed, the transformation in writing is comparable to that of spirits and gods;
it may arrive suddenly
and cease abruptly.
How could such phenomena not exist?
How could they not be considered unique?
However, just like the sheer cliffs of a mountain
or the waves of water,
they accumulate power and build momentum,
arising spontaneously.
To deliberately strive to create them
is unreasonable.
Literati are curious and
easily misled.
This is called 'mistakenly learning the gait of Hándān,'
and it is another common failing among literati.
Zhèdōng Scholarship
Although the scholarship of Zhèdōng (Eastern Zhèjiāng)
originated from Wùyuán,
since the time of the Three Yuán (Sānyuán),
most scholars honored the Lù family of Jiāngxī.
However, they were thorough in their study of the classics and ancient works,
and absolutely did not engage in abstract discussions of moral nature (déxìng).
Therefore, they did not contradict the teachings of Zhū Zǐ (Zhū Xī).
Later, Wáng Zǐ (Master Wáng) Yángmíng
proclaimed Mèng Zǐ's idea of innate knowledge (liángzhī),
which again came into conflict with Zhū Zǐ.
The Liú family of Jíshān,
starting from liángzhī, elaborated on exercising caution in solitude (shèndú).
Although they differed from Zhū Zǐ,
they did not attack him.
The Huáng family of Lízhōu
came from the school of Liú of Jíshān,
and opened up the study of classics and history for the Wàn brothers.
Even until Quán Zǔwàng
and his contemporaries, they still preserved this spirit,
honoring Lù but not contradicting Zhū.
Only the Máo family of Xīhé,
in explaining the doctrine of liángzhī,
achieved considerable insight;
but due to sectarian bias,
they inevitably attacked [Zhū Zǐ] excessively.
Even the people of Zhèdōng did not entirely agree with this.
The world respects Gù Tínglín as the Confucian master who inaugurated the current dynasty (Qīng),
but his scholarship belongs to Zhèxī (Western Zhèjiāng).
Few know that at the same time there was Huáng Lízhōu,
who hailed from Zhèdōng.
Although he stood alongside Gù Shì,
he honored Wáng and Liú above,
and opened the path for the Two Wàn below.
Compared to Gù Shì,
his source was older and his influence longer lasting.
Gù Shì honored Zhū,
while Huáng Shì honored Lù.
However, since they were not specialist lecturers
each holding sectarian views,
they mutually respected and admired each other,
and did not attack or criticize each other.
A scholar cannot be without a guiding principle,
but must absolutely not have sectarian bias.
Therefore, the paths of Zhèdōng and Zhèxī
proceeded in parallel without contention.
Zhèdōng values specialization,
while Zhèxī values extensive learning and refinement.
Each follows and practices according to its habit.
The study of Heaven, human nature, and destiny (tiānrén xìngmìng)
cannot be lectured upon abstractly.
Therefore, Sīmǎ Qiān based his work on Dǒng Shì's theories of tiānrén xìngmìng,
and created a book for statecraft.
Confucian scholars wish to honor moral nature
but take abstract discussions of principle and righteousness (yìlǐ) as their achievement.
This is why Sòng learning (Sòngxué) is criticized by the great refined scholars.
The Master (Kǒngzǐ) said:
"If I wished to entrust my ideas to abstract words,
it would be inferior to seeing them manifest profoundly and clearly in practical actions."
This is why the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals) is used for statecraft.
A sage like Kǒngzǐ,
whose words were a celestial bell,
still did not rely on abstract language to achieve victory—
how much less should others?
Therefore, those who are skilled in discussing tiānrén xìngmìng
never fail to be relevant to human affairs.
In the scholarship of the Three Dynasties (Sāndài),
they only knew history (*shǐ*) and did not know classics (*jīng*).
This was because it focused on human affairs.
Later generations valued classical studies (*jīngshù*)
because they were merely the history of the Three Dynasties.
Recent Confucians, when discussing the classics,
seem to believe that there is a separate entity called righteous principle
apart from human affairs.
The scholarship of Zhèdōng,
when discussing nature and destiny, must investigate history.
This is why it is outstanding.
The differences between Zhū and Lù,
the warring factions of their schools,
are the prison of a thousand ages,
and also the thorny forest of a thousand ages.
Investigating why they argued so vehemently,
it is only because they indulged in empty talk that was irrelevant to human affairs.
If one knows that historical studies are rooted in the *Chūnqiū*,
and knows that the *Chūnqiū* is meant to manage the world,
then one knows that nature and destiny cannot be discussed with empty words,
and those who lecture must have practical involvement in affairs;
not only will they have no factions to uphold,
but they will also have nothing by which to uphold factions.
Although the teachings of the Zhèdōng school
did not differ in origin and flow,
the circumstances they encountered were different.
Therefore, what was manifested to the world:
Yángmíng obtained it as practical achievement (*shìgōng*),
Jíshān obtained it as fidelity and righteousness (*jiéyì*),
Lízhōu obtained it as reclusion,
and the Wàn brothers obtained it as classical scholarship and historical judgment.
Although the transmission came from a single source,
their outward appearances were profoundly different,
because each had their own practical affairs and achievements.
Those who neglect practical affairs,
but only speak empty words about moral nature,
and speak empty words about inquiry and learning,
are like yellow grass and white reeds,
extremely alike in appearance,
and thus are compelled to distinguish their factions
in order to demonstrate their own view.
Therefore, only shallow scholars contend over factions.
Someone asked: Are practical achievements and moral integrity
truly comparable to literary works? I replied:
Historical studies exist to record the age;
they are certainly not empty words or writings.
Furthermore, take the Six Classics (*Lù Jīng*);
they all originated from Kǒngzǐ (Confucius).
Former scholars believed that none of them surpassed the *Chūnqiū* in merit,
precisely because it closely matched the human affairs of its time.
As for later people who talk about writings,
abandoning the present and seeking the past,
abandoning human affairs and discussing nature and Heaven,
then I cannot understand them.
A scholar who does not know this principle
is unfit to speak of historical studies.
Women's Learning.
The *Zhōu Guān* mentions female invocators and female scribes (*nǚ zhù nǚ shǐ*);
the Hàn system had internal court historians (*nèi qǐjū zhù*).
It is likely that women had some practical uses
for written words in antiquity.
The term "Women's Learning"
is found in the Inner Offices section of the *Tiānguān*.
Virtue, speech, demeanor, and work (*dé yán róng gōng*):
what it encompassed was broad,
unlike later ages which only regarded literary arts as learning.
However, the *Yì* instructs them to hold the correct position internally;
the *Lǐ* prescribes women's work in silk and hemp;
the *Chūnqiū Zhuàn* speaks of apportioning tasks and offering achievements;
a chapter in the *Xiǎo Yǎ* speaks of managing food and drink.
Thus, the professional duties of women
can also be roughly known.
The categories of Women's Learning
are virtue, speech, and proper demeanor.
Zhèng's commentary says:
"Speech means issuing commands."
Unless one is skilled in canonical rites
and practiced in writing,
it is insufficient to be called learning.
Thus we know that reciting the *Shī* (Odes) and practicing the *Lǐ* (Rites)—
the women's learning of antiquity—
was only slightly inferior to that of men.
Although the writings of later women
tend slightly toward ornamentation,
when tracing their source,
it should be understood that they received instruction.
Women's Learning was managed by the Jiǔpín (Nine Concubines),
and teaching methods were carried out within the imperial palace;
internally, reaching imperial concubines,
and externally, extending to the feudal lords’ territories.
Although the Six Statutes (*Liù Diǎn*) do not detail this,
it can be inferred by analogy.
The teacher of the *Gě Tán* poem
is recorded in the *Fēng Shī* (Airs of the States).
The gentle instruction given by the governess
is handed down in the *Nèi Zé*.
Examining all the internal and external commentaries of the *Chūnqiū*,
the wives of the feudal lords
and the inner wives of the high officials
were all able to speak eloquently and narrate historical precedents,
brilliant and well-structured.
Regarding the omen of prosperity reaching its peak,
Dèng Màn thoroughly derived it from the Way of Heaven;
regarding the principle of 'profit and persistence' (*lì zhēn*),
Mù Jiāng skillfully interpreted it based on the fundamental origin of *qián*;
the virtuous wife of Lǔ Mùbó
left behind exemplary words as instruction;
the inner mistress of the Qí Sītú
was conferred a title for her observance of rites;
when the judicial officer (*Shìshī*) died peacefully by the window,
his wife composed a funeral eulogy;
when the state warrior's soul returned from the battlefield,
his widow offered mournful words during the suburban condolence.
Down to the steady flow of spring water,
eloquently chanted in verses expressing thoughts of return;
and the swallows flying up and down,
sadly sung in the poem escorting the returning bridal attendant.
In all these canonical rites and statutes,
literary splendor and refined conduct,
what difference was there from famous ministers and high officials?
However, all these cases were involved in related affairs,
and only incidentally appear in records;
they were not specifically emphasized.
If they had appeared in later ages,
historians would certainly have dedicated entire chapters
and compiled them into the biographies of notable women.
Then, like the stories of Cáo Zhāo and Cài Yǎn,
their magnificent brilliance
would have been ten times greater than the writings of Liú and Fàn.
Thus, we know that Women's Learning was also lost in later ages.
During the flourishing of the Three Dynasties,
it was equally observed alongside the ceremonial regulations for men,
all following established precedents,
and was initially not considered remarkable or unusual.
After the *Chūnqiū* period,
when officials and teachers separated their functions,
learning was no longer restricted to official duties,
and writing flowed into private authorship.
Those men who were outstanding
all composed the works of famous schools
according to what suited their nature and temperament.
As for descending to rhetoric and style,
they also, by virtue of superior talent and beauty,
showcased their literary splendor.
And the unique intelligence and extraordinary abilities of women,
concentrated in quiet atmospheres,
also thereby manifested particularly through literature,
and were praised by people past and present.
This was merely the result of the trends of the time.
However, the flourishing of Confucian doctrines during the Hàn court,
Bān Gù said, was caused by the pursuit of profit and position.
Because the government regulations emphasized it,
talented individuals strove competitively.
The scholarly work of the literati
was equivalent to a farmer cultivating his fields—
this was naturally the case.
As for women's writings,
they were not their professional duty.
Those who occasionally excelled
did so due to superior natural talent,
not because they competed in cultural trends
or rushed after fame.
The song of *Fáng Zhōng* from Táng Shān,
Bān Jī's rhapsody on *Cháng Xìn*,
the standard and transformed forms of the *Fēng* and the *Yǎ*,
originated in the imperial palace.
Since these matters related to state affairs,
historical records included them.
The remaining pieces of poetry were scarce,
and those transmitted were few.
What is recorded in the *Yì Wén* (Treatise on Literature)
can provide a rough view.
As for the popular *Yuèfǔ* songs,
where sound and poetry were emulated—
*Mù Lán* going on military service,
*Kǒng Què* facing separation,
as well as the verses of picking mulberries on the roadside (*Mò Shàng*),
and the verses of fennel beneath the mountain,
the seasonal *Bái Zhù*,
and the fragrant *Zǐ Yè* songs—
whose sound is expansive and slow,
and whose meter is soft and delicate—
these are attributed to anonymous ancient lyrics from the two Hàn dynasties
ending with the various imitations of the Six Dynasties.
They are all verses simulated by literati,
who projected their sentiments into others.
Although the emotions are entrusted to young women and men,
the meaning is truly rooted in the tradition of *fēng* (airs).
Therefore, their language is often unrestrained,
and they do not view male and female exchanges as objectionable.
As for verses of the women's chambers
that have been occasionally transmitted,
regardless of whether the person was chaste or wanton,
their expressions all maintained boundaries.
Wénjūn
was a woman who eloped wantonly,
yet her *Bái Tóu* (White Head) only criticized Xiāngrú.
Cài Yǎn
was a woman who lost her virtue,
yet when transcribing books, she earnestly declined ten officials.
Others who lived normally and smoothly,
and those known for their chastity and integrity,
whenever they produced writings,
were invariably quiet as still water,
and gentle as a clear breeze.
Although their literary talent came from natural skill,
their standard of thought never exceeded the threshold of the home.
In this regard, although Women's Learning differed from antiquity,
it still did not contradict moral instruction.
(Airs of the States),
were all derived from the imitation by poets. If we verify this using the poems and writings of the Hàn, Wèi, and Six Dynasties periods,

there is absolutely nothing doubtful about it. The principle is the same throughout history; it is impossible that the sons and daughters of antiquity could spontaneously compose polished verses, while subsequent scholars strive hard yet ultimately fail to achieve it.
It is like a male actor,
portraying a virtuous maiden upon the stage,
who ultimately cannot resemble the refined simplicity of the boudoir.
Those who are ignorant do not understand this principle,
and mistakenly assert that even the sons and daughters of antiquity
were able to spontaneously compose polished verses,
thus claiming that women were naturally suited to *fēngyă* (Airs and Elegances).
This is like seeing actors performing ancient events upon the stage,
and mistakenly doubting that the ancient people’s every movement and stillness

must have been preceded by songs. (The texts of the songs performed by actors depicting ancient stories are exactly like the interwoven commentaries and encomiums found in historical biographies. They contain thoughts that are intentional and definitely not spoken aloud; they also contain the views of observers, absolutely not originating from the character themselves, which the lyrics do not avoid. Therefore, a *jūnzǐ* may sometimes approach self-praise, and a *xiăoxiăo* (mean person) may sometimes approach self-mockery, allowing the audience to read it like a history book while also gaining the sense of chanting and sighing. The form ought to be like this and is not objectionable. If they truly came from the mouths of *jūnzǐ* and *xiăoxiăo*, there would be no such principle.) The words of men and women in the *Guófēng* and the words that ancient people used to imitate men and women ought to be viewed exactly in this way. If one insists they truly came from the mouths of men and women, setting aside the fact that the promiscuous would never expose themselves in such a manner, even the chaste would never profane themselves so much.
In the past, Bān’s (Bān Gù) *Hànshū* (History of the Former Hàn Dynasty),
was incomplete when he died.
An imperial edict commanded his younger sister, Cáo Zhāo (Bān Zhāo),
to personally proceed to the Dōngguān (Eastern Hall)
and follow through to complete it.
Subsequently, high officials and ministers,
bearing gifts to request instruction (The great scholar Mă Róng followed her, receiving instruction on the punctuation and reading of the *Hànshū*.),
may be said to have expanded upon what had been absent for a thousand ages.
However, specialized learning and unique scholarship
have deep familial origins.
Writing cannot express everything,
and unless one is the right person, the knowledge cannot be received.
Furthermore, when Fú Qín first established schools,
widely appointing erudites and classical masters,
the Wŭjīng (Five Classics) were generally available,
but the *Zhōuguān* (Rites of Zhōu) had been lost.
The erudites submitted a memorial,
stating that Sòng Shì, the mother of the Grand Minister of Ceremonies Wéi Chĕng,
possessed the family tradition of the sounds and meanings of the *Zhōuguān*.
An edict commanded that in her family lecture hall,
120 students be appointed,
who received instruction from behind a crimson curtain,
and Sòng Shì was granted the noble title Xuānwén Jūn.
This also expanded upon what had been absent for a thousand ages.
However, at that time, scholarship and documents
flourished south of the river (Jiāngzuŏ).
The Fú clan occupied the territory east of the mountains (Shāndōng).
Lost classics and discontinued scholarship
fortunately survived with the daughter of a family of hereditary scholars.
This was not something that famous officials and ministers could forcibly access.
These two mothers,
both accomplished the tasks of men while having the bodies of women.
For transmitting classics and compiling history
concerns the Way and methods of Heaven and humanity.
Fearing that this knowledge would be buried and lost,
the rulers of the age were compelled to break convention and treat them with great respect;
it was not because their talent and brilliance were dazzling
or startled common society.
Similarly, regarding securing the frontier, there was Madame Qiáo Xĭ (Xĭ Fūrén),
and regarding assisting the Mandate, there was the Princess of Píngyáng, Chái Zhŭ.
These, too, are rare occurrences throughout the ages.
One (Qiáo Xĭ Fūrén) was specially allowed to establish an administrative headquarters
and appoint subordinate officials;
the other (Píngyáng Princess) was honored with feather banners, drums, and wind instruments,
and guards wielding ceremonial swords.
To think that the measures taken by the rulers of Suí and Táng were inappropriate
is certainly wrong;
but if one insists that ordinary women must take these examples as their standard,
not only is this wrong,
but there is also no such principle.
The Jìn people admired the Xúan (Mysterious) school of thought,
indulged their emotions, and acted unrestrainedly.
Men scorned the Six Arts,
and women likewise elegantly prized Qingyán (Pure Talk).
The conversation concerning the release of the walking screen,
and the game of the bride advising the general,
although major integrity was not lost,
the moral teachings (*míngjiào*) were utterly ruined.
Critics believe that because the Sixteen Kingdoms split apart
and the people suffered terribly,
they instead blamed *qīngtán* (Pure Talk) for destroying the rites and teachings;
this is truly an argument that delves into the root cause.
The great families of Wáng and Xiè,
although they violated the rites and laws,
yet their pure talk and famous theories
had very profound insight;
since they had already studied the Rú tradition,
they also fully understood the Xúan doctrines.
Compared to the learning of scholars,
their mistakes were like those of the middle-grounders
who drifted into being the reckless and simplistic (closer to heterodoxy, not closer to courtesans or actors).
They were not merely those who could arrange five-character or seven-character lines
and boast themselves superior to the Four Virtues and Three Obediences.
As for those whose lovely scenery
involved polite exchanges with guests,
meticulously detailing every nuance,
vividly capturing appearances,
using makeup to enhance their beauty,
and promoting themselves to adorn their false reputation—
although the Jìn people were considered empty and unrestrained,
if they had seen such things,
