they would have gathered their wives and children and fled (The great families of Wáng and Xiè, though violating the rites, were truly educated and learned, hence their thoughts were profound and far-reaching. They were not comparable to the shallow, vulgar, and fame-seeking gifted scholars and beauties).
From Táng and Sòng onwards,
the discernible talents of women
amounted to no more than spring boudoir laments and autumn grievances,
or the flourishing and withering of flowers and grasses.
Short poems and minor compositions
transmit their lofty refinement.
Occasionally, there were separate literary works,
such as the *Nǚ Lúnyŭ* (Analects for Women) by Sòng Shànggōng,
and the *Nǚ Xiàojīng* (Classic of Filial Piety for Women) by Hóu Zhèng Shì.

Although their talent and knowledge were unavoidably pedantic and shallow (Desiring to write women’s instructions, they failed to emulate the decorum of Cáo Dàjiā’s *Nǚ Jiè* (Admonitions for Women), and instead rashly imitated the Sacred Classics, akin to the hypothetical questions in the *Qī Lín*, utterly nonexistent),
their direction was still close to elegance and correctness.
The literary world praised them,
forgiving them because their intent was commendable (This is because the women's learning of the ancients had been lost, hence the achievements of those who were determined were merely this).
Lĭ Yì’ān’s (Lĭ Qīngzhào) compiling and rubbing of bronzes and stones,
and Guăn Dàoshēng’s exquisite skill in calligraphy and painting,
are rarely matched by subsequent generations.
However, the inscribed jade and bells
merely assisted in inventorying and verification at Húzhōu;
and the masterful skill in brush and ink
was merely aided by observation and discussion with the Imperial Academician (*Chéngzhĭ*).
We have never heard of the daughter-in-law of a Prime Minister
being allowed to join the three school sections to discuss literature;
(Lĭ Yì’ān and Zhào Míngchéng compiled the *Jīn Shí Lù*, and Míngchéng was still at the Imperial Academy, hence the remark.) nor of the wife of a Hánlín Academician
being able to share the whisk-and-talk sessions with the Nine Chief Ministers.
Although literature is said to be a public tool,
the separation between men and women is truly the great defense of the ages.
The awe-inspiring moral principles and standards of conduct—
how can they be falsely accused?
From Táng and Sòng until the former Míng Dynasty,
the national system did not abolish female entertainers.
When high officials entered the court for duty,
there were green sleeves and incense burners;
when officials hosted banquets,
red skirts were frequently seen assisting with the wine.
Under the *wútóng* trees by the golden well,
the post stations held autumn affairs of sensibility;
amid orchid musk and heavenly fragrance,
the Qŭjiāng River saw spring oaths of intimacy.
What is recorded in the annals
is indeed detailed.
Furthermore, due to the tyrannical governance of the previous dynasty,
whenever officials were stripped of rank and had their property confiscated,
it extended to their wives and children,
leading to great families of poetry and rites
mostly sinking into the northern quarter (prostitutes' district).
Among those who excelled in both beauty and skill,
and whose intelligence specialized in songs and poetry,
the capital’s scholars and officials
followed them with reciprocal verses;
generally, their affections were as endless as spring grass,
and their thoughts as far-reaching as autumn maples.
The exchange of gifts was akin to social acquaintance,
and their ardor led to intimacy and sweetness.
Poetic sentiment was expansive and unrestrained,
without fear of suspicion;
the compositions of the inner chambers
drummed and chimed outside the women’s quarters,
and its path was naturally such.
Moreover, although vocal poetry flourished during the Three Táng periods,
the surviving poems by women are few.
If we calculate based on that era,
those whose writings are most abundant
are none other than Lĭ Yĕ, Xuē Tāo, and Yú Xuánjī, three individuals,
and others cannot compare to them.
Thus, we know that female Daoist priests and courtesans
had numerous writings due to the frequency of their social exchanges,
while established families adhering to rites and law
had few compositions, constrained by the warning against non-decorum.
This is also clear evidence.
frequently associate with famous literati,
exchanging poems and verses.
The intention behind their composition,
combines that of spouses and friends;
this can be called skillful use of pretense.
Furthermore, when the ancients yearned for their lord or remembered a friend,
they often entrusted their deep feelings to the passion between men and women.
If poets satirized wickedness and depravity,
their writings would speak in the voice of a beautiful, mad person.
Although these three types are distinct,
their paths are slightly similar.
When evaluating rhymed compositions,
one must know how to make these distinctions.
For loyal ministers and righteous friends,
sincerity is hidden and leaps forth, preserving earnest fidelity.
When satirizing evil and hating wickedness,
meaning beyond the words reveals sorrow and distress.
When describing self-exile or abandonment,
the success or failure of the poetry vastly differs.
If the original intent is not clear,

the skill or awkwardness of the phrasing is greatly divergent. (If the woman-seeking in *Lí Sāo* is taken as genuine emotion, the language becomes disordered; if the poems about Zhēn and Wěi in the *Guó Fēng* are taken as self-narration, they are straightforward and tasteless. When treated as allegorical pretexts, the literary sentiment naturally deepens.)
Therefore, the poems of nameless men and women
perhaps contain knowledge of the principles of Tài jí and Yīn Yáng,
existing between Heaven and Earth;
thus, the wise see wisdom in them,
and the benevolent naturally see benevolence.
Famous courtesans who excelled in poetry
also understood these ancient meanings;
they, in turn, transposed the reality of mutual affection between men and women
onto the restrained and profound language of poets.
Therefore, their surviving words
are refined and principled,
genuine yet not vulgar.
Having been passed down for a thousand years,
they are able to shine in the historical records,
and cannot be dismissed because of the person who wrote them.
However, establishing language must follow conventions,
and women differ from men.
For instance, though the funeral dirge *Xiè Lù* is excellent,
it is only suitable when performed by the pallbearer.
Although the boatman's song is marvelous,
it is only appropriate when sung by a boatwoman.
Their [courtesans’] act of presenting gifts to Lǐ and Zhāng,
is due to the environment they find themselves in.
For women of respectable families in their chambers,
even their private speech is rarely heard;
how could such words
reach outside the gate in exchanged songs?
Indeed, the performance areas of the Jiàofāng (Imperial Music Bureau),
though not established by the laws of the ancient kings,
were actually continuous practices inherited from previous dynasties.
Unless one belongs to the group of masters from Lián and Luò (Neo-Confucians),
what harm is there in minor virtues having some flexibility?
Thus, there were assistants who achieved fame and brought aid to the state,
streams of loyalty and integrity,
scholars of literature and morality,
and lofty recluses and hermits;
they often found an outlet for their leisure sentiments,
recorded in books.
The prohibitions imposed by the state,
did not significantly detract from their great virtue.
However, while literature can be learned from the ancients,
institutions and regulations must follow the current era.
The rites and teachings of Our Dynasty are meticulous and strict,
distinguishing suspicions and doubts with caution.
Since the Three Dynasties,
there has never been such solemnity.
Since the Imperial Palace banned female musicians,
and the government offices discontinued the Jiàofāng,
there is no longer any context in the relationship between men and women throughout the realm
that can be used as a pretext.
Those who engage in roaming prostitution or lodging with courtesans,
profiting from sex and selling their services—
all violate the strict statutes of the law,
and receiving a beating cannot exempt one from punishment. (Officials and students are considered to have suffered a loss of proper conduct and shall never again be employed.)
Although there might be leaks (oversights) in the net that can swallow a boat,
not all are necessarily caught in the legal records;
yet the superior person keeps the penalty in mind,
so how can he intentionally constrain himself by involving the chief justice?
I often see famous literati,
whose poetry manuscripts are carved onto printing blocks.
Before examining the complete collection,
one first reads the titles.
Sometimes they record beautiful sentiments of courtesans,
sometimes they document verse exchanges in the brothels.
They claim for themselves to be refined, dashing, and unrestrained,
believing the ancients were the same.
They do not know that living in the present age,
and being a person of today,
if one is not adept at adhering to the prohibitions,
what point is there in discussing literature and writing?
Zhōu Gōng established the rites:
people of the same surname shall not intermarry.
Suppose someone born after the time of Zhōu
claimed that in high antiquity there was no distinction between men and women,
and thus violated human relationships,
acting like beasts,
and asserted that the ancients did this—
would that be acceptable?
Indeed, talent requires study,
and study values insight.
Talent without study
is considered minor cleverness.
Minor cleverness without insight
is considered lack of talent.
People who lack talent yet possess minor cleverness,
stop at nothing.

They treat frivolousness and flippancy as elegance and refinement (Refinement means correctness, contrary to vulgarity. Habitual influence of customs is called vulgarity. Frivolity and coarseness are all vulgar. Coarse vulgarity may not harm public morality, but frivolous vulgarity is a crime against refinement.),
and treat ostentatious self-promotion as reputation (Those who crave fame are never not vulgar.).
They flaunt themselves to the younger generation,
causing license among men and women.
The corruption in people's hearts and customs,
the resulting evils are too numerous to mention.
Indeed, lightheartedness arising from self-pride,
was something the ancients possessed.
But self-promoting ostentation flowing out of women,
was something previous generations did not have.
This happens because their reality is insufficient, yet they strive greedily for fame.
Though they are not men, they rely on others to gain importance.
Any man with ambition
would be ashamed to do this.
They reach a point where relationship boundaries are severed,
and the etiquette of giving and receiving is abandoned.
They immediately use compositions that indulge in romantic excess,
pretending they belong to the realm of scholarly communication,
consequently seeking to be ranked first or second in public examinations,
and asking for critical appraisals in monthly reviews.
Such actions in brothels and singing quarters,
frequently occurred in former generations.
But for quiet maidens and chamber beauties,
since the beginning of Heaven and Earth,
we have not heard of such ritual practice.
The learning of women in antiquity,
such as female historians, female invocators, and female shamans,
was based on their specific occupations,
roughly similar to how men specialized in an art and maintained an office.
As for general learning,
the essentials were virtue (Dé), speech (Yán), demeanor (Róng), and work (Gōng).
Virtue is subtle and hard to define (Only saints like Rèn and Sì can be called fully virtuous.),
and work is easy to cite, such as silk-reeling and weaving, which applies to scholars and commoners alike.
As for their learning that approached literature,
the two areas of speech and demeanor were the most important.
Indeed, from the inner rules of the family,
up to the Son of Heaven, feudal lords, high ministers, grand masters, and officials,
all studied ritual deportment.
Regarding court audiences, formal visits, funerals, and sacrifices,
the empresses, consorts, wives, and noble ladies
all had official duties.
If they did not research and prepare daily,
how could they perform correctly when the time came?
The classical masters of the Hàn dynasty,
often spoke of ritual using only sentence structure and textual segments.
It was still fortunate that Xú Shēng,
was good at illustrating demeanor,
because dignified bearing and movements
could not be fully conveyed merely by recitation and speaking.
Thus, women's demeanor must be practiced according to ritual,
a fact that even great Confucian scholars of later ages

often failed to hear about. (Just observing the recorded words of Jìng Jiāng, so strict in ritual law, shows what later classical masters and great Confucians could not attain. As for women's speech focusing on diplomatic discourse, in antiquity, private speech did not pass outside the curtained doorway; what was called diplomatic discourse was also necessarily required by ritual texts. Kǒng Zǐ said: "If you do not study the *Shī*, you have nothing to speak.")
Those who are good at diplomatic discourse
have never failed to be deeply versed in the *Shī* (Just look at the diplomatic speeches of women in the Spring and Autumn period; they are graceful and full of subtle meaning.)
We therefore know that the learning of women in antiquity
necessarily proceeded from ritual to comprehend poetry (Without ritual, one does not know demeanor; without poetry, one does not know speech).
The mastery of the Six Arts might have been something they also possessed (like Mù Jiāng discussing the *Yì*).
When women’s learning was lost in later ages,
those who were bright, intelligent, and knew literature
began to claim that women could combine the studies of scholars,
and the appearance of self-satisfaction was visible on their faces.
They do not know that women originally possessed their own learning,
and that learning must take ritual as its root.
Abandoning their fundamental profession and wrongly relying on poetry,
and furthermore, that poetry is not what the ancients meant by practicing diplomatic speech and being skilled in women's discourse—
this, even speaking in terms of study,
is like a farmer abandoning his field,
or an official losing the introductory gift needed for foreign missions.
How can this be proof of women's learning?
Alas!
The learning of women in antiquity
necessarily used ritual to comprehend poetry.
The learning of women today,
conversely, ruins ritual because of poetry.
When ritual boundaries collapse,
the state of people's hearts and customs is beyond recovery.
This is certainly caused by dissolute literati
promoting wicked theories to mislead them.
Those who truly understand women’s learning,
view these dissolute literati
as mere dirt and filth (Dissolute literati are shallow and crude in their learning, which those who truly study can easily see through.).
Why would they allow themselves to be deceived by them?
Adorning the fashionable four-horse carriage,
becoming the unsurpassed of the women's chambers.
Those who use this pretext to evaluate them either praise them excessively beyond the reality or alter and decorate their writings. ,
It is merely cherishing their beauty.
Unprincipled literati,
their intentions cannot be inquired into.
Alas!
She herself considers it talent and flaunts it,
while others consider it beauty and cherish her for it.
Not knowing the truth and rushing toward it,
is foolish.
Faintly knowing the reason,
and yet still rushing toward it,
is the foolishness of the foolish!
The best appellation for women,
is called the Jìng Nǚ,
for quietness is close to learning.
Why are those of today hailed as cáinǚ,
why are they so agitated?
Why is there such excessive commotion? Alas!
Postscript to the Fù Xué Piān
The chapter on Fù Xué,
is meant to rescue the decadent customs,
maintain the moral education of the age,
discipline the fundamental human relationships,
and distinguish between human and beast.
Truly, it was done out of necessity,
not because of a fondness for argument.
Commentators say that the interpretation of the *Shī* differs from the understanding of Zhū Zǐ,
thus violating the official regulations.
They do not know that consulting the ancient meanings across the various classics,
is not necessarily against the official regulations.
Moreover, speaking logically and reasonably,
if ignorant common men and women,
spontaneously composed verses,
far surpassed the literati of later generations,
the difference between ancient and modern times should not be so radical.
Furthermore, the span from the Spring and Autumn period (Chūnqiū) to the Two Hàns (Liǎng Hàn),
is similar to the span from today back to the Liǎng Hàn.
The poetry and prose of the Hàn rén,
that which remains today,
is all lofty, ancient, and pristine;
people consequently suspect that the talent of the Hàn era,
far surpassed later generations.
However, observing the various collections of bronze and stone inscriptions,
the writings of the Hàn rén,
which were not recorded on bamboo or silk,
but were transmitted to later generations via bronze and stone inscriptions,
actually contain much that is tangled, overly verbose, and crude,
which is not much different from modern people who cannot write well.
Thus it is known that the Hàn rén were not all talented writers;
those transmitted were merely the exceptionally good ones.
The transmitted writings of the Sān Dài,
should also be like this.
If one insists that the spontaneous utterances of the common men and women of that time,
were all sufficient to transmit classical teachings,
how can that be reasonable?
The interpretations of Zhū Zǐ,
were originally merely intended to preserve one’s own theory,
and should ideally cause no great harm.
But recently, unlearned followers,
citing them as evidence to entice ignorant scholars and women,
overstepping boundaries and casting off restraints,
eliminating the distinction between human and beast;
then the error in interpreting the *Shī*,
how is it different from misinterpreting the *Jīn Téng* and leading to Jū Shè’s regency,
or misinterpreting the *Zhōu Lǐ* and leading to the Qīng Miáo policy?
How could Zhū Zǐ have known that the resulting disaster would reach such an extreme?
Even those who argued against Zhū Zǐ in his day,
also did not know that the resulting disaster would reach this extreme.
Traditionally, poetry valued the Fēng Yǎ.
Even the *Shī Huà* of the Táng and Sòng dynasties,
although their discussions of poetry were often shallow and commonplace,
merely compared skill and crudity,
and compared phrases and sentences,
things the ancients would disdain to speak of.
Those unlearned followers,
recklessly labeled it with the term Fēng Qù,
completely erasing the distinctions between evil and righteous, chaste and lewd, right and wrong, gain and loss,
and making people seek only Fēng Qù.
They even say that the poems about gathering orchids and presenting peonies,
had little relevance, yet the Master (Fūzǐ) recorded them,
using this to prove the theory of Fēng Qù.
Ignorant scholars and women,
instantly forget modesty and restraint,
following the trend and becoming dissipated.
They thus treat the Six Classics (Liù Jīng) as tools for guiding lust and promoting debauchery,
which is to criticize the Sages and disregard the law.
Someone might say:
"The *Shī Xù* truly cannot be entirely discarded.
But to claim that the common people of antiquity,
were unable to compose poetry,
consider the songs of laborers,
and the invocations of cart drivers.
All came from the common populace,
their verses are recited even today.
Are historical records deceiving us?"
I reply:
These were the proverbs and sayings of that time,
not the refined language.
Just as earlier Confucians said regarding the decrees of Yīn Pán and Zhōu Gào,
they were rooted in local customs.
Having passed through a long period of time,
they changed into something ancient and obscure,
hence their words are often strange and rugged;
unlike the Odes of the States (Fēng Shī), which are peaceful, solemn, and refined,
having come from literary scholars,
just like the writings of the *Diǎn* and *Mó*,
which, though ancient, are not difficult to recite and understand.
Given the peaceful refinement of the Fēng Shī,
compared with the folk songs and proverbs,
they are absolutely different.
This further shows that the verses of men and women in the Guó Fēng,
all came from the satire of poets,
and were not things that ignorant common men and women could compose.
In this case, the theory of Fēng Qù,
does not need to be attacked to be defeated,
nor taught to be eliminated.
As for the Fù Xué of the ancients,
although different from that of men,
regarding the molding through ritual and the cultivation through music,
from the highest, such as kings, dukes, queens, and consorts,
down to the talented individuals among the common people,
men and women universally followed and practiced it.
Indeed, among the Four Virtues (Sì Dé),
without ritual, one cannot achieve proper demeanor,
and without poetry, one cannot speak properly.
The teaching of poetry thus leads to music,
thus the transformation inspired by the *Guān Jū* arose in the inner chambers,
and all couples under Heaven became well-ordered.
After the Sān Dài,
elementary learning was abandoned,
and the Confucians had many divergent theories from their masters;
Fù Xué was abandoned,
and scholars rarely achieved the goal of ordering their households.
When the masters' theories diverged,
heterodox teachings were able to disrupt the established education,
which has been regarded as a problem since antiquity.
As for the abandonment of learning for couples,
people merely say that household governance is not greatly cultivated.
How could they know that a thousand years later,
there would arise unlearned followers,
who created the theory of Fēng Qù,
thereby causing women of the inner chambers to be unsettled in their righteous roles,
yearning for the fame sought by base scholars.
This disaster is more severe than floods or savage beasts.
Can a Jūnzǐ who values reputation and righteousness,
fail to worry about the moral order of the world?
Formerly, Lord Ōuyáng Shì was troubled by the spread of Buddhism (Fójiào),
and wished to restore the governance of the former kings,
to consolidate the vital essence itself.
This is why the *Běn Lùn* was composed.
Now, unlearned followers,
use heterodox theories to bewitch women of the inner chambers.
This is also because Fù Xué is not cultivated,
hence women of the inner chambers are easily misled.
Although there are warnings against women exhibiting improper ritual conduct,
adhering to ritual and understanding poetry,
this is like daily necessities—food and drink,
which cannot be abandoned for a moment.
Some assume that women's duties are limited to silk, hemp, and domestic chores,
and that writing and prose should not be prioritized.
This is going too far.
Truly, intelligence and exceptional talent,
bestowed by Heaven, originally makes no distinction between men and women,
like flowers and blooms on plants,
or pearls and jade in mountains and rivers.
Even the Sages never failed to cherish them.
How can they be suppressed?
One should properly help them reach fruition.
Thus, if a woman is naturally simple and unadorned,
it is enough that she roughly understands domestic teachings,
and does not fall into error.
If she is exceptionally talented and knowledgeable in books,
one must use what she understands,
to elaborate the profound source of poetry and ritual,
advancing her toward the fundamental principles of the ancients.
Bān Jī, Wéi Mǔ—
why must she be far removed from them?
Now, if one takes Bān Jī and Wéi Mǔ as teachers,
her view of the unlearned followers
will simply be that they are reckless people.
Shī Huà
is
fundamentally derived from Zhōng Róng's *Shī Pǐn*.
However, examining the Classics and Commentaries,
they state, for example:
"The one who composed this poem,
did they understand the Way (Dào)?"
They also state:
"If one does not reflect upon this,
what difficulty is there (in achieving understanding)?"
This is discussing poetry while involving its substance (shì).
Furthermore, such as the quote: "Jí Fǔ composed the eulogy (sòng),
solemn like the pure wind.
His poetry is greatly robust,
his influence (fēng) is exceedingly good,"
this is discussing poetry while involving its wording (cí).
Substance has right and wrong;
wording has skill and clumsiness.
Extending these insights to other categories,
the enlightenment gained is indeed extensive.
Great rivers begin with a mere cupful (of water).
Although the theories of later *shīhuà* authors
are said to originate from Zhōng Róng,
the various subsequent branches have proliferated greatly,
and cannot be fully encapsulated by a single point.
The *Shī Pǐn* in relation to discussing poetry,
viewed alongside the *Wénxīn Diāolóng* in relation to discussing literature,
are both specialized masters,
the foundational ancestors codified into completed books.
The *Wénxīn* has a grand scope and comprehensive consideration;
the *Shī Pǐn* has profound thought and far-reaching intent.
Generally, the *Wénxīn* encompasses all discourses,
while the *Shī Pǐn* deeply traces the branching streams from the Six Arts (Liù Yì).
Discussing poetry or literature,
if one knows how to trace the streams and branches,
one can investigate the origins within the classics and books,
and further observe the purity of Heaven and Earth,
and the great paradigm of the ancients.
This meaning is not something the schools of later *shīhuà* authors can grasp.
The *shīhuà* of the Táng people
initially focused on discussing poetry.
Since Mèng Qǐ's *Běnshì Shī* appeared,
it allowed people to understand the intent of National Historians (Guó Shǐ) when narrating poetry;
and those who loved these matters followed and expanded upon it,
thus connecting *shīhuà* with the biographies (zhuànjì) within the History Category (Shǐ Bù).
Occasionally, they interpreted names and objects (míngwù);
thus connecting *shīhuà* with the elementary learning (xiǎoxué) within the Classics Category (Jīng Bù).
Or they broadly recounted what they had seen and heard;
thus connecting *shīhuà* with the miscellaneous schools (zájiā) within the Masters Category (Zǐ Bù).
Although the purposes of these writings are not uniform,
they generally do not stray from discussing wording and discussing substance,
inferring the author's intent (zhì),
and aiming to be beneficial to poetry instruction (shījiào)—that is all.
The *Shī Pǐn* and the *Wénxīn*
are specialized works of scholarship.
Unless one's learning is rich and talent excellent,
undertaking such work is not easy;
therefore, they devolved into *shīhuà*.
Following the stream and forgetting the source,
those who create *shīhuà*
no longer understand the original intent of the scholarly work.
It is similar to how the specialized fields of textual exegesis (xùngǔ) and the Masters/History experts
are not easy to pursue,
thus they devolved into the *shuōbù* (miscellanies/fictional narratives).
Following the stream and forgetting the source,
those who create *shuōbù*
no longer understand the original intent of the specialists.
The latter streams of *shīhuà* and *shuōbù*
are confused and indistinguishable.
When scholarship is not clear,
people's minds and customs may suffer harm because of it.
For the Sòng Confucian scholars to lecture on learning,
and personally practice what they preach,
is not easy to achieve.
Following the prevailing trend,
writing collected sayings (yǔlù) to endorse or condemn Zhū [Xī] and Lù [Jiǔyuān]
is something anyone can do.
Discussing literature and examining arts,
knowing the deep sources and branching streams,
is not easy to know.
Yielding to the habit of seeking fame,
writing *shīhuà* to factionalize and criticize opposing views,
is something anyone can do.
Using scholarship that cannot establish a distinguished school,
entering the trend of seeking fame,
wielding a pen that anyone can handle,
and producing only speech dictated by desire—
this is lamentable,
this is dangerous!
The abuses stemming from *shuōbù*
go as far as slandering the good, supporting the wicked,
fabricating names, and falsely attributing authors.
Those discussed by previous scholars,
such as the *Lóngchéng Lù* and the *Bìyún Xiá*,
are indeed too numerous to count.
This is why historians have the method of distinguishing and selecting between formal records and unofficial accounts (bàiyě).
Where events are recorded, they can be mutually verified,
but literature is subject only to the author's arbitrary conferral or dismissal.
The unreliability of *shīhuà*
may be even worse than that of *shuōbù*.
The abuses in the *shīhuà* of former generations
merely failed the impartiality of right and wrong, preference and dislike.
The abuses in the *shīhuà* of current people
even lead to harm against public morality and the people's minds (shìdào rénxīn).
A failing concerning right and wrong, preference and dislike,
is merely the common tendency of literati to belittle one another.
Public opinion will eventually settle itself,
and this trouble is not sufficient cause for anxiety.
Harm against public morality and the people's minds,
however, will intoxicate the intelligence and talent of the world,
and entrap people within the realm of beasts.
The mechanism is extremely subtle,
the method is extremely cunning,
and the resulting disasters will be inexpressible.
Gentlemen (Jūnzǐ) who uphold moral principles
must not fail to strictly guard against this and rigorously distinguish it.
Minor fiction (xiǎoshuō) originated from the petty officials (bàiguān),
consisting of trivial hearsay from winding alleys.
Even the ancients did not discard them.
However, the rustic and crude versions are largely unreliable.
Generally, the events involve ghosts and spirits,
and the retribution covers both grace and resentment.
Chapters like the *Dòngmíng* [Jì] and the *Shíyí* [Jì],
and sections like the *Sōushén* [Jì] and the *Língyì* [Zhì],
since the Six Dynasties (Liù Dài),
every family produced such books.
The Táng people then had single pieces,
separately establishing the category of *chuánqí* (tales).
For the most part, the emotions center on men and women,
not deviating from separation, reunion, sorrow, and joy.
Hóng Fú leaving Yáng [Su],
the Embroidered Jacket (Xiùrú) repaying Zhèng [Délín],
Hán [Shòu] and Lǐ [Jì] connecting their fate through falling leaves,
Cuī [Yíng] and Zhāng [Shēng] guiding their affection with the heart of the *qín* (qínxīn),
as well as Míng Zhū returning alive,
and Xiǎo Yù repaying [kindness] after death—
all of these types,
are either fabricated based on dubious similarities
or entirely attributed to fabricated sources (Zǐ Xū).
Although the emotional expressions vary greatly,
the general pattern is roughly similar.
Initially, they were merely excessive thoughts about ancient themes,
ways for frustrated literary scholars (cíkè) to express their feelings,
similar to the ancient romantic chapters (*Gǔyàn* zhū piān) of the *Yuèfǔ* (Music Bureau poetry).
Since the Sòng and Yuán dynasties,
they were widely expanded into narrative dramas (yǎnyì),
and composed into lyrics and melodies (cíqǔ).
Consequently, blind storytellers chanted them to strings,
and actors appeared on stage.
Regardless of refinement or vulgarity, men or women,
everyone was attracted by the sound, sight, hearing, and vision.
Indeed, since the petty officials were mentioned in the *Hàn Zhì* (History of the Hàn),
after three transformations, they completely lost the original source and stream of the ancients.
In the various forms of minor fiction, songs, *chuánqí*, and narrative dramas,
when describing men and women,
the men must be slight, frivolous, and shallow,
and they are euphemistically called "talented scholars" (cáizǐ) who are "romantic and elegant" (fēngliú);
the women must be seductive, wanton, and passionate,
and they are euphemistically called "peerless beauties" (jiārén juéshì).
The men in the world who possess slight cleverness but lack profound scholarship,
and the women who understand writing but are ignorant of ritual teachings (lǐjiào),
all regard the talented scholars and beauties of the *chuánqí*
as the people of antiquity,
the people of antiquity.
Now, those who write *shīhuà*
are precisely those who possess slight cleverness but lack profound scholarship.
Possessing slight cleverness but lacking profound scholarship,
supplemented by a corrupt and wicked mind,
they become base individuals (xiǎorén) who are reckless and uninhibited!
What will they not stoop to?

A Discussion on Establishing Three Types of Writing for Local Gazettes (Fāng Zhì)
Whenever one intends to manage the records and literature of a region,
one must establish three schools of study
before one can truly understand the enduring intent of the ancients.
Imitate the style of the Annals and Biographies (*jìzhuàn*) of the Standard Histories (Zhèng Shǐ) to create the records (*zhì*);
imitate the style of statutes, laws, and ordinances (*lǜlìng diǎnlì*) to create the institutional history (*zhǎnggù*);
and imitate the style of the *Wén Xuǎn* and *Wényuàn* to create the collection of local literature (*wénzhēng*).
These three books must operate in mutual support.
Missing one is unacceptable;
combining them into one
is especially unacceptable.
Fearing that people might think I deliberately seek novelty,
I therefore borrow the format of hypothetical inquiry (huòwèn) to elaborate fully on its meaning.
Someone asked:
The origin of the local gazetteers (fāngzhì) is ancient,
but there has never been a division into three books.
Why is it suddenly divided into three now?
I replied:
To make historical study clear.
Jǐa Zǐ (賈子) once said that when the ancients governed the world,
they were extremely meticulous and analytical.
I examined this in the Rites of Zhōu (Zhōuguān)
and realized that the ancients, regarding historical matters,
were never less than extremely meticulous and analytical.
The Outer Historian (Wàishǐ) was in charge of the records of the four directions (zhì),
and the commentary (zhù) states:
“They are similar to the Shèng (乘) of Jìn (晉), the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chūnqiū) of Lǔ (魯), and the Táowù (梼杌) of Chǔ (楚),”
which means the complete history of a state.
Moreover, the Traveler (Xíngrén) offered five books,

and the Grand Music Master (Tàishī) presented the Fēng Odes (fēng shī) (this is detailed in the Proposal on Gazetteer Categories (Zhìkē Yì); here, we only include what corresponds to the three books).
This shows that what the royal court obtained from the feudal states
in terms of collected documents
was certainly not just one single thing.
If one category could be omitted,
then the ancients should not have established that official position;
if they could be combined into one,
then the ancients should have first possessed a combined book.
Someone said:
The feudal system (fēngjiàn) was abolished and replaced by commanderies and prefectures (jùnxiàn),
so the present-day local gazetteers
cannot be compared to the histories of the ancient states. I replied:
The current world,
in terms of the norms of the people and the principles of things (mín yí wù zé),
has not slightly deviated from antiquity.
The reason why the local gazetteers cannot be compared to the state histories
is that, considering the officials who govern (shǒu lìng zhī guān),
they are all transferred and appointed by the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù).
Since their families are not hereditary (bù shì qí jiā),
they cannot record their own origins in the book like the feudal lords (hóu fēng).
However, regarding the collected documents submitted for the imperial court’s requisition,
how can there be any difference?
People see the independent power exercised by the various states during the Spring and Autumn period (Chūnqiū lièguó),
and thus believe that the feudal lords established their own systems,
somewhat like the histories of later separatist states (gē jù zhī guó shǐ),
and cannot be applied to local gazetteers.
They do not realize that the regulations of the Rites of Zhōu (Zhōuguān)
represented an era of flourishing governance where texts were unified and tracks were shared (tóng wén gòng guǐ).
The feudal lords receiving the royal regulations (Wáng Zhāng)
was no different from the commanderies and prefectures of later generations.
In ancient times, there were no writings from private houses (sī mén zhī zhù shù);
the Six Classics (liù jīng) were all history.
The things adopted by later generations and never abolished
are only the streams derived from the three schools of the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chūnqiū), the Odes (Shī), and the Rites (Lǐ).
The standard histories featuring annals and biographies (jì zhuàn zhèng shǐ)
are a stream derived from the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chūnqiū);
the institutional records and essential documents (zhǎng gù diǎn yào)
are a stream derived from the official Rites (guān Lǐ);
the collected literary documents (wén zhēng zhū xuǎn)
are a stream derived from the Fēng Odes (Fēng Shī).
Since the brush was laid down after the capture of the Qílín (Huòlín jué bǐ),
later scholars have rarely been able to fully grasp the grand framework of the ancients.
It is only through the accumulation of time that they have gradually inferred and demonstrated it.
Since Mǎ's History (Mǎ Shǐ) (Sīmǎ Qiān) and Bān's Book (Bān Shū) (Bān Gù),
the thread of the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chūnqiū) has already been developed.
Liú's Administrative Canon (Liú Shì Zhèngdiǎn) (Liú Zhì),
and Dù's Comprehensive Canon (Dù Shì Tōngdiǎn) (Dù Yòu),
began to develop the thread of the official Rites (guān Lǐ).
Lǚ's Mirror of Literature (Lǚ Shì Wén Jiàn) (Lǚ Zǔqiān),
and Sū's Literary Categories (Sū Shì Wén Lèi) (Sū Shì),
began to develop the thread of the Fēng Odes (Fēng Shī).
They took works that summarized the entire dynasty
and used them to verify each other,
leaving no unsubstantiated claims.
Someone said:
Master Wénzhōng (Wénzhōng Zǐ) said:
“The Sage narrated history in three parts:
the Documents (Shū), the Odes (Shī), and the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chūnqiū).”
Now, in discussing the three histories,
you omit the Documents (Shū) and add the Rites (Lǐ).
Does Master Wénzhōng’s saying refer to a different concept? I replied:
The Documents (Shū) and the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chūnqiū)
fundamentally belong to the same school of study.
Although the Bamboo Annals (Zhú Shū) cannot be entirely trusted,
the chronological style (biān nián) certainly existed in antiquity.
The chapters of the Documents (Shū) are merely a separate presentation of historical writing.
The ancients were simple and concise,
and did not combine annals and biographies (jì zhuàn).
When Master Zuǒ (Zuǒ Shì) used the Commentary (zhuàn) to supplement the Classic (jīng),
they were combined into one.
The diplomatic rhetoric within it
is the remnant of the Instructions and Admonitions (xùn gào);
the institutional facts cited
are similar to the Tribute and Models (gòng fàn).
Therefore, the Book of Zhōu (Zhōu Shū) concludes with the Oath of Qín (Qín Shì) during King Píng’s (Píng Wáng) reign (this is appended from the histories of the feudal states).
And the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chūnqiū) takes its starting point during King Píng’s reign,
making it clear that they follow sequentially.
Master Zuǒ (Zuǒ Shì) combined them, and Mǎ (Sīmǎ Qiān) and Bān (Bān Gù) followed suit,
establishing a fixed standard and rule (kē lǜ) for historians,
much like the Jiāng (江) and Hàn (漢) rivers separating at the source but merging downstream,
happening without conscious intention.
Later people failed to understand this
and separated the Book of Documents (Shàngshū) and the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chūnqiū) as records of speech and records of events, respectively,
not realizing the streams derived from the Six Arts (liù yì).
As for why the official Rites (guān Lǐ) cannot be omitted,
that has already been fully discussed in previous remarks.
Someone said:
The Music (Yuè) is lost, and the Documents (Shū) is combined with the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chūnqiū),
leaving only four of the Six Arts.
Since you claim that the Six Classics are all history,
why is there no historical stream derived from the Book of Changes (Yì) in later histories? I replied:
Ancient governance emphasized the Way of Heaven (tiān dào) and was concise regarding human affairs (rén shì);
later generations emphasized human affairs and were concise regarding the Way of Heaven.
This is due to the prevailing circumstances (shí shì),
which even a Sage cannot force.
In high antiquity, officials were named after clouds and birds,
designated by celestial timing;
only Dāng (Táng) and Yǔ (Yú) began naming them based on human affairs.
The Canon of Yáo (Yáo Diǎn) details the appointment of Xī (Xī) and Hé (Hé);
in the Rites of Zhōu (Zhōuguān), the Official for the Stars (Bǎozhāng)
is merely listed as a middle-ranking official within the Ministry of Spring (Chūn Guān).
From this, one can infer the general trend of detail and conciseness.
The Book of Changes (Yì), in its essence,
is about realizing things and perfecting tasks (kāi wù chéng wù).
The Sage established teachings through divine methods (shén dào shè jiào),
creating divine objects
for the use of the people.
Xī (Xī), Nóng (Nóng), and Huángdì (黃帝) did not inherit from each other;
the Xià (夏), Shāng (商), and Zhōu (周) dynasties did not follow established practices.
This is perhaps the same as establishing the calendar and clarifying the seasons (zhì lì míng shí),
serving as a creation and regulation of that single dynasty,
innovating the sight and hearing of the people.
Later generations only treated the issuance of the calendar and the timing of the seasons as administrative canons (zhèng diǎn),
and divination (zhān shí bǔ rì) as the duty of the officials of the Bureau of Astronomy (Sītiān zhī guān shǒu).
This is the meaning of the Way of Heaven being distant and human affairs being near,
a necessity determined by the prevailing circumstances.
This is why among later historians,
only Sīmǎ (Sīmǎ Qiān) still managed the Astronomical Bureau (Tiān Guān),
and subsequently, Bān Shì (Bān Gù) and those who followed
did not discuss celestial affairs.
Someone said:
The Six Classics evolving into the Three Histories
is a great institutional undertaking of a dynasty.
A region like a prefecture (fāng zhōu) is a small piece of land;
one gazetteer is enough to cover it entirely.
Why must we require comprehensive material? I replied:
The categories and principles do not allow for combination.
In ancient times, the Emperor’s robes
had twelve symbols (shí yǒu èr zhāng).
Dukes (gōng), Marquises (hóu), Ministers (qīng), Grand Masters (dàfū), and Scholars (shì) reduced them in degree,
down to the single symbol on the plain skirt (yuán shang yī zhāng),
which was the absolute minimum.
However, even though it is considered humble,
to combine it with the cap and shoes as a single item
is absolutely impossible.
Previous scholars compiled records for the Ministers and Supervisors (qīng jiān) of the Six Ministries (liù bù).
However, the Minister of Personnel (Lì) does not know military affairs (bīng),
and the Minister of Revenue (Hù) does not interfere with the Rites (Lǐ).
Although they encompass the entirety of the world,
in reality, they are only a partial aspect of a single office,
and one should not demand comprehensiveness from them.
Although a prefecture (fāng zhōu) is small,
what it undertakes to uphold and implement
—Personnel (Lì), Revenue (Hù), Rites (Lǐ), War (Bīng), Punishments (Xíng), and Works (Gōng)—
is all-encompassing.
This is what is meant by having all organs complete in miniature (jù tǐ ér wēi).
The national history (Guó Shǐ) draws its materials from this,
just as the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chūnqiū) borrowed from the precious records of the hundred states.
How can it be overlooked?
Someone said:
Since the existence of local gazetteers,
we have never heard of the national history relying on them as evidence.
Why do you now claim that the national history draws its materials from local gazetteers? I replied:
The tradition of local gazetteers has been lost for a long time.
What are currently called local gazetteers
are not the true local gazetteers.
The elegant ones
are merely literary amusements of scholars,
small notes and short writings,
pure discussions and collected sayings.
The coarse ones
are administrative documents and official files,
or wandering beggars’ accounts,
just conventional social responses.
Gentlemen (jìn shēn xiān shēng) often find them difficult to discuss.
The national history, having no choice,
has to resort to collecting family genealogies and funerary inscriptions (jiā pǔ zhì zhuàng),
and collected literary works and records (wén jí jì shù).
This is what is called “when the Rites are lost, seek them in the countryside.”
However, private writings
might lack factual accuracy.
Without local gazetteers to provide verification,
it is impossible to avoid the toil of verification,
and furthermore, the fault of misplaced trust
is truly hard to avoid.
Indeed, the loss of local gazetteers has long afflicted the national history.
Since the local gazetteers are not relied upon by the national history,
they are set up in vain and cannot serve their purpose.
This is what is meant by “a tablet (gū) not being a tablet.”
Alas, the local gazetteers!
Someone asked:
Now that the three works stand concurrently,
will they divide and separate the material traditionally belonging to the local gazetteers (fāngzhì)?
Or will they augment what the fāngzhì lack and stand in a tripod formation? The reply was:
There is some division,
and also some augmentation.
However, its meaning cannot be fully expressed in a single statement.
The Way of history (shǐ) is such that
the elegant speech of literati,
and the crude documentation (bó dú) of government clerks,
are both unusable;
yet, without these two,
there would be nothing to constitute history.
Mèngzǐ said:
Its events,
its writing,
its morality,
these are what the Chūnqiū takes.
That is, taking the events documented in the records (bù dú), polishing them with elegant writing,
and judging them by morality (yì)—
national histories (Guó Shǐ) and local gazetteers (fāngzhì)
are all branches and derivatives of the Chūnqiū.
Comparing it to a human body,
events are the bones,
writing is the skin,
and morality (yì) is the spirit.
When judged by morality (yì),
a work begins to establish its school (chéng jiā).
A work must establish its school
before it possesses canons and laws (diǎn fǎ),
making it suitable for recitation and recognition,
and thus able to be passed down through generations and travel far.
Therefore it is said:
The Record (zhì) is for recording (zhì),
it is intended to be enduring and memorable.
Someone asked:
Since the Record (zhì) takes administrative documents (bù dú) as its bones,
why then edit and condense these documents into Institutional History (zhǎnggù)? The reply was:
The explanation is detailed in the introductory remarks (Lìyì) to the Bózhōu Zhǎnggù;
now I shall speak of it briefly again.
The eight treatises (Bā Shū) by Mǎ Qiān
all comprehensively examine institutions and ordinances (diǎn zhāng),
and illuminate the major principles.
His Lǐ Shū states in its preface:
"Matters concerning sacrificial vessels (biāndòu zhī shì)
are preserved by the relevant officials."
This is the general principle for historical treatises and records (shū zhì).
What Mǎ Qiān referred to as being preserved by the relevant officials
are things like Shūsūn's court rites,
Hán Xìn's military laws,
and Xiāo Hé's statutes and ordinances.
Each had their official responsibility (guān shǒu) to preserve their zhǎnggù (institutional history),
and the historical text could not collect all of them uniformly.
It is a pity there were no people like Liú Zhì or Dù Yòu
to separately edit the zhǎnggù and compile them into essential canons (diǎn yào).
Therefore, those seeking Hàn dynasty institutions
have only the Bān Shū (History by Bān),
and the details and numbers are not as comprehensive as those of the Táng dynasty;
the effect of this is easily seen.
Thus, separately editing the institutional history (zhǎnggù) to supplement the Record (zhì)
is comparable to the Táng Shū having the Táng Huìyào,
the Sòng Shǐ having the Sòng Huìyào,
the Yuán Shǐ having the Yuán Diǎnzhāng,
and the Míng Shǐ having the Míng Huìdiǎn—nothing more.
Someone asked:
In today's local gazetteers (fāngzhì),
the section called "Arts and Letters" (Yìwén),
when setting up the bibliography, often selects poems and essays.
This seems to take events and writings as mutual confirmation,
thus achieving the Way of adaptability.
Why must we now compile a separate work as a Collection of Writings (Wénzhēng)?
Is the intention perhaps different? The reply was:
The explanation is detailed in the preface and guidelines (Xù Lì) of the Yǒngqīng Wénzhēng;
now I shall speak of it briefly again.
Since the Record (zhì) is compiled by imitating the historical style (shǐ tǐ),
then poems and essays related to historical structure
should be included in the Biographies and Annals (Jìzhuàn),
such as the imperial edicts, memorials, and other writings from the Hàn court recorded in the treatises and biographies of the Bān Shū;
that is permissible.
If we use the principle of selecting texts to create an Yìwén Zhì (Record of Arts and Letters),
then the Sòng Wénjiàn could be combined with the Sòng Shǐ into one book,
and the Yuán Wénlèi could be combined with the Yuán Shǐ into one book.
How would these works differ
from the writings already included in the Jìzhuàn?
Someone asked:
The tradition of selecting texts originated during the Xiāo Liáng dynasty,
and was succeeded by the Wényuàn Yīnghuá and the Táng Wéncuì;
this tradition has been long established.
Now you bring up the Wénjiàn and the Wénlèi,
and initiate the thread of the Fēng Shī (Airs) tradition.
Why is this? The reply was:
Works like the Wén Xuǎn and Wén Yuàn primarily focus on literary elegance,
not verification of actual events.
The Wénjiàn first showed an intent towards political governance (zhèngzhì),
and the Wénlèi then showed an intent towards institutional history (gùshì).
This shows that later generations, through long practice,
have views superior to those of the ancients.
Someone asked:
Writings regarding a locality or province (fāng zhōu wénzì) are not numerous.
Since essential pieces have already been included in the Classics and Biographies (Jīng Zhuàn),
if we separately compile poems and essays that can mutually verify the Record (zhì)
into one book,
I fear the number of collected pieces will be very few. The reply was:
Since it is already a separate book,
the guiding principles (yì lì) can naturally be somewhat broadened.
Even the Wénjiàn and Wénlèi,
though their main purpose is to verify history,
cannot apply the same strict rule to every single piece.
Famous writings and excellent passages
are universally appreciated;
even if they do not entirely conform to verifying history,
they should not be excluded from collection.
In general, one book has its own style and principles,
and the teaching of the Odes (Shī Jiào) naturally follows a different path from the Chūnqiū.
Regarding the Arts and Letters sections (Yìwén) in modern local gazetteers (fāngzhì),
those that are excessive and disorderly
need not be discussed.
Even those who are somewhat discerning
know to select what is useful
and cautiously choose only a small amount.
However, if judged by the principles of historical records (shǐ zhì),
even this selection is already excessive inclusion.
If one truly wishes to display the cultural richness (wénwù zhī shèng) of a locality,
even doubling the Yìwén section
would still be considered too narrow.
If we do not create a single specialized volume
to clarify the scholarship of the three works (Sān Jiā zhī Xué),
then both inclusion and exclusion will lack justification.
Someone asked:
The various styles in the Wén Xuǎn
omit nothing.
Why are we now classifying (this literary collection) under the derivative tradition of the Fēng Shī?
What is the meaning of this? The reply was:
The explanation is detailed in the chapter on the Shī Jiào;
now I shall speak of it briefly again.
The Shū (Book of Documents) states:
"Poetry expresses intent (zhì)."
In ancient times, there were no private writings.
The Classics (Jīng), Masters (Zǐ), and histories (Shǐ)
were all based on the official responsibilities (guān shǒu) of the ancients;
but poetry allowed one to express whatever one wished.
Before the Táng and Sòng dynasties,
there were no scholarly writings (zhùshù) included in literary anthologies (wénjí).
Writings that were not commentaries on classical studies (Jīng Xué), historical biographies (Shǐ Xué), or treatises on philosophical schools (Zǐ Jiā)
were what the ancients first referred to as literature (wén).
Those works that included commentaries, biographies, or treatises
were called "books" (shū) by the ancients,
not "literature" (wén).
When Xiāo Tǒng's Wén Xuǎn
combined poetry and literature and called them all "wén" (literature),
it showed that literary anthologies and poetry
belonged to the same derivative category.
Now, imitating the principles of selection to create a Collection of Writings (Wénzhēng),
although the texts included
do not all follow one rule,
they are essentially all those who spoke based on their own intent;
therefore, they are categorized with the Fēng Shī.
Someone asked:
Kǒng Yǎn compiled the Hàn Wèi Shàng Shū,
and Wáng Tōng also compiled the Xù Shū.
They both collected edicts, proclamations, memorials, and petitions
into one anthology;
this is also a derivative of the Wén Xuǎn tradition.
Yet those works are considered Shū (Book) schools,
and are not placed in the poetry section (Shī Bù).
Why is that? The reply was:
The scholarship of the Shū (Book of Documents), ever since the time of Zuǒ Shì,
has been absorbed into the Chūnqiū.
Followers of Kǒng Yǎn and Wáng Tōng
did not understand this principle but forcibly pursued such works;
therefore, their Way ultimately could not be carried out.
This is analogous to later generations,
when the Jǐ Shuǐ (Jǐ River) had already merged into the Hé (Yellow River),
but those clinging rigidly to the Yǔ Gòng
still insisted on dredging the old channels at Xíngzé and Táoqiū.
Someone asked:
Outside of the Three Books,
there are also those that continue and are not discarded,
such as the chronological arrangement of the *Tōngjiàn*
and the thematic narrative arrangement of the Benmo (Records of Events by Beginning and End).
Later generations succeed them,
and they should be like the ancestral sacrificial vessels that are never removed (i.e., forever honored).
Regarding the Liù Yì,
from where do their differing currents evolve? I replied:
They are all branches derived from the *Chūnqiū*.
Indeed, the history written in the form of Biographies and Annals (jìzhuàn)
originally derived from the academic tradition of the *Chūnqiū*,
while the *Tōngjiàn* developed from the style of the Basic Annals (běnjì)
and unified its Treatises (zhì) and Biographies (zhuàn) into one.
As for the Records of Events by Beginning and End (Jìshì Běnmò),
their source originates from the *Shàngshū* (Classic of Documents);
however, the *Shàngshū* style transitioned mid-way to enter the *Chūnqiū* tradition,
therefore it is also a divergence of the *Chūnqiū*.
From Mǎ [Qiān] and Bān [Gù] onward,
they successively developed the *Chūnqiū* through the Annals-Biography structure.
The *Tōngjiàn* took the divisions inherent in the Annals-Biography structure
and integrated them chronologically.
The *Jìshì Běnmò* then took the integration method of the *Tōngjiàn*
and divided it according to thematic events.
By naming chapters based on specific events,
it did not follow the standard models,
but instead recovered the lost method of the *Shàngshū*.
This is what is meant by affairs undergoing repeated changes and then reverting to their origin,
where embellishment (bì) is succeeded by stripping (bō),
and when stripping reaches its limit, it is succeeded by recovery (fù).
For example, burning cinnabar to produce mercury;
then taking the mercury and burning it,
it reverts back to cinnabar.
This is the principle.
This theory is discussed in detail in a separate specialized chapter,
so it is not elaborated upon fully here. (This is a side note, not discussing local gazetteers.)
Someone asked:
You are compiling a local gazetteer (fāngzhì);
why, besides the Three Books,
do you have another book called *Cóngtán*?
I replied:
This is the remainder of the materials collected.
When ancient scholars aimed for their works to establish a school (chéngjiā),
it was not by boasting of volume or seeking exhaustive detail.
However, without wide reading,
there is no basis for selective extraction.
Once the selection is made,
the remainder from the wide reading,
if forcibly inserted, would be illogical,
but to discard it would be regrettable.
Therefore, I attached it to the category of miscellaneous and unofficial narratives,
and created the *Cóngtán*.
It is like the supplementary explanations of the Classics,
the external biographies of the Histories,
or the external chapters of the Masters (Zǐ) works.
Why does it not adhere to the designation of the Three Books but is called Four?
The Three Books are all essential classics,
whereas the *Cóngtán* is not a book that is absolutely indispensable.
When predecessors compiled gazetteers,
they often appended this kind of material to the end of the gazetteer,
sometimes calling it Supplementary Compilation (Yú Biān),
or sometimes Miscellaneous Records (Zá Zhì).
Because their principles and scope for the work
had not yet been clearly established as an authoritative school (chéngjiā),
appending it afterwards
caused no harm.
Since I have established the principles of the Three Schools (Sān Jiā) of learning,
and written the three corresponding volumes,
then in terms of methodology, there is nothing regrettable (about separation);
it is better to write it as a separate compilation to find its proper place.
What the *Hàn Zhì* calls the school of Minor Talk (Xiǎoshuōjiā),
which originates from unofficial historians (bàiguān),
collecting street gossip and alley discussions,
is also the kind of material that should not be discarded when collecting local customs (cǎifēng).
Proposal Requesting the Establishment of a System for Local Gazetteer Compilation in Commanderies and Counties
I, your humble servant, grew up poor,
making a living by writing,
and I have repeatedly accepted invitations to compile gazetteers and histories.
My experience in gazetteer matters is extensive.
In the course of this, I have weighed the right and wrong of ancient people,
and considered the general rules and precedents for future gazetteers.
I have indeed spoken about these things in detail.
Essentially, all of this involves analyzing the texts for substance,
and establishing structure based on the subject matter.
As for establishing foundational laws
and creating good regulations to prevent future misuse,
these are not within the scope of my professional duties,
and I fear proposing them would be an overreach of authority.
Though sometimes discussed informally during quiet gatherings,
they have always been abandoned like a clay ox entering the sea (i.e., vanishing without effect).
Good gazetteers are not yet realized,
and my heart feels this lack.
However, since fixed regulations are not made for just one moment,
then setting forth a theory need not fear waiting for a later time.
Therefore, I wish to fully express my ideas
and await selection by those who understand.
According to the *Zhōu Guān*, among the subordinates of the Zōng Bó (Minister of Rites),
the Wài Shǐ (Outer Scribe) was in charge of the records (zhì) of the four directions.
Commentaries explain that these were like the Jìn *Shèng* and the Chǔ *Táowù*,
which were thus the compiled histories of the feudal lords (zhūhóu).
How could these compiled histories have been achieved without material support?
I have examined the Zhōu system
and thus know that the ancients, regarding historical matters,
never failed to record every minute detail.
The Sī Huì (Director of Accounting) managed the secondary copies of records, maps, and land registers in the suburbs, open country, towns, and capital cities;
the Dǎng Zhèng (Head of the Quinary-Hamlet Unit) "instructed the people to study the laws,
and recorded their virtuous conduct, principles, and skills."
The Lǘ Xū (Hamlet Headman) organized the populace,
and "recorded those who were respectful, diligent, responsible, and compassionate."
The Sòng Xùn (Director of Recitation and Instruction) "managed the dissemination of local records (fāngzhì),
to instruct people on observable phenomena;
managed the dissemination of local evils (fāngnì),
to instruct them on what to avoid and taboo,
and thereby understand the local customs."
The Xiǎo Shǐ (Minor Scribe) "managed the records of the various states,
establishing lineages
and distinguishing the relative ranks (zhāomù)."
The Xùn Fāng (Director of Regional Instruction) "managed the guidance of the political affairs of the four directions,
as well as the high and low records of those regions,
and recited the traditions passed down in the four directions."
The Xíng Fāng (Director of Regional Forms) "managed the territory of the various states,
and rectified their boundaries and borders."
The Shān Shī (Mountain Master) and Chuān Shī (River Master) "each managed the names of the mountains, forests, rivers, and marshes,
distinguishing the fauna and flora, along with their benefits and harms."
The Yuán Shī (Plain Master) "managed the place names of the four directions,
distinguishing the names of their hills, mounds, plains, plateaus, and lowlands."
Thus, between the villages (xiāng), districts (suì), cities (dū), and outskirts (bǐ),
regarding mountains, rivers, and customs,
products, and human relations,
no detail, great or small, was overlooked.
As for the Xíng Rén (Envoys) presenting the Five Books (Wǔ Shū),
the Zhí Fāng (Director of Territory) collecting maps and registers,
and the Dà Shī (Grand Music Master) arranging the Airs (Fēng) and poems,
these were the records passed upward to the sovereign.
Indeed, the institutions (zhìdù) flowed from top to bottom,
while the collection of data (cǎizhí) flowed from bottom to top.
Only when the collection of data was complete,
could the institutions become more refined.
This was the excellent legal system of the Three Dynasties (Sāndài).
In later generations, historical matters
detailed the upper levels more than the lower levels.
As the commandery-county (jùnxiàn) system differed from the feudal (fēngjiàn) system,
local gazetteers (fāngzhì) ceased to be regarded as state histories of the old kind
and fell into the domain of geographical writings.
Consequently, their content became partial and incomplete.
Moreover, these books lacked official supervisory regulations
and were left to individuals to compile voluntarily.
Therefore, their precedents were inconsistent and could not serve as canonical standards.
This was necessitated by the circumstances.
The literature (wénzhāng) after the Sāndài
may lack the remaining institutions (yízhì) of the Sāndài;
but the governance (zhèngshì) after the Sāndài
cannot but follow the remaining principles (yíyì) of the Sāndài.
If, in government regulations (zhèngfǎ), one also preserves the remaining institutions (yízhì) pertaining to the literature (wénzhāng) of the Sāndài,
why worry that literature (wénzhāng) will not attain the beauty and completeness of the Sāndài?
The governance (zhèngshì) of All Under Heaven (tiānxià)
begins in the departments and districts (zhōuxiàn)
and reaches the imperial court (cháotíng),
just as during the Sāndài, the bìlǘ (neighborhoods), zúdǎng (clans and parties),
ascended to the Six Ministers (liùqīng);
in the feudal states (hóuguó),
it proceeded from the zhǎngshuài (chiefs) and zhèngbó (senior earls)
to reach the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ).
What the Ministers (Shàngshū) of the Six Boards (Liùbù) of the imperial court (cháotíng) administer

is established by synthesizing the administrative precedents (zhǎnggù) and clerical regulations (lìdiǎn) of the Six Bureaus (Liùkē) in all the departments and districts (zhōuxiàn) under heaven (tiānxià).
Its process, from bottom to top,
also resembles the remnants of the bìlǘ, zúdǎng, zhǎngshuài, and zhèngbó of the Sāndài.
The Six Boards (Liùbù) must synthesize the administrative precedents (zhǎnggù) of all under heaven (tiānxià) for governance (zhèng) to exist;
the historiographers (shǐguān) must synthesize the records (jìzài) of all under heaven (tiānxià) for the archives (jí) to be complete.
However, the administrative precedents (zhǎnggù) of the departments and districts (zhōuxiàn),
due to matters being named according to the occasion,
and carried out by clerical functionaries (diǎnlì),
frequently add notes outside of the Six Bureaus (Liùkē).
Furthermore, the records (jìzài) of the departments and districts (zhōuxiàn)
entirely lack dedicated personnel for their custody and management,
resulting in major principles being missing.
Occasionally, there are enthusiasts
who compile local gazetteers (zhìchéng).
These generally rely on temporary interviewing and research,
the people involved are often mediocre and humble,
and the results are rarely complete;
sometimes, they even harbor private malice and make false accusations,
or use bribery to compose the text.
Because of this, when speaking of local records (fāngzhì),
gentlemen of the gentry (jiànshēn xiānshēng) often find it difficult to discuss them.
When historiographers (shǐguān) collect information from below,
if the departmental and district gazetteers (zhōuxiàn zhìchéng) are like this,
upon what will they rely for material for writing and editing (bǐxuē)?
Moreover, there is the history of All Under Heaven (tiānxià),
there is the history of a state (guó),
there is the history of a family (jiā),
and there is the history of an individual (rén).
Biographies (zhuàn), memorial inscriptions (zhuàng), and descriptive records (zhìshù)
are the history of an individual;
family annals (jiāchéng) and genealogies (pǔdié)
are the history of a family;
departmental, prefectural, and district gazetteers (bù fǔ xiàn zhì)
are the history of a state;
comprehensive recording of one dynasty (cháo)
is the history of All Under Heaven (tiānxià).
Only by combining individuals is there a family;
only by combining families is there a state;
only by combining states is there All Under Heaven.
Only when the separate parts are extremely detailed
can the composite whole select the good without regret.
Genealogies (pǔdié) are scattered and difficult to verify;
biographies and records (zhuànzhì) are private and often flattering;
when the imperial court (cháotíng) compiles history,
it must draw its standards from local records (fāngzhì).
And among the local records (fāngzhì),
the overall departments (bù) draw from the various prefectures (fǔ),
the various prefectures (fǔ) draw from the departments and districts (zhōuxiàn),
which is also the way from bottom to top.
Thus, the departmental and district gazetteers (zhōuxiàn zhìshū),
stabilize the evaluations of genealogies (pǔdié) and biographies/records (zhuànzhì) below,
and provide reliable evidence for the departments and prefectures (bùfǔ) above,
truly constituting the essential drafts for court history (cháoshǐ).
For regular meetings and projects (qīhuì gōngchéng),
taxation, imprisonment, and litigation (fùshuì yùsòng),
the departments and districts (zhōuxiàn) rely on the administrative precedents (zhǎnggù) of the clerical functionaries (lìdiǎn)
which can satisfy the demands of the Six Boards (Liùbù);
but when it comes to examining records and collecting documents (kǎoxiàn zhēngwén),
the departments and districts (zhōuxiàn) rely only on vulgar, arbitrary, and lawless gazetteers (zhìchéng).
How could these ever be sufficient for the historiographers’ (shǐguān) selection?
Since the essential records (jiéyào zhī jí) of the departments and districts (zhōuxiàn)
are not worth observing,
it is appropriate that the court historiographers (cháoshǐ) would rather seek information from genealogies (pǔdié) and biographies/records (zhuànzhì) below,
than inquire again of the departments and districts (zhōuxiàn).
Now, regarding regular meetings and projects (qīhuì gōngchéng),
taxation, imprisonment, and litigation (fùshuì yùsòng),
if the Six Boards (Liùbù) bypassed the departments and districts (zhōuxiàn)
and inquired directly among the populace,
would this be appropriate?
Then the historical matters (shǐshì) after the Sāndài
are they not difficult?
Now, literature (wénzhāng) is merely observed in governance (zhèngshì).
If there are no official duties (guānshǒu) and canonical records (diǎnjí) like those of the Sāndài,
then there is no literature (wénzhāng) like that of the Sāndài;
if there is no literature (wénzhāng) like that of the Sāndài,
even if there are accomplishments (shìgōng) like those of the Sāndài,
they cannot be brilliantly revealed like the sun and moon.
The official documents (lìngshǐ àndú) of the clerks
are scorned by literary scholars (wénxué zhī rú).
They are not worthy of mention.
But in managing government and education (jīnglún zhèngjiào),
there has never been a case of setting them aside and finding a different path.
Later generations exclusively tasked literature (wénxué) with historical matters (shǐshì),
while the official administrative precedents (guānsī zhǎnggù)
did not provide their regulations and systems (fǎzhì) for the use of the historiographers (shǐshì).
This is why, after the Sāndài,
where substance (zhì) and expression (wén) were separated,
historical matters (shǐshì) have been so difficult to discuss.
Now, the great plans (dàjì) of All Under Heaven (tiānxià)
begin in the departments and districts (zhōuxiàn),
so responsibility for historical matters (shǐshì)
should also begin with the gazetteers (zhì) of the departments and districts (zhōuxiàn).
The departments and districts (zhōuxiàn) have crude and unverifiable gazetteers (zhì),
but they do not have crude and unverifiable official documents (lìngshǐ àndú).
Gazetteers (zhì) contain righteous principles, precedents, and rhetoric (yìlì wéncí) that praise or condemn people, or judge their efforts as skillful or clumsy;
official documents (àndú) have no righteous principles, precedents, or rhetoric (yìlì wéncí) that praise or condemn people, or judge their efforts as skillful or clumsy;
this is because the recording follows a fixed method,
and the custody and management are entrusted to fixed personnel—
this is what is meant by following the remaining principles (yíyì) of the Sāndài.
Therefore, the gazetteers (zhì) of the departments and districts (zhōuxiàn)
cannot be commissioned temporarily.
Normally, among the various clerical functionaries (diǎnlì),
a specific Gazetteer Bureau (Zhìkē) should be established.
Clerical functionaries (diǎnlì) who are slightly clearer about literary methods (wénfǎ)
should be selected to fill these posts.
Moreover, established regulations (chéngfǎ) must be created,
so that they can record according to the regulations,
somewhat like official documents (àndú) having fixed forms (gōngshì).
Then there will be no defect of arbitrarily exercising ingenuity.
After accumulating records over several decades,
then those skilled in literature (wénxué) and knowledgeable about historical methodology (shǐcái) should be sought out,
to edit (bǐxuē) and compile them into finished books.
This is what is meant by waiting for the right person before proceeding.
If this process of accumulation and revision is repeated,
the task will not be arduous,
and the results will already surpass what literary and historical scholars (wénshǐ zhī rú) could achieve,
which is what is meant by preserving the remaining institutions (yízhì) related to Sāndài literature (wénzhāng) within governance regulations (zhèngfǎ).
If so, what should be done about establishing a permanent system?
The files and documents of the Liù Kē,
a rough summary should be extracted,
and the copies recorded and stored.
Regarding officials, superiors, and scholar-teachers (shīrú),
on the day they leave office,
records of their daily conduct, both good and bad, for which there is factual evidence, should be gathered,
and the complete account recorded.
Among the jurisdiction's residents,
when families compile their genealogies (pǔ),
and individuals compose their biographies, epitaphs, descriptions, or narratives (zhuàn zhì zhuàng shù),
they must present copies;
the scholar-teachers (shīrú) of the schools,
adopting public consensus,
shall verify and correct them, storing them in the Zhì Kē (Gazetteer Department).
When the people of the jurisdiction
have compiled works on the Classics and histories (jīng shǐ),
or poetry, prose, and writings (shī cí wén bǐ),
which have been finalized and edited into collections,
they must present copies,
to be stored in the Zhì Kē,
and the table of contents also recorded.
When yá xiè (yamens and offices), city walls and moats,
schools, temples, and ancestral halls,
embankments, weirs, and bridges,
are repaired or constructed,
it must be reported to the Kē (Department),
and the complete details of the project presented.
When inscriptions are cast in metal or carved in stone,
recording events or composing elaborate texts,
rubbings of the originals must be taken,
and stored in the Kē.
Whenever the Bīn Xīng (examination rituals), Xiāng Yǐn (village drinking rites),
reading of laws, or lecturing on books
are held,
the official ranks and all names involved at that time must be written down,
and what was heard and seen recorded.
A storage chamber should be set up,
safe from invasion by water or fire.
Locked chests should be provided,
sorted by department and category;
at specific times of the year,
they shall be sealed and marked for storage,
and may not be privately opened without reason.
Following the spirit of the xiāng shú (village schools) and yì xué (charity schools),
one investigator should be established in each of the four districts,
selecting gentry (shēn shì) who are upright and meet public expectations to serve,
so that they may search out forgotten writings and lost events,
and present them periodically.
The scholar-teachers (shīrú) of the schools
should be chosen carefully from experienced and mature individuals;
whenever submissions are made,
they should together maintain impartiality and verify the facts.
Rites and music (lǐ yuè) and government affairs
are interdependent, forming the inner and outer aspects of reality.
When scholars discuss rites and music (lǐ yuè),
they must consult the Zuì Zōng (Master of Ceremonies) regarding instruments and numbers,
and examine the rhythm and tempo with the engineer (gōng shī);
only then will their writings not rely on empty talk.
The files and documents of the clerks (lìng shǐ)
are what high ministers rely upon when discussing state governance,
just as Rites have the Zuì Zōng, instruments, and numbers,
and Music has the engineer (gōng shī) and rhythm and tempo.
If one discusses government affairs yet scorns the files and documents of the clerks (lìng shǐ),
or establishes rites and music (lǐ yuè) yet disdains the Zuì Zōng, instruments, and numbers,
or the engineer (gōng shī) and rhythm and tempo,
then that is writing without substance,
and cannot be used.
Why, specifically regarding the work of the historians,
is legislation not established to prevent abuses?
Can it be said that merely entrusting it to literary scholars is sufficient?
Someone might say:
Now that Zhōu Xiàn (Prefectures and Districts) have established the Zhì Kē,
there is no fear of scattering or loss of documents.
However, for materials to pass from the Zhōu Xiàn up to the official historians,
the distance is great and the structure lacks coordination and control.
Should the Fǔ (Prefectures) and the Bùzhèng Shǐ Sī (Provincial Administration Commission) not intervene and inquire? He replied:
If the Zhōu Xiàn fail to implement this sincerely,
the Sī Fǔ (Commissions and Prefectures) must certainly investigate based on the regulations.
As for the Zhì Kē,
it has already summarized the essentials of the files and documents of the Liù Kē
to preserve its registers.
The Fǔ (Prefectural) clerks must summarize the essentials of the Zhōu Xiàn Zhì Kē
to serve as the basis for compiling the Fǔ Zhì (Prefectural Gazetteers);
the Sī (Commission) clerks must summarize the essentials of the Fǔ Kē (Prefectural Department)
to serve as the basis for compiling the Tōng Zhì (General Gazetteer);
Not only will the gazetteers of the Sī Fǔ
have a basis for selection,
but they will also accumulate materials broadly,
cross-reference and verify them,
making it possible to check the veracity of the Zhōu Xiàn Zhì Kē.
Regarding senior officials who command entire regions (tǒng bù dà liáo),
the Sī Kē (Commission Department), upon their departure from office,
just as the Zhōu Xiàn Zhì Kē does for its officials, superiors, and scholar-teachers (shīrú),
shall record their daily conduct, both good and bad, for which there is factual evidence,
detailing the complete account,
and storing it in the Kē.
Regarding the officials of all Fǔ (Prefectures),
the Fǔ Kē (Prefectural Department), upon their departure from office,
shall record the same as the Zhōu Xiàn.
Thus, the clerks of the Fǔ Zhì Kē (Prefectural Gazetteer Department)
not only combine the Zhōu Xiàn department registers and store copies of them,
and the clerks of the Sī Zhì Kē (Commission Gazetteer Department)
not only combine the various Fǔ Kē registers and store copies of them,
but they also independently compile materials for their respective Sī and Fǔ,
which cannot be omitted.
Someone might say:
This is certainly beneficial
to historical matters.
But I wonder, do political governance and administration also rely on this? He replied:
Writing and political governance
are always interdependent, forming the inner and outer aspects of reality.
The files and documents of the clerks (lìng shǐ)
are the reliance of political governance.
There are cases where events happen unexpectedly
and records are lost to water or fire;
there are cases where storage is not careful
and records are damaged by moisture and decay;
there are cases where corrupt clerks manipulate the law
and secretly alter the records;
if the essentials are all recorded,
and copies stored in the Zhì Kē,
then the calamity of these numerous problems will be avoided.
This contributes significantly to sound administration.
Genealogies (pǔ dié) are not managed by the government,
which is a necessity given the difference between ancient and modern times;
the multitude of clans throughout the realm
cannot all be verified by the central government offices (jīng cáo).
However, lawsuits arise from disputes over ancestral rites and inheritance;
lawsuits arise from disputes over property and succession;
lawsuits arise from assuming false surnames and occupying registers,
or submitting and returning to the clan;
lawsuits arise from assuming false surnames and occupying registers,
lawsuits arise from marriages violating regulations;
then there is litigation;
lawsuits arise from concealing or omitting household registration and labor duties.
then there is litigation.
Sometimes genealogical evidence is lost,
sometimes corrupt individuals forge documents,
causing confusion at the moment of litigation,
