and numerous abuses multiply.
If all genealogies (pǔ dié) are presented
as copies to the Zhì Kē in ordinary times,
then the calamity of these numerous problems will be avoided.
The contribution of this
to sound administration is also significant.
In antiquity, there were no private writings and compilations;
however, since the Warring States period,
it has not been possible to restrict them using ancient methods.
Nevertheless, if texts are not subject to official supervision,
people will be overwhelmed by their own self-serving biases.
When sacred learning declines, reckless debates corrupt its teachings,
and when official historians fail, unofficial histories indulge their private views;
The vulgarity and excess of recent literary collections, biographies, and epitaphs,
and the confusion of right and wrong in fictional writings (shuō bù),
profane and disrupt historical records,
and confuse honest public opinion,
to an extent that cannot be fully recounted or condemned.
If, regarding finalized and edited works,
copies must be presented to the Zhì Kē,
and the scholar-teachers (shīrú) of the schools discuss them impartially,
then the locality being close makes it easy to verify the facts,
and the time being recent prevents reliance on hearsay,
thereby avoiding the calamity of these numerous problems.
The contribution of this
to sound administration is almost incalculable.
Therefore, it is said that writing and political governance
are always interdependent, forming the inner and outer aspects of reality.
Geographical Gazetteers and Regional Division
Hóng Liàngjí, Compiler (Biānxiū) from Yánghú,
once compiled the *Qiánlóng Fǔ Tīng Zhōu Xiàn Zhì* (Qianlong Gazetteers of Prefectures, Sub-prefectures, Districts, and Counties).
His division of regions followed the precedent of the *Yītǒng Zhì* (Comprehensive Gazetteer),
using the Bùzhèng Shǐ Sī (Provincial Administration Commission) to supervise the Fǔ (Prefectures), Tīng (Sub-prefectures), Zhōu (Departments), and Xiàn (Counties).
Ten years ago, I
visited Mr. Hóng at his home,
and told him that, under the current system, this book should refer to the Bù Yuàn (Board and Ministry) system,
and should not rigidly adhere to the outdated text of Bùzhèng Shǐ Sī.
I then recounted how the division of regions in the current system differed from the initial system,
to clarify the underlying principle.
Mr. Hóng did not agree.
Recently, I saw his published *Juǎn Shī Gé Wénjí* (Collected Writings from the Juanshige Studio),
which contained the *Yǔ Zhāng Jìnshì Shū* (Letter to Presented Scholar Zhāng),
where he extensively quoted and cited sources
and forcefully refuted the argument regarding regional division.
I, however, still dare not agree with him.
Furthermore, much of what he refuted
was what I had already analyzed previously,
and should not have been repeated thus.
It seems that my original intention
Mr. Hóng scarcely remembers.
Therefore, I have written down my divergent opinion
to preserve and show to my students and sons,
to clarify what I believe to be right;
I dare not claim that my own theory must be correct.
Regarding the system of territorial administration (tǒng bù zhī zhì),
in the era of Fēngjiàn,
there were the Fāngbó.
In the era of Jùnxiàn (Commanderies and Counties),
starting with the Hàn dynasty, the territory was divided into thirteen Bùzhōu (Departments and Circuits);
during the Liùcháo (Six Dynasties), the Zhōujùn (Circuits and Commanderies)
had continuously changing systems.
The officials administering these regions,
although they held various titles such as Dūdū and Zǒngguǎn,
established their administrative seats (fǔ) inconsistently.
Therefore, when the Táng people compiled the geography of the Wǔdài (Five Dynasties),
namely the *Suí Zhì* (Geography Section of the History of the Suí),
they could not obtain a consistent administrative system (tǒng bù zhī shuō).
They even used the Jiǔzhōu (Nine Regions) from the *Yǔ Gòng* (Tributes of Yǔ)
to delineate the Jùnxiàn (Commanderies and Counties).
That was the flaw.
The Táng people divided the realm into Dào,
and the Sòng people divided it into Lù.
Although the official regulatory power (guān zhì tǒng xiá) changed frequently,
the names of the Dào and Lù did not change.
Thus, those compiling geographic records
simply listed the Dào or Lù to clearly define the divisions.
Although the Yuán system also divided territories into Lù,
all the Lù were primarily governed by the Xíngshěng Píngzhāng,
hence they were also called Xíngshěng.
The Míng dynasty then changed the Xíngshěng into the thirteen Bùzhèng Shǐ Sī (Provincial Administration Commissions).
The officials in charge of governing the territory
were called Bùzhèng Shǐ Sī Bùzhèng Shǐ.
The Bùzhèng Shǐ Sī
is the name of the administrative division,
while the Bùzhèng Shǐ
is the official administering the division—
they must not be confused.
However, Bùzhèng Shǐ Sī,
is a phrase of four characters,
while Xíngshěng could be abbreviated simply as Shěng.
It is human nature to prefer simplicity and convenience,
so although the official system was changed,
the popular usage at the time
simply called them Shěng.
As this usage continued for a long time,
it frequently appeared in memorials, reports, and official documents,
a gradual accumulation that did not happen overnight.
In Our Dynasty, the Bùzhèng Shǐ Sī
retained the old Míng system;
and the habitual use of the term Shěng
also followed the old Míng usage.
This is similar to the Hàn system where sons and younger brothers were enfeoffed with kingdoms
and granted the rank of Wáng (King),
but imperial edicts and official memorials
referred to them as Zhūhóu Wáng.
Although they were not truly Zhūhóu (Feudal Lords) at that time,
they followed ancient custom and adopted the traditional name.
However, the initial system strictly adhered to the old Míng model,
so the official proper designation should certainly be Bùzhèng Shǐ Sī.
For over a hundred years,
adapting systems to contemporary needs,
although the name still follows the Míng precedent,
the institutional structure (tǐ zhì) gradually differs from that of the Míng.
Now Hóng Jūn's writing uses the Qiánlóng era name,
so following the name to ascertain the reality,
one must call it Bùyuàn and should not call it Bùzhèngshǐ Sī.
In the initial system, the Xúnfǔ had no dedicated territory.
During the former Míng dynasty, the Liǎng Jīng (Two Capitals) had no Bùzhèngshǐ Sī,
yet Xúnfǔ were sometimes established in Shùntiān and Yìngtiān;
outside of Shùntiān,
there was also Zhèngdìng,
and outside of Yìngtiān,
there were various Governors (Fǔ) like Fèngyáng.
This is unlike the present system, where they govern the entire department
and have their own specific territories.
This is the first reason why they should be called Bùyuàn.
In the initial system, the Xúnfǔ had no fixed official rank.
Thus, before the Kāngxī era,
Xúnfǔ varied, being Second Rank (Èr Pǐn), Third Rank (Sān Pǐn), or Fourth Rank (Sì Pǐn);
those concurrently holding the title of Shìláng were Second Rank,
those holding Fù Dū Yùshǐ were Third Rank,
and those holding Qiān Dū Yùshǐ were Fourth Rank;
now they all concurrently hold Bīngbù Shìláng and Yòu Fù Dū Yùshǐ.
This formalized system
is no longer like the old Qīnchāi system, which had no fixed rules.
This is the second reason why they should be called Bùyuàn.
Xuéchāi (Education Commissioners) relating to the Boards
all have metropolitan posts;
remove their metropolitan posts,
and the official title ceases to exist.
Now when a Xúnfǔ is newly appointed,
the Lìbù must ask whether they should concurrently hold the titles of the Ministry of War and the Dūcháyuàn.
Although traditional practice has been followed,
there has never been one who did not concurrently hold these titles;
but since there is an inquiry about whether it should be done,
then there is also a principle that they might not concurrently hold the titles.
According to the *Huìdiǎn* and *Pǐnjí Kǎo* and other books,
the Xúnfǔ is already listed as Junior Second Rank (Cóng Èr Pǐn),
with a note saying:
"Adding the Shìláng title makes it Senior Second Rank (Zhèng Èr)."
Thus, even if the Xúnfǔ does not concurrently hold the metropolitan titles,
they already have a fixed rank,
just like the Jīngcháo Guān of the Sòng dynasty,
acting as Zhī Zhōujūn or Zhī Xiànshì:
although they held metropolitan titles,
one could not say that the prefecture/county was outside of Zhífāng.
This is the third reason why they should be called Bùyuàn.
The great affairs of the state
are sacrifices and military matters.
Now military administration is specially managed by the Zǒngdū,
and the Xúnfǔ also has standard troops (Biāobīng),
which is certainly beyond dispute.
Sacrifices at altars and temples,
which were formerly presided over by the Bùzhèngshǐ,
are now presided over by the Xúnfǔ.
This is the fourth reason why they should be called Bùyuàn.
For the great ceremony of selecting scholars (Bīnxīng Dàdiǎn),
the list of successful candidates was formerly sealed by the Bùzhèngshǐ's official stamp,
but now the Xúnfǔ's seal of authorization (Guānfáng) is used.
This is the fifth reason why they should be called Bùyuàn.
In the initial system, the Bùzhèngshǐ Sī had a Right and a Left,
dividing the affairs of personnel, revenue, rites, and public works.
The Dūsī managed military affairs,
and the Àncháshǐ Sī handled criminal justice.
Thus, the two Bùzhèng envoys
internally corresponded to the Six Ministries (Liù Bù);
and the one Ànchá envoy
internally corresponded to the Dūcháyuàn.
Now, the two envoys have been reduced to one,
and the responsibility for postal relays has been transferred to the Àncháshǐ,
the Dūsī was abolished and military authority was vested in the Zǒngdū and Xúnfǔ.
Their duties and responsibilities differ from the past.
Therefore, from imperial edicts above
down to memorials and official correspondence below,
all refer to the Zǒngdū and Xúnfǔ as Fēngjiāng (Frontier Officials),
and do not call them Yáoshǐ (Carriage Envoys);
they all consider the Bùzhèng Sī as the hub for Qián gǔ (Revenue and Grain),
and the Ànchá Sī as the hub for Xíngmíng (Judicial Affairs),
and do not regard the Bùzhèngshǐ as Fēngjiāng.
This, especially due to establishing the system based on the current time,
is the sixth reason why they must be called Bùyuàn.
Although the Zǒngdū and Xúnfǔ are both called Fēngjiāng,
the Zǒngdū's title is called Bùtáng (Board Minister);
this is because the Bīngbù Tángguān,
although concurrently holding Yòu Dū Yùshǐ,
still primarily focuses on military administration.
The Xúnfǔ's title is called Bùyuàn;
this is because the Dūcháyuàn Tángguān,
although concurrently holding Bīngbù Shìláng,
still primarily focuses on supervising officials.
Therefore, in the current system outside the Auxiliary Capital (Péijīng),
there are prefectures, departments, and counties that do not report to a Zǒngdū,
but absolutely none that do not report to a Xúnfǔ.
For instance, Hénán, Shāndōng, and Shānxī
have a Xúnfǔ but no Zǒngdū.
The Xúnfǔ does not necessarily hold the Zǒngdū title concurrently.
Zhílì, Sìchuān, and Gānsù
have a Zǒngdū but no Xúnfǔ;
in this case, the Zǒngdū must concurrently hold the Xúnfǔ title.
If the powers of the Zǒngdū and Xúnfǔ are equal,
why is it that when there is a Zǒngdū but no Xúnfǔ,
the Zǒngdū must concurrently hold the Xúnfǔ title?
Precisely because the Xúnfǔ Bùyuàn
standardizes the Zhífāng system,
this concurrent title is not added randomly.
This further illustrates the current era,
requiring understanding of the present system,
and is the seventh reason why they must be called Bùyuàn.
Today there are nineteen Bùzhèngshǐ Sī in the empire,
but according to the established rules of the *Huìdiǎn*,
in the official correspondence of the Six Ministries,
such as the Lìbù's Grand Review (Dàjì),
the Hùbù's Auditing of Accounts (Zòuxiāo),
the Lǐbù's Metropolitan Examinations (Huìshì),
and the Xíngbù's Autumn Assizes (Qiūkān),
they only recognize eighteen Zhílì provinces
and do not recognize nineteen Bùzhèngshǐ Sī;
this is because there are only eighteen Xúnfǔ Bùyuàn (In reality, there are only fifteen Xúnfǔ, the Zǒngdū covers the remaining three vacancies.).
Thus, the Jiāngsū Bùyuàn
has long been habitually referred to as Jiāngsū Shěng (Jiāngsū Province).
The Sūsōng Bùzhèngshǐ Sī
and the Jiānghuái Bùzhèngshǐ Sī
separately govern eight prefectures and three departments,
yet public and private documents
do not distinguish between Sūsōng Zhílì Province and Jiānghuái Zhílì Province.
This further demonstrates the system of partitioned boards,
meaning today they absolutely should not be called Shǐ Sī,
and this is the eighth reason why they must be called Bùyuàn.
Hóng Jūn asserts that because the Xúnfǔ uses a Guānfáng (seal of authorization)
rather than the formal seal (Zhèng Yìn) of the Bùzhèngshǐ Sī,
the Xúnfǔ cannot be the proper local authority (Zhèng Zhǔ).
This can be called knowing ten but forgetting that ten is made of two fives.
According to Hóng Jūn's statement,
then his names for prefectures (Fǔ), sub-prefectures (Tīng), departments (Zhōu), and counties (Xiàn)
are also incorrect.
Fǔ, Zhōu, and Xiàn certainly have their own seals,
but the Tīng, which is administered by the Zhílì Tóngzhī (Directly Subordinate Sub-Prefect),
only has a Guānfáng and no official seal.
The Tóngzhī issues the Zhīfǔ's seal,
and yet the Guānfáng can lead Zhífāng;
the Xúnfǔ shares the Dūcháyuàn's seal,
but can the Guānfáng not lead Zhífāng?
Why is he clear about the minor issue but obscure about the major one?
This is the ninth reason why they should be called Bùyuàn.
Hóng Jūn also says that the current system of Zǒngdū and Xúnfǔ
should be compared to the Hàn dynasty system where the Chéngxiàng's Zhǎngshǐ went out to inspect the affairs of the prefecture (Zhōu),
where although the Zhōu administered commanderies (Jùn),
the *Hàn Zhì* still took the commanderies and kingdoms (Jùn Guó) as the principal entities,
and did not list the Cìshǐ among them.
This comparison is not very apt.
In the current system, only the Jiāngsū Bùyuàn
has two Bùzhèngshǐ Sī;
outside of this, the territory governed by the Shǐ Sī
is the same as the territory governed by the Bùyuàn,
unlike the Hàn system where one Zhōu necessarily administered several Jùn.
However, even based on what Hóng Jūn said,
the *Shísān Zhōuzhì* by Kàn Shì
is a dedicated book;
how could it fail to list the Cìshǐ of the Zhōu in the Zhífāng section?
This is the tenth reason why they should be called Bùyuàn.
Now, changes to the system
must have explicit written decrees.
When the former Míng dynasty first dispatched the Xúnfǔ, they and the officials of the Three Commissions (Sān Shǐ Sī) were merely
in the relationship of guest and host.
Those who were slightly more respected
were merely examples of officials of the ruler placed above the regional lords.
Thereafter, the power of the central authority (Tái Quán) gradually increased,
and the Three Commissions acted in accordance with the Tái’s decree.
However, the system had not yet changed;
all major matters like the Grand Review (Jì Diǎn), Auditing of Accounts (Zòuxiāo),
selection of scholars (Bīnxīng), and sacrifices (Jìsì),
were exclusively managed by the Bùzhèngshǐ.
Therefore, the Bùzhèngshǐ was the chief official governing the department,
and the title could not be changed simply because the Xúnfǔ's authority was light.
For more than a hundred years of Our Dynasty,
the system of official duties and responsibilities
has gradually changed.
By today, the Bùzhèngshǐ official and the Àncháshǐ official,
who separately manage revenue, grain, and judicial affairs,
are both subordinate officials of the Bùyuàn,
somewhat resembling the Cānzhèng and Cānyì found in the Xíngshěng system of the Yuán dynasty.
Regarding all major policies and ceremonies
where the duties were taken away from the Bùzhèngshǐ and transferred to the Bùyuàn,
there have historically been explicit written decrees;
this is known by both the court and the common people.
Yet, whether the governing department should still be called Shǐ Sī
or changed to Bùyuàn,
there is conversely no explicit written decree.
Why is this?
Because official and private documents
all conveniently follow common practice and use the name Zhílì Shěng (Directly Subordinate Province).
Not only does the Bùyuàn lack a modernized name,
but even the Shǐ Sī does not generally follow the old name either.
Statutes and standard regulations,
imperial edicts and official correspondence,
all use the term Zhílì Shěng;
only the *Yītǒng Zhì* still follows the old precedent,
calling it Bùzhèngshǐ Sī,
which has accidentally not been corrected.
Since Hóng Jūn entitled his work with the Qiánlóng era name,
how can he be ignorant of the contemporary affairs during the sixty years of Qiánlóng?
Someone might say:
The *Tǒng Zhì* is a book from the Imperial Library (Guǎngé),
Hóng Jūn followed the system and established the rules,
how can you criticize it?
I say that the original rules of the *Tǒng Zhì* were already fixed,
and later continuity meant they were not updated (The original rule should have naturally prioritized the Sī [Office]).
The institutional changes that transformed the Sī into the Bùyuàn [Board/Ministry and Court]
occurred gradually,
not through a single sudden act of innovation;
therefore, the Guǎngé did not update them.
When writing privately,
the rule arises from principle,
precisely because the system dictates it so.
Moreover, what I distinguish here
is not entirely directed at Hóng Jūn's book.
Those who write classical prose today,
when referring to the Tǒng Bù [Command/Administrative Division],
also say "Zhū Shěng" (various provinces),
or "Mǒu Shěng" (a certain province).
Abandoning the currently implemented system
and borrowing the names used by the Yuán people—
this is something unheard of in antiquity.
Before Yōngzhèng and Kāngxī,
classical prose also lacked the term Shǐ Sī [Supervising Office];
(At that time, logically it should have been called Shǐ Sī.) Thus, the Míng people simply abbreviated the writing,
and persisted in following the Yuán system,
which has been a flaw in classical prose for a long time.
Therefore, in my classical prose,
for matters that should be called Tǒng Bù,
the common practice might say "Mǒu Shěng,"
but I must say "Mǒu Bùyuàn,"
or abbreviate it to "Mǒu Bù;"
the common practice might say "Zhū Shěng" or "Mǒu Mǒu Děng Shěng" (various provinces or such-and-such provinces),
but I must say "Zhū Bùyuàn" or "Mǒu Mǒu Děng Bùyuàn,"
and the abbreviation is "Zhū Bù" or "Mǒu Mǒu Děng Bù;"
in this way, the names will be correct and the speech will be smooth.
If it were not for today's system,
then one must say Shǐ Sī,
or abbreviate it to Sī,
which would not be impossible,
but calling it Shěng is absolutely not permissible.
Someone might say:
Imperial edicts (Zhào Zhǐ), memorials (Zhāng Zòu), and official correspondence (Wén Yí)—
why do they still all use it?
I reply:
Using it there is harmless because it functions merely as terminology (cí yǔ),
it is not a standard precedent for classical writing.
Furthermore, for example, in Zhào Zhǐ, Zhāng Zòu, and Wén Yí,
the Bùzhèng (Administration Commissioner) is called Fān,
the Ànchá (Surveillance Commissioner) is called Niè,
and the chiefs of Fǔ, Zhōu, and Xiàn are called Shǒu, Mù, and Lìng;
such terminology is therefore harmless,
but historical writing (Shǐ Wén) has no such precedent.
Prefatory Rules for the Section on Imperial Statements (Huáng Yán Jì Xù Lì) in the *Hé Zhōu Zhì*:
In the *Zhōu Guān* (Rites of Zhōu),
the Wài Shǐ (Outer Scribe) "manages the records (zhì) of the four directions,"
and also, "when sending writings to the four directions,
then he records the commands (lìng)."
Zhèng Shì (Master Zhèng)'s commentary states that the records of the four directions
“are like Lǔ's *Chūn Qiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals),
Jìn's *Shèng*,
and Chǔ's *Táo Wù*.”
This is correct.
Recording the commands
means "recording the royal mandates and entrusting them to the envoys."
This is correct.
The Xiāng Dàfū (Village Senior Official), on "the auspicious day of the first month,
receives the teachings and laws from the Sītú (Minister of Education),
retires and promulgates them to the village officials."
Kǒng Shì (Master Kǒng)'s commentary states "this refers to the twelve teachings and subsequent items under the responsibility of the Dà Sītú (Grand Minister of Education)."
This is correct.
Now, the Six Districts within the royal domain (Jī Nèi Liù Xiāng),
were governed directly by the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ);
thus, they received the laws from the Sītú.
But the feudal territories outside the royal domain (Jī Wài Hóu Fēng),
each governed their own state,
and according to their state system, they independently compiled their *Chūn Qiū* (The histories of the feudal states were collectively named *Chūn Qiū*.).
Nevertheless, the writings from the four directions
must be registered with the Wài Shǐ;
and the issuing of written commands
was honored and treated as canonical statute.
Thus, in antiquity, states had separate writings,
but what was illuminated by the bamboo slips and scrolls
first and foremost emphasized the Royal Mandate (Wáng Mìng);
this can certainly be verified.
Therefore, the *Chūn Qiū* must record the Royal Calendar (Wáng Zhèng) at the beginning of the year,
and when Hán Xuānzǐ (Master Hán Xuān) visited Lǔ,
he was able to see the *Yì Xiàng* and the *Chūn Qiū*,
and declared that the Rites of Zhōu were contained therein.
Indeed, the writings in the four directions
must be submitted and corrected by the Wài Shǐ;
and when commands were carried out in the royal state,
they were also issued and promulgated by the Wài Shǐ.
Therefore, affairs had specialized officials,
and writings had fixed standards;
this is how the realm achieved the governance of "unified writing" (tóng wén).
I humbly suggest that under the governance described in the *Zhōu Guān*,
the historical records of the feudal states
must have had established methods
received from the Royal Court,
just like the Xiāng Dàfū received the teachings and laws,
to examine the texts,
so that nothing strange or astonishing existed.
As for the histories of Jìn and Chǔ,
which independently named their books *Shèng* and *Táo Wù*,
was this a system resulting from the decline of Zhōu authority and the loss of official positions,
where the feudal states arrogated power to themselves?
Sīmǎ Qiān’s sections on the hereditary houses of the feudal states (Hóu Guó Shì Jiā)
also preserve the meaning of states having separate writings,
and the chapter on Xiàowǔ’s Three Kings (Sān Wáng)
details the imperial edicts and pronouncements,
placing them at the head of the chapter.
The silk thread of the Royal Word (Wáng Yán Sī Lún)
is what historians value highly,
and this tradition has a long origin.
In later generations, the writings of the various regions (fāng zhōu)
suffered from disorder in their arrangement,
and their essential structure was inappropriate:
the imperial edicts and pronouncements of the court (Zhāo Gào)
were sometimes placed in the Arts and Letters section (Yì Wén);
the chapter headings
sometimes recorded only historical development (Yán Gé).
Furthermore, sometimes because a Zhōu or Xiàn was a remote corner
and had not received specific promulgations of virtuous announcements,
this resulted in the historical institutions of the Central Court (Zhōng Cháo Zhǎng Gù),
which should have been scattered throughout the records of the four directions,
being utterly missing and unable to be verified.
This is certainly because the art of compilation
has been lost for generations;
but it is also because the specialized official post of Wài Shǐ
has not been properly defined and recognized
since the Qín and Hàn dynasties.
Now, in the age of feudalism (fēng jiàn),
states compiled separate histories,
yet they still emphasized the record of the Royal Calendar at the beginning of the chapter.
In the system of Commanderies and Districts (Jùn Xiàn) subject to governance,
the administrators (Shǒu Lìng) received and executed imperial edicts,
exactly following the ancient laws of the rural administrative units (Xiāng Dǎng Zhōu Lǘ) within the royal domain.
Yet, the historical institutions managed by the Wài Shǐ
were never specifically established as separate rules.
The Zhōu Xiàn historical records of the Sòng, Yuán, and Míng dynasties
that are visible today
all follow the same pattern,
showing their extreme failure to grasp the principle of the *Chūn Qiū*!
Now, compiling and recording all existing materials within the Zhōu,
I respectfully arrange them into Volume One, the *Huáng Yán Jì* (Record of Imperial Statements),
sequencing them by era.
This brightly illuminates the beginning of the chapter,
to record the origins of the respectful mandates we receive.
Prefatory Rules for the Section on Officials and Teachers (Guān Shī Biǎo Xù Lì) in the *Hé Zhōu Zhì*:
In the *Zhōu Guān*,
the Yù Shǐ (Imperial Secretary) "manages the supplementary records,
and counts those participating in government."
Zhèng Shì’s commentary says, "It is generally numbering them and listing those currently in vacant or filled positions."
This supplements the Dà Zǎi (Grand Minister) in establishing the Six Canons and managing the historical institutions of the state governance.
Now, officials have succession,
and government has successes and failures;
the Dà Zǎi maintains the fundamental principles,
and the Yù Shǐ enumerates the relevant personnel to assist with it.
In this way, the hundred offices are organized, and all achievements flourish.
In later generations, in the chapters on official etiquette
and the rules for examination and selection (such as *Hàn Guān Yí*, *Táng Liù Diǎn*, *Liáng Xuǎn Bù*, *Suí Guān Xù Lù*),
established books existed in every era,
but the names of the officials and their posts
were so vast that they could not be fully recorded.
Thus, they had the framework of the Dà Zǎi,
but lacked the Yù Shǐ who counted those participating in government.
Bān Gù’s *Bǎi Guān Gōng Qīng Biǎo* (Table of All Officials and Dukes)
still preserves the ancient concept;
the narrative of offices at the beginning of the chapter
is a remnant of the Dà Zǎi’s Six Canons,
and the subsequent listing of officials' names and posts
is a remnant of the Yù Shǐ's duty to count those participating in government.
After Fàn and Chén,
this tradition faded away.
As for the *Táng Shū* and the *Sòng Shǐ*,
they do contain the *Zǎi Xiàng Nián Biǎo* (Chronological Table of Chief Ministers),
but they still had no time to extend this to various officials (Qīng Yǐn);
This was not solely due to insufficient consideration by the historians,
but also because the historical records were exceedingly numerous,
making a comprehensive listing naturally difficult.
Regarding those scholars who delight in antiquity,
who compile systems of rank and regulations,
who link together names and surnames,
books concerning official posts and historical precedents,
since the era of the Liùcháo,
have flourished greatly.
However, the precedents concerning the central government (zhōngcháo)
are not sufficient for the commanderies and provinces (fāngzhōu);
these trivial compilations
are difficult to include in historical records (shǐzhì);
thus, the records lacked methods,
and the sequencing lost order.
The historians of the past cannot but be held responsible for this fault.
Now, the various officials, Qīng and Yǐn,
were ordered in the central government (zhōngcháo) narrative of offices;
the administrators and magistrates (shǒulìng) of the commanderies and provinces (fāngzhōu),
were recorded by the external scribes (wàishǐ).
In the *Zhōuguān*, the Imperial Censors (yùshǐ) enumerated the officials involved in administration.
Thus, the records of the four quarters overseen by the external scribes (wàishǐ),
were not limited to mountains, rivers, and local customs;
all those who were assigned offices and received duties
must have had their records,
which were then submitted to the custody of Zhùxià.
This can be known.
The collected works of Táng literati
often contain records of names inscribed on hall walls (tīngbì tímíng zhī jì);
this was likely also intended as a narrative of offices.
However, the writings survive, but the names cannot be verified.
Unless one comprehensively searches inscriptions on metal and stone (jīnshí)
and thoroughly examines stelae (bēijié),
they cannot be known.
This is the reason why they were never compiled into specialized books.
Since the Sòng and Yuán dynasties,
up to the recent works concerning commanderies and provinces (fāngzhōu),
they frequently record the names of appointed officials;
however, they are trivial and lack literary grace (wén),
like reviewing the attendance register (mǎobù) of district magistrates (xiànlìng) and their subordinates.
Thus, this is also not the remaining legacy of Bān Gù’s historical method of weaving yearly threads (niánjīng) and monthly warps (yuèwěi).
Some compilers who arranged their material into tables (biǎo),
had introductions and prefaces that were not detailed,
and the ranks and grades (pǐnzhì) lacked sequence.
Others were limited by the size of the page (chǐfú);
if there were slightly more official ranks,
or changes in institutions over time (yángé),
they immediately separated civil and military officials into different compilations,
or recorded prefectures and departments separately,
in order to pursue easy simplicity.
They did not understand the surviving method of the historian Bān Gù, where thirty-four offices
were divided into fourteen grades.
Furthermore, the surnames of previous generations
cannot be universally known,
but the surviving compilations fully exist,
and other accounts mutually confirm them.
If one does not widely gather and extensively search,
but merely invokes the excuse of missing text (quēwén),
this is a failing that cannot be spoken of when discussing the effort of studying antiquity (jīgǔ).
Now, taking the middle ground among various sources,
I examine and sequence them chronologically.
Starting above with the Hàn Dynasty
and extending to the present day,
I compile them into a single table (biǎo),
omitting those that are doubtful.
Those who examine it later
will be able to make it more detailed.
Preface and Method for the Table of Selection and Appointment in the Hézhōu Gazetteer
In the *Zhōuguān*,
the Xiāng Dàfū, during the "Grand Triennial Assessment (dàbǐ),"
promoted the talented and worthy of one district,
and presented the written selections to the King.
The King bowed twice to receive them,
and entered them into the Heavenly Treasury (tiānfǔ)."
This was a very magnificent ritual.
The Hàn system,
with its appointments of Xiàolián (Filial and Incorrupt), Màocái (Flourishing Talent), Lìtián (Agricultural Strength), and Xiánliáng (Worthy and Good),
was essentially a remnant of the ancient system of districts (xiāngdǎng) and villages (zhōulǘ).
At that time, records concerning the selection of worthies and official documents,
and the selection and promotion of officials (pìjǔ zhǎnggù),
did not yet have specialized books;
thus, because regulations and statutes were numerous,
the rise and fall of cultural achievements (rénwén)
were scattered throughout the basic annals (jì) and biographies (zhuàn).
A dedicated scholar
could examine and know them himself.
During the Liùcháo period south of the Yangtze River (Jiāngzuǒ),
prefectures and commanderies frequently shifted their locations,
scholars were not tied to their native soil (tǔzhù),
and learning was not specialized.
Therefore, selection by district (xiāngjǔ) and village (lǐxuǎn)
gradually became difficult to implement.
When it came to the Suí regime (Suíshì),
they standardized the reliance on literature and rhetoric (wénxué cízhāng),
and established the system of selecting Jìnshì (Presented Scholars).
Since the beginning of the Táng Dynasty,
this has greatly flourished.
Since the system of selection and appointment (xuǎnjǔ) became centralized,
the qualifications became increasingly important,
regulations and statutes proliferated,
and precedents were passed down.
Consequently, literary scholars
collected statutes and precedents (diǎnzhāng),
and gathered things heard and seen.
Whether recognizing things great or small,
they all produced compiled works.
Biographical accounts and historical precedents
were mixed with humorous anecdotes (páixié),
and books on selection and appointment (xuǎnjǔ)
were amassed, equaling the collections stored by Zhùxià.
Since the compositions were numerous,
the organization and methodological principles (yìlì)
could not follow a single course.
If one seeks their purpose,
they generally fall into three categories:
Such as Cháo Jiǒng’s *Jìnshì Biānchì*
and Lù Shēn’s *Kēchǎng Tiáoguàn*,
which are books of laws, regulations, and official decrees (gōnglìng).
Yáo Kāng’s and Yuè Shǐ’s *Kēdì Lù* (Yáo Kāng sixteen *juǎn*, Yuè Shǐ ten *juǎn*),
Lǐ Yì’s and Hóng Shì’s *Dēngkē Jì* (Lǐ Yì’s two *juǎn* are lost. Hóng Shì’s fifteen *juǎn*),
are the types of records and biographies concerning inscribed names (tímíng).
Wáng Dìngbǎo’s *Táng Zhíyán*,
and Qián Míngyì’s *Sòng Yīguān Shèngshì*,
are classified as unofficial miscellaneous records (bàiyě zájì).
The official historian (shǐchén) collected historical precedents (zhǎnggù),
compiled them into treatises and monographs (shūzhì),
selected human affairs,
and sequenced them into collected biographies (lièzhuàn).
Since one era is vast and complex,
and the methodological principles (yìlì) are rigorous,
what was left over after editing and excising (bǐxuē)
was equivalent to discarded hemp refuse
or spit-out fruit pits.
However, the old, trivial compilations,
and miscellaneous records lacking literary quality (wén),
short tablets and brief writings,
cannot be transmitted through the ages or travel far.
This caused the cultural achievements of the highest ranks (jiǎdì rénwén)—
those things for which the *Zhōuguān* ordained bowing and presentation to the King and entering into the Heavenly Treasury—
to be missing and incomplete.
Therefore, the books of the commanderies and provinces (fāngzhōu)
did not follow the system whereby the Xiāng Dàfū carefully esteemed records of worthies;
this is the fault of records lacking method
and organization being unclear.
In recent times, there have been some who critically examined and established independent books for commanderies and provinces (fāngzhōu),
such as Yuè Shǐ’s *Jiāngnán Dēngkē Jì*,
Zhāng Cháoruì’s *Nánguó Xiánshū*,
and Chén Rǔyuán’s *Huáng Míng Zhèshì Dēngkē Kǎo*.
All these classify and gather the precedents of one region,
but unfortunately, they have not been seen to circulate throughout the realm.
As for the gazetteers (zhìshū) of departments and districts (zhōuxiàn),
which arrange the subjects of examination (kēmù)
and list the recommended and tribute students (jǔgòng) in tables (biǎo),
since the early Míng Dynasty,
this model has been largely preserved.
Compared to the books of the departments and commanderies of the Sòng and Yuán periods,
it can be said that they have strengths, however small.
However, their organizational principles (tǐlì) are not yet refined,
the records lack method,

and they are unfamiliar with the precedents of yearly threads and event warps (niánjīng shìwěi) (Some compilers who use tables contain many contradictions in the articles concerning recommended and tribute students, minor officials, and those granted hereditary rank by imperial grace (fēngyìn)).
They are compiled trivially and confusedly into books.
In extreme cases, they attach records of deeds;
tables (biǎo) and biographies (zhuàn) are not separated.
This has become a widespread custom,
and its errors cannot be fully enumerated (from the General Discussion of the First Chapter of the Discourse on Poetry and Biographies).
Now, collecting texts from historical records and gazetteers (shǐzhì),
I first detail the institutions (zhìdù),
and then list the inscribed names (tímíng).
Arranging them chronologically by generation,
starting from the Táng Dynasty
and extending to the present day,
I create the *Xuǎnjǔ Biǎo* (Table of Selection and Appointment).
Those granted hereditary rank (fēngyìn) or appointed via recommendation (pìjǔ),
which cannot be dated by year,
are attached at the end.
Preface and Method for the Table of Clans and Families in the Hézhōu Gazetteer, Part One.
In the *Zhōuguān*,
the Minor Historian (*Xiǎoshǐ*) "establishes the lineage sequence,
distinguishes the *zhāomù* (senior/junior generations)."
The management of genealogical records (*pǔdié*),
in antiquity, had dedicated officials.
Sīmǎ Qiān took the records of the *Wǔdì Xì* (Lineage of the Five Thearchs) and the chronicles compiled in the *Shàngshū* (Venerable Documents),
to create the *Sāndài Shìbiǎo* (Tables of the Lineages of the Three Dynasties);
thus, the origins of clans and lineages
have long had a foundation.
From Bān Gù onward,
genealogies were not included.
However, Wáng Fú's chapter on "Clans and Surnames" (the thirty-fifth chapter of *Qiánfū Lùn*),
and Dù Yù's genealogy of "Generations and Clans" (the second chapter of *Chūnqiū Shìlì*),
were specialized achievements in compiling classics and composing treatises.
They had specific expertise,
stopping when their intended meaning was complete,
and did not further pursue genealogical studies.
Since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
extending through the Six Dynasties (*Liùcháo*),
the prestige of powerful clans gradually increased.
Scholars and high officials
often followed the residual idea of the Grand Historian's (*Tàishǐ*) hereditary houses (*shìjiā*),
compiling their own family biographies.
Examples of their varied naming conventions,

such as the *Wáng Sù Jiāchuán* (Family Biography of Wáng Sù), Yú Lǎn's *Jiājì* (Family Record), Fàn Wāng's *Shìchuán* (Generational Tradition), Míng Càn's *Shìlù* (Generational Register), and Lù Xù's *Jiāshǐ* (Family History) (the *Lù Shǐ* in fifteen scrolls),
were all specialized books compiled
separate from formal genealogies,
awaiting those who would collect and record them.

As for Zhì Yú's *Zhāomù Jì* (Record of Zhāo and Mù), Wáng Jiǎn's *Bǎijiā Pǔ* (Genealogy of a Hundred Families), as well as Hè Shì's *Xìng Yuàn* (Garden of Surnames) and Jiǎ Shì's *Yàozhuàng* (Essential Records) (Jiǎ Xījiàn's *Shìzú Yàozhuàng* in fifteen scrolls),
these compiled and gathered numerous lineages,
classifying and sequencing them.
The best among them could supplement historical annals (*shǐchéng*),
while the lesser might drift into encyclopedias (*lèishū*).
Their distinctions were vast,
and must be recognized.
As clan hierarchy became stricter,
the prestige of the commandery (*jùnwàng*) grew heavier.
Such as the Liú clan of Pèiguó,
the Lǐ clan of Lǒngxī,
the Wáng clan of Tàiyuán,
and the Xiè clan of Chénjùn.
Although their descendants were scattered
or originally did not reside together,
nevertheless, when speaking of clan prestige,
they must trace back to their origin.
When the Later Wèi (Hòuwèi) moved the capital to Luò,
there were the Eight Surnames, the Ten Surnames, the Thirty-Six Clans, and the Ninety-Two Surnames,
all residing in Hénán and Luòyáng.
And the people of the Central States (*Zhōngguó*),
each ranking their aristocratic families (*ménfá*),
created genealogical registers (*pǔlù*) covering the Great Surnames of the Four Seas, the Provincial Surnames (*Zhōuxìng*), the Commandery Surnames (*Jùnxìng*), and the County Surnames (*Xiànxìng*).
During the Qí and Liáng eras,
this custom flourished even more;
Commandery Genealogies (*Jùnpǔ*) and Provincial Records (*Zhōudié*)
all had dedicated books.
Such as those recorded by Wáng Jiǎn and Wáng Sēngrú (Wáng Jiǎn's *Zhūzhōu Pǔ* in twelve scrolls, Wáng Sēngrú's *Shíbā Zhōu Pǔ* in seven hundred scrolls),
works like the *Jìzhōu Xìngzú* (Clans and Lineages of Jìzhōu) and the *Yángzhōu Pǔchāo* (Abridged Genealogy of Yángzhōu),
too numerous to count,
all tied generational prestige to provinces and commanderies.
Liú Zhījǐ of the Táng dynasty, discussing historical records and chronicles,
held that the books of clan genealogies
rightly ought to be included in history.
Subsequently, Ōuyáng's *Táng Shū* (History of Táng)
compiled the Lineages of the Chancellors (*Zǎixiàng Shìxì*);
but it overlooked distinguished families and great clans
whose members did not become chancellors,
resulting in occasional omissions.
Up to Zhèng Qiáo's *Tōng Zhì* (Comprehensive Records),
which first established the epitome of "Clans and Lineages" (*Shìzú*).
His introductory remarks
illuminated the importance of genealogical studies,
explaining why historical studies lacked proper transmission—
he frequently spoke of this with deep regret.
But later historians,
failing to follow his method,
created an omission in the historical section (*Shǐbù*).
In antiquity,
blind musicians (*gǔméng*) recited odes,
and simultaneously recited genealogies,
to admonish and encourage the sovereign.
This is what the *Guóyǔ* (Discourses of the States) meant when it said: "Teaching them the lineages,
and thereby illuminating virtue."
Therefore, matters of establishing lineage sequences,
managed by the Minor Historian,
and recited by the blind musician,
were valued by the former kings;
this was because they honored human principles and traced back to the origins.
At that time, the elders of the provinces, hamlets, clans, and parties
instructed the people to read the laws;
the District Grandee (*Xiāng Dàfū*), during the triennial grand review (*dàbǐ*),
examined virtues and skills and presented registers to the king;
thus, the materials concerning lineages and generations
must have existed as fixed registers,
which were gathered and submitted to the Minor Historian.
This is evident.
Grouping individuals forms families,
grouping families forms states,
grouping states forms the world (*Tiānxià*).
If family records are not maintained,
then upon what source
can the historical affairs of the state rely for verification?
The *Yì* (Book of Changes) says:
"Heaven and Fire make *Tóngrén* (Community).
The superior man uses this to classify clans and distinguish things."
Among great things,
none surpasses humanity.
Among important humans,
none is more important than the clan.
Miscellaneous records and commentaries
sometimes extend to insects and fish;
books of geography
must verify local products;
yet regarding how the former kings bestowed territories and divided surnames,
thereby honoring mankind and clarifying hierarchical relationships (*lúnxù*),
there are omissions and lack of records.
This does not serve to illuminate the principle of great comprehensiveness.
Furthermore, books of genealogy,
when stored in private households,
are easily scattered and lost;
if entirely incorporated into the national history,
one fears they would be too numerous.
Therefore, the gazetteers of the regions and provinces,
when examined and compiled into established editions,
can serve as a summary of various family records
and provide essential abridgements for the national history.
This is also an indispensable duty for those who hold the historian’s brush.
From the Prefatory Notes on the Table of Clans and Lineages in the Gazetter of Hézhōu.
The duty of managing the lineages and generations (jì shì) is assigned to the Minor Scribe (Xiǎoshǐ),
and the duty of managing the census (mín shù) is assigned to the Minister of the Multitudes (Sītú);
their principle is the same.
Dù Zǐchūn says:

"The recording of lineages and generations pertains to the Imperial Lineage (Dì Xì) and the genealogical records (shì běn) of the regional lords (zhūhóu), high ministers (qīng), and grand masters (dàfū)."
If so, then it is clear that
the records of the lineages
of the common people (bǐ wǔ xiǎomín), who are grouped together, do not belong to the Minor Scribe (Xiǎoshǐ).
The Village Grand Master (Xiāng Dàfū) records the number of people in the households seasonally every year,
and every three years, through the Great Comparison (Dà Bǐ), raises up the worthy and capable people of a village.
Now, the number of people in the households
is exactly the census managed by the Grand Minister of the Multitudes (Dà Sītú) mentioned above,
and the worthy and capable ones are candidates for High Ministers and Grand Masters (qīng dàfū).
This too is clear.
The common people are humble,
so only the number of households and individuals is recorded;
the High Ministers and Grand Masters are noble,
so their generational records are detailed.
This is the natural tendency of established custom.
In later historical records and gazetteers (shǐ zhì),
household registration is recorded in detail,
but the compilation of genealogies is unheard of.
This is equivalent to having common people but having no High Ministers and Grand Masters.
The *Shū* (Book of Documents) says:
"When the nine kindreds (jiǔ zú) are harmonious,
illuminate and clarify the Hundred Surnames (bǎixìng)."
Zhèng Shì's commentary notes:
"The Hundred Surnames
refers to the fathers, sons, and brothers of the assembled officials."
(See the commentary on Sīmǎ Qiān’s *Wǔ Dì Běnjì*.) Píngzhāng
means to distinguish and make illustrious.
This is the origin of the Minor Scribe's (Xiǎoshǐ) duty of recording lineages in the *Zhōu Guān* (Rites of Zhōu).
Mèngzǐ (Mencius) said:
"What is meant by an 'ancient state' (gù guó)
is not that it possesses tall trees,
but that it possesses hereditary officials (shì chén)."
Modern prefectural and county gazetteers (zhōu xiàn zhī zhì)
linger over ancient sites
and sentimentalize local connections;
but as for the records of generational lineages,
they omit them and fail to discuss them.
This means they value the tall trees while slighting the hereditary families.
Furthermore, if the national history (guó shǐ) does not record them,
and the prefectural gazetteers (zhōu zhì) do not contain them,
and the methods for genealogies
are not managed by the government,
then families will compile their own books,
and individuals will make their own claims.
Descendants may overly praise their ancestors,
and their accounts of right and wrong may deviate considerably from the national history.
Among the undeserving sort,
some falsely claim connection to worthies and sages,
or privately sell clan genealogies (zōng pǔ),
using falsehoods to corrupt the truth.
The extravagance, fabrication, and confusion
are beyond description.
As for the noble clans,
they boast of their clan status,
and arbitrarily establish names [in their records].
Taking the various families like the Wáng and Xiè (Wáng Xiè) of the Jiāngzuǒ region,
if they merely had official merit,
they immediately marked themselves for biographical inclusion.
The historical officials, holding their brushes,
were unable to decide or refuse them.
Thus, the Lǐ must be from Lǒngxī,
and the Liú must be from Pèiguó.
If one merely seeks status and prestige
without asking about origin,
then the defects of having genealogies
are worse than having none.
The omissions in historical records and gazetteers
are perhaps also the fault of our predecessors.
If the central administration (Sīfǔ) governs the prefectures and counties,
and the prefectures and counties govern the hereditary clans,
and the hereditary clans lead the common people,
then the great plan for the entire realm
can be spoken of as readily as pointing to one's palm.
In the three hundred years of the Táng dynasty, the genealogies
only recorded the chancellors (zǎixiàng).
The sheer vastness of that era
resulted from having no alternative plan.
For the records of the various prefectures,
recording those who achieved official posts through the examination system
is certainly the method by which the Village Grand Masters (Xiāng Dàfū) of the accomplished Zhōu dynasty recorded and reported the worthy and capable.
Now, following the surviving principles of the *Zhōu Guān*,
we specifically document the clans and families.
The advantages of this are generally ten.
First, historical authority will not be scattered.
The records of private families
will have a standard to mediate them.
This is the first advantage.
Second, genealogical methods will be unified.
Where the general rules of private genealogies are incomplete,
they can be referenced and incorporated.
This is the second advantage.
Third, the pure and the mixed will be separated.
Those who do not belong to the documented clans
will be unable to falsely claim association.
Social rank will thus be differentiated.
This is the third advantage.
Fourth, registered membership will be established.
When evaluating essays and selecting scholars,
the proper lineage will be available for inspection.
For those not on the register,
screening and verification will be easy.
This is the fourth advantage.
Fifth, the generational order and familial proximity
will be orderly and systematic.
Whether for the births dedicated to the worship of former worthies,
or for discussions concerning the adoption of heirs for broken lines,
the disputes over becoming an heir
will be easily settled.
This is the fifth advantage.
Sixth, ancestral lineages will be clear.
Whether the family moved here from another region
or later moved to another region,
the generational chart will be compiled in the prefectural gazetteer.
If the genealogical records
of other prefectures and counties have been lost or scattered,
this record can be used to verify those others.
This is the sixth advantage.
Seventh, regarding changes of surname,
the period of the change, the sequence, and the reason for the alteration
will be clearly noted in the record.
Thus, distinctions regarding marriage will be possible;
moreover, those who compile and clarify genealogical studies
will be able to investigate their origins.
This is the seventh advantage.
Eighth, the generational lineage will be continuous.
For respected families,
even if they achieved office through the examination system,
their genealogy might be recorded,
but their virtuous conduct, moral principles, and accomplishments
might not be included in the biographies.
To pass away unmentioned
is a shame for devoted scholars.
This record will contain no additions or deletions,
and its purpose will serve both encouragement and warning.
This is the eighth advantage.
Ninth, the local standing will be emphasized.
The archways, markers, districts, and neighborhoods
will not be set up in vain.
This is the ninth advantage.
Tenth, when gathering records and investigating sources,
and when the imperial archives (guǎn gé) issue a summons for collection,
seeking them according to the gazetteer
will be as easy as pointing to one’s palm.
This is the tenth advantage.
If so, then by compiling and clarifying this,
it can be extended to all prefectures, departments, and counties;
it is not merely the gazetteer of a single prefecture.
Conclusion to the Introductory Rules for the Clan and Family Chart in the Gazetteer of Hézhōu.
The *Yì* (Book of Changes) says:
"Things cannot be exhausted,
hence it is succeeded by *Wèijì* (Before Completion)."
Now, gathering what is scattered and lost
means that there was first scattering and loss,
and only afterwards was there gathering.
Documenting what is hidden and obscure
means that there was first obscurity,
and only afterwards was there documentation.
The biographies (liè zhuàn) in Chén Shòu's *Shǔ Zhì*
conclude with the eulogies of Yáng Xì;
Cháng Qú's *Huáyáng* records, in the preface,
generally preserve the names of both scholars and women.
These two men knew that historical materials are sometimes exhausted,
so they used eulogies and prefaces to record the names,
preserving the general outline.
They clearly marked the reason why they reluctantly preserved only what little they had.
This is also the old convention for omissions in historical records.
Hézhōu was a prominent prefecture during the Táng and Sòng dynasties,
yet the evidence from historical documents
is barely visible.
As for family genealogies and generational records,
they are few and unheard of.
When inquired of the elders,
they said that during the pirate uprising in the Yǐhài year toward the end of the Míng dynasty,
records and books were destroyed by war.
The people currently residing within the prefecture
are all the great-great-grandchildren of those who barely survived and were fortunate to escape destruction on that day.
What is heard and transmitted
stops after only five or seven generations,
and cannot be traced back any further.
Since the generations transmitted are not far distant,
and the descendants are not numerous,
the methods of genealogy are generally not maintained.
If one seeks out what records do exist,
they turn out to be private notes and informal records;
the structure and rules are unsettled,
making them difficult to establish as standard rules.
In severe cases, people cannot even trace the origins of how they received their surname.
Because of this, I sigh with deep emotion.
Now, family genealogies (jiāpǔ) are scrolls
lighter than the prefecture gazetteers (zhōuzhì);
after the devastation of war (bīngxiǎn),
no family genealogies remain.
Yet the gazetteers compiled by Zhīzhōu Yì Luán during the Jiājìng era of the Míng dynasty, and by Zhīzhōu Kāng Gào during the Wànlì era,
have existed for an even longer time,
and those books are fully preserved today;
this proves clearly that official records are easy to guard,
while private records are difficult to protect.
If we do not urgently make provisions for them now,
then even these meager ones
will later have no trace to consult.
Moreover, I observe in the *Táng Shū, Zǎixiàng Shìxì* (History of Táng, Genealogy of the Chancellors),
where their ancestors are listed,
some extend back to the Liáng and Chén dynasties,
some extend back to the Yuán Wèi and Hòu Zhōu dynasties,
but they do not trace further up the generations;
therefore, the internal records being incomplete
is not a fault of a single day or night.
In that case, recording what is verifiable
and omitting what is unknowable,
will avoid the reproach of claiming knowledge where there is none.
Each surname’s origin is traced,
serving as a resource for investigating antiquity.
The generations registered here are detailed,
settling the framework for the prefecture.
Those who achieved examination degrees (kējiǎ) or officialdom (shìhuàn) form the primary category,
while gòngshēng, jiànshēng, and shēngyuán (various student/tribute statuses), along with titled patrons (fēngjūn),
and those who purchased honorary ranks (zī shòu kōng jiē) are all included,
following their respective classifications.
If there are no examination graduates or officials,
but only shēngyuán or purchasers of honorary ranks,
no specific tables are created for them,
establishing the balance between primary and secondary importance.
For clans that produced kējiǎ or shìhuàn,
if the collateral branches are all commoners (qímín),
then the record stops with the generation of the branch division.
We do not list their sons and grandsons,
because the virtue of the superior man (jūnzǐ)
cuts off after five generations.
If all were listed,
it would be no different from the census registers (bǎntú).
Although there may be kējiǎ or shìhuàn,
if they lack a genealogy (pǔ), they are omitted,
strictly guarding against error and superfluity.
Regular tribute students (zhèng gòng) are also counted as kējiǎ,
and minor ranks are also counted as shìhuàn,
without further dividing their status or rank,
because since historical documents are not fully verifiable,
rather than erring by rejecting them,
it is better to err by preserving them,
which is the meaning of *Wèijì* (The Undone/Incomplete).
Preface to the Geographical Maps in the Gazeteer of Hé Zhōu
The study of charts and tables (túpǔ),
in antiquity had its own specialized field;
Zhèng Qiáo discussed it in detail.
Sīmǎ Qiān, when compiling history,
uniquely took the remnants of lateral and oblique lineages,
and arranged them into ten charts (biǎo);
but he did not take the regulations concerning symbols and laws held in the official courts (xiàng wèi),
and arrange them into various maps (tú).
Consequently, later historians, following this tradition,
made the charts and records increasingly numerous,
while the comprehensive maps (tújīng) gradually disappeared.
Scholars who love antiquity,
when consulting old texts,
recite the words,
but are bewildered by the images,
this is a common defect in record keeping,
and a lacuna in cultured literature (sīwén).
Zhèng Qiáo, living a thousand years later,
earnestly set his mind upon the surviving texts of the Three Dynasties (Sāndài),
and in his chapter on *Túpǔ*,
he clarified their utility;
he also deduced the reason why later generations lost their basis of documentation,
tracing it back to Bān Gù collecting texts but neglecting maps,
and spoke of this with deep emotion.
However, Zhèng Shì’s (Zhèng Qiáo’s) intention
was merely to compile records of various schools
without establishing charts and tables as a specialized field,
thus, he wished to create a separate catalogue
merely to supplement the deficiencies of the *Qī Lüè* and the four divisions (sì bù).
In reality, he did not investigate deeply;
the loss of map studies (túxué)
resulted from Sīmǎ Qiān having charts but no maps,
which led later historians, when compiling history,
not knowing how to select and record them.
Therefore, when he compiled his own *Tōng Zhì*, which included annals (jì), biographies (zhuàn), genealogies (pǔ), and outlines (lüè),
all genres were complete,
yet regarding geographical features and famous families,
he still did not create maps.
To use this to criticize Bān Shì (Bān Gù),
is this not like the saying: If Chǔ fails,
then Qí has not necessarily succeeded?
Now, the utility of charts and maps
serve as internal and external complements (bǐa lǐ).
The genealogies of the Zhōu dynasty were lost long ago,
yet the chronological order of the Three Dynasties (Sāndài),
and the years of the various feudal lords (zhūhóu),
are all verifiable today,
because Sīmǎ Qiān collected and arranged them into charts.
Since the records stored in the courts (xiàng wèi) were lost,
the names of shapes and institutions,
squareness, roundness, curvature, and straightness,
are unknowable today,
because Sīmǎ Qiān failed to arrange them into maps.
Therefore, the preservation or loss of records
depends on the editing and writing of the court historian (shǐchén)—
this is clear.
Regarding ancient maps,
let us not discuss them fully for now.
Since the time of the *Sānfǔ Huáng Tú* and the *Luòyáng Gōngdiàn Tú*,
records of capitals and cities,
have existed as complete books in every generation,
yet when later generations collected them,
less than one in a hundred survived.
Zhèng Shì (Zhèng Qiáo) uniquely devised a plan
to establish them as a specialized catalogue,
believing that if he initiated it,
no one would dare abolish it.
Yet, if we examine what Zhèng Shì collected today,
the amount lost and scattered
is not substantially different
from what was produced in previous ages;
therefore, the preservation or loss of books
is especially reliant on the editing and writing of the court historian,
and less reliant on the categorization within the catalogue
this is also clear.
Minor items like wine vessels (zūn léi),
might serve the erudite;
items like imperial processions (lǔ bù),
might display solemn dignity;
former scholars created diagrams and books for these,
which are also numerous and rich.
Court historians recognized their importance,
but had no leisure to include them all in their compilation;
Zhèng Shì listed them as a specialized catalogue
allowing them to be researched,
and finding the original book should suffice.
As for the geographical layout of provinces and prefectures,
which are of great importance to the whole realm,
if they are not arranged into a dedicated section
among the charts and records;
causing those who read the history
to be like groping blindly and stumbling over things—
how can this be acceptable?
Those who study the *Yì* (Changes) must understand the symbols (xiàng);
those who study the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals) must be conversant with the genealogies (pǔ);
maps and symbols (tú xiàng), genealogies and records (pǔ dié),
are the great foundation of the *Yì* and the *Chūnqiū*.
The *Yì* says:
“The Appendices are tied to the lines so that the words can be fully expressed.”
The *Jì* (Records) says:
“Comparing events and connecting the words—
that is the teaching of the *Chūnqiū*.”
To speak of tying the appendices and connecting the words
makes it clear that the literary text follows afterward.
Thus, maps and symbols are history without words,
and genealogies are records without literary text.
They must proceed side by side, mutually supportive,
and it is impossible to omit one, even if desired.
How much more so the geographical records (tújīng) of prefectures and commanderies,
which were highly valued by previous generations?
Someone might say:
Scholars also know that the use of diagrams and images is great.
However, texts can be transmitted and practiced,
but diagrams cannot be recited and read aloud;
therefore, books are fully preserved,
but diagrams cannot be examined or verified,
which is a natural consequence of their nature.
Although this is so,
it is not understanding the core issue.
If diagrams cannot be recited,
then tables (biǎo) are also not necessarily those that contain prose.
Tables are prominent in history,
but diagrams are not included in the compilation;
this is the reason for their loss.
Furthermore, there are two reasons why diagrams are difficult to transmit:
One is that they are disputed among skilled artists.
Because ancient people specialized in artistic skills,
they established themselves as famous schools,
but in reality, they did not correspond to the great principles and major laws (of scholarship).
Take for instance, Guō Pǔ’s 《Shānhǎi Jīng Tú Zàn》,
the eulogy (zàn) survives, but the diagrams (tú) are lost.
Now, observing the text of the eulogy,
it resembles the skill of carving dragons (flowery rhetoric),
thus we know that the diagramming and drawing
were probably also merely the technique of painting tigers (artistry over substance).
The second is that they are regarded as trivial, like peripheral matters (máo biàn).
In recent local gazetteers (fāng zhōu zhī zhì),
diagrams and images are drawn,
placed haphazardly among the prefaces and organizational rules,
without establishing a dedicated section;
they merely append famous scenic spots
to serve as recognition marks for the book,
but they actually bear no relation to the ancient study of scholarly maps and diagrams (tú pǔ zhī xué).
If they are disputed as mere artistic endeavors,
then the art is irrelevant to historical structure;
and if they are placed among the trivialities,
then bookshops carelessly use them as labels
to facilitate trade;
in both cases, they cannot speak to the refinement and subtlety of historical scholarship.
The ancients had specialized studies,
and thus had specialized books;
they had specialized books,
and thus had specialized formats and structures.
Moving horizontally and vertically,
marking and dividing into minor notes,
this is the format of genealogical records (pǔ dié).
Calculating distances by extracting square roots,
mapping and tabulating mountains and rivers,
this is the format of topographical maps (yú tú).
Where the diagram is not detailed, it is attached with explanations;
where the explanation is not clear, it is substantiated with the diagram—
this is the principle of mutual illustration.
The text is concise, yet the matter is not obscured;
the form is apparent, yet the words have a place to return (substantiate)—
this is the rule of descriptive composition.
Errors like ‘pig’ (hài) being confused with ‘fish’ (shǐ) cannot corrupt its transmission,
and editing cannot damage its substance—
this is the work meant for long preservation.
The essential aim is that even those who have not walked the land,
and those who are not deeply versed in the text,
can examine the diagram
and see clearly, like observing a fire;
this, again, is the way to universal understanding.
If there were diagrams for astronomy (tiān guān) and river regulation (hé qú),
then the Eight Treatises (bā shū) could be reduced to six;
If there were diagrams for geography (dì lǐ) and drainage ditches (gōu xù),
then the Ten Treatises (shí zhì) could be reduced to eight;
If this were the case, then today, seeking the constellations of the Tài Chū era,
and examining the maps (bǎn yú) of the Western Capital (Xī Jīng),
might not be so vast and confusing.
Moreover, regarding the books of local gazetteers,
which cite names and distinguish objects,
they should especially be detailed, comprehensive, and exhaustive,
so as to approximate a scholarly work of an established school (yī jiā zhī zuò);
Yet, why do they linger on scenery and views,
and arbitrarily attach diagrams of famous sites,
treating them merely as sights for the minor art of painting (dān qīng mò yì)?
Is this perhaps not due to their failure to study the ancient principle of ‘diagrams on the left and history on the right’ (zuǒ tú yòu shǐ)?
If diagrams cannot exist without attached explanations,
and if the detailed explanations
are identical to the book text,
is not the name 'diagram' just superfluous?
The reply is:
It is not superfluous.
The structure has its specialization,
and the intended meaning also has its focus.
Ancient books have specialized names,
and chapters have specialized meanings.
The inclusion or exclusion of specific wording is not the primary consideration,
but rather the relationship between name and reality, guest and host,
where the author merely takes the intended meaning.
Moreover, I have observed texts in previous histories:
There are tables (biǎo) that resemble treatises (zhì) [The Biǎo of Officials and Dukes in the Hàn Shū, where the beginning of the chapter chronologically narrates the official system.]
—and they are not necessarily all written in the vertical/horizontal format.
There are treatises that resemble tables [The Zhì of the Pitch Pipes and Calendar in the Hàn Shū, which arranges the cycles (sān tǒng) and the cyclical signs (jiǎ zǐ).]
—and they are not necessarily all examples of structuring facts and composing prose.
《Sān Fǔ Huáng Tú》
is now a lost book;
what is seen cited by other texts
is merely its verbal description.
Regarding the diagram of Dùn Jiǎ Tōng Tǒng,
its explanation survives today,
just as the meaning of Huá Shǔ and Yóu Gēng exists.
Even a diagram of one chí (foot)
can be attached with an explanation of xún zhàng (eight or more feet) long.
Since it is called a diagram,
it is acceptable to universally call it a diagram.
If diagrams are further arranged sequentially by category,
is that not overly complex?
The reply is:
It is not complex.
The categorization of diagrams
is like the naming of chapters in a book.
If diagrams are merely appended to the text,
then the meaning is not apparent;
if diagrams are separated and attached with explanations,
then the meaning becomes apparent.
For example, in the imperial dynasty’s 《Míng Shǐ: Lǜ Lì Zhì》,
all astronomical instruments and calculations are drawn as diagrams,
which is likely unprecedented among previous generations.
The historical officials (shǐ chén) at that time
did not set them up separately as a Diagram section,
thus they are not listed as a specialized part;
each matter has its appropriate place.
Now, the local gazetteer (zhōu zhì) divides diagrams into four categories:
First, Topography (Yú Dì);
Second, Establishment and Organization (Jiàn Zhì);
Third, Garrisons and Patrols (Yíng Xùn);
Fourth, Water Conservancy (Shuǐ Lì).
All of these are selected because they relate to fundamental principles
and are necessary for mapping specific forms and strategic situations;
they are attached with detailed explanations,
and sequenced after the Annals (Jì) and Tables (Biǎo),
to serve as a comprehensive scholarly work, and to set forth its principles in the initial introductory sections. (Hé Zhōu Zhì Tián Fù Shū Xù Lì)
The practice of demarcating land and instituting tributes,
originated in the *Xià Shū*,
which involved basing official duties on the soil (rèn tǔ shòu zhí), assigning tasks related to the land and its resources (zài shī wù dì shì), and conferring land-based offices (shòu dì zhí).
This is detailed in the *Zhōu Lǐ*;
The documentation of field taxes and levies,
and the specific management thereof,
has a long history.
Bān Shì (Bān Gù) broadly adopted the Eight Policies (bā zhèng) from the *Hóng Fàn* (Great Plan),
and structured them into the chapter on commodities and finance (*Shí Huò*),
which subsequent historians have continued to follow,
establishing it as a standard measure.
However, the maps and records of the Minister of Agriculture (Sī Nóng tú jí),
and the ledgers and registers of the auditing departments (kuài jī bù lù),
are stacked high in the archives,
and cannot be fully exhausted;
Therefore, selections are made from the middle period of a dynasty,
to serve as the established rule.
Where there are major changes,
or overall calculations of increase and decrease,
they are briefly preserved by retaining the necessary abridgements made by historians,
and the memorials submitted by financial ministers;
allowing readers to understand the situation for themselves when reviewing the text;
this is simply the inevitable outcome of the circumstances.
Such as the financial registers (*Guó Jì*) compiled by Lǐ Jífǔ and Wéi Chùhòu (Lǐ Jífǔ's *Yuánhé Guó Jì Bù* in ten scrolls, Wéi Chùhòu's *Tàihé Guó Jì* in twenty scrolls). ,
And the accounting records (*Kuài Jì*) compiled by Dīng Wèi and Tián Kuàng (Dīng Wèi's *Jǐngdé Kuài Jì Lù* in six scrolls, Tián Kuàng's *Huángyòu Kuài Jì Lù* in six scrolls). ,
these imitated the system of auditing (sī kuài suǒ èr) used by the accountant (Sī Huì) under the *Zhōu Guān* (Officials of Zhōu),
which involved written contracts and territorial maps.
Dù Yòu's and Sòng Bái's *Tōng Diǎn*,
and Wáng Pǔ's and Zhāng Déxiàng's *Huì Yào*,
are compilations of institutional history;
In these, primary importance is placed on commodities and finance,
their purpose being comprehensive review and verification,
covering matters both ancient and modern;
however, regarding trivial matters like hemp thread,
or the minute details of ounces and taels,
they no longer pursue detailed tabulation to cover everything.
Zhào Guò's proposal for the equalization of fields,
and Lǐ Áo's book on equitable taxation (*Píng Fù*),
are official documents and private discussions,
each expressing individual views;
They merely seek compromise
based on the temporary benefits and detriments of the time,
and are not the method of recording facts used by historians.
Now, the registers recorded by clerical officers,
are crude and lack literary refinement,
and cannot be transmitted across generations or travel far;
While literary works and institutional histories
are broad and comprehensive regarding the main essentials,
they are unable to deeply discern hidden details;
This is why field taxes are difficult to understand clearly,
and why comprehensive texts on the subject are rarely seen.
In antiquity, matters of finance and taxation
were collected by the Director of Fields (Zàishī, subordinate to the Grand Minister of Education, Dà Sītú). ,
and tallied by the Accountant (Sī Huì, subordinate to the Grand Master, Tài Zǎi). .
The Tài Zǎi established a system where thirty years constituted the nine standards,
equalizing and regulating the nine taxes.
From large expenditures like sacrifices and entertaining guests,
down to minor details like feed and non-standard distributions,
all had fixed amounts,
based on their expenditure,
measured against their income;
Even if one wished, outside of the established standards,
to take more from the people,
there was no means to do so.
This is why the system of regulated and precise accounting was valued for financial matters.
Since the Táng Dynasty changed the Rent, Labor, and Commutation Tax to the Two-Tax System,
and the Míng Dynasty further changed the Two-Tax System to the Single-Whip Method,
the trend has moved towards simplicity and convenience,
preventing burdensome disturbances.
By assessing the times and measuring the circumstances,
this can be considered an opportune expediency.
However, the various costs for reserves and provisions,
categories like local tribute and specialized regional products,
and funds for requisitioned or hired transport,
should all be consolidated and fully paid
to benefit the populace,
and prevent confusion and disturbance.
The documents of the responsible officials,
and the registers of the clerical officers,
should naturally include a detailed record of the previously existing articles and categories,
clearly indicating the legal reasons for their consolidation and reduction,
and then converting them according to the laws and regulations of the current time;
Only then will both the duty holders in the accounting departments,
and the registered common people,
clearly understand that the system has changed,
but the total amount has neither increased nor decreased.
As official documents become increasingly simplified,
and old records become lost to verification over time,
if only the consolidated total figures of that time are preserved,
and the various original items are not listed out,
then when official control slightly relaxes,
and officials cease to adhere strictly to the law,
they might resort to fabricating new categories,
and forcibly allocating taxes and requisitions,
claiming that this aligns with the ancient principle of "only righteous tribute."
Who would then be able to argue that this practice is contrary to regulation?
Change in law is intended to benefit the people,
but officials may sometimes use the law as an excuse for misconduct.
The function of documentary records
may sometimes be insufficient,
which is why maps and historical records serve as standards for governing the state.
However, the records of a single dynasty are immense,
and the archives of the historical bureau
cannot contain everything;
Only local gazetteers of prefectures and counties,
whose territorial scope is limited,
can enumerate the various items individually,
and include every minute detail,
thereby perhaps compensating for what the national histories fail to provide.
Since the start of the Míng Dynasty,
the records in external gazetteers
have generally been crude and disorganized;
Regarding the matter of field taxes,
it is mistakenly held that the ledgers of clerks and subordinates
are entirely unworthy of inclusion in grand and beautiful literary works,
Consequently, they rely on currently used documents,
compiling them all uniformly,
without investigating historical changes,
or thoroughly seeking out their origins;
This is like a jade cup without a base—
who can appreciate its magnificence?
The Single-Whip Method of the Míng Dynasty
was established during the Jiājìng era,
and the extant old gazetteer of Hézhōu
that can be consulted today
stops with Yì Luán's *Zhōuzhì* from the middle of the Jiājìng period.
At that time, regulations were being newly reformed,
and the prefectural gazetteer immediately adopted the new methods,
completely cutting out the old articles,
consequently making it impossible to trace the evolution since the Táng dynasty's Two-Tax System.
What a pity!
Furthermore, private discussions
and official documents
that pertain to the benefits and detriments of field taxes
should naturally be collected and included in this book;
Just as Bān Shū's arrangement placed Cháo Cuò's memorial on "Valuing Grain" into the *Shí Huò Zhì* (Treatise on Commodities and Finance),
and Jiǎ Ràng's strategy for "Managing the River" into the *Gōu Xù Zhì* (Treatise on Canals and Dykes),
so that matters are clearly presented and illuminated,
and learning leads to practical use.
Otherwise, they should be included in the biographies of the persons concerned,
making it convenient for people to cross-reference and research,
which is also the established method used for Zhào Chōngguó's proposals on military farming.
Recently, gazetteer writers typically excise literary content
and compile it separately into the *Yì Wén Zhì* (Treatise on Arts and Literature);
Yet this leaves the facts pertaining to the main sections
and the actions of the individuals concerned
sparse and lacking substance.
Is it possible that the great emphasis placed on specialized headings in the gazetteer,
specifically highlighting the principles and regulations,
resulting in compiled scrolls,
is equivalent to the hanging of a gourd,
which is looked up at but not eaten?
The old gazetteer by Kāng Gào
already exhibited traces of this trend.
Subsequent compilers
resolutely deleted such content,
repeating this action again and again,
making it impossible to retrieve;
this is truly lamentable!
Now, regarding the period before Yì's Gazetteer,
what has been lost
cannot be recovered;
But starting from Yì's Gazetteer onward,
the complete process is recorded,
and compiled into this volume.
Kāng Gào's proposal on the equalization of fields
is truly relevant to the benefits and detriments of field taxes;
Other documents in the prefecture concerning field taxes,
are all collected and recorded,
placed after the main articles;
They may also be included in the biographies,
mutually clarifying each other;
doubtful elements are omitted.
Those who review this later
may perhaps find something of use herein.
Preface and Rules for the Treatise on Arts and Literature in the Hézhōu Gazetteer
The *Yì* (Book of Changes) says:
"In high antiquity, government was conducted by tying knots;
later generations of Sages replaced this with written records and contracts,
through which the hundred officials governed,
and the myriad people were examined."
Now, the origin of writing,
is that by which the ancients established the methods of governance.
During the height of the Sān Dài (Three Dynasties),
the laws were contained in books,
and officials guarded these books.
All the skills and occupations in the world
emerged from the precedents and archives managed by the Official Masters (guān shī);
the Dào and art were unified here,
virtue and conduct were made coherent here,
and thus the world achieved governance through unified writing (tóng wén).
And the six chapters of the *Zhōu Guān* (Rites of Zhōu)
are all what the ancients used to uphold the master-traditions by adhering to the official duties.
That which was not maintained by the official duties of the Official Masters
was considered illegal (or outside the law).
Even when Kǒngzǐ (Confucius) spoke of ritual,
he necessarily consulted the archives stored beneath the pillar—this is the point.
After the Sān Dài,
writing was no longer controlled by specific official duties.
Consequently, the regulations of government offices
and the learning practiced by scholars and teachers
split into two,
leading to individuals compiling their own books
and families generating their own interpretations;
indeed, those things that flooded out and went beyond the precedents held by the hundred departments

thereupon became chaotic. (The Six Classics all belong to historical precedents, such as the *Yì* being stored by the Grand Diviner (Tài Bǔ), and the *Shī* (Odes) being held by the Grand Master (Tài Shī).)
Since books were already scattered throughout the world,
without any unifying authority,
consequently, the method of cataloging and classifying them
emerged in order to manage them,
which was also unavoidable given the circumstances.
However, since the practice of cataloging began,
scholars have treated them as mere records of numbers and registers.
Those who sought to thoroughly investigate governance through unified writing,
and preserve the legacy of understanding the duties outlined in the Six Canons (liù diǎn),
were only the books *Qī Lüè* and *Bié Lù* composed by Liú Xiàng and Liú Xīn.
