Therefore, when they differentiated the Nine Streams (Jiǔ Liú),
and discussed and classified the various Masters (zhū zǐ),
they always stated that they originated from the management of a certain ancient official,
flowed into the doctrine of a certain school,
and, through deviation, became the defect of a certain matter.
They analyzed and clarified them completely,
encompassing everything without omission.
If scholars can follow the stream back to the source,
even minor arts and small skills,
distorted words and heterodox theories,
can all be returned and made comprehensible through the Great Dào;
and those who manage these doctrines
can thereby distinguish for themselves whether their efforts have reached completion or not.
If there is a constant adherence to the source,
none will drift away;
if there is a common direction toward it,
none will be led astray.
If speech and writing
are all returned to the understanding of official duties,
then the master-traditions can be restored,
and ancient learning can flourish.
How magnificent would that not be?
Hán Yù said:
"Distinguishing the authenticity and falsity of ancient books
is as clear as the separation of black and white."
Mèngzǐ (Mencius) said:
"Distorted words—we know what obscures them;
excessive words—we know what traps them;
perverse words—we know what separates them;
evasive words—we know what exhausts them."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Listen widely,
choose the good among them and follow it."
Now, if one wishes to distinguish the authenticity and falsity of ancient books,
so as to approach understanding words,
and approach listening widely and choosing the good,
then one must deeply understand the responsibilities of the Official Masters,
and only then will one know the causes of deviation,
and ultimately the failures of the later streams.
This is why the cataloging work of the Liú family
is the crucial pivot point for the continuation or cessation of academic traditions.
If one cannot thoroughly investigate the responsibilities of the Official Masters,
one will have no means to clarify the causes of deviation,
and consequently will not know the failures of the later streams;
then the learning of the world
will lack a founding master or principle.
"To formulate intentions and issue policies,
and by issuing policies, harm affairs" —
Mèngzǐ spoke of this,
with absolute certainty.
Nevertheless, superficial scholars
are busy showing off their comprehensive talents;
experts in obscure research
are busy boasting of their narrow and biased views;
believing that the trifling documentation of catalogs,
the work of collation and editing,
can be beneficial to literary affairs. Alas!
They are mistaken.
, this means the officials (*guān*) lost their responsibilities
. The *Qī Lüè* perished and became the Four Divisions (*Sì Bù*)
, this means the teachers (*shī*) lost their transmissions
. The records (*jí*) of the *Zhōu Guān* (Rites of Zhōu) were rich
; the *Bǎo Zhāng* maintained astronomical observations
, the *Zhí Fāng* managed geography
, the *Yú Héng* regulated natural resources
, the *Wū Zhù* communicated with spirits
. Each held complete books to promulgate administrative laws
, and each refined their vocation to transmit scholarship
. This was not limited merely to the texts of the Six Arts (*Liù Yì*), the *Shī* (Odes), and the *Shū* (Documents) mentioned by the *Shī Shì* (Master Official) and the *Bǎo Shì* (Tutor Official)
. The chapter concerning the *Sī Kōng* (Minister of Works) was lost
, and Liú Xīn took the *Kǎo Gōng Jì* (Record of Examinations of Works) to supplement it
. It was not merely a supplement
; the *Kǎo Gōng* must have been an office subordinate to the *Sī Kōng*
, and what is called the *jì* (record)
, is simply the canonical record (*diǎn jí*) of the Winter Official (*Dōng Guān*)
; just as the seventeen chapters of the *Yí Lǐ* (Ceremonial Rites)
, are the canonical record of the Spring Official (*Chūn Guān*)
; and the one hundred and fifty chapters of the *Sī Mǎ Fǎ* (The Methods of the Minister of War)
, are the canonical record of the Summer Official (*Xià Guān*)
. All these were fortunate enough to be transmitted to later generations
. If the canonical records had all existed at that time
, and the three hundred and sixty chapters
, had been organized and sequenced according to official ranks (*guān zhì*)
, how could the writings have been dispersed
? After the decline of the Zhōu Dynasty
, the official system fell out of use
, and books were scattered and lost
; out of thousands and hundreds
, only one or two tenths survived
. Based on these scant survivors (one or two tenths)
, to attempt to restore the organization of the three hundred and sixty chapters
, would inevitably be forced or incomplete
. The situation made it difficult to proceed
, therefore, they were compelled to organize them into the *Qī Lüè*
. The phrase saying that a book "is probably based on the charge of a certain ancient official"
, the word *gài* (probably/perhaps) used here
, is a term of doubt or conjecture
. It intends for people to reflect deeply
, and thus spontaneously arrive at the origin of the precedents held by the officials (*guān*) and teachers (*shī*)
. Therefore, it is said: when the *Liù Diǎn* perished and became the *Qī Lüè*
, the officials lost their responsibilities
. Nevertheless
, even when the officials and teachers lost their vocation
, and reclusive scholars wrote books
, although the method (*fǎ*) was said to lack organization (*tǒng jì*)
, yet their original purpose
, was always to promote what they had studied
, so that it might be implemented in the current age
. Though their writings were loosely connected
, their main focus (*zhǐ qū*) was definable
; though their doctrines were strange and deceptive (*jué guǐ*)
, they did not become truly mixed or incoherent
. Therefore, regarding the schools of Lǎo Zhuāng, Shēn Hán, Míng Mò, and Zòng Héng
, scholars in the early Hàn Dynasty still studied their professional fields
; this is clear evidence that the transmission of teachers had not yet been lost
. Since the transmission of teachers was not lost
, the writings must have had a foundation
. Anything that had a foundation
, invariably originated from the official charges held by the ancients
. This is why the Liú family found it easy to categorize their divisions
. During the period between Wèi and Jìn
, specialized learning gradually perished
. Literary scholars
, took writing as a source of glory and splendor
; poems (*shī*), rhapsodies (*fù*), memorials (*zhāng biǎo*), inscriptions (*míng zhēn*), and encomia (*sòng lěi*)
, were structured based on specific occasions
, with the intent (*mìng yì*) differing in each case
. Their fundamental purpose was neither Rú (Confucian) nor Mò (Mohist)
, their statements were sometimes separate and sometimes combined
. When collected and arranged
, they were called Literary Collections (*Wén Jí*)
. This is the first category that cannot be separated into distinct streams
. When writings lack a foundation
, they seek assistance from rhetorical flourish
; compiling and combining the classics (*jīng*) and commentaries (*zhuàn*)
, extracting and selecting from the Masters (*zǐ*) and Histories (*shǐ*)
, it is like a physician gathering poisons
, waiting to dispense them as needed for the occasion
. Choosing 'green' (good lines) and matching 'purple' (ornate phrases)
, they adhere to no single school
, these are called Classified Anthologies (*Lèi Shū*)
. This is the second category that cannot be separated into distinct streams
. Since scholarship lacked specialization
, reading could not be precise and focused
. Various schools were abridged
, to make inspection easier and quicker
. At first, this was merely intended to provide quick reference for a time
, without any conscious intention of preserving them
. Later, they gradually became established practice
, and subsequent scholars treated them as essential guides
. If separated, the original books still exist
; if combined, they are not the teachings of a single school
, but confusingly mixed together
. These are called Book Excerpts (*Shū Chāo*)
. This is the third category that cannot be separated into distinct streams
. When inner comprehension is insufficient
, one seeks it in superficial literary appearance
. They point out whether the phrasing and rhythm are skillful or clumsy
, and judge the rising and falling tones (*gōng shāng*)
. Common masters and minor Confucians
, venerate these as models
. They dissect the classics and commentaries
, and excerpt passages from literary works for comparison
. They mark them uniformly in red and black ink
, these are called Critical Selections (*Píng Xuǎn*)
. This is the fourth category that cannot be separated into distinct streams
. All these four types
, arose because the teaching methods (*shī fǎ*) were not established
, scholarship lacked specialization
, later generations became fragmented
, and they failed to understand the grand principles of the ancients
. What later trends gravitated toward
, was truly numerous and intense
. Since these books could not all be completely burned (*fù bǐng dīng*)
, they could only be forcibly categorized into A, B, C, and D (*jiǎ yǐ*)
. But to insist on applying the old methods of the *Qī Lüè*
, to categorize the writings of later generations
, is like comparing a round mortise to a square tenon
—how could they possibly fit
? Therefore, it is said: when the *Qī Lüè* transitioned and became the Four Divisions (*Sì Bù*)
, the teachers lost their transmissions
. If one argues that historical records (*shǐ jí*) became vast and cumbersome
, and what was a dependency of the *Chūn Qiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals)
, blossomed into a great state

; (If one argues that) while the *Qī Lüè* listed the works of the Grand Historian (*Tài Shǐ Gōng*) under the Spring and Autumn School, the rise of the twenty-one Histories necessitated the separate establishment of the History Division (*Shǐ Bù*). The Míng Mò (School of Names and Mohists) became sparse and scattered
, minor sects and peripheral branches
, lost their transmission within two generations

. (The streams of) the School of Names (*Míng Jiā*) and the Mohist School (*Mò Jiā*), those who had merely a few adherents, no longer had their books in later generations. To argue that the framework of the *Qī Lüè*
, had no choice but to change into the Four Divisions
, is indeed a shallow view of the principles of cataloging books (*zhù lù zhī dào*)
but I have not heard of using books to disrupt the classification structures (bùcì).
In the early Hàn dynasty, the various masters (Zhūzǐ) and hundred schools (Bǎijiā)
were vast and lacked overall organization;
the intent of the official Rites (guān Lǐ) was lost.
The Liú clan (Liú Shì) inherited the failings of the Western Capital (Xījīng),
yet they were able to thoroughly investigate the ancient principle where officialdom (guān) and teaching (shī) were unified,
detailing it as an organized structure (tiáoguàn),
thereby tracing its source.
Thus, their management was indeed precise.
During the period between the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
literary collections (wénjí) and encyclopedia-like books (lèishū)
lacked systematic organization;
the tradition of specialized transmission became weak.
Yet, families like Xún and Lǐ
could not fully investigate the origins and development (yuánliú) of the Qī Lüè;
and regarding families like Wáng and Ruǎn,
the separation was even greater.
Subsequently, texts on technical arts (fāngjì) and military strategies (bīngshū)
were combined into the Masters (Zǐ) division (bù);
literary collections (wénjí) formed their own specialized division;
and encyclopedia-like books (lèishū) were listed among the various masters (zhūzǐ).
The four divisions (sìbù) of the Táng people
then became the unchangeable established method (chéngfǎ) for cataloging in later generations,
but the scholarship (xuéshù) of the realm
grew increasingly disorderly, lacking any controlling framework (gāngjǐ).
Generally, the Qī Lüè inherited the failings of the Six Canons (Liù Diǎn),
yet knew how to preserve the remaining methods (yífǎ) of the Six Canons;
the Four Divisions (Sìbù) inherited the failings of the Qī Lüè,
yet did not know how to preserve the remaining methods (yífǎ) of the Qī Lüè.
This means the Qī Lüè was able to manage books using classification structures,
but the Four Divisions (Sìbù) could not avoid disrupting the classification structures using books.
Furthermore, the pretexts used by the Four Divisions for being unable to restore the Qī Lüè are:
First, they say that historical writings (shǐjí) are too numerous
to be appended to the scholastic tradition (jiāxué) of the Chūnqiū.
Now, organizing the twenty-one histories (Èrshíyī Shǐ)
is not difficult;
as for books concerning official posts (zhíguān) and historical precedents (gùshì),
or the forms of genealogical tables (pǔdié) and biographies (jìzhuàn),
some originate from official ritual regulations (guānlǐ zhìzuò),
others involve the discourse of Confucian and miscellaneous schools (rú zájiā yán),
and they are not necessarily all historical statutes (shǐcái).
If one now wishes to encompass all these forms,
decisively taking History (Shǐ) as a single division,
then ritual records (yízhù) are not included in the Rites Classics (lǐjīng),
official posts (zhíguān) are unconnected to the Six Canons (Liù Diǎn),
counsel and pronouncements (mógào) are cut off from the Shàngshū,
and historical critiques (shǐpíng) diverge into the various masters (zhūzǐ);
disrupting the original intent of the ancients' writings and the established methods of classification (bùcì) merely to achieve simplicity,
how can this be permissible?
Second, they say that literary collections (wénjí) daily grow more numerous,
and if they are not listed as a specialized division (zhuānbù),
they will lack overall organization.
Now, the various masters (Zhūzǐ) and hundred schools (Bǎijiā)
did not originate from official duties (guānshǒu),
yet the Liú clan (Liú Shì) extrapolated them as branches of official duties;
if literary collections (wénjí) are not the various masters and hundred schools,
then the books to be cataloged,
why can they not be managed using the knowledge and function (shízhí) framework of the various masters and hundred schools?
Although the collection genre (jítǐ) is indeed numerous and complex,
the key is first to determine the person who created the collection.
Human temperament (xìngqíng) must lean toward something;
if one grasps their inherent temperament and inclination,
then the objects of emotional conveyance in their poetry and rhymed prose (shīfù),
the allusions used in their critiques and debates (lùnbiàn),
and the principles they highly regard in their chronicles and narratives (jìxù),
by summarizing the general purport (dàzhǐ)
and skimming the minor details (zhīyè),
what the ancients called the doctrines of one school (yījiā zhī yán)—
such as within the Rú (Confucian), Mò (Mohist), Míng (School of Names), and Fǎ (Legalist) schools—
there must be those whose branches can be ascertained.
By preserving the original titles of their literary collections,
analyzing and sequencing their sources of origin and development (yuánliú),
appending their entries after the Liú clan's (Liú Shì) classification structure,
and distinguishing between those that reached the standard and those that did not,
they can serve as a guide (jīndài) for later scholars to distinguish the paths;
then arbitrary words (zhīyán) will have nowhere to attach themselves,
and the flaws of the literary collections (wénjí)
can be somewhat mitigated.
Perhaps then words will have substance and actions constancy,
leading one from the specialized classifications of the Qī Lüè,
to glimpse the remaining statutes (yízé) of the Six Canons (Liù Diǎn)?
Once the methods of the individual schools (jiāfǎ) are specialized,
those rootless, confused, and miscellaneous items,
belonging to the categories of collected excerpts (lèichāo) and critical selections (píngxuǎn),
can be self-governed without effort.
Thus, the way of cataloging (zhùlù)
aligns with the methods of instruction (jiàofǎ);
how can one hastily rely on mere tallies of divisions and entries,
and casually discuss arrangement and sequencing (biāncì)?
However, if scholars do not first grasp the purity of Heaven and Earth,
and understand the grand structure (dàtǐ) of the ancients,
and hastily wish to classify all writings,
and delineate the various branches (liúbié),
they will struggle to achieve even a single correct statement;
This is why those specialized in cataloging (zhùlù)
prefer to speak of the Four Divisions (Sìbù),
but hesitate to hear mention of the Qī Lüè.
that historians refer to,
was fully developed by Bān Gù,
but was actually modeled after Sīmǎ Qiān.
Sīmǎ Qiān did not establish a formal methodology,
and Bān Gù inherited the scholarship of Liú Xīn but did not perfect it.
Therefore, if one speaks of the subtlety and precision of bibliography,
it still depends on thoroughly studying the work of the Liú family.
To study the work of the Liú family,
proceeding via the books of Bān Gù,
is something people know;
but to study the work of the Liú family,
one must also reference the methods of Sīmǎ Qiān,
is something people do not know.
Now, what Sīmǎ Qiān referred to as ordering the Six Schools,
distinguishing the similarities and differences in their scholarship,
investigating their advantages and disadvantages,
was based on his father Sīmǎ Tán's discussion of Yīnyáng, Rú, Mò, Míng, Fǎ, and Dàodé, which he considered the Six Schools.
This is the precedent.
The beginning of the Annals (Jì) drew its foundation from the *Shàngshū* (as seen in the encomium for the 'Annals of the Five Thearchs').
The beginning of the Tables (Biǎo) drew its foundation from the *Chūnqiū* (as seen in the preface to the 'Table of the Three Dynasties').
The beginning of the Biographies (Zhuàn) drew its foundation from what the *Shī* (Odes) and *Shū* (Documents) lacked,
extending to the texts concerning Yú and Xià (as seen in the 'Biography of Bó Yí').
All these show the origin from which the bibliographic records were initiated.
Furthermore, following the Six Arts,
regarding the Masters of the Zhōu and Qín periods,
such as the biographies of Mèng [Kē], Xún [Qìng], the Three Zōu masters, Lǎo [Zǐ], Zhuāng [Zǐ], Shēn [Bùhài], Hán [Fēi], Guān [Zhòng], Yàn [Yīng], Qū Yuán, Yú Qīng, and Lǚ Bùwéi,
he discussed and ordered their writings,
summarized their main objectives,
detailed or abbreviated their words,
and balanced and evaluated their quality;
using varied tones of praise and sighing,
his meaning was not confined to narrow limits;
when concerning a person, it was a separate Biography (Lièzhuàn),
when concerning a book, it was a Descriptive Catalog (Xùlù);
How can the intent of the ancients in naming and marking their chapters
be limited by the restrictive rules of popular scholarship?
The work of the Liú family,
regarding its methods of grouping and ordering,
was based on the Official Rites (*Guān Lǐ*);
but as for the form of the Descriptive Catalog,
they subtly derived their framework
from the Biographies of the Grand Historian (Tàishǐ, i.e., Sīmǎ Qiān).
Indeed, to distinguish the origins and streams (of thought),
to manage the confusion of the Hundred Schools,
and to guide them toward the Great Way—
this was the original purpose.
As for the order of volumes and catalog headings,
and the sequential arrangement (jiǎ-yǐ) of chapters,
although they followed a systematic progression,
orderly and not confusing,
they actually connected official functions and related tasks,
achieving success through mutual assistance.
For example, the *Guǎnzǐ* was listed under the Dàojiā (Daoist School),
but when detailing the origins of Elementary Learning,
its chapter entitled 'Dìzǐ Zhí'
was appended after the *Ěryǎ*;
thus we know that a book belonging to one school,
if its words are valuable,
can conventionally be listed separately.
*Yī Yǐn* and *Tàigōng*,
were ancestors of the Dàojiā (their books were placed in the Dàojiā section).
*Sūzǐ* and *Kuǎitōng*,
whose writings belong to the Zònghéngjiā (School of Diplomacy),
because they were respected in military strategy,
were subsequently recorded again under the category of Military Strategy and Expediency,
ranking above the various schools of Sūn [Wǔ] and Wú [Qǐ];
thus we know that morality (Dàodé) and military strategy (Bīngmóu),
wherever their main principles overlap and converge,
can conventionally be listed in multiple places (Hùxiàn).
If the sequence of chapters can be listed separately,
then the origin and stream of scholarship
will not suffer from being incomplete or having gaps.
If catalog headings can be listed in multiple places,
then dividing the main categories and separate records
will not suffer from the complication of diverging pathways and dragging limitations.
If the origin and stream of scholarship
has no gaps and is complete;
and dividing the main categories and separate records
has no diverging pathways and dragging limitations;
then the principle of the Six Ministers of the *Zhōuguān* (Rites of Zhōu) combining their official duties is preserved,

and the objective of the Grand Historian's Biographies detailing mutually related information is manifest (e.g., *Huòzhí* mentions Zǐ Gòng but avoids the 'Biography of the Disciples'; *Rúlín* mentions Dǒng Zhòngshū and Wáng Jí, who have dedicated separate biographies).
The method of compiling books,
was naturally transmitted by the ancients;
how can it be overlooked?
Ever since Bān Gù deleted the *Jílǜè* (Summary of Collections),
the concluding discussions of the Liú family were not transmitted;
(The *Jílǜè* was the general discussion of the main principles of all the books.) When he reduced the catalog headings,
the essential methods of the Liú family were not clear;
(Bān reduced those listed in multiple places by the Liú family and merged them into one.) Consequently, scholars did not understand the method of bibliography,
which was used to distinguish the Hundred Schools,
and connect them to the Great Way (The 'Tiānxià' chapter of the *Zhuāngzǐ* also holds this meaning),
but merely regarded it as a necessity for sequential enumeration (jiǎ-yǐ) and counting.
It is no wonder that scholarship lacks specialized fields,
and books lack hereditary custodians,
and instead, it is less reliable than the talismans and registers of shamans and priests, or the secret formulas of physicians,
which at least retain the method of continuous transmission from teacher to disciple.
Zhèng Qiáo's brief work on Collation and Editing (*Jiàochóu*)
forcefully corrected the errors in the categorization found in the *Chóngfāng* (Catalogue of Books),
criticizing all subsequent works starting from Bān Gù.
However, Zhèng did not clearly understand the origins and streams of bibliography,
which ought to trace back to the Official Rites (*Guān Lǐ*),
merely meticulously correcting that a certain book should be Category A but was mistakenly Category B,
or that a certain book should be Category C but was erroneously Category D.
Now, the confusion and disarray in grouping and ordering,
although caused by the loss of the hereditary methodology,
is also due to the ease of confusing the Rú (Confucian) and Ză (Syncretist) schools,
and the multiplicity of ways to categorize official duties and historical precedents.
These books were originally open to either classification,
and were not initially bibliographic errors.
If the Liú family's methods of separate listing (Biéchū) and multiple listing (Hùxiàn)
are not made clear to later generations,
even if the Grand Historian (Tàishǐ) were reborn,
and Yáng Xióng appeared again,
concerning the methods of grouping and ordering,
they would still be bewildered and unable to impose order.
Zhèng was able to criticize Bān's *Zhì* (Treatise) for the inappropriateness of appended classifications,
but he could not correct Bān's inappropriateness in merging and reducing classifications.
He may be said to have known the 'ten' but not known the 'two times five'.
Moreover, I observe the bibliographies of later scholars:
some separately list the *Xiǎo Ěryǎ* and assign it to the *Lúnyǔ* (Analects) (originally a chapter title in the *Kǒng Cóngzǐ*; the *Suí Jīngjí Zhì* separately lists it under the *Lúnyǔ*).
Some separately list the *Xià Xiǎozhèng* and place it under Seasonal Ordinances (originally a chapter title in the *Dà Dài Lǐ*; the *Wénxiàn Tōngkǎo* separately lists it under Seasonal Ordinances).
How can this be sufficient to understand the ancient method of separate listing (Biéchū)?
They simply forgot the book from which the piece originated,
appending it to a class and thereby losing its basis.
The *Jiāruì Jì* (Record of Auspicious Omens) was entered under the Five Phases (Wǔ Xíng),
and also listed in the Miscellaneous Biographies (Zá Zhuàn) (as per the *Suí Shū Jīngjí Zhì*).
The *Xījīng Zájì* (Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital) was entered under Historical Precedents (Gùshì),
and also listed in the Geography section (as per the *Táng Shū Yìwén Zhì*).
How can this be sufficient to understand the ancient method of multiple listing (Hùxiàn)?
They simply forgot that the book had already been recorded,
resulting in duplication and consequently error.
Now, the fragmented nature of late scholarship,
leading to classification without basis,
and duplication resulting in error,
can be considered extreme.
Investigating the reason for this divergence and error,
we find that the principle itself inherently causes doubt,
and the circumstances inevitably lead to it.
If one merely adheres rigidly to the established sequence (jiǎ-yǐ) methodology,
and does not analyze the subtle principles underlying
the ancients' reasons for separate listing and multiple listing,
without a clear understanding,
this failure is certainly the result.
However, if collators and editors
cannot delve deeply into the origins and streams of scholarship,
and they are allowed merely to cut up chapters for separate listing,
or sever categories for multiple listing,
they will create fragmentation and disorder,
losing all standards and regulations.
In this case, saving the failure would only multiply the failure.
Therefore, the traditional methods of collation and editing
must be transmitted,
and specialized experts in bibliography
must be established.
The chapters on literary works (Yìwén) in local gazetteers (zhìchén) of the prefectures (zhōu) and counties (xiàn),
must be thoroughly discussed.
In ancient times, the officials (xíngrén) collected documents (cǎishū),
the Grand Historian (Tàishǐ) managed the records,
and literature and writings (wénzhāng zàijí)
were all centralized above (in the court).
Therefore, outside of what the government offices maintained,
there were no private repositories of books (fénjí).
In later ages, people wrote books themselves,
and each family kept its own version of the narrative.
Even when encountering an era that honored literature (yòuwén zhī dài),
or a period of purchasing classics (gòudiǎn zhī qí),
those that could enter the imperial archives (mìfǔ)
and be overseen by the historical officials (shǐguān),
seven or eight out of ten failed to do so.
This is the natural tendency of things.
When literature is scattered throughout the world,
and historical officials lack sole guardianship,
then the governance of unified texts (tóngwén zhī zhì)
can only be achieved if schools and scholars (xuéxiào shīrú) study and practice them,
and if the local gazetteers (zhōu xiàn zhìchén) organize and categorize them,
establishing them as fixed methods
maintained in every region (fāngzhōu).
This is done in order to prepare for the collection of customs (cǎifēng) by light carriages (yóuxuān),
and to await the discussion and final determination by the Imperial Library (Mìshū);
Should there be peculiar, surprising, or incorrect narratives,
they can also be examined based on what has been heard and seen,
collated and corrected;
Thus, literature and classics
would have a unified origin (tǒngzōng),
and academic thought and human character (xuéshù rénxīn)
would acquire standards (guīfàn).
In the past, when Cài Yōng (蔡邕) rectified and established the Stone Classics (Shíjīng),
he said that scholars from all directions
went so far as to bribe people to alter the lacquer writings (qīshū) of Lántái
so they would match their private family texts.
This is clear evidence that the versions transmitted and studied in the commanderies and states (jùnguó) at that time
were inconsistent with the Imperial Library (Zhōngshū).
If mere characters and strokes,
which belong to elementary studies (xiǎoxué zhī gōng),
still show variations in transmission and study across the four regions,
how much more so for recorded accounts and hearsay,
private books, and separate records?
If schools do not transmit their instruction,
and gazetteers do not manage their categorization,
then literature will be scattered and widespread,
confusing what is likely and what is suspicious.
How can later generations rely on any basis to examine and finalize them?
Zhèng Qiáo (鄭樵) discussed the method of seeking books,
holding that one must seek them based on the location (yīndì)
and seek them based on the person (yīnrén).
Therefore, the regional recording of literary works (Yìwén) by the various provinces (fāngzhōu)
must surely be the crucial outline (yàoshān) for seeking based on location and person.
If previous dynasties, when searching for and collecting books,
did not offer generous rewards,
then rare books and secret texts
could not be assembled.
But if generous rewards were offered,
then ancient lost works would be fabricated,
hoping wildly for deceptive acceptance.
The *Yì* (易) of the Sān Fén (三墳)
and the *Shū* (書) in Ancient Text script
are clear examples of this.
If we had regional records of categorization (bùcì zhī shū) in the various provinces,
which corrected the lists of private family collections below,
and borrowed verification from the Imperial Library (Zhōngmì) above,
then the writings of the world
would all be recorded in registers.
Although one might wish to hoard them privately, one could not,
and although one might wish to fabricate them, one could not;
this is a certainty.
Even the proliferation of the population
is checked against registers (bǎnjí);
the products of the land and water
are listed in the geographical records (zhífāng).
How much more so for classics and literature,
which are the source from which academic thought originates
and the record of administrative achievements that are passed down?
If we do not use the prefectural and county gazetteers (zhōu xiàn zhìshū)
to categorize and itemize them,
and manage their crucial outlines,
how can we prevent the documents and records (wénxiàn) of a given region from being incomplete or lost?
Preface and Rules for the Chapter on Administrative Strategy (Zhènglüè) in the Gazetter of Hézhōu (和州).
The local gazetteers of prefectures and counties (zhōu xiàn zhìchén),
when compared to the historical records of the ancient feudal states (lièguó shǐshū),
are of high esteem.
The lords of the feudal states established their countries and inherited their lines;
their status was exalted and their power distinct.
Historical records list them in Hereditary Houses (Shìjiā),
placing them above ministers and commoners;
this was naturally the correct method.
The chief administrators of prefectures and counties (zhōu xiàn zhǎnglì)
are merely the equivalent of the ancient Grand Masters (dàfū) or city magistrates (yìzǎi).
Their tenure is not long,
and their office is not hereditary.
If they leave a beloved legacy (gāntáng liúyìn),
and their conduct is worthy of emulation,
they should be categorized in biographies (lièzhuàn),
ranked among those noted for literature and administration (wénxué zhèngshì);
this is also appropriate.
What the former records contained
is now unknowable.
Examples include the *Dānyáng Yǐn Zhuàn* (丹陽尹傳) compiled by Liáng Yuándì (梁元帝) (which appears in the *Suí Zhì* (隋誌) and totals ten volumes)
and the *Xián Mù Zhuàn* (賢牧傳) compiled by Sūn Zhòng (孫仲) (which appears in the *Táng Zhì* (唐誌) and totals fifteen volumes).
These specialized compilations
generally followed old precedents.
The chapter on Upright Officials (Xúnlì) by Mǎ [Qiān] (馬) and Bān [Gù] (班)
is essentially unchangeable.
As for comprehensive prefectural and county gazetteers,
when categorizing the local inhabitants,
they take Distinguished Officials (Mínghuàn) as the main category,
dividing them equally into sections
alongside categories such as Local Worthies (Xiāngxián), Virtuous Women (Liènǚ), Immortals and Buddhists (Xiānshì), and Sojourners (Liúyù).
This is merely an excerpted and comparative encyclopedia (lèishū),
a miscellaneous compilation by men of letters (círén),
which, although it slightly imitates the list of names appended in Yuè Shǐ’s (樂史) *Tàipíng Huányǔ Jì* (太平寰宇記),
is truly just preparatory material for the collection of flowery phrases in the Rabbit Garden (Tùyuán).
If one wishes to emulate the tradition of the *Chūnqiū* (春秋) (Spring and Autumn Annals),
where the unofficial historian (wàishǐ) managed historical accounts,
individuals were compiled into biographies,
and events were recorded from beginning to end,
yet officials and commoners are recorded together,
with no difference in format,
it is unavoidable that, like Décāo (德操) visiting the home of Páng Gōng (龐公),
in one room it is hard to distinguish guest from host.
I humbly suggest that the admiration of Wén Wēng (文翁) in Shǔ Jùn (蜀郡)
and the remembrance of Shào Fǔ (邵父) in Nányáng (南陽)
stems from their having acted on behalf of their regions
by promoting benefits and eliminating abuses.
Although those people have departed,
their lingering kindness remains among the populace;
this is the reason.
Even if Bó Yí (伯夷) was pure
and Liǔxià Huì (柳下惠) was compassionate,
they should not be excluded from the same category.
Alternatively, perhaps before they took office,
local opinions were not unified;
or after they left office,
their integrity failed later in life;
yet if they served as honest and upright officials for a period,
how does that harm the good governance of the region?
If we take administrative achievement (zhìjì) as important,
and their remaining conduct as minor,
when comparing the personalities within the prefecture,
examining their entire lives from beginning to end,
judging their flaws and merits,
distinguishing between them clearly,
and compiling them into categorized lists,
the principle is fundamentally different [from other categories].
To separately title this section
and call it "Administrative Strategy" (Zhènglüè),
is this not appropriate?
The term *lüè* (略) (Strategy/Outline),
is a grand structure for administrative principles
and a magnificent title for compilation.
Writings like those of Huáng Shí (黃石) and Huáinán (淮南) bore this title (*Huáng Shí Sān Lüè* (黃石三略), *Huáinánzǐ Yàolüè* (淮南子要略)).
Figures like Zhāng Wēn (張溫) and Yú Huàn (魚豢) used it for their records (Zhāng Wēn’s *Sān Shǐ Lüè* (三史略), Yú Huàn’s *Diǎn Lüè* (典略)).
This usage is derived from the legacy of strategic planning (móu lüè),
and is not solely limited to the twenty sections of Zhèng Qiáo (鄭樵) (*Zhèng Qiáo Tōng Zhì* (通誌) twenty *lüè*).
To use it to categorize administrative affairs,
and compile achievements and merits,
is sufficient to oversee the people of the state,
and to crown the biographies (lièzhuàn).
When measured against historical documentation,
the format perfectly conforms,
and it does not mean merely adopting the essence of summarized extracts,
as Péi Zǐyě (裴子野) did when he abridged the *Sòng Lüè* (宋略).
General Discussion of the Biographies (Lièzhuàn) in the Gazetter of Hézhōu (和州).
The Monograph says:
The writings of biographies (zhuàn) and monographs (zhì),
in antiquity, had no fixed style.
The various writings, such as the *Jūn Zhì* and *Zhōu Zhì*, cited by the *Zuǒ Shì*,
are commentaries (zhuàn).
The questions concerning the parks and preserves of Tāng and Wǔ, which Mèngzǐ answered,
all said, "It is recorded in the commentaries (zhuàn),"
which are records (zhì).
If the Six Arts (Liù Yì) are taken as the Classics (jīng),
then the writings of the *Lún Yǔ* and *Lǐ Jì* are called commentaries (zhuàn).
If the hexagrams and lines (Guà Yáo) are taken as the Classic,
then the *Tuàn*, *Xiàng*, and *Wén Yán* are called commentaries (zhuàn).
Since the *Zuǒshì Chūnqiū* interpreted the meaning based on the Classic [the *Chūnqiū*],
it simultaneously adopted the historical record as its standard.
And Sīmǎ Qiān's seventy collective Biographies (Liè Zhuàn),
briefly referenced this pattern;
firmly, with the Twelve Basic Annals (Shí'èr Běn Jì),
he secretly compared them to the *Chūnqiū*.
Now, as for his individuals being separated into chapters,
and following in succession by category,
when considering the *Zuǒ Shì*,
one feels they are somewhat formal and severe,
but he set his own unique standard
and generally modeled himself on the various Masters (zhū zǐ).
Examining the origin of its naming,
the reliance of the various biographies (zhuàn) on the *Chūnqiū*
is merely like the various records relying on the ritual classics (jīng lǐ);
the form was determined by the name,
it did not contain hidden profound meanings.
Thus, Qū Yuán of Chǔ
was combined in a joint biography with Jiǎ Shēng of Hàn;
Zōu Yǎn, who discussed Heaven,
was attached to the chapters of the great Confucians Mèng and Xún;
Using individuals to find correlations,
his critique and judgment knew no bounds,
and his elevated sighing and chanting

was perhaps also a remnant of the *Lǚ Shì Liù Lùn* (The Twelve Annals of *Lǚ Shì* resemble the Basic Annals; the Eight Views resemble the Eight Treatises; the Six Treatises resemble the Collective Biographies).
Within a single volume of Bān's History (Bān Shǐ),
individuals are divided into beginning and end,
once the names of the biographies (zhuàn) were fixed,
the regulations were extremely strict.
However, the likes of the Yìmín (Recluses) and the Sì Hào (Four Graybeards)
were merely subordinates appended to the biographies of Wáng Gòng.
People such as Wáng Jí and Wéi Xián
were a separate branch of the *Rú Lín* (Confucian Scholars) section.
An appended subordinate is like Zhuānyú attached to Lǔ—
its designation is not heard;
a separate branch is like the Tián and Chén families residing in Qí—
they open a new heading again;
When discussing literature, Xiāngrú elaborately displayed his rhapsodies;
when discerning customs, Dōngfāng did not shy away from humorous words;
truly, his outstanding judgment and grand standards
still cannot be measured by a single track.
As for the work concerning the Eastern Hàn by Fàn Shì,
its topics were numerous and fragmented,
resembling grains of rice or salt;
the names listed in the biographies (zhuàn),
must have their courtesy names (zǐ) annotated at the beginning of the chapter.
Consequently, the style of the collective biographies (liè zhuàn)
became like registering official credentials:
the ancestral line is cited at the beginning,
descendants and great-grandchildren are attached at the end,
chronologically arranged in sequence,
fearing only that something would be lost.
If one seeks examples like Chén Shòu's account in the *Shǔ Zhì*,
which broadly collected material for *Jì Hàn Fǔ Chén* (Supporting Ministers of the Later Hàn),
or Shěn Yuē's biography of Língyùn,
which generally discussed the literature and history of the Six Dynasties (Liù Cháo),
not being restricted by rigid rules,
and retaining slightly the intent of the author,
it is startling, like the sound of footsteps in an empty valley.
However, since Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù (Shī Bān) are no longer writing,
the standards and rules still remain.
To compile a collection according to these standards,
and wait for the capable ones;
to harmonize with, but not originate (hé ér bù chàng),
seems appropriate and feasible;
but because there are many schools of writing,
people of comprehensive talent and profound insight
should not be bound by this triviality.
As for books of miscellaneous records
outside of the official histories (zhèng shǐ),
such as those on Gāozǔ and Xiàowén,
which discuss their strategies and edicts,
all are called biographies (zhuàn) (The *Hàn Yìwén Zhì* lists thirteen chapters of *Gāozǔ Zhuàn* and eleven chapters of *Xiàowén Zhuàn*).
These are thus the ancestors of anecdotal records (gù shì).
The *Mù Tiānzǐ Zhuàn* and the *Hàn Wǔ Nèi Zhuàn*
belong to the category of minor tales (xiǎo shuō).
Liú Xiàng's *Liè Nǚ Zhuàn* (Biographies of Eminent Women),
and Jī Kāng's *Gāo Shì Zhuàn* (Biographies of Eminent Scholars),
are records of specialized fields.
Wáng Sù's *Jiā Zhuàn* (Family Biographies),
and Wáng Póu's *Shì Zhuàn* (Hereditary Biographies),
are books focusing on a single family.
The *Dōngfāng Shuò Zhuàn* and the *Lù Xiānshēng Zhuàn*
are records of the actions of a single person.
As for the monographs (zhì) of commanderies and districts,
then from the time of Dōngjīng (Eastern Capital/Later Hàn) onward,
up to the end of the Six Dynasties (Liù Cháo) and back,
such as the *Chénliú Qíjiù Zhuàn* (Biographies of Elders of Chénliú),
and the *Kuàijī Xiānxián Zhuàn* (Biographies of Former Worthies of Kuàijī);
those not named biographies (zhuàn),
such as the *Xiāngyáng Qíjiù Jì* (Record of Elders of Xiāngyáng) and the *Yùzhāng Zhì Hòu Zhuàn* (Later Compilation of the Yùzhāng Monograph);
The writings are numerous and abundant,
impossible to count.
They encompass what was lost and scattered,
and compile what was previously heard,
like many streams rushing toward a ravine,
discarding nothing, great or small;
or five metals in a foundry,
both sharp and dull being cast together.
Sīmǎ Qiān said:
"The words of the Hundred Schools (Bǎi Jiā) are not refined,
it is difficult for gentry scholars (jìn shēn xiān shēng) to speak of them."
He also said:
"Those who do not depart from the ancient texts (gǔ wén) are close [to the truth]."
He further said:
"Select those statements that are particularly refined."
The collected documents are extremely broad,
allowing reconciliation via the Six Arts (Liù Yì).
Although the *Shī* (Odes) and the *Shū* (Documents) are deficient,
the Yú and Xià periods can still be known."
If this is the case, then by extensively inferring and subtly demonstrating,
combining what is heard and what is seen,
making the hidden manifest and the obscure clear,
and reconciling them to the ultimate propriety,
the text must be well-formed and the standard established.
How can one be constrained by merely following a marked line on the ground?
To combine sweet and spicy flavors to achieve taste,
and to interweave compilation to form text,
to compare and contrast eras,
and evaluate the ethos of scholars,
is the study of judging the age (lùn shì).
To compare virtues among contemporaries,
and to append them to equally compiled sections,
is the method of categorical ordering.
When emotion is intense yet seems calm,
or when the purpose appears critical but is actually regretful,
this is the power of granting and denying [historical judgment].
Sometimes counter-evidence serves as comparison (bǐ),
sometimes a distant quote serves as allusion (xīng);
the detail or brevity of one event depends on comparison,
and different writings are suddenly compiled together—
this is the principle of categorization and modulation.
If words lack refinement,
they will not travel far.
If one gathers public and private records,
and examines the strengths and weaknesses of the Hundred Schools,
but cannot establish one's own judgment,
and merely meticulously acts as a clerk checking indices,
how can one inspire the reader,
and forthwith desire to publish a work that lasts eternally?
Moreover, the national history must consult external records (wài zhì),
and external records must consult family archives (jiā dié);
only if the consulted sources are extensive,
can they provide a basis for concise selection.
Today's external records (wài zhì),
do not distinguish between annals and biographies,
and the names and actual contents often differ.
Having already designated Biographies of Eminent People and Eminent Women (Rénwù Liè Nǚ) as specialized fields,
they also separate the Literary Garden (Wén Yuàn) and Local Worthies (Xiāng Xián) into fixed categories;
cutting and controlling historical biographies,
deleting and summarizing facts,
and appending notes to every entry,
resembles the rules of an encyclopedia (lèi shū) excerpting and comparing,
and is no longer the historical biography study of the ancients;
If one intends to create books divided by state,
or monographs divided by districts,
is it not difficult?
Furthermore, for officials (shì huàn) of the highest rank (jiǎ kē),
sometimes the details of their examinations and selection (xuǎnjǔ) are emphasized;
records, eulogies, and stele inscriptions (zhì zhuàng bēi míng)
are listed within the chapter on arts and literature (yì wén).
The deeds of one person
are seen repeated and duplicated,
sometimes noted in the biography detailed in a certain volume,
or noted in the facts found in a certain entry;
This is truly similar to materia medica (běn cǎo) annotating medicines,
where roots and fruits are collected in different sections;
or dictionaries (yùn shū) classifying sounds,
where level (píng) and oblique (zè) tones are mutually marked for use.
If the writing is not elegant and refined,
it is difficult for scholars to discuss.
Now, using the common standards of official history (zhèng shǐ),
specifically marking the collective biographies (liè zhuàn),
extensively inferring and mutually verifying,
and compelling it to be a specialized field,
it would benefit the extant writings of ancient history above,
and serve as a reserve for later generations to gather material below;
It is hoped that there will be authors
who can conduct research and seek it out.
If one holds otherwise,
I ask that we await future sages.
Hézhōu Monograph: Preface and Principles for Collective Biographies (Draft, Awaiting Consultation)
Kǒngzǐ said:
“I still reached the point where historians left gaps in the text.”
He also said:
“Hear much but set aside what is doubtful,
and speak cautiously about the rest.”
Now, in collecting what has been scattered and lost,
and deducing from the bamboo slips and texts,
what is seen and heard
sometimes leads to uncertainty (doubt and similarity).
This does not mean valuing omissions while failing to investigate.
Indeed, the [cases of] Guō Gōng Xià Wǔ [in the Chūnqiū]
originally held no hidden meaning;
the discussion of plows and fishing nets [lěi sì wǎng gǔ]
is also preserved in treatises.
Yet the *Chūnqiū* still retains its old titles,
and the *Shàngshū* begins definitively with the *Yáo Diǎn*;
what is doubtful is omitted and not exhaustively pursued,
and what is omitted is preserved and not deleted.
This is caution (shèn).
Sīmǎ Qiān said:
“There are gaps where the texts are missing,
but the lost content sometimes appears in other accounts.”
The traces of doubt and resemblance
are not necessarily without other accounts to consult,
but the ancient slips take the ancient script (gǔ wén) as their standard,
and the hundred schools choose refinement and orthodoxy (yǎ xún).
Knowing this intent in our hearts,
we should deeply reflect on scholars who are fond of learning and deep thought.
Bān Gù, in the *Dōngfāng Shuò Zhuàn*,
believed that bizarre sayings and strange language
attributed to him were many,
so he extensively recorded the trivial conversations involving humor, riddles, and hidden meanings
to show that Shuò’s [deeds] truly stopped there.
This is the historical tradition of historians resolving doubts.
Chén Shòu, in the *Shǔ Zhì*,
since Zhūgě did not establish a history official,
and records of Shǔ affairs were exhausted by searching and interviewing,
he thus recorded Yáng Xì’s encomiums (zàn) on the famous officials of Jì Hàn,
briefly preserving their names
to convey his meaning.

This is the established convention for handling textual gaps in historical records. Shòu separately compiled ten scrolls of the *Yì Bù Qí Jiù Zhuàn*, meaning Shòu never neglected Shǔ. The *Yì Bù Qí Jiù Zhuàn* was not included in the *Shǔ Zhì* because each had its appropriate structure. Some criticized Shòu for this, which is wrong. .
Since historical scholarship was lost,
mediocre historians failed to grasp the meaning of textual gaps (què wén).
Those fond of verbose accounts
sometimes mixed in bizarre and astonishing theories;
those who favored conciseness
sometimes deleted essential words.
The *Jìn Shū* liked to adopt minor fictional accounts, and the *Táng Shū* often deleted memorials and reports (zhāng zòu). The principle of hearing much was not followed,
and the instruction to speak cautiously was misunderstood.
If, because facts lead to propagating doubts,
or events are prone to forced interpretation,
one cannot definitively decide when holding the brush,
and old records are difficult to verify,
and thus believes that entire chapters should be deleted
to align with the theory of textual gaps (què wén);
this is merely extinguishing what is doubtful,
and how can it still be considered an omission (què)?
Zhèng Qiáo, in compiling the *Jiào Chóu Lüè*,
stated that when imperial libraries sought books,
there traditionally existed a catalog of missing books.
Anyone who investigates texts
must record the sections and sequence
and search for them throughout the land.
His argument can be called precise.
I humbly suggest that what applies to classical texts
also applies to human records.
All who compile history
should, besides the material arranged and discussed,
also consider those who are noted but whose deeds are incomplete,
or those whose biographies diverge and whose accounts are inconsistent;
as well as those clearly listed among the famous,
but whose facts cannot yet be verified;
those whose purity equals Yí Qí [Bó Yí and Shū Qí],
but whose act of gathering ferns on Xī Shān is missing from the record;
those whose learning is as prominent as Yán Zēng [Yán Huí and Zēng Shēn],
but whose achievements in the eastern state are not passed down.
If we apply the principle of ‘raising one corner to find three’ (yī yú sān fǎn),
such cases are truly numerous.
Perhaps they resulted from accidental deletions by scribes,
or perhaps they were generalized entries based on vague reputations.
It is difficult to rely on subjective judgment,
so they should be relegated to the category of ‘passing down doubts’ (chuán yí).
When the biographies (liè zhuàn) are about to conclude,
a separate section for ‘omissions requiring search’ (què fǎng) should be established,
to fulfill the instruction of speaking cautiously (shèn yán).
Later readers
will thus be able to investigate and seek them out.
If this were done, like Chén Shòu's famous officials of Jì Hàn (see above),
or Cháng Qú's notable persons of Huáyáng (The preface to the *Huáyáng Guó Zhì* contains a record of notable persons, listing only their names, stating that their deeds are incomplete.),
would it not be excellent?
As for the gazetteers (zhì) of prefectures (zhōu) and districts (xiàn),
their structure ought to be even more detailed than general histories.
However, the gazetteers compiled heretofore,
when listing rules for biographies (rén wù),
are limited to short spaces,
picking facts for comparison,
and adding brief summary notes,
which is roughly equivalent
to the categorical classification of local products and native goods.
Furthermore, the facts noted therein
often resemble evaluation comments in recommendation reports
or sentencing documents in judicial cases,
using parallel and balanced phrases,
making judgments without narrative description.
Scholars are said to be filial, friendly, upright, and square;
kindly, benevolent, and peaceable;
officials are praised as honest, capable, clear-minded, and cautious;
loyal, trustworthy, benevolent, and good.
Their learning is all complete Yì Rú scholarship,
and their chastity is that of Jiāng Nǚ.
It is a thousand pieces conforming to one pattern,
vague and like reeds,
so what is there to observe?
Now, employing the universal criteria of historians,
we specially designated the biographies (liè zhuàn).
We strove to select those whose writings are worthy of recitation
and whose facts are suitable for recording.
What the former gazetteers omitted
we have exhaustively searched for and investigated.
Other cases, such as those listed by name with brief notes,
where facts are difficult to verify,
where the era is distant and the years have vanished,
making searching impossible—
if preserved, there is no reliable source to return to;
if deleted, potential virtue will not shine forth.
All such cases
are compiled as the *Què Fǎng Liè Zhuàn* (Biographies Requiring Search and Omission),
to await the selection and judgment of those who come later.
Preface to the Biographies in the Former Gazetteer of Hé Zhōu, Part One.
The *Jì* (Record) says:
"To thoroughly understand the past and grasp the distant future,
that is the teaching of the *Shū* (Classic of History).
To compare events and arrange the phrasing,
that is the teaching of the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals)."
This means the modes of composition are different,
and thus the influence and instruction vary.
Mèngzǐ said:
"To chant their poems
and read their writings,
is it acceptable not to know the person who wrote them?"
This means that although the ancient records are fully preserved,
the intent of the author
must necessarily be discerned.
In antiquity, the officials in charge of history (*shǐguān*) each had established methods;
the profound meaning of the rhetoric and text
resided in the person who composed it.
What Mèngzǐ referred to as "the text is history,"
and what Kǒngzǐ considered "the principle (or righteousness) is selectively adopted,"
clarifies that the established statutes of the *shǐguān* were immutable,
but the principles and ideas were subject to the sole judgment of the sage.
If that is the case, then excellent historians and well-written histories
must also follow a proper path.
The officials who held the history post in high antiquity cannot be fully investigated,
but among the good historians of the various states during the *Chūnqiū* period,
such as Dǒng Hú and the Nán Shǐ (Southern Historian) with their unswerving writing,
and Zuǒ Shǐ Yǐ Xiàng with his extensive learning and refinement,
these are the general criteria.
I venture to suggest that figures like the Nán Shǐ, Dǒng, and the Zuǒ Shǐ
must have had traditions and teachings passed down from teachers at the time.
However, because this specialized field
is distant and the transmission was lost,
we cannot now fully investigate it.
Sīmǎ Qiān collected what was scattered and lost,
gathered old accounts,
and compiled them into one hundred and thirty chapters,
thereby continuing the work of the *Chūnqiū*.
Regarding the historical writings (*jiāyán*) styled as *Chūnqiū* during the waning Zhōu and Warring States periods—

such as the works by Yàn Yīng, Yú Qīng, and Lǚ Bùwéi (the *Yànzǐ Chūnqiū*, the *Yú Shì Chūnqiū*, and the *Lǚ Shì Chūnqiū*), all of which employed the style of comparing events and arranging phrases. (This indicates that the historical writings of the *Chūnqiū* school at that time each had different branches and were not all uniformly based on the standard of 'Spring, King, First Month.') —
he recorded the general outline of their writings,
collecting, comparing, and organizing them;
thereby clarifying that he extensively gathered from various schools,
reconciled them with the Six Arts (*Liù Yì*),
and when tracing the origin and distinguishing the branches,

he had to detail where the tradition came from. (Sīmǎ Qiān's *Zìxù* [Self-Preface] states that he continued the work of the *Chūnqiū*. This means he traced its different lineages back to their sources, and these were not merely presumptuous words.)
After the death of the Sīmǎ family (Sīmǎ Qiān),
Bān Gù composed his work.
In organizing the historical events of the Western Capital (Western Hàn),
he fully recorded the *Tàishǐ Zìxù* (Self-Preface of the Grand Historian),
expanding on its principles and methodology,
which is practically in the same category as the biographies of Xiāngrú and Yáng Xióng.
Fàn Wèizōng, in his description of Bān Gù in the *Hòu Hàn* (Later Hàn History),
followed and completed the established practice,
rigidly adhering to the old methods,
never exceeding the prescribed rules;
although he lacked the talent for independent judgment,
he still preserved the practice of offering a live sheep at the new moon announcement (*xīyáng gàosuò*),
a case where the ritual was discarded but the form was maintained.
When the *Sòng Shū* (History of Sòng) came to write the biography of Fàn Wèizōng,
and the *Jìn Shū* (History of Jìn) wrote the biography of Chén Shòu,
they either mixed them among the ranks of men of letters
or crudely compiled them among contemporaries.
They no longer paid attention
to the origins of historical study
or the methodology of the author's school.
This, too, was the gradual accumulation leading to the loss of historical methods.
As for the two histories, the *Jìn* and the *Suí*, compiled during the Táng dynasty,
they relied only on collective effort.
Since the talents were dispersed,
those who worked together
could not all be known;
some were attached to the end of another person's biography,
others were sporadically mentioned by one or two men of letters in their writings.
There was no longer separate documentation.
This caused the scholarly tradition of the *Chūnqiū* school
to lose its bridge and pathway,
and the transmission between teachers and historians
became vast and indistinct, like the Milky Way (*Hé Hàn*).
This is analogous to a clan having no one to gather its members,
leading to the family records becoming confused;
or the Buddhist monks (*zīliú*) being driven away and dispersed,
leaving the Buddhist monasteries (*fànshà*) desolate.
It is a necessary outcome of circumstances,
and a natural consequence of principle.
Now, the history writing of Mǎ (Sīmǎ Qiān) and Bān (Bān Gù)
is equivalent to the classic transmission by Fú (Fú Shèng) and Kǒng (Kǒng Ānguó).
The great principles and subtle words
were transmitted from heart to heart and taught orally;
some desired to store their work on famous mountains
and pass it on to the right person;
others made great Confucian scholars remain in the imperial library (*fúgé*),
receiving instruction from their younger sister (Bān Zhāo).
How could this be like the biographies and annals of later generations,
where the meaning is exhausted within the slips and scrolls,
and the writing is the same as that of a petty clerk (*xūshǐ*),
rigidly bound by general rules,
leaving nothing concealed upon a single glance?
Nevertheless, the *Rúlín* (Confucian Scholars) chapters of Mǎ and Bān
were able to use the Six Arts as the warp
and the tradition passed down by teachers and scholars as the weft.
Like tying a cord through pearls,
they formed their own structure;
thereby demonstrating the continuous succession of teaching methods

and tracing the origins without fail. (The format of the *Rúlín Zhuàn* (Biographies of Confucian Scholars) uses the classics as the warp and the individuals as the weft, unlike ordinary biographies that detail the life of a single person. This tradition was lost after the *Hòu Hàn Shū*.)
For the biographies of historians in later generations,
if one could thoroughly study the teaching methods of the ancients,
briefly imitate the precedents set by the transmission of classic scholars,
designate the history itself as the warp,
and then use the branches of historical writing
to weave them together.
Taking Mǎ and Bān as an example,
the sources they drew upon beforehand
were the *Shìběn* and the *Guócè* for Qiān’s (*Shǐjì*),
and Yáng Xióng and Líu Xīn for the *Hàn Shū*.
Those who subsequently expanded the transmission
include Yáng Yùn distributing Qiān’s History (*Shǐjì*),
and Mǎ Róng receiving the *Hàn Shū*.
Those who separately created commentaries and annotations
include Xú Guǎng and Péi Yīn for Qiān’s History,
and Fú Qián and Yīng Shào for the *Hàn Shū*.
All such examples
should be compiled according to type,
clarifying the scholarly tradition,
taking the book itself as the principal focus,
and no longer naming the chapter after the life story (beginning and end) of a single person.
In that case, the world-ordering principles of the *Chūnqiū*,
even if one were to say they still exist today, would be acceptable.
As for the histories of the Later Hàn,
the works of Líu Zhēn and Yuán Hóng,
and the books of Huà Qiáo, Xiè Chéng, and Sīmǎ Biāo,
should all be broadly included and listed alongside the work of Fàn (Fàn Wèizōng).
Regarding the histories of the Jìn family (Jìn dynasty),
the authors, such as Wáng Yǐn, Yú Yù, Hé Fǎshèng, Gàn Bǎo, Lù Jī, and Xiè Língyùn,
totaled eighteen schools of writers;
this was certainly a flourishing era.
Yet later historians, when compiling histories,
were unable to categorize the styles of these various schools,
discuss and arrange the merits and flaws of the collected books,
and gather them into a single chapter.
This is like the man of Yǐng who was skilled in cutting,
but if the substance is lost, what is there to seek?
The rites of Xià can be spoken of,
but without evidence, they cannot be believed.
Furthermore, when gathering a multitude to compile a book,
setting up supervisors and recorders,
one should especially examine and determine the chapters and sections,
and repeatedly review the text:
which record is documenting a certain book,
who compiled it,
and which treatise or which biography
was authored by whom.
This allows the reader to examine their merits and faults
and determine what is right and wrong;
nearly ensuring that even if the Jīng and Wèi rivers are mixed,
the Zī and Mǐn rivers can still be distinguished;
thus, the excesses of later generations
may still rely on preventive measures.
However, the various historians of the Táng and Sòng dynasties
ultimately had no dedicated record,
allowing the classical scholars who wrote formulaic essays (*tiēguā*)
and the literary men who specialized in shallow rhetoric (*diāochóng*)
to chirp and chatter in the hall of Bān and Mǎ,
and lay claim to the profession of the chroniclers (*hànqīng*).
Preface to the Biographies in the Former Gazetteer of Hézhōu.
Zhì Yú of Jìn established the *Wénzhāng Zhì*,
narrating the lives of literary figures,
and discussing the origins and details of literary writings;
this provided the model subsequently imitated by the historical genre of the *Wényuàn Lièzhuàn*.
Since then, records and biographies of literary figures
have been compiled in every generation,
and the inclusion of the literary genre into historical works
was also subsequently adopted as an established convention.
However, concerning the schools and streams of historiography,
discussions are unheard of,
and the merits and demerits of historical officials
are also placed outside the realm of consideration.
How profound it is,
that the world finds it easy to speak of literature but is afraid to speak of history.
Indeed, the works of Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù
did not establish a *Wényuàn* section;
it was not because they lacked literary figures.
Lǎo Zhuāng Shēn Hán, Guǎn Yàn, Mèng Xún, Sīmǎ Xiāngrú, Yáng Xióng, Méi Chéng, and Zōu Yáng,
for whom biographies were compiled,
were all figures whose contributions to scholarship and authorship
they never failed to pay great attention to.
They did not label it *Wényuàn*,
in order to discuss and order the learning of specialized scholars.
That *Wényuàn* now has biographies
is probably due to the lack of specialized scholars in learning,
which signifies the decline of literary arts.
Yet, when historians wield the pen,
they extravagantly speak of *Wényuàn*,
but regarding the schools and traditions concerning the *Chūnqiū*,
its branches and origins,
they never give the slightest thought to them.
I do not know what they claim their own historical work to be?
The tradition of the *Wénzhāng Zhì*,
after Zhì Yú,
was continued by Shěn Yuē, Fù Liàng, Zhāng Zhì, and others,
who prolifically compiled and recorded—Fù Liàng wrote the *Xù Wénzhāng Zhì*, Shěn Yuē the *Sòng Shì Wénzhāng Zhì*, and Zhāng Zhì the *Wénshì Zhuàn*—,
and their number is too great to count.
However, the historians who collected this material,
preserved only the general outlines,
and these recorded works
are now all lost.
Thus, concerning the origins and details of the historical tradition,
and the ancient traces of compilation,
when these histories were being written and compiled,
public records and private manuscripts
might not have been entirely without evidentiary basis.
But since previous historians did not establish dedicated sections,
and later scholars do not know the essential principles,
even if traces existed,
they are ultimately lost and nothing remains.
This has consequently caused what the ancients referred to as "officials guarding their books,"
and "families inheriting the profession,"
to be, instead, inferior to literary talent and stylistic writings,
which are still managed to be included in the list of Cháng Bǎodǐng’s *Wénxuǎn Zhùzuò Rénmíng*. (The book has three volumes.)
Lǐ Zhào of the Táng dynasty wrote the *Jīng Shǐ Shì Tí*,
and Zōng Jiàn annotated the *Shísān Dài Shǐ Mù*.
These works were categorized under the bibliography section,
and thus failed to fully grasp the grand scope of records and biographies.
Kǒng Píngzhòng of the Zhào Sòng dynasty
once wrote the *Liáng Shǐ Shì Jì*,
but that book is also lost today,
and the recorded entry for it is merely one volume,
which means it is too meager and trifling to be worth studying.
Now, the precedents established by historians,
each have their underlying basis.
The *Liènǚ* genre originated with Liú Xiàng,
Filial Piety and Righteousness originated with Xiāo Guǎngjì (a Jìn person who wrote the *Xiàozǐ Zhuàn*),
Loyalty and Righteousness originated with Emperor Yuán of Liáng's *Zhōngchén Zhuàn* (thirty volumes),
and Recluses originated with Huángfǔ Shì’s *Yì Shì Zhuàn* and *Gāo Shì Zhuàn*.
These were all general practices of former historians,
who formulated the guiding principles according to their era.
The *Rúlín* biographies of Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù
were based on the studies undertaken by the Erudites;
it is regrettable that they did not take the responsibilities of the historical officials,
and compile them into a dedicated work.
Later generations' learning and knowledge
are inferior to those of their predecessors,
thus preventing them from obtaining this legacy,
and rendering them unable to contribute.
When Hàn Confucians transmitted the classics,
the master-disciple methodology was lost.
Although the *Rúlín* chapters of later histories
could not follow the methods of charting its structure and origins,
they never failed to select the Confucian masters of their own generation,
and concerning their respective studies,
record the scholarship of the age.
If Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù wrote history,
and the school tradition was already lost,
why could the work of historical officials in later generations,
even if they could not harmonize with its principles and structure,
not select the general outlines of contemporary compilations,
and the scholarly lineage across time,
discuss and order them into biographies,
to complete the achievement of a single history?
Now, the *Rúlín* manages the classics,
and the *Wényuàn* discusses the arts.
The profession of historians
lies in the middle of these,
and compiling history is also something one must know what to prioritize.
Some might use the categorization of the Arts and Literature section,
to record its contents,
and in the postscript commentary,
briefly indicate the author's intention,
claiming that the essential meaning of the history section
is already revealed in the general outline.
But they do not realize that the commentaries and annotations of the masters of classics,
and the literary writings of scholars,
the Arts and Literature section never fails to record their categorization;
whereas the *Rúlín* and *Wényuàn* chapters,
examine their lives in detail,
provide separate evaluations,
and must be examined side-by-side and mutually verified.
How can they be neglected?
If, perhaps, the records of their deeds are numerous,
and a separate special biography is listed,
making it impossible to combine into one chapter,
then within the chapter concerning historical officials,
their names should still be recorded,
with a note indicating that a separate biography exists.
The precedents set by Dǒng Zhòngshū, Wáng Jí, and Wéi Xián

already have established procedures (Dǒng Zhòngshū studied the *Chūnqiū*, Wáng Jí studied the *Máo Shī*, and Wéi Xián studied the *Lǔ Shī*; all appear in the *Rúlín* but also have separate biographies),
and neither causes hindrance to the other.
If Xún Qīng wrote discussions on the *Lǐ* and *Yuè*,
yet they were not categorized as books of the Twelve Masters,
and Zhuāng Zhōu indulged in wild and absurd pronouncements,
still, they discussed masters like Qín Huá and Mò Zǐ.
If one wishes to complete a work belonging to a single school,
but fails to clearly analyze the treatises of predecessors,
distinguishing the categories clearly,
tracing the sources and origins,
and establishing the most appropriate balanced judgments;
then even though one wishes to be beneficial to predecessors,
and bestow favor upon future students,
it is like stepping backward yet seeking to advance,
and one will never attain the ultimate goal.
Section following the Preface to the Biographies in the former gazetteer of Hézhōu Zhì
Prefectural and county gazetteers,
which discuss and order the writings of predecessors,
and specifically compile biographies,
are establishing a precedent.
By taking this example and extending it throughout the land,
causing the world-regulating principles of the *Chūnqiū*,
and the school methodology of historians,
to brilliantly illuminate the world,
then once the regional gazetteers are ordered,
and books have a unified structure,
the essential abridgement of the national history
can be spoken of with assurance.
Nevertheless,
there are three things difficult to narrate,
and three things that must not be left unnarrated.
Scholars who hold the pen
must carefully study this discussion.
What are the three difficulties in recounting (histories)?
First, the writings lack established methods (jiāfǎ),
the prose is not worth reading,
and they are easily scattered and lost.
After the Táng and Sòng Dynasties,
the methods of historiography were lost,
especially regarding the specialized work of Mǎ [Sīmǎ Qiān] and Bān [Bān Gù];
they could not be recovered.
However, regarding the established rules for Annals (Jì) and Tables (Biǎo),
and the old precedents for Treatises (Zhì) and Biographies (Zhuàn),
they persisted unchanged over time,
resembling the formalized structures of the Imperial Examinations (Kējǔ Chéngshì),
and the regulations of official mandates (Gōnglìng Tiáolì).
Even mediocre historians (shǐguān),
could manage to conform to the standards,
and roughly organize the material;
therefore, although these writings varied in quality,
showing both strengths and weaknesses,
the reader could still use the established format to judge the editing and revision.
For local gazetteers (wài zhì), the rules and structure are utterly lost,
the style has no standard,
extracts resemble encyclopedias (lèishū),
notes and records are like account ledgers,
the plain language resembles that of minor clerks (xūlì),
and the literary phrases are like short letters (chǐdú);
readers are bewildered,
unable to grasp the fundamental purpose.
Literary scholars (wénxué zhī shì)
disdain and ignore them;
as soon as a new compilation is finished,
the old gazetteer immediately vanishes.
This is like changing hats and clothes with the seasons,
or a posting station retaining passing guests;
if one tries to find and preserve them,
is this not difficult?
Second, the compilers of these various works,
their actions and careers are not detailed,
making it difficult to write their biographies.
When the Historiography Office (Shǐguǎn) employs scholars,
they are generally men of literature,
holding official rank in the court (cháoshēn),
and sometimes include famous dukes and ministers (gōngqīng).
Their writings might appear in the bibliography sections (Yìwén),
and their careers might be detailed in the Biographies (Lièzhuàn);
comparing and verifying them,
they are still easy to collect.
The gazetteers of prefectures and counties (Zhōuxiàn Zhìshū),
are merely the work of temporary visiting officials (yóuhuàn zhī shì)
who happen to pass through;
starting the bureau and completing the writing (shāqīng),
takes no more than a few months,
and the discussions and deliberations
do not go beyond the local district (zhōulǘ).
These people might have hidden virtues that are not recorded,
or commendable achievements that are not apparent;
where they traveled is not known regularly,
and what they studied is not known professionally.
They are like gathering floating duckweed traces (píngzōng zhī jù),
and retaining the footprint of a swan (hóngzhǎo zhī liú);
even if one wished to imitate the collected biographies of the Literary Figures (Wényuàn),
or follow the biographies of the Confucian Scholars (Rúlín),
how could this be achieved?
Third, the titles and prefaces (tíxù) are disorganized and excessive,
the essential structure has long been lost,
making it difficult to find precedents for recording (the biographies).
The biographies compiled by Mǎ [Sīmǎ Qiān] and Bān [Bān Gù]
all include their own prefaces (zìxù).
This is because their life events and careers,
along with the general principles of their editing,
were already made clear in their self-prefaces;
based on the original text, they were written directly,
and compiled into the Biographies (Lièzhuàn).
If readers can grasp this themselves,
then they will understand more than half of the book.
The original purpose of writing catalogue prefaces (xùlù),
although stemming from the *Yì* [Yìjīng] Appendices (*Yì Xì*) and the Odes (*Shī* Piān),
for the sake of historians, required pruning.
This practice truly originated with the various scholars of collation and editing (jiàochóu zhūjiā),
who especially valued their structure (tǐ).
That which Liú Xiàng called 'detailing the chapter titles,'
'summarizing the main points,'
and 'recording them in a document presented to the throne,'
was generally clear, profound, and pure,
providing definite illumination
regarding both the books and the people involved.
The introductory remarks at the beginning of the bamboo slips (jiǎn shǒu tící),
benefit later students;
this is why.
Later generations of writing lack essential structure,
and are not duties of collation;
everyone can spontaneously take up the writing brush (cāogū).
Whenever there is a book or compilation (jiǎnbiān),
a preface (biànyǔ) is always affixed,
the statements come from official circles,
but the principles are all generalized and vague.
If one hides the contents and organization,
and quickly reads the preface,
one does not know to whom it refers,
or what events it praises.
Yet literati have perpetuated this ingrained habit,
unable to reform themselves—
this is indeed bewildering.
In compiling local gazetteers (Zhōuxiàn Xiū Zhì),
they especially take pride in having many prefaces;
clerical script (lì) and cursive script (cǎo) vie for prominence in the writing,
and various calligraphic styles compete.
The shade of the sweet pear tree (Táng Yīn) is filled with flowers,
first serving as an encomium for upright officials (xúnlì);
water surges and mountains stand high,
then forming a general praise for local culture and talent (rénwén tōngzàn).
A thousand books follow a single pattern,
leaving the reader feeling dry and dull.
Moving it to book A or B is permissible,
or assigning it to book C or D is permissible.
How can one still gather the prefaces from the old gazetteers,
record the general rules (fánlì) of the previous books,
use them as source material for biographies (Lièzhuàn),
and establish the organization of the entire work?
These three matters,
are what make the recounting (or compilation) difficult.
What are the three things that must not be omitted from the narrative?
The first is that if a previous gazetteer was inappropriate,
and a later gazetteer corrects it,
the original should be retained for mutual corroboration.
The eyes and ears of the world are infinite,
but the intelligence of one person is limited.
The text in the *Yǔgòng* (Tribute of Yǔ) regarding Mínshān is ancient,
but upon obtaining the *Miǎn Zhì* (Gazetteer of Miǎn),
the source of the river is described in detail at Jīnshā.
Zhèng Xuán’s explanation of *suōzūn* is old,
but upon obtaining Wáng Sù’s account,
it is understood that the metal casting involves carving the back of the sacrificial animal (*xī*).
In the study of the Classics,
the later scholar may sometimes surpass the earlier one;
how can the talent for compiling gazetteers
be fixed once established and never subject to change?
However, when subsequent compilers determine and edit a new work,
they do not necessarily retain the old record immediately.
If the account of the previous gazetteer is lost,
how can we know the painstaking effort behind the revision,
or recognize the utmost appropriateness of the differentiation and determination?
Therefore, discussing and arranging previous records,
is not merely to preserve the names of the authors of the old gazetteer,
but also to clarify the specific editorial choices made for the new gazetteer.
The second is that if a previous gazetteer has verifiable evidence,
but a later gazetteer mistakenly alters it,
the original should be kept available for selection and verification.
Human minds differ,
just as their faces do,
and it is the same for writing works.
It is the accumulated habit of historians
to enjoy changing old texts,
choosing to easily conform to general rules,
not fundamentally intending to be overly critical.
However, when Huáiyīn wore a sword,
it is unclear who is being referred to;

Sīmǎ Qiān’s *Hán Xìn Zhuàn* (Biography of Hán Xìn) says that a youth in Huáiyīn insulted Xìn, saying, “Though you are tall, your heart is timid.” Bān Gù removed the character *ruò* (若), and the meaning of the text became obscure. When the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) carried a head,
whose head was borrowed?

Earlier people criticized the *Xīn Táng Shū* (New History of Táng) *Duàn Xiùshí Zhuàn* (Biography of Duàn Xiùshí), saying that Liǔ Zōngyuán’s account quoted the Grand Commandant as saying: “I have brought my head.” The meaning is self-evident. The *Xīn Táng Shū* changed it to: “I have brought the head.” Whose head is this? If the original text of the day is not preserved,
then after three revisions by different hands,
it will not merely be errors transmitted like mixing up *hài* (亥) and *shǐ* (豕),
but rather the character forms will change entirely like insects and fish replacing each other.
The third is that gazetteers should be sequentially continued,
and not repeatedly overhauled,
and should adhere to general guidelines.
Sīmǎ Qiān’s writings (Shū) drew upon the *Shìběn* and the *Guócè*,
and assembled the chronological records of the *Shàngshū*.
The *Nán Běi Shǐ* (Histories of the Southern and Northern Dynasties) compiled the works of the eight families of Shěn, Xiāo, Yáo, and Lǐ.
We have never heard that once a new compilation was finished,
the old books were immediately sealed up and stored away.
Regarding the meager gazetteers and records of prefectures and districts (Zhōu Xiàn Zhì Chéng),
since they lack distinct understanding or new editorial judgment,
