they ought simply to narrate and not create. Yet, recent writers,
strive only to show off their superiority,
without having peeked over the fence of Lóngmén (Sīmǎ Qiān’s residence),
but first practice the tactics of the Gibbon Keeper (*Jū Gōng*),
changing three into four,
and mutually replicating in circles—
this is what is called bringing trouble upon oneself.
Now, thirty years constitutes a generation,
during which forgotten writings can be supplemented and collected,
and historical facts gathered.
Thirty years later,
the omissions should be left for future worthies,
so that Compendium A and Record B,
newly succeed one another,
much like Bān (Gù) continued Mǎ (Sīmǎ Qiān),
and Fàn (Yè) succeeded Bān (Gù)—
would this not be good?
Suppose the established principles and examples of the former work were incomplete,
and the general table of contents had omissions,
and later people newly establish them,
wishing to supplement the missing texts,
they should also act as Sīmǎ Qiān did not include a geography section,
but Bān Gù’s *Zhì* (Treatise) directly traced back to the *Xià Shū* (Book of Xià);
or as the Liáng and Chén Dynasties had no official histories (Zhì),
but the *Suí Shū* (History of Suí) extended upward to include five dynasties (Wǔ Dài).
Liáng, Chén, Běi Qí, Hòu Zhōu, Suí are the five dynasties. Rules are established based on appropriateness,
how could this not be acceptable?
Yet, instead, they roughly revise the general table of contents,
and record the old text entirely;
forgetting the trap once the fish is caught,
which is akin to plagiarism.
How can this be acceptable?
However, if the *qín* (zither) and *sè* (lute) are out of tune,
they must be re-tuned and adjusted.
Now that this book is being newly established,
it cannot be strictly bound by the rule of sequential continuation;
perhaps this will be called using a spear to pierce one's own shield,
I do not decline the charge;
those who come after
perhaps will appreciate the sincerity of the intention.
By sequentially narrating the previous gazetteers,
and preserving their structures,
it also shows that the establishment of new principles for this new compilation,
was not done willingly.
These three matters, in general,
are what is meant by that which must not be omitted from the narrative.
Preface and Principles for the Literary Collection of Hézhōu
In the thirty-ninth year of Qiánlóng (1774),
I compiled forty-two chapters of the *Hézhōu Zhì* (Gazetteer of Hézhōu).
After the compilation was finished,
I proceeded to select works and writings from the prefecture that benefited literary records,
or whose literary style was elegant and impressive in appearance,
assembling them into two volumes of Memorials (Zòuyì),
three volumes of Collected Narratives (Zhēngshù),
one volume of Discourses and Writings (Lùnzhù),
and two volumes of Poetry and Rhapsodies (Shīfù),
totaling eight volumes titled *Wénzhēng* (Literary Collection),
comprising an unspecified number of articles.
After itemizing these divisions,
I proceeded to narrate the reasons for the selection and compilation,
writing this preface and record for it.
The preface states:
The writings of the ancients,
each established their own school,
and there was no practice of selecting and compiling the works of various people,
and combining them into one collection.
Since specialized learning dispersed,
the trend of private anthologies became increasingly frequent.
Although the writings were not uniform,
yet their words sometimes possessed merit,
thus the work of selection and compilation arose.
Regarding what is included in the history section (Shǐ Bù),
the Hán Dynasty was still relatively ancient.
Although Xiāngrú, Yáng Xióng, Méi Chéng, and Zōu Yáng,
but only their ornate prose and rhapsodies were taken,
and compiled into their biographies (Liè Zhuàn);
the original intention of the court historian,
while certainly preserving the literary elegance of the time,
was also that humanity is not uniform,
and the importance of literature,
is not something that cannot be included in the biographies alongside their deeds;
it was not entirely like later generations that narrowly focused on the meaning of texts,
and only recorded conduct and achievements in the biographies.
But the atmosphere of the Western Capital (Xī Jīng, i.e., Western Hán) was simple and plain,
and Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù themselves compiled works that formed their own schools,
thus allowing for the use of their principles and examples.
Later literature,
like streams proliferating into great rivers,
if not separated into divisions and collected separately,
then the records would pile up to the roof,
and become immeasurable.
Liú Zhījǐ of the Táng Dynasty once worried that historical biographies contained too many textual records,
and wished to take the imperial edicts of the court,
and the memorials and petitions of the officials,
imitating the specialized principles of tables and treatises (Biǎo and Zhì),
to create a separate style.
Although classifying them within the chronological records and biographies
was a commendable intention.
However, since the chronological records and biographies cannot entirely omit literary writings,
and if literary writings were specially compiled into the histories,
it is also feared that the bulk would be too vast to finish.
This is why later generations maintained the theory,
but ultimately were unable to implement it.
Now, the writings of historians
have very broad principles and structures;
the forms of the *Shī* and the *Shū*
differ from the *Chūnqiū*.
Such as the twelve sections of the *Guóyǔ*,
and the fifteen sections of the *Guófēng*.
What are called canonical instructions and folk ballads
each have their proper place.
Therefore, the Grand Master presented poetry (shī),
and the External Scribe (Wàishǐ) also managed the records (zhì) of the four directions;
I have not heard that preparation relies solely on one type of text.
Following Kǒng Guǎn's *Wényuàn* and Xiāo Tǒng's *Wénxuǎn*,
the Táng dynasty had the *Wéncuì*,
and the Sòng dynasty had the *Wénjiàn*.
All of these compiled selected writings across the eras,
broadly gathering various forms.
However, their intent in establishing the general principles
still did not escape the habits of talented scholars discussing literature,
nor the style of examination-essay students filling templates.
Regarding historical matters,
they were not very relevant.
As for the *Wénlèi* compiled by people of the Yuán dynasty,
after the practice persisted, they gradually realized its flaws;
therefore, when compiling the literary compositions,
they always preserved the historical meaning,
and the preface and structure already clearly stated this.
Nevertheless, the categories were not yet clearly distinguished,
and regarding the origins and development of literature,
little discussion or ordering was provided.
Furthermore, the ancients said:
"To recite his poetry,
to read his books,
but not know the person, is that acceptable?"
The major events of the author's life,
as well as the titles of the books they wrote,
seem appropriate to be retained according to Lǐ Shàn's commentary style in the *Wénxuǎn*,
and slightly supplemented with evidence and explanation.
As for presenting suggestions and making arguments,
often the literary brilliance is outstanding,
inspiring readers,
but at the end of the piece, one wrings one's wrists,
not knowing the full details of the original event.
This is perhaps like dreaming of an ancient person and suddenly waking up,
or listening to a marvelous tune that does not finish.
It inevitably makes one feel deeply unsatisfied.
All cases like this
show that they have more than enough literary discussion,
but insufficient historical verification.
Future scholars who study history
must deliberate carefully on this matter.
As for the selection of writings in various regions and provinces (fāng zhōu),
the doctrines of *Guóyǔ* and *Guófēng* are far removed.
Like the recent collections such as *Zhōngzhōu* and *Héfén*,
and the various pieces from *Liángyuán* and *Jīnlíng*,
all manage to delineate boundaries when discussing literature,
and slightly convey the intention of historical compilation.
This too is acceptable.
But how is it that those who compile gazetteers (zhì jiā) and order literary and artistic works,
not understanding the structure of various historical writings,
instead use poems, lyrics, songs, rhymed prose (fù), records (jì), biographies (zhuàn), and miscellaneous essays,
entirely imitating the structure of selected anthologies,
and list them within the gazetteers and records?
This can be called ignorance of proper classification.
Therefore, utilizing the leisure time while editing the gazetteer,
I collected various styles,
roughly drafting a structure and regulation,
approximately grouping them by category,
to narrate and record their differences and development,
so that those who follow this endeavor
may thereby enhance its brilliance.
Memorials (Zòuyì) – First Category
For a collection of writings (Wénzhēng) to begin with Memorials (zòuyì)
is like a gazetteer beginning with the Imperial Annals (jì).
Since Xiāo Tǒng selected writings,
he took the rhymed prose (fù) as the crown of the book.
If discussing chronology, Bān Gù comes after Qū Yuán;
if discussing literary form, the *fù* is merely a branching development of the *shī* (poetry).
How can this principle and structure
be treated as canonical and essential?
Yet later scholars who selected literature
revered it as an ancestor never to be superseded for a hundred generations.
This is truly strange.
Now I take Memorials (zòuyì) to head the list,
and attach official government documents (wényí) to them.
Memorials are analogous to the Imperial Annals (jì),
and official documents are analogous to the Summaries of Government (zhènglüè);
they are all repositories of historical institutions.
Documentary Records (Zhēngshù) – Second Category
Documentary Records (zhēngshù)
include the forms of records (jì), biographies (zhuàn), prefaces, narratives, inscriptions (zhìzhuàng), and stele inscriptions (bēimíng).
Their texts, alongside the official biographies (lièzhuàn) and collected writings (túshū),
serve as reciprocal details and summaries.
This is because historical scholarship became dispersed and texts were not monopolized by specialists;
within the individual collections of literary figures,
works preserved from correspondence and social interaction
often include various forms of records (jì) and biographies (zhuàn),
which can supplement historical matters.
At the time Xiāo Tǒng selected his writings,
this was not yet common.
In later literary collections that incorporate historical forms,
those compiling histories and biographies often draw upon them.
Thus, the texts of Documentary Records (zhēngshù)
are truly invaluable.
Treatises and Writings (Lùnzhù) – Third Category
Treatises and Writings (lùnzhù)
are the lingering tradition of the Hundred Schools of Thought (zhūzǐ),
whereby people in antiquity established words (lìyán) to achieve immortality;
their origin lies here.
Liú Xié stated that the naming of the *lùn* (discussion/treatise)
began with the *Lúnyǔ* (Analects);
his statement is correct.
Master Cháo's *Dúshū Zhì*
cites "discussing the Way and managing the state (lùn dào jīng bāng),"
which comes from the *Shàngshū* (Book of Documents),
and therefore criticizes Master Liú's oversight.
However, the *Zhōuguān* chapter comes from the forged ancient text;
Master Cháo did not investigate this,
which is also his confusion.
When the style of the Hundred Schools of Thought declined,
literary scholars' collections then included various forms like treatises (lùnshuō) and expositions (biànjiě).
As for categories like letters (shū dú) and colophons (tíbá),
these establish arguments based on specific events,
and are also branches of Treatises and Writings (lùnzhù).
Poetry and Rhymed Prose (Shīfù) – Fourth Category
Poetry and Rhymed Prose (shīfù)
are the legacy of the Six Principles.
The genre of the *Guófēng*
is actually close to the collected writings (wénzhēng) of the prefectures and counties.
Regarding the *Gānquán* and *Shànglín* [fù],
Bān Gù recorded them in the Biographies (Lièzhuàn);
this was permissible given the practices of that time.
In later generations, literature flourished,
and it should certainly be organized into a separate specialized book.
However, the tradition of poets and writers of *fù*,
up until recent times,
has become immersed in flowery diction,
failing to grasp the intention of the ancient National Historians when they presented the *Shī* (Poetry);
they foolishly argue over the skill or clumsiness of the wording,
and cannot discuss the principles of a collected literary history (wénzhēng).
Here I take the *fù* and poems of previous generations,
and arrange them sequentially,
to preserve the legacy of *Fēng* and *Yǎ* (traditional poetry styles).
Those of the present generation
are generally relegated to an appendix,
to await subsequent discerning selection.
Table of Contents: *Wénshǐ Tōngyì*
◀ Previous Chapter | Chapter 7 | Next Chapter ▶
Preface and Structure for the Imperial Annals Section of the *Yǒngqīng Xiàn Zhì*
The inclusion of Annals (jì) in history
originated with the Twelve Monthly Annals (Shí'èr Yuè Jì) in the *Lǚ Shì Chūnqiū*.
Sīmǎ Qiān used this structure to record the deeds of emperors and kings,
crowning his 130 chapters;
this was likely the old method derived from the *Chūnqiū*.
Thereafter, the Twenty-one [Dynastic] Histories
successively inherited and followed this tradition.
The style was solemn and the precedents were strict,
like legal statutes.
However, the gazetteers of the regions and provinces
are mostly confused by the structure of geographical encyclopedias,
and are not known to follow this principle.
This is like shaking a robe but not knowing how to lift the collar,
or listing details but being unable to grasp the main thread.
It is therefore predictable that they are sprawling and disorganized,
and lose the meaning inherent in the essential selection principles of national history.
In antiquity, during the feudal age,
the various states had their own historical writings.
However, the first month of the year necessarily referred to the King of Zhōu,
and the history of Lǔ must refer to the Zhōu statutes (Hán Xuānzǐ, having seen the *Yì Xiàng* and the *Chūnqiū*, believed that the *Zhōu Lǐ* was entirely contained in Lǔ. This is it.).
This demonstrates the origin of showing subordinate adherence [to the central authority].
In later generations, the prefectures and counties,
even if situated ten thousand *lǐ* away,
should follow the ancient system of the royal domain (jīdiàn).
Yet when they divide the sections and categorize the classes,
they entirely lack rules and formal structure.
How can this accord with the meaning of the External Scribe (Wàishǐ) in the *Zhōuguān*?

The External Scribe (Wàishǐ) in the *Zhōuguān* manages the records of the four directions (He manages the communication of book titles to the four directions. This shows that the texts of the various states could not be compiled arbitrarily, but had to adhere to the established standard of the External Scribe.). This shows that the various writers of gazetteers,
are at fault for not understanding historical scholarship.
The twelve monthly ordinances of Lǚ Shì,
were merely titled Jì (Chronicles);
but later figures like Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù
referred to them as Běnjì (Basic Annals).
Examining the meaning behind the term Běn (Basic):
Sīmǎ Qiān intended to follow the method of the Chūnqiū;
considering that the specialists of Zuǒ Shì, Gōng, and Gǔ
while Qiān's work was a book by a single person,
who also authored treatises (shū), tables (biǎo), and collected biographies (lièzhuàn) to serve as the supporting warp (wěi),
thus he added běn to jì,
making it clear that his Jì served as the main thread (jīng). His established name followed the old appellation of the Shìběn.
Bān Gù failed to grasp this intention,
and consequently titled the ten treatises (zhì) as Běnzhì (Basic Treatises) as well.
If that is the case, the reason the tables and biographies were not given the běn appellation
is specifically because the tables were called Niánbiǎo (Annual Tables),
the biographies were called Lièzhuàn (Collected Biographies),
and these, along with Běnjì, were all established using two characters.
Since Zhì was merely a single name,
he forcefully matched its character count,

unaware that this harmed the meaning of the main thread (jīng) and supporting warp (wěi) structure of chronicles and biographies. (It was common in antiquity to match single and double characters, such as Fāng in Qī Lüè being called Jīngfāng, and Lùn in Huáinánzǐ being called Shūlùn, and so on. This was only permissible if it did not harm the meaning of the text.)
As for the rule that method should arise from meaning (yì qǐ),
when compiling the chronicles (jì) for a local gazetteer (fāngzhì),
and treating it as the main thread (jīng) of the book,
that is appropriate.
If one also follows the historians (shǐ) and calls it Běnjì,
then the name and reality become confused,
which is not the way to uphold the solemnity and dignity of the national history.
Furthermore, consider the poems and essays written by literati in later generations
that concern the actions of contemporary sovereigns (jūnjūn).
Although the text itself is not in the chronicle (jì) format,
it is also called Gōngjì (Respectful Record) to express reverence,
which fundamentally causes no harm to the meaning.
If it were called Běnjì,
there would be no rationale for it.
Therefore, what the local gazetteer calls Jì,
compared to the tables and biographies (biǎo zhuàn) within the same book,
is the lighter form (tǐ);
but when compared to the Běnjì of the national histories,
it becomes the supporting warp (wěi).
This is why it is called Jì and must not be called Běn.
Following Qiān and Gù,
although the Běnjì imitated the Chūnqiū,
because they included edicts (zhào gào) and commands (hào lìng),
they also mixed in the style of the Shàngshū.
It was not until Ōuyáng Xiū compiled the Xīn Tángshū
that he began to use the method of ‘grand writing’ (dà shū zhī fǎ),
exercising strict and careful editing.
He thus surpassed Qiān and Gù;
this can indeed be called excelling at following the Chūnqiū as a model.
As for the compilation of chronicles (jì) in local gazetteers (fāngzhì),
the purpose is to supplement omissions in the unofficial histories (wài shǐ)
and to preserve the respectful accounts (zhī fèng) of a locality.
This is what is meant by following the central courtyard and porch to measure the sun's illumination,
or occupying the window slit to peer through the penetrating light of heaven.
The goal is careful collection and detailed recording,
without having to borrow from the principles of event recording used in the Chūnqiū.
Therefore, imperial pronouncements (huáng yán) are respectfully copied and recorded,
and placed at the beginning of the volume.
These mutually serve as the main thread and supporting warp
alongside the principles of the historiographers,
and one should not rigidly adhere to a single rule to constrain them.
"Great are the words of the King (wáng yán),"
originates in the Shàngshū;
"The King's words are like silk,"
originates in the Lǐjì.
This is because the Son of Heaven during the Three Dynasties was called Wáng (King),
and thus the Son of Heaven’s words were called Wáng Yán.
Later generations continued to use Wáng Yán,
treating it as an historical allusion.
However, they fail to realize that after the Three Dynasties,
Wáng was also a title for a minister;
to still refer to the Son of Heaven’s edicts and announcements as Wáng Yán
is to be bound by adherence to antiquity,
and fails to keep pace with the times.
Now, in the texts of the Shàngshū,
ministers and sons referred to themselves as Zhèn (I, the Sovereign),
and their pronouncements could also be called Gào (Announcement).
Since the honored appellations of later generations
have been uniformly established,
the terminology must surely match the reality of the name.
How can one rigidly adhere to ancient examples
and fail to change them?
Therefore, we change the old term Wáng Yán,
and use the majestic appellation Huáng Yán (Imperial Pronouncements),
hoping that the facts follow their substance
and the name and reality are not confused.
The songs praising Heaven (chì tiān zhī gē)
are recorded in the Módian (Book of Documents);
while the basic annals of later historians
only record edicts and announcements (zhào gào).
This is because poetry and songs express sentiments,
while edicts and announcements apply to governmental affairs.
Therefore, what the History Section (shǐ bù) collects
each has its proper place.
As for the structure of the local gazetteer (fāngzhì),
the meaning lies in revering the exalted subject,
and it is not proper according to precedent to make arbitrary selections.
The Jīfǔ Tōngzhì compiled by the former Governor-General Lǐ Wèi
began by listing the two categories of Zhàoyù (Edicts and Instructions) and Chénzhāng (Imperial Compositions),
which is comparatively fitting in terms of meaning.
As for the county of Yǒngqīng,
it is close to the southern capital region (Jīnán),
and naturally received no specific edicts or instructions.
If these concern the various prefectures and counties collectively,
or cover the entire Zhílì province,
then they ought to be recorded in the Tōngzhì (General Gazetteer),
and it is not permissible, simply because Yǒngqīng is included within that area,
to misleadingly record them in this book.
If there were acts of imperial grace such as tax remissions (ēncì juān bū) or famine relief (zhèn xù),
those facts are respectfully entered into the Chronicle of Imperial Grace (Ēnzé zhī Jì).
Since the scope of edicts and instructions is broad,
we dared not cross boundaries and record them here.
However, extended acts of imperial grace (tán ēn kǎi zé),
such as commendations and posthumous enfeoffments (bāo zèng yí fēng),
are certainly the glory of a family’s lineage records
and the coronet of the county records.
Therefore, they have been compiled and recorded here.
The Imperial Poems (Yùzhì Shīzhāng)
only contain one piece, the "Bīngjiào" (Icehouse),
and since it cannot be placed in a separate fascicle,
it is respectfully recorded after the edicts and instructions,
to mark the brilliance of the Heavenly River.
Preface to the Principles of the Chronicle of Imperial Grace in the Yǒngqīng County Gazetteer
In antiquity, the Left Historian (Zuǒ Shǐ) recorded words,
and the Right Historian (Yòu Shǐ) recorded events.
Zhū Zǐ (Zhu Xi) believed that words belonged to the category of the Shàngshū,
and events belonged to the category of the Chūnqiū;
this interpretation seems plausible.
However, the system of the Shàngshū
does not entirely record words;
and the method of recording events
is also not entirely confined to the formula "In the King’s First Month of Spring."
The methods of the five historians (wǔ shǐ) in the Zhōu Guān
are detailed and comprehensive;
yet, the books of records and notes
from later generations cannot be fully detailed.
Apart from the Shū and the Chūnqiū,
those available for reference
are only the Jízhǒng Zhōu Shū, which resembles the Shàngshū,
and the Zhúshū Jìnián, which resembles the Chūnqiū.
Nevertheless, the Mù Tiānzǐ Zhuàn
uniquely approximates the notes of the imperial daily life (Qǐjū zhī Zhù).
Although that book may not be entirely trustworthy,
it is also evidence of the ancient method of recording,
where the main threads (jīng), supporting warps (wěi), exterior (biǎo), and interior (lǐ)
each had their focus.
It was not strictly limited to the two forms of the Shàngshū and the Chūnqiū,
and asserting that the methodology was perfected there
can also be understood.
After the Three Dynasties,
on a small scale, there were court historians,
such as the Hàn Wǔ Jìn Zhōng Qǐjū Zhù
and the Mǎ Hòu Xiǎnzōng Qǐjū Zhù;
these are examples.
On a large scale, there were records of contemporary governance,
such as the Táng Zhēnguān Zhèngyào
and the Zhōu Xiǎndé Rìlì;
these are examples.
Timely records include
the successive dynastic Qǐjū Zhù (Records of Imperial Daily Life);
these are examples.
Comprehensive compilations include
the Veritable Records (Shílù) since Liáng Tàiqīng;
these are examples.
The virtue of the sovereign is like Heaven;
measurements of gnomon shadows and planetary movements,
calculations using jade armillary spheres and standard measuring rods,
and comprehensive systems of law
must be instituted so that nothing is overlooked.
Therefore, the established canons (lì diǎn) in the Zhōu Guān
must be thoroughly understood in their meaning,
and the Lǐjì’s mention of the duties of the Left Historian and Right Historian
shows that neither can truly be dispensed with.
The Annals (Jì) and the Biographies (Zhuàn),
were used by the ancients to differentiate the warp and the weft (main narrative vs. detailed accounts),
and were originally not used to distinguish between high and low status.
This is why Sīmǎ Qiān’s *Shǐ Jì* contains Annals (Jì) that lack specific years,
a point which Liú Zǐxuán first raised as criticism.
Bān Gù, in the self-preface to his *Hàn Shū*,
referred to the Twelve Annals (Shí'èr Jì) as "Annals for Examination in the style of the *Chūn Qiū*" (*Chūn Qiū Kǎo Jì*).
His intention is thus ascertainable.
However, since Bān Gù and Sīmǎ Qiān,
successive historians [in their arranged histories] have followed suit,
all treating the Annals (Jì) as an honorific title,
while Biographies (Zhuàn) are exclusively designated for ministers and subjects.
If this is the case, there is no way to explain the inclusion of the *Mù Tiānzǐ Zhuàn*
and the Biographies of Gāo Zǔ and Xiào Wén (who were emperors).
Now let us discuss the drawback of emperors in the arranged histories having Annals but no Biographies.
The actions of the sovereign,
are not detailed as thoroughly as those of their ministers.
The beginning of the chapter describes the spiritual omens,
and the end of the chapter summarizes the general outline of their reign.
The rest follows the chronological order of years and months,
recording only governmental affairs,
serving as the framework for treatises (Zhì) and biographies (Zhuàn).
Because the literary format cannot further accommodate other matters,
this is due to the structure of the warp and the weft (Jīng and Wěi),
which naturally cannot be combined.
If we truly judge based on the main objective of the *Chūn Qiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals),
then the Basic Annals (Běn Jì) should only include the accession in the first year,
up to the major principles and laws,
which is sufficient to serve as the subject headings.
In terms of principle, this is satisfactory.
The actions of the sovereign,
should be supplemented by the biographical format (Zhuàn tǐ),
detailing their life story,
and placed foremost, above the collective biographies of Empresses and Consorts (Hòufēi Lièzhuàn).
This is also evidenced by the *Zuǒ Shì Zhuàn*,
where the few phrases concerning [Lu] Huì Gōng's principal consort,
which precede the events in the Classic (Jīng),
immediately belong to the biographical text under the heading of [Lu] Yǐn Gōng.
They can be mutually authenticated.
However, the differentiation between Annals (Jì) and Biographies (Zhuàn) as high and low status
has long been established;
treating the sovereign and the ministers identically
is not sound in principle.
Therefore, it would be best that upon the conclusion of one emperor's Annals (Jì),
that emperor’s Biography (Zhuàn) immediately follows his Annals.
Similar to the example of Zhèng Shì's commentary on the *Yì* (Classic of Change), where the *Xiàng Zhuàn* and the *Tuàn Cí*
are appended after the main hexagram,
and moreover, the name is elevated to *Dà Zhuàn* (Grand Biography/Commentary),
without being mixed with the regular collective biographies (Liè Zhuàn).
In that way, the name and the substance correspond,
and it seems to be one reasonable path of compromise.
As for the records in local gazetteers (Fāng Zhì),
they separate matters and events,
and are uniformly named Jì (Annals/Records).
This is presumably done to prepare for the rectification by external historians (Wài Shǐ),
and it originally did not follow the established rules of the *Chūn Qiū*.
For this reason, changes should not be debated.
Preface to the Table of Officials in the Yǒngqīng Xiàn Gazetteer
Official posts and examinations (elections),
when included in local gazetteers,
are all in the format of Tables (Biǎo tǐ).
But those who compile local gazetteers today
say that histories contain treatises (Zhì) on the Hundred Officials (*Bǎi Guān Zhì*) and on Elections (*Xuǎnjǔ Zhì*),
and they take imitation of the ancients as their example,
establishing grand titles,
and compiling them all as treatises (Zhì).
This is pedantic, generalized, and inappropriate.
Now, for the text of standard treatises (Zhì),
the Treatise on Official Posts details their systems,
and the Treatise on Elections clarifies their regulations.
This text might emulate the classic format (Jīng) of the *Zhōu Guān* (Rites of Zhōu),
or mix the styles of annals and biographies.
Compiling these as treatises (Zhì),
is this not appropriate?
As for what is written in local gazetteers,
it merely involves the dates of officials served [in sequence],
and the years of the examinations (Jiǎ Gēng),
where years are the warp (Jīng) and events are the weft (Wěi),
sufficiently clear and distinct,
allowing for investigation and search,
and verification according to the structure.
For practical purposes, this is enough.
But the current format for compiling these treatises
categorizes and groups officials such as the Zhīxiàn (Magistrate), Diǎnshǐ (Sub-Prefectural Clerk), Jiàoyù (Instructor), and Xùndǎo (Assistant Instructor).
This consequently causes a Qiánlóng Magistrate
to be placed before a Shùnzhì Sub-Prefectural Clerk,
and a Kāngxī Assistant Instructor
to be sequenced after a Yōngzhèng Instructor.
If there is a need to check the temporal sequence of events,
and reference is required,
or if one wishes to verify the years
when colleagues served together;
this method forces people to repeatedly search,
making it difficult to find the conclusion,
pointlessly taking up space,
without knowing what should be cut.
I do not understand why people are fond of creating such trouble for themselves!
Now, the compilation of Collective Biographies (Lièzhuàn)
is the grand scheme of the historical sections.
But for the records compiled in local gazetteers,
I have not heard that they must follow this pattern.
As for official posts and elections,
they are fundamentally the same despite differing names.
To skillfully force their attachment [to the biographical format],
is like the pacing steps used at the iron foundry in Yǒngzhōu (Yǒngzhōu Tiělú),
which has caused lamentation throughout the ages.
The Imperial Secretary (Yùshǐ) in the *Zhōu Guān*
was in charge of recording the succession of officials,
and Zhèng Shì's commentary states that this means "listing their present official positions."
Thus, a book recording official titles and names
must have existed in antiquity.
For the three hundred and sixty official departments,
to be recorded based on their succession and numbers,
I suspect there must have also been a method for this.
The general rules concerning the warp and weft of the Zhōu Chronology (Zhōu Pǔ)

were probably not used entirely for the branch of astronomical calculation. (Liú Xiàng combined chronologies (Pǔ) and calendars (Lì) into one branch, categorized under numerology (Shù Shù). But Sīmǎ Qiān's reference to the Zhōu Pǔ indicates it was not a book of numerology. I suspect that the ancients frequently used the chronological chart format (Pǔ tǐ) for methods of accumulation and calculation.)
Bān Gù’s *Bǎi Guān Gōng Qīng Biǎo* (Table of the Hundred Officials and High Ministers)
has a structural outline that is entirely in the style of a treatise (Zhì tǐ),
yet it is not named a Treatise (Zhì).
This shows that records of successive officials require the method of chronological tables (Pǔ fǎ).
Taking the structure of the *Zhōu Guān* as the warp (Jīng),
and the method of the Hàn Tables (Hàn Biǎo) as the weft (Wěi),
the legislative approach of the ancients
was extensive and yet not loose—
this can be generally observed.
time of Dōngjīng
(the Eastern Capital), there have only been records of official positions (zhígūan zhì).
However, the histories of the Táng and Sòng dynasties
include tables of Chief Ministers (zǎifǔ biǎo).
This also implies that the hundred posts held by high officials (qīngyǐn) are too numerous to include completely.
As for specialized books,
records of official regulations (guānyí bùzhuàng),
since the Hàn dynasties,
have been compiled in every age.
But using tables organized by year (biānnián)
only became frequent in the Sòng era;
examples include Sīmǎ Guāng’s *Bǎiguān Gōngqīng Biǎo* in 150 *juàn*. Records of successive officials and their terms (jìshù) are also seen,
but they are often neglected due to their plain style and are thus easily lost.
Regarding the records of provinces and prefectures (fāngzhōu),
the inscriptions (tímíng) on the hall walls during the Táng and Sòng
were buried over time.
The ancient system of illustrated records (*tújīng*)
no longer compiles officials by category.
Is this not a serious omission?
Since the Yuán and Míng dynasties,
the gazetteers of prefectures and counties (zhōuxiàn zhìshū)
often preserve records of successive office holders (lìrèn),
but because the methods of recording are flawed,
it easily leads to confusion.
This is something that must not be left uncorrected.
Some say that creating tables of officials (zhígūan lièbiǎo)
should only be applied to the highest ministers (sāngōng zǎifǔ)
and to local gazetteers (fāngzhì) of prefectures and counties.
In the former case, the status is revered and the rules are strict;
in the latter, the number of officials is small and easily summarized.
As for the gazetteers of major departments (bù) and prefectures (fǔ),
the official posts are numerous,
and a single sheet of paper (chǐfú) is difficult to complete.
If all are presented in tables,

one fears that the warp (jīng) will be simple but the woof (wěi) will be difficult. (The text notes: The upper rows of months and years form the warp, the first row of official ranks forms the woof. When officials are numerous, there is no space left in the grid.)
If the method is not established precisely,
and people merely argue about the difficulty of summarizing the records,
this is why, after Mǎ [Qiān] and Bān [Gù],
histories became voluminous but events were incomplete.
The table of *Bǎiguān* (Hundred Officials) in the Bān history (*Bān Shǐ*)
is not excessively large,
yet the records detail even the Nine Ministers (jiǔqīng).
The tables of Chief Ministers (zǎifǔ) during the Táng and Sòng
are many times larger,
yet the records are limited to the counselors and assistants (chéngbì).
It is not that ancient texts were simple
while later histories were methodologically complex.
Rather, because the method Bān used—grouping and appending by category—
was not practiced when organizing years as warp (jīng) and events as woof (wěi),
it is understandable that they vacillated and lost solid footing,
making it difficult to grasp the essentials and manage the complexity.
Looking at the Bān history,
the table lists 34 officials,
and the grid only has 14 ranks (jí).
Sometimes due to evolution and change,
the chief officials are noted in the first section, such as Xiàngguó, Chéngxiàng, Fèngcháng, Tàicháng, and similar titles.
Sometimes due to related official duties,
they occupy the same space in the grid;
for example, Dàxíng Lìng and Dàhónglú share a space, and Zuǒ Fénɡyì and Jīngzhào Yǐn share a space. The space is simplified and easy to manage,
the categories of events follow clearly,
hence allowing readers,
by examining the records, to avoid omissions.
If we were to create comprehensive departmental tables,
then officials belonging to the rank of Dūfǔ, Tízhèn,
would be combined into one cell (gé).
Officials belonging to the rank of Bùàn, Xúnshǒu,
would be combined into one cell.
The rest can be categorized by prefecture (fǔ) and department (zhōu),
and the officials belonging to the prefecture
can be grouped within the same cell.
There is certainly no harm in this.
When compiling the gazetteers of prefectures (fǔ) and departments (zhōu),
if each department and county occupies one cell,
omissions can still be avoided.
Therefore, there is absolutely no lack of applicable methods
for creating tables of successive officials.
Moreover, in a county gazetteer, couldn't each official position naturally occupy its own cell?
Below the name,
their native place (xiāngguàn) and examination success (kējiǎ) should be noted.
This is because these individuals are not fully recorded in the administrative narrative (zhènglüè).
Noting their beginning and end [of tenure]
also helps reduce the need for biographies.
Those without such details should be left blank.
As for records derived from bronze and stone inscriptions (jīnshí jìzǎi),
if other sources provide evidence
and are included in the gazetteer,
then the date derived from the inscription should be used as the heading.
We will no longer elaborate on the year they first entered office
or the month they left the post,
as this is simply necessitated by circumstances.
As for those whose years and months cannot be verified but whose names are known,
they should be placed at the end of the chronological (jīngwěi) table,
listed horizontally to preserve their entry.
This is an approach of reserving judgment and awaiting later clarification.
Preface and Rules for the Examination Candidates Table in the *Yǒngqīng Xiàn Zhì* (Yǒngqīng County Gazetteer)
The table of successful examination candidates (xuǎnjǔ)
is the remnant of the ancient custom of compiling lists of worthies (xiánshū).
In antiquity, candidates were selected
without establishing specialized departments.
Worthies were promoted to leadership,
and the capable were appointed to administer.
Talent that was recommended was immediately seen in use,
and the utilization of personnel was immediately reflected in affairs.
The Xiánliáng, Xiào, and Xiù candidates of the Hàn dynasties,
along with those appointed by prefectures and counties (zhōujùn císhǔ),
had their deeds recorded in the annals and biographies (jìzhuàn).
There was no need to seek out specialized books on selection and examination (xuǎnjǔ).
Since the Suí and Táng dynasties,
the examination system became specialized,
and qualifications became increasingly important.
Regulations and rules proliferated,
precedents were handed down,
and books on selection and examination (xuǎnjǔ)
piled up, filling the rafters.
Thus, those recommended were not necessarily all employed,
and those employed were not necessarily all reflected in records of events.
Old regulations and established precedents
could no longer be sought within the annals and biographies (jìzhuàn);
instead, the writings on selection and examination (xuǎnjǔ)
became a specialized section in histories and gazetteers.
Those who compile gazetteers (zhìjiā), when recording successful candidates,
do not understand the method of making years the warp (jīng) and events the woof (wěi).
They habitually divide candidates into categories such as Jìnshì, Jǔrén, Gòngshēng, and military selections (wǔxuǎn),
each forming a separate section.
They also place the Jìnshì first,
and list the Jǔrén and Gòngshēng subsequently.
Consequently, for one individual who progressed from Gòngshēng to Jǔrén and finally became a Jìnshì,
one first sees the year of their Jìnshì examination,
then searches for the time of their provincial examination (xiāngjǔ),
and only at the end of the section does one finally find the year they became a Gòngshēng.
This is a reversal of the chronological order of events,
and doesn't the text become needlessly repetitive?
Occasionally, there are those who use the chronological (jīngwěi) method to create tables,
but they also include factual notes
in the side columns and diagonal spaces.
Using the style of biographies (lièzhuàn) to create chronological tables (niánbiǎo)
is the flawed method employed by the Yuán compilers of the *Liáo* and *Jīn Shǐ*.
It wastes column space
and also obscures the main points.
I do not understand what benefit they derived from this.
A table in a historical work
serves as an index for the biographies (lièzhuàn).
If a name is listed in the table,
but no biography exists for that person,
it is because they have no virtue worth praising,
and their events are recorded briefly.
If a biography is written but the name does not appear in the table,
it is because the event is worth recording,
and a special writing format (tèshū) is used.
Nowadays, compilers of gazetteers,
beneath the sections for successful candidates (xuǎnjǔ) and officials (zhígūan),
often intersperse one or two facts.
As for the major points of a person’s life,
they use a broad summary
and place it in the section on notable figures and officials (rénwù mínghuàn).
Then, they take the complete text of the biography or inscription
and place it within the literature section (yìwén).
Here, it states, "See Section X for details,"
and there, it states, "Already listed in Item Y."
The affairs of one person
are thus repeated multiple times.
And those who are capable of creating tables
still cannot avoid adding notes beneath the names in the table
stating that a biography exists.
How extremely disruptive and imprecise this is!
Among tables, some can be structured chronologically (jīngwěi),
and some cannot.
For example, the annual tribute students (suìgòng) of Yǒngqīng
before Jiājìng,
numbering seventy-seven individuals whose years cannot be verified.
To include them leaves them nowhere suitable in the grid,
but to delete them is ethically unsatisfactory.
Therefore, their names should be listed before the Jiājìng examination candidates,
and placed after the Zhèngdé examination candidates.
This follows the principle of the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals) listing residual items at the end,
and the *Yì* (Book of Changes) concluding the hexagrams with *Wèijì* (Before Completion).
Shǐ Qiān’s *Sāndài Shì Biǎo* (Table of the Lineages of the Three Dynasties),
starting from Xià Xiè onwards,
lacked verifiable chronology (jīngwěi).
Thus, he simply listed them sequentially without adhering to the longitudinal and horizontal table structure.
This is also an ancient method that remains applicable.
Preface and Rules for the Gentry Table in the *Yǒngqīng Xiàn Zhì* (Yǒngqīng County Gazetteer)
(tǔzú)
generally derives from ancient methods,
and is not the creation of a new precedent.
The *Xiǎoshǐ*
(Minor Scribe) section of the *Zhōuguān*
states: "Establish the lineage generations
and distinguish the *zhāomù*
(senior and junior lines)." Dù Zǐchūn's
commentary says: "Lineage generations (xìshì)
are similar to the lineage records (xìběn) of the Zhūhóu, Qīng, and Dàfū." This
is correct. The *Shū*
(Classic of History) says:
"Clarify and illuminate the hundred surnames
(bǎixìng)." Zhèng Kāngchéng
said: "The hundred surnames refer to the fathers, sons, and brothers of the officials."
To clarify and illuminate (píngzhāng) means to distinguish and make them manifest.
The former kings granted land and divided surnames
(fēnxìng);
the reason for honoring the human order and clarifying the moral hierarchy (lúnxù)
is universally derived from this.
Therefore, if one wishes to harmonize the myriad states
(wànbāng), one must first clarify and illuminate the hundred surnames.
This statute is critically important.
The gentry (shì) are also the people (mín).
To detail the gentry clans (shìzú)
while briefly mentioning the common surnames
(mínxìng) is also following the ancient way.
The *Xiāng Dàfū*
(District Grand Master) section of the *Zhōuguān* states:
"At the seasonal occasions, register the size of the households (fūjiā)."
Every three years, using the Great Comparison (dàbǐ), promote the worthy and capable individuals of a district.
The common people (mín) were humble while the gentry (shì) were esteemed.
Therefore, the number of large and small households
was merely registered;
but for the worthy and capable ones who became Qīng Dàfū,
their lineage records (shìxì zhī dié) were detailed.
Thus, the lineage records
were considered more important than the household registration books,
which is clearly evident.
In recent times, the local gazetteers
invariably detail the household registration,
but the documentation of lineages
is completely unheard of,
which is a failure to grasp the principle of relative importance.
Indeed, combining individuals forms a family,
combining families forms a state,
and combining states forms All-under-Heaven
(tiānxià). The vastness of All-under-Heaven
begins with the combination of individuals into families.
Families cannot all be enumerated,
therefore, the aristocratic clans (shìzú)
are esteemed.
If the aristocratic clans
guide the common people (Qímín),
the prefectures and counties (Zhōuxiàn) lead the aristocratic clans,
the administrative offices (Sīfǔ) lead the prefectures and counties,
and the ministries and courts (Bùyuàn) lead the administrative offices,
then one manages the complex by grasping the simple,
and All-under-Heaven can be wielded in the palm of one’s hand.
Mèngzǐ
said:
"What is meant by an old state
(gùguó) is not having tall trees,
but having hereditary ministers (shìchén)."
If the records of the prefectures and counties
can categorize and sequence the aristocratic clans,
and thereby transmit this information up to the Sīfǔ
and Bùyuàn,
then the moral hierarchy (lúnxù) will be interconnected,
and the order and transformation (zhìhuà) will have a structure to belong to.
Nowadays, those who compile gazetteers
often dwell upon ancient ruins
and attach importance to native places (sāngzǐ),
but the compilation of genealogical records (pǔdié)
is conspicuously lacking.
This is precisely what is meant by esteeming tall trees but slighting hereditary families (shìjiā).
If genealogical records are managed by the government,
then affairs will have a central coordination,
people will have registered status,
and the general state of All-under-Heaven
can be harmonized and stabilized.
Currently, south of the great river
(Dàjiāng),
cultural attainments are considered flourishing,
but customs may lean toward superficiality.
The genealogical records of private families
often falsely connect themselves to famous worthies
and exaggerate their virtues and achievements;
their error lies in deceit.
North of the great river
(Dàhé),
the customs are simple and rustic,
and the people are generally unsophisticated and uncultured.
The practice of genealogical record keeping
is lacking and incomplete.
Often, descendants do not know the names of their great-grandparents and great-great-grandparents.
What is occasionally recorded
is sparse and difficult to verify;
their error lies in crudeness.
Indeed, what place is without people?
What person is without ancestors?
Yet, the biased deceit and biased crudeness,
leading to such severe malpractice,
occurs because genealogical records are not managed by the government
and historical authority lacks centralization.
Some may say that the ancients valued hereditary families,
but later this practice developed flaws
leading to the competition for status
(mén dì). After the Wèi
and Jìn Dynasties, the Wáng,
Xiè,
Cuī,
and Lú clans constantly crushed each other based on social rank.
And even among the worthy, the reputation of one's family line
did not prevent the creation of distinctions in rank.
How can this serve as a model?
This is not the case.
Regarding the selection criteria of the Ministry of Personnel
(Lìbù) and the local recommenders
(Zhōujùn Zhōngzhèng), it is correct
that they should not cling to aristocratic status
(ménfá) to determine appointments.
However, if the genealogical records
are managed by the section chiefs and clerks
(Cáoláng Lìngshǐ),
this serves precisely to prevent loss and suppress fraudulent claims,
and initially causes no harm.
Furthermore, if the clerks manage the lineages
while the Lìbù
promotes the most outstanding individuals,
then the prominent and great clans
who have no worthy individuals to be promoted to office
or no capable persons to govern
will be motivated to strive to distinguish themselves.
This is also a way to inspire worthy talent.
Shǐ Qiān's
tables of lineages (shìbiǎo)
only document the origins of the Sānwǔ
(Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors);
and the clan records (shìzú) within the *Chūnqiū*
(Spring and Autumn Annals) only preserve Dù Yù's
genealogical records (shìpǔ).
Consequently, historians have lost knowledge of clan lineages.
Ōuyáng's
*Zǎixiàng Shìxì*
(Lineages of Prime Ministers)
seems to have grasped the subtle implications of preserving history;
the *Shū Zhì* chapter of the *Shǐ Tōng*
(Generalities on History) intended to establish records of clans (shìzú zhì), but the intention was subject to deliberation, not Liú's
original aim.
Moreover, the Hán clan of Dèngzhōu,
though having no prime ministers,
was recorded in the chapter
because of Tuìzhī
(Hán Yù).
This also created a precedent that was not pure.
Wèi Shōu's
*Guān Shì*
(Official Surnames) and Zhèng Qiáo's
*Shìzú*
(Clans) only recorded the origins and flow of surnames,
and did not systematically list the branch lineages.
Thus, the historical practice of tabulating lineages
is only seen in Ōuyáng,
but later generations did not follow it as a consistent system.
Perhaps they were observing that Ōuyáng's
precedent was not pure?
I humbly believe that in covering an entire era,
the records are immensely voluminous.
What is valuable is maintaining the essentials
and having clear judgment sufficient to decide what to omit or include,
which then results in an unchangeable statute.
Lineages
need not all be strictly restricted to prime ministers (zǎixiàng).
If the prominent families (yòuzú) of a dynasty
whose reputation spanned the dynasty's beginning to end
are compiled into tables,
the resulting volumes would also not be numerous.
If the section title is simply designated "Aristocratic Clans"
(shìzú),
how could it result in an impure precedent?
Liú Xīn
said:
"Rather than erring by omission,
it is better to err by inclusion."
This refers precisely to that principle.
The official histories already maintain the essentials,
and the records of the ministries, prefectures, and counties
should gradually become more detailed.
This is what is meant by starting near to travel far,
and starting low to climb high.
The broad collection of information by the prefectures and counties

is intended to prepare the material that the official histories summarize and select from. Some might ask: Prefectures and counties vary in size, and impoverished districts may not all be able to provide complete genealogical records. However, within a single county, there are certainly gentry and common people (shì and mín). The common people can be counted by household registration, and the gentry naturally need not worry about lacking a lineage. Someone else might say: Those who hold the title of *Shēngyuán* (Government Student) or above are all called gentry (shì). In a large state renowned for its scholarship, one fears that the records would be too numerous to collect. In this case, the scope of inclusion should be determined by the prosperity or decline of the region, and stricter or looser standards applied. Perhaps use the *Jǔgòng* (Recommended Tribute Students) status as the benchmark, or use the *Jìnshì* (Presented Scholars) status as the benchmark. As for the records of the ministries and prefectures, perhaps use officials reaching the fifth rank or the third rank as the benchmark, and there would certainly be no concern about excessive bulk. The documentation of events in the gazetteers is like a mirror reflecting an image. A mirror of only an inch in diameter fully captures the form, though miniaturized. For mirrors larger than a foot, the reflected form is commensurately expanded. There is never a case where the object is so vast that the mirror has nowhere to cast its shadow. If the records of the prefectures and counties fully compile the genealogical records, then the ancestral homes of officials and candidates can be inspected and verified; lawsuits regarding disputed succession can be fairly resolved; unauthorized private family records can be checked and corrected; the errors in the government genealogical records can be verified through mutual comparison; the pure and corrupt classifications of social status can be distinguished; harmony in marriage, filial piety, and fraternal kindness can be encouraged; and all measures that aid governance and benefit the gentry and common people can have their essential outlines derived from these records.
The former kings (Xiānwáng) granted land and divided surnames,
establishing people by land,
how could they ever have established land by people?
When the feudal system (Fēngjiàn) ceased,
people no longer settled exclusively on the land.
However, concerning the eminent clans (Jùnwàng) of the Six Dynasties (Liùcháo),
if you ask about Xiè, you know they are from Yángxià;
if you ask about Cuī, you know they are from Qīnghé.
This means that households were fixed by registration,
and residential sections (fāngbiǎo dūlǐ)
were not established without purpose.
As for Méilǐ and Zhèngxiāng,
they represent the expectations based on human relations (rénlún zhī wàng),
and the towns and villages were made prominent or obscure based on the people therein.
Therefore, in the charts of clans (shìzú zhī biǎo),
the sequence is determined entirely by the village or town where they reside.
First, the center of the city (chéngzhōng),
which is the principal land governed by the county (xiàn).
Next, the East,
next, the South,
and then the West villages.
If the North region is absent, it is omitted,
recording the reality of the situation.
Inside the city, the North Street (Běijiē) precedes the South Street (Nánjiē);
the cardinal direction is North as superior and South as inferior;
the cardinal directions within the city are fixed.
The four villages (sì xiāng) prioritize Southeast before Northwest,
following the principle of the Yǔgòng which prioritizes Qīng and Yǎn,
followed by Yáng and Jīng,
and concluding with Liáng and Yōng.
However, this is not a fixed rule;
according to the topography of a specific county,
any arrangement is acceptable.
All those who are scholars (shì)
are permitted to be listed in the chart,
but those without a genealogy (pǔxì) are omitted.
Descendants who are not scholars are not included,
but elder and younger brothers, even if not scholars, are recorded,
in order to determine their generational sequence.
Those who have been adopted as heirs (wéi rén hòu zhě)
are recorded below the person they succeed,
and their birth lineage is not detailed again.
The text of the gazetteer (zhì wén) follows brevity;
the family genealogy (jiāpǔ) itself can be detailed.
Even if there are only a sparse few people,
they are also allowed into the genealogy;
if the earlier generations cannot be traced (shī kǎo),
this fact is still recorded in the chapter.
Since private records (sī shū) are easily lost,
while official genealogies (guānpǔ) are easily preserved,
we hasten to record them,
hoping that later generations may detail and confirm them.
This is what is meant by setting forth a precedent first.
Private genealogies (sī pǔ) that describe official ranks (guānjiē) and imperial honors (fēngzèng)
contain many errors.
For example, the Assistant Prefect (Tóngzhī Tōngpàn) is called Fēnfǔ,
and the Garrison Commander (Shǒubèi) is called Shǒufǔ;
these follow the designations used by common custom.
A Battalion Commander (Qiānhù) of the Brocade-Clad Guard (Jǐnyī)
is called Guāndài Jiāngjūn (General with Cap and Sash),
or Yùqián Jiāngjūn (General Before the Emperor),
or is called Jīnwú (Golden Crow),
which is extremely coarse and vulgar,
making it impossible for people to understand what office they actually held.
Now these are all being clarified and corrected.
Furthermore, many in the genealogy are designated as Shěngjì Guān (Officials for Observing Sacrifices);
it is unclear what title this is.
We keep the term now
but state that they are not included in the total count of officials.
Preface and Principles for the Map of the Territory in the Gazetteer of Yǒngqīng County (Yǒngqīng Xiàn Zhì Yúdì Tú Xùlì)
The essential principle of the History section (Shǐ Bù) is that
the Basic Annals (Běnjì) serve as the warp thread,
and the various other categories serve as the weft.
Those with textual narratives
are called Shū (Treatises)
and Zhuàn (Biographies);
those without textual narratives
are called Biǎo (Tables)
and Tú (Maps/Charts).
The abstract and the concrete complement each other,
the detailed and the brief are seen in conjunction,
thereby making it possible to avoid omissions.
Formerly, Sīmǎ Shì (Sīmǎ Qiān) established 130 chapters.
He only knew how to base his work on the genealogies of Zhōu to create Tables (Biǎo),
but he did not know how to trace back to the tripods of Xià to create Maps (Tú).
Consequently, the generational sequence, years, and months of the ancients
can be sought and investigated,
but the topography, names, and forms of former ages
cannot be traced.
This means he learned the principles of chronology and genealogy from the Chūnqiū (Spring and Autumn Annals),
but did not know how to trace the Yì Xiàng (Images of the Changes) to grasp the connection of diagrams and documents (tú shū).
The Biographies (Lièzhuàn) require Tables (Biǎo) to be orderly,
just as Treatises and Gazetteers (shū zhì) require Maps (Tú) to be clear.
Former scholars (xiānrú) once said that if the Tables are missing, the Biographies must necessarily be voluminous;
but they failed to realize that if the Maps are missing, the Treatises and Gazetteers must necessarily be verbose.
Alas!
Since Mǎ [Qiān] and Bān [Gù],
two thousand years have passed,
yet no one has established this precedent.
This is truly getting to the root and tracing the end (qióng yuán jìng wěi),
and deeply regrettable for the 130 chapters [of the Shǐjì].
Zhèng Qiáo's brief work on Maps and Genealogies (Tú Pǔ)
he claimed as his uniquely acquired scholarship;
this was merely a method for recording book titles
and organizing chapters and sections.
In reality, the grand scope of the History section
requires comprehensive collection and broad selection,
incorporating private familial scholarship (jiā xué)
to guard against loss and oblivion.
Qiáo was also unable to foresee this aspect.
Take, for instance, the Tōngzhì.
Its Annals and Biographies (Jì Zhuàn) entirely follow the ancients.
It reversed Tables into Genealogies (Pǔ),
and renamed Treatises (Zhì) as Summaries (Lüè).
Its structure can also be considered complete.
Why, then, did he only know how to collect the titles of maps and genealogies,
but fail to invent his own map structure
to supplement what the former histories lacked?
If he boasted of this, claiming that the scholars of the Hàn and Táng Dynasties could not have conceived of it,
would he not be ashamed?
Furthermore, when Qiáo recorded maps and genealogies,
he designated them by section and sequence, claiming,
"Centralized means easy preservation;
dispersed means easy loss."
This statement seems reasonable.
However, if we now check ancient maps
according to Qiáo's sectional headings,
the extent of their loss and scattering
is actually not significantly different from before.
Therefore, specialized scholarship
must be included in the grand historical compilation (shǐ shì hóng biān);
it is not the case that merely recording it in sectional catalogs
guarantees its preservation without loss.
Sīmǎ Qiān created Tables,
and the residual method of the Zhōu genealogies
survives even today.
Rèn Hóng recorded Maps,
yet the ritual system (yí zhì) of the Hàn court
could no longer be verified by the Wèi and Jìn Dynasties.
Therefore, the merit of merely recording existing works is small,
while the merit of establishing a new historical structure is great.
This principle is easy to understand.
If a history does not establish Tables,
the generational sequences, years, and months
can still be patched together from the text.
If a history does not establish Maps,
the shapes, names, and forms
certainly cannot be sought incidentally in the written words.
This is why treatment via the ear differs from treatment via the eye,
and the essential meaning of Maps
is therefore even greater than that of Tables.
Ancient scholarship passed down by word of mouth
includes things that written words cannot fully record;
it is valued because one understands it in the mind and grasps it spiritually.
As for the scholarship of diagrams and images (tú xiàng),
this also cannot be transmitted merely by word of mouth;
it is valued because one sees it with the eye, and the principle exists therein.
With the scholarship of Zhèng Kāngchéng,
if he relied on written characters to seek understanding,
then the commentary on Suō Zūn was explained as the Dance of the Phoenix.
But when the sacrificial vessel (xī) with the carved back appeared,
Wáng Sù’s interpretation prevailed.
With the scholarship of Kǒng Yǐngdá,
if he approached the text and interpreted its meaning,
the source of the river (Jiāng Yuán) was said to originate from Mínshān.
But when the route of Jīnshā was opened up,
the flow described in the Miǎnzhì was proven to be further away.
There is nothing else to this;
one case was constrained by the loss of diagrams from the Three Dynasties (Sāndài),
and the other was constrained because Bān Gù’s Dìlǐ (Geography) lacked the study of maps.
Even though there are scholars who love learning and deep contemplation,
if they read history without seeing the accompanying maps,
they cannot avoid traveling blindly and groping for information.
The records of the prefectures and commanderies during the Táng and Sòng dynasties
mostly took *Tú Jīng* (Illustrated Classics/Records) as their designation.
And comprehensive geographical maps
originated when Xiāo Hé collected the maps and registers.
As for these maps that existed in antiquity,
every generation had such books,
but specifically because they were not included in the History section (*Shǐ Bù*),
their influence could not survive alone through the ages.
Moreover, concerning their form,
they had no text that could be recited and studied,
nor could they be concisely compiled and collected;
the matters belonged to the learning of specialists,
and the work was not something literary scholars could accomplish;
if the *Shǐ Bù* did not participate in compiling and editing them,
then after two generations, they would lose their original form.
Furthermore, titles like the *Sān Fǔ Huáng Tú*
and the *Yuán Hé Tú Zhì*
now both exist as text but lack the maps.
How could this be due to events of only one day or night?
This is because in antiquity there was no woodblock printing,
making the study of maps difficult to copy and illustrate;
and the form of bamboo and silk scrolls was cumbersome,
making it difficult for every household to possess a copy.
The specialized learning of Mǎ [Qiān] and Bān [Gù]
did not establish and fix the form (of maps);
and later generations followed the stream and forgot the source.
It is therefore fitting that they collectively neglected this practice.
Explaining the classics often results in errors,
and reading history is like being lost—
all due to this reason.
Modern local gazetteers (*fāng zhì*)
often include maps,
but we do not hear of any that can serve as exemplary models.
Their defects are two:
One is that they pursue scenic views,
depicting landscapes
and excelling in the art of painting,
but this is irrelevant to historical standards.
The second is that they are relegated to the prefaces, tables of contents, and general rules,
treated as useless ornaments,
without being given names or explanatory accounts,
or having their sequence of chapters fixed.
Thus, they cannot establish an independent form.
Now, charts have coordinates but no descriptive text,
and maps have images but no coordinates.
Both are essential supplementary elements to monographs, gazetteers, and biographies;
yet common practice follows the tradition
of carelessly using them merely as devices to please the eye and ear.
If they are transmitted for a long time,
hoping that they will still retain the text, like the *Sān Fǔ Huáng Tú* or the *Yuán Hé Tú Zhì*,
is already impossible,
let alone being able to supplement what Mǎ [Qiān] and Bān [Gù] failed to achieve
and create a magnificent spectacle within the *Shǐ Bù*!
Maps generally lack coordinates (latitude and longitude),
but geographical maps should slightly retain coordinates.
Méngzǐ said:
"The implementation of benevolent governance
must begin with the fixing of boundaries (*jīng jiè*)."
The *Shì Míng* says:
"North-south lines are *jīng* (warp/meridians),
east-west lines are *wěi* (weft/parallels)."
The need for coordinates in geography has long been established.
Modern maps of prefectures and counties
often use the actual breadth and narrowness of the paper sheet
to dictate the extension or compression of the map's form;
this is the old habit of painting and drawing,
and it cannot be admitted into the universal standards of the *Shǐ Bù*.
Now, we take the measurement of squares and distances (*kāi fāng jì lǐ*) as the meridians (*jīng*),
and the counties, townships, and villages as the parallels (*wěi*);
so that later readers,
checking according to the grid,
make no error even of a hair's breadth.
This is the true meaning of *Tú Jīng*.
Yǒngqīng Xiàn Zhì: Preface and Rules for the Map of Institutional Establishments (*Jiàn Zhì Tú*)
The system of the standard towers (*xiàng wèi*) mentioned in the *Zhōu Guān*
cannot be verified.
Later generations' maps, such as the *Sān Fǔ Huáng Tú* and the Map of the Luòyáng Palaces (*Luòyáng Gōng Diàn*),
are what cities, capitals, and palaces were based on and imitated.
Jiànzhāng Gōng had a thousand gates and ten thousand households,
and Zhāng Huà was consequently able to list all their names;
Zhèng Qiáo believed this was the result of viewing maps,
not the result of reading books.
Therefore, is the importance attached to maps of institutional establishments
not great?
Zhū Zǐ once wrote the *Yí Lǐ Shì Gōng* (Explanation of Palaces in the Book of Etiquette and Rites),
believing that if the layout and structure were not understood,
then the proper ceremonies, regulations, and measurements
would have nothing to attach to.
Since ancient and modern palaces differ in appropriateness,
scholars seeking understanding through descriptive text
fail to grasp the meaning.
Thus, if the map is missing, the text also becomes useless and abandoned.
Later generations viewing the present
are just like the present generation viewing antiquity.
The cities and towns, government offices,
altars and temples—
these institutional codes and systems
are what the state and the people hold in high regard.
If we do not carefully produce their maps,
then later generations reading the gazetteer
will also not know where to look or what to seek.
Since the time of Qiān (Sīmǎ Qiān) and Gù (Bān Gù),
histories have contained no maps of institutional establishments;
this is why, following the Yuán and Chéng eras,
there have been numerous and disparate interpretations
regarding the Míng Táng (Luminuous Hall) and Tàimiào (Grand Ancestral Temple).
Shào Zǐ said:
"The Way of Heaven is manifest in the south
and concealed in the north;
hence, people know what is before them
but are ignorant of what is behind them."
Now, the nature of all things
is mostly to turn their back to the north and face the south.
Therefore, map drawers
must place the south at the bottom and the north at the top.
The direction of mountains and rivers,
and the breadth and length of the geography,
when set out on a map,
can still place the north at the bottom and the south at the top,
yet this already loses the appropriateness of orientation.
If the institutional establishments of temples, shrines, and government offices
are depicted with north at the bottom and south at the top,
then the eaves, plaques, and doors
will no longer have their proper places.
Huáng Shì Zhī Jùn of Huátíng,
holding the map of the Eight Trigrams (*Bā Guà*),
where Qián (Heaven) resides in the south at the top
and Kūn (Earth) resides in the north at the bottom,
consequently argues that all maps should place south at the top.
This is because he does not realize that the River Chart (*Hé Luò*) and the Diagrams of Earlier and Later Heaven (*Xiān, Hòu Tiān Tú*)
first became prominent in the Sòng dynasty,
and he mistakenly considers them ancient objects.
Moreover, the fundamental nature of principles and numbers (*lǐ shù*),
established symbolically from the formless,
must strictly follow their original position.
Mountains, rivers, palaces,
and all tangible things
are depicted on maps starting from their visible appearance,
and must necessarily be viewed face-to-face in order to be accurate.
Furthermore, when drawing a person viewing the *Bā Guà* Diagram,
if that person is sitting facing south,
the viewer must be facing north.
Therefore, the *Bā Guà* Diagram
must have south at the bottom and north at the top.
This is the ultimate expression of the nature of things.
Formless principles
are like the sun shining on the eaves;
not an inch or fraction can be exceeded.
Tangible objects
are like a mirror reflecting an image;
facing them causes mutual reversal.
This is the inevitable characteristic of drawing maps.
Those who like to speak highly of antiquity
but do not understand the proper arrangement of facts and principles
are similarly unfit to discuss written works.
Institutional establishments (*Jiàn Zhì*) are recorded to document regulations and systems.
If something does not belong to the established system,
it should not be included under *Jiàn Zhì*.
Modern gazetteers
sometimes include ancient sites (*gǔ jì*).
However, ancient sites were not originally established institutionally.
Others include Buddhist and Daoist temples (*sì guàn*),
but these are not sufficient to be considered institutional establishments.
The maps in old gazetteers
do not detail the regulations and systems,
but instead draw maps of the Eight Views (*Bā Jǐng*).
Their titles include:
Autumn Water at the South Bridge (*Nán Qiáo Qiū Shuǐ*),
Spring Rainbow at the Three Pagodas (*Sān Tǎ Chūn Hóng*),
Remaining Horns at Hánchéng (*Hán Chéng Liú Jiǎo*),
West Wind at the Hàn Temple (*Hàn Miào Xī Fēng*),
Layered Verdure of the West Mountain (*Xī Shān Dié Cuì*),
Tolling Bell of Tōngzhèn (*Tōng Zhèn Míng Zhōng*),
Drum Rhythm of the Numinous Spring (*Líng Quán Gǔ Yùn*),
and Honking Sound at Wild Goose Mouth (*Yàn Kǒu Shēng Pǔ*).
The naming is vulgar and shallow,
the conceptual structure is forced,
and they lack substance.
Therefore, everything related was eliminated from this gazetteer,
leaving no room for inscriptions or poems,
thus solemnizing the historical style.
Furthermore, things like wind and moonlight are inherent to nature,
and the seasons of spring and autumn are inevitable,
yet they forcefully link scenery,
patching things together loosely and arbitrarily—
where does it end?
Even within a single room,
morning glow and evening light,
rising sun and clear breeze,
East, West, South, and North—
anything can be named by association.
Of what value is this?
As for those today who are fond of making inscriptions and poems,
who delight in competing for temporary fame,
changing daily and renewing monthly,
pursuing folly without realizing it—
they should cease this practice.
Yǒngqīng Xiàn Zhì: Preface and Rules for the Map of Waterways (*Shuǐ Dào Tú*)
Sīmǎ Qiān composed the *Héqú Shū* (Treatise on Rivers and Canals),
Bān Gù composed the *Gōuxù Zhì* (Treatise on Ditches and Channels).
This is because geography is the warp (principle),
and waterways are the weft (details).
Geography is fixed,
but water shifts and is inconstant;
this is why Mr. Bān separated the *Gōuxù* from the *Dìlǐ* (Geography).
However, rivers (*hé*) are established by Heaven,
whereas canals (*qú*) are man-made.
Qiān used *Héqú* for the title,
which combines the meaning of natural obstructions and human effort;
but Gù’s naming it *Gōuxù* (Ditches and Channels),
refers to the methods of hydraulic engineering and land division,
including the system of *jǐngtián* (well-field), *kuài* (larger channels), and *quǎn* (smaller furrows),
which belong exclusively to the craftsman (*jiàngrén*).
I do not know if the measurement of four *chǐ* being a *xù*,
and double a *xù* being a *gōu*,
truly corresponds to the great events of the Yellow River bursting at Hùzǐ and entering the sea at Jiéshí.
If so, the titling in later histories,
following Mǎ (Sīmǎ Qiān) and not Bān (Bān Gù),
was not without reason.
The *Hé* (Yellow River) is the name of a single great stream (*dú*),
on par with the Jiāng (Yangtze), Hàn, Huái, and Jǐ.
The title of Qiān’s book, *Héqú*,
probably encompasses the methods of managing the Yellow River during the Hàn Dynasty,
named by linking it with the various canals like the Zhèng Qú and the Bái Qú.
It never touched upon the waters of the Jiāng, Huái, Wèn, or Sì,
thus it was uniquely titled using *Hé*.
In the histories of the Sòng and Yuán Dynasties,
they generally covered hydraulic engineering projects across the entire realm,
such as the dikes and sluices along the Biàn, Luò, Zhāng, Cài, Jiāng, and Huái Rivers,
all preserving their systems,
and their title was also *Héqú*.
Furthermore, they took various northern streams,
and uniformly designated them as *hé* (river) — not saying Biàn but Biàn Hé, not Luò but Luò Hé, and so on, too numerous to mention.
This is nearly equivalent to drinking the water while forgetting its source. (The *Shuǐ Jīng* [Classic of Waters] refers to various streams, but none use the character *hé* as a generic term.)
Now, to use the water of a single great stream
to generically name all the canal-digging systems in the realm,
encompassing reservoirs and sluices—
although it is said the naming follows antiquity,
it inevitably loses the opportunity for adaptation and change.
Mèngzǐ said:
“Yǔ’s water control
followed the Way of Water.”
If we take *shuǐ* (water) as the generic term,
and the *dào* (way/system) preserves the institutions,
and title the entry in the treatise
as *Shuǐdào* (Waterways/System of Water),
would this not be better and less prone to error?
The name Yǒngdìng Hé,
was bestowed by the Holy Ancestor (Emperor Kāngxī);
Húnhé and Lúgōu,
were already named so in antiquity;
to title it *Héqú*,
is certainly appropriate;
however, the waters of Jiǎnshuǐ and Yǎba, among others,
do not all flow entirely into one river.
Thus, if we title it *Shuǐdào*,
then all the waters in the whole county
can be generally included therein.
Geographical texts
broadly follow three patterns:
historical evolution (*yángé*), topography/configuration (*xíngshì*), and hydraulic engineering (*shuǐlì*).
Historical evolution should be presented in tables,
while the structure of topography and hydraulic engineering should be illustrated in maps,
and neither can be fully sought through written descriptions alone.
Since the time of Qiān and Gù,
they only composed treatises and records,
but did not draw maps,
which leads readers to rely on rote memorization,
only preparing them for policy proposals and examination success.
For the general configurations of the realm,
readers must clearly see them with their eyes,
before they can fully understand them in their hearts.
If a person discusses matters with great clarity,
but cannot put them into practice on the ground,
is this not the fault of adhering to rhetoric without seeking practical application?
The historical evolution of place names
can be managed through tables,
whereas the historical evolution of hydraulic engineering works,
cannot be managed solely through tables.
A table serves to standardize names and entries,
but it cannot standardize physical forms.
A map can convey physical forms,
but when physical forms undergo historical evolution,
it is not something that a single map can generally cover.
Therefore, following the historical evolution of the physical forms,
a separate map should be made for each stage,
so that viewers can understand the entire situation at a glance.
The *Yǔ Gòng* (Tribute of Yǔ) recorded geography
by using mountains and rivers as markers,
and the boundaries of the Nine Provinces
were determined based on them.
Later scholars thus argued that mountains and rivers are fixed,
while boundaries are impermanent.
This, however, refers to the general structure.
The shape of the Yǒngdìng Hé frequently shifts;
often, within only a few years,
its configuration immediately changes from its former appearance.
Using this to define boundaries
is untenable.
Now, we take villages (*cūnluò*) as the warp (fixed reference),
and use squaring and distance calculation (surveying),
to establish a fixed method.
The changes in the river's shape
are then mapped based on the square area measurements relative to the villages,
this is the meaning of mutual verification used by the ancients.
The treatise is written for a single county,
yet waters that do not belong to Yǒngqīng [County]
are also included generally in the map.
What is the meaning of this?
It is done to clarify the source and ramifications of the water,
and to show the sequence in which water control measures were implemented.
Bān’s history only recorded matters concerning the Western Capital,
yet his *Dìlǐ Zhì* (Treatise on Geography)
traced its origins back to the *Yǔ Gòng* and the *Zhōu Guān* (Rites of Zhōu).
This also shows that the source and ramifications have an origin.
However, the methods of squaring and distance calculation,
and the reasons for historical evolution and change,
are detailed only within Yǒngqīng,
and do not extend to the configuration of the entire river.
This illustrates the principle of prioritizing the main subject over secondary ones.
If all prefectures and counties bordering the river
were to imitate this approach,
then the complete record of the administration of the Yǒngdìng Hé course
would be properly organized.
Discussion on the Principles of the Six Treatises in the Yǒngqīng County Gazetteer
The unified form of historical texts and treatises
is a remnant of the ancient system of Official Rites (*Guān Lǐ*).
The Rites of Zhōu were preserved in Lǔ,
and in the *Zuǒ Shì Chūn Qiū* (Zuo Tradition)
the institutions and regulations are brilliantly displayed.
Since it was impossible to fully reconstruct the complete set of offices,
they used the method of following the Classic (the *Chūn Qiū*) and arranging by year,
appearing interspersed as events occurred—
circumstances necessitated this.
Since Sīmǎ Qiān’s Eight Books,
and Mèngjiān’s (Bān Gù) Ten Treatises,
they followed their own inclinations and methods,
ignoring the text of the Six Canons (*Liù Diǎn*),
leading to the great institutions of a dynasty
being difficult to organize and control systematically.
Later historians followed suit,
and in terms of detail, brevity, rejection, and selection,
they lacked a consistent standard.
The origin of this flaw
has been long-standing.
Zhèng Qiáo once said that the origin of historical texts and treatises
derived from the *Ěr Yǎ*.
He certainly emphasized categories like the *Liù Shū* (Six Scripts), *Qī Yīn* (Seven Sounds), and *Kūnchóng Cǎomù* (Insects and Plants),
desiring that the Classics and Histories mutually serve as warp and weft.
This can be accepted as forming a school of thought for himself.
However, if we discuss literary composition,
