fully adhering to the Official Rites,
then what he called the *Liù Shū* and *Qī Yīn*,
nomenclature, and exegetical studies,
all fundamentally belonged to the Ministry of the Multitudes (*Sītú*),
specifically the officials known as the Instructor (*shīshì*) and Guardian (*bǎoshì*);
this was their duty.
But the great principles and great laws,
which systematically govern Heaven and humanity and spread the Kingly Way (*Wáng Dào*),
the scope of the *Ěr Yǎ*
is insufficient to encompass them all.
The meaning of the Official Rites,
is broader than historical texts and treatises,
and ought not to be attributed to the *Ěr Yǎ*;
this principle is easy to see.
Yǔwén [Tai] imitated the *Zhōu Guān*,
and the Táng people composed the *Liù Diǎn* (Six Canons).
Although they did not fully conform to antiquity,
they were still the regulations of their respective dynasties.
Yet followers like Niú Hóng and Liú Xù,
failed to grasp the fundamental organizational principles,
to organize the institutions of their dynasty.
Consequently, works like the *Huì Yào* (Essential Documents) and *Huì Diǎn* (Collected Statutes)
could not be unified with the historical treatises and records composed by historians.
This is something that requires deep and prolonged reflection.
Ancient and modern records,
when combined, are easy to preserve;
when separated, are difficult to rely upon.
If it is said that governmental precedents (zhǎng gù) are fully prepared in the *Huì Yào* and *Huì Diǎn*,
but the treatises (shū zhì) within the histories,
might still intend to focus on what is considered important;
then the *Hàn Zhì* (Treatise of Hàn) did not use the Hàn official system as its framework,
and the institutions (Yí) of Yīng Shào,
are fragmented and incomplete;
the *Jìn Zhì* (Treatise of Jìn) did not take the Jìn official system as its framework,
and the ranks (pǐn) compiled by Xú Xuān Yú (the Xú clan possessed the *Jìn Guān Pǐn*),
are lost and non-existent.
The great principles (dà jīng) and grand statutes (dà fǎ) within them,
because of this, cannot be seen in their entirety,
and these cases are not few.
Moreover, intending to focus on what is important
is the private view of a single school,
difficult to serve as an established rule.
If literature (wén zhāng) is based on institutions (zhì zuò),
and institutions depend on official responsibilities (guān shǒu);
and pushing this to its extreme,
then in establishing offices and creating systems,
even the Sages did not regard the realm as their private domain;
how then can scholars who bear the pen
use their own opinions to determine detail or brevity?
The format of the treatises (shū zhì) should be uniform,
yet historians fail by making them uneven.
The format of the biographies (liè zhuàn) is fundamentally uneven,
yet historians fail by making them uniform.
Regulations, statutes, and systems (diǎn zhāng zhì dù),
are based entirely on the Official Rites (*Guān Lǐ*),
the structure and pattern of which are fundamentally distinct.
However, some histories have a Treatise on Officials (*Tiān Guān*) but lack a Treatise on Geography (*Dì Lǐ*);
some separate Rites (*Lǐ*) and Music (*Yuè*) but combine Military (*Bīng*) and Penal Law (*Xíng*);
they fail to understand that the official positions of that contemporary era should serve as the framework (gāng jì);
their failing is fragmentation.
Biographies are based on the *Chūn Qiū*,
originally having no fixed style,
but were shaped by Sī Mǎ [Qiān],
who briefly showed how to distinguish them.
They contain criticism and praise (yì yáng), lamentation and admiration (yǒng tàn),
granting and withholding, separating and combining—
they possess the straightforward writing style of the *Chūn Qiū*,
while also incorporating the subtle delicacy of the poets,
it is difficult to judge them all by a single measure.
Later historians separated categories and classes,
ordered sequences,
clung rigidly to official ranks,
down to the smallest detail (zī zhū chǐ cùn),
not daring to deviate slightly;
their failing is rigidity.
Fragmentation,
and rigidity,
are not the universal standard for writing.
When prefectures (zhōu) and counties (xiàn) compile local gazetteers (zhì),
it is, in ancient times, the record of a state enfeoffed by a lord.
The affairs of Officialdom (Lì), Revenue (Hù), Military (Bīng), and Justice (Xíng),
are embodied therein, though on a small scale.
Today, although the [ancient] offices no longer exist, the clerks (lì) do,
which is where the actual responsibilities lie;
no source of governmental precedents is more complete than this,
and no source of governing methods is more complete than this.
Moreover, the officials and clerks (fǔ shǐ) belonging to this group,
the *Zhōu Guān* records their number in detail,
and the *Huì Diǎn* also preserves their system;
and the regulations of a county that they manage,
are truly comprehensive and can serve as the framework;
but because these persons are humble and not discussed by the gentry (jìn shēn),
gazetteer compilers do not use them as a standard.
However, when entering a region and asking about its affairs,
without this [information], one cannot know the essentials.
Therefore, the scribal clerks (shū lì) are called Command Clerks (Lìng Shǐ),
and the chief officials are called Registry Clerks (Diǎn Shǐ).
To understand the histories (shǐ) of the Command Clerks (Lìng Shǐ) and Registry Clerks (Diǎn Shǐ),
is to understand the historical records of the principles and precedents (gāng jì zhǎng gù);
from which the essential meaning of gazetteer compilation can be derived.
The prefectures and counties of today,
have varying degrees of administrative complexity (fán jiǎn yì shì),
and the Command Clerks dealing with precedents,
establish systems according to circumstances;
they are not all based on the Six Bureaus (Cáo) of Officialdom, Revenue, Military, and Justice.
Nevertheless, if one documents the affairs of a single county,
and uses the system of that county to structure the book,
and enumerates its general categories,
the overall situation (shì shì) of the county can be seen even more clearly.
Although official documents (àn dú) and registers (bù jí) lack literary quality (wén zhāng),
the true institutions (wén zhāng) of a county,
must certainly be traced back to this source;
common people use them daily but remain unaware.
Now, to extract their framework,
to revise and clarify these records,
to enable people, based on the records, to abide by the statutes and systems (fǎ dù),
and based on the systems, to clarify their duties,
and consequently to refine the work and ensure the transmission reaches the right person—
what the ancients called "records and contracts made easy, and all officials governed well,"
is precisely this principle.
Some say that books of governmental precedents,
each managed by a specialized official,
would merely be repetitive (literally: placing beds side-by-side, adding beams atop a house),
a scope that the treatise format cannot fully encompass;
therefore, they are stored in the *Huì Diǎn* and *Huì Yào*,
and historical treatises adopt a different approach.
This view also cannot be called discerning.
The *Zhōu Guān* grasps the grand framework of an entire era,
yet the three thousand rules of Ceremonial Rites (Yí Lǐ)
are not known to be wholly contained within the Spring Office (Chūn Guān);
the six chapters of the *Sī Mǎ Fǎ*
are not known to be wholly contained within the Summer Office (Xià Guān);
however, by preserving the duties of the Minister of Rites (Zōng Bó) and the Minister of War (Sī Mǎ),
the essentials of Rites and Military affairs
can be discussed with utmost clarity.
Furthermore, Mǎ [Qiān] compiled the Treatise on Officials (*Tiān Guān*),
but the astronomical data of the Tài Chū calendar (Lì Xiàng)
are not fully seen in the relevant chapter.
Bān [Gù] compiled the Treatise on Literature (*Yì Wén*);
but Liú Xīn’s *Qī Lüè* (Seven Summaries),
did not entirely preserve its discussion.
Historians selectively extract governmental precedents,
to serve as an essential abstract for scholars.
That they cannot be expected to be as detailed
as specialized, fully formed books
is simply the natural course of things.
Since detail is not sought,
yet there is also no framework (gāng jì) to control and govern the material,
the result is disorganized and unstructured writing.
To rely on disorganized and unstructured writing
and attempt to categorize the regulations of an entire era,
is understandably difficult!
Some say that if precedents are sought from the Command Clerks (Lìng Shǐ),
and Officialdom, Revenue, Military, and Justice are taken as the framework,
then the formats of Annals (Jì), Tables (Biǎo), Diagrams (Tú), and Treatises (Shū)
cannot be separated again.
For example, the Tables of Selection and Appointment (xuǎn jǔ zhī biǎo)
should belong to the Treatise on Officials (Lì Shū);
the Diagrams of Riverways (hé dào zhī tú)
should belong to the Treatise on Works (Gōng Shū).
If categories are filled completely,
then one gazetteer would only contain the Six Treatises (Liù Shū) and nothing else;
how then can the various formats be separated again?
This view also cannot be called discerning.
When the ancients wrote books,
each had its own functional category (yì lèi);
once functional categories are separated,
they cannot be forcibly combined.
The Sī Mǎ clan based their Tables (Biǎo) on the genealogy records (pǔ) of the Zhōu,
however, the records of genealogy and succession,
were managed by the Grand Historian (Tài Shǐ),
and the format of horizontal and diagonal flow [i.e., tables],
is not known to have been mixed into the Six Statutes (Liù Diǎn).
Maps and genealogical records (tú pǔ) each have their specialized books,
whereas the treatise (shū zhì) format,
focuses exclusively on regulations and systems,
it naturally follows that the official posts of the contemporary era should serve as the unifying framework.
This does not mean that specialized works designed for separate formats
should all be mixed into it [the treatise];
only then is it called comprehensive summarization.
Furthermore, consider the Six Arts (Liù Yì), all managed by the Zhōu officials,
yet the *Yì* [Classic of Changes] is not recorded under the Grand Diviner (Tài Bǔ),
and the *Shī* [Classic of Odes] is not recorded under the Grand Music Master (Tài Shī);
however, the names of the three *Yì*
are never absent from the Grand Diviner's records;
and the titles of the four collections of *Shī*,
are again never absent from the Grand Music Master's records.
This is the meaning [of inclusion].
The Six Ministers (Liù Qīng) coordinate their affairs,
and their achievements appear interactively;
this is why previous scholars have questioned why the Winter Office (Dōng Guān) is scattered among the other five statutes (diǎn).
Prefectures and counties adapt systems to local conditions (yīn dì zhì yí),
and are particularly lacking a single fixed methodology.
For instance, population figures (dīng kǒu) are managed by the Revenue Bureau (Hù Fáng),
but the compilation of household records and census lists (yān cè)
belongs to the Justice Bureau (Xíng Fáng);
because the census lists are not for taxation purposes,
but are intended to investigate deceit.
Military students (Wǔ Shēng) and military candidates (Wǔ Jǔ) belong to the Ministry of War (Bīng Bù),
but the processing of their affairs is handled by the Rites Bureau (Lǐ Fáng);
because students (shēng yuán) are not differentiated by civil or military status,
all are placed under the schools,
and the schools are linked to the system of official recommendation (Gòng Jǔ).
In the distinctions between separation and combination, detail and brevity,
if one investigates the reasons why they are so,
what is there that is not scholarship?
Preface and Regulations for the Administrative Summary of the Yǒng Qīng County Gazetteer.
Recent gazetteers
take figures/biographies (*rénwù*) as the main structure (*gāng*),
and the categories of Distinguished Officials (*Mínghuàn*), Local Worthies (*Xiāngxián*), and Sojourners (*Liúyù*),
are marked and divided into sub-headings (*mù*).
This convention was likely established by the *Yītǒng Zhì* (*Comprehensive Gazetteer*) of the Yuán and Míng dynasties.
Furthermore, when departments (*bù*), prefectures (*fǔ*), subprefectures (*zhōu*), and counties (*xiàn*) are separately designated and compiled into books,
they also utilize the classified compilation (*lèizuǎn*) method of the comprehensive gazetteers (*tǒngzhì*),
which can be said to have lost its proper form.
Now, concerning why biographies (*rénwù*) should not be classified and compiled (*lèizuǎn*),
the principles (*yìlì*) are detailed in the introductory section of the Biographies (*Liè Zhuàn*) chapter;
concerning why Distinguished Officials (*Mínghuàn*) should not be included among the Biographies (*Rénwù*),
this shows a failure to grasp the proper style of historical writing,
and thus ignorance regarding the balance and principles (*quánhéng yìlǐ*) involved.
In antiquity, marquises were enfeoffed and governed hereditarily.
The various states naturally possessed their own Spring and Autumn Annals (e.g., *Yángshé Xī*'s *Jìn Chūn Qiū*, and the *Yān Chūn Qiū* cited by Mòzǐ).
Thus, when the ruler presided over his domain,
the first year merely observed the King’s calendar (*wáng zhèng*) and nothing more.
When the feudal system (*fēngjiàn*) was abolished and replaced by commanderies and counties (*jùnxiàn*),
the administrators (*shǒu líng*) received and executed imperial edicts and statutes.
Even officials thousands of *lǐ* away
were treated like those maintaining territory within the capital region (*jīnèi*).
The poem *Gāntáng* praising Shào Gōng,
the songs of the people of Zhèng about Zǐchǎn,
and the biographies of Excellent Officials (*Xún Lì*) by Mǎ [Qiān] and Bān [Gù],
all illustrate adaptation to changes in the era.
As for specialized works concerning prefectures (*zhōu*) and departments (*bù*),
outside of the standard histories (*zhèng shǐ*),
authors existed in antiquity,
and the principles (*yìlì*) they used are not impossible to trace.
Liáng Yuándì had the *Dānyáng Yǐn Zhuàn* (listed in the *Suí Zhì* as ten scrolls).
The Hè clan had the *Kuàijī Tàishǒu Zàn* (listed in the *Táng Zhì* as two scrolls).
People of the Táng dynasty had the *Chéngdū Mùfǔ Jì* (listed in the *Táng Zhì* as two scrolls, starting in Zhēnyuán, ending in Xiántōng).
All these collected those who administered that specific region,
recording their names and achievements.
These books were compiled separately

and were initially not haphazardly mingled in the same volumes as the *Guǎnglín Lièshì Zhuàn* (compiled by Huá Gé, seen in the *Suí Zhì*), the *Kuàijī Xiānxián Zhuàn* (compiled by Xiè Chéng, seen in the *Suí Zhì*), or the *Yì Bù Qí Jiù Zhuàn* (compiled by Chén Shòu, seen in the *Suí Zhì*).
This means that the long-term administrators (*cháng lì*) who served under the shade of the sweet pear tree (*Tángyīn*)
and the famous scholars (*míng liú*) of the local community (*Zǐlǐ*)
were originally not grouped together like clouds and dragons (i.e., people attracted to each other by innate affinity);
they were indeed matters as distant as wind and horses (i.e., unrelated).
When listing Distinguished Officials (*Mínghuàn*),
they should not be placed in the same section of Biographies (*Liè Zhuàn*) as Local Worthies (*Xiāngxián*).
This is not only because the guest (official) and the host (local) occupy different roles,
but also because they demand styles of compilation that differ in detail and conciseness.
When a high official (*cháng lì*) governs this land,
we select those whose efforts benefited this region,
promoting advantage and eliminating harm,
leaving behind virtue among the people,
and they should immediately be treated with utmost reverence.
Otherwise, if their learning resembles Yán [Huí] or Zēng [Shēn],
and their conduct matches Lián [Pō] or Huì [Sī],
but they offered no benefit to the county,
the gazetteer's pen cannot cross boundaries to record them;
this is also the principle.
If, before they took office,
local opinion did not approve of them,
or after leaving office,
their later years were not virtuous until the end,
but they were momentarily excellent and benevolent officials (*xún liáng*),
then their good governance (*shàn zhèng*) in this region must be recorded.
Wú Qǐ killed his wife,
yet his achievements were reported in Xīhé;
in the gazetteer, we should not dwell upon his past actions.
Huáng Bà served as Chancellor (*xiàng*),
but his reputation was less esteemed than when he was in Yǐngchuān;
in the gazetteer, we should not predict his future failings.
We take governance (*zhèng*) as paramount,
and all other matters are considered secondary.
How can this be compared to the people of this very land,
whose lives are investigated from beginning to end,
and who are compiled into Biographies (*Liè Zhuàn*),
sharing the same format?
Old gazetteers, under the section for Office Holders (*Zhígūan*),
fully record administrative achievements (*zhèng jì*).
But the Distinguished Officials (*Mínghuàn*) section occupies only empty pages,
where beneath the name,
a note simply says that the matter is already detailed earlier.
This is not only a reversal of the guest and host roles,
but also a failure to distinguish between praise, blame, rejection, and inclusion,
completely losing the *Chūn Qiū*'s principle of recording events truthfully as they happened.
Now, selection and examination (*xuǎnjǔ*) form the structural framework for Biographies (*rénwù*),
just as Office Holders (*Zhígūan*) form the structural framework for Distinguished Officials (*Mínghuàn*).
That the selection and appointment of Office Holders (*Zhígūan*) does not calculate merit or demerit
is analogous to the way Distinguished Officials (*Mínghuàn*) and Biographies (*rénwù*) do not calculate high status or low status;
the conventions are not identical, but the underlying principles are mutually supportive.
If a list of selections (*xuǎnjǔ*) exists but names are absent from the Biographies (*Liè Zhuàn*),
or if a list of Office Holders (*Zhígūan*) exists but no record is found in the Administrative Summary (*Zhènglüè*),
observers can check the chronological order,
demand facts corresponding to the name,
and although the words themselves contain no praise or blame, the meaning implicitly holds encouragement or criticism.
How could this not serve as an exhortation for future generations?
The form of the Biographies (*Liè Zhuàn*) is detailed and literary,
while the form of the Administrative Summary (*Zhènglüè*) is direct and concise.
This is not due to a difference in the act of writing,
but rather because the facts and principles necessitate it.
Biographies (*Liè Zhuàn*) encompass the great and the small,
evaluating and assessing individuals (*rénwù*).
Sometimes they follow categorization like a clan (*zú*),
sometimes they are divided into sections like a well (*jǐng*);
their variations are unrestricted—
this is the image of the *Yì* (*Book of Changes*);
they disseminate principles and set forth strategies—
this is the substance of the *Shū* (*Book of Documents*);
they criticize, praise, and lament—
this is the purpose of the *Shī* (*Book of Odes*);
they are intricate, detailed, and subtly nuanced—
this is the order of the *Lǐ* (*Book of Rites*);
they correlate events and organize language—
this is the fundamental meaning of the *Chūn Qiū* (*Spring and Autumn Annals*).
Possessing insight into human relations (*rénlún*),
exhausting the principles of things and affairs,
harboring ambitions for a thousand ages,
culling the essence of the Classics (*jīng*) and Commentaries (*zhuàn*),
and issuing forth as literary works,
they are incomparable.
Therefore, the talent of Mǎ [Qiān] and Bān [Gù]
was not fully displayed in the Basic Annals (*Běnjì*), Tables (*Biǎo*), and Treatises (*Zhì*),
but was fully displayed in the Biographies (*Liè Zhuàn*).
As for the form of the Administrative Summary (*Zhènglüè*),
its principle demands strict adherence to facts,
its purpose lies in providing remedy and assistance,
chronology is constrained by sequence,
and the narrative must focus on statecraft (*jīnglún*).
Its form must be lofty and pure,
so that it can govern the people of the state,
crown the Biographies (*Liè Zhuàn*),
intertwine the warp and the weft,
and hold the key central point.
This is indeed difficult for a mere literary scholar (*wén shì*) to achieve.
Books written by the ancients that possess the warp but lack the weft
are generally named *lüè* (Summary/Outline).
When Péi Zǐyě excerpted Shěn Yuē's *Sòng Shū*,
and titled his chronological work a *lüè*,
this was also an example of that.
However, Liú Zhījǐ criticized Péi's book for being named a *lüè*,
yet its writing was unavoidably voluminous.
This also shows a failure to grasp the intent of the ancients.
The *Huáng Shí* (referring to *Huáng Shígōng Sān Lüè*) and *Huáinán* (referring to *Huáinánzǐ Yào Lüè*)
are chapters from the Masters (*Zhūzǐ*).
Zhāng Wēn and Yú Huàn (referring to Zhāng Wēn's *Sān Shǐ Lüè* and Yú Huàn's *Diǎn Lüè*) are writings from historical records.
Within these, there is also the meaning of strategy and outline (*móu lüè*).
Why should the meaning be entirely derived merely from condensation?
The achievements of excellent officials (*xún lì*)
are harder to record in a gazetteer than those of local worthies (*xiāngxián*).
Governance involves rewards and punishments.
When rewards and punishments are issued, favor and resentment arise.
The lack of uniformity in public opinion
is the first difficulty.
Affairs involve failure and success.
Failure and success differ, making difficulty and ease distinct.
The reciprocal view of the present and the past
is the second difficulty.
Officials come and go.
Unlike local villagers whose descendants are all present,
officials whose traces are distant easily vanish.
This is the third difficulty.
Excellent officials (*xún lì*) are sincere and unembellished,
while clever officials (*qiǎo huàn*) are skilled at ornamentation.
Memorial tablets erected upon departure (*qù sī zhī bēi*)
are half filled with words of shame,
and words of praise and celebration
are difficult to verify with actual achievements.
This is the fourth difficulty.
If the official is promoted to an important position,
the compiler dare not speak plainly.
If he transfers his administration to a neighboring domain,
how can the officials looking on be without partiality?
This is the fifth difficulty.
The law of the world naturally involves many scruples,
and human sentiment judges talent based on success or failure.
If one accidentally encounters an impeachment report listing errors,
people immediately say that person was not good.
This is the sixth difficulty.
Old gazetteers recorded without method,
and stone inscriptions amidst the dust and wind easily disappear.
Even if one manages to roughly list the general facts,
the chronology of beginning and end cannot be investigated.
This is the seventh difficulty.
Knowing these difficulties,
yet daring not to fail to record what has been heard and seen in order to preserve an outline,
leads one to the extreme of having no choice,
and thus necessitates greater caution.
Biographies (*Liè Zhuàn*) begin by listing the name,
followed by narrating the official position and lineage (*gōng fá*);
this is the fixed convention of historical writing.
The Administrative Summary (*Zhènglüè*) takes the official post (*guān*) as the heading.
Not only is this proper due to the principle of guest and host,
but it is also the intention of considering the name and contemplating the meaning (*gùmíng sīyì*),
which must not be neglected.
Old gazetteers classified and ordered
officials such as magistrates (*Zhīxiàn*) and assistant magistrates (*Xiànchéng*)
without adhering to the chronological order of their service.
This is not the intent of the Administrative Summary (*Zhènglüè*),
and thus is not worthy of criticism.
Preface to the Principles of the Biographies Section of the *Yǒngqīng Xiàn Zhì*
A *zhuàn* (commentary/biography) is designated in contrast to a *jīng* (classic),
serving to transmit and teach exegesis,
elaborate upon the deeper meanings,
and it is what is committed to writing only when unavoidable.
Zuǒ Shì compiled his precious book,
detailing the entirety of the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals),
while the Sīmǎ Shì designated separate chapters based on individuals,
marking them with the name *zhuàn* and placing them in series;
this is how they were named.
The purpose of the *jīng* is simple and rigorous,
but the text of the *zhuàn* is ornate and beautiful.
Consequently, scholars followed the current and forgot the source,
leading one another to compose *zhuàn* that lacked a corresponding *jīng*.
Thus, among the literary collections of the Táng and Sòng dynasties,
there is an abundance of the *zhuàn* style.
Recently, some have claimed that since scholars are not official historians (*shǐguān*),
they are not entitled to write *zhuàn*.
Indeed, regarding the topic of interpreting classics,
they pursued the branch while abandoning the root.
If constrained by proper rules,
they truly have no defense.
Yet, they speak of the official historian,
condemning him for overstepping his bounds (*yuè zǔ*),
causing that person to retaliate with a sneer,
saying, "Gōng and Gǔ were not the Grand Historians of Lǔ,
so why do they also have *zhuàn* texts?"
In that case, that person would have no means to justify himself.
Moreover, even if one is a historian,
if there is no *běnjì* (basic annals),
how can one immediately create *lièzhuàn* (arranged biographies)?
This is a principle of the *zhuàn* format that must be clearly understood.
*Zhuàn* without *jīng*
are the collections of literary men.
*Jīng* without *zhuàn*
are the records (*zhì*) of regions and prefectures.
Literary collections err on the side of being flowery and deceitful,
while regional records err on the side of being brief and vulgar.
Since the capture of the *lín* (unicorn) and the laying down of the brush,
official historians have not understood the meaning of the precious books of the hundred states.
The historical records of the prefectures and commanderies
were named *tújīng* (illustrated classics/records);
after many generations passed,
the illustrations were lost and the texts were isolated,
the *zhuàn* style was not detailed,
and thus their books became disjointed and scattered (*hùluò*).
Yuè Shǐ’s *Huán Yǔ Jì*
adopted the style of the *Yuán Hé Zhì*,
in which famous scenic spots and historical sites
were merely included as ornamentation.
Subsequently, the Yuán and Míng dynasties’ *Yī Tǒng Zhì* (Gazetteers of the Empire)
thus classified and sequenced categories such as distinguished persons (*rénwù*), exemplary women (*liènǚ*), noted officials (*mínghuàn*), and temporary residents (*liúyù*),
together with mountains, rivers, temples, and tombs.
This pertains solely to geography;
it briefly embodies the idea of categorized compilation,
meant to supply literary writers with timely material,
and was originally not considered important or trivial.
The records (*zhì*) of prefectures and counties
fundamentally possess the historical structure of a single state,
but those who write them instead adopt the headings of generalized compilation found in the *Yī Tǒng Zhì*.
How can one say this is done for broad inclusion, enabling succinct extraction for the national history?
The purpose of titles in *lièzhuàn*
is that the affairs outweigh the individual.
Chapters like the *Rúlín* (Confucian Scholars) and *Xúnlì* (Good Officials)
were originally not established for individuals like Shī, Mèng, Liáng Qiū, Gōng, Huáng, Zhuó, or Lǔ.
As for the various types of other people,
they are not merely tens, hundreds, or thousands, but tenfold, hundredfold, or thousandfold!
If one insists on using two characters as a heading for all of them,
the Master (Kǒngzǐ) also spoke of "categorizing people,"
but I would not have the leisure for that.
In Ōuyáng Xiū’s history of the *Wǔ Dài* (Five Dynasties),
every person is labeled with a category,
how can this compare to the *Chūnqiū*’s purpose of regulating the world,
where the Sage discussed but did not make definitive judgments?
The records (*zhì*) of regions and prefectures
extract and abbreviate events,
dividing them into categories for compilation.
Readers find this dull and flavorless,
like peering into a ledger for summoning ghosts.
As for famous worthies and exemplary women (*liènǚ*),
there are separate epitaphs (*zhuàng*), records (*zhì*), biographies (*zhuàn*), and inscriptions (*míng*).
This leads to splitting the chapters,
and separately listing them under the section for arts and literature (*yìwén*).
Consequently, having no other choice,
they simply add sub-notes:
"See details in certain chapter here,"
"Already listed under certain entry there."
The repetition is redundant,
making reading laborious.
I do not understand why they enjoy creating such self-imposed vexation!
This is another aspect of the *lièzhuàn* in gazetteers that demands deep and sustained consideration.
It is certainly proper
for recent generations
to compile and sequence *lièzhuàn*
based on what they have seen and heard.
If there are people from antiquity
already detailed in previous histories,
recording the exact text of their biographies and histories
without any alteration
also reflects the principle by which Mǎ (Sīmǎ Qiān) and Bān (Bān Gù) successively revised and compiled
without presuming to display their own cleverness.
Nevertheless,
when historians compose biographies,
within a single work,
they vary in detail and brevity in relation to each other,
which readers can understand by reviewing the whole.
Thus, in the *Chén Yú Zhuàn*,
the deeds of Zhāng Ěr are also detailed;
the governance of Guǎn and Yàn
is fully accounted for in the chapter on Tàigōng;
these are clear proofs.
Now, having cut historical accounts to insert them into the gazetteers,
yet still retaining the original *lièzhuàn* text
without incorporating the cross-references found in the historical writings,
how is this different from carving a mark on the boat
and seeking one’s old sword?
If historical texts contain errors,
and the gazetteer writer corrects them,
they must certainly demonstrate the reason
and show that their alteration
was originally not undertaken lightly.
This is also due to the circumstances of the time;
therefore, Sīmǎ Shì’s *Tōng Jiàn Kǎo Yì*
cannot adhere to the Mǎ and Bān principle of setting one’s own standard for antiquity.
As for historical texts containing praise and condemnation,
since the *Chūnqiū*,
no one has ever changed them.
Yet, writers of gazetteers
often select the person’s strengths while concealing their weaknesses.
In that case, it would be better not to use the text at all;
one might at least forget it without realization.
The gazetteer writer selects historical biographies to include in the arts and literature section,
titling them "The *Lièzhuàn* of So-and-so from So-and-so's History."
But upon reviewing the *zhuàn* text, it does not match the historical intention.
If one seeks the reason for the deletions and abbreviations,
there is no corroborating evidence.
This is an attempt to conceal a weakness,
but they do not realize they are merely exposing it.
The sequencing of historical biographies
is generally arranged by dynastic order;
otherwise, figures like Qū and Jiǎ, or Lǎo and Zhuāng, would have specific intentions assigned to them separately.
Comparing events and assigning words
is the teaching of the *Chūnqiū*;
this is where comparison (*bǐ*) and arousal (*xīng*) reside.
Clarifying and articulating what is distant
is the teaching of the *Shàng Shū*;
this is where the phenomena of change are collected.
To write *lièzhuàn* without understanding that the spiritual illumination resides within the person
is merely to compile an autobiography detailing their age and origin.
Introductory Principles for the Biographies of Exemplary Women in the *Yǒng Qīng Xiàn Zhì*.
The biographies of exemplary women,
transmit their good fortune.
In the biographies categorized and titled by historians,
such as the chapters on *Rúlín*, *Wényuàn*, *Zhōngyì*, *Xúnliáng*,
and extending to the chapters on *Liènǚ*,
none fail to be sequenced by category.
Since the time of Wèi Zōng and Bó Qǐ,
this structure has generally been followed without change.
However, *Rúlín* and *Wényuàn*
have their own family biographies;
*Zhōngyì* and *Xúnliáng*
have their names engraved on metal and stone.
Moreover, such individuals are rarely seen in the world,
and their merits are multifaceted,
making it easy for the Grand Historian to collect and
identify them.
Chaste maidens and virtuous wives (*zhēnnǚ jiéfù*)
are humble in person and hidden in deeds,
yet they uphold the great principles
and crown human relationships.
The region is not without such people,
and people are not without such deeds,
but the light carriage (official inspectors) is far away and difficult to gather from,
and public opinion is accustomed to them and takes them for granted.
If they are unfortunate and do not meet their time,
or if they meet their time but entrust themselves to the wrong person,
although they possess lofty conduct and exceptional integrity,
they fade away like the wilting grasses and trees.
Is this not regrettable!
In the old *zhì* of Yǒng Qīng,
the names of exemplary women were few and far between;
reviewing the text,
the facts and deeds cannot be verified,
which is the consequence of entrusting them to the wrong person.
After the old *zhì* was written on bamboo slips,
and before the new compilation was assembled,
spanning several decades,
there was little worth recording,
which is the consequence of not meeting the right time.
Now, having widely collected and extensively inquired,
detailing their actions and facts comprehensively,
is it not their good fortune
that they are able to be included in the *lièzhuàn*?
We celebrate their encounter (with fortune),
and thus deeply mourn those who did not have such an encounter!
of Worthy Women (Liènǚ)
follows the model of Liú Xiàng,
and is not exclusively for Chaste/Martyr Women (Liènǚ).
Cáo Zhāo was valued for her learning;
had she been a man,
she would have been selected for the Forest of Scholars (Rúlín).
Cài Yǎn was famed for her talent;
had she been a man,
she would have been material for the Garden of Literature (Wényuàn).
Liú Zhījǐ criticized Fàn Shǐ (Fàn Wèi’s History) for including Cài Yǎn’s biography;
his assertion is extremely erroneous;
yet later historians upheld this as a fixed rule,
specifically dedicating a section only to those upholding Chastity and Martyrdom (Jiéliè).
If we fully follow this principle,
then in historical records concerning men,
it would suffice to only include biographies of Loyal Ministers (Zhōngchén);
this is called not knowing how to categorize properly.
Among the Worthy Women of Yǒngqīng,
there are certainly none selected for the Garden of Literature or the Forest of Scholars,
yet, if a husband died before the wife reached thirty,
and she lived beyond fifty,
the period she lived as a widow in between
must have been at least thirty years;
if she unfortunately died young,
it must also have been after fifteen years,
and the husband must have been over forty years old—
legal statutes (lǜlìng) require no less than this standard.
The merit or lack thereof in feminine virtue
cannot be judged by age rules.
The death of Mù Bó
was not necessarily before Jìng Jiāng was thirty;
the death of Qǐ Liáng's wife (Qǐ Liáng Qī)
was not necessarily fifteen years after the battle of Jǔ.
Judging by this reasoning,
one should only verify truth and falsehood,
and no longer be restricted by age and year requirements.
Local prefectural and county records
are close by and easy to verify facts,
unlike the broad scope covered by legal statutes,
which must retain restrictions.
The works of Qiān (Sīmǎ Qiān) and Gù (Bān Gù) do not omit Worthy Women,
they merely do not title a separate chapter for them;
Bā Qīng is recounted in the Monograph on Money Makers (*Huòzhí*),
Wén Jūn is attached to Xiāngrú's biography,
Táng Shān is included in the Monograph on Arts and Literature (*Yìwén*),
and Tí Yíng appears in the Treatise on Punishment (*Xíng Zhì*);
some were chaste, others filial,
some scholarly, others literary;
they appear scattered brilliantly.
This is not limited only to Yáng Chǎng having a wise wife,
or Mǎi Chén having a foolish wife.
This is because the methods of Mǎ and Bān were concise,
still preserving the style of the *Zuǒ Zhuàn* and *Guó Yǔ*,
and they were not overly meticulous in making detailed classifications;
this is also why the Four Whiteheads (Sì Hào) and Jūn Píng were not labeled as Recluses (Yǐnyì),
nor were Zōu (Yáng), Méi (Shèng), Yán (Zhù), and Yuè (Yáng) listed under the Garden of Literature (Wényuàn).
Lǐ Yánshòu's two histories, *Nán Shǐ* (Southern History) and *Běi Shǐ* (Northern History),
originated from the same family;
the *Běi Shǐ* maintained the original section titles from Wèi and Suí dynasties,
specifically featuring *Liènǚ* (Worthy Women);
but the *Nán Shǐ*, because it lacked the original *Liènǚ* heading,
placed Xiāo Jiǎo's wife Yáng and those who followed
mixed within the chapter on Filial Piety and Righteousness (*Xiàoyì*);
consequently, within a single volume,
there was no distinction between men and women,
and since this was not done to derive a separate meaning,
it must simply be called confusion and disorder,
and cannot wrongly invoke the precedent set by Mǎ and Bān.
As for chapters grouping by clans,
this also follows the lingering concept of hereditary aristocratic houses (*Shìjiā*);
for example, descendants and collateral relatives of the Wáng, Xiè, Cuī, and Lú clans
are grouped together across different generations in the same chapter.
(In the original histories, Wáng, Xiè, Cuī, and Lú were separated by dynasty, but Lǐ combined them into one place.) Furthermore, the strengths of Lǐ (Yánshòu)
should not be obscured by a single flaw.
Now, regarding the chapter on *Liènǚ*,
we establish our own principles.
Those included by association,
whether they are respected mothers-in-law (wēigū) who are advanced in years and possess fine virtue,
or young daughters-in-law (zǐfù) who demonstrate exemplary conduct,

are all introduced following the precedent of Liú Xiàng. (Liú Xiàng's precedent: *Liènǚ* compiled all categories of women's conduct and was not strictly restricted to chastity and martyrdom. Attaching mother-in-law and daughter-in-law together also follows the lingering concept of aristocratic houses.)
They are compiled together in sequence;
this is what is meant by "what others reject, I adopt."
If their deeds relate to the Three Obediences (sāncóng)
and their conduct is detailed for the entire clan,
although this falls under the standard meaning of constancy and chastity (zhēnjié),
it is also classified separately;
for example, the wife of the Liú clan maintaining chastity is placed in the biographies under the Gūiyì Mén category. Hopefully, the events will have coherence
and the principles will not be fragmented,
not being rigidly constrained by the chapter titles as a standard,
thus retaining the scholarly method of the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals);
this, conversely, is what is meant by "what others combine, I separate."
The biographical format of Fàn Shǐ (Fàn Wèi’s History)
features a separate chapter for each person,
and a separate appraisal (lùn) for each chapter,
completely losing the principle of Mǎ and Bān of combining biographies

and following the *Chūnqiū* method of arranging affairs and composing language. (Mǎ and Bān's organization and arrangement of chapters, whether separate or combined, contained deep meaning, unlike Fàn Shǐ, which merely aimed to fill a scroll. Therefore, the former *Hàn Shū*, in places where the volume of bamboo slips was heavy, preferred to divide a single chapter into 'Upper,' 'Middle,' and 'Lower,' rather than splitting the chapter into 'One,' 'Two,' and 'Three.')
As for the chapter on *Liènǚ*,

the introductory remarks clearly state that it is not restricted to one type of conduct. (The preface states: "We record their highly outstanding qualities, not specializing in one type of conduct" only.)
Yet, it is compiled in a mixed sequence,

without separate appraisals being placed for individuals. (In other biographies, often once a person's affairs are finished, an appraisal is immediately established, destroying the coherence of the form. Here, where division is appropriate, there is no appraisal.)
How is it that these conflicting practices each result in errors?
In the biographies of the current Gazetteer (*Zhì*),
I dare not arbitrarily decide on combining or separating entries,
or break the format by writing appraisals (lùn zàn).
However, for this chapter on *Liènǚ*,
I incorporate the remaining intent of Liú Xiàng. (The biographies are not constrained to a single conduct, and there is an encomium for each person.)
I draft individual commentaries;
this also follows the meaning of the poets' singing and sighing.
If the deeds are ordinary
and the meaning is not particularly remarkable,
then I will not append a description.
The titles used by the Grand Historian (Tàishǐ, Sīmǎ Qiān)
were not constrained by standard rules. (Biographical titles directly mention Zhāng Tíngwèi, Lǐ Jiāngjūn, and the like.)
This preserves the intent of the scholars of the Spring and Autumn period (Chūnqiū Zhūzǐ) to title chapters based on meaning.
When it came to Bān (Gù)'s biographies,
the names and titles were no longer borrowed.
The biographies in Fàn Shǐ
all utilize Bān's biographical method;
yet in the chapter on *Liènǚ*,
the beginning of each section uses the husband's name and geographical origin (jùnwàng),
since this is not a geographical treatise (*Dìlǐ zhī Zhì*),
why is the place name placed first?
Furthermore, since this is not an account of men,
why must the husband's name appear first?
This has already missed the point of titling the *Liènǚ* chapter. (It should say: 'So-and-so's wife, of such-and-such commandery,' not: 'So-and-so commandery, so-and-so's wife, so-and-so.')
Furthermore, regarding the two women Cáo É and Shū Xiān Xióng,
the title 'Filial Daughter' (Xiàonǚ zhī chēng)
is placed above their names—
why was Wèizōng (Fàn Wèi) not averse to such elaboration?
Since the chapter title already denotes Worthy Women,
we do not hear of Cáo Zhāo being labeled 'Worthy Mother' (Xiánmǔ),
nor Cài Yǎn being labeled 'Talented Woman' (Cáinǚ),
nor Huángfǔ being called 'Martyr Wife' (Lièfù),
nor the Páng clan woman being called 'Filial Wife' (Xiàofù)—
so how can the addition of embellishments for É and Xióng
align with the principle of the *Chūnqiū*
of recording events truthfully so that good and evil are self-evident?
In later generations' writings,
when recounting the deeds of worthy women,
there are cases where the surname is not written,
but the words 'Chaste Maiden' (Zhēnnǚ) or 'Chaste Wife' (Jiéfù) are used directly instead of the name;
how is this different from the examination essay (kējǔ zhìyì) format
where, in the opening section, the person is not called by name
but referred to by categories such as 'The Sage,' 'The Great Worthy,' 'The Worthy Man,' or 'The Person of the Time'?
This practice was truly initiated by Wèizōng.
Now, I title the section with the woman's surname,
and place the husband's name and paternal lineage after it,
and also detail her village and hamlet
to serve as verification for future divisions of townships and counties.
Regarding the deeds of constancy, martyrdom, chastity, and filial piety,
observing the text will make them fully clear,
and I will not forcibly elaborate the title,

allowing the reader to study the details. (It is acceptable for women to be referred to by surname, such as Zhang or Li. People nowadays, if they do not call them 'Chaste Wife' or 'Chaste Maiden,' refer to them as 'Mrs. [X]'; the ancients had no such precedent. Calling them 'Chaste Wife' or 'Chaste Maiden' is like an essay's opening line. Referring to them merely as 'Mrs. [X]' is like petitioning for official certification.)
The sequence is generally arranged by historical period.
Those originating from the same clan
are grouped into one place;
for those whose era cannot be detailed,
they are roughly appended to the end.
Even if there are no deeds to narrate,
I must detail the dates of her marriage,
and her age when she was still living.
The reason she is not the same as every other person
lies merely in these minor details. Alas!
People may even consider this to be unnecessary elaboration. (Those for whom the age and year are not recorded were simply cases where inquiry failed to yield the information.)
Preface to the Biographies in the Yǒngqīng County Gazetteer (Worthy Women section pending investigation)
The principle of historians omitting questionable text (quēwén)
is fully contained in the *Chūnqiū*.
Since the era of the Two Hàn (Liǎng Hàn),
Fú Shēng and Zhèng Xuán transmitted the Classics,
and Mǎ (Sīmǎ Qiān) and Bān (Bān Gù) compiled histories.
The Classics adhere to the masters' doctrines,
but history relies on personal judgment.
Thus, while the Six Classics (Liù Yì) have omitted and simplified texts,

the Three Commentaries (Sān Zhuàn) lack the principle of mutually preserving differing accounts. Differing accounts in the *Gōngyáng* and *Gǔliáng* are not recorded in the *Zuǒshì* (Zuǒzhuàn); separate observations in the *Zuǒshì* are not preserved in the *Gōngyáng* and *Gǔliáng*.
Now, the Classic is revered while the commentaries treat their texts separately;
hence, even if one is treated as master and others as slaves,
the structure does not prevent their simultaneous inclusion.
History, being straightforward and its narrative unified,
then, by excising questionable elements, the writing is clarified.
The rule cannot permit both versions to coexist;
this is simply the nature of the situation.
Master Sīmǎ (Sīmǎ shì) initiated his methodology based on the *Chūnqiū*
and created the annals-biography (jì zhuàn) format.
Regarding differing accounts in transmitted reports,
his mediation, selection, and rejection
can be called prudent indeed.
However, in the stone chambers and metal caskets,
records and documents were preserved;
through famous mountains and great rivers,
observations and hearing were increased and enriched.
In his methodology, what is meant by "omitting the doubtful" (yí zhě quē zhī),
or the divergence in ancient texts,
or the existence of gaps in the written record,
or missing details frequently seen in other accounts, and so on—
he only records what he adopted,
but does not clarify the reason for adopting it;
he regards it as omitted (quē),
but does not preserve the explanation for the omission.
This is like placing one's foot and reaching the Yellow Springs;
everything beyond the space needed for the foot
is abandoned material.
The Master (Fūzǐ) said:
"Hear much, omit the doubtful,
and speak cautiously about the remainder."
Wishing to hear much, yet retaining the omission of the doubtful,
is the height of caution.
Following Mǎ and Bān,
they preserved what was certain but did not record the doubtful points to await inquiry.
This is simply what is called "excising the doubtful" and nothing more;
what omission (quē) is there then?
There are three examples of omitting the doubtful (quēyí):
The first is one event with two accounts that are difficult to synthesize into one,
such as when the *Chūnqiū* records the death of Chén Hóu Bào,
and simultaneously preserves the texts recording the jiǎxū and jǐchǒu dates.
The second is where the text was previously recorded, but now the explanation for it is lost,
such as the *Chūnqiū*'s record of the principle concerning Xià Wǔ Guō Gōng.
The third is cautiously recording observations without providing one's own explanation,
such as the *Chūnqiū*'s record that the fixed stars (héngxīng) were not seen,
but not stating that the fixed stars had fallen.
Hán Fēi's *Chǔ Shuō*,
when comparing and arranging events of the Chūnqiū period,
whenever there were differences or similarities,
always added "or it is said" and so on,
recording it beneath the main text.
This is the example of the jiǎxū and jǐchǒu dates.
Mèngzǐ spoke of Xiànzǐ’s five friends,
but only recorded two people.
This is the example of Guō Gōng Xià Wǔ.
The *Tángōng* records that the horses panicked and the army was routed,
but does not record that the horse was struck by a stray arrow.
This is the example of the fixed stars (héngxīng) not being seen.
Following Mǎ and Bān,
those who recorded their observations and implied a meaning
indeed existed;
but recording one event in two ways,
or merely preserving the title of an event without content,
is absolutely unheard of.
If it is argued that the Classic texts became clear through transmission,
and that the historian’s pen is inconvenient for simultaneously recording and explaining doubtful items,
then separately preserving a list of items
and clearly recording these omissions (quēyí) to await inquiry
does not seem to harm the literary format.
If history lacks a chapter for awaiting inquiry (quēfǎng),
its drawbacks are ten.
When one person's opinion
mediates among various theories,
if it slightly misses the mark of fairness,
later generations have no means to distinguish and correct it.
This is the first drawback.
Talented scholars tend to focus on the novel,
and literati often find it difficult in principle to relinquish favored material.
If inappropriately mixed into the book,
it harms the structure of the history.
If excised and not recorded,
it omits the context and nuance.
This is the second drawback.
Transmitted reports must contain differences and similarities,
and it is practically difficult to completely erase their traces.
If a general catalogue is not provided,
then miscellaneous narratives and accumulated stories
will arise and cause confusion.
This is the third drawback.
If initially, because the facts were unclear,
they were temporarily put aside and not recorded,
later even the title of the event is omitted,
which is equivalent to a mud ox entering the sea (being utterly lost).
This is the fourth drawback.
Records are easy to disperse but hard to gather.
If a brief supporting outline is not preserved,
then the books of that era
consequently perish along with their titles.
Even if later generations wish to research them,
the source has no guide.
This is the fifth drawback.
At that time, based on what was seen and heard,
it is easy to preserve the record.
In later generations, patching up deficiencies with great difficulty
wastes words and exhausts the mind,
and furthermore, it is difficult to obtain the truth.
This is the sixth drawback.
The *Chūnqiū* had the benefit of oral transmission;
Mǎ and Bān had specialized scholarship.
The core tradition of historical writing has long been lost.
It is difficult to expect it from Mǎ's maternal grandson
or Bān's female relative (Bān Zhāo).
If the omission and inquiry are not preserved,
it results in the author's intentions being difficult to clarify.
This is the seventh drawback.
The intentions and titles of historical biographies,
such as the chapters on Lǎo Zhuāng or Qū Jiǎ,
or categorized accounts based on topic,
such as the chapters on Xún Lì or Rú Lín—
in terms of historical methodology,
these all have a fixed placement,
and absolutely no supplementary text can be appended.
For all matters that are briefly mentioned but not detailed,
or are doubtful and difficult to resolve,
if a chapter for awaiting inquiry (quēfǎng) is not preserved,
they must be appended within the main text.
The classifications become unclear,
and the prose is difficult to call pure and clean.
This is the eighth drawback.
When commencing the compilation of books under an official bureau,
disputes regarding right and wrong erupt.
Descendants wish to glorify their ancestors,
and political factions each pursue their private interests.
If there is no verification from bronze or stone,
and transmitted reports are hard to trust,
by not establishing a section for awaiting inquiry (quēfǎng)

in order to prevent petitions and requests (stating: Since the facts are still incomplete, and what has been said is thus, we diligently preserve the outline, allowing for later investigation. Then, even narrow-minded people will have no means to start a dispute.),
there is no means to refuse biased statements.
This is the ninth drawback.
If the historian lacks unique discernment and judgment,
he is merely a document clerk.
But if he possesses unique discernment and judgment,
and does not use the awaiting inquiry (quēfǎng) section as a remedy,
then if his talent is not that of an unthroned king (Sù Wáng, i.e., Confucius),
his editing and excising will certainly often lack fairness.
This is the tenth drawback.
Someone might say that historical writing reached its pinnacle with Mǎ and Bān,
and we have never heard of such fastidiousness.
Now, must we look far back to the *Chūnqiū* for models,
while recently rejecting the *Shǐjì* and *Hànshū*?
Have historians of later generations also realized this point?
I reply:
Later historians all took the *Shǐjì* and *Hànshū* as their model.
The methodologies not included in the *Shǐjì* and *Hànshū*
were invented by later people according to their own ideas,
and mostly approach categorized collections of books,
all of which Mǎ and Bān cast aside and did not adopt.
Even following the footsteps of Mǎ and Bān,
they still fear they cannot measure up;
how much less can they innovate to remedy the mistakes of Mǎ and Bān?
Nevertheless, those who glimpsed one or two points
and slightly retained the underlying intention—
their merit cannot be entirely denied.
In Chén Shòu's *Shǔ Zhì*,
because Zhūgě Liàng did not establish official historians
and the facts concerning Shǔ were difficult to obtain through searches,
he consequently, at the end of the fifteen biographies (liè zhuàn),
uniquely included Yáng Xì's *Jì Hàn Fǔ Chén Zàn*
and the *Yì Bù Qí Jiù Zá Jì* to supplement them.
In Cháng Qú's *Huáyáng Guó Zhì*,
because the scholars and women of Hànzhōng were known for their virtue, fidelity, and integrity
and these accounts had been transmitted for a long time,
yet for their inherited sayings and scattered incidents
there were no verifiable records,
in the *Xù Zhì* chapter
he listed all their names
without editing or excising them.
This seems to grasp the meaning of "hear much, omit the doubtful" (duō wén quē yí).
It is a pity that they failed to establish a general standard and set up a specific methodology,
or specially compose a dedicated chapter.
Later people did not take the time to search for the hidden meaning,
which led to the scholarship of sole determination
and books of categorized comparison
continuously following one another in the world,
and the meaning of the *Chūnqiū* became obscured.
routinely compile a section on biographical subjects (Rénwù),
placing it among mountains, rivers, temples, tombs, local products (Fāngwù), and native specialties (Tǔchǎn).
However, regarding the structure of the biographical chapters (Lièzhuàn) in previous histories,
no further consideration is given to it.
Whether they achieved great merit and splendid accomplishments,
or possessed hidden virtue and subtle brilliance,
all are constrained by abbreviated summaries measuring barely an inch.
The arrangement and compilation,
are roughly like a lexicon (Lèishū);
Since the form is already superficial,
the content collected is also indiscriminately excessive and immoderate.
In the records contained in the old gazetteers,
the number of biographical subjects (Rénwù) is sparse,
yet in the praise offered,
scholars are all Fú Shēng and Zhèng Xuán,
there is carelessly no distinction made:
talents are entirely Bān Gù and Yáng Xióng,
officials must be Gōng Suì and Huáng Bà,
and conduct is only Zēngzǐ and Shǐ Yú.
Furthermore, the literary style used,
is especially incomprehensible.
Sometimes it resembles superficial social remarks,
sometimes it resembles official documents and communiqués.
It is filled carelessly with parallel phrases,
intermixed with conventional examination-essay (Tiěkù) sentences.
Following the names and seeking the substance,
one is utterly lost upon opening the volume.
In all such cases,
they may be ordinary deeds of local villagers,
pleaded for and indiscriminately included;
or they may be famous figures of the day,
whose facts have been lost.
To delete them would cause the deceased (Jiǔyuán) to suffer injustice,
but to compile them makes them difficult to assign to the standard biographical structure (Zhuànlì).
Furthermore, when one event has two accounts,
with discrepancies and similarities mixed,
to favor one leads to huge differences in praise or censure,
but to include both makes the balance of praise and blame unsettled.
If one seeks to match name and reality without regret,
placement is truly difficult.
As for people of recent times,
whose deeds are submitted for inclusion,
we must inquire into the details from beginning to end,
leaving out nothing, however trivial,
and fully compile them within the biographical chapters (Lièzhuàn),
without setting any limits of era or time.
Among these, there are also names that are heard of,
but whose actual deeds are not prominent.
If included indiscriminately in a comparable category volume,
they might perhaps be hidden away,
but entering the format of the historian (Shǐ Shì),
they are difficult to lend themselves to inclusion.
Now, having made separate deletions and omissions,
and occupying the same space as the biographical chapters (Lièzhuàn),
each is given a heading
so that they can mutually illustrate
the official biographies (Zhèngzài Zhū Zhuàn).
Therefore, I relate the principles and precedents (Yìlì),
waiting for those who come later to know how to judge and decide.
Preface on the Precedents for the Biographies in the Former Gazetteer of Yǒngqīng Xiàn
When historians (Shǐ Jiā) compile and complete a work,
they must draw upon the writings of predecessors,
collecting and categorizing them.
This is to distinguish the origins of the school tradition (Jiāxué),
and clarify the sources of the compromises made (Zhézhōng).
Sīmǎ Tán's discussion of the scholarship of the Six Schools (Liù Jiā),
resembles Zhuāngshēng’s (Zhuāngzǐ) recounting of Qín Zhāng and Mò Dì (Mòzǐ),
or Xúnzǐ’s criticism of the teachings of the Twelve Schools.
As for Sīmǎ Qiān’s narrative in the *Table of the Twelve Feudal Lords* (*Shí'èr Zhūhóu Biǎo Xù*),
concerning the various schools of Lǚ Bùwéi (*Lǚ Lǎn*), Yú Qīng, Duó Jiāo, and Zuǒ Qiūmíng,
and their respective *Spring and Autumn Annals* (Chūnqiū) school traditions,
he repeatedly expounded and clarified the essential purposes of their writings.
This is the source relied upon by the one hundred thirty chapters. (Sīmǎ Qiān’s adherence to the *Chūnqiū* reflects the intent of Yú, Lǚ, Duó, and Zuǒ. People who mock his presumption are wrong.)
Bān Gù composed a biography (Lièzhuàn) for Sīmǎ Qiān,
and Fàn Yè composed a biography for Bān Gù,
wherein the school traditions (Jiāxué) are fully preserved.
But when Shěn Yuē wrote the biography of Fàn Yè,
and Yáo Sīlián wrote the biography of Shěn Yuē,
they did not prioritize a specialized chapter focused on historical matters (Shǐ Shì);
consequently, historians no longer adhered to the method of tracing the lineage and origins (Zǔshù Yuānyuán).
Now, compiling this gazetteer,
if we do not compose a biography for the former gazetteer authors,
that is tantamount to openly seizing what belongs to others and submerging their names,
which is even worse than Shěn Yuē and Yáo Sīlián failing to preserve the school tradition (Jiāxué).
This is because old gazetteers of prefectures and counties are easily lost,
and do not possess the power of Fàn Yè’s History (Fàn Shǐ) or Shěn Yuē’s works to long endure.
The importance of recording the duties of the official historian (Shǐ Guān),
is like the importance of the Classicist (Jīng Shī) in the *Biographies of the Confucians* (*Rúlín*),
or the importance of the literary author in the *Biographies of the Literary Figures* (*Wényuàn*).
The *Biographies of the Confucians* (*Rúlín Lièzhuàn*) ought to clarify how the great Way (Dà Dào) was disseminated and recorded,
and the origins of the transmission from master to disciple (Shīshòu Yuānyuán);
the *Biographies of the Literary Figures* (*Wényuàn Lièzhuàn*) ought to clarify the changes in literary trends (Fēnghuì Biànqiān),
and the various schools of literary men (Wénrén Liúbié).
This is what is meant by the works of the historian (Shǐ Jiā):
they do not merely record events,
but also illuminate the Way (Míng Dào).
If the *Rúlín* and *Wényuàn* fail to illuminate the essentials of the Way,
merely relating one or two deeds of scholars and literati,
they have already lost the original meaning of the ancients in naming those chapters.
Furthermore, the importance of historical scholarship,
traces its lineage far back to the *Spring and Autumn Annals* (*Chūnqiū*),
yet later historians do not establish specialized chapters.
This causes the work of specialized writing and compilation
to be buried and untraceable.
Is this not a great lack of consideration on the part of the historians?
When established histories (Liè Shǐ) fully exist,
yet specialized biographies are not established,
the defect is already so great.
How much more so for books from prefectures and counties,
whose records are minor and easily obscured,
how can they be without specialized records?
Before a book is completed,
there must be sources relied upon,
such as Sīmǎ Qiān’s History drawing on the *Shìběn* and the *Guócè*,
or Bān Gù’s book relying on Féng Shāng and Liú Xīn.
This is correct.
Once a book is completed,
there must be those who transmit it,
such as Yáng Yùn disseminating Sīmǎ Qiān’s book,
or Mǎ Róng receiving the Han History.
This is correct.
Once a book establishes a school (Chéng Jiā),
there must be those who study and practice it diligently,
such as Xú Guǎng and Cuī Yīn annotating Mǎ Róng (i.e., Sīmǎ Qiān’s work),
or Fú Qián and Yīng Shào explaining Bān Gù.
This is correct.
This is why the origins of the school tradition (Jiāxué Yuānyuán) must rely on specialized chapters and biographies (Lièzhuàn) to be illuminated.
After Mǎ Róng and Bān Gù,
the family tradition (Jiāxué) gradually declined (the family tradition passed down through generations).
But the scholarship established by heroic and outstanding individuals (Míngjiā zhī Xué) arose,
characterized by specialized scholarly institutions.
Such as the various schools concerning the *History of the Later Han* (*Hòu Hàn Shū*), including Sīmǎ Biāo, Huá Jiào, Xiè Chéng, and Fàn Wèizōng (Fàn Yè),
and the eighteen schools concerning the *History of Jìn* (*Jìn Shū*), including Hé Fǎshèng.
This is correct.
When the records of one dynasty are simultaneously compiled,
and the historians (Shǐ Chén) do not serve under one specialized official,
then people compile their own versions,
and each school offers its own explanation.
If they are not narrated and discussed,
and gathered within a single chapter,
how can a balanced compromise (Zhézhōng) be achieved?
This is why the different branches of these schools must rely on specialized chapters and biographies (Lièzhuàn) to be illuminated.
Since the Six Dynasties (Liù Dài),

specialized scholarship (Míngjiā) has again ceased (the father-son hereditary tradition constitutes the family tradition [Jiāxué]; individual, specialized authorship constitutes the specialized scholarship [Míngjiā]).
Instead, the method of gathering many people to compile a book became prevalent,
such as the Táng people compiling the *History of Jìn* (*Jìn Shū*),
or the Yuán people compiling the three histories of Sòng, Liáo, and Jīn.
This is correct.
The Supervising Ministers (Jiānxiū Dàchén)
are named prominently at the start of the bamboo slips (the text),
but the officials responsible for compilation, editing, and collation
are inconsistently hidden or visible.
Even if the individuals and their roles in historical compilation are sometimes noted,
it is unknown who compiled which Basic Annals (Jì) or Table (Biǎo),
or who edited which Treatise (Zhì) or Biography (Zhuàn);
who established the initial framework and regulations,
or who polished the literary quality.
If they are not properly organized and linked,
tracing back each source,
it is unavoidable that within a single work,
merits and flaws appear side by side,
and credit and blame are difficult to determine.
This is why the effort expended on a single book must rely on specialized chapters and biographies (Lièzhuàn) to be illuminated.
As for the methods of the Daily Records (Rì Lì) and the Activity Records (Qǐjū),
the collections stored in the Yán Gé (Pavilion) and Guǎng Nèi (Inner Treasury),
the system of submitting memorials to propose posthumous titles (Yì Shì),
and the evidence drawn from unofficial accounts (Bàiguān Yěshǐ),
sometimes these are explained in detail in a preface of precedents (Xùlì) at the beginning of the biography,
clarifying the system;
or sometimes they are discussed in a concluding commentary (Lùnshù) at the end of the biography,
explaining the reasons.
There is no method that is unsuitable.
This is also like the introductory narratives in the *Rúlín* biographies,
where the educational system is clearly established,
manifesting the inherited intention of establishing scholastic officials (Xuégūan).
Truly, if this intention is grasped and applied throughout the historical writings,
yet one still worries that historical scholarship (Shǐxué) will not flourish,
or that the Way of History (Shǐ Dào) will not be illuminated,
I have never heard of such a case.
The local gazetteer (zhìchéng 誌乘) is the book of a xiàn (county)
—that is, the history of a guó (state) in ancient times—
yet contemporary people overlook it;
this is because family learning (jiāxué) is not established,
the master's methods (shīfǎ) are lost to transmission,
the writing is not refined and elegant,
and it is difficult for models and standards to be passed down.
When a new compilation is completed,
and the old books are covered and stored,
it is not necessarily the case that the new book is entirely superior
and the old gazetteer is entirely inferior.
What the old gazetteer contains,
the new gazetteer repeatedly records,
and whether its textual emendation and deletion (bǐxuē) is good or bad,
there is initially no time to distinguish;
but what the old gazetteer failed to record,
the new gazetteer must have augmented,
thus, this is one reason why old gazetteers are easily dismissed.
Compilers and authors,
like to show off their own strengths,
and later books
are prone to attacking and finding fault.
I often see that all those who compile gazetteers,
when first establishing the organizational principles (fánlì),
if they do not say that the old books are crude and negligible,
then they claim that the previous authors were unfounded,
and then they are again attacked by those who follow,
a continuous succession of bad examples.
In reality, it is like the ape-keeper (jūgōng 狙公) merely reversing the sequence of three and four
—fundamentally there is no great divergence;
but since the previous authors are gone,
there is no way to verify them with evidence,
thus, this is the second reason why old gazetteers are easily dismissed.
The books of the zhōu (prefecture) and xiàn (county)
are mostly crude and negligible,
and literary men and scholars
bundle them up and do not read them.
Those who make a special effort to search and collect them,
and cite them elsewhere for investigation,
do nothing more than use this to prove that,
and are initially not fond of the book itself.
When the new and old versions
are placed mixed together before them,
those who flip through them
are like candidates in the imperial examinations
who seek to buy model essays (chéngmò),
or like practitioners of Yīnyáng
who consult the annual almanac (xiànshū 憲書),
they take the new and discard the old—
this is the natural tendency of circumstances,
fundamentally not due to any special selection,
thus, this is the third reason why old gazetteers are easily dismissed.
Now, Suǒ Suī’s 《Chūnqiū》 (Suǒ Suī compiled the 《Qiánliáng Chūnqiū》)
relied heavily on Biān Liú;
(Liú received the mandate from Zhāng Jùn and compiled the inner and outer affairs of Liáng.) Cháng Qú’s 《Guózhì》 (The 《Huáyáng Guózhì》)

was half copied from Qiáo Zhōu’s work. (The 《Huáyáng Guózhì》 records the beginnings and endings of the Lǐ family. Its two histories of the Liú family are largely derived from Qiáo Zhōu’s 《Shǔ Běnjì》.)
This means that a book concerning one region
cannot be without reliance upon the records of that same region,
yet gazetteer authors fail to list the biographies (zhuàn) of previous authors.
Is this not 'forgetting the fish trap once the fish is caught' (déyú wàngquán),
an unexamined habit?
Furthermore, why should we wonder that gazetteer writings
are lost and difficult to examine?
The official who supervised the compilation,
and the scholar who held the brush,
when writing their composition,
did not distinguish between name and reality (míngshí);
this is the first reason why previous gazetteers are difficult to transmit.
The prefaces and postscripts were set up perfunctorily,
providing no illumination of the book;

this is the second reason why previous gazetteers are difficult to transmit. (If there were illumination, they would be like Mǎ [Qiān] and Bān [Gù]'s recording of their "Self-Preface" (Zìxù), which can serve as a biography.)
The people who compiled the gazetteers,
their actions and achievements (hángyè) are not detailed;
this is the third reason why previous gazetteers are difficult to transmit.
The source material used for the book,
is not labeled by section title;
this is the fourth reason why previous gazetteers are difficult to transmit.
Gazetteers should be continuously supplemented,
and unless absolutely necessary,
they should not be repeatedly revised;
a repeatedly revised book,
if one wishes to preserve them all together,
becomes overly complex and burdensome;
this is the fifth reason why previous gazetteers are difficult to transmit.
Amidst what is difficult to transmit,
I compose biographies for them [the old gazetteers],
which is done out of necessity to preserve them,
to illuminate their origins,
and to serve as a model for future generations.
Yǒngqīng Xiànzhì Wénzhēng Xùlì (Preface and Principles for the Collection of Writings in the Yǒngqīng County Gazetteer)
The 《Yǒngqīng Xiànzhì》 has been completed,
divided into six categories: Jì (Annals), Biǎo (Tables), Tú (Maps), Shū (Books), Zhènglüè (Administrative Strategy), and Lièzhuàn (Biographies),
establishing twenty-five chapters,
with each chapter having its own principles.
Furthermore, we selected the historical events and writings collected during a certain period,
choosing those related to Yǒngqīng but which could not be included in the main gazetteer,
and categorized them according to type,
separating them into Zòuyì (Memorials), Zhēngshí (Verification of Facts), Lùnshuō (Discourses), and Shīfù (Poetry and Rhapsodies),
each forming one volume,
totaling four volumes.
Each volume has a summary record (xùlù) as follows,
and a general introduction summarizes the main points
to head the compilation.
The introduction states:
In ancient times, when there were officials with specialized duties,
there were corresponding affairs managed by them;
when there were specialized fields of study,
there were corresponding scholarly writings;
never was there a practice of widely collecting from various schools
and compiling various literary forms
like the selections of literature (wénxuǎn) done in later generations.
With the decline of official institutions and the disappearance of schools of study,
literary works became increasingly abundant.
Based on what one values,
one gathers famous and excellent works,
such as Xiāo Shì’s 《Wénxuǎn》
and Yáo Shì’s 《Wéncuì》,
which are examples of this.
Tracing the flow back to the source,
and extending it to reach the principles of governance,
the 《Sòng Wén zhī Jiàn》 is an example of this.
Comparing and examining the texts,
and proceeding to serve as an auxiliary to history,
the 《Yuán Wén zhī Lèi》 is an example of this.
The intentions of these few authors
can be said to be consummate.
However, if we analyze the core principles of the fifteen 《Guófēng》 and the eight guó 《Guóyǔ》 in ancient times,
as well as the Jìn Chéng (Annals of Jìn), the Chǔ Táowù (Annals of Chǔ), and the various states' Spring and Autumn Annals (Chūnqiū),
then the historical books of the feudal states
and their textual records, manifestos, vocal verses (wén gào shēng shī)
complemented each other.
In the past, there was not an absence of such precedents.
Liú Zhījǐ of the Táng dynasty once worried that historical writings contained too many trivial utterances,
and wished to take imperial edicts, memorials, and similar items,
categorize them by type,
and form a separate literary style
to be included in the biographical histories (jìzhuàn zhī shǐ).
This shows he failed to observe the ancient custom where each type had its own established book,
complementing and enriching each other.
However, observing the books of the ancients,
when the 《Guóyǔ》 records words,
it must narrate the beginning and end of the event;
the meanings of the 《Chūnqiū》 were transmitted via the Zuǒ family (Zuǒ Shì),
and the 《Shī》 (Book of Songs) has narratives provided by the state historian (guóshǐ),
so even if the events are a thousand years in the past,
readers are perfectly clear and have no doubts.
Later authors who selected literature
collected texts and phrases,
but no longer fully provided their beginnings and endings,
such as when a memorial (zòuyì) is worth reading
but the response (bào kě 報可) is not recorded;
when the spoken words had a purpose
but the era and circumstances are not recounted;
when the poetry and songs held symbolic meaning
but the causes of the events are not attached;
then readers have no way to reach a definitive conclusion,
and how does that benefit historical affairs?
The 《Wénxuǎn》 and 《Wéncuì》
are certainly beyond reproach;
but the 《Wénjiàn》 and 《Wénlèi》,
whose vision did not extend this far,
are they not cases where "even a foot has its limitations"?
Contemporary compilers of gazetteers,
fail to list book titles in the 'Arts and Literature' (yìwén) section,
and indiscriminately include miscellaneous forms of poetry and prose;
their shortcomings are self-evident;
this is also because at the time of compilation,
they already failed to recognize that it ought to be compiled according to the standards of a state history,
thus, all sorts of crude and disorganized writings
are included,
so why should this be surprising?
Now we have slightly rectified this,
creating a separate section for the 《Wénzhēng》,
and still, after the section for poetry and prose,
briefly outlining the beginnings and endings [of the events],
to facilitate reader viewing,
omitting anything doubtful.
This is merely an explanation of the principles
to articulate the main idea.
Zòuyì Xùlù (Summary Record for Memorials)
serve
to manage affairs and synthesize matters,
widely setting forth the principles of governance (Zhìdào);
the utility of literary composition (Wénzhāng zhī yòng),
none is more important than this.
However, when Xiāo Tǒng selected literature,
he used the Rhapsody (Fù) to lead the collection;
later generations compiling various authors,
accepted this as a fixed law and rule (Kēlǜ),
thereby also losing the meaning of proper emphasis and priority.
If one says that those (selections) are merely literary works (Cízhāng jiāyán),
fundamentally inappropriate for historical precedent (Shǐlì),
then the Rhapsody is merely an appendage to the Six Principles (Liù Yì)
yet is listed before the poetry (Shī);
the Lament (Sāo) is the ancestor (Bǐzǔ) of the Rhapsody,
yet is separately placed after the poetry—
its arbitrary and inverted arrangement,
is likewise difficult to justify (Zìjiě).
And [works like] the *Wényuàn* and the *Wénjiàn*,
followed and honored this arrangement—
what explanation is there for this?
Now, by placing the Memorials and Proposals (Zòuyì) at the beginning,
taking this as the general rule for compiling writings (Jíwén tōnglì),
I humbly compare it to the annals (Běnjì) preceding the biographies (Liè Shǐ) in historical works.
Historians' practice of adopting memorials and proposals (Zòuyì),
is like the *Shàngshū* recording instructions and admonitions (Xùngào):
those concerning the institutions of a specific era (Zhìdù),
are cut and placed into the chapters of treatises (Shūzhì);
those concerning the establishment of an individual's reputation,
are compiled within the biographies (Lièzhuàn).
However, the scope of the annals and biographies (Jìzhuàn piānfú),
is each limited and fixed,
while the documents of memorials (Zòudú) of one era,
are numerous in words,
extensive inclusion would make the historical style (Shǐtǐ) dissimilar,
while omitting favorite parts would leave textual gaps.
Observing Bān Shì’s *Hàn Shū*,
it details the writings and memorials,
yet upon re-examining the *Yìwén Zhì*,
those related to the Shíqú memorials and proposals (Zòuyì),
and the accounts of Gāozǔ and Xiàowén’s discussions, pronouncements, and edicts (Cèzhào),
never failed to have specialized books
separate from the standard history (Zhèng Shǐ).
Therefore, the compilation of memorials and proposals (Zòuyì),
is indeed related to the veritable records (Shílù) and diaries of activity and repose (Qǐjū Zhù) as inner and outer components.
Previous scholars compiled the *Hàn Wèi Shàngshū*,
and recent times saw the compilation of *Míng Chén Zhāngzòu*,
both possessing rigorous structure and great utility,
unlike the style of literary scholars selecting texts.
Those who do not know this,
often overlook and fail to observe it,
which is truly regrettable.
Dù Yòu, in compiling the *Tōng Diǎn*,
apart from the institutions and systems of successive dynasties (Zhìdù),
separately compiled more than twenty volumes of ritual discussions (Lǐyì),
regardless of whether those words were adopted or not,
but because the discussions contained truth,
he preserved their essential principles (Mínglǐ).
This is the unique decision (Dúduàn) in writing the book,
and the general standard (Tōngcái) for its arrangement;
its intention can be intuitively grasped,
but its arguments cannot be traced or rigidly adhered to.
However, specialized books (Zhuānmén zhī shū),
make their own determinations and rules;
whether deleting or abridging,
there is certainly nothing wrong with that.
The forms of historical treatises (Shǐzhì zhī tǐ),
each have recognized functions;
when collecting texts to supplement the deficiencies of the treatises,
then recording them without explanation
follows established precedents (Jiùzhāng).
Now, having collected four pieces of memorials and proposals (Zòuyì),
and three pieces of detailed consultations and petitions (Zīxiáng Bǐngtiè),
these are also included as appendices,
because these official documents (Guānfǔ wénshū),
are close to memorials and proposals,
thus they are categorized together.
Their sequence is uniformly ordered by year and month,
thus providing the full details of the events.
Record of Evidential Narratives (Zhēngshí Xùlù)
Evidential texts (Zhēngshí zhī wén),
are a branch stream of the biography category in historical literature (Shǐ Bù zhuànjì).
In antiquity, historical laws (Shǐfǎ) were strict,
and the styles of documentation (Jìshù zhī tǐ),
each had their specialists.
Therefore, from the Wèi and Jìn dynasties onward,
literary figures generally had separate collections (Biéjí).
However, the biographies (Lièzhuàn) in various histories,
recording the writings of their lifetime,
