only mention categories such as poetry (Shī), rhapsody (Fù), admonitions (Zhēnmíng), eulogies (Sòng), and dirges (Lěi),
totaling a certain number of pieces, and nothing more.
We have never heard of them recording a certain number of narratives (Jì),
a certain number of biographies (Zhuàn),
a certain number of epitaphs (Zhì),
or a certain number of explanatory writings (Shù).
Observing from this,
it can generally be known
were, for the ancients, each specialized books,
and were initially not scattered within general literary collections (Wénjí).
that the forms of narratives, biographies, epitaphs, and explanatory writings (Jì Zhuàn Zhì Shù zhī tǐ)
Since the Táng and Sòng dynasties,
the trend of literary collections (Wénjí zhī fēng) has flourished daily,
while specialized scholarship (Zhuānmén zhī xué) has faded away.
Consequently, within a single collection,
poetry and rhapsody coexist with classical exegesis (Jīngjiě),
discussions and narratives are included together;
and in these books compiled into collections,
it becomes difficult to determine where the specialization of the school (Jiāxué) lies.
Regarding compiled anthologies,
Xiāo Tǒng's *Wén Xuǎn* did not include biographies (Zhuànjì),
while the *Wényuàn* and *Wénjiàn* gradually began to be more detailed—
this was due to the trend of the times (Shíshì).
That the collections of literary figures
can be used as historical sources (Shǐcái)
is because their learning was not specialized,
and their affairs often branched out—
is this not truly the case?
Regarding the forms of evidential texts (Zhēngshí zhī tǐ),
besides recording affairs (Jìshì),
there are also texts recounting precedents (Shǔdiǎn zhī wén),
which scholars of textual verification (Kǎojù zhī jiā)
use to differentiate from narrative texts (Xùshù zhī wén).
Applying the rules of historical methods (Shǐfǎ) to categorize them,
recording affairs (Jìshì) is the remainder of the annals and biographies (Jìzhuàn),
and recounting precedents (Shǔdiǎn) is the descendant of the treatises (Shūzhì)—
these are what are called texts having the same source but different streams.
The source of recording affairs
originates from the *Chūnqiū*,
while the source of recounting precedents
is based on the official *Lǐ* (Rites);
this is the general principle.
Texts recounting precedents (Shǔdiǎn zhī wén),
in antiquity also had specialists.
After the *Dài Jì* (Records of Dài),
such as Bān Shì’s *Báihǔ Tōngyì*,
Yīng Shì’s *Fēngsú Tōngyì*,
Cài Shì’s *Dúduàn*, and others of this kind,
are countless.
As for their inclusion in literary figures' collections,
prior to the Suí and Táng dynasties,
this form was particularly unseen.
When specialized learning declined,
and literary figures occasionally relied on what they had gained,
writing them down as textual investigations (Kǎobiàn),
or publishing them as explanatory discussions (Shùyì)—
these were insufficient to form a complete book,
yet regrettable to discard.
Consequently, having no alternative,
they were compiled into literary collections,
taking up a category
alongside poetry, rhapsody, letters, and memorials (Shūbiǎo).
This is why later generations compiling texts had no choice but to include them.
Evidential texts (Zhēngshí zhī wén),
and the narratives (Jìshì) in this current book,
are particularly related as inner and outer components;
therefore, many works differing in style have been collected and collated.
Regarding the texts of biographies and accounts (Zhuànzhuàng zhī wén),
some are comparable to the biographies (Lièzhuàn) in the main treatise.
This is precisely so that detailed and abbreviated versions coexist,
and also to show the origin from which the biographies were selected and excerpted,
so that whether the editing (Bǐxuē) was good or bad, skillful or clumsy,
can be left to later generations to distinguish, select, and judge.
I dare not hold this as my private decision.
Texts from stone inscriptions (Bēikè zhī wén),
which sometimes are not included in the category of epigraphy (Jīnshí),
have been recorded in full text;
the emphasis is on establishing the facts of the matter.
The inscriptions (Kuǎnshí) of the stone carving are still attached at the end of the chapter,
so that they can be viewed in conjunction with epigraphy.
Record of Discussions and Explanations (Lùnshuō Xùlù)
The genre of argumentative writing,
its origin lies in the *Lúnyǔ* (Analects).
Zhèng Shì's commentary on the *Yì* (Classic of Change) says:
“When clouds and thunder gather (as in the Tún hexagram),
the noble person uses them for governance and organization (jīnglún).
This refers to discussing principles, composing texts, establishing rituals,
and delighting in implementing policies.”
Thus, when they are put into use,
they become canons, plans, instructions, and admonitions;
when they are not yet put into use,
they become argumentative compositions, discussions, and deliberations.
The creations of the Sages,
although their uses differ,
their foundation arises from a single source.
The various Masters of the Zhōu and Qín periods
each maintained their specialized school.
Although their doctrines had purity or impurity,
and their language had evenness or unevenness;
yet, tracing their original intent,
they all took that which they wished to implement but could not,
and wrote it down in books,
rather than intentionally creating texts for literary beauty or spectacle;
this is the fundamental nature of argumentative writing.
Since scholarship ceased to be specialized,
and writing pursued gorgeousness,
literati thus compiled collections,
and discussions and deliberations became numerous.
Among these, isolated insights,
and those statements that happened to coincide [with ancient wisdom],
often also aligned with the ancients;
but their foundation was not deep,
their ultimate purpose was not outstanding,
or various styles emerged haphazardly,
leading naturally to inconsistency;
or when viewed collectively, both early and late pieces,
they ultimately became repetitive;
this is why the argumentative writings found in literary collections
differ from the doctrines of the specialized Masters.
Táng Mǎ Zǒng compiled the *Yì Lín* (Forest of Meanings),
editing and selecting from the various Masters,
highlighting their famous and excellent parts.
This also embodied the intention of discarding the weak points and adopting the strengths.
Now, in selecting texts here,
we preserve those arguments that are congruent;
this is also the general principle of compilation.
The various arguments in the *Wén Xuǎn*,
such as the chapters *Guò Qín* and *Biàn Wáng*,
are intended for rhetorical flourish, praise, and lamentation,
their purpose is not deep analysis and elucidation;
these belong to the category of historical critiques and encomia,
their origin is somewhat close to the tradition of poetic comparison and association (bǐ xìng),
and compared to the arguments of the Táng and Sòng eras,
they are similar in name but different in substance.
However, chapters like *Yǎng Shēng* and *Bó Yì*
already possess their own thematic intentions;
this certainly happened when literary collections flourished
and the style of the Masters declined.
Xiāo Shì did not discern this,
and compiled them together as one category,
which misses their true nature.
The style of the Masters changed once into the arguments found in literary collections,
and changed again into the informal notes (zhájì) of miscellaneous prose (shuōbù).
This was the juncture where Sòng people dedicated themselves to learning
and sought to return to simplicity and sincerity (fǎn pǔ huán chún).
However, as their interests were diverse,
they could neither completely discard the habits of the literati,
nor treat the subject matter too easily,
nor could they achieve deep mastery and effortless fulfillment.
Reviewing all the authors
and investigating their methods,
they mostly collected remnants from literary collections,
taking what they gained coincidentally,
and what they had not immediately been able to structure into formal compositions,
noting and recording them.
Accumulating little by little to form a large quantity,
they compiled them into volumes.
Therefore, the general principles are often worth observing,
but the ultimate aim is difficult to fully explore.
The literary records of Yǒngqīng are sparse.
Argumentative writings
were unavailable for selection.
We have reserved approximately one piece
merely to complete the category,
not daring to claim that it aligns with the standards of the ancients.
Record of Poetry and Rhapsodies (Shīfù)
Poetry and Rhapsodies
are the fanfare of the Six Classics,
and the embodiment of rhythm in literature.
In ancient times, sung poetry established education;
the resonance was practiced under the Director of Music (Sī Yuè),
and the poems and verses were recorded by the Grand Scribe (Tài Shǐ);
the matter was managed by specialized officials,
and the craft was passed down by scholars.
If one wished to understand the way of sound and rhythm,
or sought to know how moral education was implemented,
they inquired of those in charge of historical records,
and the details were clearly extant,
preserved in their entirety.
Since the streams of poetry and music diverged,
common artisans only practiced musical notation (gōng chǐ),
and literati merely focused on trivial romantic verse (yuè lù);
consequently, the way of sung poetry
did not connect with governance;
and the craft that was maintained by specialized officials
and preserved in historical records
is now largely forgotten and cannot be recovered.
However, from the Hàn and Wèi dynasties onward,
the songs, narrative poems, and music bureau pieces (yuèfǔ)
pointed to events and paralleled sentiments;
if we examine the finest among them,
we can still study their vocabulary
and confirm the events of their time.
After the Táng and Sòng dynasties,
although they were said to be the occupation of literati,
authors arose successively,
elucidating subtle hidden meanings
and expounding on policies and doctrines;
selecting the most exceptional among them,
they too can stand proudly alongside the ancients.
Therefore, when selecting texts regarding poetry and rhapsodies,
if we can avoid falling into the habit of frivolous literary language,
that will be close enough to the mark.
In Liú Shì's *Qī Lüè* (Seven Summaries),
the records of the Fēng Shàn rituals were placed in the *Lǐ Jīng*,
the official memorials of Qín and the *Tài Shǐ Gōng Shū* were placed in the *Chūn Qiū* category,
but *Shīfù* (Poetry and Rhapsodies) was established as its own separate summary,
not subordinate to the *Shī Jīng*.
This was because the bulk of the texts was large,
and they could not but be classified separately.
It is regrettable that its preface
failed to fully explain the origin and process,
which led to the later confusion where poetry, rhapsodies, and literary collections became undifferentiated and could not be clearly distinguished.
As for the rhapsody (fù), it is one of the Six Principles of Poetry,
and its form is recited but not sung.
Yet, the number of pieces included in the Liú Summary
was five times greater than the poetry.
Consequently, the rhapsodies were placed first,
while poetry and miscellaneous forms
were appended afterwards.
This caused subsequent compilers, such as the *Xiāo Xuǎn*,
to regard this arrangement as a fixed regulation,
which can be called a failure to properly weigh their importance.
Furthermore, his classification divided poetry and rhapsodies into five categories.
For instance, the category of Miscellaneous Rhapsodies
did not list specific authors by name,
a format resembling how later general collections differ from individual collections.
The category of poetry and songs
formed a separate class.
Although there was no preface explaining the classification,
readers could still use their judgment to distinguish them
and know the proper category.
Regarding the twenty schools starting with Qū Yuán,
the twenty-one schools starting with Lù Jiǎ,
and the twenty-five schools starting with Sūn Qīng,
since the categories were divided into three,
there must have been an explanation at the time.
However, the preface is missing (like the explanations found after the listing of the Masters, clarifying that the origins of certain schools derived from specific ancient officials, and so forth),
and unlike the volumes on the Masters,
the origins were not comprehensively explained.
This made the summary on poetry and rhapsodies
the subject where later generations, seeking to investigate the remaining texts,
could not ascertain the guiding principle.
When collecting local writings from prefectures and districts,
the selection and compilation of poetry and rhapsodies
is the lingering intent of the ancient *Guó Fēng*.
The poems regarding the Eight Views found in the old gazetteers
were quite tainted by the habits of the literati,
and were therefore all deleted,
in order to enforce strict historical standards.
The lyric verse (cí) of Wén Chéngxiàng and the *Jì Luò Hé Wén*
are recorded together although they are not strictly poetry or rhapsodies,
because rhymed compositions,
such as inscriptions (míng), admonitions (zhēn), eulogies (sòng), and laments (lěi),
are all remnants of ancient poetry.
Bó Zhōu Zhì Rénwù Biǎo Lì Yì Shàng (Discussion of the Precedent for the Table of Figures in the Bó Zhōu Gazetteer, Part One)
*Gǔjīn Rénbiǎo*
has been criticized and reviled by the world for a long time.
Viewed from the present,
histories focusing on a single dynasty (dynastic histories)
might perhaps not need a Table of Persons (*rénbiǎo*);
but comprehensive histories spanning all ages
cannot be without a Table of Persons.
Gù took a single dynasty as the scope of his book,
continuing Qīan's (*Shǐ Jì*) work;
whatever categories the Historian Qīan's writings lacked,
Gù supplemented them.
It was not merely listing the deeds of sovereigns and ministers, as detailed in the Basic Annals and Biographies (*jìzhuàn*),
merely using the Western Capital (Xījīng) as the chronological boundary.
Therefore, the Treatise on Geography (*Dìlǐ Zhì*) extended to the *Yǔ Gòng* and the *Zhōu Guān*;
the Treatise on the Five Elements (*Wǔ Xíng Zhì*) listed matters from the Spring and Autumn (*Chūnqiū*) and Warring States periods.
The principle behind the Table of Persons,
can be similarly inferred.
The fault of the Table of Persons
was inappropriately classifying people into nine ranks,
forcibly assigning positions,
and wantonly evaluating
them as Sages (*shèng*), Humane (*rén*), Wise (*zhì*), or Foolish (*yú*),
thereby failing to capture the strict impartiality of the *Chūnqiū*.
Moreover, Liú Zhījǐ pointed out that it included the ancient but omitted the contemporary,
and that the names did not accord with reality;
this explanation is also quite reasonable.
Other various criticisms arguing that it should not have been compiled
are not sufficient to be considered flaws in Bān's work.
If one were to remove those nine ranks of superiority and inferiority,
and the designations of Humane, Sage, Foolish, and Wise,
and instead use status (noble and common, high and low) to categorize their place;
or use different headings based on administrative divisions (capital or state division);
arranging them horizontally as the warp (fixed columns),
and marking the chronological sequence above
as the weft (connecting rows);
and clearly state the purpose, saying
that it was created to supplement Qīan's writings
and serve as a reference guide for the Biographies (*lièzhuàn*);
then the principle established
would definitely have become a fixed rule for later writers of comprehensive histories,
and how could it have ended up being reviled by others?
Alas!
A good method from antiquity
has been submerged amidst widespread condemnation,
without any historian of discerning judgment
saving it from its flaws and making good use of it.
In recent times, Mr. Mǎ's (Mǎ Suì) *Yì Shǐ*
seems to have used this principle.
However, Mr. Mǎ's book
fundamentally belongs to the category of compilations,
not original compositions.
Inferring its intent,
it was merely that the Three Dynasties (*sāndài*) are too far removed from the present,
the accounts and writings are scattered,
and without beginning or end;
listing them in a Table of Persons
merely serves as a study of transmitted names.
Furthermore, he still disparaged Bān's Table,
failing to understand that it could fill gaps in Qīan's writings;
nor did he understand that expanding its scope
could serve as a comprehensive standard for historians.
He merely called it a Table of Persons;
if it were created for the sake of the *Yì Shǐ*,
then he was not one who understood the category (of historical writing).
Now, comprehensive histories spanning all ages,
the deeds and events recorded
are mostly derived from ancient bamboo slips and records;
unlike contemporary records
obtained through hearing and seeing,
where authenticity and fabrication can be mutually verified.
Since a work is compiled
and claims expert authority,
then in the selection and rejection of materials for the Biographies,
the author must have unique insight and judgment
to form his school of thought.
It is inevitable

treating it the same as a compilation. For example, events from the *Zuǒ Zhuàn* were included in the *Shǐ Jì*. Yet, people like Zǐchǎn and Shū Xiàng could not all be included in separate biographies. How
that he cannot include everything by category,
Regarding the deeds of former people,
found scattered throughout various records and biographies,
the appearance or obscurity of their names
inevitably shows variation in detail and completeness.
If what remains after the selection and omission process for the Biographies
is not collected in the Table of Persons to capture the essentials,
then those omitted will lead to criticism of oversights,
and those detailed will be slandered for showing favoritism.
Even later readers of my book
will feel that something is missing and lacks proper structure.
Therefore, Bān's Table of Persons
likely drew inspiration from antiquity,
and should not be lightly criticized.
(From the middle section of "Discussion on the Principles of the Table of Persons in the Bózhōu Gazetteer")
Someone might say:
That comprehensive histories require a Table of Persons
is true.
Regarding dynastic histories,
your statement that they "might perhaps not need a Table of Persons"—
the word "perhaps" (*huò*) used here
indicates uncertainty.
If a dynastic history does not need to cite antiquity,
why should it have a Table of Persons? I reply:
Dynastic histories are not all of one type;
generally, they fall into three categories.
However, none of them can be without a Table of Persons.
Compared to comprehensive histories,
the need is naturally slightly less urgent;
but having one,
would be excellent.
A history having Biographies
is like the *Chūnqiū* having the *Zuǒ Shì*.
The *Zuǒ Shì* follows the Classic and orders events by month and year;
the Biographies divide people and apply headings.
Their form is slightly different;
but their function
is similarly to provide sufficient detail for the beginning and end of the Classic (*Chūnqiū*) (referring to the Basic Annals, *běnjì*).
Scholars who study the *Zuǒ Shì*
have compiled the *Gōngzǐ Pǔ* (Genealogy of Princelings) of the various states.
Among those who compile texts using the Basic Annals and Biographies format for a single dynasty,
there is only Bān's *Shū* (referring to *Hàn Shū*) and the Table of Persons,
which, immediately upon being recorded, was subjected to a barrage of criticism.
Who would dare to discuss the organization of figures again?
The various genealogies like the *Chūnqiū* [Genealogies], *Gōngzǐ* [Genealogies], and *Shì Zú* [Genealogies] (compiled by Dù Yù and others),
and various records like *Míng Zì Yì Tóng* (Differences in Names and Forms) (compiled by Féng Jìxiān and others) –
those who work on chronological histories
are detailed to that extent.
Yet histories using the Basic Annals and Biographies format
merely have a Table of Contents for the Biographies,
and the number of Biographies is limited.
Even the Chronological Tables (*niánbiǎo*) and Hereditary Family Tables (*shìbiǎo*)
only record kings, marquises, generals, and ministers;
thus, they naturally cannot encompass all figures
and categorize them properly.
Therefore, when scholars discuss eras and understand people,
or examine the principles of selection and omission in historical accounts,
these matters are generally obscure and hard to know.
Thus, that the Table of Persons is indispensable
is certainly true.
Gù Yánwǔ said:
"If a history lacks Chronological Tables,
then the Biographies inevitably must be numerous;
when the Biographies are numerous,
the text becomes verbose, yet events are still overlooked."
He therefore claimed that this fault began with Chén Shòu,
and that authors like Fàn [Yè], Shěn [Yǔe], Yáo [Sīlián], and Lǐ [Yánshòu]
all suffered from this shortcoming.
Gù's statement
can be described as knowing one thing but not the other.
Chronological Tables naturally cannot be discarded;
but how much space
devote to kings, dukes, generals, and ministers
did the histories of Fàn, Shěn, Yáo, and Lǐ
The histories of the Táng and Sòng dynasties
re-established Chronological Tables,
yet the verbosity of the Biographies
was several times greater than the books by Fàn and Shěn.
How did the Chronological Tables help mitigate the proliferation of Biographies?
If a Table of Persons is not established,
then the Biographies inevitably must be numerous;
Chronological Tables are merely secondary to this need.
Since the Table of Persons is ridiculed by historians
and they dare not attempt it again,
it is understandable that they busily compile biographies,
as if filling out household registers,
finding it difficult to make firm decisions
on selection and omission.
Now, for comprehensive histories spanning antiquity,
the ancient records they draw upon
are fully preserved in documents;
if they do not establish a Table of Persons,
perhaps they can, like Historian Qīan's writings, wait for Gù to supplement them,
which would not be too late.
As for dynastic histories,
whether they are based on official records and registers,
or derived from firsthand accounts,
it is impossible to record everything by category.
Yet, one cannot ensure that the events do not exist,
being involved or connected.
Therefore, summarizing names broadly
and categorizing them into a table
is sufficient to demonstrate the general principles,
and also to enforce strict, comprehensive judgment in the Biographies.
How can one wait for later generations?
Now, dynastic histories
include the superior works, like the specialized masterpieces of Bān and Chén;
the secondary works, like the collections of strengths from the Jìn and Táng dynasties;
and the inferior works, like the forced divisions and suppression/matching found in the Sòng and Yuán dynasties.
For histories by specialized masters,
a Table of Persons is essential to clarify their unique insights and distinct methods.
For histories that compile the strengths of many,
a Table of Persons is essential to prevent discrepancies and overlaps.
For histories based on forced division and matching,
a Table of Persons is essential to control their confused, excessive, and disorderly nature.
Therefore, I say that
dynastic histories,
generally divided into three categories,
none can be without a Table of Persons.
(From the latter section of "Discussion on the Principles of the Table of Persons in the Bózhōu Gazetteer")
Regarding the tables of distinguished persons (rénwù) in local gazetteers (fāngzhì),
what are they modeled after? The answer is:
They are intended to remedy the defects of local gazetteers;
they are not necessarily intended to imitate historical writings (shǐ).
However, the structure of history (shǐcái) is also present within them, and nothing more.
Those who compile local gazetteers now,
in recording distinguished persons (rénwù),
leave nothing suitable for inclusion in tables.
Moreover, the distinguished persons they do record,
on the contrary, resemble tables of distinguished persons (rénwù biǎo),
and there is no longer anything that can be called a monograph of distinguished persons (rénwù zhì);
yet, the table is not even a proper table.
The defects of local gazetteers have indeed been long-standing!
Since Sīmǎ [Qiān]'s time in history (shǐ),
the structure of biographical collections (lièzhuàn)
has never been altered.
Since local gazetteers (fāngzhì) are modeled after national history (guóshǐ),
when listing distinguished persons (rénwù) and composing biographies (zhuàn),
they ought to be more detailed than the national history.
But those who now record distinguished persons (rénwù)
delete and simplify the facts,
summarize the main ideas,
roughly constrain the format,
and categorize them into distinct sections.
Their writings are neither narrative nor discourse,
they seem like prose (sǎn) and yet like parallel prose (pián);
the polite formalities of letters (chǐdú hánwēn),
the conclusive statements of ledgers and documents (bùshū jiékān),
are indiscriminately collected and vulgarly included,
with no proper editing or selection remaining.
As for character, they are all Zēng [Zǐ] and Shǐ [Qiān];
their governance is entirely Bào [Yǒng] and Huáng [Bā];
their learning is invariably that of the Hàn Rú;
their chastity is that of Jiāng Nǚ;
their appearance is identical,
and their true disposition is hard to find.
This truly amounts to "from Kuài, without censure,"
and they might as well be recorded but not discussed.
Even if there are one or two outstanding individuals (jiǎojiǎo)
who elegantly adhere to distinctive selection criteria,
then their descriptions are overly brief,
falsely claiming lofty antiquity.
Some imitate the records and annotations of the Bamboo Annals (Zhúshū Jìzhù),
or emulate the inscriptions on stone steles (shíkè tímíng);
although they contain no useless or shallow talk,
they truly lack comprehensive structure and insightful understanding.
What results are things that resemble tables but are not tables (sì biǎo fēi biǎo),
and resemble annotations but are not annotations (sì zhù fēi zhù);
this deep-seated fault has existed for a long time.
Therefore, national historians (guóshǐ) would rather take from family genealogies (jiāchéng)
than collect local gazetteers (fāngzhì).
This is the reason for it.
Now, gazetteers (zhì),
are records (zhì).
Biographical collections (rénwù lièzhuàn)
must adopt unique perspectives and methods,
following the rigor of the Chūnqiū,
and embodying the allegorical spirit (bǐxīng) of the poets.
Through arrangement, combination, selection, and rejection,
they form their own school of thought (jiāyán);
although they are called the records of a single locality (yīfāng zhī zhì),
they are also the embodiment, though minor, of national history (guóshǐ).
Now, by making tables of distinguished persons (rénwù lièbiǎo),
there are generally three advantages.
If emperors (dìwáng) of previous dynasties are mentioned,
whose ancestral homes (gùlǐ) still exist today,
for gazetteer writers (zhìjiā) to include them among distinguished persons (rénwù),
is ethically inappropriate;
but to omit them entirely
also seems like neglecting a custom (quēdiǎn).
Therefore, when local gazetteers (fāngzhì) encounter this,
there is much contentious debate,
and those who rely on private cleverness and forced interpretation (sīzhì chuānzuò zhī liú)
often selectively excerpt from the basic annals (běnjì),
cleverly change the titles,
and twist the arrangement,
never achieving accuracy.
Now, by removing such figures from the biographies (zhuàn)
but listing the emperors (dìwáng) in the tables (biǎo),
then both omission and inclusion become appropriate,
establishing a permanent system.
This is the first advantage.
Historical biographies (shǐzhuàn) are inherently detailed regarding distinguished persons (rénwù),
yet gazetteer writers (zhìjiā) conversely summarize them briefly.
This is fundamentally an extracted comparison from reference works (lèishū),
and is truly not the comprehensive structure of the historian (shǐshì).
However, having cited the records and documents,
and returning to their essential meaning,
then the bamboo slips and documents (jiǎncè) containing names
must also not be collected indiscriminately,
as in an encyclopedic compilation (lèizuǎn).
Thus, regarding ancient figures recorded in historical documents (shǐcè),
if they are inappropriate for inclusion in the biographies (zhuànlì),
listing their names in the table of distinguished persons (rénwù zhī biǎo)
will ensure that it is detailed without being excessive,
and sparse without being incomplete.
This is the second advantage.
In the accounts of historians (shǐjiā),
what is seen is detailed over what is heard,
and they are lenient toward the present but strict toward antiquity;
circumstances naturally necessitate this.
As for the virtues cherished in the locality (xiāngdǎng zìhǎo),
and small acts of goodness in the family,
deeds of righteousness (yìxíng) are often only preserved as headings,
and integrity (jiécāo) merely listed under annual entries.
If historical standards (shǐfǎ) do not include them,
gazetteer writers (zhìjiā) ought to provide them.
If the biographies (zhuàn) lack substantial facts that can be recorded,
then the text will not be overly verbose;
if the tables (biǎo) contain specially distinguished names,
then the principle of righteousness (yì) will not be suppressed.
This is the third advantage.
All three of these points
are the common flaws of recent gazetteers (jìn zhì),
and are difficult matters for the author (zuòjiā) to address.
Therefore, I say:
The creation of tables of distinguished persons (rénwù) in local gazetteers (fāngzhì)
is intended to remedy the defects of local gazetteers.
Bózhōu Zhì Zhǎnggù Lìyì Shàng
The creations of the former kings (xiānwáng),
preserved in the Six Arts (Liùyì),
once their structure is clarified,
can the world be shown in the palm of one's hand?
The Shū [Jīng] discusses governmental affairs (zhèngshì),
the canons (diǎn), counsels (mó), tributes (gòng), and patterns (fàn),
which can serve as essential classics.
However, the details and calculations of the Zhōu Guān [Rites]
were not included in the documents of the Four Dynasties.
The Xià Lǐ and the Yīn Lǐ,
though the Master (Fūzǐ) could speak of them,
their records no longer exist today.
Indeed, the major aspects of governance, teaching, canons, and instruction
constitute specialized books;
whereas the detailed complexities of personnel, offices, and objects
are separately recorded in their own documents.
Their purposes (yì) each have their appropriate place.
Therefore, even with the governing principles of Zhōu [Gōng] and Kǒng [Zǐ],
they could not be merged into one single volume.
Sīmǎ Qiān followed the methods of the Chūnqiū,
and composed the Twelve Basic Annals (Shí'èr Běnjì).
His chronological tables (niánbiǎo) and biographical collections (lièzhuàn)
were organized sequentially as chapters,
sufficient to encompass the full account of events.
But concerning institutional statutes and systems (diǎnzhāng zhìdù),
which serve to regulate human relations (rénlún)
and structure the universe (shìzhòu),
he separately composed the Eight Treatises (Bā Shū)
to discuss them.
Bān Shì [Gù] expanded this into Ten Treatises (Shí Zhì).
Later historians followed this,
with mutual additions and deletions,
which then became the fixed methodology for historians.
In the past, when Hán Xuānzǐ saw the Yì Xiàng and the Chūnqiū,
he said that the Rites of Zhōu (Zhōu Lǐ) were preserved in Lǔ.
Zuǒ Shì [Qīumíng], compiling the records of the Chūnqiū,
frequently cited the Rites Classics (Lǐ Jīng).
The origin of the writings (shū) and treatises (zhì),
was likely derived from official Rites (guān lǐ).
The Tiānguān [section] not yet having been changed to Astronomy (Tiānwén),
and the Píngzhǔn [section] not yet having been changed to Food and Money (Shíhuò),
still preserves one or two terms from the Hàn Shū,
which can be imagined.
However, Zhèng Qiáo asserted:
“The great origin of the treatises (zhì)
comes from the Ěryǎ,”
which is not the essence of the matter.
Nevertheless, [Sīmǎ] Qiān and [Bān] Gù, in their writings and treatises (shū zhì),
selected the main outlines,
and discussed the general principles,
so that those who recite and study them can ascertain the general outline of a dynasty,
and obtain mutual illumination with the Annals (jì) and Biographies (zhuàn).
This is sufficient.
As for names of objects, ritual vessels, and numbers,
they believed that specialized books existed for these,
and did not seek complete coverage.
This is like Zuǒ Shì [Qīumíng]'s citing of classics and referencing texts (shǔ diǎn zhēng wén),
not needing to possess every single detail of the Zhōu Guān.
The end of Sīmǎ's Treatise on Rites (Lǐshū) states:
“Matters concerning ritual vessels and dishes (zǔ dòu zhī shì)
are preserved by the relevant officials.”
The implication for other matters can thus be understood.
Since Shěn [Yuè] and Fàn [Yè],
the substance of discussion gradually diminished,
and the addition of technical details and measurements gradually expanded.
Reaching Ōuyáng [Xiū]'s *Xīn Táng Shū* treatises (zhì),
with thirteen categories (míngmù),
the book totaled fifty volumes (juǎn).
Official documents and registers,
and notes on currency (quánhuò),
were classified and categorized,
as if fearing they were not detailed enough.
The *Sòng Shǐ*, *Jīn Shǐ*, and *Yuán Shǐ* are even more excessively voluminous,
filling couches and stacking tables,
making it difficult to grasp the essential principles.
This is almost like wishing to take the official duties
of the *Zhōu Guān*, and the rituals and demeanors of the canonical rites,
and put them entirely into the *Chūn Qiū*,
before calling it complete.
If so, then the Master (Kǒng Fūzǐ 孔夫子) in editing and composing the *Lǐ*, *Yuè*, *Shī*, and *Shū*,
would not have needed to divide the Classics into six.
Now, the treatises (shū zhì) of Mǎ [Qiān] and Bān [Gù],
when they were first created,
generally preserved the remnants of the Hundred Schools (zhūzǐ).
Works like the *Guǎnzi*, the *Lǚ Lǎn*, and the *Hóng Liè*,
in the chapters describing astronomy, geography, official maps, and music systems,
collected rules and numbers,
applied their own judgment,
and compiled them into the doctrines of a single school—
this is what [Mǎ and Bān] imitated.
How could Mǎ [Qiān] and Bān [Gù] not know that names, numbers, and physical artifacts
should not be overlooked?
It is because they considered that these items each had their own established texts,
and were not suited for inclusion in the doctrines of a single school;
they merely sought comprehensiveness indirectly.
If one wishes to seek comprehensiveness indirectly,
the writing will inevitably be voluminous and disordered,
the structure (lì) inevitably complex,
and the matters discussed may conversely become obscure and unclear.
However, as for works compiled by Classicists as policy summaries,
or by classifiers as essential collections,
they are fundamentally not creative compositions.
They merely aim for encompassing all matters
and facilitating searching and checking.
Such voluminous simplicity is not worth criticizing.
Historians (shǐjiā) govern and manage various discourses,
intending to achieve permanence,
but if they focus only on trivial technical details and measurements,
picking them up without pause,
this shows ignorance that the spirit of the *Chūn Qiū*
and the *Guān Lǐ* (Official Rites) may be sought mutually,
but their organizational principles (lì) cannot be mixed.
[From the] Bózhōu Gazetteer, Discussion of Precedents for Official Systems (Zhǎnggù), Part I (Zhōng): Since detailed registers
and documents are not to be mixed
with historical treatises,
and the fundamental structure (Jiǎ Yǐ zhāng běn) used by the ancients
cannot be known by later generations,
then if one wishes to research ancient systems and ascertain their details,
where should one seek the path? The answer is:
The regulations of Shúsūn [Tōng],
the military law of Hán Xìn,
and the statutes and ordinances of Xiāo Hé,
were all essential canonical texts of the early Hàn dynasty,
just like the Six Canons (liù diǎn) of the *Zhōu Guān*.
The *Hàn Zhì* could not encompass and preserve
the rites, music, punishments, and laws,
partly because those texts themselves belonged to the imperial offices,
and people could consult the relevant officials and obtain them.
When officials failed and books were lost,
it was because their form was overly complex and heavy;
naturally, they could not circulate widely.
This has been true since antiquity;
it was not unique to the Hàn dynasty.
Ōu [Xiū] and the Sòng compilers
did not understand this reason,
and thus wished to use the power of history to transmit [those details].
Literary works (wénzhāng) are easy to transmit,
but measurements and systems (dù shù) are hard to maintain over time.
Thus, more than half of the *Lǐ*
was lost, and the *Yuè Jīng* completely disappeared.
If the Six Arts (Liù Yì) are already like this,
how much more so historical writing?
Furthermore, the *Táng Shū* is double the size of the Hàn histories,
and the *Sòng Shǐ* is double the size of the Táng histories;
they already seem impossible to handle.
The nature of all things
is to reach a limit.
If later generations were again to double the size of the Táng and Sòng histories to complete a work,
it would be like linking beds and building upon houses.
Leaving aside the fact that human attention and capacity would certainly be insufficient to cover it all,
the longer it is delayed,
the eventually it must also perish.
In this way, due to the complexity and bulk of the systems and measurements,
they paradoxically cause the historical texts themselves to perish as well.
How then could the power of history still preserve those systems and measurements?
If so, then should the regulations and precedents of former dynasties
simply be allowed to perish? The answer is:
Historical studies (shǐxué) declined in the Táng dynasty,
and historical methodology (shǐ fǎ) was also not fully established in the Táng.
Before Ōuyáng's *Táng Zhì* was published,
Táng scholars already perceived that canonical systems and institutions
should not be sought completely within the historical treatises (shǐ zhì).
Mister Liú [Zhìjī] had the *Zhèng Diǎn*,
and Mister Dù [Yòu] had the *Tōng Diǎn*.
Both imitated the Six Canons of the *Zhōu Guān*,
encompassing institutions and precedents,
gathering both major and minor details;
the books filled a hundred bundles.
They did not fail to say that the achievements of rulers and ministers
could be detailed in the Basic Annals and Biographies (jì zhuàn),
but that systems, names, and numbers
were difficult to fully encompass in the treatises (shū zhì).
Therefore, they urgently undertook this compilation.
As for the early Sòng, Mister Wáng [Pǔ] had the *Táng Huìyào* and the *Wǔ Dài Huìyào*.
Later, Mister Xú [Tiānjié] further created the *Liǎng Hàn Huìyào*.
These works filled in gaps in antiquity
and summarized entire dynasties.
Although they shared the same source
but followed different currents
compared to the canons (diǎn) of Liú and Dù,
they all generally synthesized and examined institutions and precedents, kept separate from the historical treatises (shǐ zhì).
Their guiding principles (yì lì) are clearly established
and immutable.
Since the essential canons compiled during the Táng and Sòng
were already like this,
later people compiling the Táng and Sòng histories
should immediately adopt that method
to organize the Táng and Sòng systems,
allowing them to proceed alongside
the history of Basic Annals and Biographies (jì zhuàn).
Then the traditions of the *Chūn Qiū*
and the *Zhōu Lǐ* would continue their flow side by side.
If followed through successive generations,
would this not be excellent?
Why did Ōuyáng [Xiū], when narrating the Táng,
and the Yuán compilers, when compiling the Sòng,
instead take technical details and measurements not collected by previous histories,
and excessively list them?
This shows they did not skillfully estimate the appropriate balance for the time. ”
Some say that the works like the *Tōng Diǎn* and the *Huìyào*
are merely more detailed in form than the historical treatises of Mǎ [Qiān] and Bān [Gù].
As for the names, numbers, and artifacts they contain,
they still cannot completely select, synthesize, or encompass them.
Therefore, researchers of antiquity must inevitably consult other texts.
This, however, is not a wise observation.
If ancient objects happen to exist today,
even household registers
and ledgers of market currency
can all be used for supplementary research and verification.
If one wishes to preserve everything without selection or control,
then Mount Dài (Dàiyuè) would be insufficient to house the archives,
and the blue sea (cānghǎi) would be insufficient for ink.
Therefore, considering the long-term strategy for historical studies,
the Basic Annals (jì), Tables (biǎo), Treatises (zhì), and Biographies (zhuàn)
should generally follow the established structure.
Furthermore, extending the remaining intent of the *Zhōu Diǎn*,
selecting from the official registers and records,
editing and extracting names, objects, technical details, and measurements,
organizing them with some structure,
to preserve the official systems (zhǎnggù) of that period,
serving as a complement to history without encroaching upon it—
this can be a regulation immutable for a hundred generations,
and is acceptable.
[From the] Bózhōu Gazetteer, Discussion of Precedents for Official Systems (Zhǎnggù), Part II (Xià):
The origin of official systems (zhǎnggù)
began with the *Guān Lǐ* (Official Rites).
Since the functions of the hundred officials are fully established in the imperial court,
only the treatises (shū zhì) of the national history
should extract their essential points,
while the canonical statutes and summaries (huì diǎn huì yào) of the state
should fully prepare their objects and numbers.
For those who compile local gazetteers (fāng zhì),
why must the gazetteers (zhì) and the official systems (zhǎnggù) be separated? The answer is:
The gazetteers of the Ministries (Bù), Courts (Sì), Grand Masters (Qīng), and Directorates (Jiān)
are the official systems (zhǎnggù);
comparing them to the *Zhōu Guān*,
they are just as the Office of Summer (Xià Guān) had the *Sīmǎ Fǎ* (The Methods of the Sīmǎ)
and the Office of Winter (Dōng Guān) had the *Kǎogōng Jì* (Record of Trades).
The gazetteers of the Prefectures (Bù), Circuits (Fǔ), Departments (Zhōu), and Districts (Xiàn)
are subdivisions of the National History (Guó Shǐ);
comparing them to the Zhōu system,
they are like the *Jìn Chéng*, the *Chǔ Táowù*, and the *Lǔ Chūn Qiū*.
Since the commanderies and districts (jùn xiàn) differ from the feudal system,
the official systems (zhǎnggù) must all derive from the institutions of the imperial court.
The functional duties of the Six Ministries (Liù Cáo)
are promulgated and carried out by the higher authorities,
and accepted and executed by the lower authorities.
Compared to the National History,
they are comprehensive yet detailed (jù tǐ ér wēi).
The gazetteers (zhì) and the official systems (zhǎnggù)
each have their immutable character
and must not be mixed.
of today
are vulgar, mediocre, and common.
Judged by the principles and precedents (yìlì) of historians,
they resemble gazetteers but are not gazetteers;
they resemble historical archives (zhǎnggù) yet are not historical archives.
Truly, there is nothing to criticize them for being.
However, administrative records and official documents (bùshū àndú),
promulgated by official regulations (gōnglìng)
and maintained by bureaucratic statutes (lìdiǎn),
possess fixed rules and standards (kēlǜ).
Even if one possesses extraordinary talent,
they cannot add to them;
even if one is foolish or clumsy,
they cannot diminish them.
Famous and prosperous major states (dàbāng)
are no different from desolate, poor, and small towns (lòuyì).
There is no distinction.
Therefore, if one seeks historical standards (shǐcái)
of the ancients in today’s gazetteers, they cannot be found.
However, if one seeks
the statutes and systems (zhāngchéng zhìdù) of the ancients in today’s official documents, they can indeed be seen.
Hence, it is said:
"If the rites (lǐ) are lost, seek them in the countryside (yě)."
Now, those who compile the national history (guóshǐ),
extend the national history to include historical archives (zhǎnggù).
If the methods of history (shǐfǎ) are not yet lost,
but the proper meaning of historical archives (zhǎnggù) is unclear,
then history suffers.
Those who compile local gazetteers (fāngzhì)
must instead start from historical archives (zhǎnggù) to correct the gazetteers.
This is because the true meaning of gazetteers (zhìyì) has long been lost,
but the preservation of historical archives (zhǎnggù) has not yet collapsed.
By improving the historical archives,
the meaning of gazetteers can in turn be clarified.
The *Yì* (The *Classic of Changes*) says:
“When one reaches the extreme (qióng), one changes (biàn);
when one changes, one becomes interconnected (tōng);
when one is interconnected, one lasts (jiǔ).”
The principle of gazetteers (zhìyì) requires them to be concise yet clear,
yet the material (shì) must be complete.
Historical archives (zhǎnggù) require them to be orderly and systematic,
yet the essentials (yào) must not fail to be summarized.
Merely taking brevity and omission as the essence of a gazetteer—
this is the shallow understanding of the gazetteers of Cháoyì and Wǔgōng.
If one only knows that detailed completeness constitutes historical archives (zhǎnggù),
then minor clerks (xūshǐ) will excel at compiling them,
failing to realize that this is impractical.
Now, the gazetteer (zhì)
is a record (zhì).
Beyond its events (shì) and its text (wén),
there must be underlying principle (yì).
This is what is called the way of concise control (cāoyue zhī dào).
But some mistakenly equate combining and omitting events (shìjì)
and deleting passages of text (wénzì)
with being concise (jiǎn).
How far
are they not from the standards of the ancients?
When famous scholars (míngjiā) write,
where their intent lies,
there must be a distinct selection (biécái).
Sometimes they elaborate on what others abbreviate,
sometimes they discard what others adopt.
Initially, there is no single established method.
The crucial point is that readers
admire and preserve it for a long time,
and suddenly recognize the underlying principle (yì) between the events and the text.
This then has relevance to orthodox moral teaching (míngjiào).
However, if historical archives (zhǎnggù) are not organized
and separately made into specialized books,
then the gazetteer (zhì) will also be unable to reveal its true intent.

First Letter in Reply to Xiùcái Zhēn Concerning the Compilation of Gazetteers
The magistrate (zǎi) of Wén'ān has invited and paid you (bì pìn) to compile the gazetteer.
You, my brother (xìng), have long been devoted to historical matters;
having rarely had a minor chance to test yourself,
you should be highly motivated for this trip.
What knowledge do I possess
that you should condescend to ask me?
Nevertheless, your earnest intention must be responded to.
I venture to summarize a few points
that I usually pay attention to,
hoping for your enlightened selection!
If there are parts that are incorrect,
please inform me.
One: Although prefectures and commanderies (zhōujùn) are all subordinate to the Bureau of Geography (Zhífāng),
and thus cannot have separate histories like the states of the feudal period (fēngjiàn zhī guó),
the established principles (yìlì) must still be clear.
For example, biographies (zhuàn) and gazetteers (zhì)
are fundamentally two different forms.
In compiling gazetteers today,
since institutions and biographies (rénwù diǎnzhì) are generally referred to as *zhì*,
then categories like famous officials (mínghuàn) and local worthies (xiāngxián)
should not establish separate headings (sèmù) labeled *zhuàn*.
If *zhuàn* (biographies) are separately divided into headings,
then subjects such as Rites and Music (lǐyuè), Military, and Penal Law (bīngxíng)
should not continue to use the general designation of *zhì* (gazetteer).
I humbly suggest that *zhì* (gazetteer) should be the general name for the whole book.
Imperial favors and celebratory events (qìngdiǎn)
should be recorded as External Records (Wàijì);
appointments and transfers of officials and teachers (guānshī quánchú)
should be categorized as Chronological Biographies (Niánpǔ);
statutes and legal systems (diǎnjí fǎzhì)
should be compiled as Studies (*Kǎo*) to document them;
and individuals and famous officials (rénwù mínghuàn)
should be listed as Biographies (*Zhuàn*).
By changing the designations,
there is no suspicion of usurping the style of history (jiànshǐ).
With the main themes grasped and the categories deployed (gāng jǔ mù zhāng),
there is also no worry of omission.
Other items should be attached according to their category.
For matters that do not fit into existing categories,
principles should be initiated according to necessity (yì qǐ),
and separate, new structures (chuàngzhì) may be created.
Trivial and overly complex details
that have no bearing on admonition or encouragement (chéngchuàng)
may be eliminated and not preserved.
Only when detailed, complete, clear, and comprehensive,
orderly and standardized (huàyī),
can the work be used as source material for the national history (guóshǐ).
Otherwise, even if extremely brilliant,
it is merely the novel (xiǎoshuō) of one family,
and what benefit does it provide?
One: Those who compile the Arts and Literature section (yìwén) today
mostly select poems, rhapsodies (fù), records, prefaces, and miscellaneous essays (záwén) written by senior officials (chánglì) and local gentry (yìshēn),
attaching them according to category.
Moreover, even descriptions of wind, clouds, moon, and dew (fēng yún yuè lù) that have no bearing on admonition or encouragement (chéngchuàng),
or eulogies and inscriptions for shrines (shēngcí bēisòng) that completely lack factual evidence (shízhēng),
are all included by the clerks.
Setting aside whether this is right or wrong for the moment,
even if all the prose conforms to standards,
and the poetry is refined and elegant,
the process of collating and categorizing the record,
striving to include every style,
is merely the standard for selecting literature (xuǎnwén),
and is no longer the form of a gazetteer (zhìshèng).
If one is to record Arts and Literature (yìwén),
one must emulate the intent of the *Sāntōng* and the *Qīlüè*,
taking the compiled books and selections written by scholars (xuéshì) of that region,
dividing them into categories and collections (bù huì).
First, list the table of contents,
then describe the sequence of their origins and endings,
eliminate the mediocre and select the outstanding,
extract the main purport,
discuss their merits and faults,
and compile them by comparison and category.
Only then will later generations have material for examination and evidence (kǎojù),
and perhaps be used as source material for collation by the Imperial Libraries (Guǎngé chóujiào).
This would not deviate from the gazetteer form (zhìshèng tǐ).
As for inscriptions (bēimíng) for altars and temples (tánmiào),
records concerning city walls and embankments (chéngtí jìshù),
treatises discussing benefits and drawbacks,
and poems describing local products (tǔwù tíyǒng)
—these should be appended to the Studies (*Kǎo*) sections on Products, Land Tax (Tiánfù), Customs (Fēngsú), and Geography (Dìlǐ),
in order to show the causes of gains and losses
and the history of evolution and change (yángé zhī gù).
This follows the precedent of Bān Shǐ (Bān Gù's *History*), which placed the memorials of Yánnián and Jiǎ Ràng into the *Héqú Zhì* (Treatise on Canals and Waterways),
and the memorials of Jiǎ Yì and Cháo Cuò into the *Shíhuò Zhì* (Treatise on Food and Money).
This is acceptable.
If scholarly writings (lùnzhù)
can reveal the author’s lifelong aspirations and ambition,
they should be fully recorded in their respective Biographies (*Zhuàn*).
This follows the precedent of Bān Shǐ, which recorded the *Tiānrén Sāncè* (Three Strategies of Heaven and Humanity) in the *Dǒng Zhòngshū Zhuàn* (Biography of Dǒng Zhòngshū),
and recorded the *Zhì'ān* (On Governance) memorials in the *Jiǎ Yì Lièzhuàn* (Collective Biography of Jiǎ Yì).
This is acceptable.
As for epitaphs (mùzhì), biographies, and laudatory inscriptions,
if they verify the facts without falsehood
and already possess an established structure (dìnglún),
they should be directly adopted as the text for the biographies (*zhuànwén*).
This follows the precedent of Bān Shǐ, which retained the *Shǐjì Zìxù* (Grand Historian’s Self-Preface) to create the *Sīmǎ Qiān Zhuàn* (Biography of Sīmǎ Qiān),
and retained Yáng Xióng’s *Zìxù* (Self-Preface) to create the *Yáng Xióng Lièzhuàn* (Collective Biography of Yáng Xióng).
This is acceptable.
These are fixed precedents
about which there should be no doubt or concern.
Yet, if people follow the old practices without changing them,
how difficult it is to achieve historical insight (shǐshí)!
1. Generally, those who donate funds to compile gazetteers,
establish bureaus, and invite scholars
have not grasped true learning,
but have first widely promoted compilation rules
to make things fresh and novel,
and abruptly discard old books.
In reality, this is just turning things upside down like the ‘mocker of the duke’ (jūgōng),
what genuine insight is there?
The establishment of gazetteers for prefectures and counties
imitated the practice of the former Míng dynasty.
At the time of their initial establishment,
although the principles and models (yìlì) were not very uniform,
the writing style still valued truth and realism,
and the cutting and editing often stemmed from the authors themselves.
This was unlike the prevalent habitual formulas of recent times,
where frivolous and immature young scholars,
who have not fully learned historical characters (shǐzì),
can all take up their brushes recklessly to compile
and surreptitiously claim stipends (xīfǔ).
Yet, out of these books, hardly one in a hundred survives.
This is all due to the later overriding the former,
where those compiling new gazetteers
appropriate the records of the old gazetteers,
but destroy the names of the original authors.
If we extend this principle,
once the Hànshū was published,
should the Shǐjì have been handed over to Zǔlóng (Qín Shǐ Huáng)?
Once Ōu(yáng Xiū) and Sòng (Qì) completed their books,
could the Jiù Tángshū (Old Book of Táng) then be used to cover an urn?
I believe that those compiling gazetteers
should continue the records of their predecessors,
not destroy the completed books of their predecessors.
Even if a former gazetteer's principles were unclear,
or its writing was erroneous (guāichuǎn),
and I create a separate structure
and revise the completed book;
it should still be allowed to circulate alongside the new one,
with the new continually succeeding the old.
One must not wantonly destroy the former.
The merits and demerits of both
will naturally be judged fairly by observers.
Furthermore, the index of chapters and volumes of the former book,
and the names of the authors,
should be recorded in the Yìwén Kǎo (Bibliography Section) of the new gazetteer,
to prevent their loss.
Thus, we might achieve the spirit of great impartiality (dàgōng wúwǒ),
and moreover, I would not risk being destroyed by later generations.
2. The gazetteer as a literary form
should contain more detail than standard histories (shǐ),
yet the contents of current gazetteers
are less than one-hundredth of what they should be.
This is due to nothing else than:
in collecting and compiling materials,
the eyes and ears of one generation are hard-pressed to be comprehensive;
and for historical records (zhǎnggù) to be fully stored,
there is no dedicated supervisor responsible for this task on a daily basis.
I once proposed that relevant officials,
if they wish the gazetteers to have no omissions,
should establish a Gazetteer Section (zhìchéng kēfáng) daily,
staffed by junior clerks (qiān yuánlì) who are moderately literate.
Regarding all administrative and educational precedents (zhèngjiào diǎngù),
facts implemented in the court (tángxíng shìshí),
records from the Six Boards (liùcáo àndú),
everything should be routed to them for collation.
The indexes and original documents
should be collected in volumes and stored in the repository.
When the bureau is opened for compilation in the future,
they will have abundant material to draw upon.
Although this should not be compared to the Historiographers of the various states (lièguó shǐguān),
it might still resemble the traditional idea of local historians and clerks (zhōulǘ shǐxū).
Since this is no longer achievable today,
we should propose it as a method for the future.
3. The gazetteer is a historical form (shǐtǐ),
originally belonging to the public domain,
not like a family tomb epitaph or birthday eulogy (mùzhì shòuwén),
which can be arbitrarily filled with superficial praise
to please people's eyes and ears.
I hear that in recent compilations,
bribery is often openly practiced,
and petitions for biographies are commissioned (qǐngtuō zuòzhuàn),
entirely without factual basis.
Although this is the doing of unworthy, frivolous literati,
the punishment and commendation of good and evil
should naturally not be abandoned.
Current gazetteers
never record anything negative.
One reason is the conventional habit of wishing goodness to prevail (shànshàn yùzhǎng),
and the other is the apprehensive fear of incurring future trouble.
I believe that satire and censure (jībiǎn) should not primarily constitute the gazetteer form,
but by stating the facts directly (jùshì zhíshū),
goodness and badness will naturally be apparent.
This is akin to the idea of being lenient with the hidden and highlighting the obvious (kuānyǐn zhāngzhī).
One must not exclusively pursue flowery writing (fúwén)
and make superficial praise the main task.
4. The value of historical and gazetteer writings
in benefitting customs and education (fēngjiào)
stems from transmitting the stories of loyalty (zhōng), filial piety (xiào), integrity (jié), and righteousness (yì).
These stories, vivid and stirring (lǐnglǐng lièliè),
with sound and color (yǒushēng yǒusè),
ensure that for a hundred generations to come,
the timid will become brave,
and the greedy will establish integrity (liánlì).
The Shǐjì favored knight-errants (hǎoxiá),
writing much about assassins and eccentric individuals (cìkè jīliú),
which was still enough to encourage people to disregard life and increase spirit.
How much more so the great virtues and righteousness between Heaven and Earth,
upon which the ethical principles (gāngcháng) rely for support,
and the world's education (shìjiào) relies for stability?
I often see that when literati compile gazetteers,
they dwell excessively on scenery and objects (jǐngwù liúlián),
places where their writing can be displayed,
or on the textual research of precedents (diǎngù kǎodìng),
areas where they can boast of erudition,
writing lengthily and enthusiastically (jīnjīn lěidú).
But when it comes to filial sons and loyal ministers,
righteous husbands and chaste women (yìfū jiéfù),
they are dismissed with just a few sparse strokes;
some even merely preserve the name,
not detailing a single word of their biographical sketch (xíngshù),
making the reader feel as if they are reviewing the county magistrate's register of signed-in staff (máobù).
What is the purpose of this?
I believe that county gazetteers only collect information spanning a few decades,
and conduct interviews within a radius of only one hundred miles.
The information gathered is naturally factual.
Effort should be dedicated to collecting these records
and extensively transmitting their stories,
so that observers are inspired.
Beneath the autumn fields covered with long grass (sùcǎo qiūyuán),
there will certainly be those who bow before the official records (tóngguǎn) and weep in the autumn rain.
Furthermore, special attention should be paid to
the unique acts and extraordinary integrity (jīxíng qíjié) found in remote villages and secluded areas (qióngxiāng pìrǎng),
where descendants are hindered by lack of means,
or are restricted by existing regulations (chénglì),
and thus cannot be officially commended and rewarded.
As long as their traces are verifiable,
efforts must be made to write biographies for them,
to be seen by those gathering public sentiment (cǎifēngzhě).
This would truly embody the spirit of wishing goodness to prevail.
The six points above
are based on my observations;
I dare not claim they are absolutely correct.
However, the gazetteers currently published in the world
indeed have aspects that I find unacceptable.
A man, if he cannot be a historiographer (shǐchén) in life,
should at least follow famous nobles and high officials (mínggōng jùqīng),
hold the brush, and serve as a secretary (shūjì),
thereby gaining the opportunity to discuss current affairs
and be employed for his literary talent.
Compiling gazetteers (zhuǎnxiū zhìchéng)
is also one such task.
Today’s so-called compilation of gazetteers
is driven by magistrates merely seeking empty fame,
while the authors often lack learning and insight.
At best, the superior motive is to document diligent service for merit assessment (tú zhùqínshì kǎochéng);
at worst, the inferior motive is merely to obtain board and lodging stipends (guǎngǔ lùlì).
Moreover, local gentry use it to initiate competitive maneuvering (bēnjìng),
and literati use it to practice dishonest writing (wǔ qǔbǐ).
The host and guest each harbor their own preconceptions,
and those in the same bureau sometimes clash.
In such a case regarding the compilation of the gazetteer,
it would be better not to do it at all.
However, as you, Sir (zúxià), possess historical talent (shǐcái),
you have often lamented not having the opportunity for a minor demonstration (niúdāo xiǎoshì).
Having previously discussed and consulted with you back and forth,
I observe your underlying thoughts (dǐyùn),
and believe you are not doing this haphazardly.
Furthermore, Wén'ān Jūn is able to listen with an open mind (xūxīn qīnglǐng),
sending gifts and earnestly inviting you.
You will surely break completely with previous ingrained habits.
Before the final drafts are complete (shāqīng wèibì),
observers will be startled
and consider it a ground-breaking work.
How could it be merely the book of one county,
when it is truly a book for all under Heaven?
In this matter, I am unable to render service (wúnéng wéiyì),
but since you have honored me by asking for my humble opinion (rǔcún shāngquè),
I offer my rigid and simple thoughts (gùlòu zhīzhōng),
in the hope of adding a glow, like a firefly (yíngzhú zēnghuī).
Do you, my Brother (xiōng), have anything to teach me in return?
Second Letter in Reply to Xiùcái Zhēn Regarding the Compilation of the Gazetteer
A few days ago, I respectfully offered my final suggestions.
Being of meager learning and shallow experience,
I presumptuously lacked firm opinions.
It was certainly not hoped that they could supplement your profound insights,
but merely served as a way to fulfill my duty.
Yet, I have been honored by your instructional reply,
wherein you kindly bestowed excessive praise.
Your standards are lofty and your citations far-reaching,
and your language and intent are sincere and heartfelt.
Reading it truly fills me with shame and awe!
Your Excellency possesses the talent of a great historian.
You are knowledgeable yet decisive.
Looking majestically upon antiquity,
your intent and ambition are clearly to surpass Fàn [Yè] and outstrip Chén [Shòu].
A petty county or prefectural gazetteer (*zhì chéng*),
is surely like using an ox-cleaver to slaughter a fledgling.
Yet, though your talent is vast, your heart is humble,
and you are not ashamed to repeatedly seek my humble advice.
For someone as common and limited as I,
how can I match the disposition of one whose mind is like a deep valley?
My previous letter roughly outlined the main points,
for which I received excessive and undeserved praise,
and you further wished to inquire about all the details.
Although I am not the right person (for this task),
I must immediately respond, based on the profound sincerity of your noble sentiments,
and dare not fail to offer a reply.
I hope you will consider and select from these points.
I. The structure and style should follow historical principles.
County and prefectural gazetteers (*zhì chéng*),
are often mixed up and lack order.
Since they are not formal histories (*zhèng tǐ*),
dividing them into Annals (*jì*) and Tables (*biǎo*),
would also be inappropriate presumption.
Therefore, in my previous letter, I mediated and established a structure,
primarily based on the four categories: External Records (*wài jì*), Chronological Biographies (*nián pǔ*), Monographs (*kǎo*), and Biographies (*zhuàn*).
This is to avoid the suspicion of presuming to write history,
while still seeking the truth of the documentation.
However, while the nominal titles should avoid those of national histories,
the actual method should emulate the ancients.
Categories like External Records (*wài jì*) and Chronological Biographies (*nián pǔ*),
are rarely seen in modern gazetteers (*zhì chéng*),
perhaps only in one or two out of a hundred.
As for the Monographs (*kǎo*) and Biographies (*zhuàn*),
although they are now commonly called gazetteers and biographies (*zhì zhuàn*),
the actual substance of these two categories,
is never entirely absent;
the reason why they cannot conform to the excellent methods of ancient history is that
the Monograph structure (*kǎo tǐ*) often errs on the side of complexity and fragmentation,
and the Biography structure (*zhuàn tǐ*) often errs on the side of being generalized and indistinct.
The structure of the Monograph (*kǎo*),
is made in imitation of the Treatises (*shū*) and Monographs (*zhì*).
Zǐcháng’s eight Treatises (*shū*),
Mèngjiān’s ten Monographs (*zhì*),
comprehensively examined the institutions and statutes,
and covered an extremely wide scope.
The Fàn History (*Fàn Shǐ*) divided them into thirty Monographs,
and the *Táng Shū* expanded them to fifty chapters,
which was already gradually expanding.
When the Yuán dynasty compiled the *Sòng Shǐ*,
the Monographs were divided into over one hundred and sixty.
Critics mocked this as being merely the files and registers of government clerks.
However, this was merely a failure in structural organization,
leading to excessive verbosity;
it is not like today's county gazetteers,
which divide topics into too many headings,
resulting in endless material that lacks overall coherence.
For example, astronomical fields (*xīng yě*), borders and territory, and administrative evolution,
mountains, rivers, and local products,
all belong within the Monograph on Geography (*Dìlǐ Zhì*).
Population census, taxes, and corvée duties,
state monopolies, tariffs, and market trade,
all belong within the Monograph on Food and Commodities (*Shíhuò Kǎo*);
Calamities, auspicious omens, and folk songs,
unusual changes, floods, and droughts,
all belong within the Monograph on the Five Phases (*Wǔxíng Zhì*);
Court audiences and congratulations, altars, temples, and sacrificial rituals,
village drinking ceremonies, and selection of talent,
all belong within the Monograph on Rites and Ceremonies (*Lǐyí Zhì*).
All matters, great and small,
can be inferred by analogy.
The beginning of the chapter should be headed by a general name,
beneath which the details should be meticulously itemized,
compiled together into a unified section.
Not only does this make the collective material easy to view,
but it also ensures carefulness, strictness, and proper style.
These kinds of entries,
simply require reorganization.
But modern gazetteers are vulgar, petty, complex, and fragmented,
being nothing less than the account ledgers of market currency,
dealing with trivial, confused, and miscellaneous details.
What value is there in that?
Some might argue that writing long, major chapters,
like Bān Gù’s *Shíhuò* [Treatise on Food and Commodities],
or Mǎ Qiān’s *Píngzhǔn* [Treatise on the Standardization of Prices],
is extremely difficult to structure.
How can they not know that once the literary form adheres to historical principles,
even if the phrasing is as systematic as arranging calculation rods,
it will naturally exhibit admirable order,
and be practical and useful.
The writing does not need to be obsessively worried about,
and should not delight in being overly verbose.
II. Completed writings should indicate the author.
When Bān [Gù] inherited [Sīmǎ] Qiān’s History (*Qiān Shǐ*),
the events before [Emperor] Xiàowǔ,
largely utilized the original text,
without making further distinction;
because the *Shǐ* [Jì] and *Hàn* [Shū] documented the same period,
and Qiān’s History had long been in general circulation,
thus there was no impropriety.
Other instances, such as imperial edicts, decrees, memorials, and petitions,
were clearly narrated alongside the person and the context of the event,
and thus there was no impropriety in copying the finished text.
When the *Shǐjì* commented on the Qín,
it entirely used Jiǎ Shēng’s three treatises (*lùn*),
introduced by the phrase, “Excellent! Jiǎ Shēng thoroughly discusses this,”
to lead into the quote.
The *Hàn Shū*’s Biography of Qiān (*Qiān Zhuàn*) entirely used the *Shǐjì*’s Postface (*Zìxù*),
concluded by the phrase, “This is what Qiān’s Postface says.”
to conclude the quote.
Although finished text was used,
the distinction between the host (the historian) and the guest (the quoted source) was clear,
and it was not merely plundering the work of others.
Since gazetteers (*zhì*) are historical documents,
it is unavoidable that finished writings will be cited within them.
If these are like common literary anthologies,
then the original name of the author,
should naturally be marked below the table of contents.
If, now, the included literary texts are edited out,
and categorized into various forms of Monographs (*kǎo*) and Biographies (*zhuàn*),
the original name of the author is easily omitted during the editing process.
It is necessary, therefore, to adhere to the precedents of the *Shǐ* [Jì] and *Hàn* [Shū],
and explicitly mark the source.
If a text is excessively long,
and requires abridgment,
it should be introduced by the three characters, “Its summary says,”
used to introduce the quote.
This follows the precedent of Mèngjiān citing Jiǎ Yì’s memorials.
This is acceptable.
If citing old text,
which is sufficient in itself for discussion,
then one may follow the precedent of the text within the *Bóyí Lièzhuàn*,
which inserts the phrase, “Its biography says,”
followed by the passage.
This is acceptable.
Furthermore, regarding the prefaces (*xù*) or introductions (*yǐn*) attached at the beginning,
or the critiques (*lùn*) and encomiums (*zàn*) appended at the end,
modern compilers
often use titles like “The Unofficial Historian says,”
or “The External Historian says.”
Judging these based on principle,
neither is fully appropriate;
nothing is better than directly imitating the method used during the Eastern Hàn dynasty,
and marking the text with the forms *Lùn yuē* (The Critique says) or *Xù yuē* (The Preface says) for safety.
As for repeated attempts to discern the truth,
recording doubts, or including divergent views,
adding *Àn yuē* (The Note says) is also acceptable.
Otherwise, just integrate it directly into the main text,
without adding a heading.
Using discretion according to the situation,
depends entirely on tailoring the garment to fit the body.
First, the style of the biography (*zhuàn*) should be unified.
Including biographical narratives (*lièzhuàn*) into the Treatise on Literature (*Yìwén Zhì*),
previous books have already pointed out its error.
However, when the National History (*Guóshǐ*) draws material from the Local Gazetteers (*Yìzhì*),
characters are particularly crucial.
This is because statutes and ordinances,
the state has its compiled institutes,
officials have their records,
and these matters proceed from the top downward;
therefore, they are universally consistent throughout the realm.
Even if occasionally there are omissions or errors,
there is no worry that there will be no way to verify them.
As for the category of individuals,
unless they hold a position of prominence and renown,
unless the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*Tàicháng*) discusses their posthumous title,
and the historians establish a biography (*zhuàn*),
then their names have no means of reaching the Capital (*Jīngshī*).
Those secluded and solitary scholars,
those chaste and virtuous women,
if they happen to receive commendation and reward,
upon consulting the relevant archives and records,
they are truly nothing more than simple muster rolls or registers of names.
It is necessary to wait until an imperial decree orders compilation,
for the establishment of an office and the submission of documents,
only then can they be verified.
Therefore, their affairs proceed from the bottom upward.
If the Local Gazetteers (*Yìzhì*) are not detailed and complete,
then how can they be verified in the future?
Now, the biography (*zhuàn*) is precisely the biographical chapter (*lièzhuàn*) format of historical texts (*shǐ*).
The (*Rúlín* - Confucian Scholars) and (*Yóuxiá* - Wandering Knights),
these were the comprehensive titles first marked by *Shǐ Qiān*'s historical work (*Shǐjì*);
(*Wényuàn* - Men of Letters) and (*Dàoxué* - Neo-Confucianism),
the *Sòng Shǐ* further divided these into three categories.
Earlier Confucians criticized this labeling system for instigating controversy,
but this criticism only targeted the labels themselves for lacking careful consideration.
This is unlike later generations, where gazetteers (*zhìchéng*) compiled biographical accounts and stele inscriptions,
collectively listing them in the Treatise on Literature (*Yìwén*).
When compiling biographical chapters (*lièzhuàn*) for individuals,
they must also specifically label the categories,
such as Loyal Ministers, Filial Sons, Famous Worthies, or Men of Letters (*Wényuàn*),
and arrange them successively in compiled order.
Each person often takes up no more than eight or nine lines,
or sometimes only one, two, or three lines,
and these are called 'Abridged Biographies' (*Zhuànlǜè*).
Now, a gazetteer (*zhì*) claims to be a ‘factual record brought by the light carriage,’
it ought to be more detailed than the history (*shǐ*),
yet it proceeds using the abridged format—
what is the rationale for this?
Furthermore, when a category label cannot fully encompass the subject,
the principles of classification should allow for supplementary attachments.
If *Dǒng Xuān* were not included in the 'Harsh Officials' (*Kùlì*),
then in the chapter on *Zhōu Chén*, *Hán Tōng* would be lacking.
Examining the seventy biographical chapters (*lièzhuàn*) in the *Shǐjì*,
only the nine chapters beginning with 'Upright Officials' (*Xúnlì*) and 'Confucian Scholars' (*Rúlín*),
have comprehensive titles marked out.
In the *Hànshū*, the seven chapters beginning with 'Imperial Relatives' (*Wàiqī*) and 'Flatterers and Favorites' (*Nìngxìng*),
have comprehensive titles marked out.
The biography of *Jiāngdū* lists three strategies,
it need not be listed under 'Confucian Scholars' (*Rúlín*);
*Dōngfāng* especially enjoyed humor,
he need not be categorized under 'Humorists' (*Huájī*).
Since the rules for biographies (*zhuàn*) are broad,
one can record extraordinary conduct that lies outside the realm of law;
those whose conduct is similar,
can be grouped together and attached;
those whose writings are numerous,
can be recorded and included.
One must only guard against inclusion based on mediocrity, redundancy, or personal favoritism,
and not be restricted by the length or brevity of the chapter.
This is the best possible approach.
Second, critical discussions should adhere to strict gravity.
*Shǐ Qiān*'s concluding remarks and judgments at the end of prefaces and introductions,
all used the phrase, "The Grand Historian (*Tàishǐ Gōng*) says,..."
This was done to distinguish them from the narrative text,
and not specifically to label categories.
Since *Bān Gù* composed praises (*zàn*),
and *Fàn Shǐ* compiled discourses (*lùn*),
there has already been a slight decline in quality.
The various histories of the Southern Dynasties (*Náncháo*),
at the end of the biographies (*zhuàn*) and treatises (*zhì*),
used prose to write discourses,
and also used rhymed language,
imitating *Mèng Jiān*'s autobiographical style to write praises,
attaching them after the critical discourses.
This is like putting a roof upon a roof;
this constitutes excessive writing.
Subsequent practice followed this trend,
and the composition styles were not uniform.
When the Míng Ancestor (*Míng Zǔ*) commissioned the compilation of the *Yuán Shǐ*,
he instructed *Sòng Lián* and others to record facts plainly,
without adding critical discourses or praises.
Although this contained an intent for gravity and strictness,
it was not the way of public affirmation.
I, however, believe that affirming right and wrong, and offering praise and criticism,
only requires that it be balanced (impartial);
the discourses and praises may be attached;
but one must not deliberately exalt or demean,
nor deliberately indulge in startling paradoxes.
If the right and wrong is plainly obvious,
and does not require argumentation,
or if the biographical text has already thoroughly expressed praise and condemnation,
and there are no remaining unexpressed sentiments,
it is unnecessary to forcibly compose a conclusion
just to fulfill the required quota.
Third, statutes and institutions should be fully detailed.
When I said that statutes proceed from the top down,
and can therefore be handled more briefly than individuals,
I was merely emphasizing that the biographies (*zhuàn*) should be even more detailed.
Schools, sacrificial rites,
and all matters recorded in the compiled institutes,
if they are regularly implemented by the prefectures and counties,
how can they be omitted?
The compiled institutes are numerous and extensive,
and it is not easy to purchase and read them.
If they were distributed throughout the various gazetteers of the prefectures and counties,
then everyone could view them.
Would this not be a splendid arrangement?
Moreover, the statutes implemented by prefectures and counties,
require merely the expense of ten-odd wooden blocks (for printing).
Current gazetteers mostly omit them by deletion;
I do not understand the reasoning behind this.
Fourth, self-annotations should be added after careful consideration.
The self-annotations in *Bān*’s history (*Hànshū*) are especially numerous in the Ten Treatises (*Shí Zhì*).
In the writings of subsequent historians,
self-annotations were frequently used.
When the Sòng people published the spurious *Sū Zhù Dù Shī* (Sū's Commentary on Dù's Poetry),
those parts that could not be forcibly interpreted,
were arbitrarily labeled with the three characters
“*Gōng* self-annotated.”
Later people who recognized the forgery,
retorted by correcting it, saying:
The writings of the ancients
never contained self-annotations.
If so, then what about texts like *Sīmǎ*'s *Qián Xū*,
which adds its own commentary (*xiàng zhuàn*)?
What then?
Since the format of the gazetteer (*zhì*) aims for detail and completeness,
while the style of writing values conciseness,
and seeks to use the methodology of topical compilation
while applying the biographical (*jìzhuàn*) style of writing,
if self-annotations are not added,
how can clarity be achieved?
