However, regarding the factual matters contained within the main text,
those that require detailed investigation into their beginning and end
may be added as self-annotations.
As for the *Qián Xū*’s self-explanation of the meaning of the text,
that is not suitable for the gazetteer format.
1. The collected literature (Wénxuǎn) should mutually assist [the history].
Including mixed styles of poetry and prose into the Treatise on Literature (Yìwén Zhì)
is certainly not the proper format;
this is why the previous book desired to take all different styles and assign them to Biographies and Investigations.
However, the writings of the Western Capital were extremely abundant,
yet outside of what was collected in Bān Shǐ,
few others are encountered.
This is because when scholars compiled writings,
they were only collected if they conformed to historical criteria,
and all poetry, prose, rhapsodies (fù), and hymns
lacked figures like Zhāomíng or Lǐ Fǎng
who came forward first to gather and compile them.
Historical forms are viewed longitudinally (vertically);
treatise forms are viewed laterally (horizontally);
their purpose in comprehensively examining matters is the same.
However, comprehensive examination details events,
and consequently touches upon literature.
There are quite a few writings
that concern local customs and human affairs,
and history certainly cannot collect all of them.
For this reason, since Zhāomíng,
collections have spanned across dynasties:
the Táng dynasty had the Wényuàn,
the Sòng dynasty had the Wénjiàn,
the Yuán dynasty had the Wénlèi,
and the Míng dynasty had the Wénxuǎn.
These were broadly selected and organized,
collecting everything regardless of size,
and those [texts] that can verify deficiencies in historical records
are plentiful.
Thus, when Zuǒ Shì organized and compiled the Guóyǔ,
he never failed to quote proverbs and verify ballads;
and the Fifteen Guófēng
were also always compiled as a separate section
and placed under the Grand Historian.
This is clear proof that literary selections and local gazetteers
mutually support and benefit each other.
Recently, the Governor of Chǔ (Chǔ Fǔ), beyond the Húguǎng Tōngzhì,
also compiled the Sānchǔ Wénxiàn Lù.
Jiāngsū Sòng Fǔjūn hired Shào Pílíng to compile the Míng Wén Lù; in addition,
he further authored collections like the Sānwú Wénxiàn Lù,
which also supplement the deficiencies of the Jiāngnán Tōngzhì.
I am ignorant and poorly informed;
I do not know if all other provinces do likewise.
However, even based on this single example,
one can generalize.
Why not briefly imitate the lingering intent of the Guófēng,
taking those [writings] concerning popular customs and social practices,
using them for mutual comparison and verification,
and serving as material for investigation and review?
If divided into styles such as poetry, prose, records, and prefaces,
and compiled into a book for a single district,
to assist the gazetteer,
it should also not be without benefit.
But this is not something within your power to accomplish;
why not take the opportunity to inform the relevant authorities?
1. There should be separate biographical categories for Distinguished Women (Liènǚ).
The famous biography of Distinguished Women
was originated by Liú Xiàng.
It was divided and compiled into seven chapters;
its principle is close to that of the Masters (Zǐ);
it includes hymns (Sòng) and describes odes (Yǎ);
its learning is connected to the Shī [Classic of Poetry];
and yet, in comparing events and arranging words,
it is truly a historical record.
The two histories by Bān and Mǎ [Bān Gù and Sīmǎ Qiān]
both lack this biography.
It was only starting from Fàn Wèizōng’s Dōnghàn Shū
that the Liènǚ biography was included.
Later historians followed suit,
and it thus became a fixed rule.
However, what later historians called Liènǚ
refers to chastity and martyrdom (Jiéliè),
whereas what Liú Xiàng narrated
refers to comprehensive enumeration (Luóliè).
If the ‘Liè’ of Jiéliè (martyrdom/ardor) is used for the Liènǚ biography,
then chastity (Zhēnjié) and dying for virtue (Xùnliè)
are already inherently different;
if filial daughters and righteous wives [are considered],
they are even less compatible.
Furthermore, refined ladies and talented wives,
Daoist nuns and celestial maidens,
will forever lack a precedent for inclusion in a biography.
If a woman achieves nothing related to the path of husband and wife,
it might originally be acceptable to slightly omit those
outside of Jiéliè, filial piety, and righteousness.
However, the great virtue of Bān Jī,
the historical talent of Cáo Zhāo,
and the literary skill of Cài Yǎn—
how could they possibly be inferior to those belonging to the classes of technicians/diviners or court performers,
leaving them with no way to be recorded?
In Liú Xiàng’s biography,
besides Jiéliè, filial piety, and righteousness,
those talented like the concubine Jìng,
those unique like the Woman of Lǔ,
were all included;
even down to Shī [Yí] and Dàn [Jǐ],
they were attached.
The meaning of ‘Liè’ (to enumerate/distinguish)
can thus be considered expansive.
Since the Eastern Hàn dynasty,
later histories mistakenly took the ‘Liè’ of enumeration (Luóliè)
to mean the ‘Liè’ of martyrdom (Xùnliè).
Consequently, outside of legal constraints,
few others could be recorded,
and even the inclusion of Cài Wénjī into history
was debated by people.
Now, a separate biography for Chastity and Virtue (Zhēnjié) should be established
to record names deserving commendation.
For those outside of the main records,
if they possess outstanding talent and emotion,
or unconventional moral integrity,
or if their literary achievements are noteworthy,
or if they possess a unique, superior skill,
it would not be inappropriate to include them in the Liènǚ biography,
following the precedent of biographies for Technicians, Literary figures, and Solitary Practitioners (Fāngjì, Wényuàn, Dúxíng).
Thus, the virtues of women would not be limited entirely to Jiéliè,
and anyone possessing a singular commendable skill
would not suffer the lament of being forgotten.
These are foolish words,
I hope you will wisely choose [what to use].
Written hastily while drunk,
do not blame me.
Letter to Xiùcai Zhēn discussing the Principles and Precedents of Wénxuǎn (Part Two)
I am honored to receive your demonstration regarding the principles and precedents of Wénxuǎn.
It is extremely insightful;
had you not intimately known the joys and pains of this field,
how could you have achieved this?
I merely have a few points to discuss in reply.
Indeed, following existing practice and adding embellishments
is easier for later generations.
When compiling comprehensive selections spanning multiple dynasties,
one must view them through the criteria of historical writing.
Zhāomíng’s initial draft
was slightly similar to that of Mǎ Qiān.
Viewing the Two Hàn dynasties from the perspective of the Six Dynasties,
there were omissions,
and the pre-Qín era was even more omitted.
Regarding the Zhōu dynasty,
apart from Zǐxià’s Poetry Preface and Qū Zǐ’s Lísāo,
there were no other writings.
Similarly, when the Heavenly Hàn viewed the pre-Qín era,
there were omissions,
and the Zhōu dynasty was even more omitted.
Regarding the Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns,
apart from the brief entries in the Basic Annals,
they are not detailed further.
Zhāomíng covered eight dynasties;
Shǐ Jì collected three ancient eras;
and since they were pioneering works,
the precedents were broad and the text concise.
Wényuàn and Wénjiàn
each encompass a single dynasty;
Hànshū and Táng Shū
each specifically record one court;
and because they relied on former regulations,
the articles are detailed and the text is exhaustive.
Wényuàn’s supplementary records of the Chén and Suí dynasties
compensate for what Zhāomíng left unfinished;
Wénjiàn’s parallel inclusion of official examination papers
expands upon what Zhāomíng did not list.
This is analogous to Bān Gù's Dì Zhì simultaneously adopting the Zhífāng and Yǔgòng,
or the treatises in the Suí Shū supplementing the records of Liáng, Chén, Zhōu, and Qí.
Precedents arise from meaning;
adjusting them, either by reducing or increasing,
is certainly permissible.
The historical accounts do not detail all the literature of an era;
The historical accounts do not detail all the literature of an era;
we rely entirely on large-scale comprehensive selections.
They allow texts from various sections, outside of official statutes, to be recorded,
compared, and verified,
which can compensate for the deficiencies of the Twenty-one Histories.
This undertaking is extremely important,
and fundamentally differs from critics who merely evaluate literary skill.
Whether the texts are skillful or clumsy, voluminous or concise,
one should not meticulously quibble over repetition.
Readers should merely glean the main ideas
to broaden their knowledge of antiquity,
which is where the benefit lies.
Second Reply Letter Refuting the Principles and Precedents of Wénxuǎn
The letter received said:
“I strongly disagree
with the principles and methods you discussed regarding the *Wénxuǎn* (Selections of Literature).
The path of literature
covers a vast scope,
and history is merely one category within it.
The principles of selection anthologies
are complex, voluminous, and unsystematic;
within the Four Divisions and Nine Schools (Sìbù Jiǔliú),
what is not included?
Yet you generally wish to compare it to history.
Whether it is Sīmǎ Qiān (Mǎ) or Bān Gù (Bān),
whether it is biographies (biǎo) or epitaphs (zhì),
you meticulously insist on using the selections made by Xiāo Tǒng and Táng Rén (Xiāo Táng zhū xuǎn),
cutting off the toes to fit the shoe (xuē zhǐ shì lǚ),
seeking to find even one point of compliance.
Are you perhaps suggesting that Chén Dàshì, when first learning formal essays (shíwén),
should tailor all his family letters into the Eight-Legged Essay (bāgǔ) format?
Literary texts from the two capitals (Dōng Jīng and Xī Jīng, Eastern and Western Hàn)
that were included in selections are few,
yet the structured compilations of the two histories, *Bān Shǐ* (Bān Gù's history) and *Fàn Shǐ* (Fàn Yè's history),
thus became the definitive versions.
Only Lǐ Líng's letter from beyond the frontier
was not recorded in the *Bān Shǐ*.
If this approaches the practice of the petty literati of the Qí and Liáng dynasties,
is it that the selections fall short of benefiting history?
Or that history falls short of benefiting the selections?
Chronological history has the *Gāngmù* (Summary and Details),
and biographical history has the Twenty-One Histories (Niàn Yī Shǐ);
the events of past dynasties are already clear as the sun and stars.
For you now to seek to supplement them with the *Wénxuǎn*
is like building a house upon a bed (redundant effort).
How can words relating to wind, clouds, moon, and dew (fēng yún yuè lù zhī cí)
supplement the archives of the Historiographer (Zhù Xià zhī Zàng)?
The practice of selection anthologies originated during the Six Dynasties (Liù Cháo),
and the structure of history also deteriorated from that time.
It is clear that selection anthologies do not benefit history.
The task of examining ancient and modern affairs,
and discussing merits and flaws,
belongs to outstanding scholars (zhuólùo zhī shì),
who do not rigidly adhere to sentences and phrases;
songs of children and sighs of women (rǔ gē fù tàn)
can all be observed and collected.
Are they all equivalent to history?
In the past, people called Dù Fǔ's poetry 'Poetry-History' (Shī Shǐ),
but Yáng Wànlǐ refuted this,
asking whether the *Shījīng* (Classic of Poetry) could truly encompass the *Shàngshū* (Classic of History)?
Your reading of books has always been exceptional,
but your current comments seem constrained by exegesis and philology (xùngǔ).
I secretly dislike this.
If I am wrong in any aspect,
please quickly grant me your judgment and instructions!”
Your valued letter is eloquent and discerning.
How could the instruction you have given me
be considered insignificant?
However, it seems our intentions and meanings are still not fully clear to each other,
but your gracious intent must not be disregarded.
Therefore, I venture to reply by letter.
The path of literature (wénzhāng yī dào)
did not originally follow uniform structures,
but its origins each derived from different sources.
The writings of the ancients,
in their beginning, emerged profusely and mixed together,
serving only the purpose for which they were suited.
How could they meticulously establish a single category
and rigidly seek conformity?
If we say that literary matters are inherently vast,
and history merely occupies one category within them,
then the categories would be endlessly complex.
The biographies of Bó Yí and Qū Yuán, among others,
blend narrative and commentary;
while the writings of Zhuāng Zhōu and Liè Zǐ
often use fabricated narratives to execute the text.
If you believe that the rules for selection anthologies cannot be uniform,
then how should these types of texts
be categorized?
The Classics (Jīng), Histories (Shǐ), Philosophers (Zǐ), and Anthologies (Jí)
have long been categorized into the Four Divisions (Sìkù),
and their origins are not distant.
If we discuss the beginning of the Six Arts (Liù Yì),
then the category of Classics (Jīng) fundamentally did not exist.
The Great *Yì* (Classic of Changes) was not revered as a book of the sages;
it was merely a book of the Zǐ division.
The *Shū* (Classic of History) and the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals)
were merely two historical records.
The Three Hundred Pieces of the *Shī* (Classic of Poetry)
were a literary collection.
The *Yílǐ* (Book of Rites) and *Zhōuguān* (Rites of Zhōu)
were simply legal codes and administrative statutes.
Apart from the *Yì* being stored with the Grand Diviner (Tài Bǔ),
the remaining four
were all subordinates of the Historiographer's archives (Zhù Xià zhī Jí).
Later generations took them to verify the merits and flaws of antiquity and modernity,
but I have not heard of anyone fastidiously selecting those resembling the *Gāngmù* or the biographical records
and exclusively classifying them as history,
while other styles, being complex and extensive,
were immediately excluded from selection.
The *Chūnqiū* was written after the decline of the *Shī*.
The *Shī* is analogous to today’s literary anthologies (*Wénxuǎn*);
why then could it also exist alongside history from beginning to end?
Local customs being disparate,
and the rise and fall of human affairs—
these are details that biographical records cannot elaborate upon,
and chronological histories cannot fully record.
But through mutual verification and examination,
those texts that align with this purpose
include the *Chī Xiāo* (Owl) concerning the *Jīn Téng* (Metal-bound Coffer),
and the *Chéng Zhōu* (Riding a Boat) concerning the *Zuǒ Zhuàn* (Zuo Commentary);
those that lie outside this strict scope
include the *Qī Yuè* (Seventh Month) relating the ancestors of Zhōu,
and the *Shāng Sòng* (Odes of Shāng) encompassing affairs of different eras.
Is it not the case that literature and historical matters
naturally exist together throughout time?
The writings of the two capitals (Liǎng Jīng)
that were selected are very few,
not equaling the amount included by Bān Gù and Fàn Yè.
Had there been someone then, like the compilers of the *Wényuàn* (Garden of Literature),
to compile them into a vast, magnificent canon,
then the deeds of the two Hàn Dynasties
would, I know, be even more glorious, as though they happened yesterday.
The structure of history deteriorated during the Six Dynasties,
and the general atmosphere has declined since then;
this is not the fault of the *Wénxuǎn*.
It is only regrettable
that Zhāomíng’s selections (the *Wénxuǎn*) are too brief.
As for your point about not rigidly adhering to sentences and phrases,
if one need not include literary works within history,
yet meticulously insists on placing literary works outside history,
can such a perspective still be called exceptional?
Yáng Wànlǐ did not understand the intention of the Grand Historiographer (Tài Shǐ) regarding the observation of popular customs (guān fēng),
and therefore refuted the theory of ‘Poetry-History’ (Shī Shǐ).
Why should your outstanding insight
be misled by him?
Ten Proposals for Compiling the Gazetteer (Presented to Magistrate Hú Míngfǔ of Tiānmén)
There are two advantages (èrbian) in compiling a gazetteer:
closeness in location makes verification easy,
and closeness in time makes the traces authentic.
There are three strengths (sāncháng):
sufficient knowledge to determine general principles,
clarity to decide what to accept or reject,
and impartiality to prevent lobbying or undue influence.
There are five difficulties (wǔnán):
the difficulty of clarifying astronomical measurements,
the difficulty of verifying ancient boundaries,
the difficulty of harmonizing public opinions,
the difficulty of widely soliciting rare books,
and the difficulty of preemptively preventing disputes.
There are eight taboos (bājì):
taboo against confusing organization,
taboo against imbalance in detail and brevity,
taboo against excessive focus on literary style,
taboo against overly beautifying famous sites,
taboo against arbitrarily overturning old records,
taboo against superficially recording achievements,
taboo against clinging rigidly to the ancient and refusing change,
and taboo against greedily including legends.
There are four forms (sìtǐ):
Imperial favors and celebratory ceremonies should be presented as Annals (Jì),
records of officials, teachers, and examination graduates should be presented as Genealogies (Pǔ),
codes, statutes, and legal systems should be presented as Treatises (Kǎo),
and records of famous officials and notable persons should be presented as Biographies (Zhuàn).
There are four essentials (sìyào):
it must be concise (jiǎn),
it must be rigorous (yán),
it must be verifiable (hé),
and it must be elegant (yǎ).
I now propose to leverage the two advantages,
fulfill the three strengths,
avoid the five difficulties,
eliminate the eight taboos,
establish the four forms,
and achieve the four essentials.
Allow me to briefly discuss the reasoning behind this in ten articles.
We should first present the necessary affairs
and then establish the general principles,
hoping thereby to achieve the intent of "drawing a palace on a wall."
Article One:
Discussing Responsibilities (Yì Zhízhǎng).
The Director (Tí Diào) shall be solely responsible for deciding right and wrong.
The Editor-in-Chief (Zǒng Cái) shall be solely responsible for literary revisions and excisions.
Those submitting documents shall narrate but not comment.
Those consulting the documents shall comment but not decide.
This will ensure that responsibilities do not overlap,
and that each task has its designated person.
Second,
Discussion on Research and Verification.
Although the gazetteer of the prefecture (yì zhì) is small,
its structural principles must be fully prepared.
Verification and research should be exhaustively thorough and detailed;
balancing different sources should strive for the utmost perfection.
All required books,
in addition to the gazetteers of the province, prefecture, and neighboring regions,
such as the *Èrshí'èr Shǐ*, the *Sān Chǔ Wénxiàn Lù*, the *Yītǒng Zhì*, the Imperial Compilation of the *Fāngyú Lùchéng Tú* by the Shèngzǔ Rén Huángdì, the *Dà Qīng Huìdiǎn*, and the *Fù Yì Quánshū*,
must all be diligently sought out and consulted.
Furthermore, local gentry's private histories (yě shèng), personal records, collected writings, minor histories (bài shǐ), genealogies (jiā pǔ), and maps/charts (tú dié),
all sources that can aid research,
must also be publicly requested and collected,
observing widely and extracting concisely.
Regarding the official documents (àn dú) of the Six Boards (liù cáo),
statutes, laws, and official correspondence (wén yí),
that concern governmental regulations, institutional precedents (diǎn gù), local customs, or advantages and disadvantages,
all must be ordered to be copied,
and uniformly sent to the bureau (guǎn)
to serve as the basis for detailed and careful selection and arrangement.
In this way, nothing, great or small, will be omitted,
and a reliable historical record (xìn shǐ) will be eternally preserved.
Third,
Discussion on Gathering Reliable Information (Zhēng Xìn).
Prefecture gazetteers especially prioritize biographies of individuals (rén wù),
and in selecting and rejecting material, discerning truth from falsehood is vital.
Regarding the biographies listed in the old gazetteer,
the rule is to allow additions/revisions but no deletions.
For individuals in the new gazetteer,
they must rely entirely on the family's descendants to submit a detailed account to the office (guì),
which, once verified as factual and sound,
will be sent to the bureau for inclusion as a biography.
These points are not open to discussion.
However, the submitted biographical accounts (xíng zhuàng)
must contain verifiable facts worthy of record,
listed in full detail,
to await selection,
only then permitting inclusion.
For example, when submitting an account for an esteemed official (míng huàn),
it must detail what post he held,
what benefit he truly brought,
what abuse he truly eliminated,
and what specific action benefited the nation's economy and the people's livelihood (guójì mínshēng);
only this meets the requirement.
If the account merely states "incorruptible, diligent, and cautious,"
or "benevolent, compassionate, strict, and fair,"
without any concrete evidence,
and is written in the style of official evaluation remarks (kǎo yǔ),
it will be entirely rejected.
Similarly, for those of distinguished conduct (zhuó xíng), it must be listed how their conduct was distinguished;
for literary figures (wén yuàn), it must be listed what books they authored
that earned the respect of the scholarly community (shì lín);
for Confucian scholars (rú lín), it must be verified what classical texts (jīng) they contributed to,
and what works they published that related to the orthodox doctrines (míng jiào);
for those known for filial piety and fraternity (xiào yǒu), it must be specified in what deeds their ability to be filial and fraternal was demonstrated.
Regardless of whether the character is common or extraordinary, flawed or complete,
it must have genuine deeds (zhēn jì),
making verification easy.
Otherwise, if conduct is all like Zēng [Zēng Shēn] and Shǐ [Shǐ Yú],
scholarship all like Chéng [Chéng brothers] and Zhū [Zhū Xī],
writing all like Mǎ [Mǎ Qiān] and Bān [Bān Gù/Bān Zhāo],
and character all like Yí [Bó Yí] and Huì [Liǔ Xiàhuì],
in such a chaotic jumble (yú yú lù lù),
how can truth and falsehood be distinguished?
Furthermore, if there are indeed omissions regarding individuals recorded in the former gazetteer,
or if
the major events of their life
were not recorded in full detail,
they are also permitted, along with newly included individuals,
to submit accounts in the same manner,
to be verified and supplemented.
Fourth,
Discussion on Collecting Literary Works (Zhēng Wén).
Next to Biographies (rén wù),
Collected Arts and Literature (yì wén) is essential.
Those who compiled Arts and Literature in recent gazetteers
generally collected poems, prose, essays, and prefaces;
their format was simply that of a literary anthology (wén xuǎn);
but the bibliography of the prefecture’s writings
and the full context and development of the authors’ lineages
were not researched,
which is not the proper gazetteer style.
We now propose to revise the general principles:
We will imitate Bān [Bān Gù]'s *Zhì* and Liú [Liú Xiàng/Liú Xīn]'s *Lüè*;
we will categorize and divide the works into sections,
excise the superfluous and select the excellent,
write postscripts describing their origins and conclusions,
and independently compile a study (kǎo).
This can provide material for future cataloging and collation in the imperial library (guǎn gé),
and will thus be beneficial to historical documentation (wénxiàn).
However, for Arts and Literature to be included in the gazetteer,
the rule is that inclusion requires the subject to be deceased and their reputation finalized (gài guān lùn dìng);
living individuals,
even if they have published works,
are generally not included in the gazetteer.
This adheres to the established practice of the Imperial Compilation and Continuation Verification Bureau (Yù Zuǎn Xù Kǎo Guǎn chéng fǎ),
and differs from modern gazetteers
which merely collect poems and essays,
taking temporary inscriptions and eulogies,
and widely printing them in short tracts.
For scholars and literary figures of the current dynasty or previous eras,
who truly established themselves as masters
and whose work can achieve lasting fame (bù xiǔ zhī yè),
regardless of whether they belong to the Classics (jīng), Histories (shǐ), Philosophers (zǐ), or Anthologies (jí) categories,
or if they are related to technical arts (fāng jì) and miscellaneous schools,
Buddhist canon (shì mén dào zàng),
painting manuals and charts (tú huà pǔ dié),
examination essays (tiè kuò) and philological commentaries (xùn gǔ),
they may all submit clean copies or duplicates
to the office, to be sent to the bureau
for verification and compilation.
However, the submitted works
must be widely recognized;
even if they have not been published,
they must be acknowledged as complete collections,
before inclusion is permitted.
If they are copied manuscripts,
incomplete pages or fragments,
or books that have never been formally evaluated with prefaces or postscripts,
they will be entirely excluded from the compilation,
in order to adhere to the principle of judging by reputation and demanding substance (xún míng zé shí).
Only works that were originally listed in the old gazetteer’s bibliography,
but whose volumes have since been lost or scattered,
are still permitted entry into the gazetteer,
but below the listing,
the character "Wáng"
shall be annotated to distinguish them.
Fifth,
Discussion on Biographical Rules (Chuán Lì).
In the creation of historical biographies,
the rule is to require the subject to be deceased and their reputation finalized (gài guān lùn dìng);
biographies are not written for living people.
Reviewing historical accounts since the Hàn dynasties,
biographies such as *Fēiyǒu Xiānshēng* and *Lǐ Chì*
all treated the biography form as a jest.
Works like *Wū Zhě* and *Tuó Tuó*
used the biographical form to express opinions.
As for the biographies of *Hé Fán* and *Fāng Shān*,
they were used as prefaces for commemorative gifts.
By the time of the Sòng people,
it became common to write biographies for living people,
but this is truly not historical method.
The biographies in the prefecture gazetteer
will entirely follow historical precedent;
all currently living persons
are generally excluded from biographies.
However, for women who maintained chastity (shǒu jié)
and have already received official commendation (jīng diǎn);
or those who have not yet been commended,
but whose age meets the standard rule,
and whose moral integrity is pure,
they may be universally included by exception.
This is because a woman who adheres to one man until the end
has no other aspiration;
her lifelong duty is completed,
and there is no need to wait until her death.
Moreover, such impoverished families
do not necessarily have the access to the gentry enjoyed by literary figures or those of distinguished conduct;
they may be in remote, desolate areas,
their descendants struggling without resources,
or they might accidentally violate a standing rule.
If they are not recognized today,
it is feared that subsequent gazetteer compilations
will inevitably miss them,
hence the urgent effort to seek them out.
As for officials who have left office,
if their political achievements during their tenure were outstanding and worthy of transmission,
and public opinion unanimously praised them,
without any objections,
even if they have not passed away and their reputation finalized,
they are legally permitted to have a biography written.
Since the gazetteer is compiled for this county,
if a magistrate has achieved merit for this county,
his example may be preserved like the sweet pear tree (gān táng);
even if he was impeached for some reason,
or if local opinion is unclear,
how can his currently implemented deeds be erased?
Furthermore, since the person has already departed,
there is no suspicion of flattery,
and having crossed provincial boundaries (fāng zhōu),
there is no standard procedure for remotely verifying whether the person is still alive or not.
Only if the person is currently residing in this county,
or has currently been promoted to a higher official position in this province or holds jurisdiction over it,
will no biography be written;
this is to avoid the suspicion of seeking favor
and to prevent debate over right and wrong.
For individuals who are permitted a biography according to these rules,
the submitted biographical accounts (xíng zhuàng)
must focus on the major events of their life that align with historical standards,
listed with careful detail;
petty trivialities (xiān suǒ dìng dòu),
and anything that constitutes excessive prose,
should all be expunged.
Those matters that involve the strange and bizarre,
or which are not intended to encourage or warn;
or those that invoke gods and spirits,
or speak of unusual dreams,
even if supported by evidence,
will not be included,
so as to avoid the ridicule of being disjointed and chaotic (fú lǚ yáng míng).
Six,
Discussing the Method of Writing.
Historical events should be compiled as monographs (kǎo),
figures should be compiled as biographies (zhuàn),
The adoption or rejection of these two forms
must be determined and executed perfectly,
possessing both structure and essential elements.
Only then can they be considered books worthy of being engraved (i.e., enduring works),
and serve as models for future generations.
For example, the monograph form should only emphasize government, education, and rituals,
and the customs and practices of the people,
while those that excessively praise topographical advantages
or artificially connect them with scenic views
should be omitted.
If there are ancient relics and excellent scenic spots
that are reliably verifiable,
or inscriptions and verses by famous people
that are truly worthy of record,
they should also follow the method of separate annotation using smaller script,
and be judiciously appended below the main monograph;
this is to rectify the historical style
and differentiate it from anecdotal histories.
Indeed, the gazetteer form may be compared to managing a household:
The main halls and prime residences
may be called the official residence (fǔzhái).
Structures built against cliffs,
or pavilions spanning water,
may be called auxiliary estates (biéyè),
but cannot be called the main dwelling (zhèngqǐn).
Jade ornaments and crimson silk ribbons
may be called immortal attire (xiānfú),
but cannot be called the robes and tablets of officials (shēnhù).
This constitutes the distinction between local gazetteers (jùnxiàn zhìchéng)
and compiled works like *Wòyóu* and *Qīngfú*.
The Biographies (lièzhuàn) should also prioritize famous officials (mínghuàn) and local worthies (xiāngxián),
those distinguished by loyalty, filial piety, integrity, and righteousness,
and notable scholars (rúín zhuóxíng).
Those skilled in literature (wényuàn) or specialized techniques (fāngjì) who have visible achievements
come next.
For instance, officials (zhíguān) who lack memorable achievements,
or degree holders (kēmù) who lack notable accomplishments,
by rule, may not have biographies established.
This is because gazetteers belong to reliable history (xìnshǐ);
they are not like official registers and records,
which are organized purely by rank, title, and dress.
For those who should not have biographies established,
officials and teachers (guānshī) should have a separate chronological table of their successive appointments (lìrèn niánpǔ),
while local gentry (yìshēn) should have a separate chronological table of their examinations and degrees (kējiǎ niánpǔ).
Under the framework of years and months,
only the names should be noted,
and no flowery rhetoric should be inserted.
Even if some among them deserve biographies,
it is unnecessary to further
note the phrase "has biography" within the tables,
in order to maintain uniformity.
If we follow the common contemporary practice,
then those recording officials and teachers:
first have the Monograph on Officials (Zhíguān Zhì),
which records the dates of their assumption of office,
and then have the Monograph on Famous Officials (Mínghuàn Zhì),
which records the administrative achievements of their successive appointments;
and other matters found in commemorative stele, praises, or prefaces recording administrative achievements
are further collected into the Monograph on Arts and Letters (Yìwén Zhì).
Those recording local gentry:
first have the Monograph on Examinations (Kēmù Zhì),
and then have the Monograph on Figures (Rénwù Zhì).
They also separate the year of passing the examination and the professional achievements of a lifetime into two monographs;
and if their achievements are found in epitaphs, biographies, or funeral orations,
they are again collected into the Monograph on Arts and Letters (Yìwén Zhì).
The matters concerning a single person
are redundantly seen in three or four categories.
Consequently, in one place, they note "biography found in X volume,"
and in another place, they note "details found in X monograph,"
the notations are confused and scattered,
the facts are disordered,
and the structure is excessively fragmented;
nothing is worse than this.
When compiling gazetteers today,
it is especially necessary to first reorganize and standardize them,
and immediately break this conventional practice.
Seven,
Discussing Quotations.
When histories and gazetteers quote established texts,
the goal is to clarify facts,
not to admire literary style.
If it relates to the facts,
even documents written by clerks
should be collected,
let alone texts superior to these.
If it is irrelevant to the facts,
even the writings of Bān Gù and Yáng Xióng
should not be adopted,
let alone texts inferior to these.
However, if the literary pieces recorded in the Arts and Letters sections of old gazetteers
are now all scattered and placed under the sections detailing the achievements of the person concerned,
then the resulting arrangement of pieces will lack uniformity in length and complexity;
when integrated into the space allotted for monographs and biographies,
it is inevitable that they must be edited and pruned.
If there is a concern about appearing to plagiarize,
then above the main text,
the author's name should still be clearly marked,
to indicate the source, and nothing more.
As for the method of labeling the citations,
it should entirely imitate the usage in the *Shǐ Jì* (史記) and the *Hàn Shū* (漢書).
When the *Shǐ Jì* and the *Hàn Shū* quote the masters of the Zhōu and Qín Dynasties,
if only common words or phrases are deleted or modified,
they do not differentiate it further,
but directly use the three-character phrase
"Qí Cí Yuē" (其辭曰, 'Its text says') to introduce the passage.
Only when there have been substantial deletions or modifications,
and the original scope of the essay is no longer maintained,
do they then use the three characters
"Qí Lüè Yuē" (其略曰, 'Its summary says') to distinguish it.
The memorials of Jiǎ Chángshā and others are examples of this.
The quotations used now
should all follow this model.
However, among various literary forms,
each has places where it ought to be quoted,
but the form of poetry and rhapsodies
has very few applicable uses.
Only within the Monograph on Geography (Dìlǐ Kǎo),
in the section on famous sites,
under the separate annotations,
a small amount may be recorded
to attest to their spiritual excellence.
As for others, such as works expressing inner spirit,
or those dealing with wind, clouds, moon, and dew—
if they are truly fine compositions—
they should naturally be kept in separate manuscripts,
or placed in books specifically dedicated to literary selection;
they should not be intermixed within histories and gazetteers,
as this is the correct approach.
Moreover, since ancient times, the Fifteen *Guófēng*
and the Twelve *Guóyǔ*
have proceeded side by side without conflict,
and it is unheard of that they could be combined into one book.
Therefore, the extensive selection of poetry and lyrics
is also a conventional practice that must be urgently reformed.
However, if, within the chapter on Customs (Fēngsú Piān),
there are places where folk songs must be quoted,
this does not fall under that prohibition.
This aligns with the principle by which the *Zuǒ Zhuàn* and the *Guóyǔ* quote proverbs and cite folk songs.
Eight,
Discussing Selection and Editing.
Taking all texts that should be recorded in the Yìwén (Arts and Literature) section,
and assigning each to the biography of the person concerned,
there is nothing objectionable in this.
However, regarding various genres that should be recorded in the Biographies (zhuàn), Records (zhì), and Conduct Accounts (xíngzhuàng),
they are now all deleted;
and instead, the texts are taken and edited into the Lièzhuàn (Collective Biographies).
In this process, there are three difficulties:
First, those for whom, according to established rules, a biography should not be established,
and texts which the biography should not fully include;
the stele inscriptions and narrative accounts of the time,
perhaps because of the perceived importance of the writing style,
were not without indiscriminate inclusion.
Second, the Lièzhuàn (Collective Biographies) in the gazetteers (zhì)
do not have much scope,
yet the original accounts sometimes contain expansive, lengthy articles;
if the original text is fully recorded,
the imbalance between length and brevity will be improper;
if the events and deeds are deleted,
it will invite resentment and criticism.
Third, when using existing texts
and incorporating them into the main studies (kǎo) or main biographies (zhuàn),
this originally belonged to the style of textual citation,
thus allowing the author's name and the three characters, "qí cí yuē" (其辭曰, 'its text says'),
to be marked,
so that it adheres to the style of citation.
If we now take the old biography directly
and edit it into a new biography,
since it is connected and compiled as a single continuous piece,
it is not convenient to additionally mark the author’s name.
For example, when Bān Shǐ (the historian Bān Gù) wrote the 'Biography of Sīmǎ Qiān' (Sīmǎ Qiān Zhuàn),
he used the entirety of the 'Preface to the Shǐjì' (Shǐjì Zìxù);
he used the phrase, "Qiān zhī zìxù yún ěr" (遷之自序雲爾, 'This is what Qiān’s own preface says'),
as a single sentence
to clearly distinguish the guest and the host.
This is because the Grand Historian's (Shǐ Gōng) 'Preface' (Zìxù)
was originally not the main biography (běn zhuàn),
thus allowing this sentence to be used for differentiation.
However, regarding the annals and biographies (jì zhuàn) before [Emperor] Kǎo-Wǔ,
where the existing text of the Shǐjì is used entirely,
no further differentiation is made;
this is because the annals (jì) are these specific annals,
the biography (zhuàn) is this specific biography,
the eulogy (zàn) is this specific eulogy,
and the style does not permit the marking of the words "Sīmǎ Qiān yuē" (Sīmǎ Qiān says).
If we now rashly adopt this same precedent,
since this type of style has rarely been seen recently,
there will certainly be accusations of plagiarism and imitation.
Regarding these three points,
there is definitively no other method to handle them;
only the precedent of using large text with separated annotations
can satisfy both concerns.
The method is to take that old biography,
conform it to the principles and precedents of the current gazetteer (zhì),
and edit it into a new biography.
As for matters that should be deleted according to the rules,
but which are inconvenient to delete immediately,
these shall also be treated as small characters in double rows,
along with the author's full name,
and the reason for deletion or refinement,
all uniformly attached as a note beneath the main text.
In this way, the documents confirming facts from the old gazetteer (zhì)
will not be entirely omitted,
and the rigorous style of the new gazetteer (zhì)
will also not be hindered.
If the original text is not too disorganized
and still conforms to the precedent of rigor,
it shall remain as it was,
to show that there is no inherent fondness for unnecessary change.
Nine,
Discussing Titles and Headings.
In recently circulated gazetteers and records (zhì chéng),
where selection and rejection lack order,
and the crude and superficial are not worthy of study,
it is not only that the text lacks essential structure,
but even the headings
already fail to adhere to historical principles (shǐ fǎ).
For instance, when gathering historical facts (diǎngù) to compile Studies (kǎo),
the major sections like Tiānwén (Astronomy), Dìlǐ (Geography), Lǐyí (Rites and Ceremonies), and Shíhuò (Food and Money/Economics)
are fundamentally sufficient to encompass all sub-items.
However, modern people are always fond of excessive analysis;
thus, Tiānwén is split into two Records (zhì): Xīngyě (Stellar Fields) and Zhānhòu (Prognostication);
and Dìlǐ is split into several chapters: Jiāngyù (Territorial Limits) and Shānchuān (Mountains and Rivers).
Binding volume after volume, page after page,
they suddenly divide things into dozens of categories.
Yet the precedents of the eight treatises (shū) in the Shǐjì and the ten records (zhì) in the Hánshū
are clearly established—how often have they resorted to such complexity and fragmentation?
Similarly, when seeking out personalities and establishing biographies (zhuàn),
sections like Mínghuàn (Famous Officials), Xiāngxián (Local Worthies), Rúlín (Confucian Scholars), and Zhuóxíng (Outstanding Conduct)
are fundamentally insufficient to encompass all types of people, ancient and modern.
Yet modern people are always fond of forced merging;
thus, upon finding a reclusive talent (yì cái),
they do not ask how exceptional their career or conduct was,
but first try to categorize which heading (sèmù) they belong to;
upon finding a versatile talent (quán cái),
they do not ask how comprehensive their learning and conduct were,
but first try to categorize which section should take precedence;
leading to contradictions and strained interpretations,
wrapping them up by category.
The historical texts featuring collective biographies (hé zhuàn) and individual biographies (dú zhuàn) are established—
how often have they necessarily prefixed the section heading?
The reason for this
is that the documents providing historical facts (diǎngù) and evidence
are not assigned to the main Studies (běn kǎo) but to the Yìwén Zhì (Record of Arts and Literature).
In that case, lacking sources and consequences for events,
they inevitably must be scattered throughout the text
to hide the disgrace of superficiality.
The documents comprising Conduct Accounts (xíngzhuàng) and Stele Inscriptions (bēi bǎn)
are not assigned to the main Biographies (běn zhuàn) but to the Yìwén Zhì (Record of Arts and Literature).
In that case, the person lacks a complete biography,
and they must be forcibly combined
to meet the required number of items.
Therefore, the structure of the gazetteer (zhì) is ruined because the headings do not adhere to historical principles (shǐ fǎ);
and the headings are ruined because the Yìwén section does not conform to historical precedents (shǐ lì);
and the origin of the Yìwén section not conforming to historical precedents
stems from the time when county and prefecture gazetteers (jùn xiàn zhì) were first compiled,
mistakenly imitating the wide recording of poetry and prose found in topographical records of famous mountains (míng shān tú zhì).
Now, compiling a gazetteer for a prefecture or county (zhōu xiàn zhì) is different from compiling one for a famous mountain.
The latter takes topographical features and scenery as its focus,
and skillful, lifelike depiction as its craft.
Inscriptions on cliff faces,
records hidden on walls,
as well as traces of thunder, lightning, ghosts, and monsters,
texts related to grotto-heavens (dòngtiān) and talismans (fújiǎn),
and the works of famous people, ancient and modern, regarding their travels and scenic views—
are collected without exception,
serving to demonstrate profound scholarship.
Indeed, historical principles (shǐ fǎ) were originally not needed there.
As for the gazetteers and records of prefectures and counties (zhōu xiàn zhì chéng),
they are the book of a region or state at that time,
covering the people, the altars of soil and grain (shè jì),
government, education, and historical facts (diǎngù).
Their applications are extremely broad;
how can they be treated under the same precedent as the others?
Since the Míng dynasty,
this practice has been followed without change.
Therefore, although some prefecture and county gazetteers (zhōu xiàn zhì chéng)
are better than others,
in the end, few possess the outstanding quality of independent judgment,
establishing historical precedents (shǐ lì)
that can serve as permanent models.
Today, we must especially break this long-standing habit
to restore the proper structure of historical writing (zhèng shǐ tǐ cái).
Ten,
Discussing Supplementary Sections (Wài Biān).
Among the twenty-one dynastic histories,
besides the four main sections of Annals (jì), Tables (biǎo), Treatises (zhì), and Biographies (zhuàn),
the Jìn Shū (History of Jìn) has Zàijì (Records of the Sixteen States),
the Wǔdài Shǐ (History of the Five Dynasties) has Fùlù (Appendices),
the Liáo Shǐ (History of Liáo) has Guóyǔ Jiě (Explanations of the National Language);
and when the Míng Shǐ (History of Míng) was compiled during the present dynasty,
in addition to the Chronological Tables (nián biǎo),
there were also Túshì (Diagrams and Forms).
Although the materials used differ,
the precedents are all established based on necessity,
aiming to ensure nothing is omitted and nothing is included indiscriminately.
If the local gazetteers (yì zhì) are mixed and confusing,
making them resemble unofficial or minor novels (bàiyě xiǎoshuō),
they certainly do not constitute the proper style;
but if they are immediately treated solely by the rigorous and concise precedents of the national histories,
this also defeats the purpose of broad collection for later selective use.
For all matters that are trivial but should not be omitted,
such as giving birth to triplets,
people living to one hundred years old,
traces of immortals (shénxiān),
glorious events related to the imperial examinations (kēdì),
and all new, strange, and delightful anecdotes,
although these are not emphasized in the style of historical writing,
it is also difficult to immediately discuss deleting them.
These should be placed after the main biographies (zhèng zhuàn),
using the style of miscellaneous writings (zá zhù tǐ),
recorded sporadically;
it may be named Wài Biān (Supplementary Section)
or Zájì (Miscellaneous Records),
forming a separate structure,
allowing the scattered small details
to first have a section they can belong to,
precisely to clarify the structure of the main record (zhèng zài).
Popular songs and proverbs (yáogē yànyǔ),
and street gossip and rumor (xiàng shuō jiē tán),
if they contain anything noteworthy,
should all be governed by this rule.
In the late winter of the Jiǎshēn year,
Hú Míngfǔ of Tiānmén proposed compiling the County Gazetteer (Xiàn Zhì),
therefore I composed this piece,
to attach for discussion.
The general meaning of its discussion on the principles of selection and deletion (bǐxuē yìlì),
is consistent with the two previous letters in the old *Dá Zhēn Xiùcai* (Reply to the Scholar Zhēn).
However, the first five articles of this discussion,
concern matters suitable for pre-preparation,
which those letters did not cover.
Regarding the articles laid out in those letters,
this discussion does not include all of them,
because this (current text) focuses on the immediate matters at hand,
while the remaining ideas, which are extrapolations outside of the compilation work,
have not been addressed here.
As for the discussion concerning the pitfalls of sticking rigidly to common practices,
this piece is clearer than the previous letters;
and the section on Arts and Letters (Yìwén yī zhì),
is discussed repeatedly and in particular detail.
This is because, upon reviewing the origins of the defects found in common practices,
none fall outside this scope;
therefore, I wish to offer a discussion that pulls out the root and stops the source,
and decisively implement newly defined principles,
which is certainly not merely indulging in making changes.
Readers should take the two documents and compare them,
so that during the process of compilation,
they might derive a small benefit. (End of self-postscript).
Preface to the Examination of Arts and Letters in the Tiānmén Xiàn Zhì (Appendix: Discussion on Arts and Letters)
Alas!
This examination of Arts and Letters,
is not only for recording the prosperity of literature,
but also for lamenting its decline.
Scholars with ambition,
bearing extraordinary genius within their hearts,
reaching the point of contradiction, obstruction, and frustration,
inevitably express it through literature—
how lamentable!
Yet, this very literature,
often consumes decades of work by firefly light and snowy desks,
amidst bitter rain and chilling wind,
where one carves into the liver and kidneys,
expends heart and blood,
and produces it with great seriousness.
However, not a few generations pass,
before a solitary cup (of writing) is lost,
existing or vanishing among men,
subjected to cold dew and drifting wind,
returning together to ruin—
how overwhelming the sorrow!
Fortunately, when light carriages carry brushes (i.e., when officials compile histories),
they can be transmitted to future generations.
Nevertheless, among those recorded in the Hàn histories,
several individuals are missing from the *Suí Zhì*;
among those recorded in the *Suí Zhì*,
several families (of works) are fragmented and lost in the *Táng Shū*;
the *Chóngwén Zǒng Mù*,
the *Zhōngxīng Shū Mù*,
the *Wényuān Gé Mù*—
across a thousand years,
the general trend is the same.
Is it that the Creator envies talent,
and wishes to keep the finest essence secret?
Or is it that the compositions themselves,
lack sufficient brilliance,
and are unworthy of long-term transmission?
Yet, since the time of the Two Hàns,
miscellaneous works of hundreds of schools,
mixing the refined and the vulgar,
including vulgar and trivial writings,
also remain in existence;
thus, among them, there is inherent fortune and misfortune.
The old *Jǐnglíng Jiù Zhì*,
did not list bibliographic entries in the Arts and Letters section,
consequently, the works of former people
were not all gathered;
although the biographies often appended records of their life’s writings,
even now, not many are generally visible.
If that is the case, among the works collected in this examination,
if another few decades pass,
how much of their dispersal, loss, and disappearance
will compare to the present day?
This is why I profoundly lament the works of all these authors.
Now, gathering the various authors,
compiling them into one examination,
there are four categories:
namely Classics (Jīng),
namely Histories (Shǐ),
namely Masters (Zǐ),
and namely Collections (Jí).
There are three distinctions:
works transmitted through the generations,
works preserved in private collections—
both are categorized into the four divisions;
and works lost,
which form a separate category,
appended to the end of the chapter.
Discussion:
Recent gazetteers, in their Arts and Letters section,
completely abandon the ancient method,
grouping poetry and prose together,
but omitting bibliographic listings—
this is not without intent.
When literature is collected and arranged in systematic sequence,
those pieces that aid historical matters,
allow events to be detailed more easily through collateral evidence,
and literature, by being comprehensively included, is made complete.
Therefore, since Zhāomíng (Prince Liú Tǒng),
the Táng Dynasty had the *Wényuàn* (Garden of Literature),
the Sòng Dynasty had the *Wén Jiàn* (Mirror of Literature),
and the Yuán Dynasty had the *Wén Lèi* (Categories of Literature)—
these comprehensive anthologies spanning entire dynasties,
presenting both the refined and the vulgar,
all served to assist the official histories,
broaden knowledge,
and illuminate literature.
The fifteen *Guófēng* (Airs of the States),
and the twelve sections of *Guóyǔ* (Discourses of the States),
ought, by principle, to exist as separate compiled works;
logically, they should not be mixed.
Recently, many gazetteers emulate the structure of *Guóyǔ* when compiling local records,
but one does not hear of imitating *Guófēng* by collecting the poetry and prose of a single locality
to form a specialized anthology;
Is this the reason why, out of fondness and unwillingness to delete,
they are constrained and contradictory,
completely abandoning the established principles of Arts and Letters?
Now, the historical form values solemn rigor,
while the work of selection values broad collection.
Inserting such poetry and prose into the gazetteer,
already feels excessive,
but judged by the standards of selection for anthologies,
it would then be considered too few.
Therefore, it is clear that the two ought to be compiled as separate works,
mutually aiding and assisting each other.
As for the catalog of authors’ works,
the importance is immense,
and it should not be lightly discussed for removal.
Therefore, we now exclusively employ the ancient method,
to conform to historical standards.
Those writings which I am particularly reluctant to delete,
are temporarily placed in the appendix.
Should one follow up on this endeavor and enhance it,
further compiling the works into a book,
to supplement the gazetteer’s shortcomings—
Alas!
Perhaps there will be others who, hearing of this, will continue the compilation?
Preface to the Examination of the Five Phases in the Tiānmén Xiàn Zhì
The floods during Yáo’s reign, the droughts during Tāng’s reign,
even in a sage’s era, there cannot be freedom from calamity.
Revolving stars and reversed fire,
how can external things not cause abnormalities?
Nevertheless, the stone yè must be recorded,
and the presence of armyworms and locusts must be carefully noted,
in order to rectify human affairs,
and respond to celestial changes.
Since the *Yuán Shén* and the *Gōu Mìng*,
the use of talismans and prophecies has been absurd,
thus losing solemn rigor.
Yet, the records compiled by Bān (Gù) and Fàn (Yè),
all adhere to Liú Xiàng's commentary on the *Hóngfàn* (Great Plan),
connecting categories and making analogies,
matching evidence to human affairs;
although they retain the function of warning,
they are inevitably not without forced interpretation.
Regarding the juncture between Heaven and man,
the Sages were cautious.
During the two hundred and forty-two years of the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals),
the calamities and auspicious signs of the Five Phases,
appeared mixed and varied;
the Sages merely recorded them carefully,
without meticulously trying to match them,
saying which event corresponded to which matter,
or which corresponded to which person.
It was not that they were unable,
but rather, by preserving the general principle
that omens reflect the constant and the changing,
it is sufficient to warn the hearts of men;
if one insists on forcing connections between events,
it will inevitably lead to discrepancies,
perhaps causing doubt that calamities are not to be feared,
thus aiming for caution but achieving negligence?
Anomalies in plants and trees,
misfortunes caused by insects and beasts,
historians categorize all these under the Five Types,
listing them according to the Five Matters.
I believe that while auspicious and strange occurrences do happen for a reason,
there are also cases that are not necessarily so,
and are difficult to fit through forced interpretation.
Therefore, I record events plainly based on facts,
without dividing them into categories,
without annotating their correspondences,
strictly sequenced by year and month.
Relevant human affairs,
are found interspersed in other chapters,
where they can be understood independently.
Preface to the Examination of Schools in the Tiānmén Xiàn Zhì
Quèlǐ has prepared its family chronicles;
Chéngjūn has collected its historical narratives.
Schools everywhere,
the world shares the same customs.
Why bother with continuous compilation and collection,
or creating a specialized examination?
However, since the period of the Liǎng Hàn onward,
governance and education each had their object of veneration,
and schools have seen flourishing without obsolescence.
They built palaces by the water,
dusted the bell stands and wiped their shoes;
when there were affairs, they were lectured upon, clarified, and executed within these halls;
when there were no affairs, elders and youth
would use them for visiting, viewing, and self-improvement,
and thus rites, laws, punishments, and governance,
human constants and universal principles,
all originated from this.
Therefore, schools were indeed the exterior and interior counterparts of administrative governance.
The classic models are extant,
but the lost lineage is indistinct.
Stroking the bells and drums and contemplating their musical elegance,
one can be suddenly inspired to action.
Discussing the Gazetteer Style with Wáng Míngfǔ, Magistrate of Shíshǒu.
The gazetteer is crafted historically;
the complete work must have its own definitive style.
The text within the gazetteer
must adhere to historical methods,
thus the wording and phrasing used throughout the complete work,
must also possess standards, rules, and guidelines,
which cannot be neglected.
Although style originally has no fixed standard,
it is sufficient that the entire work is internally consistent
and avoids mutual contradiction;
there is no need to change it casually
due to differences in individual opinion.
Even the originally established eight major categories,
divided into dozens of sub-sections,
require slight adjustment,
which is enough to establish a consistent framework
and submit the table of contents for review.
However, those who write records, biographies, and narratives
must rely on historical scholarship.
If historical scholarship is ignored,
then the texts of records, biographies, and narratives
will completely lack methodology.
This leads to the writings of gazetteer compilers,
who follow custom unexamined.
Not only is the prose unrefined,
but it also harms the factual context.
Zēngzǐ said:
“When expressing words and tone,
one must distance oneself from vulgarity and perversity.”
Vulgarity means the prose is unrefined,
and perversity means it harms the facts.
Scholars are limited by customary habits,
each boasting of their own preferences,
competing intensely over intangible qualities like flatness, ingenuity, richness, or simplicity.
This is like how human minds differ
and faces vary;
how can one compete,
and why must one compete?
But regarding methodology and textual principles,
if one fails to deliberate,
not only will the language be unrefined,
making it difficult to be carried far;
but it also harms the factual context
and loses the purpose for which the words were spoken.
Now that corrections have been made along with the text,
I have attached recommendations for discussion.
Fearing that the reasons for mandatory corrections are not fully understood,
I briefly list several points
to serve as a general outline.
Then not only will the gazetteer style be pristine,
but even extending this to the writing of records, biographies, and narratives,
it will invariably be clear, rigorous, and clean,
practical and useful,
thus preventing flowery prose from obscuring actual facts.
For example, the *Shíshǒu Xiàn Zhì*,
frequently refers to the county as *Shí Yì*,
which harms the factual context.
If a two-character place name
has only one character extracted,
how can those with the same character
be differentiated?
For instance, if Shíshǒu is referred to as Shí,
among ancient county names,
the Hàn Dynasty had Shíchéng,
the Qí Dynasty had Shíqiū,
the Suí Dynasty had Shínán,
the Táng Dynasty had Shíyán,
today Sìchuān has Shízhù Tīng,
Yúnnán has Shípíng Zhōu,
Shānxī has Shílóu Xiàn,
Jiāngnán has Shídài Xiàn,
and Jiāngxī and Guǎngdōng both have Shíchéng Xiàn.
How will later readers
know this refers to the present-day Shíshǒu?
Furthermore, referring to a county (*xiàn*) as an *yì*,
is also a custom followed without examining its reality,
and cannot be taken as precedent.
*Yì* is a general term for fortified cities.
Large cities, like metropolitan capitals, provincial capitals, prefectural seats, and departmental seats,
can all be called *yì*.
The *Shī* refers to *Jīng Yì*,
and when states in the Chūnqiū period sought friendly relations,
they referred to themselves humbly as *Bì Yì*.
How can this term be exclusively reserved for the modern county name?
Even small fortified villages,
or settlements of ten families,
can all be called *yì*.
How could this only refer to the county administration?
Furthermore, calling the current County Magistrate (*zhī xiàn*) *zhī mǒu xiàn shì* (Administrator of Affairs of a Certain County),
is also inaccurate.
The Sòng Dynasty used capital officials to administer external county affairs,
treating them with more respect than the County Head (*xiàn lìng*).
Their concluding title still carried their capital rank,
hence the usage "Such-and-such Official Administrator of Affairs of Such-and-such County."
If we now adopt that designation,
later generations will certainly confuse the Sòng system with the current system.
As for *Yì Hóu* or *Yì Dàfū*,
these are terms of respect used by those governed;
They are acceptable in rhetorical prose,
but using them in factual narrative
is both vulgar and perverse.
*Yì Zǎi* was an office from the Chūnqiū period.
Although people of the Hàn Dynasty used it in stone inscriptions,
ultimately, it cannot be taken as a standard.
*Lìng Yǐn* is also an ancient official title
that should not be misused and confuse later generations.
When official titles ignore the established system and rely heavily on literary phrases,
it greatly harms the factual context.
I recall someone referring to an ancestor as *Sīmǎ Gōng*.
When I tried to verify the ancestor’s identity,
I was confused for several days
and could not find the answer.
This is because common practice favors literary phrases,
using the *Sīmǎ* of the *Zhōu Guān*
to designate the modern Ministry of War (*Bīng Bù*);
Yet the Minister (*Shàngshū*), Vice Minister (*Shìláng*), and their subordinate officials
can all generally be referred to as *Sīmǎ*.
Distinction is already difficult.
Moreover, the Prefectural Associate Administrator (*Fǔ Tóngzhī*)
is popularly also called *Sīmǎ*,
and the Department Associate Administrator (*Zhōu Tóng*) also has the title *Zhōu Sīmǎ*.
From the Minister of War (*Bīng Bù Shàngshū*) down to the Department Associate Administrator (*Zhōu Tóng*),
their offices are immensely separated.
The three characters *Sīmǎ Gōng*,
people today already cannot distinguish which official it refers to,
much less those of later generations?
They use the ancient *Chéngjūn* to refer to modern Imperial Academy students (*Guózǐ Jiàn Shēng*);
and use the ancient *Xiáng Xù* to refer to modern *Lǐn Zēng Fù Shēng* students.
*Míng Jīng* was originally a category separate from the *Jìnshì* exams,
but is now a general designation for Tribute Students (*Gòngshēng*).
However, there are ten grades: *Ēn*, *Bá*, *Fù*, *Suì*, *Yōu*, *Gōng*, *Lǐn*, *Zēng*, *Fù*, and *Lì*—
if differentiated, they become indistinguishable.
For high and distinguished noble officials,
their posthumous names (*shì*) often include Gōng, Wén, Yì, or Mǐn;
For scholars and students,
their literary names (*hào*) are frequently Fēng, Yán, Xī, or Quán.
The posthumous name is rendered as *Gōng*,
and the literary name as *Xiānshēng* or *Chǔshì*.
Sometimes the phrasing resembles a longevity dedication,
sometimes it resembles an official prayer for the departed.
The origin of this style is unknown.
Xiàng Jí said:
“Writing should be sufficient to record names and titles.”
Now, reading these books
and seeing the deeds,
yet not knowing the person’s name,
how can this be considered the method for historians writing history?
Moreover, regarding double names where only one character is used,
the ancients long ago pointed out this error.
For example, if Dù Tái Liǔ is referred to as Qīng,
the phrase is incomplete,
yet Xún Qīng and Yú Qīng
can both be used generally.
If Ān Zhòng Róng is referred to as Róng,
the phrase is incomplete,
yet Huán Róng and Kòu Róng
can both be used generally.
Furthermore, referring to Qùjí as Jí,
Wújì as Jì,
or Bùhài as Hài,
is also contrary to the intent of the naming itself.
How can one still claim to be referring to that person?
Women who have personal names are referred to by their name;
those without personal names are referred to by their surname.
Since the time of the Zuǒ [Zhuàn] and Shǐ [Jì],
there have been none who changed this practice.
Now, writers of local gazetteers omit the surname and refer to the clan name (shì),
sometimes even calling them "Gāi Shì" (that clan).
This is illogical in meaning,
and stylistically, it is also coarse and clumsy.
Nowadays, when composing writings for virtuous and martyred women,
one often fails to mention their full name,
but immediately refers to them as "Virtuous Wife" (jiéfù) or "Martyred Woman" (liènǚ).
This is especially harmful to reason.
For a woman to maintain her integrity
is comparable to a man expressing his loyalty.
If one were to write biographies for officials like Féng or Bǐ,
and failed to refer to them by the names Féng or Bǐ,
but instead called them "Loyal Minister, and so on,"
would there be any sense in that?
When classical scholars composed the Civil Service Examination essay (shíyì),
they first used two phrases to begin the topic (pòtí).
By rule, the pòtí does not record the person's name;
thus, the Founding Master is called "the Sage" (shèngrén),
the disciples are called "the Worthies" (xiánzhě),
and Yán, Zēng, and Mèngzǐ are called "the Great Worthies."
This system likely imitates the beginning of regulated verse prose (lǜfù),
starting vaguely and then becoming concrete.
This is simply the nature of the examination essay format.
Now, using this method to refer to the loyal and filial,
is truly what is meant by "being accustomed to something without examining it."
Liǔzǐ said:
"Consult the Grand Historian (tàishǐ) to establish its purity."
There has never been historical writing that was impure.
How should writing be pure?
In selecting vocabulary, one desires it to be refined and not mixed (with irrelevant material).
When the ancients read the Yì [Jīng], it was as if the Shū [Jīng] did not exist.
This is what is meant by "not being mixed."
Even though they are both classics,
and both the words of the Sages,
if one were to mix
the imagery of "dragon's blood and demon carriages" into the text
or take the dreams of "bears, snakes, and fish banners"
and link them to the sequence of "The King’s First Month of Spring";
then the work of the Sages would be spoiled,
and the texts of the Six Classics would become impure.
Now, when writing biographies for virtuous wives,
instead of narrating the virtuous wife’s deeds,
they often refer to her as having "vowed her intent in the Cypress Boat" (shǐ zhì Bǎi Zhōu).
The literary allusion is then impossible to understand clearly.
Now, Bǎi Zhōu
is merely a boat made of cypress wood.
The poet uses it as an initiating metaphor (qǐ xīng);
Bǎi Zhōu is not therefore a factual deed of chastity.
The Guān Jū can inspire the idea of a virtuous lady,
but the osprey (jūjiū) cannot therefore be pointed to as the virtuous lady;
the Lù Míng can inspire the idea of an honored guest,
but how can the braying deer be therefore pointed to as the honored guest?
The principle is quite obvious.
Why, then, in descriptive writing,
are flowery and embellished literary phrases from poetry and fu inserted?
The Master (Fūzǐ) said:
"The essential thing is the rectification of names (zhèng míng)!"
Written language is the accumulation and manifestation of names and statements.
"If names are not correct, then speech will not be appropriate,"
and thus, the facts and principles cannot be made clear.
Therefore, documents have structure,
and writing has rules and standards.
This is unavoidable for the superior man (Jūnzǐ).
If one follows custom without damaging principle
or harming the facts of the matter,
although this might not be what the ancients practiced,
one may naturally invoke the principle of flexible adaptation according to the times.
Today, I am also not completely inflexible about this.
Record of Discussing Gazetteer Compilation with Dài Dōngyuán
In the summer of the Guǐsì year of Qíánlóng 38 (1773),
I met Dài Dōngyuán at the office of the Níngbō Circuit Intendant.
Fényúnbì (Mr. Féng) was then serving as the Circuit Intendant of Military Defense for Níng[bō], Shào[xīng], and Tái[zhōu] (Níngshàotái Bīngbèidào).
Mr. Dài was profoundly versed in classical scholarship;
his name had long been celebrated among the high officials,
but he did not understand historical studies.
When he heard me discuss historical matters,
he would often treat me with an air of arrogance.
Upon seeing my Draft Guidelines for the Hézhōu Gazetteer (Hézhōu Zhì Lì),
he then said:
"As for the structure
and guidelines, these are very archaic and elegant,
but gazetteer compilation does not value archaism and elegance.
When I compiled the various gazetteers, such as Fénzhōu,
I followed popular custom,
differing in no way from others.
I also had no fixed rules or precedents;
whatever was convenient was fine.
The purpose of a gazetteer is to investigate geography.
If one only applies one's mind to the changes and evolution of the geography,
the work of the gazetteer is complete.
Why excessively discuss historical documents and scholarship (wénxiàn)?
How can that be called urgent business?"
I replied:
"In terms of structure and guidelines,
I merely sought what was correct,
I had no intention of seeking archaism and elegance.
However, those who achieve what is correct
invariably conform to archaism and elegance.
If one claims that one must merely follow custom,
then any common person could compile it.
Why, then, must one select a specific person to take part?
Local gazetteers are like the national histories of antiquity;
fundamentally, they are not specialized geographical works.
If one claims that only evolution and change are important,
and that wénxiàn is not urgent,
then simply composing a single essay on the investigation of evolution is sufficient.
Why gather people and open an office,
collect thousands of pieces of gold for expenses,
use humble language and generous gifts
to invite you to travel great distances,
spend long periods of time,
resulting in a book that fills several boxes?
Moreover, the evolution of antiquity and the present
is not something that can be achieved through my own conjecture.
Those who investigate evolution
draw resources from existing records.
Since the records are all there,
anyone can examine them.
Even if I make an error today,
later generations can still correct it.
As for the wénxiàn of a particular locality,
if they are not collected in a timely manner,
if the arrangement is improper,
or if the selection and rejection are inappropriate,
then in the future, there will be material lost and difficult to trace,
disappearing without notice.
Now, the key to planning any undertaking
is nothing better
than devoting one's attention to those things that later generations will not be able to recover or correct.
Therefore, according to my view,
while researching antiquity certainly requires meticulous care,
if circumstances compel us and we cannot achieve both simultaneously,
it is better to prioritize wénxiàn and treat evolution lightly."
Dài looked away and said to another person:
"If the evolution and change are incorrect,
then the entire book is incorrect.
It is nominally the gazetteer of this Prefecture or State,
but in reality, it is not that Prefecture or State. How can this be acceptable?"
I replied:
"The idea that if the evolution is wrong,
the whole book is wrong,
merely means that incorrect ancient events traceable in the records might be included.
If ancient events are mistakenly included,
they can also be corrected based on ancient texts.
The matter is the same as with evolution.
As for scattered and extraneous lost texts and neglected documents
from within the last three hundred years,
along with that which is transmitted orally,
we cannot guarantee that these will not be lost to future generations.
And the benefits and disadvantages of local projects
that are crucial for the practical needs of the locality—
these are all verifiable and factual,
and there is certainly no case where an error in the investigation of evolution
would make them irrelevant to this particular Prefecture or State."
FÉNG Jūn said:
"A local gazetteer (fāng zhì) that integrates antiquity and the present
is what constitutes a complete book.
How can it be only established for matters within three or four hundred years?"
I replied:
"Books in the historical category (shǐ bù)
detail the near and summarize the distant;
this is generally the case for all schools,
not only for local gazetteers.
Shǐ Tàigōng's Book (《Tàishǐgōng Shū》) details the institutions of the Hàn dynasty,
yet its accounts of Yú, Xià, Shāng, and Zhōu
often clearly contradict the Six Classics (liù yì).
There are quite a few such instances.
However, the Six Classics are entirely extant,
and people can rely on them to correct the errors of Shǐ Qiān;
thus, even if Shǐ Qiān's book is mistaken,
it still does no harm.
For the period spanning the Qín-Chǔ transition
down to the Heavenly Hàn (Tiān Hàn) era,
a stretch of over a hundred years,
people will rely solely on Shǐ Qiān's book.
If Shǐ Qiān is not detailed in this area,
how can later generations examine these events?
Moreover, those who compile local gazetteers today
insist on integrating the present and the past,
mainly because the previous compilers of these gazetteers
were mostly crude and superficial,
offering no standard for selection.
They have no choice but to establish new general principles and formats,
as if creating something from scratch.
If the previous gazetteer had no shortcomings,
one should simply continue what it contained.
If the previous gazetteer had omissions,
one should merely supplement what it lacked.
The compilation of a local gazetteer
for the distant past should not exceed a hundred years,
and for the recent past, not more than three or four decades.
Now, we set the distant limit at three or four hundred years,
because although the work is sequentially revised,
its nature is equivalent to a creation from scratch.
We are just generously broadening the scope.
If the previous gazetteer is genuinely usable,
there is no need for every gazetteer to necessarily account for three or four hundred years.
The purpose of compiling a gazetteer
is not to display beauty,
but to seek practical utility.
Times differ and circumstances change,
so old gazetteers cannot cover everything.
That is why, whether for the distant past of a hundred years
or the near past of three or four decades,
revisions are necessary.
If you claim that only tracing institutional development (yán gé) is important,
and other things are not prioritized,
then if the institutional development is obvious,
and there is no need for research and verification,
then prefectures and counties might as well stop compiling gazetteers."
FÉNG Jūn suddenly realized and said,
"Indeed."
Dài Fúyī (Dài Fúyī) promptly left.
The next day, he showed me the Gazetteer of Fénzhōu Prefecture (《Fénzhōu Fǔ Zhì》) and said:
"Apart from institutional development,
I am not without original and insightful selection criteria.
The category for 'People' (Rénwù mén lèi) in the old gazetteer
listed famous monks first.
I wanted to delete this,
but the documented facts
were so outstandingly clear,
that they could not be removed.
However, how can a monk be counted as a person?
The arrangement of the 'People' section in other gazetteers
shows extreme ignorance.
I considered that famous monks must reside in ancient temples,
and ancient temples belong in the 'Historical Sites' (Gǔjī) category.
Therefore, I took the facts concerning famous monks
and assigned them to 'Historical Sites.'
Mediocre historians do not understand this innovative principle."
I said:
"Historical Sites are not the focus of a gazetteer.
They should be marginally noted on geographical maps (Yúdì zhī Tú),
and should not constitute a dedicated section.
Establishing a dedicated section for Historical Sites
is a category name found in comprehensive compendiums (tǒng zhì lèi zuǎn míng mù).
Crude scholars plagiarized this
and included it in local gazetteers.
This is not a balanced selection criterion.
If you claim that a monk cannot be counted as a person,
then what exactly is that body of flesh and blood,
which is neither wood nor stone?
What kind of thing is it, after all?
The rules for editing (bǐ xuē) are extremely strict,
reaching their peak in the Spring and Autumn Annals (《Chūnqiū》).
Its condemnations
are reserved for rebellious ministers and treasonous sons.
Even then, it only rectifies their name and condemns them,
but I have never heard of them being excluded from the category of 'person'
or the writing style being different from that used for the circle-headed and square-footed kind (i.e., humans).
Moreover, the 'People' section emulates historical precedents (shǐ lì).
History, even concerning treacherous ministers and rebel bandits,
still lists them alongside the loyal and good in biographies (zhuàn);
I have never heard of them being excluded from the category of 'person'
and appended to the geographical treatise (Dìlǐ Zhì).
To excise the deeds of monks and not record them
is merely the view of a vulgar scholar.
If you use 'Historical Sites' as the trace left by famous monks
and refuse to categorize them as 'People,'
then the Gazetteer of Kuàijī (《Kuàijī Zhì》) includes the Yǔ Cave (Yǔ Xué),
but the 'People' section should lack Yǔ;
the Gazetteer of Yǎnshī (《Yǎnshī Zhì》) includes Tāng's Tomb (Tāng Mù),
but the 'People' section should lack Tāng;
the Gazetteer of Qūfù (《Qūfù Zhì》) includes the Kǒng Cemetery (Kǒnglín),
but the 'People' section should lack Kǒngzǐ.
How fortunate are those famous monks
to be considered worthy of the same respect as Yǔ, Tāng, and Kǒngzǐ?
To lack understanding yet forcefully attempt to rationalize the work
is indeed worse than the vulgar practice, which at least avoids becoming bizarre and absurd."
A Reply to Huáng Dàyǐn of Guǎngjì Regarding Gazetteer Compilation
I received the draft of the gazetteer you showed me.
The style is concise and esteemed,
and the structure is rigorous.
Given your earnest request for my opinion,
and fearing I might fail your great expectations,
I will briefly raise just one or two points based on my humble views,
for your consideration and selection,
though they may not necessarily be correct.
The failings of local gazetteers have been long-standing.
Superficial and crude popular books
can, of course, be ignored.
However, works compiled with elegant intent and rigorous refinement,
enough to establish a school of thought,
are often encountered.
