Broadly speaking, there are books by literary scholars (wén rén zhī shū),
books by academic scholars (xué rén zhī shū),
books by rhetoricians (cí rén zhī shū),
books by explication writers (shuō jiā zhī shū),
and books by historians (shǐ jiā zhī shū).
Only the historian's approach adheres to the orthodox tradition.
Among historians, there is the history of original authorship (zhù zuò zhī shǐ)
and the history of compilation and editing (zuǎn jí zhī shǐ);
their paths are not uniform.
Histories of original authorship
have rarely been seen
since the Sòng dynasty.
As for compiled histories,
they prioritize extensive scholarship,
aiming for every character to have documented evidence.
Interweaving, arranging,
refining, and having judicious selection—
this is what makes them excellent.
Your current draft largely imitates Zhū Shì's Old Narratives (《Jiù Wén》) (Zhū Shì 's 《Jiù Wén》),
which is the superior kind of compilation.
However, when applying this model, it seems impossible to standardize the style.
When Zhōu Shūchāng and Lǐ Nánjiàn jointly compiled the Gazetteer of Lìchéng County (《Lìchéng Xiàn Zhì》) previously,
not a single character lacked a documented source.
For matters clearly stated in old books and previous gazetteers,
they definitely annotated the name of the original book.
Even for newly collected matters
for which no book could be cited,
if taken from official documents,
they annotated the words "found in a certain department's case file" (mǒu fáng àn juàn).
If taken from submitted private accounts,
they annotated the words "presented private family account" (jiā chuán chéng zhuàng).
If obtained through verbal testimony,
they annotated the words "verbally recounted by a certain person" (mǒu rén kǒu shù).
This clearly shows that the entire book contains not a single word attributable to the authors themselves,
thus truly imitating and standardizing the model of Old Narratives.
In your gazetteer, sometimes the words 'Newly Added' (xīn zēng) are annotated,
and sometimes not,
which seems inconsistent with the principles.
Furthermore, the 'Chronological Record' (Shì Jì) section has too many omissions.
Local developments recorded in histories and gazetteers
have not yet been fully collected,
and other parts also seem to lack structure.
This section seems not yet ready for use.
Regarding the academies within the city,
recording the musical pieces (yuè zhāng) and the placement of former worthies and Confucian masters (xiān xián xiān rú pèi wèi)—
these matters are universal across the realm
and promulgated by imperial decree (lìng diǎn),
so they fundamentally do not need to be recorded.
If they are recorded now,
yet you do not annotate them as originating from the Collected Statutes (《Huì Diǎn》),
but instead annotate them as originating from the old gazetteer,
this also seems to lose the original source.
Furthermore, when including poetry and prose in the gazetteer,
careful deliberation is appropriate.
My personal preference was to establish a separate section for Collected Writings (Wén Zhēng).
If you now imitate the precedent of Old Narratives,
and include them under the relevant section,
then the rule should also be standardized.
According to Old Narratives, whether poetry or prose,
they are generally segregated and recorded in a lower register.
In your draft, however, entire poems are recorded
only in the 'Mountains and Rivers' (Shānchuān mén) section,
while prose pieces that should be included in the 'Biographies, Treatises, Records, and Narratives' sections (zhuàn zhì jì xù zhī wén)
are mostly abridged and not listed as the main text.
Although conciseness may be achieved,
I fear it fails to be comprehensive.
Furthermore, concerning the organizational format of the tables,
the vertical and horizontal framework (warp and weft)
is intended to clarify the outlines,
and condense the chapters.
The principle is excellent.
Currently, the tables for official positions (Zhíguān) and selections (Xuǎnjǔ)
are still scattered and noted like a roster (Huāmíng Bù).
Though named "tables,"
they are not truly tables.
The table for household registers (Hùjí) is well done;
however, noting the names of the family heads (Tújiǎ) is sufficient;
now there are those who note individual names (Rénmíng),
making it unclear whom they refer to.
This seems suitable for rigorous review.
Regarding the rules for the Literature and Arts (Yìwén) section,
all four categories—Classics (Jīng), Histories (Shǐ), Philosophers (Zǐ), and Anthologies (Jí)—
should be included.
The authors of these works
do not all belong to the category of Literary Figures (Wényuàn).
Now, biographies belonging to Wényuàn are being cut and placed into Yìwén,
claiming to imitate the *Shūlù Jiětí*.
In reality, Liú Xiàng’s *Qīlüè Biélù*
never failed to list the person (the author),
which is somewhat similar to the biographical format.
However, when Bān Shì compiled this into the *Hàn Yìwén Zhì*,
each person had their own separate biography,
and under the category of *Yìwén*,
only the two characters "Yǒu Zhuàn" (has a biography) were noted.
This is the proper format.
Now, we have inevitably allowed the guest to become the host.
All the points mentioned above,
I am acutely aware are the views of a blind and ignorant person (gǔméng),
and are not suitable for selection or adoption.
Furthermore, I do not measure myself (my competence)
by offering advice that exceeds my position.
Therefore, I dare not present these trivial points presumptuously;
however, since you have consulted me,
I dare not fail to mention the general outline.
Reply to a Letter from Cuī Jīngzhōu
Last month, when I called upon you,
it was precisely when official duties were overwhelming (Pángwǔ),
yet I was favored with your gifts and the grant of a boat.
I feel deeply uneasy about this.
Due to the limited perspective of a scholar (Cuò Dà),
I failed to appreciate the urgency and circumstances of official life.
I have repeatedly presumed upon you by writing,
leaving me utterly ashamed!
As winter cold sets in,
I respectfully trust your health has been recently excellent.
The draft gazetteer (Zhìgǎo) that was entrusted to me—
due to the haste of casting off the moorings,
I did not manage to open and look at it (immediately).
I had previously written
that I would wait until returning to the provincial capital to report back.
While on the boat, having nothing to do,
I also quickly glanced over it,
and sighed in admiration of your Excellency's clear discernment (Míngjiàn)—
something others cannot match.
Previously, when we met in the provincial capital,
when the draft gazetteer was sent,
Your Excellency did not stay many days,
and immediately said:
"The gazetteer is quite meticulous and appropriate;
any errors within it,
are also easy to correct."
These few words constituted the final verdict.
Now, all the officials and gentry (Jìnshēn),
after reviewing and scrutinizing it for more than a month,
have made countless revisions and criticisms (Qiān Zhāi rú má),
even repeatedly adding slander, condemnation, and ridicule,
completely losing the manner of refined scholarship (Yǎ Dào).
This makes your humble servant utterly ashamed!
However, after thorough deliberation,
it is merely that in the two tables, Zhíguān (Official Positions) and Kēmù (Examinations),
the names are inverted or misplaced;
and in the chapter on collected writings and stone inscriptions (Wénzhēng Bēijì),
the eras are not arranged chronologically.
These are indeed contradictions (Dǐwǔ).
However, correcting texts (Jiào shū) is like dealing with an enemy,
and discussing rites (Yì lǐ) leads to litigation.
For compiling a book to involve back-and-forth consultation and criticism,
is merely normal practice.
Otherwise, the ancients would not have needed to establish the study of collation (Jiàochóu);
nor would modern people, when compiling books,
need to list the titles of collators, editors, or consultants.
Furthermore, concerning the two tables, Zhíguān and Kēmù,
there are indeed places where the arrangement was erroneous;
and also cases where the registers provided (Kāisòng Cèjí)
were originally incomplete.
As for Wénzhēng, because the chapter was compiled first,
and later there were supplementary inclusions,
this led to chronological discrepancies.
Although these are mistakes,
they are not entirely without cause.
Yet, beyond mere criticism, the various gentry
add harsh slander and abuse,
treating the compiler like a tutor addressing a child (Rú Zǐ),
or an official addressing a clerk (Xū Lì).
This is excessive.
Moreover, if their literary reasoning (Wén Lǐ) were truly clear and profound,
and their criticisms were indeed without error,
why would your humble servant find it difficult to regard them as strict teachers?
Now, let us look at the very first point in the book (Kāijuàn Dì Yī Tiáo).
The original text of the General Rules (Fánlì) says: "Local gazetteers (Fāngzhì) serve as the essential abridgement (Yàoshān) of the National History (Guóshǐ),"
the phrasing is fundamentally clear.
Yàoshān (essential abridgement)
is equivalent to saying that the essential parts are abridged for future use.
The phrase originates in the *Shǐjì*,
and is by no means obscure.
Yet, the criticism changes it to Yàodiǎn (essential canon or great classic),
which implies that the National History relies on the local gazetteer for importance.
This violates factual principle,
and the wording is also confusing.
In the Wénzhēng section, in the *Èrshèng Cí Jì* (Record of the Two Sages Shrine),
the text above says, "stood before the transforming/dying image (Lì huà xiàng qián),"
and the text below says, "was revived after a moment (Shí qǐng fù huó)."
Huà (化) here means death or transformation into an immortal;
hence, in lexicography, the character Sǐ (死) incorporates half of the character Huà (化).
The text is itself clear.
Now, the criticism remarks on the phrase Lì huà, saying: "There is an error,
otherwise the 'revival' mentioned in the text below has no basis."
Judging from this,
that person’s literary reasoning (Wén Lǐ) is fundamentally unclear and insufficient;
it is fitting that he abuses and scolds arbitrarily,
ignoring the dignity of refined discourse (Sī Wén Yǒu Miànmù).
As for the tables for Zhíguān and Kēmù,
mistakes should certainly be corrected.
However, Zhíguān includes civil and military, principal and subordinate roles;
Kēmù also includes civil and military, first and second classes.
If we have already divided the content into seven columns based on the seven subordinate counties,
and then take the Zhíguān and Kēmù from each jurisdiction
and divide them into individual sub-columns,
a single sheet of paper (Chǐ Fú) cannot contain them.
Therefore, we only divided them into seven columns,
and placed the specific titles for each category
below the names of the individuals.
This method is based on the *Hàn Shū Bǎiguān Biǎo* (Table of Official Posts in the Book of Hàn),
which takes thirty-four official titles,
and lists them together in fourteen columns,
while still noting the specific titles within the table itself.
It is an excellent method for handling complexity with simplicity (Zhíjiǎn Yùfán).
Now, the criticism points out, saying:
"Merging them into one table
makes the outlines unclear."
Furthermore, in Wénzhēng, the texts are divided and compiled according to their various literary forms,
following a single rule throughout the entire section.
If occasionally the sequence of the stone inscriptions (Bēijì) contains errors,
it should naturally be criticized and corrected.
Now, the criticism suddenly states:
"Records of Schools (Xuéxiào zhī Jì) should come first;
records of administrative offices (Shǔ Xiè) should be placed after that;
and temples and monasteries (Sì Guān) should follow again."
This means that within one literary form (Yī Tǐ),
sub-classification is required.
Sub-classification is not impossible,
yet other forms like memorials (Biǎozòu), prefaces and discussions (Xùlùn), poetry, and prose (Shī Fù)
are not classified,
nor are they noted for change.
Thus, the rules of the book
contradict themselves.
From this perspective,
that person is originally unfamiliar with the stylistic rules (Tǐ Lì) of book compilation,
and is not well-versed in them.
He only knows how to curse and scold arbitrarily,
and does not understand that there is courtesy and propriety (Lǐ Yì) in communication.
There are many other instances where the criticism criticizes what should not be criticized, and refutes what should not be refuted.
I will tentatively list one or two examples to illustrate the rest.
Therefore, the critical notes (Qiān) offered by the various gentry
may not be entirely reliable.
In the section on customs (Fēngsú) in the *Jīng Zhì*,
the old text was adopted,
stating that scholars cherish honesty and yielding (Shì Dūn Lián Ràng).
Now, observing the critical suggestions (Qiān Yì) in this book,
which originate from the various gentry,
they show they understand neither the principles of phrasing and structure (Zì Jù Fǎn Zhèng Xū Shí) in literary reasoning,
nor the sequencing of categories (Kuǎnmù Qián Hòu Biāncì) in stylistic rules.
They indulge solely in reckless abuse and condemnation,
approaching the extreme of vulgar absurdity (Yōng Wàng zhī Yóu).
It is difficult to speak of literary customs and scholarly habits (Wén Fēng Shì Xí) here.
I therefore recall how Your Excellency, within the space of a few days,
evaluated the merits and demerits of the draft gazetteer.
Compared to the gentry who convened for many days,
making countless confused criticisms,
yours was vastly superior.
I am filled with the utmost admiration.
However, at this moment, Your Excellency has no leisure for this matter,
and your humble servant is pressed for his return date.
I shall wait until next year to report back with the corrected notes,
and await your decision to proceed or desist.
Preface for the Gazetteer of Dàmíng Xiàn, written for Zhāng Jífǔ Sīmǎ
, I
was transferred from Magistrate of Féixiāng to the crucial post of Dàmíng.
Since Dàmíng was merged with Wèi and the administration moved to the prefectural city
, it has been called a strategic hub in the southern Jī Nán region;
but the county gazetteer had not yet been compiled into a complete book,
and the documentary evidence
was lacking and incomplete.
I intended to collect the materials,
but at the beginning of my tenure
, I provisionally lacked the leisure.
By the 49th year,
I then discussed and deliberated with the local gentry,
collecting the old gazetteers of the two counties,
cross-referencing and revising them,
supplementing them with what I had subsequently seen and heard,
and compiling them into a volume;
I obtained two chapters of Illustrated Explanations (Túshuō),
two chapters of Tables (Biǎo),
seven chapters of Treatises (Zhì),
and five chapters of Biographies (Zhuàn),
totaling sixteen chapters.
The Preface and Table of Contents (Xùlì Mùlù) listed at the beginning of the scroll,
and the miscellaneous collected notes (Zácǎi Zhuìjì) attached at the end of the scroll,
are not included in this count.
In the first month of spring of the 50th year,
the book was completed.
Coincidentally, I was transferred to Hèjiān Fǔ as Sub-prefect (Tóngzhī)
, and shortly thereafter was dismissed from office due to an error (guàwù),
remaining stranded in the area of my former administration.
The person who succeeded me in governance
was Gentleman Wú of Xiūníng,
who transferred here from Lóngpíng to govern this county.
Gentleman Wú had previously been renowned as an exemplary official (xúnliáng) in the Sān Fǔ region
. Moreover, he possessed great literary elegance (dàyǎ),
and his scholarship was deeply rooted.
When I met him
, we became deeply congenial.
Consequently, I entrusted the draft gazetteer to him for editing and finalization
, before submitting it to the printer (zǐrén).
Therefore, I recount the reasons for compiling the gazetteer
, and present them to Gentleman Wú
, saying:
Formerly, while in the official residence in Féixiāng
, my friend and colleague Zhāng Xuéchéng of Kuàijī
discussed the matter of compiling gazetteers with me.
What Gentleman Zhāng said
differed from the views of contemporary gazetteer compilers.
I asked him to explain his theory,
and Gentleman Zhāng said:
"The gazetteers and histories (zhìchéng) of prefectures and counties
are the legacy of the historians (shǐguān) of the various states during the Fēngjiàn period;
but modern compilers of gazetteers
mistakenly imitate the Geographical Atlases (Tújīng) of the prefectures and circuits during the Táng and Sòng dynasties, thereby losing the correct path.
In the *Zhōuguān* (Rites of Zhōu), the Outer Scribe (Wàishǐ) managed the records (zhì) of the four directions.
The commentary notes that these records were like the *Chéng* of Jìn
, the *Táowù* of Chǔ
, and the *Chūnqiū* of Lǔ
. This means that the history of one state
recorded everything
, and could thus be utilized by the historian compiling the history of the entire dynasty (cháoshǐ)
. When the Master (Fūzǐ) composed the *Chūnqiū*
, he necessarily consulted the treasured records (bǎoshū) of a hundred states
; this is the underlying meaning.
As for the function of the Túijīng
, it is strictly geographical specialization.
According to the *Tiānguān Sīhuì* (Celestial Offices, Director of Accounting), who managed the documented contracts and maps (shūqì bǎntú)—the commentary states:
*Bǎn* refers to the household registers,
and *Tú* refers to the depiction of the land
and the extent of fields
—this is what later generations used as the model for the Túijīng
. Therefore, the local gazetteer (Fāngzhì) and the Geographical Atlas (Tújīng)
are fundamentally different in form;
but later generations have failed to distinguish between these categories
, and this has been the case for a long time."
I asked:
"Are the old Túijīng
still available for examination today?"
Gentleman Zhāng replied:
"The ancient Túijīng
are now unavailable
. Occasionally, the text survives but the map is lost,
such as the *Wújùn Túijīng* and the *Gāolì Túijīng*;
furthermore, they are fragmentarily seen in citations by various books,
such as the *Shuǐjīng* (Water Classic) and other geographical records (dìzhì)
, but one cannot obtain them in their entirety.
The modern Túijīng
are the maps (yútú) of the prefectures and counties,
along with the registers outlining the Six Categories of Regulations (Liùtiáo Xiàngāng)
—these are their scattered documents.
Works like the *Yītǒngzhì* (Comprehensive Gazetteer) of the Yuán and Míng dynasties
are their comprehensive compilations.
The scattered documents
are preserved in government files,
inherently lacking literary structure,
and scholars disdain to discuss them.
The comprehensive compilations
are certainly specialist geographical works,
but the categories like Figures and Sojourners (Rénwù Liúyù)
, Strategic Sites and Local Products (Xíngshèng Tǔchǎn)
, and Ancient Sites and Shrines (Gǔjì Címiào)
are selectively extracted according to geographical criteria
and are adopted merely to provide material for literary compositions
, not serving the original purpose of the book.
Therefore, strategic sites must be described using balanced, parallel prose (piánlì)
; biographies are limited to essential summaries
; ancient sites dwell upon the scenery
; and shrines also record sight-seeing tours
. These are classified compilations within the field of geography
and it is perfectly obvious that they do not serve as comprehensive records of local documentation (wénxiàn)."
I asked:
"In that case, are the principles (lì) of the comprehensive gazetteers (Tǒngzhì)
incorrect?
Yán Ruòqú asserted that books of the Tǒngzhì type
ought not to include biographies (rénwù)—
is his assertion truly worthy of being followed?"
Gentleman Zhāng replied:
"The Tǒngzhì originated in the Yuán and Míng dynasties,
and their form was based on the Táng and Sòng
. Although the substance and style were modified and adjusted
, they had a clear heritage
and cannot be considered inherently wrong.
The *Yuánhé Jùnxiàn Zhì*
crowned each chapter with a map (tú) at the beginning,
followed by descriptions of the four cardinal and eight intervening directions (sìzhì bādào)
; apart from the rivers and mountains
, nothing extraneous was attached
. This is the essential nature of the Túijīng.
The record of the *Tàipíng Huányǔ Jì*
introduced biographies (rénwù) and literature (yìwén)
—this is what is meant by following a precedent and adding embellishments.
The *Jiāxī Fāngyú Shènglǎn*
excessively detailed famous scenic spots and ancient sites
, along with travel accounts and poetic essays (cífù)
—it drifted with the current and became decadent.
The principles of the *Tǒngzhì*
supplemented the remnants of the *Huányǔ*'s original intent,
deleted the superficial descriptions of scenic spots,
found a balance among earlier works
, and had a basis
. Yán Shì (Mr. Yán) was excessive in criticizing it.
However, its form inherently contains emphasis and subordination,
and one cannot strictly adhere to its classified headings
while attempting to cover the entirety of local documentation
; this is very clear."
I asked:
"What were the principles and format (yìlì)
of the ancient local gazetteers?"
Gentleman Zhāng replied:
"During the Fēngjiàn system of the Three Dynasties (Sāndài)
, and among the regional powers (gējù zhī xióng) of later eras
, states generally established their own systems
, and their forms were certainly not comparable.
In the age of commanderies and counties (jùnxiàn zhī shì)
, the accounts compiled by the Hàn people—such as the *Rǔnán Xiānxián*, the *Xiāngyáng Qíjiù*, and the *Guāndōng Fēngsú*
—were inherently biased and incomplete,
and the surviving transmissions are moreover not the original texts.
Among those visible today are
more than ten Sòng-dynasty gazetteers
. Although they were not without merits and flaws,
because the classified headings typical of the Tújīng were not yet widespread at that time,
the historical tradition (shǐshì jiāfǎ) was still preserved.
This is unlike today's practice of directly taking classified subheadings
and using them as the entire gazetteer
, treating them as immutable natural and moral laws (tiānjīng dìyì)."
I asked:
"Among those more than ten Sòng gazetteers,
where do their merits and flaws lie?"
Gentleman Zhāng replied:
"Fàn Shì's *Wújùn Zhì*
and Luó Shì's *Xīn'ān Zhì*
are the particularly good ones.
The *Luó Zhì* is voluminous but lacks refinement,
and the *Fàn Zhì* is brief and lacks detail
—these are their shortcomings.
The *Luó Zhì* was intended as a narrative work (zhùshù)
, and the *Fàn Zhì* excelled in editing and selection (jiǎncái)
—these are their strengths.
Few later people understood the narrative intent.
Those who only knew selection and editing (jiǎncái)
produced writing that was lean but not rich,
and events that were repressed but not smoothly expressed
. Their understanding
did not transcend the usual habits of literati
and could not achieve the grand structure of the historian
. The gazetteers like Kāng Shì's *Wǔgōng Zhì*
and Hán Shì's *Cháoyì Zhì*
are prominent examples of this.
What are the habits of literati?
They imitate Hán Tuìzhī's *Huà Jì* (Painting Record) when describing mountains, rivers, and products
, unaware that the form of the Eight Treatises and Ten Treatises (Bāshū Shízhì)
must not be abandoned.
They imitate Liǔ Zǐhòu's *Xiānyǒu Jì* (Record of Deceased Friends) when recording biographies (rénwù)
, unaware that the format of the Seventy Biographies (Qīshí Lièzhuàn)
must not be forgotten.
However, this is merely the flaw of literati seeking superficial fame.
As for those of lower quality
, they are not even worth mentioning."
I said:
"According to what you have said,
how must a gazetteer be compiled to be acceptable?"
Zhāng Jūn said:
"A zhì (gazetteer)
is a record (zhì).
Beyond its facts and its text,
it must contain underlying principles,
which are the subtle intent (wēizhǐ) of historical works.
When dealing with the historical traditions (zhǎnggù) of a region,
why choose the work of only one person?
However, if it is not entrusted to a written work,
then it cannot be transmitted through the generations and travel far.
Official documents and ledgers
are not unclear or inexplicit,
but it is especially difficult for them to last long.
Therefore, expertise (zhuānjiā) is valued.
The core meaning of expertise,
which is spiritual and enlightening,
resides in the person
and cannot be conveyed in words.
That which can be conveyed in words,
which are the rules, standards, and methods (guījǔ fǎdù),
must clearly understand the comprehensive structure (tōngcái) of general history."
"How does one achieve a clear understanding of the comprehensive structure of general history?" He replied:
"If one recognizes that a local gazetteer (fāngzhì) is not solely a book on geography,
then mountains, rivers, cities, neighborhoods, landmarks, and scenic spots
should all be integrated into the geographical section,
and must not occupy separate chapters,
thereby losing the principle of host and guest.
If one recognizes that a local gazetteer provides material for the national history (guóshǐ),
then biographies (rénwù) must be detailed in the tradition of historical biographies (shǐchuán),
and not merely abridged summaries;
arts and literature (yìwén) must fully record book titles,
and must not merely select poems and prose by category.
If one recognizes that a local gazetteer is an essential excerpt (yàoshān) from the historical division,
then clerks' documents (xūlì àndú)
and flowery rhetoric from literati (wénshì qǐyán)
are useless,
and the style and structure must comply with historical methods (shǐfǎ).
These are the things that can be spoken of.
Now, families have genealogies (pǔ),
prefectures and counties have gazetteers (zhì),
and the nation has histories (shǐ);
their underlying principles are the same.
However, if a family genealogy has evidence,
the county gazetteer draws from it.
If the county gazetteer has evidence,
the national history draws from it.
Now, when compiling the history of a dynasty,
they might draw material from family genealogies.
We have not heard of them drawing from county gazetteers.
This means they are vague and unreliable (huānglüè wú jī),
something that officials and scholars (jiànshén xiānshēng) find difficult to discuss.
However, the reason for this
actually starts with the mistaken imitation of the table of contents (míngmù) used in the *Tú Jīng Zuan Lèi* (Illustrated Classics and Classified Compendia).
This must be clearly distinguished."
Alas!
The words of Zhāng Jūn,
I could not fully fathom.
Nevertheless, concerning the matter of gazetteers,
I truly dared not treat it lightly.
The Two Maps (Èr Tú) encompass the geography;
I dared not linger on scenic spots
or exaggerate the scenery.
The Seven Treatises (Qī Zhì) distinguish the main topics and subheadings;
I dared not lose organization by adhering superficially
and causing fragmentation.
The Two Tables (Èr Biǎo) analyze the warp and woof (principles);
I dared not turn them into flowery lists
and make them messy.
The Five Biographies (Wǔ Chuán) fully detail the facts;
I dared not abridge or embellish them
and lose authenticity.
The local gentry (xiāng jiànshén) did not dismiss me,
but diligently discussed,
and compiled this gazetteer.
Hopefully, the historical traditions of this region
will not fall into the geographical bias (piān) mentioned by Zhāng Jūn.
If one seeks accuracy in this gazetteer
and wishes to categorize it with the works of experts (zhuānjiā),
then I must apologize for my inadequacy.
Preface to the *Chángdé Fǔzhì* written for Grand Secretary Bì Qiūfán.
Chángdé is an ancient renowned prefecture (jùn).
To its left, it encompasses Dòngtíng,
and to its right, it controls the Wǔ Xī.
During the Warring States period, it was the location of Chǔ's Qiánzhōng Commandery.
When Qín and Chǔ contended for power,
they had to secure Qiánzhōng to serve as a key (tuóyào).
This is what is meant by adjacent control over the Xī Mán tribes,
passage south to the Lǐngjiào (mountain passes),
whence advantages extend to the Nánhǎi (South Sea).
During the Later Hàn, the seat of Jīngzhōu was sometimes moved here.
This was because by externally controlling the various Mán tribes,
the interior of the province (zhōu bù)
remained tranquil for a thousand *lǐ*.
Since the Suí and Táng dynasties,
it has increasingly served as a crucial hinge for the entirety of Chǔ (Húběi and Húnán).
When the Mǎ clan during the Five Dynasties annexed Lǎngzhōu,
it subsequently stood tall and dominated the view,
and no other military region dared to resist it.
Is it not true that
it screens Jīngzhǔ to the north,
borders Chángshā to the south,
and serves remotely as the gateway to Diān and Qián (Yúnnán and Guìzhōu),
truly making it an area of critical control?
During the generations of peace inherited by Our Dynasty,
the Mán and Yí tribes were generally submissive.
Both the north and south of the Great Hú Nán (Húnán province)
became interior territories (fùdì).
In the 22nd year of Kāngxī,
the Mǎnzhōu General was stationed at Jīngzhōu.
Consequently, the military command of the Provincial Commander (Tídū Jūnmén) was moved
to govern and control Chángdé.
Although later Húnán and Húběi were divided into two governorships (Bù Yuàn),
the military systems connect the two regions,
breathing in coordination,
so the duty of overall command
is still unified.
When I served as the official in charge of the Two Hús (Liǎng Hú),
I once inspected Chángdé.
Viewing its mountains, rivers, and strategic landscape,
I reflected with emotion upon the mechanisms of order and chaos
since the opening of the communication routes in the Qín and Hàn eras,
the advantages and disadvantages of administration and control,
as well as the method of dwelling in peace and considering governance,
and transforming customs to suit the people.
Thereupon, I instructed the local chief administrators (shǒutǔ zhǎnglì)
to study and meticulously investigate these matters.
The Prefect (Zhīfǔ), Lǐ Dàhóng from Sānyuán,
is a sincere and earnest official (kǔnfú lì).
The Six Articles of Investigation
had already been roughly prepared in sequence.
The previous prefectural gazetteer (fǔzhì), compiled in the 9th year of Kāngxī,
was rudimentary and sparse,
making thorough verification impossible.
Moreover, the documentation (wénxiàn) from the past hundred-plus years
was remote and lacked evidence.
Therefore, he requested the task of heavy revision.
I believe this shows he can grasp the important matters.
Nonetheless,
local gazetteers (fāngzhì) now exist throughout the world (huányǔ).
While capable administrators (xián zhǎnglì) understand that governance must be constant,
the writers (zàibǐ zhī shì)
fail to recognize that the rhetoric should value substance and essentials (tǐyào).
They are vulgar, disordered, excessive, and confusing (wěi wú zá làn),
which attracts no criticism.
Even if some correct this trend, move beyond common practices,
and claim to be experts (chéngjiā),
perhaps a man of letters takes pride in his literary embellishment,
or a scholar boasts of his comprehensive collection,
but concerning matters related to statecraft (jīngjì),
or writing adhering to historical structure (shǐcái),
they have not yet discussed these things.
Zhāng Xuéchéng
, studied under my guidance
He frequently spoke to me about historical matters
and his words were remarkably resonant with my own thoughts
I commended the intent of Lí Jūn
and consequently charged the clerk
to compile and arrange it
completing the work after one year
In total, the book comprises twenty-four chapters
two are designated as Annals (Jì)
arranged chronologically to summarize the major events of the prefecture

with years as the warp and events as the weft
thereby recording the names and surnames concerning the Feudal System (Fēngjiàn), Official Posts (Zhíguān), Selection (Xuǎnjǔ), and Notable Persons (Rénwù)
one is designated as Summaries (Lüè)

collecting and compiling biographical records
incorporating personal observations and hearsay
to record the deeds of Famous Officials (Mínghuàn), Local Worthies (Xiāngxián), the Loyal and Filial (Zhōngxiào), and the Chaste and Righteous (Jiéyì)
When the main structure is lifted, the details spread out
when the framework is established, the application can be achieved
Popular gazetteers tend to strain connections to ancient sites
writing poems and praises for the Eight Views (Bā Jǐng)
Lacking substance and filled with superfluous rhetoric
they have generally been omitted and deleted
Regarding those memorial essays and prefaces
poems and songs
sufficient to verify facts

which gazetteer compilers traditionally record as the Arts and Letters (Yìwén) section
now, since the Arts and Letters (Yìwén) section is specifically for recording bibliographies

We have separately compiled the *Wénzhēng*
forming a separate book

Furthermore, from the surplus materials gathered

which are irrelevant to grand administration (jīnglún)
but which assist in conversation
have been further compiled into the *Cóngtán*
None of these are included in the main chapters of the gazetteer
All these divisions and classifications
serve to clearly distinguish purposes and functions
and return the work to essential structure
Thus, the historical precedents of Chángdé
can be spoken of as easily as pointing to one's palm
Now, a gazetteer does not merely
When reviewing the geographical maps
seeing the mountains and towns like Shàndé and Táoyuán
and the rivers and marshes like Jiàn, Qián, and Cānglàng
one naturally envisions the pure character of the ancients
which can inspire later customs
Seeking out past traces
there are figures like Mǎ Fúbō and Yīng Sīlì
who controlled the Miáo-Mán tribes during the Hàn era
and people like Lǐ Xízhī and Wēn Jiǎnyú
who initiated water conservancy projects during the Táng period
Adapting measures to local conditions
and responding to changes as they occur
they all serve as instructors concerning the past deeds of civil and military chief officials
Studying the past is used to verify the present
and daily deliberation
must not be neglected beforehand
For establishing permanence in governance and adhering to the essentials of expression
are fundamentally not two different things
those ignorant of governance fail to perceive this
I therefore, because Lí Jūn understood his duties

so that they might serve as a standard for those seeking good governance
Preface written for Bì Qiūfān, Governor-General (Zhìfǔ), upon his compilation of the *Jīngzhōu Fǔ Zhì*
Jīngzhōu
dominating during the Three Kingdoms, Six Dynasties, and Five Dynasties
and was a strategically vital and difficult place during the preceding Míng dynasty
Although it governs only seven cities today
among the eleven prefectures and departments within Húběi Province
it is still considered of great importance
When the Three Dynasties divided the land into provinces (zhōu)
the territory of Jīng
a scale that need not be discussed
The Hàn dynasty divided it into Nánjùn
which was governed by Jīngzhōu
Kuǎi Yuè advised Liú Biǎo, saying
"Jīngzhōu
guards Xiāngyáng in the north
and the eight commanderies can be pacified simply by sending a written summons
Zhūgě Zhōngwǔ
"Jīngzhōu
its benefits extend to the South Sea (Nánhǎi)
it is connected to Wú and Kuàijī in the east
and it links to Bā and Shǔ in the west
truly a region for military endeavor
The Six Dynasties fought fiercely over it during the Xiāo Liáng period
and the Five Dynasties saw the Gāo clan claim supremacy there
Though numerous brilliant strategies and military counsels were presented at that time
and the elaborate discussions were many
they generally did not go beyond the few words spoken by Kuǎi and Gě
However, at that time
actually included commanderies such as Wǔlíng and Guìyáng
its territory encompassing the boundaries of Húnán
It was not until the Míng dynasty changed Zhōngxīng Lù to Jīngzhōu Fǔ
its boundaries became those of the present-day Jīngzhōu
At that time, it was the fiefdom of princely states
flourishing as a great metropolis
Our dynasty followed the old Míng system of governance
initially stationing a Regional Commander (Zǒngbīngguān) to guard the area
later changing it to the Manchu Garrison (Mǎnyíng)
establishing the system of a General (Jiāngjūn) and a Lieutenant-General (Dūtǒng) and others below them as regulated
In the thirteenth year of Yōngzhèng

establishing the two prefectures of Yíchāng and Shīnán
In the fifty-sixth year of Qiánlóng
Yuǎn'ān was again subordinated to Jīngmén Zhōu
Consequently, the jurisdiction of Jīngzhōu
was limited to seven districts
Nevertheless, its strategic position remains foremost among the prefectures
Jiānglíng truly combines the critical North-South route
and its command over the East and West
and its connectivity, remain as before
Regarding differing requirements necessitated by the times

so that civilians and soldiers do not disturb one another

The Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) looked southward, consulting widely

At that time, I

Over the following year,
