The Prefect (Zhīfǔ), Zhāng Jūn of Shānyīn, who was just taking office,
first intended to organize the historical records (zhǎnggù) and precedents,
to serve as guidelines for future adherence;
but he soon left due to an assignment.
The one who succeeded him in office,
Cuī Jūn Lóngjiàn of Yǒngjì,
then gathered the chief magistrates of the seven counties and discussed compiling the Prefectural Gazetteer (Fǔzhì).
Cuī Jūn began his career as a renowned Jìnshì (scholar-official),
excelling in scholarship before taking office.
Regarding this gazetteer,
he was meticulous and dared not compile it carelessly.
Furthermore, the gazetteers of Jīng (Jīngzhì) documented in antiquity
are double that of other prefectures and commanderies.
Shèng Hóng had the *Jīngzhōu Jì*,
Yǔ Zhòngyōng had the *Jiāng Jì*,
Zōng Lǐn had the *Jīngchǔ Suìshí Jì*,
Emperor Yuán of Liáng had the *Jīngnán Zhì*,
and also the *Dānyáng Yǐn Zhuàn*.
Although these books no longer exist,
their sections and headings can still be investigated,
and fragments of text and scattered phrases
are still occasionally seen cited in various books.
The *Jīngzhōu Fǔzhì* compiled during the former Míng Dynasty
is only found listed in records but the document itself is missing.
During the Kāngxī era,
the version compiled by Hú Zàikè
was reputed to be an excellent edition,
yet it is also rarely seen in the world.
The gazetteer by Yè Yǎnggāo currently remains.
He himself claimed that much of it retained Hú Shì’s old text.
Its structure and style are strict and rigorous,
and in compilation, the source of every entry must be noted,
demonstrating the excellence of its methodology.
As for Cuī Jūn’s approach to this gazetteer,
he uniformly upheld historical standards (shǐcái).
Amidst detailed thoroughness and broad elegance,
he applied the principle of independent judgment and distinct selection.
The first section is a Chronicle (Jì) structured according to the method of annals (biānnián shǐfǎ).
The next section is a Table (Biǎo) detailing the succession and eras.
Historical precedents are preserved in the various Treatises (Kǎo).
Notable individuals are detailed in the Biographies (Lièzhuàn).
Thus, the framework is established and the details are spread out.
He also believes that historical and gazetteer writings
should focus primarily on recording events.
The section on Arts and Letters (Yìwén) is still a chapter that records titles,
but recent gazetteer compilers
indiscriminately select miscellaneous styles of poetry and prose.
Those who attempt to correct this
instead abridge and segment the poetry and prose,
classifying them under the related Events (Běnshì),
both of which lose the categorized distinctions of the ancients.
Now, following historical precedents, he compiles the Fǔzhì,
and further imitates the selection standards to compile the Wénzhēng (Collection of Texts).
He himself said:
The gazetteer follows the standard of the *Guóyǔ* of the Eight Masters (Bā Jiā),
and the Wénzhēng follows the standard of the fifteen *Guófēng* (Airs of the States).
By making them separate books,
they are able to complement each other without causing confusion.
Furthermore, regarding miscellaneous matters and exceptional sayings (suǒshì jīyán) remaining after collection and compilation,
including them violates the standard,
but discarding them is regrettable.
Recent authors compile them into a *Zhì Yú* (Gazetteer Supplement),
which is also not historical methodology.
Now, he separately created a book titled *Cóngtán* (Collected Discussions),
which incorporates both major and minor details,
and yet is orderly and methodical,
a practice rarely seen among contemporary gazetteer compilers.
Previously, Luó Yuàn compiled the *Xīn’ān Zhì*,
describing it as a scholar’s book (Rúzhě zhī shū),
unlike simple transcripts or records.
The compilation by Cuī Jūn today
has deep and distant origins.
Compared to the elegant standards of Luó Shì,
it surpasses him and does not fall short.
Coincidentally, Húběi Province was undertaking the project of the General Gazetteer (*Tōngzhì*).
Zhāng Diǎnjí Xuéchéng of Kuàijī was hired
to organize the relevant matters.
Zhāng Jūn possesses refined historical insight (shǐshì),
and our discussions were in agreement.
Cuī Jūn also frequently consulted with the Diǎnjí (Record Keeper),
debating and discussing back and forth,
and sometimes also sought my judgment.
I am therefore fully informed of the beginning and the end of this project,
and thus I write this preface at the beginning of the volume.
Preface for the Shíshǒu Xiàn Zhì (Stone Head County Gazetteer) written for Bì Qiūfān Zhìfǔ (Governor-General Bì Qiūfān)
Shíshǒu is a prominent county of Jīngzhōu.
During the Two Hàn dynasties, it was originally Huáróng territory.
When the Jìn Dynasty pacified Wú,
it divided Huáróng and established a county,
naming it Shíshǒu after a mountain.
During the Zhào Sòng Dynasty, the government seat was moved to Diàohóng
and the name was changed to Jiànníng.
Soon after, it was moved again to the west of Xiùlín Mountain,
and the name was restored to Shíshǒu.
In the Dàdé era of the Yuán Dynasty,
it was moved again, to the foot of Chǔwàng Mountain.
From the Míng Dynasty until now,
its cultural achievements and reputation
have been celebrated throughout the Jīng region.
The County Gazetteer has not been revised
for nearly sixty years.
The old gazetteer was incomplete and flawed,
lacking proper organization and classification,
and furthermore omitted facts and events covering several decades.
The County Magistrate (Zhīxiàn) Wáng Jūn Wéipíng of Yùtián,
because I was compiling the General Gazetteer (*Tōngzhì*),
issued official requests for records from prefectures and counties.
He then organized and classified the county's affairs,
thoroughly examining eight sections,
combining the beginning and the end into ten chapters for the book,
to comply with the requisition,
and moreover asked me to write a preface for it.
I perused and reviewed this book,
and thereby knew that Lord Wáng (Wáng Jūn) is someone with whom governance can be discussed.
Now, those governing must first establish structure and discipline (gāngjì);
those compiling records must clarify the essential organizational principles (tǐyào).
Recently, those compiling gazetteers (zhì) for prefectures and counties,
sometimes rely on clerical records and dossiers,
which are disorganized, confusing, and lacking proper structure;
sometimes they focus on scenery descriptions and poems,
which are superficial and lacking substance;
but if one seeks what constitutes their proper nomenclature and purpose,
or what is emphasized in governance and education,
they are utterly clueless as to the core points.
Now, governance (zhèng)
is action (shì).
A gazetteer (zhì)
is description (yán).
In this world, there are those whose descriptions are elegant,
yet they fail to grasp the corresponding actions;
I have never heard of descriptions that still lack proper coherence and structure,
yet the actions they describe turn out to be orderly and well-sequenced.
Now, Lord Wáng’s (Wáng Jūn) gazetteer
contains dozens of items
organized into eight sections (bā mén).
It is like a net held by its main rope (gāng),
orderly and uncluttered.
The first is called "Chronology" (Biānnián),
preserving the method of history.
A gazetteer is governed by historical precedent (shǐ suǒ qǔ cái);
history records events,
and without chronology, it cannot serve as the structure (gāng).
Next is "Geography" (Fāngyú),
investigating topographical features.
The reasons why the county was established,
its mountains, rivers, and historical sites,
are classified and sequenced.
And water control (shuǐlì) and river defense (jiāngfáng)
occupy the essentials here.
Next is "Establishments" (Jiànzhì),
the constructions completed by human effort.
City walls and moats, government offices,
down to altars and temples,
are attached in sequence.
Next is "Civil Administration" (Mínzhèng),
where laws and regulations are established.
Household registration, fields, taxes, and labor services (fùyì) belonging to the Minister of the Multitude (Sītú),
and postal stations, transport, military, and defense (bīngfáng) belonging to the Minister of War (Sīmǎ),
are all the constant principles of the Eight Objects of Government (Bā Zhèng) mentioned in the Hóng Fàn.
Next is "Official Ranks" (Zhìguān),
to illustrate those who uphold the standards.
Chief officials, subordinates, teachers, and scholars (shī rú),
are those through whom governance and education originate.
And those who are outstanding
are recorded in this section’s biographies.
Next is "Selection" (Xuǎnjǔ),
to bring forth talented individuals.
Discussing the excellent and advancing the worthy,
this is central to the Wáng Zhì;
promoting the virtuous and giving scope to the capable,
this is detailed in the Zhōu Guān;
those compiling local records (bāng shèng)
must not neglect this.
Next is "Eminent Persons" (Rénwù),
and next is "Arts and Letters" (Yìwén).
One uses documentary evidence,
the other examines records of the past,
both gather forgotten and dispersed materials,
carefully guarding against omissions,
and are thus the vital tasks of the present era.
The "Eminent Persons" must rely on verified deeds,
and not use endorsement to create false fame;
"Arts and Letters" carefully lists titles and categories,
and does not use miscellaneous poetry and prose merely to fill pages.
The "Eminent Persons" section follows the tradition of the Biographies (Lièzhuàn) in Sīmǎ Qiān’s (Mǎ Shǐ) Historical Records,
and "Arts and Letters" follows the model of descriptive catalogs established by Bān Gù (Bān) and Liú Xiàng (Liú);
actions must emulate the ancients,
only then can they serve as a model for the contemporary world.
Divided into these eight sections,
the structure is thus fully articulated, with the main points grasped and the details displayed.
As for the prefaces, rules, maps, and research (xù lì tú kǎo),
they are placed at the beginning of the volume;
miscellaneous texts and leftover discussions,
are attached at the end of the fascicles;
these are arranged in separate chapters
and are not included in the Eight Sections (Bā Mén).
This is comparable to the nine farmers partitioning the land (jiǔ fū huà jǐng),
or the eight formations (bā zhèn) arraying the army;
the organizational structure (jīngwěi) is brilliant,
and the substance (tǐ) and function (yòng) are fully realized.
Thus, I realize that a local gazetteer (fāng zhì) is the essential framework for regional governance,
and not merely a collection of elegant literary pieces
used by chief magistrates to adorn themselves with the reputation of cultured refinement.
Furthermore, since Shíshǒu County (Shíshǒu) was established,
it has been moved three times.
The topographical situation of the present county seat
is truly stable;
in the midst of the vast, flat plain surrounding it,
a cluster of mountains rises up close to the county seat.
To the east is Lónggài,
to the south is Mǎ'ān,
to the west is Xiùlín,
and to the north is Chǔwàng.
It occupies a central, crucial position,
making governance easy to spread evenly;
therefore, from the Míng Dynasty until now,
it has been continuously governed from this location.
Now, administration must rely on topographical features,
governance must depend on structure and discipline (gāngjì),
and compiling records must value essential organizational principles (tǐyào)—
these are all the same principle.
Lord Wáng (Wáng Jūn), who entered officialdom through Confucian scholarship (rú shù),
knew what the priority tasks were.
In compiling this book,
he truly grasped the essential organizational principles (tǐyào),
and later generations who carry on
will benefit, just like the county seat location.
Furthermore, the ancients said:
“One who sits and speaks expects to rise and act.”
If what is compiled in this book today
can truly be manifested in practical governance,
then one must not consider ledgers, records, and dossiers to be sufficient for one’s profession,
nor flowery rhetoric and embellishment sufficient to establish fame;
if this is the case, although this is only a gazetteer for one county,
it is truly a compilation of governance by Lord Wáng (Wáng Jūn) himself.
Even the fine historians of antiquity
could not surpass this.
I have high hopes for Lord Wáng (Wáng Jūn).
A Note Written After the Wǔgōng Gazetteer (Wǔgōng Zhì).
Kāng Hǎi’s (Kāng Hǎi) Wǔgōng Zhì is in three volumes,
further divided into seven sections (piān),
each with its own heading:
The first is "Geography" (Dìlǐ),
the second is "Establishments" (Jiànzhì),
the third is "Shrines and Sacrifices" (Císì),
the fourth is "Fields and Taxation" (Tiánfù),
the fifth is "Palace Officials and Teachers" (Gōngshī),
the sixth is "Eminent Persons" (Rénwù),
and the seventh is "Selection" (Xuǎnjǔ).
Kāng Hǎi (Kāng Shì) first imitated the writings of the ancients,
arranging the text in separate chapters,
placing himself highly,
almost without deference,
and yet the world widely praises it.
Wáng Shìzhèng (Wáng Shìzhèng)
also said: "The writing is concise, the facts are precise,
and the instructive language is refined" (xùn cí ěryǎ).
Later generations even wished to treat it as a model for compiling gazetteers,
which may be fortunate indeed.
Now, Kāng Hǎi (Kāng Shì) used roughly twenty thousand characters,
completing three volumes,
to write one county gazetteer,
and he considered this to be lofty and concise (gāo jiǎn).
But looking at his book now,
it is exceptionally messy and disordered.
This is because he did not understand the standards of historians
or the proper form of literature;
he merely used the reduction of volumes and chapters
to call it "lofty and concise" (gāo jiǎn).
If that is the case, who cannot achieve "lofty and concise"?
Gazetteers are historical judgments;
if they are irrelevant to events or principles,
they conventionally do not indiscriminately include poetry and prose.
Mr. Kāng [Kāng shì] concerning famous scenic spots and historical sites,
carelessly included useless poetry and prose.
How much difference is there
between this and the vulgar practice of compiling gazetteers
which uses the model of the *Wén Xuǎn* for the Arts and Letters section?
Furthermore, feudal lords do not cite the Son of Heaven [Tiānzǐ] as their ancestor,
and high officials do not cite feudal lords as their ancestors;
this is to strictly maintain proper social hierarchy.
Emperors, kings, empresses, and consorts throughout the generations,
are honored by historical annals and biographies,
and do not rely on local gazetteers.
Those who compile local gazetteers,
upon encountering the former hometown of an emperor, king, empress, or consort,
may state that fact.
Listing emperors and kings under Biographies,
and recording empresses and consorts under Eminent Women,
not only confuses the proper hierarchy,
but also consider that rulers take the whole world as their home;
what relevance do they have to a single county?
Mr. Kāng [Kāng shì], under Biographies,
first lists Hòu Jì up to King Wén [Wén Wáng],
excerpting the Grand Historian’s *Zhōu Jì*;
next, he lists Emperor Gāozǔ of Táng [Táng Gāozǔ] and Emperor Tàizōng [Tàizōng],
again excerpting the *Táng Běn Jì*.
The contradictions are too numerous to enumerate.
Local gazetteers should not presumptuously list emperors and kings;
let us set aside this principle for the moment.
Just following his own precedent,
why then are those after King Wǔ [Wǔ Wáng]
deleted?
If he argues that those who later possessed the empire
were not the former residents of Bīn County?
Yet the Grand King [Tài Wáng] once moved to Qí,
and King Wén later moved to Fēng;
why are they still listed under Wǔgōng Biographies?
If he argues that King Wǔ truly possessed the empire,
and those before King Wén
were merely posthumously titled kings,
and thus they are recorded?
Then on what principle
are Emperor Gāozǔ and Emperor Tàizōng of Táng included?
If he argues that Gāozǔ and Tàizōng grew up in that region,
and thus they are recorded?
Then why are the two ancestors, Xiǎn and Yì,
deleted?
Among the empresses and consorts, from Jiāng Yuán above,
down to Tài Jiāng below,
why is Tài Rèn alone missing in the middle?
Jiāng Yuán was not granted a fief in Wǔgōng,
yet she is included among the Eminent Women of Wǔgōng.
If he argues that the wife follows the husband?
Then Empress Dòu, Consort Tàimù of Táng Gāozǔ,
and Empress Zhǎngsūn, Consort Wéndé of Tàizōng,
all had reputations for virtue,
why are they not recorded?
Recording what should not be recorded,
which is extraneous and presumptuous,
demonstrates insufficient scholarly understanding.
Even within the general rules he set for himself,
he arbitrarily adds and deletes entries,
making it impossible to ascertain his true intention.
Can anything in the world like this be called loftily concise?
What is especially strange is this:
the gazetteer is divided into seven chapters,
why is the map section not included in the chapter order?
Presumably, this also follows common vulgar practice.
The beginning of the volume is topped with maps,
but there are only two maps.
Yet the diagram of Ms. Sū’s *Xuán Jī*
is placed side-by-side with the territorial map.
This demonstrates that the author has absolutely no logical sense of classification.
Now, placing the territorial map at the beginning,
perhaps imitating the ancient model of geographic records,
serves to display the overall layout of the county;
this is still understandable.
The diagram of *Xuán Jī*
is nothing more than the writing of a single person.
Perhaps following the example of Mr. Fàn [Fàn shì] recording Cài Yǎn’s *Bēi Fèn Shī*,
it could have been included in the biography of Eminent Women.
If he argues that a diagram cannot be included in a biography,
it could have been appended after the biography.
Suddenly taking it and placing it at the beginning,
is Wǔgōng County,
specifically made prominent because of Ms. Sū the woman?
If that is the case, extending this principle,
since King Wén is listed under Biographies,
why not take the diagram of the Sixty-Four Hexagrams and place it at the beginning?
Since Emperor Tàizōng of Táng is listed under Biographies,
why not take the diagram of the Six Battle Formations and place it at the beginning?
Although this would be called circuitous, erroneous, and unreasonable,
it would still be better than the *Xuán Jī Tú* being prominent merely due to the name of one woman.
Only the *Guān Shī Zhì*
applies both praise and criticism, thus preserving the standard of forthrightness,
slightly rising above the common practice.
Written after the *Cháoyì Zhì*
Hán Bāngjìng’s *Cháoyì Zhì* is in two volumes,
comprised of seven chapters:
The first is *Zǒng Zhì* (General Record),
the second is *Fēng Sú* (Customs),
the third is *Wù Chǎn* (Products),
the fourth is *Tián Fù* (Land Tax),
the fifth is *Míng Huàn* (Famous Officials),
the sixth is *Rén Wù* (Biographies),
the seventh is *Zá Jì* (Miscellaneous Notes).
In total, it is only six or seven thousand words,
using sixteen or seventeen quires of paper.
Among gazetteers and records,
none is simpler than this.
Kāng’s *Wǔgōng*, which sought extreme brevity,
looks far inferior to this.
Kāng [Kāng shì] wrote a preface for it,
also praising it highly.
Now looking at the writing style,
compared to Kāng’s, it is indeed perceived as simpler and purer;
only the General Record, within the section on ancient sites,
included several Táng poems, which makes it extraneous.
Mr. Kāng and Mr. Hán [Hán shì] were both literary men,
but they did not understand historical methodology,
and furthermore, they sought to be different from others.
Therefore, the resulting books
are so inappropriate,
that the knowledgeable ought not bother discussing them.
However, Mr. Kāng still maintained the general structure used by contemporary compilers of gazetteers.
Thus, when judging it by the methods of gazetteer compilation,
faults and errors emerge everywhere.
Mr. Hán’s work, however, cannot even be considered a gazetteer.
It is merely a rhymeless *Fù* of Cháoyì,
and also a *Kǎo* of Cháoyì with arbitrarily separated categories.
If placed among the small books and short notes of the Six Dynasties,
such as *Chénliú Fēng Sú* or *Luòyáng Qiélán* and other such records,
and if we do not demand that it follow the standard methodology of historians,
it might still be acceptable.
Therefore, regarding the gazetteers of the two authors, *Wǔgōng* and *Cháoyì*,
I consider *Cháoyì* to be slightly superior.
However, although the faults of the *Cháoyì Zhì* are few,
recording Chéng Jǐ serving Emperor Jiànwén
indiscriminately uses unofficial histories,
without verifying the facts.
This is the first fault.
Combining the section on officials selected through examination with the Biographies section,
but failing to record the examination year for *Jǔrén* and *Jìnshì*.
This is the second fault.
When recording his father's affairs,
he refers to his father as “the former Lord Hán,”
so that to this day, people do not know his father's actual name.
In the Eminent Women section, there is Madam Zhāng, Consort Tài Yírén of Hán,
who is obviously Hán Bāngjìng’s honored relative;
but she is recorded in such a way that people still do not know whose wife she was,
or whose mother she was.
The ancients did not avoid naming names when writing.
Some say that Sīmǎ Qiān avoided the name of his father Tán by replacing it with *tóng*;
however, in the *Huájī Zhuàn*, the phrase *tán yán wēi zhòng* appears,
thus he did not avoid the character *tán*.
I suspect the theory of name avoidance is not accurate.
Even if he avoided it,
when narrating his family background,
he must properly state his father’s name,
so that later generations have something to verify.
Now Bāngjìng avoids naming his father,
leaving people ignorant of who he was;
he refers to his honored relative as Tài Yírén,
leaving people ignorant of whose wife or mother she was;
this means submerging the deeds of his ancestors.
Seeking to enhance their reputation, he instead diminishes it.
This is the third fault.
Regarding the names of chapters and fascicles:
Ancient people used bamboo slips as chapters (piān);
when the slips and tablets were too numerous,
they would separate them into separate volumes (biān),
marking them with jiǎ and yǐ,
for ease of cross-referencing.
Later people used silk fabric to form scrolls (juăn),
which carried more text compared to what the bamboo slips contained.
Therefore, piān (chapter) was used for the beginning and ending of a piece of writing,
while juăn (fascicle/scroll) was generally measured by what the scroll axis could hold.
This is because piān has structural meaning,
but juăn does not.
In recent times, books are written in paper booklets (cè),
which can be increased by five or ten times
compared to scrolls.
Naming them juăn
is merely preserving an ancient name.
If accumulated paper does not require being separated into separate booklets,
then those texts divided into piān,
do not need to be further divided into juăn numbers,
because the latter inherently lacks structural meaning.
Now, the two gazetteers of
Wǔgōng and
Cháoyì,
their intention seems to dislike the way common compilations categorize things by headings,
and their general titles all use piān names.
This can be said to capture the essence of the ancients.
The Wǔgōng Gazetteer used more than sixty sheets of paper,
which one booklet was sufficient for,
yet it had to be divided into seven piān making up three juăn.
This division already lacks justification.
The Cháoyì Gazetteer only used just over ten sheets of paper,
not enough for one booklet,
yet it was also divided into seven piān making up two juăn.
What explanation is there for this?
Some might say:
This is a trivial detail,
unrelated to the meaning of the text; why bother nitpicking?
They do not understand that these two authors pride themselves on being writers,
yet they fail to grasp the intention of the ancients regarding such chapter titles and headings.
Thus, their every stroke of the brush and every deletion,
attempting to emulate former sages,
without properly assessing their own virtue and capability,
can generally be known.
Postscript to the Wú Jùn Zhì
Fàn Chéngdà’s Wú Jùn Zhì is in fifty juăn,
divided into thirty-nine piān:
titled 'Historical Evolution' (Yán'gé),
titled 'Divisions and Enfeoffment' (Fēnfēng),
titled 'Households, Taxes, and Rents' (Hùkǒu Shuìzū),
titled 'Local Tribute' (Tǔgòng),
titled 'Customs' (Fēngsú),
titled 'City Walls' (Chéngguō),
titled 'Schools' (Xuéxiào),
titled 'Military Camps' (Yíngzhài),
titled 'Government Offices' (Guānyǔ),
titled 'Granaries and Treasuries' (Cāngkù),
with 'Markets and Taxes' (Chǎngwù) appended thereto,
titled 'Neighborhoods and Markets' (Fāngshì),
titled 'Historical Sites' (Gǔjì),
titled 'Feudal Titles' (Fēngjué),
titled 'Governors' (Mùshǒu),
titled 'Inscriptions' (Tímíng),
titled 'Officials' (Guānlì),
titled 'Ancestral Shrines and Temples' (Címiào),
titled 'Gardens and Pavilions' (Yuántíng),
titled 'Mountains' (Shān),
titled 'Tiger Hill' (Hǔqiū),
titled 'Bridges' (Qiáoliáng),
titled 'Rivers' (Chuān),
titled 'Water Conservancy' (Shuǐlì),
titled 'Notable Figures' (Rénwù),
with 'Chaste Women' (Liènǚ) appended thereto,
titled 'Inscribed Names of Jinshì' (Jìnshì Tímíng),
titled 'Local Products' (Tǔwù),
titled 'Palaces and Daoist Monasteries' (Gōngguān),
titled 'Temples within the Prefectural City' (Fǔguō Sì),
titled 'Temples Outside the Suburbs' (Jiāowài Sì),
titled 'County Records' (Xiànjì),
titled 'Tombs' (Zhǒngmù),
titled 'Immortal Affairs' (Xiānshì),
titled 'Buddhism' (Fútú),
titled 'Technicians' (Fāngjì),
titled 'Strange Events' (Qíshì),
titled 'Unusual Stories' (Yìwén),
titled 'Textual Research' (Kǎozhèng),
titled 'Miscellaneous Poems' (Záyǒng),
and 'Miscellaneous Records' (Zázhì).
At the beginning of the volume is a preface dated Shàodìng second year
by Zhào Rǔtán of Biàn.
It states: "When the Shíhú Gazetteer was completed,
the administrator had the necessary wood prepared for carving.
At that time, there were those who requested that certain matters be appended to the record but failed,
and they cried out,
'This book is not written by Shíhú!'
The administrator dared not engrave it,
so it was stored in the Confucian Temple.
In the initial year of Shàodìng,
Lǐ Hóu Shòupéng of Guăngdé, having been appointed Administrator from the position of Shàngshū Láng.
His ancestor, the Duke of Dùzhī, Jiāyán,
was a guest of Shíhú.
Upon visiting the school and asking about the old affairs,
he was astonished and said,
'Has this book still not been published?'
Another day, he paid respects at the Shíhú Ancestral Shrine,
and sought the remaining writings from his family,
and compared it with the school's version, finding no differences.
However, the book stopped at Shàoxī third year,
and later major constructions,
such as the Bǎiwàn Cāng, the new settlement of Jiādìng, the Xǔpǔ Navy Base, and the relocation of troops at Gùjìng, were all not recorded.
Thereupon, he convened the School Inspector Wāng Tàihēng,
and they consulted with the literary scholars,
following the precedent of Chǔ Shǎosūn,
to supplement the omissions,
and correct the errors,
without setting them apart as a separate continuation."
It further states:
"While Shíhú was alive,
he frequently consulted with the three local scholars, Gōng Yí, Téng Chéng, and Zhōu Nán Hòu.
Gōng especially presented many things he had heard to the Duke,
which caused differing opinions to arise.
The stele placed at the Duke's tomb by Yìgōng
recorded the book he wrote,
and the chapter titles can be verified,"
and so on.
He was highly esteemed by people in this manner.
Today, scholars discussing Song Dynasty local gazetteers
also praise Luó's Xīn'ān Zhì and Fàn's Wú Jùn Zhì as the foremost examples,
without any dissenting views.
I carefully examined it;
the writing style is indeed clear and concise.
The vulgar and base habits of later gazetteers (fāngzhì)
had not yet begun at that time,
and the arrangement was also elegant and clean.
Furthermore, its structure details the Commandery (jùn) but omits the County (xiàn).
From the sections on historical changes (yángé), city walls and pools (chéngchí), and lists of officials (zhíguān tímíng),
all cover the Commandery but none the County.
The two juan (scrolls) dedicated to County records (xiànjì),
however, only record official residences (guānshǔ),
occasionally touching upon the pavilions and terraces (tíngtái) within the residences,
sometimes quoting inscriptions from stones without listing the names and surnames (míngxìng) of the authors,
and the structure is inconsistent and uneven.
This was the standard structure for gazetteers of that era,
and it is completely different
from the recent Prefectural Gazetteers (fǔzhì) which are compiled by combining the records of the Departments (zhōu) and Counties (xiàn).
I have a separate, specialized essay discussing this matter,
so it can certainly be ignored here.
However, while detailing the Commandery and omitting the County in other matters
might be considered acceptable organizational practice (tǐlì);
having historical changes (yángé) for the Commandery but none for the County,
is to lose all clear outline.
It is no wonder that they used Píngjiāng Lù Fǔ
to improperly replace the old name of Wú Jùn,
placing it at the head of the entire gazetteer without realizing the mistake.
Moreover, when the historical changes narrative enters the Sòng Dynasty,
it says: "In the first year of Kāibǎo,
the King of Wúyuè changed Zhōngwú Jūn to Píngjiāng Jūn.
In the third year of Tàipíng Xīngguó,
Qián Chǔ surrendered his territory."
Consulting the histories,
it had already been changed to Sūzhōu at that time,
but the gazetteer text fails to mention the change to a Department (zhōu).
Below this, it abruptly continues:
“In the third year of Zhènghé,
Sūzhōu was elevated to Píngjiāng Fǔ.”
Having no mention of Sūzhōu above,
it suddenly introduces the elevation of the Department (zhōu) to a Prefecture (fǔ);
the meaning of the text is also unclear.
The entire text compiles material gathered from historical records (shǐjí), poetry, essays, and literary miscellanies (shuōbù),
and is edited into its current form.
It still notes the source below the relevant entry.
This is certainly an acceptable method for compilation (zuǎnlèi),
but it is not the style of original authorship (zhùzuò tǐ).
The section on customs (fēngsú) mostly draws from the poetry critiques (shīhuà) of Wú Xià,
and occasionally verifies local pronunciations (fāngyīn),
which is correct.
The assemblies of the Nine Elders (Jiǔ Lǎo zhī Huì), such as Xú Yòu and his peers,
and the assemblies of the Venerable Elders (Qí Yīng zhī Huì), such as Zhāng Hù and his peers,
were merely incidental grand events of the time,
and ought not to be included in the section on customs (fēngsú).
Schools (xuéxiào) are in juan 4,
while County records (xiànjì) are in juan 37 and 38.
Since the official residences of the County administration (xiànzhì guānyǔ)
are already included in the County records,
and Schools covers both Prefectural and County education,
this means that the school information appears before the County name itself.
Markets and wards (fāngshì) are not appended to the city walls (chéngguō),
but rather appended to the official residences (guānyǔ);
this also lacks proper sequence.
The lists of officials for the Surveillance Commissioner (Tídiǎn Xíngyù Sī) and the Salt and Tea Transportation Commissioner (Tíjǔ Chángpíng Yán Chá Sī)
are not included in the main category of Governors and Administrators (Mùshǒu Tímíng),
but appear appended after the official residences (guānyǔ);
this is also contrary to proper regulations.
For the list of Surveillance Commissioners (Tídiǎn Xíngyù tímíng),
the names and surnames are written prominently at the top,
while the origin and the months of arrival and departure are annotated separately below;
for the Salt and Tea Transportation Commissioners (Tíjǔ Chángpíng Yán Chá),
the official rank, names, and surnames are written prominently at the top,
while the months of service are annotated separately below.
This lack of uniformity in structure (tǐlì) is also inconsistent.
Famous people are recorded under Governors and Administrators (mùshǒu),
but the lists of officials (tímíng) are placed afterward;
this is an inversion.
The grades, systems, and quotas (pǐnzhì yuán'é) for officials and functionaries (guānlì) are not recorded,
but only those worthy of transmission (chuan) are selected;
this is also too abbreviated and careless.
The registrars (gōngcáo) and subordinates (yuànshǔ)
are interspersed and mixed in with the Magistrates (língzhǎng).
Furthermore, it is awkward that the names of the Magistrates (língzhǎng) appear before the County records (xiànjì).
Ancient Sites (gǔjì) are considerably mixed up

with ancestral temples (címiào), official residences (guānyǔ), gardens and pavilions (yuántíng), tombs (zhǒngmù), palaces and monasteries (gōngguān), temples (sì), mountains (shān), and rivers (chuān).
If one separates Hǔqiū into its own section outside of the Mountain category,
and does not understand the method of categorizing, linking examples, detailing, abbreviating, and cross-referencing,
then every attempt will encounter thorns and obstacles.
The section on eminent figures (rénwù) is not originally authored,
but cuts and condenses historical biographies (shǐchuán);
this is also the standard practice for compilation (zuǎnlèi).
It is compiled into eight consecutive juan,
and does not use categorized headings,
which is still broadly elegant.
However, for great families like the Zhāng and the Gù,
who produced famous people across generations,
it would naturally be appropriate to gather them into sections by clan.
Within a single clan,
they should then be arranged by chronological generation.
Instead, they are sometimes divided and sometimes combined,
and the chronological order is also occasionally inverted,
unlike the Lù families (Zhū Lù), which are gathered into one compilation
where the sequence is not confused.
Perhaps the current edition is erroneous
and does not reflect Fàn Shì’s original arrangement?
Immortal Affairs (xiānshì), Buddhists (fútú), and Technical Arts Practitioners (fāngjì)
are also branches of the Eminent Figures (rénwù) section.
Even if one wishes to strictly separate them,
they should still be placed after the Eminent Figures section,
with distinct headings provided.
Now, after the Eminent Figures section,

they are interspersed with the lists of successful candidates (jìnshì tímíng), local products (tǔwù), palaces and monasteries (gōngguān), temples inside the prefecture city (fǔ guō sì), temples outside the city (jiāowài sì), county records (xiànjì), and tombs (zhǒngmù).
After these twelve juan,
the three categories starting with Immortal Affairs (xiānshì) suddenly appear.
Consequently, events, institutions, and human affairs
are confused and unclear,
which can be called the ultimate example of disorderliness and lack of refinement.
The collection of local products (tǔwù) is extremely broad,
and the verification of facts is also good.
However, the swords of Gànfǔ, Mò Yé, and Shǔ Lòu,
and the hooks of Wú Hóng and Hù Jī,
are miraculous objects recorded in biographies and anecdotes of a specific era,
and are difficult to fully trust.
Including them wholesale in the section on local products (tǔwù)
is not appropriate for their category.
The Strange Affairs (qíshì) section (one juan)
and the Unusual Reports (yìwén) section (three juan)
have no real distinction upon close examination.
The verification of sources is broad but not simplistic.
Poetry, odes, and miscellaneous essays (shīfù záwén)
are already annotated under their respective categories,
yet those that have no category to return to
are separately placed into a Miscellaneous Verse (zá yǒng) section.
Although the material collected is not bad,
it is rather criticized for being vague and irrelevant.
I often see recent gazetteer compilers,
whose judgment is insufficient to make decisive cuts,
and who, being greedy for the strange and fond of the trivial,
cannot bear to omit anything.
They therefore compile a Miscellaneous Records (zázhì) section at the end of the volume,
or call it Remaining Chapters (yúpiān).
This happens because the categorization of the whole gazetteer
is treated like arranging abacus beads,
without distinct discerning judgment.
Therefore, when subjects are difficult to attach to a category,
they simply create this juan
to serve as a pickle jar for snakes and dragons (i.e., miscellaneous junk),
which is highly pointless.
Now, looking at the end of Fàn Shì’s gazetteer,
it also has a Miscellaneous Records (zázhì) section,
so this custom was pioneered by the predecessors.
In reality, everything contained therein
has a category it could belong to.
It is a pity that Fàn Shì's analytical categorization was not refined.
In its fifty juan,
the appellations for official titles and place names are irregular,
and the names and titles of people are randomly filled in without rigor.
This reflects the style of Sòng Dynasty literary critics (shīhuà jiāfēng),
which drastically alters the established conventions of historical writing.
That this is inappropriate for a specialized gazetteer (fāngzhì zhuānjiā)
or the standards of an official historian (shǐguān shéngchǐ),
goes without saying.
The reason why it is praised by the world
is because Shíhú (Fàn Chéngdà) was virtuous and learned,
and was also prominent and respected at the time.
Although his cutting and editing (jiǎncái bǐxuē)
does not conform to historical methods,
compared to the current generation of those who are vulgar, excessive, incompetent, and ignorant,
it is certainly an improvement.
Its good reputation is thus not accidental.
However, to consider this the standard of a fine gazetteer (fāngzhì),
is inaccurate.
Written after the Gūsū Zhì.
*Gūsū Zhì* consists of sixty *juàn* (volumes).
The beginning covers the evolution of the Commanderies and Districts (*jùnyì yángé*).
Next are the Prefects and Magistrates (*gǔjīn shǒulìng*) of past and present.
Next are the Examination Graduates (*kēdì*).
All of these are presented in tables (*biǎo*).
Next is Evolution (General History) (*yángé*).
Next are the Celestial Fields (*fēnyě*).
Next are the Boundaries (*jiāngyù*).
Next are Mountains.
Next are Waterways.
Next is Water Conservancy (*shuǐlì*).
Next are Customs (*fēngsú*).
Next is Population (*hùkǒu*).
Next are Local Products (*tǔchǎn*).
Next are Land Taxes (*tiánfù*).
Next are Walls and Moats (*chéngchí*).
Next are Wards and Lanes (*fāngxiàng*).
Next are Townships and Metropolis Areas (*xiāngdū*).
Next are Bridges.
Next are Government Offices (*guānshǔ*).
Next are Schools.
Next are Military Defenses (*bīngfáng*).
Next are Granaries (*cāngchǎng*).
Next are Postal Stations (*yìdì*).
Next are Altars and Temples (*tánmiào*).
Next are Buddhist Monasteries and Daoist Temples (*sìguàn*).
Next are Official Residences (*dìzhái*).
Next are Gardens and Ponds (*yuánchí*).
Next are Historical Sites (*gǔjì*).
Next are Tombs (*zhǒngmù*).
Next is the History of the Wú Clan (*Wú Shìjiā*).
Appended are Enfeoffments, Titles, and Clans (*shìzú*).
Next are Accounts of Pacifying Rebellions (*píngluàn*).
Next are Official Achievements (*huànjì*).
Next are Biographies (*rénwù*).
Within Biographies,

it is divided into Famous Officials (*míngchén*), Loyal and Righteous (*zhōngyì*), Filial Piety and Fraternity (*xiàoyǒu*), Confucian Scholars (*rú lín*), Literature (*wénxué*), Distinguished Conduct (*zhuó xíng*), Recluses (*yǐnyì*), Recommended Officials (*jiànjǔ*), Arts (*yìshù*), Miscellaneous Skills (*zá jì*), Sojourners (*yóuyù*), Exemplary Women (*liènǚ*), and Buddhists and Daoists (*shìlǎo*),
totaling thirteen categories.
The final section consists of Records of Anomalies and Miscellaneous Matters (*jìyì záshì*).
However, the number of volumes assigned to each section,
does not correspond uniformly to the sectional headings.
Official Achievements (*mínghuàn*) is divided into six *juàn*.
Famous Officials (*míngchén*) within Biographies (*rénwù*) is divided into ten *juàn*.
Loyal and Righteous (*zhōngyì*) and Filial Piety and Fraternity (*xiàoyǒu*) are combined into one *juàn*.
Confucian Scholars (*rú lín*) and Literature (*wénxué*) are combined into one *juàn*.
Granaries (*cāngchǎng*) and Postal Stations (*yìdì*) are combined into one *juàn*.
Such instances,
are numerous.
The total sixty *juàn*
were roughly compiled according to the quantity of paper needed,
without systematic structure.
The nomenclature of the Suzhou Gazette (*Sū Zhì*) is inconsistent.
Fàn Chéngdà, for instance, titled his gazette of Sūzhōu as *Wú Jùn Zhì*,
which already lacks logic.
Previous critics, however, only fault Wáng Shì for inappropriately naming the Gazetteer of Sūzhōu Prefecture (*Sūzhōu Fǔ Zhì*) as *Gūsū Zhì*,
which is a case of valuing what is heard over what is seen.
However, local gazetteers (*zhìchéng*) for commanderies and districts,
have rarely been good editions, past or present.
Works like those by Fàn Shì and Wáng Shì,
although not considered exemplary by historians,
still stand out above the vulgar and wretched common run of books.
They are comparatively superior.
The existing edition of the *Sūzhōu Fǔ Zhì* has many commendable aspects,
largely because the inherited old documents were sufficient to draw upon.
Nevertheless, there are absurd and irrational points,
which are not even worth a laugh.
Even a minor clerk (*xūlì*)
who barely understands the format of official documents,
certainly would not commit such errors.
For instance, the three tables at the beginning demonstrate this.
Table One is titled "Evolution of Commanderies and Districts" (*Jùnyì Yángé*).
To treat the Prefecture (*fǔ*) and District (*xiàn*) as Commanderies and Districts (*jùnyì*),
is an error too obvious to mention.
The table headings use *zhōu*, *guó*, *jùn*, *jūn*, *fǔ*, and *lù*.
It only lists the superior administrative units (*zhōu*, *jùn*) but lacks the districts (*xiànyì*).
Setting aside the inappropriate formal structure,
since they themselves titled it "Commanderies and Districts,"
is this not self-contradictory?
Furthermore, the list of officials includes the District Magistrate (*zhīxiàn*),
but the evolution section lacks district names.
To what jurisdiction are these officials like the *zhīxiàn* supposed to belong?
What is particularly strange is that,
in the form of a table,
vertical columns and horizontal rows are used to distinguish the warp and weft.
This is typically employed when events occur in the same year and month but in different places,
or when events belong to the same generational sequence but different branches.
This is known as "same warp, different weft."
When things are uneven and not uniform,
they cannot be clearly distinguished merely by sequential writing.
Therefore, the vertical and horizontal (warp and weft) format is used to differentiate them.
In a table of Prefects and Magistrates (*Shǒulìng Biǎo*),
the Prefect (*shǒu*), Assistant (*chéng*), Judge (*pàn*), and Secretary (*lù*) of the commandery,
and the Magistrate (*lìng*), Assistant (*chéng*), Registrar (*bù*), and Commandant (*wèi*) of the district,
must be arranged horizontally as the warp;
and the dynasties, years, and months,
must be arranged vertically as the weft.
When later generations want to check the years and months of appointment,
they find the era from the vertical headings,
and from the horizontal rows, they know which *shǒu*, which *lìng*, which *chéng*, or which *lù* was serving,
whether before or after,
or concurrently.
Consulting the table is as clear as pointing to the palm of one's hand.
If events occurred sequentially,
and definitely not at the same time,
then there is no need for anything other than listing the items in sequence.
There is certainly no reason to use the warp and weft table format.
The table divides its cells based on *zhōu*, *guó*, *jùn*, *jūn*, *fǔ*, and *lù*.
Now, *zhōu* refers to Sūzhōu.
*Guó* refers to the State of Wú.
*Jùn* refers to the Commandery.
*Jūn*, *fǔ*, and *lù* refer to Píngjiāng Lù Fǔ (Route-Prefecture).
These are all sequential names reflecting the administrative evolution of the single territory known as Sūzhōu Fǔ.
When it was called the State of Wú (*Wú Guó*), there was no Sūzhōu.
When it was called Sūzhōu, there was no Wú Jùn.
When it was called Wú Jùn, there was no Píngjiāng Lù Fǔ.
Since there are no elements that occurred concurrently in different places, unevenly, and difficult to standardize,
simply listing them by item,
the reader would understand automatically.
Instead, they created a vertical and horizontal table,
leaping up and down without logic,
lacking any systematic structure.
This merely confuses the eyes and ears of the reader.
The official documents of a clerk (*xūlì*)
would not be so chaotic.
The Table of Ancient Prefects and Magistrates (*Gǔ Shǒulìng Biǎo*)
divides its cells based on Grand Administrators (*tàishǒu*), Commandants (*dūwèi*), and Acting Officials (*quánshè*).
Now, Grand Administrators and Commandants
certainly may have had concurrent terms in office.
As for Acting Officials (*quánshè*),
they are like the current officials holding temporary seals of office.
If there is a sitting Prefect (*shǒu*), there is no acting Prefect (*quánshǒu*).
If there is a sitting Commandant (*wèi*), there is no acting Commandant (*shèwèi*).
The acting official and the main official
absolutely cannot appear concurrently.
Thus, there is certainly no need for the vertical and horizontal table format.
Now, they separately list these categories,
needlessly taking up space.
This, too, is something a clerk would not do.
When listing officials,
names should be designated according to the institutional rules of the time.
The table of Prefects and Magistrates (*shǒulìng*),
should be titled "Table of Fǔ and Xiàn Officials,"
treating the later terminology as encompassing the earlier. This would be acceptable.
Now they call it the Table of Ancient Prefects and Magistrates (*Gǔ Shǒulìng Biǎo*).
In terms of literal meaning, this is perhaps harmless.
However, regarding the Table of Current Prefects and Magistrates (*Jīn Shǒulìng Biǎo*),
"Current" refers specifically to the contemporary institutional system.
Yet they still use the old titles *shǒu* and *lìng* to refer to the Míng Dynasty officials *zhīfǔ* and *zhīxiàn*.
The error in name versus reality
is too obvious to mention again.
For Prefecture officials (*fǔ guān*), they only list the Prefect (*zhīfǔ*),
omitting the Sub-prefects (*tóngzhī*) and lower ranks.
For District officials (*xiàn guān*), they only list the Magistrate (*zhīxiàn*),
omitting the Assistants (*chéng*) and Registrars (*bù*).
What is the reasoning for this?
Furthermore, if a table uses warp and weft;
the function of the warp and weft method
is to compare and combine similar categories,
thereby forcing dissimilar items to follow their appropriate category.
Therefore, categories (*lèi*) and tables (*biǎo*),
are fundamentally incompatible.
A table cannot serve as a category list.
A category list has no use for a table.
This is also something commonly understood by clerks.
The Table of Examination Graduates (*Kēdì Zhī Biǎo*),
divided into upper, middle, and lower sections,
due to the differing systems in antiquity and modernity,
where the records are numerous and heavy,
dividing the volumes by historical era would have been acceptable.
The proper format should be to list the family background and affiliation horizontally as the warp,
and list the hometown, metropolitan exam, and year of the session vertically as the weft.
Provincial Graduates (*jǔrén*) and Presented Scholars (*jìnshì*)
are all Examination Graduates (*kēdì*).
Now, they use *kēdì* as the general title,
but then divide *jǔrén* and *jìnshì* into two separate tables.
This is a method of classification (*fēnlèi*),
not comparison (or coordination) (*bǐlèi*).
Furthermore, those ranked as *jìnshì*
must first have attained the *jǔrén* degree.
Now they place the *jìnshì* first,
and list the *jǔrén* later.
This is an inversion of the proper sequence of events,
confusing the reader’s senses.
This, again, is something a clerk would not do.
All these errors and blunders,
committed by Wáng Shì Ào,
who was styled an erudite man (*tōngrén*),
were perhaps not created by him personally.
He was probably generally weak in historical structure (*shǐcái*),
and indulged in the habits of literati,
holding that the tables lacked literary merit worth looking at,
and thus paid no attention to them.
He allowed the ignorant people of the time
to recklessly compile the content,
unaware that he would bring ridicule upon himself from knowledgeable individuals,
to such an extent.
Therefore, I say that literary men (*wénrén*) cannot be trusted to compile gazetteers.
Regarding the establishment of government offices,
pavilions, towers, and galleries,
and the steles, inscriptions, prefaces, and postscripts of previous authors listed,
retaining their original text is permissible.
The gazetteer text narrates original constructions and major renovations,
but within a single section,
it suddenly refers to the location as a Zhōu (Prefecture),
and suddenly refers to it as a Jùn (Commandery),
mostly retaining the original text of the *Fàn Zhì*;
they did not realize that the *Fàn Zhì* is not worthy of emulation.
According to historical records, during the Sòng Dynasty, before the fifth year of Zhènghé [1115 CE],
it was named Sūzhōu.
After the fifth year of Zhènghé,
it was named Píngjiāng Lù Fǔ (Píngjiāng Circuit and Prefecture).
Throughout the duration of the Sòng Dynasty,
there was no name Wú Jùn (Wú Commandery).
Since the title of the *Fàn Zhì* was already erroneous,
then the rules and structure of the gazetteer text
were akin to the proverb "having nothing to censure oneself in Kuài."
Wáng Shì (Mr. Wáng) did not know to revise this,
which is what is meant by the error.
Furthermore, regarding the narrative of military events since ancient times,
to list it as a category titled Píng Luàn (Pacifying Disorder),
I also cannot understand the reasoning.
Mountains and rivers, fields and taxes,
neighborhoods and customs,
households, post stations, military, and granaries,
these are all categories for statistical records;
official careers, temporary residences,
prominent figures, and exemplary women,
these are all literary forms for biography and narration.
Naming a section Píng Luàn
is neither similar to the statistical records of a chronicle,
nor is it equivalent to the biographical style identifying specific persons.
It should naturally be discussed and recorded separately,
ensuring proper organization;
otherwise, the entire gazetteer should be revised to resemble a chronological record of events (jì shì běnmò),
so as not to incur criticism for being ill-categorized.
However, only those skilled in historical methodology
can distinguish this,
and it is perhaps not a point of criticism applicable to this gazetteer.
As for the remaining minor textual flaws,
and occasional errors in compilation,
they are not worth scrutinizing further.
The *Sū Zhì* (Sūzhōu Gazetteer) is highly praised by the public,
which is why I felt compelled to make these distinctions,
not to willfully be demanding,
or to seek to find fault with previous worthies.
Postscript to the *Luán Zhì* (Luán Gazetteer)
My family possesses four fascicles of the *Luán Zhì*,
the woodblock printing is blurred,
with missing characters and inversions,
making it impossible to read straight through.
This is because in the forty-seventh year of Qiánlóng [1782 CE],
when I was lecturing in Yǒngpíng,
Cài Jūnxūn of Ānyuè, the former Zhī Zhōu (Prefect) of Luán Zhōu,
wanted to commission me to compile the Zhōu Gazetteer.
He consequently took the old gazetteer to show me,
and that is this copy.
According to the "Bibliography Treatise" (*Yìwén Zhì*) of the *Míng Shǐ* (History of Míng),
there is Chén Shìyuán's *Luán Zhōu Zhì* in eleven volumes.
Chén (style name Yǎngjūn),
was a native of Yìngchéng, Húguǎng.
He obtained the *jìnshì* degree in the *Jiājìng jiǎchén* year [1544 CE],
and served successively as the Zhī Zhōu of Luán Zhōu,
and enjoyed great fame.
His writings were numerous,
many of which are seen in the *Míng Zhì* (Míng Gazetteer),
yet the official history does not include a biography of him.
The *Yìngchéng Xiàn Zhì* (Yìngchéng County Gazetteer)
contains a biography but no list of his works.
Nevertheless, the county residents still speak highly of him today.
When I resided briefly in Yìngchéng in my youth,
I searched for his writings,
but saw absolutely none.
I heard that the former magistrate, Jīn Céng of Jiāngpǔ,
took all the manuscripts stored in his family collection when he left,
which I regretted greatly.
This gazetteer is still referred to as Mr. Chén's original edition.
During the Kāngxī period,
Zhī Zhōu Hóu Shàoqí continued and supplemented it according to the established framework.
Although the original sequence of the eleven volumes
cannot be recovered,
the categories and methodological structure
were not altered.
The preface at the beginning of the volume was written by an unknown person,
and contains the following statement:
"In the past, when I served as an official in Zhōngzhōu,
I met with Duke Guō Qīngluó to discuss revising the *Xǔzhōu Zhì*.
The Duke said:
'Among all gazetteers in the realm,
Lǐ Cāngmíng's *Qīngzhōu Zhì* is the first,
and the next is the *Luán Zhì*.'"
This seems to refer to Mr. Chén's original edition.
Both the book and the man
were highly praised by their contemporaries.
That is why Mr. Hóu followed the example and dared not propose major changes.
Now, looking at the book,
it is exaggerated, misleading, esoteric, and strange,
rather colored by the habit among mid-Míng Dynasty people of being curious without having studied properly.
When the literary style reaches this point,
it is truly beyond commentary.
Mr. Chén was known for his extensive learning,
yet the *Luán Zhì* is so mediocre and absurd.
I do not know what his
other writings might be like.
And that Mr. Guō Qīngluó praised it so rashly,
is incomprehensible.
The book is divided into four sections:
First, Shì Biān (Chronology of Eras);
Second, Jiāng Lǐ (Territory and Administration);
Third, Rǎng Zé (Land Regulations);
Fourth, Jiàn Zhì (Establishments).
The Shì Biān uses the chronological format,
imitating the style of the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals),
but is actually unfounded and wildly extravagant.
At the beginning of the chapter, it is prominently written:
"Emperor Dì Kù established the Nine Provinces,
our Jì (Ji Province) division."
The commentary says:
"Why is this written?
It records the beginning."
And so on.
When examining the divisions of the Nine Provinces,
it is again prominently written:
"The Yellow Emperor (Huángdì) expelled the Hūnròu."
The commentary says:
"Why write Hūnròu?
It is our border commandery."
It is also prominently written:
"In the thirteenth year (*sì*) of King Wǔ of Zhōu (Zhōu Wǔwáng),
Yí Qí (Bó Yí and Shū Qí) starved to death on Shǒuyáng Mountain,
and Zhào Gōng Shì was enfeoffed in Yān.
This is our Yān division."
These are all parts of Mr. Chén's original compilation,
so bizarre and reckless that they are not even worth a smile.
The *Chūnqiū*
is a chronicle of the state of Lǔ.
The language used by the minister-scribe
distinguished between the internal and the external (Lǔ vs. other states).
Therefore, Lǔ is referred to as 'our,'
not because it grants special status to the ruler over the rulers of other states.
Moreover, since the Lǔ history already uses the name of the state,
it would naturally be inconvenient for the text to refer to the state repeatedly as Lǔ.
This is appropriate literary style,
and nothing more.
In the age of commanderies and counties,
the realm is united under one sovereign.
Those who wield the brush to compile Zhōu and Xiàn gazetteers
are all subjects of the imperial court.
Why use the term 'our'?
As for the commentaries of Gōng (Gōngyáng) and Gǔ (Gǔliáng) on the Classics,
they originate from the teachings passed down by classical scholars.
The subtle intentions
are difficult to explain immediately,
so they utilize fictitious questions and answers to clarify them.
This is not standard historical practice.
The gazetteers of prefectures and counties
are produced by a single hand.
The compilation does not contain obscure meanings left by a predecessor
waiting for the compiler to clarify.
To write and explain oneself,
to question and answer oneself,
since this is not a performer acting in a play,
why engage in this isolated dialogue and exchange?
Furthermore, Liú Shì's *Shǐ Tōng* (Generalities on History)
discusses the *Jìn Jì* (Annals of Jìn) and the *Hàn Jìn Chūnqiū* (Annals of Hàn and Jìn),
and severely criticizes previous authors for baseless imitation,
where the use of the term 'our' and hypothetical questions and answers
are both targeted for rejection.
Mr. Chén was reputed to be learned and comprehensive;
did he alone fail to examine this?
If this applies even to national histories,
how much more so to Zhōu and Xiàn gazetteers?
The phrase "In the thirteenth year (*sì*) of King Wǔ of Zhōu (Zhōu Wǔwáng)"
is particularly erroneous in its wording.
The term *sì* (祀) was used for the annual sacrifice during the Yīn Dynasty,
and the two [systems] do not overlap.
Although the *Hóngfàn* (Great Plan) was presented by Jīzǐ to the Zhou court,
its use of historical terminology is an exception [to the Zhou standard],
not the proper designation.
Mr. Chén, for the sake of Yí Qí,
changed the term for 'year' to *sì*.
The subsequent reference to the enfeoffment of Zhào Gōng
is included under the same text.
Does this imply that Zhào Gōng was considered a man of Yīn?
Moreover, Yí Qí, who refused to eat the grain of Zhōu
and starved to death on Shǒuyáng Mountain,
means they refused official stipends and died in destitution and hunger,
not that they deliberately starved themselves to death as martyrs.
To prominently record their year of death,
is this not extremely inappropriate?
If just these few points are considered,
is it still necessary to investigate the rest?
Its historical divisions are categorized into three sections:
The first is called the Former Dynasties,
the second is called Our Dynasty,
and the third is called the Restoration (Zhōngxīng).
The section designated Our Dynasty
concludes in the 28th year of Jiājìng (嘉靖) during the reign of Shìzōng (世宗);
the section titled Restoration (Zhōngxīng)
is defined as starting in the 29th year of Jiājìng (嘉靖),
which in truth is also incomprehensible.
The categories concerning Territory (Jiānglǐ) are six:
namely, Boundaries (Yùjiè),
Governmental System (Lǐzhì),
Mountains and Rivers (Shānshuǐ),
Places of Interest (Shènggài),
Customs (Fēngsú),
and Historical Remains (Wǎnjì).
The categories concerning Economics (Rǎngzé) are seven:
namely, Households and Population (Hùkǒu),
Land Taxes (Tiánfù),
Salt Administration (Yánfǎ),
Products (Wùchǎn),
Horse Administration (Mǎzhèng),
Military Administration (Bīngzhèng),
and Post Stations (Yìchuán).
The categories concerning Constructions (Jiànzhì) are eleven:
namely, City Walls and Moats (Chéngchí),
Offices and Yamen (Shǔxiè),
Confucian Schools (Rúxué),
Granaries and Storehouses (Cāngkù),
Post Houses (Pūshě),
Streets and Markets (Jiēshì),
Wards and Signboards (Fāngpái),
Towers and Pavilions (Lóugé),
Bridges and Ferries (Qiáodù),
Official Sacrifices (Zhìsì),
and Temples and Monasteries (Sìguàn).
However, Officials and Teachers (Guānshī Rénwù),
and Examinations and Selections (Kēmù Xuǎnjǔ),
are all included within the chronological annals (Biānnián).
For Officials and Teachers, the year and month are written in large characters,
stating that a certain official (Mǒu Guān Mǒu Rén) arrived to take office;
if that person has commendable deeds,
then, imitating the style of the *Zuǒzhuàn* (左傳),
their actions and achievements are annotated below.
For Examinations, it states,
so-and-so was a Recommended Scholar (Gòng) from the School,
so-and-so was selected in the local examination (Jǔ Yú Xiāng),
and among them, so-and-so was a successful candidate (Jìnshì) on a certain list (Mǒu Bǎng);
if there are praiseworthy deeds,
the same rule as for Officials and Teachers is applied,
otherwise, it is omitted.
Cases of Filial Piety, Righteousness, Fidelity, and Martyrdom (Xiàoyì Jiéliè) which received commendation (Jīng),
are recorded under the date the commendation was received.
However, Confucians (Rú) who practice virtue in obscurity,
and scholars who excel in writing (Néng Wén zhī Shì),
but who did not enter through the examinations (Kēmù),
along with chaste and filial women (Jiéxiào zhī Fù),
and virtuous and pure girls (Zhēnshū zhī Nǚ),
if they happened not to receive commendation,
then there is no precedent for them to be included in the gazetteer.
What is particularly unusual is that
the gazetteer continued and presented by Lord Hóu (Hóu Jūn Xù Chén),
in the 47th year of Wànlì (萬歷) of the Míng (明) dynasty,
writes in large characters, "The 4th year of Tiānmìng (天命) in the Jǐwèi (己未) cycle, of Our Gāohuángdì (高皇帝), the Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ),"
and separately annotates the Míng (明) era name below;
it further writes in large characters that Féng Yùntài (馮運泰) successfully passed the Jìnshì (進士) examination on the list where Zhuāng Jìchāng (莊際昌) was also successful,
and also records that Lín Yìngjù (林應聚), the Prefect (Zhīzhōu), arrived to take office.
Now, the territory of the Former Míng (明)
had not yet entered the domain of Our Dynasty;
the historical writings of the Imperial Dynasty,
when recording Míng (明) affairs
that were not related to the legitimate calendar (Zhèngshuò),
did not even dismiss the Tiānqǐ (天啟) and Chóngzhēn (崇禎) era names.
Even if one invokes the principle of a subject (Chénzǐ zhī Yì),
centering the current dynasty and externalizing the Former Míng (明),
since the Tiānmìng (天命) era name is written above,
then affairs that occurred during the Former Míng (明) period
must necessarily have the character Míng (明) added to distinguish them;
this would allow readers to know which is the host and which is the guest,
which is also an immutable principle.
Now, Féng Yùntài (馮運泰) was a *Jìnshì* (進士) of the Míng (明),
and Lín Yìngjù (林應聚) was a Prefect (Zhīzhōu) of the Míng (明),
yet they are subordinated under the era name of the present dynasty,
and lack the character Míng (明) to differentiate them—
is this not directly taking the *Jìnshì* and Prefect of the Míng (明),
and treating them as examination degree holders and officials of the present dynasty?
Is this not a fabrication!
As for the title of the *Luán Zhì* (灤誌) [Gazetteer of Luán],
it is also quite vulgar and careless.
Luán (灤) is merely the name of a river,
and the Prefecture (Zhōu) took its name from the river.
Now, by removing the character *zhōu* (州, prefecture),
and calling it the *Luán Zhì* (灤誌),
then readers looking at the title label
will suspect it to be a gazetteer of the Luán River (Luánshuǐ Zhì).
However, the *Yìwén Zhì* (藝文誌) of the Míng (明) records that Chén Shìyuán (陳士元) compiled the *Luánzhōu Zhì* (灤州誌);
therefore, the removal of the character *zhōu* (州) from the title
might have been the work of Hóu Shàoqí (侯紹岐).
Yet, looking at the entire book,
such matters are still trivial,
and are not worth criticizing.
Colophon to the Língshòu County Gazetteer (Língshòu Xiànzhì).
If a book is valued because of the person who wrote it,
it is permissible to value the person and overlook the book;
if a piece of writing has good intentions but its language is inadequate,
it is permissible to value the intention and overlook the language.
Lù Shì Lǒngqí (陸氏隴其) of Pínghú (平湖),
a famous Confucian master of Neo-Confucianism (Lǐxué),
how can he be lightly criticized?
Nevertheless, he was not deeply versed in historiography.
The *Língshòu County Gazetteer* (Língshòu Xiànzhì) that he compiled
was extremely well-intended,
but he did not fully grasp literary structure (Wénlǐ).
Therefore, it is permissible to value Lù (Lù) as a person,
and accept the fundamental intention behind the compilation of the gazetteer.
To value the person,
and consequently value the book,
asserting that it should be a model praised by gazetteer experts,
is merely accepting hearsay.
I observe that Lù's (Lù Shì) *Língshòu County Gazetteer* (Língshòu Xiànzhì) has ten chapters (juǎn):
Chapter One is Geography (Dìlǐ),
with Historical Events and Local Dialects (Jìshì Fāngyīn) appended;
Chapter Two is Constructions (Jiànzhì);
Chapter Three is Sacrificial Canons (Sìdiǎn);
Chapter Four is Calamities and Auspices (Zāixiáng);
Chapter Five is Products (Wùchǎn);
Chapter Six is Land Taxes (Tiánfù);
Chapter Seven is Officials and Teachers (Guānshī);
Chapter Eight is Notable Figures (Rénwù);
within Notable Figures,
it is further divided into Empresses and Consorts (Hòufēi), Famous Ministers (Míngchén), Official Merits (Shìjì), Filial Piety and Righteousness (Xiàoyì), Hermits (Yǐnyì), and Eminent Women (Liènǚ);
Chapter Nine is Selections (Xuǎnjǔ);
Chapter Ten is Arts and Literature (Yìwén).
However, Land Taxes (Tiánfù) and Arts and Literature (Yìwén) are each divided into upper and lower parts,
while Sacrificial Canons (Sìdiǎn), Calamities and Auspices (Zāixiáng), and Products (Wùchǎn) are all combined into one,
which means that the chapter divisions
also lack a consistent structure (Yìlì).
The book is generally brief,
but the Land Taxes (Tiánfù) section is uniquely detailed,
which shows that he knew what was important.
The *Preface and Rules* (Xùlì) all state:
"Since the land is barren and the people are poor,
those in office must not recklessly change regulations and accumulate wealth,
and the natives must not be extravagant or contentious."
This is especially the benevolent and moderate speech of a humanitarian.
The general principle of the entire book is based on this objective,
and his intentions truly do not fall short of the good and honest officials (Xúnliáng Lì) of antiquity.
At the end of the chapter, he uses his own statements to request instructions from the superior (official),
concerning what should be promoted or abolished in his county,
and concludes the compilation with back-and-forth discussions concerning the general rules for compiling the gazetteer with the county resident Fù Wéiyún.
His detailed proposals regarding promotion and abolition,
were certainly practical and useful;
however, his arguments about the gazetteer compilation rules,
were circuitous, mistaken, and irrelevant.
I fear that people of the world will pursue reputation and forget reality,
and thus I must offer a detailed critique below.
For instance, regarding the geography section at the beginning of the chapter,
it is acceptable to append local pronunciations,
but it is erroneous to append historical records (jìshì).
Jìshì (Historical Records),
are the major events of previous dynasties concerning Língshòu,
recorded chronologically.
This is equivalent to having, within a single county,
what are the Basic Annals (běnjì) in a standard history.
If Jìshì can be appended to Geography,
then the *Shùn Diǎn* (Canon of Shùn) can be appended to the *Yǔ Gòng* (Tribute of Yǔ),
and the Basic Annals of history can be included in the geographical treatise.
Recording events is valuable when it is concise and structured (has method);
to append them in this manner,
is indeed concise,
but how can it be considered a proper method?
In the chapter on Establishments (jiànzhì),
he deletes the memorial arches (fāngbiǎo),
and says that what is important lies in the people,
not in the arches.
This argument is circuitous and preposterous.
No person is more important than Kǒngzǐ (Confucius),
and no person relies less on written records to be detailedly known
than Kǒngzǐ.
If one assumes that what is important lies elsewhere,
and the gazetteer consequently removes records concerning him,
then the gazetteer of Quèlǐ,
could be burned down.
The importance of memorial arches lies in the people (they commemorate),
just as the importance of schools lies in the Dào (Way),
and the importance of government offices lies in governance (zhèng),
and the importance of city walls lies in defense (shǒu).
If one believes that the true importance lies elsewhere and therefore does not record the physical structure,
then schools, government residences, and city walls can all be removed,
and the entire volume on Establishments,
can simply have its entire entry list omitted.
To delete temples and monasteries and not record them,
claiming it is to ward off evil and promote the orthodox,
is also circuitous and irrelevant.
The *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals) emphasizes the recording of construction projects.
Everything that should not have been built, but was built,
is recorded in detail,
in order to serve as a warning and admonishment.
If we follow Lù Shì’s argument,
we merely need to delete the text,
claiming to ward off evil and promote the orthodox.
A thousand generations later,
who will still know that it was evil and should be avoided?
Moreover, within temples and monasteries,
inscriptions (jīnshí) can be investigated,
lost writings circulate,
and ancient events can be sought.
This is the first reason they should not be removed.
The offices for monks and Daoists,
are established by state regulations.
Their residences must have their designated land,
and those they govern must have their followers.
This is the second reason they should not be removed.
Prayers offered during floods and droughts,
relief provided during disasters,
the adoption and care of abandoned infants,
and the maintenance of offerings (xiānghuǒ) at the shrines and tombs of former worthies—
local officials often choose temples and monasteries to serve as public places,
and often select monks and Daoists to manage and maintain them.
In matters of business, reliance upon them is great,
and they frequently appear in memorials (zhāngzòu) and official documents.
They have never harmed the principles of governance (zhìtǐ).
These types of establishments, temples, monasteries, monks, and Daoists,
were regarded by people of the past as honoring heterodoxy;
recently, they have been used to assist official business.
Even if Zhōu Gōng and Kǒngzǐ were resurrected,
taking advantage of the circumstances and guiding them beneficially,
they would surely have means to appropriately classify and manage them,
and would not necessarily expel all the people and tear down their residences.
Lù Shì, by removing them and failing to record them,
intends to show his defense of the Dào (Way).
How narrow his perspective is!
Regarding officials, teachers, and selection (guānshī xuǎnjǔ),
he details only the current dynasty,
claiming to follow the old gazetteer's intent of starting the cutoff from the beginning of the Míng dynasty.
This is especially erroneous.
The old gazetteer was unable to extensively investigate previous dynasties,
and took the beginning of the Míng dynasty as its cutoff point.
This was already a fault of the old gazetteer;
however, it never discarded what it actually possessed.
Now, Lù Shì clearly saw the old gazetteer,
yet he deleted those names.
His irrationality requires no further debate.
Since ancient times, feudal lords (zhūhóu) do not list the Son of Heaven (tiānzǐ) as their ancestor,
and high officials (dàfū) do not list the feudal lords as their ancestors.
This is dictated by reason and circumstance.
All compilers of local gazetteers,
regarding the emperors and empresses of former dynasties,
should only record their origins,
and must not list them as "Figures" (rénwù).
This point has been frequently debated by earlier scholars,
but the conclusion of the argument has never been settled.
In reality, listing them under "Figures,"
is erroneous.
Setting aside for a moment whether it is appropriate based on reason and circumstance,
let us ask about the general rule for "Figures."
If it comprehensively records figures from ancient times to the present,
since the local gazetteer has already listed emperors and empresses of former dynasties
under "Figures,"
then one compiling the gazetteer of Jīngzhào (the capital area),
must include the reigning dynasty’s emperors and empresses under "Figures."
This is known to be impossible without even asking.
Therefore, Lù Shì’s gazetteer placing empresses and consorts at the beginning of the "Figures" section,
is exceedingly lacking in rigor.
Reaching the end of the chapter,
concerning the discussion with Fù Wéiyún,
at first, his views were merely biased,
but after debating back and forth repeatedly,
his forceful arguments became illogical and unreasonable.
He himself said:
“The conduct and words of famous officials,
such as Yuè Yì and Cáo Bīn,
those clearly recorded in the standard histories,
only their summaries remain.”
Wéiyún, however, said that “Regarding the sages of the Three Dynasties (Sān Dài) and earlier,
whose deeds are already recorded in the classics (jīngjí),
Sīmǎ Qiān (Shǐ Qiān) still included them in the *Shǐjì* (《Shǐjì》);
the events before Emperor Xiàowǔ narrated by Sīmǎ Qiān,
Bān Gù still included them in the *Hànshū* (《Hànshū》);
they were not omitted merely because they were seen elsewhere.
Historical biographies and literary collections from previous generations,
especially in remote small counties,
are rarely seen completely by people.
Therefore, texts like Yuè Yì’s *Letter in Reply to the King of Yān* (《Bào Yānwáng Shū》) and Hán Wéi’s *Discussion on the Temple of Xīzǔ* (《Xīzǔ Miào Yì》) in the Arts and Letters sections,
should not be censored or cut.”
His statement is correct.
Mr. Lù (Lù Shì) then said:
“Among the figures of the Spring and Autumn (Chūnqiū) period,
none is greater than Kǒngzǐ (Confucius),
and in literary works, none surpasses Kǒngzǐ.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* (《Zuǒ Zhuàn》) is less detailed regarding the affairs of Kǒngzǐ
than it is regarding Shú Xiàng and Zǐ Chǎn;
concerning the writings of Kǒngzǐ,
it includes less than it does for Shú Xiàng and Zǐ Chǎn;
his service as minister in Lǔ and his journey to Chǔ,
his editing of the classics and correcting of music (shān shū zhèng yuè),
those deeds illustrious for ten thousand generations,
are not seen even once;
the *Xiàojīng* (《Xiàojīng》), the *Lúnyǔ* (《Lúnyǔ》),
the *Wényán* (《Wényán》), and the *Xìcí* (《Xìcí》),
texts glorious for ten thousand generations,
are not seen even once.
Because Kǒngzǐ is the sage for ten thousand generations,
there is no need to lavishly praise him in a single book—
this is the way to honor Kǒngzǐ.”
This is certainly not Mr. Lù’s (Lù Shì’s) original intention;
running out of words,
he made grand statements,
trying to overwhelm others with bombast,
disregarding whether his reasoning held water,
and still retaining the habitual tendency to slander Yángmíng.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* (《Zuǒ Zhuàn》) was compiled by editing and selecting from state histories;
all matters recorded concern the nation and state,
its principles forming the warp and weft for the *Chūnqiū* (《Chūnqiū》).
Zǐ Chǎn and Shú Xiàng
were virtuous and eloquent,
and served in government for the longest time.
Therefore, the affairs of Jìn and Zhèng
frequently involved the words and deeds of these two men.
This was not intentional detail,
but because these matters related to the governance of their respective states.
Kǒngzǐ did not find favor with the times.
Only when he served as minister under Duke Dìng (Dìng Gōng) for the Jiágǔ meeting,
when the people of Qí came to return the land of Wènyáng,
were these events related to state affairs.
When did they fail to be recorded in detail?
His wandering throughout the four directions
and establishing teachings at Zhūsì
were matters unrelated to state administration.
Mr. Zuǒ (Zuǒ Shì) arranged the text chronologically attached to the classic (jīng);
its style is direct and straightforward.
It is not like the structure of biographies and annals (jì zhuàn) found in later histories,
which allowed for special biographies focusing on figures in the Daoist studies (dàoxué), Confucian scholars (rúlín), or literary figures (wényuàn),
narrated in a nuanced way
and given emphasis according to the person.
Even if he had wanted to detail Kǒngzǐ uniquely,
there was no means to do so.
How can one say this was done to honor Kǒngzǐ?
As for saying that the *Xiàojīng* (《Xiàojīng》), *Lúnyǔ* (《Lúnyǔ》), *Wényán* (《Wényán》), and *Xìcí* (《Xìcí》) were not included in the *Zuǒ Zhuàn* (《Zuǒ Zhuàn》),
also as a way for Mr. Zuǒ (Zuǒ Shì) to honor Kǒngzǐ,
this specious error is generally the same as his previous argument,
and needs no further refutation.
But if, according to what he says,
non-inclusion means honor,
then the recording of Yáo and Shùn in the *Canon of Yáo* (Dì Diǎn),
and the recording of Dà Yǔ (Great Yǔ) in the *Counsels and Tribute* (Mó Gòng),
would mean the historians did not honor Yáo, Shùn, or Yǔ;
the singing and praising of Kings Wén and Wǔ (Wén Wǔ) in the *Èr Nán* (The Two Nán) and the *Zhèng Yǎ* (Correct Odes)
would mean the poets did not honor the former kings of Zhōu;
Kǒngzǐ’s editing and narrating of the *Classic of Poetry* (《Shī》) and the *Classic of History* (《Shū》)
would mean Kǒngzǐ did not honor the Two Emperors and Three Kings (Èr Dì Sān Wáng).
Can such an argument possibly be maintained?
Moreover, habitually invoking Kǒngzǐ as a standard for comparison
is merely the old trick of a pedant (xué jiū) seeking to intimidate others.
If we try to ask Mr. Lù (Lù Shì) about his original intention in compiling the gazetteer,
did he view people like Yuè Yì, Cáo Bīn, and Hán Wéi
as worthy of standing in place of Kǒngzǐ?
He further cited the encomium in the *Biography of Guǎn Zhòng and Yàn Yīng* (《Guǎn Yàn Zhuàn Zàn》) by the Grand Historian (Tài Shǐ Gōng), which says:

“I have read the *Guǎnzǐ* (《Guǎnzǐ》), *Pasturing the People* (《Mù Mín》), *Mountain Height* (《Shān Gāo》), *Driving Horses* (《Chéng Mǎ》), *Weight and Lightness* (《Qīng Zhòng》), *Nine Treasuries* (《Jiǔ Fǔ》), and the *Spring and Autumn Annals of Master Yàn* (《Yànzǐ Chūnqiū》).
These books are widely available in the world,
therefore I do not discuss them.”
It can be seen that those things widely available
need not be detailed.
This argument is somewhat reasonable.
However, he also misunderstands the subtle intent of Mr. Sīmǎ (Sīmǎ Shì);
primarily, the focus was on anecdotal history (yì shì),
which is why he made that statement.
Furthermore, when recording the works of the various masters,
it is impossible to cut and include all of them into the biographies.
Hán Fēi’s biography includes his *Difficulties in Persuasion* (《Shuō Nán》);
was this not included because his book was widely available in the world?
The inclusion of literature in standard biographies
differs from its inclusion in local gazetteers’ Arts and Letters sections (fāng zhì yìwén);
the circumstances are different.
Standard biographies are fundamentally narratives of events,
so selection and editing must be strict;
whereas in the Arts and Letters sections of local gazetteers,
even though poems and essays are sometimes carelessly inserted due to common practice,
since the standard is already lenient,
excellent pieces may naturally be selected and included.
If one must satisfy both requirements without regret,
I have a separate set of rules and principles (yì lì),
which I will not detail here.
